I have had Limbo in my gaming library for the longest of times, and I have always looked for the right time to bring it out of the darkness and into the light and start playing it through (analogy intended ;) .
However I also wanted to wait and play Limbo the way I think this type of game was meant to be played, and that is with a controller on a big TV screen.
I can't emphasise enough the importance of playing Limbo with a gaming controller. Now, not everyone has to agree with me on this, but if you are going to play this game, don't go at it on a "small" computer screen with a keyboard, its a little like playing FPS games with a ps/xbox controller, it just doesn't make the game proper justice. You have been warned.
With that said, lets get on with the game L-I-M-B-O. And what a game it is. So well designed and directed, I am absolutley speechless. Limbo is not quite a platformer, and it's not quite a puzzle game, I could make it easy for myself and say it is a mix of both genres but... I would like to describe Limbo more as an immersive feeling, the game touches you without even a word being uttered throughout the whole game. Limbo takes you to places of lonelyness and war, a desolate place with trees and animals in a forest, there are gruesome deaths, machines and children, without any context and meaning, yet it all makes sense somehow.
You, as a player, are totally commited to playing this through and through, and throughout the whole 4-5hours that I played, I never once got bored, only touched and amazed.
The graphics and sounds mix seamleassly and completing one another in the most subtle ways and in what appears to be a minimalistic design, however such is not the case. Each section of the game has been carefully planned to the slightest detail, to mesh together seamlessly, hence the excellent minimalistic black and white design and the subtle sounds of the world of Limbo.
Limbos art direction scales aways so much clutter and color and thus as a player your are solelyl left to focus only on the feeling- , exploring, and advancing the game.
At this point you are probably wondering what the h**l is the game about, if you haven't heard or read about Limbo, I strongly suggest you youtube it and find some gameplay.
Simply put, the game is the modern trendsetter for the puzzle/platformer games/genre, where its not about being able to jump over enemies and getting extra lives ala Super Mario Bros, but solving situations with the help your characters abilities, which is your brain, because the character, the little boy, himself, does not posses any abilities actually, outside of jumping and grabbing ledges.
There is only one way to solve each problem, which is fine, and only once or twice did I have to youtube the solution to a problem.
And for this review I would like to take the time to highlight one thing that probably most gamers never take into consideration, the game tester of Limbo that have done a tremendous job. This game is totally successfull because of game testers feedback has been right on point. Since in no part of the game do you really get stuck with a puzzle for too long, and this is 99% doing of the actual game testers. The testers have to understand what challenges each player faces and put their "new player" glasses on everytime they play the game. Don't get me wrong, the planning and direction and all that is the doing of the team, but where many puzzle games go wrong, is that you are at times lost of what to do next and how to do it, especially in this genre of games, but in Limbo, 99% of the time you know what to do intuitively or at least have a clue of what you are supposed to do, and what you can do to achieve the solution.
Final verdict: Get this game and start playing if you haven't dones so already, no questions asked, hands down (preferably on a controller ;) & Happy gaming!

-Casual gameplay
-Easy to learn
-Intriguing plot
-Varied characters and events
-Clever combat system
-Repetitive
-Combat system poorly explained
This game started out on mobile, and got ported to PC.  So as you might expect, the layout is pretty basic, the controls are easy, and it's a game that can be played in short bursts.  It's great for when you have a few minutes here or there, and the game is fairly replayable.
The game relies on sliding left or right for every decision or action.  You have to juggle the power of the army, population, church, and treasury, and if any one gets too powerful or too weak, you lose.  The events are randomized, and eventually you will die, only to start again as the next king in the lineage.  It's simple and fun.
There is a combat system, which also uses the left/right mechanic in a turn based minigame.  However, the game does a terrible job explaining how combat works.  It doesn't even tell you how to win.  In short, if you buy this game, look up a guide for how to do combat.  A few community members have made good ones.  Combat is not hard, but the game simply doesn't explain it.
Aside from that, the only "drawback" is that the game is repetitive.  You just say yes or no to every decision, and after a while you start to memorize the outcomes of decisions as you see the same events over and over.  But there are enough unlockable events and things that there's always some new variation waiting.
There is an overarching plot, and it's actually pretty good.  But this is the type of game you play for the gameplay.  If you don't enjoy it, the game's plot won't make you keep playing.  If you do enjoy the gameplay, then the plot is a good reason to keep going.
Personally, I found it a very relaxing and easygoing game that relieved some stress.  Worth it if you want a casual, fun experience.
$3 is nothing, and it goes on sale occasionally for half off.  Easy recommend.

So original and so replayable. Such a wonderful casual game yet it seems like it isn't. You take the role of king of your kingdom. A very well-worn theme for a game. Many games of this sort were very hands on and very "castle defense" about the whole thing where you actually raise an army. Send them around. Have combats, manage resources etc. Castlles in the 90s is the one I remember most. I think "Castle Defense" has since become a term for the kingdom Simulator. But this takes that whole premise and simplifies it into an attractive and silly animated card game. You deal out cards, each card that comes up is one of your advisors. They give you a choice. YOu say yay or nay. YOu have four things that will effect: Church, people, military, and money. Once one of those hits zero you lose. I did not actually realize that was WHY I kept losing for quite awhile :). And it didn't matter. THe characters of your court are very charming. DOne in a very cool art style and each uses a distinct voice that speaks in gibberish. YOu basically see how far each king can get. And it KEEPS TRACK. You see each king on a grand timeline of kings, some are even called things. LIke if you arrange a marriage between two werewolves (persay) you are called "the Tender". Hmmm I just realized maybe the wolves themselves gave me that name! :O So fun and so addictive. Can pull that up whenever you need a laugh. Love the legacy feel and the achievements from Steam really add to this.

While this game may only be in Alpha, DotE is quickly becoming one of my favorite games of the year.
With beautifully designed rooms (who says pixel sprites can't look great), an array of unique and rather charming heroes to play with and a learning curve not impossible to work with, Dungeon of the Endless is a seemingly simple Rouge-Like Defense game with more happening than it is letting on. Dungeon of the Endless has so much to offer once development has finished, and is already offering so much in its current form.
Trying to balence your heroes who are defending with those exploring takes much trial and error, a number of game over screens facing you before a rhythm of sorts is developed. Finding which heroes work better against which enimies, of which there are a number, also takes time. Once again, it may take several game over screens for a rhythm to develop.

All in all, a game well worth your $10-15 to play as it develops.

Downsides:
- The game progresses way too fast. I had passed three levels by the time I figured the controls out. I have no idea how the first few titans even looked like.
- The gameplay itself is way too slow-paced even though I expected a 3D bullet hell. Bullets/lasers, enemies and I are too slow. This disappointed me the most.
- Easy. The enemies are stupid, predictable and fragile. Their weak points are brightly highlighted on titans as they fall apart after a few shots. It is as though they wanted to remind the players of transiency of life. Time seems to be the only major constraint (which further contributes to the allegory). There are few levels I would call challenging.
- Expensive. The price is too high for a game that almost feels unfinished.
Upsides:
+ The game overall is very fun.
+ Dejobaan Games' absurd and cnidarian sense of humour.
+ Nice references sprinkled around make the game a lot more entertaining.
+ "Provoking" soundtrack.
+ Bright graphics make you really feel in a Douglas Adams inspired gaudy cyberpunk world.
+ Allows me to change my FoV. I wish more games let me do this.
Overall, I recommend this if you are looking for simple fun and don't have high expectations from the price.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a relatively cheap indy open-world shooter. While the gameplay is somewhat repetitive, it is too short to outstay its welcome too much.
At its heart SYaBH is a stealth game and you won't survive for long if you use your weapons too much. In this game, as the title suggests, you are the quarry. For those that enjoy permadeath, I think this game is well suited to it. Such an approach would no doubt add grist to the extended-play mill.
While I quite enjoyed SYaBH, it could potentially have been a very, very good game, and the developers seem to have settled for a game that is okay to good. Various interesting items and opponents appear in the game that add to the variety, but after the first couple of hours, careful players will learn how to keep out of trouble. From then on it's just a matter of going through the motions. Nothing happens that really shakes things up. There is no second (let alone a third) act to this game.
Like Betrayer (which I also reviewed recently, and to which this game bares some similarity) this game has oodles of flavour and atmosphere, but not a lot of variety. Unlike Betrayer, SYaBH makes your goals clearer and there is a little bit more to be found on the islands. There is also a lot more humour in this game. While Betrayer was a very pretty looking game and SYaBH falls a little short in that regard, the graphics are more than adequate to create the 'baskervillian' moors.
Verdict: If you like sandbox (or stealth) games, you are a bit of an anglophile and the game is on special, give it a go.

This is a really fun and strategy-heavy game. You definitely need to plan out your moves to survive, so if you like games with endless amounts of "stop and think about what you should do next" kinds of moments, you will just love this one. Be warned, though, that the robots in this game are a lot smarter than they look, so you should never take the enemies lightly, no matter how good/safe you think you are (I had to find this out the hard way by firing my rifle at one robot that looked alone, which rapidly escalated into a 1-on-10+ robot shootout within roughly a minute).
The random level generator tool keeps the game constantly new, fresh and exciting to play, also, so you will always have a unique set of challenges to overcome whenever you decide to create a new save file. The ultimate objective is present, but how you go about winning the game is entirely up to you. You can go direct and win as fast as possible, or you can take your time and explore the islands at your own leisure. Nothing is timed, so you do not have to worry about rushing to do everything before a deadline arrives.
I would have to give this game a 10/10, if the option was available here.

This game seems really interesting at first glance. Four hunters chasing down a lone monster in an epic fight to the death. Unfortunatly this game ultimately just turns into a very long game of tag. The monster barely hides. It is more efficient to just run from the hunters and feed little by little until you hit stage 3 and just turn on them. Hunters in the mean time simple follow along at a slow pace contantly needing to recharge their jets, due to the overwhelming number of cliffs that require traversing, slowly dying to all the wildlife they encounter along the way. Unlike the zombies from the Left 4 Dead series, which dealt overall minor damage to most players except when utilized properly by the infected, the creatures in this game seem dead set on seeing you.... well dead. Too much of the wildlife perma-traps hunters, until they get rescued by a teammate, and kill them. This mechanic, along with the monsters sneak attack on hunters, restricts players from doing anykind of real 'split and corner' strategy efficiently. If you have a full team of five people to play with this game might be a bit more fun but for $60 a person just doesn't seem to be worth it. Not to mention the fact that the season pass doesn't include any of the optional skins that they sell in the shop. Actually the season pass doesn't even mention, at the time of writing this review, what it actually includes at all.

LIMBO is one of those games where you find yourself in the middle of an emotional storm from the beginning to the very last second. It's very quick to grab your attention with its fantastic atmosphere, music, colour scheme and lack of explanation as for what's actually going on around you. This is why LIMBO keeps you intrigued, makes you play the game from start to finish in one go because it's nearly impossible to stop playing. You want to know what's going on, why the boy is there, what his goal is, what LIMBO actually means.
The best thing about this game is the ending, which left me thinking about several explanations for the ending scene, for the story in general. A game that can draw out so many different theories can't be anything but a fantastic game, and that's what LIMBO is. Cannot recommend this title enough.

I'd probably give this a neutral if I could. Leaning toward "Yes" because it is a pretty charming and enjoyable experience.
The two main flaws are the length and simplicity. I 100% completed this in just under 2 hours and I goofed off a bit at some parts. The game is also very simplistic. The combat is basic 3D swordplay like something out of Ocarina of Time but without any of Link's gadgets. There aren't many enemies, though, so the lack of complex combat isn't a huge deal, IMO. The levels are like 20% fighting and 80% puzzling/platforming.
The story and voice acting are pretty amateurish but at the same time they're kind of charming so, again, not a huge deal for me but my finding them charming is subjective so I wouldn't fault anyone for hating on them.
The mechanics are pretty basic but not braindead. In a few of the latter levels I found myself having to go back and forth to find things I missed or to figure out a puzzle. Each level adds like 1 new enemy type and 1 or 2 new puzzle/platform mechanics so it does stay fresh as you progress. There are some interesting mechanics you don't see very much in puzzle/platformers.
Overall, I had an enjoyable 2 hours but for $8 some might have a problem with the length, the simplicity or both. In that case it might be worth it when it goes on deep discount during a sale.

Dear Reader,
There are many merits to judge a game by. Design Choices. Artistic Representation. Compelling Writing. Fluid and Fun Mechanics. More than this of course.
These are all great things that we've come to expect in one part or another from our video games. Some might lay claim that without these core tenets, a game can be called
. If that is you, I challenge you to play The Beginner's Guide and see if you don't change your mind.
Yet reader, have you paused for a moment to ask that a game may seek to exist of its own merit? That a game can simply be good, regardless of rating or score?
If we were to stop judging games as a mechanical contraption with quantifiable measurements of success, how would we know what a good game is?
How about that game fulfils its own goals. The Beginner's Guide exists as a game that seems to disregard traditional measurements of merit for its art form.
I'd be remiss to give this game it a category or box to put it in. The Beginner's Guide is a narrative, which takes you through the relationship between two game developers. One, being the creator of the Stanley Parable and the other being Coda.
It explores how Coda creates games, not with the purpose of being played by anybody or even beaten. But simply as a representation of his emotional landscape. The narrator goes to tell us about how Coda creates games as an outlet for... whatever might weigh on him.
Without spoiling too much, I can highly recommend The Beginner's Guide to anybody who either suffers from depression or loves somebody that does (or did). The game offers some perspective that you, the human being reading this, may already know and want to share. Or perhaps it helps expand on emotions not yet spun into words.
Perhaps the game offers you a brief window into the torturous landscape of a loved one's depression, only to remind you that the window is locked.
If any of these could be true, then I suspect you, the human being reading this, will find meaning in The Beginner's Guide. This is not a game that it fulfils the traditional meritorious measurements of a good game. It is simply a game that exists to be true to itself.

Before I got Dungeon of the Endless I had no idea what this game is about. I thought I would. But I didn't. Although I checked a few let's play videos I missed so many aspects of the gameplay.
Dungeon of the Endless is a roguelike science fiction turn-based real-time strategy game (yeah, whatever!) in the universe of Endless Space (isn't it?). Your space ship crashed into a dungeon and you have to move your power generator and your team of heros to the exit. Dungeon of the Endless is turn-based. Every door you open triggers certain events. You get more resources. Monsters spawn. Each turn is played in real-time and can be paused. You can build stuff. Your heros fight. You don't. You can only tell them in which room they have to go. You can power up a few rooms. Which means you can build stuff in here and monsters will not spawn into this room. Until now there are three resources: industry (build), food (heal, level up), dust (energy, currency). You can build generators for producing industry or food and gain dust by killing monsters or trading items. The resource science will follow. It is not implemented yet.
But Dungeon of the Endless is not about killing all monsters, finding great items and trading them, leveling up your team, going to the exit. This is not an action game. You do all this stuff. More or less. However Dungeon of the Endless is a strategy game. It's about building a base and protecting it. Every door you open changes the dungeon. It adds a room and often you can decide where and you should. This influences the shape of your base and the world. Sometimes you don't have much of a choice or it doesn't matter. Nevertheless sometimes you really should think about it. Before you open a door you have to consider many issues:
Which door should I open next?
Where do I put my heros when I open the door?
Which hero should open the door?
How many of each resource should I produce?
Which Rooms should be powered?
Dungeon of the Endless is an Early Access game. Though this alpha version is pretty stable. The drawback is the content. Many things are missing. It is short and needs more difficulty balancing. But each game is different because the world is randomly generated. Every game has its own story. Dungeon of the Endless is a nice strategy game. It has a enjoyable pace and is not very pushy. I hope they don't screw it up. So far I had a lot of fun.

[Long Review: The initial review was since the released of the game]
After many updates...
-They've implemented 1 skill for some characters like increase damages or speed.
-New rooms like the one where you can do some researches (the most interesting add in this game because it was highly unplayable before). The Merchant is good too, you have to decide if you keep dust to energize your rooms or use it as a currency with the merchant to buy new gear for your heroes.
-New characters with their backgrounds. In my humble point of view it was not important because I've found the game really annoying with the previous heroes.
To conclude:
Even with updates this game is still boring. You will never have this feeling of "epicenes" or "punch" this kind of game has in general. Too much slow paced with a bad atmosphere: heroes background are quite mature but in the dungeon the music is totally at the opposite of the gloom and the violence of the game in general (enemies dies like flies, heroes are cannon fodder and the global situation: you crash on a planet and you kill everything on your path... the trailer shows how gratuitous is the violence). Even the gameplay is awkward; mixing Endless Space's resources management, a tower defense and a dungeon crawling. Instead of focusing on fights; you will be forced to put heroes on nodes to get the resources you need. Couple that to the fact that each "turns" depends of the next door you will open or the last moment of each level where you have to bring your crystal to the exit...
And you had a really unbalanced game which will send you from calm moments (zen music in a derelict alien underground base...what a joke!) to huge crisis where the single mistake is synonym of game over (and the death of your keyboard).
Dare to try this game if you judge the rating of this review.

Ah, Drunken Robot Pornography... no other game has caused so much... controversy over its name.  Well... except for all the ones that started lawsuits.  But I digress!   Drunken Robot Pornography (which will now be shortened to Drunken) is a first person bullet hell shooter.  While the name is what made me click on the link out of morbid curiosity, it was the concept which made me buy the game.  (Well... the concept
watching those 3-D Touhou fan made videos...)
Control and mechanic-wise, Drunken is mostly solid.  Movement and shooting is done without feeling tanky, aiming is fair (as long as it's in the crosshairs, it's good; you don't need to be absolute dead center), the power-ups are useful without feeling overpowered, and there's a good variety of them.  My biggest complaint about the controls is the mode of flight - the jetpack.  The flight time per burst always felt way too short, and it's nearly impossible to overcome inertia once you start to fall (the last point being the most damning for me).  While I did get used to the controls, I still wished the strength of the jetpack from the jet boost power up was the standard for it.
The level design and difficulty curve is done decently... for the most part.  For me, I believe the challenges of a stage should come from the enemies and bosses, and not the stage layout itself.  If you're having to fight the stage more than the enemies or bosses, there's something wrong.   That said, there's not much to say about  the good side - the beginning levels are easy, and the later levels are hard - as it should be.  On the bad side, there are two points - level 25 Waterspires, and level 48 Tightrope.  When you encounter these stages, it's like running into a brick wall.  Both contain super tiny platforms with bosses which have far too many parts, and an extremely strict time limit.  The problem with the time limit is if you fall out of bounds, you lose five seconds.  It took me over 100 tries before I could beat Tightrope; it got to the point where if I ever fell off/couldn't reach a platform, I would immediately start the stage over because there was no chance of completing it.  It went far beyond "tough challenge" and straight screaming into "pounding on your keyboard like an enraged howler monkey" territory.  Like I said though, the other levels were fairly good, and many of them were the good sort of hard where it felt like the game over was your fault and not the game's.  (Like the last level - it took numerous tries, but when I finally beat it, I felt happy instead of exhausted.)
As you may guess from just the name, Drunken has a fair amount of humour in it, most of it leaning towards lowbrow.  Personally, I like that, but I also know many people don't like that sort of humour.
Overall, I felt this was a good game, and I'm glad I bought it.  If you're on the fence about it, check out a few videos of the game play on youtube to get a better feel of it.  If you're a fan of bullet hell and/or non-realistic first person shooters, I'd suggest it just for the unique feel it has.

I think this game is worth getting so long as you understand that its value proposition is different than that of most games on steam. It's a game that you probably won't play for more than an hour before you get fed up with how unfair it is and quit, but the next day you'll come back (because it was super fun while it lasted) and you'll be a little better and get a little farther before you rage quit. Before long it has become a habit and you can't imagine what your life was like before this game. DRP is like the arcade games of old. It didn't matter that their gameplay never changed or that you found yourself playing the same section over and over before you were able to beat it because the gameplay was fun and the difficulty meant you got a REAL sense of achievement from acomplishing something. Unlike those old arcade games which were short on content, DRP has near infinite content with the built in levels, modes, and arenas supplimented by those bosses and levels created in the steam workshop and by the developers themselves every week for the Battle Royale weekly challenge. This constant stream of new content but old gameplay lends itself well to a game that you play in short bursts for a long period of time.
If you're looking for a game with progression, or that holds your hand, or that sucks you in for hours at a time then DRP is not for you, but if you are looking for a game in the spirit of arcade classics which offers scores of content and several game modes then I highly recommend it.

There is a visibility meter with an eye that gains rings as you become more visible.  They eye goes away completely when you are completely hidden.  The rings are sort of ambiguous. I like Evolve, but I don't think its worth the price; I think it has leveling and balance issues.  Also, buying the Season Pass does not get you all the DLC, only some of it.
First, Leveling in the game is required if you want to gain access to the more useful hunters or more potent monsters.  If you jump into this game late, and you play with people who have been playing for a while, expect to get your butt handed to you perpetually until you level up (which might take a long while because your XP is dependent on whether you win).  Playing the monster as a new-comer against people who have played for a while is a brutal course in futility: the hunters will find you and kill you quickly and relentlessly, and there is nothing you can do about it.  If you play a hunter as a n00b, you'll generally be riding the coat-tails of your more experienced companions, unless the more experienced monster finds you, in which case you'll just be killed in short order (and possibly eaten).  I think the game would be better if, like so may other games out there that require leveling, you could create a private game that was completely unlocked for everyone and pick the hunters/monsters you wanted, but sadly that is not an option in this game.
And then there are Balancing issues; if you join a group of players that have 6 or more levels on you, be prepared to be at a significant disadvantage.  It seems that everything you do is at a noticeable degradation compared to the other more experienced players: you seem to run slower, have less jet pack energy, weapons do less damage, healing takes longer, etc.  Because you'll die a lot, you can spend time spectating the bots and see what your abilities will be like once you do level, but when you take that bot over your abilities will degrade and you'll be forced into fighting an uphill battle to get little scraps of XP so you can level.  The leveling also seems to take forever when you try to level with groups that have a lot of experience on you because they will pick the best of their class (whether that is a hunter or monster) and you'll be stuck with the starter class.  I think the game would be better if the various playable classes (both monsters and hunters) were more equally balanced; because there's a huge disparity between the various classes gainable by leveling, as a new player, you end up on the receiving end of an exponentially longer and harder row to hoe to get to where those that have gone before you are.  My advice if your new: only play as a hunter in groups of experienced people; only play solo as the monster until you get the wraith monster; otherwise, only play solo until you get leveled.
Until some of these issues are fixed, or the price goes down, save your cash.

Sir/Madam is a creative and unique approach to stealth-based combat in setting, aesthetics, and gameplay. If you like sneaking past guards, looting buildings, or assassining then you'll probably enjoy this. However if you like replaying 20-30 minute sessions because of the rare save points and punish difficulty, then you'll likely get frusterated very quickly. The goal of the game is to scavenge for goodies, avoid starvation and detection, and find pieces of a mysterious device in a five randomly generated environments.
The biggest problem currently with the Mac verion of Sir is the fairly frequent yet unpredictable crashes every 90-120 minutes. These seem to occur most often in some of the more exotic areas. Being that save points are infrequent, and that there are incentives to not to save often, this gets to be a big problem.
Gameplay-wise the biggest problem is the difficulty. I'm a big fan of high difficulty games, but there is not a large skill ceiling here, so it gets very frusterating even in the early stages. However because of the limited inventory system (and consumable nature of supplies) it is almost impossible to "defeat" the game by "snowballing" large amounts of supplies later on, so while Sir is punishly hard from the beginning, it stays consitent until the end.
Another big problem is the most basic enemy type, (which is also the most common enemy type) a bipedal robot with a shotgun. Having a low tier enemy, or a common enemy with shotgun in a stealth-based combat game is very frusterating. The purpose of stealth based combat is to sneak in close proximity to enemies, either to kill them or get to objectives; but if they have a shotguns, then the closer you get the stronger they get. This creates incentives to battle from a larger distance (which isn't viable), or to avoid combat altogether (which also isn't viable). Getting killed in 1-2 shots from full health is can work if it is clearly your fault, and the stealth detection system works well, just not the inability to deal with enemies regularly.
Bandages are also another problem with Sir, being that when you take damage it is possible to start bleeding out until you die. Bleeding can only be stopped by bandages, which are uncommonly found and very rarely dropped by enemies. This makes combat frusterating because even a low-damage, grazing shot on yourself (especially with the abundant shotgun enemies) can be can be lethal if you don't have a bandage. Or if you use your bandage to stop the bleed, only to get another one put on yourself by the next shot.

Playtime: two hours.  Might still be in the honey moon phase, but I'm really enjoying this game.  You have to shake the notions you've become accostumed to in, say L4D, where you have to stick together.  Really, at the start of a match the monster is more analgous to the L4D survivors than the hunters are.
I suggest really, really knowing how to be present in the game world as the monster.  You leave tracks if you run, but not if you sneak.  Hunters can hear you (actually hear you, not they get an HUD display necessarily) to get vague position, so even if you aren't setting off alerts, if you're being noisy, they'll find you.  More than once I've managed to hide and have the hunters walk within 20 feet of me, then turn around.  Don't be hasty, and think ahead.  Know what your abilties do, whether hunter or monster, and be smart.
The game doesn't play itself.
EDIT:
After playing the game some more, I can confidently say this game joins Strike Vector and Titanfall on the list of the most fantastic games that are going to fail.  Here is why.
Simply put, the complete reliance on matchmaking nullifies the possibility of ad hoc gaming communities.  I'd have never played TF2 for as long as I did if I hadn't found a server with a great community.  L4D/2 had a similar problem, but I had a great number of friends who played it, so it was a non-issue.  Evolve scared away a number of people with the DLC non-sense (which, it turns out, really amounted to nothing more than speeding your character through normal progression-based unlocks and exclusive-but-mediocre monster skins), but in my opinion it is *at least* as much fun as L4D, and plenty more if you draw in friends with you.
Let's talk about the biggest problem, though.  The gameplay is severely asymmetrical.  This is fine, though.  Hell, I applaud it.  However, that means there is a lot of pressure to perform as the monster.  In addition, the monster role is not something that a lot of people are going to pick up on the sublties of right away, and that's just the nature of gaming.  That, combined with what I'm not going to start referring to as a sin: leaving a player with no one to talk to.  Yes.  Granted, a monster that is doing poorly never gets taunted or teased or verbally abused, but without a method to converse with your opponents, you'll never get that random person that offers advice and makes your play experience better.  You'll never be able to celebrate a victory or play off a defeat.  As much as I like it, even at the end of an evacuation campaign, the "winner" is fairly ambiguous.  In the context of a larger mythos, this would be intriguing, but as it is it just leaves one uncertain about how to feel in the end.  At the end of each match, I feel either bad because I got roflstomped or guilty because I did the roflstomping.  I feel like being able to communicate during the match would do more to ease such things than it would to scare people away.
In the end, I *do* still recommend it.  If you had a cadre of friends who played L4D/2, and they are interested in Evolve, I'd say go for it.  Right now.  If the mechanics appeal to you, then you'll be playing it together often.  If you're just interested in the game but 60$ seems a bit steep... you're not wrong.  I can safely recommend a purchase to individuals interested in asymmetrical gameplay who are willing to go it alone and able to learn as they go.  For everyone else, unable or unwilling to fight against the current a bit, I'd suggest picking it up on sale.  Mechanically, the game is absolutely worth playing, though whether it will hold your attention for an extended period of time... that I don't know.  If my experience here is anything like my experience with Titanfall, my win/loss ratio will begin to approach 1 and I'll get bored with it.  Though, to be fair, even the last match of evacuation I played where I was rofl-stomping the hunters, they did manage to pull it out in the end thanks to the auto-balancing.  And, again, to its credit, I've found the community to be neutral to friendly, if a little on the quiet side.
It is, verily, a flawed game.  Intended for AAA, I think it will find itself more niche.  The real tragedy, then, is if you never pick up the game when it is right up your alley.

I reviewed this game for Game Walkers.

Words:
It’s easy to get the details wrong. If I told you that this game only lasted an hour and a half, you would probably immediately think that I was saying it wasn’t worth the $7.99 price tag. That’s not necessarily true. I do think you should be hesitant but I will get to that.
Forward to the Sky is about a princess who’s eager to prove herself. Everyone thinks that she can’t handle herself and so, to do this, she has set off on an adventure to defeat the evil witch that has taken control of the Sky Tower with nothing but her sword, her wits, and, of course, her hot air balloon. It’s a charming story about getting the details wrong, details you uncover by collecting crystals that hold memories of the place they reside in. It’s a largely predictable story but a charming one, nonetheless.
This story is brought to life by a great 3D anime style and some rather good voice acting done by one or two people. Don’t worry, the voice acting is all in English. And yes, it is good. I was actually pretty shocked by the overall production values. The game is clearly an indie effort, as the gameplay is simple, and it consists of only six levels, but the author(s) made a clear effort to make it look and sound the best they could within the confines of their budget.
The gameplay wasn’t lucky enough to get such polish. For starters, the combat is incredibly simplistic. With an awkward dodge and no way to block, the only way to really go about things is to brute force it by taking out any long-ranged opponents, or mages, in later levels, and then taking out any melee opponents by simply beating them up and dodging back whenever they go to attack. This may not be ideal, depending on how many melee opponents are attacking at once, however, and it can eventually turn into a mess of jumping around, trying to take out whoever you can whenever you can. With only two combos that vary solely based on how many times you hit their respective button, it gets old fast. I was extremely grateful that enemies seemed to be limited to 25 crystals-worth per level, with larger enemies giving you three. Considering the limited amount of attacks and the fact that most players who even sort of figure it out will have more health than they need, meaning they will almost never be at risk of dying, it easily starts to feel a bit like a chore. You don’t ever feel like you’re in danger and the larger enemies can take a long time to take down.
The gameplay isn’t the most polished, either. The AI are extremely dumb, mostly just chasing after and attacking you in a very slow fashion. Archers are dimwitted and shoot at a location you haven’t been at for about five seconds. If they can’t reach you by pathfinding across a flat surface, melee enemies will kind of dance back and forth in place until they can. If you jump onto certain platforms that act as elevators, rather than just walking onto them, you will fall through them. There are some layering issues on one level where platforms have to be activated by hitting crystals with projectiles. There are a lot of clipping issues in terms of platforms that aren’t in one place permanently There are way too many places you can get to unintentionally by falling off of a level. There are some audio issues when a sound is played repeatedly. In short, there are a lot of little issues that add up to a less polished feel.
Fortunately, the puzzles and platforming make up for that. Every single level is themed around a different set of objects and mechanisms that are used to both reach statues that give you crystals when destroyed and get to your hot air balloon to end the level. There are 100 crystals in total on each level and each statue gives you 25. There end up being three statues per level and, while not mindbending, the puzzles do take some thought. Most are relatively isolated, though, and only give you as much as you need to solve the puzzle, rather than putting you into situations where you can mess up by altering something further back than the puzzle you’re on. In fact, the game really doesn’t allow you to mess up at all, as it has a generous checkpointing system for when you fall off the level, the hot air balloon somehow catching you and dropping you off at a nearby platform. I don’t know what happens when you die but I assume you just restart that level.
The puzzles themselves are rather varied in nature. One second you’re flipping switches to align things correctly or to set up elevators in the right places and the next you’re walking on a boulder, trying to avoid lasers. Once you’ve left a level, you have left behind that kind of puzzle and an entirely new kind is headed your way. The amount of variety is extremely welcome due to the fact that it is a short game. It would have made a lot less lasting of an impression on me if I were solving the same kind of puzzle repeatedly for an hour and a half, especially when you consider that only five of the six levels are puzzle levels. The last one is a boss.
When it comes down to it, it is really hard to recommend Forward to the Sky. It is a charming game with an entertaining, if predictable, story, and it has quite a lot of puzzle variety but it just isn’t substantial enough. It’s a mere six levels, set in scenery that feels the same from level to level, that might take you two and a half hours if it takes you a while to figure the puzzles out. It would be much easier to recommend if it were twice that. Unfortunately, it is not.

SUPERHOT proves that innovative and fun are not mutually exclusive.
I’m sure you already know the premise here. A first person shooter where time moves as you do. You may notice that 90% of reviews of this game use the exact phrase “the most innovate shooter I’ve played in years.” It’s hard to say if those are sincere opinions since you'll learn that line is synonymous with classics like “would you kindly” and “the cake is a lie.” It’s a disingenuous meme that halts actual discussion about the game.
As I vaguely allude to the story, I’ll say this: I thought it was really predictable. Here’s a challenge: Play the game up until you get thrown back to the main menu for the first time. Then write down what you think the story is. Odds are, you’re probably very close if not on the nose.
So here’s where we get into the gameplay itself. The gameplay is OK. It’s very very ok. Although the entire game relies on a time mechanic, SUPERHOT isn’t as good as other games’ time mechanics. A number of needless pain points arise because of the time mechanic. For example, doing an action (like picking up a weapon) jumps time forward 0.30 seconds, while normal walking moves time 0.10 seconds a step. Bending over to pick up that pistol can have you immediately killed because not only does it move time forward 0.30 seconds, you're also moving the camera down and then back up and then on an enemy, all of which waste time. To put all this into context, a lot of speedrun missions have a par time of 4.00 seconds. Just picking up a weapon uses 1/13th of that total time.
This should not have been a first person shooter. Neither the art style or the gameplay complement a first person shooter. Why? First of all, your hitbox is bigger than your screen. Bullets will clearly whiz above your head and then immediately kill you. There’s no crouch button and no way to know if you actually dodged the bullet until it kills you. This could have been solved with a third person shooter where you can see your hitbox.
Another pain point of the FPS is that a lot of missions in the second half drop you in the center of the action. This means that enemies will spawn from all directions. But wait a second, time moves as you do. So spinning the camera 180 degrees moves time forward 4-5 seconds. Again, there’s no crouch feature; you can’t take cover behind that pool table. Add to this that enemies make a sound when they die and when they fire their guns, but they don’t make a sound when they appear. Due to the game’s minimalist style, there’s almost no sound at all. This means that you often won’t know enemies spawned behind you until your corpse hits the floor.
SUPERHOT isn’t a puzzle game as many would have you believe. It’s more like Hotline Miami if you died every time you looked behind you. Yet every single problem in the last two paragraphs could be solved if this game was third person. With a third person camera we could see the enemies coming without breaking the flow and you could still have a minimalist and mostly soundless art direction BUT allow players to inform themselves about the environment.
Also, I have to laugh and laugh and laugh that the game's description calls itself "polished." Bullets, especially from shotguns will often go through walls. Don't believe me? Try the train level. If the hitboxes on the PC are poorly defined and the hitboxes on the buildings are poorly definied, then the devs still have a lot of work to do, even a 1.5 years after release.
I won’t spoil, but the game doesn’t even properly use its full arsenal. Toward the end of the game, you’re granted a game-changing feature. The problem is that they take it away for the finale. To understand what an objectively bad piece of game design that is, think about how most games teach. You learn how to play and you’re tested on that element. Then you learn some more and you use what you learned before with the new. SUPERHOT’s finale is like spending a week studying for a math test. The assigned homework is ¾ multiplication and ¼ division. Then the day of the test comes and none of the questions mention division. That’s SUPERHOT.
For a $20 game with a 2-hour run time, I can’t recommend SUPERHOT to anyone, despite it’s positive reputation. The gunplay is more irritating than innovate due to the previously mentioned design choices that make the game more trial and error than puzzle. The story kept me going, but ultimately disappointed. But hey, at least we got some memes.
If you like paying too much for too little, by all means, buy SUPERHOT.

(The plot of this story itself seems to switch halfway through as if two different people wrote it...).
Overall, the game tries harder to be a meta, psychological story than a challenging game.
If you like entertainment that just tries to screw with your mind, then you might like this game. But if you were looking to play a challenging shooter with bullet time based puzzles you may find yourself disappointed.

Ok, I'm going to start this off by saying that I have beat Cuphead and I am currently on the way to beating the game with all A's and on expert mode. So I have felt the full grasp of the game, and I would say, enough to write a thorough review.
As most people have learned by now, Cuphead is not a simple game. It takes determination and perseverance to complete each boss and level. I personally love that fact about the game. After beating a boss the player is rewarded with a great feeling of satisfaction and completeness that many games are lacking in this time. Now, I am not stating that you will have all fun with this game, but I am stating that once completing certain levels or the entire game itself, it will feel worth it as you spent that time learning and understanding how the game mechanics work in that specific stage.
I would also like to point out the amazing art style that completely gives the game a touch apart from other games. It doesn't look anywhere close to realistic with the graphics (which many games are attempting to master at the moment). It gives an old-cartoonish style that is pleasant to the eyes, yet not overwhelming when playing the game. The balance between emphasis and beauty is almost perfect in my opinion. Again, at certain times throughout the game, (partially one or two bosses) the art style may seem to get in the way or distract you in some way, but I found this to give a sense of difficulty as you must look beyond the art, to recognize attacks and maneuver in a way to avoid them, while also paying attention to where the character is.
Now, as much as I can go on and on about the game, there are a few flaws in my eyes that came to my attention. These flaws are small, but can sometimes be frustrating to the player. First, parrying. Sometimes when attempting to parry an object for various reasons it seemingly doesn't work, or you parry the object and you still take damage. I found this slightly annoying throughout levels when attempting to get A's on all bosses, because I would have to completely restart when taking damage in some cases. I know this is most likely my fault entirely, but it is one part of the game that brought me a great deal of frustration.
Another problem I encountered, although it was very rare, is that sometimes the bosses would almost "bug out" while fighting them, and they may just sit their until hit enough to advance to the next phase. This "bug" never once took away from my experience in any way, but I thought I might as well include it in this review so you are not thrown off if this may happen to you.

Overall, Cuphead is a well developed and challenging game not suitable for everyone, but while advancing through the game a great deal of satisfaction will fill the player after trying time and time again to complete a stage. Although, like all games, it has its "bugs" they do not take away from the players overall experience of the game.
Cuphead is a great game, and I would give it a rating of 9/10 or even 9.5/10 for the sheer enjoyment I had while playing the game.
It is a very tactical game and has many achievements to obrain which always keeps you going.

One of the most fantastic but frustrating games I have ever played.
To start off, the game is fantastic in the sense that 2K & Irrational games have created a game that is truly unique and vastly different than any other game at the time.  Almost 10 years later, Bioshock has aged very well and can easily be played for many more years to come.  The weapons & combat system offer great variety and satisfaction.  Shooting an enemy with a pistol to taking photos of hideous splicers for damage buffs, each weapon offers something unique for every combat situation as well as enjoyability.
Visually, Bioshock is beautiful; considering it's age, the graphic design really is ground breaking compared to many other games that were made of the same year.  There are many small details that Irrational games added to give a strong emotional feel towards Rapture - the environment and atmosphere in particular.  The water and fire effects are pleasing to look at.  I believe the graphics in Bioshock will withstand the test of time.
The story is very well done.  From beginning to end you will most definitely be engaged,  I don't want to put any spoilers on this review so I will keep this part short; the game's story is very good.
Now,  this is the kicker for this game - not the game in particular, but, STEAM's version of the game.  There are MAJOR MAJOR MAJOR bug issues with this game on STEAM.  First of all, you cannot play this game without a microphone plugged in; don't even bother starting it up because you're game is just going to crash before you even hit the main menu.
The next part is where Bioshock on STEAM will make you drop to your knees and cry.  The game WILL CRASH ON YOU.  I have tried everything in my power to make this game fully operational but nothing worked.  I had to save this game EVERY 30 seconds to a minute.  Since Bioshock does NOT have autosave you have to do it yourself; guess what happens when you forget to save the game? That's correct! You lose all your progress! YAY!
I somehow managed to finish this game, considering how much I enjoyed it while it managed to run for 10-15 minutes at a time before I had to reboot it.  If you can withstand this kind of frustration and headache then you will love this game - otherwise, just buy an XBOX 360 and play this game on the console.

I'd previously written a review of the game that criticized a lot of its UI/control elements, frustrated as I was after dying for like the thousandth time due to general 'clunkiness'.
After thinking about it though I realized that ultimately I could live with these minor annoyances, given that this is indeed a zombie survival game, and one of the few I've played that gives as much freedom as it does. I was being a little unfair because a lot of the positive points about the game more than make up for some of its technical shortcomings.
So I will give a little credit here. I like that this game can actually get you scared because there's a great deal of risk involved (at practically all times), you never quite feel safe in this game (getting ambushed by zombies in your 'home' because you forgot the front door open will scare the pee out of you). And the idea of greater risk leading to higher potential awards is also implemented very well (as the downtown areas that have the most goodies are also the most zombie-infested).
So after playing it as long as I have (50+ hours), the reason why I'm still not giving my recommendation is the lack of any sort of content beyond raiding and stealing stuff. The game is really fun until you've managed to stake out all the 'richer' areas and get the good stuff. What then? Farming? Not going to hold me in the same way, and there's only two maps...
I recognize the game is still in development, but until there's more to do (maybe rescue survivors, start mini-colonies, move from one town to another, maybe even have a final objective like discovering a cure) I think it's still just the shell of a game. A very nice shell, but just not quite enough... (I guess I'm also a little concerned about early releases and devs' ongoing committments to them). I will gladly change my recommendation once there's more content to keep me interested.

I haven't even played this game for ten hours and I'm already hooked. Despite not actually being pornography (though that word in the title is what initially caught my attention), this game is a solid title that any fan of bullet hell should pick up.
The basic gameplay is that you have a jetpack and a gun, the goal in each stage is to either get a certain number of points or destroy one or more titans, which usually has a time limit. My only issue with the control is that when on the ground it's hard to change direction while moving and the jump has a lot of up, but not a lot of over.
Some would say it's too easy once you've destroyed a titan's weapons (no♥♥♥♥♥♥sherlock), but that doesn't take into account the fact that there's almost always something shooting at you, not just the titan.
My only real problem comes about ten or so stages in, the game starts off easy with a slow and steady difficulty curve, then the difficulty suddenly spiked and then went back to a steady rise from where it jumped to, nothing to really break the experience. You can just play on the easy setting if you can't handle it, and you won't have to start over for each difficulty you play, which I like.
One last thing to mention, the music. While I wouldn't say the songs get stuck in my head, they are pretty darn enjoyable and sound like something you'd hear in a bar.
Definitely a game you should get, assuming you don't mind dying a lot.

I normally hate zombie survival games, but I love this one. The devs are working hard to improve the gameplay, and update often enough. Most importantly, for those of you who are looking to opt in during early access, the game is not only playable, but very fun. While not feature complete, it could be released as is and be a perfectly solid, complete game. This is an example of early access done right.
As for the specifics of why this game is worth a buy (at any stage of its development), it has a lot going for it in terms of gameplay. It feels desperate, and it's tough as nails, but you never feel like you got screwed randomly. You're in control of how much risk you take on in your endeavors, and with increased risk comes greater reward. Scavenging in a mall may be far more lucrative than in a trailer park, but there are far more zombies in a mall, for instance.
It's unlike other survival games in that it isn't all about endlessly spamming crafting, though crafting does play a vital role. It's not like other zombie games in that the zombies are actually what made zombies cool 25-30 years ago (as opposed to lame and played out in 2015). They're terrifying in numbers, but are a total joke individually. That said, a moment of negligence could end your life.
You won't regret buying this, and now that Steam offers easy refunds, why not give it a go? It's potentially a classic in the genre. You'd be cheating yourself if you passed this up.

I like Evolve, but I don't think its worth the price; I think it has leveling and balance issues.  Also, buying the Season Pass does not get you all the DLC, only some of it.
First, Leveling in the game is required if you want to gain access to the more useful hunters or more potent monsters.  If you jump into this game late, and you play with people who have been playing for a while, expect to get your butt handed to you perpetually until you level up (which might take a long while because your XP is dependent on whether you win).  Playing the monster as a new-comer against people who have played for a while is a brutal course in futility: the hunters will find you and kill you quickly and relentlessly, and there is nothing you can do about it.  If you play a hunter as a n00b, you'll generally be riding the coat-tails of your more experienced companions, unless the more experienced monster finds you, in which case you'll just be killed in short order (and possibly eaten).  I think the game would be better if, like so may other games out there that require leveling, you could create a private game that was completely unlocked for everyone and pick the hunters/monsters you wanted, but sadly that is not an option in this game.
And then there are Balancing issues; if you join a group of players that have 6 or more levels on you, be prepared to be at a significant disadvantage.  It seems that everything you do is at a noticeable degradation compared to the other more experienced players: you seem to run slower, have less jet pack energy, weapons do less damage, healing takes longer, etc.  Because you'll die a lot, you can spend time spectating the bots and see what your abilities will be like once you do level, but when you take that bot over your abilities will degrade and you'll be forced into fighting an uphill battle to get little scraps of XP so you can level.  The leveling also seems to take forever when you try to level with groups that have a lot of experience on you because they will pick the best of their class (whether that is a hunter or monster) and you'll be stuck with the starter class.  I think the game would be better if the various playable classes (both monsters and hunters) were more equally balanced; because there's a huge disparity between the various classes gainable by leveling, as a new player, you end up on the receiving end of an exponentially longer and harder row to hoe to get to where those that have gone before you are.  My advice if your new: only play as a hunter in groups of experienced people; only play solo as the monster until you get the wraith monster; otherwise, only play solo until you get leveled.
Until some of these issues are fixed, or the price goes down, save your cash.

EDIT:
After playing the game some more, I can confidently say this game joins Strike Vector and Titanfall on the list of the most fantastic games that are going to fail.  Here is why.
Simply put, the complete reliance on matchmaking nullifies the possibility of ad hoc gaming communities.  I'd have never played TF2 for as long as I did if I hadn't found a server with a great community.  L4D/2 had a similar problem, but I had a great number of friends who played it, so it was a non-issue.  Evolve scared away a number of people with the DLC non-sense (which, it turns out, really amounted to nothing more than speeding your character through normal progression-based unlocks and exclusive-but-mediocre monster skins), but in my opinion it is *at least* as much fun as L4D, and plenty more if you draw in friends with you.
Let's talk about the biggest problem, though.  The gameplay is severely asymmetrical.  This is fine, though.  Hell, I applaud it.  However, that means there is a lot of pressure to perform as the monster.  In addition, the monster role is not something that a lot of people are going to pick up on the sublties of right away, and that's just the nature of gaming.  That, combined with what I'm not going to start referring to as a sin: leaving a player with no one to talk to.  Yes.  Granted, a monster that is doing poorly never gets taunted or teased or verbally abused, but without a method to converse with your opponents, you'll never get that random person that offers advice and makes your play experience better.  You'll never be able to celebrate a victory or play off a defeat.  As much as I like it, even at the end of an evacuation campaign, the "winner" is fairly ambiguous.  In the context of a larger mythos, this would be intriguing, but as it is it just leaves one uncertain about how to feel in the end.  At the end of each match, I feel either bad because I got roflstomped or guilty because I did the roflstomping.  I feel like being able to communicate during the match would do more to ease such things than it would to scare people away.
In the end, I *do* still recommend it.  If you had a cadre of friends who played L4D/2, and they are interested in Evolve, I'd say go for it.  Right now.  If the mechanics appeal to you, then you'll be playing it together often.  If you're just interested in the game but 60$ seems a bit steep... you're not wrong.  I can safely recommend a purchase to individuals interested in asymmetrical gameplay who are willing to go it alone and able to learn as they go.  For everyone else, unable or unwilling to fight against the current a bit, I'd suggest picking it up on sale.  Mechanically, the game is absolutely worth playing, though whether it will hold your attention for an extended period of time... that I don't know.  If my experience here is anything like my experience with Titanfall, my win/loss ratio will begin to approach 1 and I'll get bored with it.  Though, to be fair, even the last match of evacuation I played where I was rofl-stomping the hunters, they did manage to pull it out in the end thanks to the auto-balancing.  And, again, to its credit, I've found the community to be neutral to friendly, if a little on the quiet side.
It is, verily, a flawed game.  Intended for AAA, I think it will find itself more niche.  The real tragedy, then, is if you never pick up the game when it is right up your alley.
Kill zombies.  Explore caves.  Build stuff.

When I initially heard about Sir, You Are Being Hunted it sounded too good to be true. A procedurally generated open world stealth survival game that's systems driven rather than on rails? Even the AAA developers hadn't pulled off anything that ambitious. I held off for as long as I could, but when the game hit v1.0 my curiosity got the best of me and I picked it up. What I found was one of the most unique and enjoyable experiences in recent history.
The only bit of background information you get is that an experiment went wrong leaving you trapped in some transdimensional Brittain where surprisingly polite robots hunt humans for sport. The only way to get back is to collect 17 pieces to power the standing stone which are spread throughout the games 5 islands. How you go about that and what order you do it in are entirely up to you. What follows is an experience that truly makes one feel like they are being hunted, which is refreshing since so many games cast you as some invincible badass.
They didn't overcomplicate things either. There are a few weapons to choose from, different options as far as traps and distractions, and if you're lucky you'll come across some dynamite which will blow the tweed suited robots to bits. This is not a game that is built to be played combatively, so running and gunning rarely works, but guerilla tactics and hit and runs prove gloriously viable. The stealth indicator is accurate and easy to understand, and I'm happy to report that I had few if any instances where the enemy took notice of me when it shouldn't have.
The games health system is intuitive and well balanced. You'll use bandages for when you're bleeding, but other than that its a matter of keeping yourself fed. When your fed, your health regenerates automatically while when your vitality ticker reaches zero your health slowly starts to decrease. The need to find food will keep you from skirting the maps and avoiding danger. Sometimes you have to enter a dangerously populated town just to get a pack of mints to keep you alive for the next five minutes. It's a brutal game, and the camp of gamers that enjoys a good challenge will find a lot to love here.
Enemy and environment design are brilliant. The red eyes of the robots work as stellar indicators of vision cones and the different enemy varieties kept me on my toes. One in particular that I only encountered in the last quarter of the game was downright terrifying and the loud noise it made will stick with me. The environments are believable which is great considering the world is generated differently each time. My favorite of the Biomes was the mountainous one which is perhaps the most scenic and with the most clausterphobic environments.
I've just completed my first playthrough and I'm already ready to jump back in. I haven't gotten a chance to use the Blunderbuss yet and I want to figure out the strategic advantage of the choo-choo train set. If your a fan of stealth or survival games this is a must have. I'd even recommend it to those looking for an experience outside the norm. Sir, You Are Being Hunted deserves a tip of the top hat and a polite bow; They have developed a game that exceeds expectations, and as a result I'll be sure to watch their future work closely.

Before I begin my review, I would like to say that I have not reached endgame nor have I partaken in EOS's PvP feature. That's not my cup of tea and I prefer to play through an MMO's story rather then fight other players.
Starting off, the games story, to me, is very well put together. The lore of the game is told to you on the run, as in most MMO's, and it's not too difficult to understand. I also appreciated their use of Norse mythology in the lore, because in my experience of MMO's I have never come across one that has used Norse mythology.
The quests in the game are the standard one's that you will find in any MMORPG (collect a certain number of items / kill a certain number of enemies). However, the quests are spread out in a way that you can grab all of your quests, finish them, and head to the next zone. There are usually no quests that you have to go out of your way to complete. TERA did a very nice job of using that same quest mechanic.
The combat is smooth and responsive, it reminds a bit of ArcheAge in the sense that you stand still and attack, rather than move around and attack your enemy, whilst dodging their attacks. The combat could be more exciting and challenging but it is fun for the most part.
One addition that this game has that I have never seen is it's aggro *ding* sound. When you aggro an enemy there will be a *ding* that tells you that you have aggroed an enemy. Another mechanic they added is the compass next to the quest and the distance to your location.
Overall, the game isn't polished, but no MMORPG ever is. It has it's flaws at points and it can seem boring to some, but I have throughly enjoyed my time with this game. Do I recommend it? Of course I do, it's very fun and if you are looking for an MMO as a beginner or you're a sucker for a PvE lore-influenced game like myself, you'll have no problem enjoying this game.
TL;DR: Echo of Soul, despite it's negative reviews due to it's Cash Shop, PvP, and more, is still a very fun game and if you at all enjoy MMO's, a game with rich lore, or RPG's, you'll have a great time with this game.

Disregard all of the dlc whining people do about this game, most of them were probably only part of the Alpha. Evolve is a genuinely fun game, that while seeming repetitive, manages to stay fresh even after 70 hours. Sure, there are balancing issues with some of the monsters, sure, some hunters need slight nerfs or buffs but the game has only been out for 11 days as of the time of this review.
- Fun Co-op experience combined with a great solo experience as in co-op with hunters and solo/lone wolf gameplay with the monster.
- Evacuation campaign that, while short, always plays different every time as different maps mean different adjacent maps and effects for victory or loss on each.
- Very strategic (Monster needs to avoid hunters until stage 3 and hunters need to hunt the monster down and kill it meaning that you will need to position and move strategically to win.)
- Doesn't require a large investment of time (Characters are unlocked quickly and matches last about ten minutes on average)
- Bots are very good (The bots are actually better than most mid-level players at doing their job.)
- Rewards good tactics and team play (Hunters are super powerful if they can work together properly but the monster can be just as powerful if he uses terrain, mobs, sneaking, good timing and other tactics to beat the hunters.)
- Free maps and gamemodes (All future maps and gamemodes will be free to all owners of the game)

- Sometimes can bug out (like you will spawn in as an Ebonstar soldier occasionally instead of the class you chose)
- Unbalanced characters and monsters (Some characters and monsters need tweaks to make them work better. e.g. The Wraith)
The whole DLC fiasco is a bit of a mess. Firstly, I want to mention, all of the DLC aside from the Hunting Season Pass and the Monster Expansion Pack is cosmetic. Sure, its a bit expensive but if you intend on continuing to play the game and like the skins, why not buy them? If you don't like them, don't.
The Hunting season pass is NOT as SEASON PASS as in gives all the DLC. It is a "pass" for the next 4 hunters that are released.
The Monster Expansion Pack includes Behemoth and a Goliath skin.
All other DLC packs are merely cosmetic skin packs for the monsters or hunters, nothing more.

I am honestly surprised by this game, while it doesn't exactly shine in graphics or feel the most modern and polished mmo I have played. I find myself enjoying it a lot. Especially the PvP battlefields, they are fast paced generally capture point driven and combat is relatively balanced regardless of your level. Another feature I like is the ability to solo dungeons, it's doable as pretty much any class and any level. You can get all the gear in the game and never party up if that's the way you want to do things. You can also of course party up, the strangest mechanic there is there is no dedicated healer class in this game. It takes some getting used to. They compensate for that by making potions, revives, and heal scrolls easily and cheaply obtainable at the npc in game shops. I could go on for awhile but despite a lot of complaining and bad reviews I found myself considering this a good game, and will likely give it even more time, and maybe even spend a few bucks on that cash shop just to show my appreciation. Usually these korean cross over mmo's aren't very enjoyable, but this one reminds me of what WoW used to be before they turned it into the lowest common denominator crap that it is now.
I highly suggest giving the game a few days and 20-40 levels to make an impression on you. If you can see past it not having the greatest graphics I'm pretty sure you'll find yourself enjoying it. TL;DR? Forward to the Sky is a charming, but short, puzzle action-adventure that's definitely worth the small price tag, especially if you have fond memories of older-school Playstation and Dreamcast action-adventure titles (^-^)
--
I've just pulled myself away from playing this after having played a bit of the 5th Chapter of the game. 5 of 6, so that's a little bit of a bummer. But it's a bummer simply because the game is fun, well-made and good-looking, and I totally would love to play more of it. On the flipside, this is one title that definitely won't be cloggin up your Steam backlog; this is a title that you will actually finish :)
So it's short; that's not necessarily a bad thing. What matters is if it's good, and Forward to the Sky certainly is. As a rookie effort from a small studio, this is a very well made game. They do a lot with a little, and despite only having 6 chapters, every chapter introduces new mechanics that mix up the style of gameplay. One brings in elevators and fan-platforms (jump on the blades), another will bring wind that pushes you around and "air gates" for you to ride in, the next will bring in crystal prisms that shoot lasers around to activate hidden platforms and stairs, etc. These things do a great job of changing the platforming gameplay & puzzles from Chapter-to-Chapter.
They also do a good job with the limited art assets, changing the time of day/skybox/lighting to make the Tower levels look... well as different as you can, even though the assets are pretty much identical throughout. It's just amazing what a change of lighting can do. It's not as varied as a bigger production, but for what it is, it's very smart and well-done.
The combat is the most simple part of the game. It's not bad; it's almost like a 3D Secret of Mana or classic Zelda title. You have a simple combo, and then a charge attack (which you can also combo). The depth comes from handling the different types of enemies, which they do manage to mix up as you proceed to the game. So there's enough enemy variety here to make the encounters feel fresh Chapter-to-Chapter. They have guys that fire arrows, shielded foes that use charge attacks, sorcerers that can freeze you in ice if you get too close with a wave of their wand, etc. They introduce a new unit every Chapter, and fighting different combinations of them is engaging. There's definitely a little bit of strategy here; trying to pull some guys away so you can take them out before projectile-users start firing on you from across the map, or rushing in and trying to kill the archers before they become a nuisance... and how best to take on a bigger enemy one-on-one; can you get a combo in before they wreck you, or should you try to get their rhythm down, and doing hit-and-run tactics instead? That sort of things. It's old-school, and it does it's job. It's engaging enough without getting monotonous. Besides, combat is there but it's not really the focus; it takes a back seat to the puzzle-platforming.
The worst part of the game (which isn't that bad overall) does affect the platforming though, which is a tad floaty. The physics though, they're not that much of a problem - a floaty jump is fun and forgiving in most cases, and that rings true here. What's awkward is that jumping will KEEP YOU jumping in that direction until you change direction in mid-air. So for a game with some precision jumps (especially in the Second Chapter with the fan-platforms), you end up doing this silly move where, to land your jump accurately, you pass over your platform and then start quickly moving in a tiny circle in mid-air so as not to overshoot as you wait a beat for your fall to actually drop you on your destination. It's never really putting you in serious risk (if you DO fall from the Tower, the Princess will summon her Hot Air Balloon to catch her and plop her close by to where you fell), it's just a little less polished than you'd hope for.
Plus, oddly enough, while the lighting is good overall, there is no shadow underneath the character. The oldest-school trick in the 3D gaming book to help with this sort of thing. Weird.
Beyond that though, I honestly have no issues with the game. I mean, it's fun. It looks good. It sounds good. It's got a simple, cute story (with simple, cute voice acting). And it's a really well designed, very small production that successfully hearkens back to the age of really charming Japanese action games. It's like someone took the design principles for titles like Threads of Fate, Tenerezza, Gurumin, Dual Hearts, Dawn of Mana, Brave Fencer Musashi, even Dark Cloud and decided to make a new game like that with modern tech. Which is awesome! It's just short and doesn't feel quite as good as you'd like it to.
But make no mistake about it, I'm definitely recommending it! Plus, $7 is not that much for a fun experience and to support a promising developer, especially if you have anything in your Steam Wallet to knock that down even further. It could be $6, $5 or even lower for you. So don't let the length dissuade you if you enjoy titles like those I just listed. This game will definitely entertain you and charm your socks off, just like games used to do (^-^)
Highly recommended. Very fun. AnimuGames is a small developer to watch in the future, for sure!
