I hope people on the fence about this game take note of the very polarized community of those playing this game, but not let it dominate. This game is incredibly fun, and it does take a bit of practice. Yes, the season pass is way too expensive. Does that one attribute land this game unending grief? Yes. SHOULD it? No!  People should realize they aren't being forced to buy anything, and if they don't put in the time to get all the facts on what they are buying, that's on them. Am I planning on buying the season pass? No. Am I happy with the game? Yes! Both factions are fun to play. Both factions can win. Fair, balanced gameplay. I find it replayable. The tracking and footprint system really keeps the monster on its toes; they need to be sneaky before they stage up. Humans need to track while balancing speed of pursuit, prediction of the monster, and evasion of natural hazards. (The wildlife can be fearsome if you don't pay attention, much like a rattlesnake.)
If you look at the people who have put time in to review this game, you'll notice a trend.
-No one is making claims that the game is unbalanced. The game IS balanced, very well!
-They usually say "Don't get me wrong, I love this game" because it is FUN.
-The people complaining about DLC prices have their point, but the content within the DLC's are not something they should be griping over. This isn't a pay to win game.
The only consistent problem players have with this game are as follows-
Pricey <- A bit, yes. If this is the only grievance that seems to prevail, there are things called STEAM SALES. WAIT. If you feel you are above waiting, fork out the money. I did, and I'm very happy with this game. Pricey DLC's shouldn't land the game a negative review. Save the hate for the company forums.
"ONLY FUN WITH FRIENDS" <- Not true.  Of course playing with friends makes the game more fun, but that's the way the teams are set up. Until Evolve gets a gametype with multiple monsters, playing with friends is way more fun. If you find out you don't like it when that inevitable troll or noob refuses to understand the concept of teamwork, play monster! Problem solved.
I hope this review helped you understand the situation surrounding Evolve, so you can make a decision best suited for you.

7th Legion is a unique oldie RTS. Heavily underrated.  It's gameplay features many common RTS elements such as tech trees and base building mechanics. However, it also features so unique features. Its first unique setup is that instead of farming resources, you're killing enemies. This allows boosts to your periodical budget allotment, which gives you free money. With a much heavier emphasis on combat, its nice to throw aside your usual chains to resources and just mow down some Chosen scum. Its other unique mechanic is Cards. Just like your perodic budget allotment, every few cycles you'll get a unqiue card. These Cards all feature different effects. To illustrate, the Chaos card causes all characters within it's radius to start fighting each other, friend or foe. The Stealth card cloakcs your units, kaing them invisible, etc. This might sound like tacky gimmick, but this is a real game changer, these cards can easily turn the courses of battle.
So, unto my problems with this game. Firstly, THIS GAME IS UNOPTIMIZED. In order to play, download DXwind and look over the game's forums here on Steam to find more in-depth tuts. Also, there are two factions in-game: 7th Legion and the Chosen. The Chosen quit the Earth centuries ago when it ran out of resources, and left most of humanity behind. They returned later on, thinking humanity had died out, only to find several warring factions, whom all teamed up when they found the Chosen returning. So, now both sides are fighting for the Earth. I haven't beaten the campaign, but the story seems paper-thin and more just a backdrop than anything else. the two in game factions are just recolors of each other; one being red and the other blue. I don't believe there is any stat differences or unit alterrations.
So, to summerize, this game features some unqiue mechanics and an awesome soundtrack, only really held back by my nitpacks. However, the fact it is on Steam but not optimized at all for newer tech is practically heresy. It is disgusting to see them merely throw something on Steam with little reguards for the consumer, and force the consmer to work for hours trying to get their product to work. Consumers shouldn't have to waste time on trying to fix a product. That's the developer's job, if someone puts a game on Steam, even if its an older game, they need to patch it up. Period. Due to the nonexistant optimization, I must downvote this game. Should the publisher patch the game, I'll upvote it. In the mean time however, no.

If you have problems getting the game to work then forget using the enclosed DXWrapper. Use DXWnd instead which you can download from their sourceforge webpage. Once installed If you look in the DXWnd 'exports' folder you will find compatibility templates. Just pick a template for a similar DirectDraw game from that time period, unless you want to create your own. Make sure to change the path to your legion.exe and untick 'run in window' or choose resolution, etc.
Features;
Action Card System that is used to change the dynamics of the battle.
A.I. uses the Action Card System as well.
Units rank up with experience.
Earn resources from destroying enemy units.
Can put units into squads with [CTRL]+[1] or [CTRL]+[2] and then quick select with [1] or [2], etc.
Can select all units in screen view by right clicking on a unit.
Random crate drops on battlefield.
Random events can occur throughout battle.
FMV cutscenes between campaign missions.
Music is interesting if you don't mind electronical/industrial metal.
Can only build one infantry or tank unit, etc at a time even if you have multiple barracks or factorys, etc.
Pathfinding can be a little annoying sometimes but is manageable if you keep things simple.
This is an old skool RTS game and therefore the mechanics are quite simple by modern standards. Basically, just build a large army as quick as you can and try to overpower the enemy. The randomness from the Action Card System, the drop crates, and the random events can be a blessing or a curse.

Hackers, pay to win and a game team full of man childs, that summarizes Metin2 .
There is a steep learning curve that it's similar to games like RuneScape. Unless you've played Metin2 before, you're going to find it difficult to understand the game mechanics and you won't know what you have to do.
Tutorials and guides are minimal on the internet, this game is mostly dead with the exception of a few countries that currently dominate the game: Poland, Romania and Turkey to name the most predominant ones.
Therefore, most other servers set in UK, US, or other countries in EU are going to be empty or close to empty. The global server, you guessed it, is going to be populated by these three countries, and the community is not very friendly.
You won't find help in-game, the game offers no form of instruction for new players, the current players are usually greedy and take advantage of new players and internet tutorials and guides are often minimal, hard to find and usually meant for players that already played Metin2 before and regularly .
The game recieves an important update every 4-5 years , anything else you see in the News section are events meant to make you to top-up money. They are limited "15% more dragon coins!!11!! Top-up nawww!!11!!" , "Whelp Box now in store!!11! FOR JUST 50 DRAGON COINS!1! TRY YOUR LUCK AND AFTERWARDS BUY MORE" kind of offers and they usually are meant for old players.
It's not your average MMO, you don't get into this game with the end-game in mind, because if you do, you're setting yourself for a waste of time and money, because without 24/24 grind you won't make it to end-game OR even be able to resist it.
The game is designed with the ideea of you topping up . Up until level 50-55, you are forced to either grind constantly for hours and hours (and that's going to be impossible for new players) or, take the shortcut, and pay for the itemshop. Either way, at one point, YOU WILL have to pay for in-game currency to take advantage of itemshop offers, otherwise you will quickly become underpowered.
If you take the shortcut and top up in this game, you're entering a never-ending circle of topping up, because there is no way for you to stay at the top without putting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of money constantly. Even this way, you'll find yourself extremly underpowered compared to experienced players that currently dominate the game and the safest bet is to stay away.
This game is alive because of people that topped-up and now can't just quit, because they'll lose huuge investments that they've made along the years and because people keep comming back due to nostalgia (but quickly give up or top-up and join the constant playerbase). New players are RARE and usually quit, and with a good reason, it's not a good game.
GameForge is quickly losing playerbase and it's obvious that the game is declining. They recently started to close down private servers and force private server owners to buy a license in order to keep their servers and playerbase (a desperate action to bring people back to the official servers) and they keep pushing more and more offers and new items into the store, more regularly than before, so that they can make as much money as possible!
If you ever make the mistake of getting this game, PLEASE don't fall into the trap of the itemshop and purchase anything from there!!
I recently got back into this game as a joke, and I can't tell you how many people I've seen purchasing scarfs (an itemshop item that gives you in-game bonuses) and buying over 50-100 boxes (that cost 50 DC each) to get a pet, but not actually knowing how to play the game and thinking this is like any other MMO out there, such as WoW . They eventually quit and lose their investments , and it's not worth it! It's a dead game, published by greedy devs that have 0 interests to please the community.
TL;DR - A dead, unfriendly to new players type of MMO, that forces people to get into the cycle of topping-up real cash in order to stay relevant.
If after all this, you are still interested for some reason, to try out Metin2, PLEASE, join one of the many alive private servers. They are usually highly populated, and due to their nature of being a private branch, people are usually more friendly. It's easier to get a grip on the game and private servers have everything that the official servers have in the itemshop, available in-game for Yang (the free currency) and pay-to-win is not THAT bad (but still existent - you can't say Metin2 without saying Pay2Win).

Superhot is an FPS game that revolves around the concept of time moving when you do, and is good fun. You are tossed into one of many arenas in the game that resemble the real world, with monochrome visuals. Your only enemies are red characters weilding 1 of 4 weapons, a machine gun, shotgun, pistol, and sword. Each takes one hit to kill. It becomes somewhat puzzle like at times, as you have to prioritize your enemies, and know how to use the time mechanic to your advantage. Another mechanic is hot-switching, which lets you take the spot of enemies while disposing of your body, though it does have a cooldown. The story, while found pretentious by some, is pretty okay. It's relatively simple and doesn't get in the way of the game TOO much. My only gripes with the game is that it's relatively short, and somewhat unforgiving at times. I reccomend this game, however, not for the price it's at. Get this game on sale.

I am absolutely in love with this game. The art is insane, the bosses are super fun and the game is very hard but not in bad ways. Sadly when a very difficult game is released, flaws are much more easily noticed.
There are a few issues that hold me back from truely enjoying this game, getting in the way of the fun and making my experience far less pleasant than it should be. The most prominent negatives are:
1. The game crashes far too often when pausing during a boss fight.
2. It is a common occurence for my Xbox 360 controller to be stuck vibrating for seemingly no reason until I take a hit of damage, which is something you never want to be forced to do. I have confirmed this to not be due to my controller being damaged as it has happened with 2.
3. If you're playing co-op, two players can not parry the same object at the same time. This is actually a massive oversight in my opinion. For example: there is a level where you must parry the objects in order to change gravity and avoid a large line of enemies, or successfully reach certain jumps. This is the only way to not take any damage, but me and my co-op partner found ourselves consistently taking damage because of this. It would be completely fine with only one player, but I did not buy this game just to play by myself.
3. Probably the most annoying for me, why is there absolutely no way in the game to unequip power ups? I can imagine this only being an issue early on, but it's an issue that has affected my gameplay quite harshly. For instance, the super moves. Allow me to explain. There is a power bar where cards fill up as you shoot enemies up to a maximum of 5 cards. When a card finishes filling, you are able to shoot a more powerful shot at the cost of a single card
I find myself commonly stockpiling my cards to the maximum in order to use them at the more difficult boss forms. Thats when I came across a power up called a 'super' which can only be used when you have the maximum amount of cards, and, when used, removes all your cards aswell. The first super I found to be quite lacking in any use, and I would have definitely preferred to unequip it so I would be able to stockpile my cards again without worrying that when I hit the maximum, I don't need to waste all my cards on a crappy super and instead use the more powerful shots. But apparently the only way to remove this is to find another super, with absolutely no way of unequipping it unless I rummaged through the save files manually. This, too me, seems like a massive oversight with very annoying consequences.
This could also be solved by changing the super move button to one of the numerous unused buttons in the game, but there is no way to do that as of now.
This game is great, and I have been waiting for it for so long, and it sucks that I can't get myself to reccomend it at this time. if it wasnt held back by these little problems I would enjoy it double as much, and if they do get fixed, I will change this to a positive.

Ugh. Pretty badly pretentious. It has some nice music sometimes and an interesting mechanic here and interesting ambience there, but never really ropes them together into anything but a motley collection of taking one's work too seriously.  The Stanley Parable is by far superior to this one, and I think that game at least demonstrates that this studio really can do very engaging and compelling work in principal.
I look forward to their next work, because everything you do isn't going to be a hit and that's perfectly fine. But this one really ran on rails and did far more telling than showing.
To put another way, you can't really make somebody feel like a prisoner until they've at least been allowed to become acquainted with a taste of freedom first. Parable hits this mark better because while it represents a treatise on choice and futility, you are at least granted a modicum of choice belying a far grander illusion of freedom. Branching paths, and a game designer predicting what you might have previously thought was unpredictable? That's innovative. Window dressing on boxy hallways with M. Night Shamayalan narration and zero opportunity for the *player* to express themselves, or gain any reactive validation from the game environment? Nah, not really.

Full review:
Yes, the title is a bit strange and doesn't really have anything to do with what the game is other than the fact that it includes robots, and not the drunk type.
The game has you flying around various arenas in a jetpack, equipped with a gun that acts more like a pea shooter than a gun. The gun has infinite ammo and doesn't have any recoil to it, but it can be upgraded with various abilities found throughout the different arenas. It’s really find to slide around and fly between the various platformers, spewing bullets whilst doing so. However, while moving, it often feels like you’re skating on ice, which was actually quite fun.
There are several types of robots and “titans” that can be found throughout the experience. They’re all very easy to defeat, and I had no trouble progressing through the multitude of levels offered by the game. There was even a type of robot that resembled a burger and attacked in swarms. The titans are these massive robots that look very cool, but can deal massive damage if not dealt with quickly. They need to be taken down piece by piece in order to be defeated.
Although the game is fun, the variety of weapons and upgrades available are really limited. If there was a wider weapon variety offered, such as the variety offered in Serious Sam, then the game would be a whole lot better and not feel like the same, repetitive experience everytime it’s played. The level variety is top-notch. Each level looks and feels different and it’s always a joy to fly around, bounce off jump pads, and such, all while spraying bullets about.
I can’t say the game is worth $15, but it would certainly be worth $5, so try to pick it up during a sale. The amount of content offered is large and replayability is high.

As usual with Davey Wreden's games, I cannot say much about this game without spoiling the fun of it. However, here is what I can say:
-It is nothing like The Stanley Parable. It is not a bad thing at all, but just be aware of that before playing it. It is not a comedy. Many people go into playing The Beginner's Guide thinking it'll be Stanley Parable 2, and they are heavily disappointed because of that.
-It speaks a lot to game developpers (or aspiring ones). It still has some sort of meta commentary. It should be played more than once to fully appreciate it.
Now if you don't mind knowing a bit more about the game (again without any spoil, but it can affect a bit your experience knowing that beforehand):
It has a very mature, personnal story to it. Not many games dare to take that angle, or to have different layers of interpretation, and I'd really love to have more of that kind of games in the future.
Finally, if you REALLY want to know more about the game, this is the biggest thing I can say without spoiling anything. Beware though, it's better to discover most of The Beginner's Guide by playing it, but I feel like you can know that and still be surprised by the game and be into it:
You will play different prototypes of games that were made throughout the years, as shown in the trailer. The experience is ever-changing, and they all have an interesting concept or twist, that is explained by the narrator. It is like going through a game dev's archives of all the games they've made to learn the craft. It really makes the statement that you can get to know about a person only by experiencing their work (in this case, games). It defends this point very well, and I'm happy it does.

One of the first games I've ever felt overwelmingly compelled to write a review for, and even at that, I'm only halfway through. It discusses something that I feel is close to the heart and soul of all good video games. Creating a game doesn't have to be about telling a story or pretty graphics or even fun intense gameplay. A game can just be an experience, a pice of art that you can walk through and interact with in a world not grounded in reality. It can be an experince that might be entirely subjective, involkes strange feelings, or just makes you think about life.
Games are going to be hyper realistic and just visually fantastic. Experiments with the abstract is nothing new, but this is something different. These short experiences are like stepping into brief poems or sneaking through an artist's  abandoned studio. I really hope that this niche collection experimental levels inspire more develoupers to turn everything they've been taught about story telling on its side.

If you've never been drunk with robots, I suggest you give it a try. You might want to skip the pornography however. Using a super powered suit, you jet pack around a disco colored world of robots shooting everything and collecting alcohol for extra points. This is a bullet hell shooter, done in the first person view and mixes a frantic feeling of platforming, item collection and bullet hell stying shooting and dodging.
The game is set across multiple stages, that don't usually last that long. You have to complete a series of goals, ranging from beating a score to defeating titans, which is good and bad. It's good because it mixes things up, but sometimes bad because a level can hit you out of nowhere and keep you stuck for awhile. I cruised along without any failures until level six, which took me about 10 tries to beat, after that I beat the next few stages without much trouble. The game is a bit uneven to say the least.
I love what they are trying to do here, you get a wacky shooter, with a fun theme and a bunch of robots that look like, well, porn for robots, of fans of the Transformers movies. The titan design is great, and the bosses all have weak points that require you to run around and shoot them all over. I don't like the collection mini game much, and score based levels are not as fun for me, but I do enjoy running around shooting and blasting bosses while homing missile bots try to crush you.
The game is slick, has amazing music and throws a bunch of jokes at you, so of course some will lay flat and most of the emails are boring to listen to, but the voice acting is great, reminds me a lot of characters on Archer.  Overall, I would say this is a solid title, with frantic shooting that borders on hard, to impossible, until you keep trying and beat it.

Blair Zuppicich, the composer for 7th Legion and most other Vision Software titles is an unsung master of video game music. Sadly, his works always tend to end up in rather flawed games, and 7th Legion is no exception. The game's premise is great, though a bit too heavily influenced by Warhammer 40000, especially when it comes to unit designs.
It also has some pretty interesting mechanics, most importantly a card game system, which it probably was the first RTS games to have, even though we've seen it more recently (and better executed) in games like Divinity: Dragon Commander and Battleforge.
7th Legion sadly has issues with many of the genre's fundamentals - path finding and mouse interface among the worst offenders, often making you struggle against the UI to get even basic stuff done (especially since modern CPU's are too fast to give you the intended delay from clicking to getting the unit behavior menu that's only supposed to appear after you've held the left mouse button for a second. You'll also notice the main menu animations going way too fast, but the in-game cutscenes work as intended).
All in all it's a pretty interesting title from the era when we saw the creative peak of the genre, it's a deeply
flawed RTS, certainly not at the level of classics like Dark Reign or Total Annihilation, or even Krush Kill 'N Destroy but over all I think it's worth experiencing.

Pros:

Yes, they were difficult (and moon logic-y), but I'm not afraid of walkthroughs, so I was happy to turn to one when needed.  I really liked the fact that this made the gameplay reflect the story, and hence become part of the narrative itself.  Besides, the puzzles sort of reminded me of those in Monkey Island 2, where

This is a no-frills re-release of the 1997 Game. If you liked it then, you'll like it now. No fresh coat of paint, no additional features, nothing. For better or worse, it is exactly as it was.
For the uninitiated, 7th Legion is an RTS about two factions, the 7th Legion and the Chosen. The Chosen are comprised of the rich, powerful, and uber smart that evacuated Earth when pollution rendered the planet uninhabitable. The 7th Legion are so-called because they were the ones left behind, and this is the seventh generation after the evacuation. The Chosen come back from deep space to reclaim the planet, the 7th Legion resists, and that's about it. There's no real story beyond the intro video.
As far as play styles go, the infantry are mirrored on both sides. It's in the vehicles and Assault Chassis (mechs) that the two factions diverge. The 7th Legion has hard-hitting vehicles, and The Chosen have awesome AC's.
The game's economy is gifted in regular intervals of time. The player's rank will determine how many Credits are given during these intervals. Rank is achieved through a hidden XP system. Killing units, completing objectives, and destroying buildings all contribute. Credits can also be earned in the same fashion plus some additional means such as collecting crates and from "card" effects (more on that below).
The game has a unique system that adds an additional layer of strategy, playing cards. These cards are gifted every other interval or found in crates and have a wide variety of effects. They can instantly grant soldiers, burn the enemy in an area, gain control of an enemy vehicle, or steal credits. These cards are outlined with colored borders to indicate how they should be played: green for play on yourself, blue for neutral, and red for play on the enemy. Exploiting these cards at the right time often will have devastating effects on your enemy. The enemy has their own cards that can be played on you, too, so be careful.
The game's missions are challenging, and maps are usually large enough to explore different routes. The 7th Legion's missions tend to be more strategic, expanding beyond merely amassing an army and steamrolling across the map. In one mission, you only have one guy with a bomb, and you have to blow up a base with it before you are granted reinforcements. There are a few others where you don't even have a base, and have to make do with small squads and limited resources.
There are also infantry based missions indoors. In these scenarios, three soldiers enter a facility to either get to a certain point on the map or kill everyone inside. Each member of the squad can be equipped with three weapon types, the default laser gun, grenade launcher, or a sniper rifle. Frankly though, the sniper rifle is vastly superior, and it's the only weapon I use. The game for either faction will last a handful of hours to complete.
Although the game is a lot of fun, there are a number of caveats. It's far from perfect. Pathing in large groups is an exercise in frustration. Units will get stuck behind trees, on different elevations, or will ignore orders altogether. They do this thing I call the "F You" response. Say for example you want to attack a vehicle bay. Instead of doing that, sometimes tank turrets or AC chassis will spin 180 degrees and just sit there. Or just as bad, units sometimes won't recognize move and attack orders that are placed very near to the unit.
The enemy AI is about as intelligent as a pile of rocks. My favorite tactic is to wall off paths to my base,then build power plants or barracks until I can literally build well behind enemy lines. They never destroy the walls and only attack buildings that are invading their space once in a while. However, never is the AI's stupidity more evident than when playing a particular card, "Armageddon". It wipes out the whole map of friendlies and enemy alike, destroys every building, and critically damages both bases. No matter how intricately the mission map was planned out, the AI won't even repair the base. They build one or two power plants, barracks, basic infantry, and that's it. Left to its own devices, the AI is worthless.
This game was developed in a time where balance wasn't a huge factor, and patches were difficult to distribute. It is possible to upgrade infantry to the degree of being near-godlike. With top armor upgrades, some infantry can survive being crushed by tank treads quite handily. Sure, you can upgrade vehicle and AC armor and weapons, but upgrading infantry is much more economical and effective.
If you are willing to forgive the game's shortcomings, there's a lot to enjoy here. Some of the cut-scenes are pretty cool, and the title theme is still an awesome jam. The card system and how the economy works are both unique features that I haven't seen reproduced in any RTS since. For the price, give it a try. You only have a few bucks and an afternoon to lose.

The game started out promisingly enough with insomniac Mizuki pacing her room, the source of her affliction, a red-eyed dwarf, vowing that as long as he couldn’t sleep, neither could she. The smooth animation, fully voice acted script, and bizarre, but beautiful artstyle created a distinct atmosphere and I was eager to find out how I’d be able to dispel Mizuki’s demon.
From there, the game makes a nosedive.
In typical point and click fashion, your protagonist is given a laundry list of tasks to complete in order to move the plot forward. Memoranda’s journal/quest log of choice called a memoranda and Mizuki updates it when you get something new to do. Unfortunately, she scribbles down personal notes the way one might in their own private journal, meaning that it may or may not make sense to someone other than the person who wrote it while these scribble notes fit in with the game thematically, a lot of them only gave the vaguest sense of what actually needed to be done.
This meant that I spent more time travelling from screen to screen, trying my most recently acquired item on people and trying to combine random items in my inventory.
Even the townspeople, who could have very well have made a helpful suggestion such as “Hey, have you spoken to so-and-so?” just continued to spit out one of their three pre-programmed lines, so they were of no help. I finally broke down and used the only guide posted in the community hub, which is why my playtime is only 4 hours.
One of those four were spent trying not to tear my hair out and the other three were actually spent playing the game with the occasional, infrequent glance at my handy, dandy guide.
In conjunction with the oftentimes obscure memoranda is the story itself. It’s based off of a collection of short stories, so perhaps it’s my own fault for not having read that first, but the game just seemed to be a Frankenstein of parallel story paths that were strangely disjointed, but somehow relevant to the fact that Mizuki had trouble remembering her name.
The dwarf I mentioned earlier, for example, I had assumed had something to do with the missing name, but it turned out that he was just another random weird part of Mizuki’s life. Add to that a near-suicidal man who wants to be a fish, an investigator who is looking for a weirdly human-sized elephant and the runaway man who’s harboring him, a duck doctor who brews mysterious potions, a “dragon”, an opera singing man-cat, a deadbeat who vomits the peanut punch he was so desperate for a war between an army of frogs and a giant worm, a girl who killed herself and feared a monkey would steal her name - the list goes on and the majority of these tangents go on without a resolution.
Instead, you end up with a lot of unanswered questions and the sour taste of “that’s it”? When the credits roll, not too long after the game starts.
If this was an episodic game, fine. The confusion would likely be answered by subsequent chapters. As a completed work, however, Memoranda is like a machine with too many complicated working parts--Some of the parts just don’t function the way they should and instead serve as clutter.
In trying to make this plot complex and many layered, the creator only manages to needlessly convolute the main plot—that is, the problem with Mizuki’s memory—with a bunch of fetch quests and 1-dimensional characters that serve no other purpose than to move the main plotline along.
And that fact shows. The other characters are people who Mizuki’s seems to be very familiar with and as such, it seems that she doesn’t need to explain anything about them other than their name and occupation. The art in Mizuki’s mind, however, nor have we shared any of her 30 years on Earth and so these strangers she chats with so warmly are held at arm’s length and are made stranger still by the fact that we have no idea why we should care about them or their problems.
This utter lack of character development makes the game feel even more like a chore because at no point do you feel empathetic towards any of the characters that appear once, say their peace, and a re never heard from again. There is nothing memorable about them other than the fact that they are strange people or creatures in a strange world--their motivations, likes and dislikes, and what makes them more than a plot device is lost.
Phil is the perfect example of an interesting characters rendered one dimensional by loose ends. He's mentioned early on and, indeed, his story seems to run parallel of Mizuki's because she spends much of the game trying to figure out where he was located and, upon finding him, protecting him from being located by someone investigating the disappearance. After completing a few tasks geared towards helping him become a human, you find out that this weirdly proportioned elephant doesn't actually want to be a human and the man who said he did was actually lying to keep you busy.
Which is insult to injury considering these are clearly fetch quests meant to pad your short game time.
After that, that's it. You don't find out why the elephant has gone missing, why the runaway man is harboring him, or where they end up in the end. You just leave the elephant sitting in an armchair and talking gibberish  (apparently elephants speak gibberish) and the man cooking spaghetti. For all of eternity.
The game looks great and the music is quite nice. The voice acting, however, leaves something to be desired. Personally, I found the main character's very noticeable lisp maddening. Other voice actors sounded phoned in--as though they were recorded in a large, echo-y room or passed through some other medium like a phone and then recorded by a device.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
I found Memoranda to be subpar in terms of story and gameplay elements. Strange is fine, but the disjointed, random events that make up this surreal tale border on the nonsensical and, by the end, you have more questions than answers.

You're going to die. You're going to bleed to death, you're going to starve to death, you're going to be shot with shotguns, or blugeoned with giant robo-canes, or gnawed on by vicious robo-hounds, or spmething equally unfair.
That's sort of the point though. This game isn't at all fair, and it makes that the central theme. You, Sir (or Madam) have been unceremoniously deposited in an alternate dimension. In Britain. Your interdimensional whatever has exploded all over five islands, and in order to get home, you needto find the smoking remains and cram them in to a conveniently sized hole in a magic rock.
Also, there are a lot of robots, and no people.
Robots have a pretty good idea what you want, and despite some clearly worded letters to the contrary they aren't inclined to give it to you. They'll do a pretty decent job of patrolling, on foot, in baloons, with robo-hounds, and they'll make a habit of frequenting the places where you find things you need to not starve to death or die from being mauled by robots.
As you retrieve the pieces of your gizmo, the robot hunt will intensify, adding new types of robots to the hunt and increasing their number.
Luckily, you have the opportunity to save your progress at the aformentioned magic stones, or at the boats that carry you between islands. You should do that, because you're probably going to die once or twice.
Aside from weaponry (which is pretty scarce) there are plenty of insteresting gizmos to spice up your experience including bear traps, fire, trombones, alarm clocks, toy trains, hallucinogenic mushrooms, and a slow of other useful or just fun to find stuff to help, hinder, or amuse you along the way.
I highly reccommend this game to anyone who enjoys a decent stealth experience, roguelikes, or those who like survival games like DayZ or Nether but don't appreciate the PvP focus found there.

It's exactly what it says.  You're on a group of islands in the English countryside, where a bunch of robots dressed as hunters and gentlemen are stalking you as the last human alive on the island.  This isn't a shooter; you are prey.  Run, hide, ambush, loot, survive.
An interesting game mechanic (besides not allowing save-anywhere, which is as it should be for a game such as this) is that your health is constantly draining.  You need to eat to keep up your health, and you need to forage to get food.  This keeps you in constant motion and heading in new directions rather than camping.  A second mechanic which I haven't seen in a game before is that messing with inventory doesn't stop the world...do you finish moving your inventory around to pick up more loot, or do you keep an eye out for hunters?  It adds a decent sense of fear to the game.
I haven't played much of it yet, but it is unlike anything I've played before, and has a sense of whimsy to cover up what is essentially a horror/survival game.  Definitely a fun game.  Unlike how I normally play shooter-type games (slow, learn the ground, keep to defensible positions), this game forces you to take risks, to keep moving, to get out of your comfort zone.  It's done a good job of that and I hope as I learn the ropes that it will continue to be as enjoyable.

I also found the artwork striking and fresh for an adventure game and the premise itself (you have lost your name) very amusing. The hint system is somewhat elegant (and it gets the job done most of the time), but not the puzzles themselves. Sure, it's hard already trying to make good puzzles in a straightfoward narrative game, try doing it in a surreal one, where logic itself is warped. The game tries to acommodate this shortcoming by gating you out of areas and characters - sadly, most of the time by logically randomic means. You might feel you should do something at a point via the "memoranda hints" - put you can't, unless you somehow devise the unlogical trigger which you let you then access said areas or use said items.
Also: the main character's "i don't wanna do this" messages ("some people get lucky and make it, im not one of them"and "Maybe I would have done it in the old days") drove me CRAZY. Basically, the most repeated phrases in the whole game are the most random and badly written.
ALSO 2: someone may have mixed up surreal with "quirky" while coming up with a lot of this game's writing.
HOWEVER: I know I'm being extra picky - as I said, I had hopes for the game.
I'll sum it up:  if you enjoy adventures, this one is different and worth a shot if only for the artwork and the weird and amusing universe it creates. So, if nothing else, maybe consider it when it's on sale?

I am excited to see a multiplayer co-op element introduced in future updates!  I have seen some people discourage introducing multiplayer but as long as the single player sticks around, multiplayer would just make this game that much more fun.  The controls are fairly well setup, it would be nice if changing controls were introduced so that players can at least edit the hotkeys to their personal preferences.   The game also has a nice, simple background story that is really fitting. It would be nice if they gave a little bit more of an explanation of why you are carrying your crystal around everywhere, but that is still at least explained a little bit.  It does have a very well thought out backstory on the Steam page and it would be nice to see that implemented on the main menu (like an option that plays a cutscene that tells the backstory).  While I love the idea behind the storyline, I think it would be beneficial to add a truly 'Endless' mode where you keep going through levels until you die.  Also, it would be nice to see the level cap of 5 be increased (later in development) because level 5 is reached to easily if you know what you are doing. All in all, this is a great game and I am very excited to see the final product!

One more door. Just one more door.
I am not a huge fan of tower defense games, but this little rogue-like has me hooked. Beyond the simple build-and-defend mechanic at the heart of every TD, DotE adds a compelling risk-reward element in the choice between doubling down and heading to the exit with the resources you've collected, or opening one more door in hopes of finding treasure or an ally at the risk of multiple waves of enemies threatening to destroy everything you have built. Striking that balance is key to your survival.
Dungeon of the Endless is still in its early stages, but this little monster has a lot of potential. More items, more enemies, more levels, more non-combat encounters, story elements, heroic side quests, and party management mechanics are sure to come, but I would love to see competing parties of survivors taking resources (multiplayer plix?), the ability to relock doors (albeit either as limited use item or heroic ability), and different environments (with more incredible music added to what is already a killer soundtrack).
I cannot wait to see how this game develops. I am officially pumped.

Hinterland had a special relationship with its fans.  It felt like we knew the developers, and they cared about us....  They showed this by being open and honest with us when they failed to meet a   release deadline, or when their progress between sandbox updates was slower than expected....
But, we were ok with this...  Because we understood that perfection takes time, and even in pre-release alpha, TLD was pretty damn good... Spectacular even.
we rewarded this behaviour with loyalty and praise.  Giddy excitement.
And we trusted that this is how it would be.
My opinion of Hinterland games has changed a bit today.
22 days ago, a countdown timer was posted on the Long Dark website.  This was an obvious tease that hinted at the fan base finally receiving Story mode and many promised updates.... Or at least something, because Hinterland wouldn't mess around with a countdown clock.  If it were only a countdown to an announcement, well they would tell us that, wouldn't they?
I would surmise that a lot of people jumped on board and purchased TLD during these 22 days, hoping to get in a last minute pre-release price...
Only to be rewarded with another 90 day wait at the endo of the timer countdown.
On first glance, this seems to me like it may have been a last-ditch money grab leading up to the now-promised August 1st release.  Why the smoke and mirrors?  You could have given it to us straight and we would have understood.  As we have in the past.
Hinterland doesn't make me think of a small, enthausiastic venture by a close knit team of developers anymore.  Now I think of them as just another corporation that cares mostly about the bottom line.  Now that the big console money is at stake, this is how we'll be treated.
I expected better of you, Hinterland.
Is the game worth $21.99 in its current state?  Absolutely. Yes. Definitely.
Do I feel like I am supporting a passionate, tight group of indies that care about quality above all?  No.  The warm fuzzy feeling is gone.
I expect a marketing position to open up soon at Hinterland.
-------
My introduction to the The Long Dark was through a totally unrelated search for a trailer for a movie name I couldn't remember.  (I believe it was 30 Days of Night..)
Anyway, the Youtube link for one of the TLD play videos came up and happened to grab my eye with its interesting artistic style and the Canadian flag.  I decided to watch.
I was pretty engrossed right off the bat.  See, I am not into heavy, mindless, button-mashing action... I am not into unrealistic player abilities like magic, flight, etc... I am not into being dazzled by graphics to hide a lame game.  My wishlist is simple.  Realism, depth, sandbox-style freedom and the ability to immerse me.  The Long Dark is a perfect fit for me.
The thing that amazes me is that how I have to keep telling myself that this game is still an alpha, yet I have never felt such immersion...
There is room for improvement and refining of a the stat balancing in the game... There's also one or two very minor graphic anomalies, but once again... It's an alpha.
The issues this game has in alpha pale in comparison to some of the issues you would find in highly marketed big box releases.
If you want to feel the biting coldness of a winter storm through your computer screen, the chill that runs down your spine when you hear a wolf howl, the primal fear of being prey as you hear a bear's footsteps nearby... This is the game for you...
If you want to feel the elation of finding shelter after a long, hopeless hike in a storm...  The relief of finding a simple candy bar when you are starving...  The heart-pounding excitement of the hunt...  TLD is for you.
This hasn't even touched on the beauty of this game.  The morning sunrise.. The evening sunsets.  The calm.  The quiet.  And sometimes the awe of nature's anger.
Simple survival that is made to feel very, very real.
Man against nature.  Or maybe man against himself.
The Long Dark is simply the most immersive game (simulation?) I have ever experienced.  For me personally it is perfection...  (It's an alpha....  What's to come?)

This is an Early Access Review, so read with that in mind.
Dungeon of The Endless, portrayed as a ''Roguelike Dungeon-Defender" game. Roguelike seems to be more equivalent with ''PermaDeath'' these days than actual Roguelikes, because *real* Roguelikes these days are rare. While Dungeon of the Endless *does* kind of fall flat in that department, the gameplay and visuals are still great and the game is a joy to play.
What do you do?
You crashlanded on a planet in your escape pod. Two of your crew members survived but the escape pod is totally ruined. It is up to you to exit the space shuttle, explore the hallways of some unknown facility, and escape with the power core that still happened to be intact. It is reminiscent of tower-defense games, in that there is a distinct turn-based mechanic going on in-between the real time segments. Every time you explore a new room, you get additional resources plus a chance to spawn some event. There's an event for the room you just entered (Resources / Items / Monsters / Nothing / NPCs) and a possible event for several rooms that have been exploded and abandoned (Monster spawns).
As soon as you open a door to explore a new room, you potentially trigger a ''tower defense wave''. If nothing happens? Lucky you! Continue to build / scout / play around and open another door.
The power core itself also plays a role, with its health being shared as both currency and power-limiter, you will have to keep it safe to ensure the option of building a safe route throughout the dungeons that you will be exploring. Almost every room has a specific amount of small nodes and big nodes which can be used to build towers that either attack, help defend, or give other supportive boons that affect either your heroes or the resource generation per room explored.
Although the Early Access is relatively limited, it is already noticeable that a lot of work went into this game, and as far as I can tell, it should only get better and better as time goes on.
The only downsides for the early access (other than limited content) are the few bugs, of which some can be quite annoying (and even gamebreaking at times) They happen sparingly though, and with the dedication Amplitude has shown on their other games, this should get fixed relatively fast.
So, would I recommend this game?
If you are looking for an *actual* Roguelike in the same style as NetHack / ADOM / mAngband, then no.
If you are looking for a fun strategical Tower Defense meets Dungeon Crawler RPG game, then it's an absolute yes.

I thought I'd have quite a bit of fun with this. Flying around in a jetpack, shooting giant octopus laser robots, what could go wrong? And yet somehow it still manages to be frustrating and boring. Yes, even with a name like that.
The gameplay is basically the same throughout the whole thing. Jump across the platforms, shoot the smaller enemies until the big enemies ("Titans") appear and then shoot the big enemies. You have a jetpack to give you a short (and I mean very short) boost, but you're stuck with the one gun throughout the whole game. Which is a shame, because it's not even remotely fun. It looks pretty neat I guess, but it's one of the least satisfying guns I've ever seen in a game. It barely even makes a sound, and the only indication that you're hitting your target is a brief flash of red. It's basically a NERF gun with flashing lights on the side.
The enemy deaths aren't any better. The titans are made up of plenty of smaller parts, and you have to destroy all of these to finally take out the core. But the parts just turn red and float off with barely a sound. No explosion, no impact, no fun.  Same issue when the thing finally goes down. There's an actual explosion this time, but it's still kind of weak. It's more of a light show than anything else.
And then there's the platforming. As mentioned before, your jetpack keeps you in the air for a few seconds at most before you plummet to the ground. If you're lucky, you'll land on a platform. And you do need luck. It's first person, so you basically have no way of telling what you're going to land on without looking straight down, which will of course require you taking your eyes off the enemy. And you can't do that. Thanks to the stupidly short time limits, you have to be shooting the titans pretty much constantly to have any chance of winning. And thanks to the huge amount of enemies and bullets, you can't afford to keep still either. So that means lots of jumping and lots of falling off. And once you do fall off you'll need to make your way to one of the jump pads to get back up, wasting even more time.
There are a few powerups as well, but they're not fun and not massively useful either. I counted about four powerups in total. Not impressive.
There's also a plot but there might as well not be. Your former robot workers have gone mad and invaded Boston (I think). So go shoot them. It only exists as some brief pre-level descriptions of each Titan, which are silly but not funny, and the few actual jokes they have are repeated many times. "Ha, it's funny because the evil death robot used to be a stripper/bartender/cleaner/whatever", every damn time.
It's pretty much forgotten about entirely in the levels too. The titans look nothing like anything that could do any sort of work, which seems to be missing a big oppurtunity. Why make jokes about the robot having a silly name or job if it doesn't come across in the enemy design. It's the same with the levels. The descriptions seem to imply uniqueness and personality, but they're all the same collection of floating platforms and jump pads.
I could point out more flaws but there isn't much point. This game isn't worth your time.

Red Orchestra 2 is the best ptsd simulator I have and may ever have played. It isn’t one of the best first person shooters or multiplayer games out there, and not necessarily the best WW2 game, and its single player isn’t particularly good at all. But without a doubt, the killing, the being killed and the plenty of in-between there is in this game makes Red Orchestra 2 a terrifying but great experience.
In this game, you are in one of four armies, Stalin's Russia, Hitler's Germany, Tojo's Japan or Roosevelt's Americanos. A large percentage of the time spent in this game is having your back to the wall sh*t scared. There's bullets and shrapnel flying from every direction and you've got sh*t in your pants and countless deaths already. Every corner in this game, every room, nook and cranny can and will conceal someone from the opposing team, firing at you from every possible angle imaginable. The cover system in this game isn’t necessarily great (although the blind firing is pretty nice) but it works, so I'll give it that.
You've seen an enemy soldier, he's shot you or you've shot him and now he's dead. It's exactly like a million other games, but it feels nothing like any other game. the little things that make the difference, such as the sound of your own breathing when you lifted the rifle to your eye, and the way it bobbed around slightly in your hands. It's in the mark on your enemy's chest where the bullet hit, and the way his blood spurted from his back, making the mark of entry. The way they fell, with some weight to it like a real person. The way he clutches his stomach, yelling in German, the way he clutches and pulls the trigger madly firing the last ammo in his gun before departing.
The developers of this game thought that if the main interaction of the game is to kill, and kill and kill. You should probably make it feel great. It's the attention to detail that turns this from a generic war shooter to a battlefield. It makes it something great, making you feel more like you're the one actually pulling the trigger. The limited hud really adds to this; and I love the fact that you have to check the ammo in your magazine rather than having a counter in the corner of your screen.
The game modes are also great and fairly interesting. The most popular one is Territory, in which the offensive team is meant to capture multiple points on the map, whilst the other is to defend them. In this game each team has reinforcements which spawn every 15-20 seconds. The maps are made and designed to support 64 players. The reinforcement system works greatly because it finds a good way to deal with respawns and involve them with the setting of the game. These reinforcements allow the players to concentrate on the shifting frontline, going backwards and backwards until the offensive team has taken the map. Countdown mode has similar objectives, but players get just 1 life per round, where the teams swap sides halfway through, similar to how it works in games like competitive game modes in games like Counter Strike. Firefight, a team deathmatch variant to the game is fairly popular but feels as if it doesn’t really belong in the game. Territory is the only real active gamemode as of now.
The weapons feel remarkable, and the classes that carry them are fairly familiar from other games. The assault class with an SMG, a marksman sniper class, a rifleman and an elite rifleman variant as well as a few others like the tank commander or engineer. The few inventive classes such as Commanders or Squad leaders do little to change the flow of gameplay however. Both roles have valuable abilities but the players on public servers rarely interact with one another asking for smokescreens or giving commands as the squad leader.
Tanks don’t add much to the experience. They require a different set of skills to use well and have lovingly detailed interiors. They are an easily disposed of or ignored nuisance on the few maps that actually allow the players to utilize them.
The many deaths you will go through in this game put you constantly on the edge of your seat. Death is so violent and sudden that you’re constantly kept on edge, an experience made suspenseful by the little pieces of information kept from you by the game.
While this game was greatly enjoyable for me for the time i played it, it does not come without its flaws. RO2's bots barely funciton. The AI bots are almost blind, and will walk past and into the opposition without firing, and when they do it appears more to be in their general direction than an accurate shot. They're incredibly indecisive and will keep jumping through the same window and into the same trench repeatedly. If an AI is close enough he will quickly become a master swordsman, attempting to behead you with a katana or stick you with a bayonet like a pig; but, this can all be countered by walking backwards where he will infinitely chase you, most likely never firing.
In this game I've seen a machinegunner set up a gun with their backs to the enemy. I've seen them set up on a cabinet, I've seen them set up in their own trench facing away from gunfire. The soldiers have ran in infinite circles where they're unable to navigate a corner or a hallway of a buulding; infinitely retracing their own steps. I've seen allied and enemy tanks aline drive in a figure of eight indefinetly, or stop in front of me and never fire. This lack of the Artifical intelligence's intelligence makes the single player gamemode completely worthless, as it's a carbon copy of the multiplayer with a few slideshows of historical background inbetween.
RO2 is what it is. It’s a realistic World War 2 shooter that does what it does well. It’s a suspenseful and at times terrifying shooter with a unique twist to it. The game immerses you and doesn’t take you out for a while. It caused me to feel sadness upon watching a comrade of mine drop to the ground, and genuine fear when being aimed upon behind flimsy cover by a mounted gun in an apartment building.
I enjoyed this game greatly, and as such will give it an 7/10. It’s a fast paced and enjoyable game but nevertheless there are bugs and flaws that lower the rating.

Evolve is a game that I never really paid attention to before release.  I heard occasional muttering about DLC practices, something about being made by the Left 4 Dead studio, and a gameplay mode focused on asymmetrical gameplay, with 4 people playing as human hunters hunting one player playing as a monster.  It sounded ok in concept, but nothing too exciting.
A week ago, the game officially released.  I watched a few videos...and knew that I needed to play this game.
After playing it 50 hours over the past week, I cannot understate how much I enjoyed this game.  I played a lot of Left 4 Dead in the past, both against AI and in Versus, and Evolve is just a huge step forward of that.  The gameplay is balanced and incredibly tight, with both hunters and monster feeling they have to use good strategy and tactics every moment of a match in order to get the advantage.  Each of the 12 hunters plays in a unique fashion, which is already enjoyable and fun to experiment with, but seeing them all come together into cohesive 4 man teams? Feels like a dream. Similarly, playing as a solo monster trying to outsmart the 4 man teams feels exhilirating, always watching for those moments when a hunter makes a fatal misstep, creating an opening to start tearing into their team with tooth and claw, fiery breath and lightning bolts.
The negative aspects of DLC practices in this game are fairly exaggerated.  For all of the negative outcry about the DLC, the only actual game-content DLC to purchase costs at most $40, and that's without it going on sale, which it likely will in the near future. Other than that game-content DLC, the game only has cosmetic character skin DLC, which is barely noticeable in game and not worth spending money on or worth discussing. When they do release future content, you will never be stopped from playing with your friends if they bought DLC and you didn't.  The game is built to let people build any group they want and play together, no matter who has bought DLC or not.

What Evolve lacks in single player content, it makes up for in an incredibly well crafted multiplayer game that is a huge step ahead of every other game like it. If you're a fan of team-based FPS combat with a unique twist, I can't recommend this game strongly enough.

Coming into the game primarily because of the Murakami inspiration, the atmosphere and aesthetics of Memoranda won me over. I'm not the biggest point-and-click fan, having only played a handful of the classics, but the puzzles were largely reasonable (though the hints, which may have been added in an update [?] are a welcome addition in some cases) if not always feeling connected to the story or anything. The ones I found confusing mostly made more sense in hindsigh, which is more than can be said for some of those classics I've played. I did spend a little time thrashing about, trying fruitlessly to combine objects in the inventory with each other and the environment, but that was almost always resolved by taking a break and coming back to the game later.
The English script and voice work (can't speak for any other/future languages) is a little stilted and awkward, but I found the characters endearing overall. Like in a lot of Murakami's work, everything and everyone feels just at arm's length and a little out of focus; whether intentionally or not, I felt like it fits the jigsaw puzzle of a story. The music and art are lovely, giving it an off-kilter storybook feel, and I'd definitely be interested in more games with this art style. I don't often replay games, but this is short and pleasant enough that it might be nice to return to after some details of the story and puzzles fade, just to soak up the atmosphere.
My overall impression: this is a thoughful game, and feels to me like it was made with a lot of care and passion. I only found Memoranda well after release, but would've been happy to have been a Kickstarter backer and received this game in return.

BioShock is one of those classic games that people are going to be playing like 20 years from now. In my opinion it's one of the best shooter games that has ever been made, and hell, it might be my favorite. And right now is a good time to pick it up, something I'll touch on in a second.
In a genre that has become stagnant on generic military men shooting generic foreigners, BioShock stands tall as an FPS that isn't afraid to explore more mature themes. And by mature, I mean less 'nudity' and more 'philosophy and♥♥♥♥♥♥. The voice acting feels superb, the environment is unforgettable, the game can look and sound gorgeous even years after it's release and the first few hours of this game scare the hell out of me.
However, it's not without it's flaws. There's a bit of an RPG side to this game, but it's basic and uninteresting. The combat becomes easy after a point. Once the combat becomes easy, the game ceases to be scary. Especially as you come to realize that those respawn tanks scattered around will revive you infinitely at no cost. Unless you turn those off (which is thankfully an option), you will eventually lose any sense of fear you might have had.
The game's also got a morality system. I won't spoil the details, but suffice to say this game is the poster boy for why moral choice systems in games are garbage. You have the choice to be either an unreasonable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or Jesus Christ reincarnate, not much middle ground, and all you get for not being good is a terrible ending. It feels hacked in and unnecessary, and just stupid. It really makes you wish more games had Walking Dead style morality where you can actually debate things and the right choice isn't always clear. Y'know, like how real life is.
Aside from that, there's not much to complain about. The game holds up pretty well and is very fun to play. There are some stressmarks like how human characters don't look so good and the game relies on tapes rather than living characters for exposition, but it makes it work well enough.
If you haven't played it yet, do so! Now's a great time, like I said, because the game has this issue, right, where all the animations are in choppy 30 fps no matter what your framerate is. Well, someone's released a mod to fix that! Google the BioShock Physics Unlocker.

Actual review after 30 hours in (Not just complaining about DLC)
Evolve is an online PvP 4v1 Shooter (You can play solo with AI but it takes away from the fun of the game.) Four hunters (depending on the game type)  must either hunt and kill a monster, destroy the monsters eggs, rescue survivors or defend a refueling ship.  Each mode requires different tactics for successful completion.  Weather playing as the hunter or the monster different classes (or monsters) can be used to give you more of an edge for the game mode you are currently playing.

There are a few bugs with the game, the most annoying one in my opinion is sometimes the mouse cursor doesn't go away and can be distracting during a match.  I hope this will be fixed in an upcoming patch.  It's not game breaking, but it is annoying.

I haven't noticed many balancing issues, all hunters have their strong and weak points and the same goes for the monster.  The Kraken is a little over powered and seems to have a great advantage in any game mode.  But the more me and my friends play the better we get at facing it by changing the hunters we use to better suit the fight.  The rescue game mode gives favor to the monster because the AI controlled objectives are not very bright and are easy to kill.  We tend to stay away from this mode trying it every now and then as we get better at our respective classes.  In the game mode where you must destroy the monsters eggs the monster can hatch one egg at a time and gain a minion.  The minion isn't very difficult but it will focus the healer and (for the most part) ignore everyone else until the healer is dead.

Coordination is key to Evolve, communicating with your fellow hunters makes all the difference in any game mode.  You can use the in game voice chat or the ping system to communicate with each other. And by coordinating your class abilities you really gain an edge over the monster.  If you just worry about yourself, this is not a game for you.

Explanation of game modes:

1) Hunt:  In hunt you'll find yourself facing off against a single monster, you'll have to track it down, trap it and kill it before it can destroy the generator when it reaches stage 3.  At first it took several minutes to find the monster but not the entire match usually lasts 5 to 7 minutes  facing off against the monster (or hunters) several times before either winning or losing the match.

2) Nest: In nest you must destroy the monsters eggs before the time expires (or the monster kills the hunters).  The monster can hatch one egg at a time and gain a minion, there can only be one minion active at a time.  The game mode usually lasts about 4 to 5 minutes and many different tactics can be use to achieve victory.

3) Rescue: In rescue the hunters must revive and get 5 survivors to the escape pods.  The survivors spawn separately.  There are fist 2 to rescue, after they are saved there are 2 more and the there are 5.  The monster has a great advantage in this mode, the survivors AI isn't the greatest and they are easy to kill.

4) Defend:  Defend is the last game mode in Evacuation.  In defend you must defend 3 objectives from a wave of monsters.  You defend them one at a time moving to the next one after the current one is destroyed.  The monsters has AI controlled minions that for the most part damage the objective and ignore everything else (until they are almost dead, then they will attack the hunters or the turrets that the hunters have to help them). If the monster is killed or time expires the hunters win.

There are a few different ways to play. Evacuation is a 5 day game mode that starts with hunt and ends with defend.  In between the 4 hunters and the one monster get to vote of the next map. After hunt you get a choice between Nest and Rescue and depending on what you pick it will either be Rescue or Hunt or Nest and Hunt for the next day and then Rescue and Nest for day 4.  Depending on who wins each day a buff is rewarded to help in the next map.  Sometimes the buff is useless in the next game mode chosen and sometimes it is very beneficial.  This can be played Solo, Co-Op or PvP.

Skirmish is a one match random game mode. Again it can be played Solo, Co-Op or PvP.

You can also set up custom matches with friends or solo choosing the game mode (Evacuation, Skirmish, or a specific game type) You can set up unique rules giving favor to either the hunters or monster.

I have no complaints about the DLC as I don't plan to buy any skins but the game needs to make money to maintain the servers, bring out additional content and fix bugs. I may buy hunter/monster DLC's in the future if the hunter/monster looks interesting and fun to play.  All future game modes and maps will be free which I like.  Usually DLC upsets me when games release truly additional content on day one that you pretty much have to buy to fully enjoy the game (eg. extra game chapters, maps and modes, etc)

DLC is common practice these days, everyone does it, most of them do it wrong.  If people stop buying it companies will stop doing it, but that will never happen.  In order to fully enjoy evolve with my friends I need only spend 60$, I miss out on nothing except having a different color monster or gun (not important, I don't look at that stuff anyway, to busy concentrating on the game)

Overall I really enjoy the game and enjoy playing with my friends.  Win or lose we all have a great time.  Every now and then I play with random people, but it is defiantly more enjoyable playing with people you know.

A lot of great ideas put together into a game with a fundamentally bad structure. You run around islands collecting fragments and then lugging them back to the center. That's your objective. This means that you'll be going through the same areas over and over as you run back and forth like a courier to the centermost section of the center island. This is tedious, needlessly time-consuming, and not very fun.
There is a reason stealth action games have not historically been open world/sandbox games. When you have all the space you need to navigate, you can just avoid most dangers by taking a wide route around them. There is no tension 90% of the time you are playing. It's just running, running, and more running. The amount of time you spend not playing the game and instead running and searching from place to place is absurd. It's seriously as bad as an MMO.
There are plenty of other small issues: Houses and buildings don't actually exist, they're just gigantic loot crates where you can click on the door to search them. There are huge inconsistencies in what qualifies as grass you can hide in and grass that's just there for show. AI is not any more intelligent than in other games, even though the developers brag about it in the description.
Fortunately, most of these issues can be fixed post-release, if the devs pay mind to them. Change the objective of the game in some way so that we aren't running back and forth, make the entire world WAY more dense with both loot and enemies (so that players are never just mindlessly sprinting across an entire island), and add more stealth elements to the game than just hiding in grass or behind a building every now and then.

Evolve is a multiplayer focused FPS.
The game pits 4 hunters against 1 monster. In the base game, there is a total of 12 hunters and 3 monsters available to choose from. The game offers no customisation aside from a selection of skins, of which only 1 per hunter/monster are not DLC. The progression system is purely linear and makes for a very unbalanced experience. Hunters/monsters work in tiers, where the next hunter/monster is better than the last, and only the same level of hunter/monster can have a good chance against other hunters/monsters. For example, four tier 1 hunters will find it near-impossible to take down the tier 3 monster, and vice-versa.
As well as balancing issues, the game is plagued with people of varying skill so it's always a game of chance as to whether or not your team will actually work as a team.
The game offers very little replayability due to the sheer lack of proper progression and customisation, and the lack of content, most of which is cut to be sold as DLC.
Speaking of DLC, this game is chock-a-block full of it. The game itself costs $60. From launch, 12 items of DLC are available to purchase, one of which is a season pass that includes none of the other content available to purchase. You can buy skin packs which offer 1 new skin for each 3 hunters in a class, that's 3 skins in total, for the low low price of $6. Or, you can buy one skin for each of the 3 monsters at the low low price of $10. The season pass itself is $25-30 depending on your region, and includes 4 new hunters (when they release). New monsters will also be available to buy for the grand total of $15-20.
You'd think for all the money they're charging, they'd at least release a game relatively bug-free and well polished. But no, that sadly is not the case. The game still has issues that were around in both alpha and beta. On top of this, the graphics are console quality, and the few CGI cutscenes are so badly compressed, my toaster could render a higher quality image.
The game is a total rip-off, and that itself is enough for me to not recommend this game. However, DLC♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥aside, the game's lack of serious progression and replayability is once again not enough for me to recommend a purchase. Maybe a year from now when the complete pack is $15-20, then you should pick it up. However at that point the game will be dead MP wise, and as SP isn't even worth mentioning, what's the point?

I was in the kickstarter for this, and completely missed that it already released in January.
This is a slow, calm, contemplative little point & click adventure game, with a wonderful, dreamlike, surreal atmosphere, surrounding a number of little short narratives our main character comes across during her attempts to recover her name. Some of them are more succesful than others, but they are all interesting and enjoyable. There's a fair bit of humour, but the game isn't out to make you laugh, but rather smile wistfully.
The puzzles have an in-game logic that makes sense once you've figured them out, but before that, because of the non-linear order you may solve some of them, you will end up in situations where you have no idea what to do next. If you find those moments incredibly frustrating in old-school adventure games, then consider this a fair warning. The developers have mercifully added a hotspot reveal button, and some of the bigger puzzles screens have multi-stage hints that you can use if you need. Even then you will occasionally get stuck, and will backtrack through screens trying to find what you've missed.
I very much enjoyed my time with the characters, and greatly appreciate the tone and the introspective nature of the little journey you take. The visual style is gorgeous and the superb soundtrack greatly adds to the atmosphere. It all feels like you're going on a little walk through a poem, while someone plays jazz vinyls on an old gramophone.
8/10
