Cool concept for a game. Basically you control a succession of reigning monarchs and make binary decisions which guide your kingdom. The decisions you make effect your kingdom in a number of ways improving or worsening the situation of 4 competing interests: the church, the people, the army and the treasury--if any get too strong or too weak you die, and are replaced by the next king.
Throughout the game there are multiple story lines which develop and a bigger conflict which pervades the whole succession of monarchs. It tells an interesting story and is just plain fun to play, and also makes you think about how difficult it would be to actually rule as a king.
Music and graphics work well with the game and provide a nice backdrop to the game. As you continue to play the game some aspects can get repetative, but it is also interesting to try to figure out all the different things you can do (including the inumerous ways to die).
I will mentiont that there was a glitch which would sometimes hang up the game for a second, but it didn't interefere too much, and never prevented me from playing after just a moment.
At $3 the price is very fair for this type of game, and if it is on sale I highly recommend. This game will probably keep you interested for about 3 hours or so, and if you are a completionist certainly much longer.
I give this game 8/10, and recommend it.

As hauntingly beautiful as it is disturbing, Bioshock is the spiritual successor to System Shock only this time you are underwater in a dystopian “Me-first” society somewhere along the lines of Atlas Shrugged. The first thing anyone will notice and admire about this game is how it just oozes style and detail in every crack and crevice of this underwater hellhole, along with the bizarre and fascinating characters and enemies one will encounter. The gameplay is a perfect mix of weapons and powers with the weapons consisting of pistols, machine guns, shotguns, grenade launchers, flame throwers and wrenches. While the powers consist of shooting fire, lightning, wind, BEES and ice along with buffers and telekinesis. The gameplay is just as creative as this unique world. The only drawback to the game would be the “Hacking” which is so bland and stale compared to the rest of this fantastic game along with a plethora of fetch quests spread all over a middle act that tends to drag story wise, but otherwise it is a sensational game that everyone should give a try.

Nice, relaxing game to play on mute while you're listening to an audio book or something. For each color in the level, you have to make a path connecting two marked blocks. Each colored block can only be visited in the path of that color, neutral blocks have to be visited a certain number of times, and paths can only cross at those neutral blocks. That's it. Pretty simple.
Most levels are extremely easy (5 seconds), but many take a bit longer, and a few are pretty hard, in which case you're trying things for 10 minutes.
There are 26 sets (A-Z) of 25 levels each, and up to 3 randomly generated sets every day, varying in difficulty. Solving sets unlocks themes and gets you closer to the magical "999 points" that the menu encourages you to reach. Because of the sheer volume it's a good time killer.

This is one of those "hidden gems" of a game that holds up VERY WELL for its age even though it is over 10 years old.
This game is just not that well known, but it should have been.
There is no reason why this game should not have been made into a sequel (notice I said SEQUEL, not REMADE or "upgraded" to HD because it already natively compatible and rarity for that period).
There is a reason is it a cult classic on Good Old Games and among certain players on the internet.
Think of of Sims+Ghosts+Strategy, rolled all together in a concise manner.
You essentially control a team of ghosts and apparitions of your choosing (or earned) to scare the living daylights out of humans.
However, many missions although not linear in HOW YOU DO IT have specific objectives and even time limits.
One of the best parts is the parodies and mission backgrounds it uses from movie franchises such as Evil Dead, Ghostbusters, Poltergeist, and quite a few others.
I think most older players will recognize the movie tie ins.
Not sure how they got away with some of the similarities back then based on copyright infringement "gray areas", but it was a good choice for humor.
Graphics are very acceptable for this period, and look very good at Ultra HD resolutions.
You can easily modify the game to crank it up well above 1080p.
Soundtrack is solid, fun, and upbeat, and game narration is well done.
The only really negative sides are the somewhat archaic camera system that can make it a bit difficult to see what you want to see (although the camera is never "fixed"), overlay complicated UI, dificulty in understanding WHAT specific ghosts skills REALLY DO, synergy BETWEEN ghosts needed, and cryptic nature of how to complete some of the puzzles.  Sometimes you need VERY SPECIFIC ghosts to perform tasks, other times your creativity is the limit.
You will need to "upgrade" your ghosts with plasm to be able to maximize their performance in game and multitask.
This is just one of those game for its price you should give a crack at in terms of time, especially for $5.00.
It is likely that even after you complete the ENTIRE game (it is fairly lengthy), you will probably go back again and see if you can do a better job a second time.
If you do not mind a challenge, and have a good solid strategy head on your shoulder you should have no problems.
You will get a good laugh at the same time and its worth the entertainment.

This is already, without a doubt, the best survival game I have ever played. It takes so many elements from the countless other survival games out there and puts them into one fantastic experience. Everything works seamlessly well together and I am kept busy the entire time. Things like the log sleds, tree houses, and just small things like actually chopping trees down are great ideas that are definitely missing in other survival titles.
Along with all of that, the graphics are a 10/10. Beautiful game.
But the other great thing about this game is that it is not just a survival game. The developers went beyond that and added a horror aspect to it all with the cannibal mutants. Not many games actually scare me, but this one does a nice job of creeping me out when it turns nighttime. The uncertainty of where the cannibals are at and hearing them scream in the distance makes for a thrilling experience. And somehow it gets even better, because there is a story to this game, and a good story at that.
This game keeps me interested, it keeps me engaged, and most of all it makes me want to come back for more. I highly recommend this game (play it with friends if you can) , especially for it being on sale for 10 dollars.

This is one of those low-price gems that gets overlooked and underplayed because of the understated appeal or oldschool graphics. Its developer, Sick Puppies, went under shortly after publishing and the game was met with poor sales and coverage and an awful console port put the final nail in the coffin until it was released on Steam years later.
It's a great little game and still unique to this day. You tactically chose, place and manage a variety of your ghouls to interact with the environment in a home or building, often using the history of the building to your advantage. It's whacky, but has a surprising depth of writing and even your ghouls and residents have a line or two of character or backstory.
Figuring out different approaches to solving the level is great fun and very satisfying.
* Friendly tone and humour, all the characters, good and evil, have stats and personality information delivered in a fun way
* Can be casual fun or quite deep strategic planning based on your gameplay preferences
* Many different ways to reach level completions
* Ridiculously cheap
* Overly complex User Interface and controls
* Some AI problems
* Fairly dated
Priced at just £2.99/4.99€/$4.99 and clocking in at 15 hours+ gametime, it's already worth its asking price, despite being dated. It's cheapest on Steam and the Steam version includes the most up to date/complete package (including an extra level). It's also available on GMG, IndieGala, GMG, GOG, etc at a higher price. It regularly goes for up to -90% during Steam Sales.
* There's a Fan-made project already on Greenlight for a Ghost Master 2 for those who might be interested, it includes a free demo

Arms Race - The Cold War Era is pretty promising with the way game mechanics work and the AI is good. The recommended strategy in the guide section doesn't work reliably for me and I ended up using a different strategy. The AI is also pretty good at adapting to what you are doing. The limited 3 budget changes ends up meaning every decision has long term implications.
Most games turn out slightly differently due to the AI choosing different tactics and the randomness of global crisis events.
The game isn't as full fleshed as say Hearts of Iron but I feel like the mechanics are well thought out and the AI provides a challenge even on easy. It does a good job of abtracting the cold war and reducing decisions to the macro level ('meaningful decisions') compared to HoI3/4 which features considerable micromanagement. I personally prefer macro level games (less micromanagement) but it's not everyone's cup of tea. If you prefer to play M&T in EU4 vs base EU4 or if you prefer to play Darkest Hour/HoI2 vs HoI4 then this is the game for you.
In terms of improvements I think some additional work on fleshing out global crisis (ex instead of random have triggers) as well as UI work would be helpful. There's quite a bit of promise with what exists in the game.
Make sure to read the manual and watch the online tutorials since there isn't an in game tutorial or tooltips. The UI Does take a while to get used to. Also I HIGHLY RECOMMEND playing in TURN BASED OR on SLOW so you have plenty of time to consider strategic decisions without needing to 'button mash' as mentioned in some other reviews.
One warning is to not expect replayability on the level of Paradox Games since this is made by a small indie. I would say expect ~10-15 hours out of the game if you want to try all the possibilities.
I wish the development team the best of luck as the Hearts of Iron series has gone in the direction of too much micromanagement and I would like to see a competitor that is more in the vein of Ho2.

Frustrating puzzles. Shaky jump controls. Platforming that often requires perfect timing. Dark lighting that is more often a hindrance than a mood-setter. And if you want to check it out as an artsy game? Don't bother. There's so little story, the title tells you more about what's going on than the events within the game.

I'm afraid i can't in the least bit recommend this game. I so wanted to love it, and it seriously looked amazing on the trailers.
It had such promise, and it manages to cash in pretty much none of that. There's no feeling of bullet hell of any sort, outside of the gun you're firing when it's actually powered up. You don't need to even concider dodging bullets or beams, because the game's bosses, titans, are actually extremely brittle, and it's trivial to shoot out their weapons in an instant, leaving them as little more than static pieces of scenery.
The only threat in the game comes from the seemingly infinitely spawning random little drone enemies, as well as an indescribably silly decision to put in a time limit.
The game looks great, the bosses look great, so much so, that i'm very sure 80% of the development time went for polishing the graphic quality, at the cost of such small, to them, seemingly less important concepts like gameplay, entertainment, or challenge. The intro song to the game is actually far more entertaining than the game itself, and i think whoever wrote that has a great career ahead of them.
It tells a great deal, that after 15 levels during the writing of this, the leaderboards have only 10 entries, where in the beginning, there were hundreds. The vast majority of people grew bored of the game in less than an hour. With that being said, i can't understand why there are so many positive reviews of it... One citing especially how it has improved over time. I would not have wanted to see the earlier revisions, then.
The creation of your own arena and boss would be an extremely interesting thing, and it was the main draw in the game for me... sadly, however, there's little to no enjoyment in the game, so there's little to no point in taking the effort of creating anything for it.
On a personal note, the vast majority of the game's in-level music is also awful, but it is easy to turn it off. I shouldn't need to do that, however. The music in the trailers are, outside of the theme song, the sole good tracks in the game. The rest are the worst of the worst kind of dubstep.
PS. I think the game would be far, far, far more interesting, if the health pools of the bosses were 10x the value of all parts combined, and you could not shoot off parts. The decision not to do a unified health system, but allow the players to completely make the bosses harmless baffles me to no end.

This is a game that deals with the art of balancing. Balancing the budget, the need to compete in space, the need for armed forces, the need for better weapons and so on.
Each year you can place three "pips" in various fields (or all in one), and there quite a few places to put those "pips". Do you boost national economy, increase spy gain, increase diplomat gain, increase research in one of three military field, boost funding in one of the two space race fields or increase troop gain? Go too agressive in one field and you are bound to fall behind in others. As said, a balancing art.
I can not put the finger on one specific thing that makes me like the game, instead it is the mix of it all, to me it feels like I am constantly putting out real/imagined/potential fires all over the world, while trying to get the upper hand of my opponent.
PRO:
-several ways to win
-each faction has 4 leaders, each of those 4 leaders have 1 fixed stat and 1 customizable
-fun and interesting
-alot of historical information (lots of info about the space race project and about various weapon platforms)
-flipping nations by civil war or diplomacy
-quite decent AI (atleast seems so to me)
CONS:
-manual. I needed a game to figure out some of the stuff, and asked a few questions on the discussion board before I could really enjoy the game properly. This has been agreed upon by the devs who said an improved manual is something they will do in a patch.
-not everything is intuitive, so as mentioned, I needed a game where I simply pressed the various buttons to see what happend.
Instead of a thumb up/down, how do you rate it?
I would say this is around 82% for me, but please note that I am a history geek, so this might influence my rating somewhat.

Each time you play, the levels give you a different style of gameplay, so it keeps the challenge bar set pretty high, especially set on the right difficulty for your experience in shooters. Having played many of the survival games available on Steam and elsewhere, I became upset at the state of things. Most were either too gamelike, too stylized, or hardly even survival-focused.
The Long Dark was exactly what I was looking for - a good balance of realism and fun, no trendy environmental threats, a survival-atmoshpere. My first few attempts ended with freezing to death or starving. Then I ran across wild animals that were not particularly hospitable. Then froze to death again because I got caught in a blizzard with insufficient clothing, no firewood, too much weight in my inventory and no clue about where I was due to poor visibility.
If you are looking for an honest survival game that does not hold your hand, does not throw unreasonable threats at you, and actual aims to provide an enjoyable and authentic survival experience, this is likely the game you were looking for.

Disclaimer: I was given my copy of this game by the developer(s?) for a review I wrote of their prior title. I enjoy their work. That said, this took me a few tries to finish.
At its core, this is a narrative-focused title. You've got two storylines running in parallel, that of your player character, and that of the people "playing" the game in real life. It's decidedly designed to bring up the era of pirate game design, where things are glitchy, frustrating, and sometimes literally painful to play. This is not a game I would call "fun". The final stage actually gave me a splitting headache but I refused to stop because there is no save function (the game can be beaten in about a half-hour or so, it makes sense).
Like their prior title (NPPD Rush), this game received a post-launch patch adding new content and cleaning up some gripes people had with it. I played this after the Director's Cut patch, and so I already know some of the things on the store page/from my launch week failed attempt to beat the game were changed. Mostly it's for the better, although from the sound of it, the final painful stage was also one of these additions.
Despite the criticism above, I'm still glad I played through this, as it's basically what you'd get by mixing a fever dream with WarioWare like "microgames", since each stage is short from start to finish. It's just on stages 2/4 you will probably die. A lot. It's a surreal narrative that's more focused on introducing some concepts that are slightly based upon interpretations of actual texts, rather than just being 1:1 translations. (Seriously. Google some of this. If you want a more coherent take on some of the same material, go find the console-only title El Shaddai: Ascension of the Metatron.)
A tip from me to you: on stage one, blow up a few asteroids and then immediately beeline to the corner of the map to stay still after your Faith begins rising. You will complete the stage with a little patience and minimum harassment.

I finally got Echo of Soul to work and wasn't too impressed. I only played one class up to level 9 to at least give it a chance, but it didn't hold out.
Playing to Game
In order to actually play this game, I downloaded it through Steam, only to have to download it again from the game's actual website. After transfering some files, the game could be played through Steam. If you're interested in checking this game out for yourself, a walkthrough on how to play it through Steam can be found at the following link. Just click on "Getting EoS to work through Steam" on the right hand side.
Character "Creation"
First, is the classes. I'm not overly fond of classes after some of the other mmo's I've played where you can use any (or most) of the skills, equipment, etc. If you don't care whether a game has classes or not, then go ahead and disregard this one, it's just a personal thing for me.
Second, classes are gender locked. Every warrior is a big, muscular dude with a big sword. Every rouge is a lithe dude who looks like a kid. Every mage is a little girl. You can customize their hair, eyes, face, the colors, and some sizes, and that's all free (at least at creation. I don't know if you can change it later or not). To me, this is picking a character to play and customizing their appearance a little.
Quests
To be completely honest, I skipped over the dialouge portion of the quests, so I don't have any story other than cutscenes and bosses. I found the quests to be lackluster. Even the MMO's I do like have some of this, but the quests seemed to be sending me to talk to someone, kill some monster, or get something. In addition, each quest was only one task long. While this does get you to the reward faster, it's not as challenging and, in my opinion, is just too simple. I faced, and defeated, two bosses before I was level 8, and that was solo. (that could possibly be a balancing issue, or it could just be simplicity itself).
New, better equipment for your class is also given away as quest rewards. While this is useful in saving money and not having to bother with shops (I didn't even look at those), it further simplifies the game. If you ever have to use a shop, it'd probably be to sell things and clean out your inventory. Everything you need is given to you when you need it.
Skills
Again, I only played one class, and not for very long, so I don't have all of the details on this. What I did notice is that your skills are automatically learned and hotkeyed as you level. This does remove the hassle of picking out skills each level, but it also removes the ability to customize your class and play the way you like. Then again, you could just not use the skills you don't care for, but why have them anyway? I'm fine with getting preset skills in other RPG's, but I prefer to customize my MMO characters, whether it's their appearance, gender, or skills.
Cash Shop
Many free to play mmo's have this, so I'm not going to complain about it too much. They do have to make money somehow. However, there is at least one quest, albeit optional, where you are to buy something from the cash shop. You are able to abandon the quest, but there'll always be a marker in the second town for a quest you haven't done, because you haven't paid for it.
Graphics

A concept game at its heart, Superhot is unique in the “me-too” first person shooter space and provides a compelling if unfulfilling gameplay experience that doesn’t outstay its brief welcome.
The concept was initially born from a game jam, and later, from a browser demo that was popular enough to create crowdfunding demand. I remember playing that browser demo that journalists raved about and enjoyed the simple concept. It was the perfect lunch hour gaming fix. So imagine my surprise to see it become a full release title, as the initial unique hook, as fun as it was, didn’t feel like it could sustain a full game.
However, the Superhot team have created a slick and entertaining game that has some smart ideas and shows a lot of restraint. The initial hook of having time only move when the player does is elevated by a minimal but no less thought-provoking plot.
With the main gameplay concept out of the way, you are left with a minimalist world, with the meta being you are sent a cracked version of this very game, which then begins to push you from being an observer to participant. I won’t spoil the story, as nominal it is, but it treads on the well written ground of cyberpunk, corporate control and espionage. The saving grace is the fetching and very disconcerting interface and UI, which administers a constant perception of paranoia and anxiety.
Determining the perfect line of attack, as you need to kill the enemies in order to proceed is the order of the day then, with Superhot providing an arresting puzzle in how you position yourself, when to shoot and when to dodge. The first few levels quickly get you acclimated and the game barely pushes you further, as you will know all you need to in the first five minutes.
The levels are short, and the enemies spawn and act always in a certain way, allowing you to pinpoint your moves and learn from your mistakes. It almost feels perfectly set up for speed-runners, and once completed, challenges are available which time your prowess, yet this rings hollow.
Since a single bullet or punch is enough to kill you, you will die a lot in your first playthrough. However, seeing the levels are short and getting the right pattern is so satisfying, this is rarely an issue. There is very little complexity and the game isn’t to frustrating.
When the credits rolled on Superhot I was mostly impressed with the restrained discipline the developers had for this singular idea. That they managed to stretch a game out of it is a remarkable feat and one that should be applauded. It lacks bloat and its concise nature wraps up the story and the gameplay hook before they become boring.
It’s one –note gameplay may support the style over substance argument, but that isn’t completely the case here. It blends the two seemingly, providing a cohesive package that is a fun short burst of creativity. Recommended.

Its challenging and interesting. With game elements such as Tower Defense and Turn-Based/Real-Time components, the current alpha will take some thinking to get through, even if it is only a few levels.
The goal of the game is to explore the "Dungeon" to find the exit point. The exit point isnt for your characters, but rather an Artifact that you must protect and transport. The Artifact isnt solely for the Capture the Flag purpose, it must be defended whilst you are exploring the dungeon, since all damage done is taken out of an important resource that can only be gained through exploring, killing enemies and selling items (from what I have discovered).
By Turn-Based, we can classify the turns as the opening of a new room. You build up your defenses and manage resources/heroes in real time, with no chance of being attacked. As soon as a door is opened, there is a chance of gaining loot, meeting a character, or initiating a wave of aliens. The aliens may not only come from that room, but other rooms that you have opened that have no line of sight. So by using the free time, you prepare your defenses for the eventuality that the aliens come. You move your characters in Real Time and can build structures during alien waves (albeit at a slower rate) to defend.
When you are completing the goal of transporting the diamond to the end point, it triggers an All or Nothing alien swarm spawn, with large, endless waves of aliens preventing you from completing the final goal. Yes, you may get the diamond to the end, but can all your heroes survive? Their deaths will carry on to the next level, and you need all hands on deck. Did you use too many resources levelling up/healing or building structures? The leftovers also carry over to your next game.
The graphics are not really an issue. There is a factor of fun I really enjoy. I am not sure if multiplayer could be incorporated into this game, uunless it is a coop - pvp fight against the aliens, cooperating or fighting to get the artifact to the exit first. Many hopes for this game that it turns out as well as i had fun playing it.

Dungeon of the Endless is a rougelite spin off of the 4X stratgey series Endless Space, A lot of people on seeing Dungeon of the Endless (here on called DotE) may compare it to The Sword of The Stars spin off The Pit (If you haven't already I implore you to check out The Pit as well!) but besides being spinoffs of 4X series they are very diffrent games, where as The Pitt was a rougelike purists dream DotE is a rouglelite mixed with tower defense and RPG team managment. Although the game is in a very raw early acssess state one can see where the dev team is heading, in the TowerD part of the game you power up a limited number of rooms in the dungeon making paths to rooms that could modules to assist you in clearing the dungeon. After the room is powered you set up in the room an array of turrets and relays that will buff your party in combat against enemies that will come from new rooms and waves that may spawn from unpowred rooms, and if the room contains a slot for it you may place a module that will collect resources for you to use (the end game plans to have 3 but only two are currently avalible). The resources are used to build, trade with merchants, power rooms, or to hire and upgrade heroes, the third as of yet unimplamented resource will allow you to research a tech tree and upgrade buildings. The combat side of the game is a party based RPG where you move your party in real time either using them to explore or boost modual output. You can pause the game at anytime so as to give you time carefully layout plans as things can get quite tense as your heroes are not super powered space marines (at least not at the start) and will be mobbed and killied quickly if not managed properly. Overall in its raw form DotE is a fun experiance brining new ideas to both rouglites and tower defense and I'm egarly awaiting to see what the the devs will breakout in the future.

60 hours of play so far, and this game still succeeds at failing to present a recurring tactical scenario. In Left 4 dead 2, you know the Tank is going to appear at certain points during a campaign, you're always "Survivor" and you will always have one of a small set of weapons/healing items which minimally impact the environment.... Evolve is never quite like that.

The monster might have skilled up a different skillset and chosen different perks than you anticipated

You might drop the trap dome with some advantageous high ground
You might drop the trap dome giving the monster a cave to hide in
You might drop the trap dome with hostile wildlife that wants to fight you

It might start snowing

Project Zomboid is basically the epidome of a top down 3D zombie survival game. With little help and little direction you literally are thrown into an open world to do as you please. Character customization is fairly indepth which is impressive considering I was not expecting it because you do not get to customize a character in the demo. You can select an occupation which gives certain strengths (selecting a doctor improves your healing stats, the fitness instructor impoves your stamina, etc.), and you can even select what color you want your shirt/pants to be, as well as your hairstyle. The game itself as said is an open immersive world and you find buildings, houses, food markets, and other places in which you can loot items and even set up a base by barricading windows and such and spend the night. I'm not gonna lie the game is somewhat challenging because they don't really tell you how to do stuff, and there are no objectives/quests (for now) so you will often find yourself wandering around not really knowing what to do with yourself. You have to figure out how to do things on your own such as building stuff, farming, fishing, etc. The game is still early access so there is hope for many more features. If any of this sounds appealing to you, you will probably like the game and get plenty of hours of enjoyment out of it and then some. I'd give it an 8/10 right now!

I've seen a lot of review and I find most of them to be quite vague, so here's my own attempt at explaining what the "game" is about.
It's a series of thoughts and reflexions about something. Basically, it's kind of as if you took a philosophical question and made a narrative game about it. The author could've taken "What if robots could be human? What if they were able to have feelings? etc." and he would've ended up with a similar game.
Except here the question and thoughts aren't about what I just presented as an example. I'll let you discover what the game wants to think about and show you.
In a bit more detail, mainly based on my own experience, the thoughts that the game raises aren't particularly original or unique or revolutionary or whatever. I've had most of these thoughts myself and so I'd say that the ideas aren't on genius level.
Though I'll have to put in that the game develops and presents the thoughts really well. This is a pretty wishy-washy subjective thing and I can't really explain it, so I'll just say that the part about "what the game wants to show and how it does it" is really well done.
Also, some reviews mentioned that the game "is relevant if you're into game design", they're not wrong but any creative activity helps for that. I don't do game design, I just compose crappy music on a russian software that is built as if it had to fit in the 90s, but the thoughts still felt relevant. If you're a visual artist or whatever, the game's thoughts will probably concern you too.
In one sentence: The author asked himself questions on a nearly philosophical matter about something and then put his conclusions into this game.
I hope this helps for people who don't really know what they're looking at before buying the game. It's not perfect, it's not all that revolutionary either, and it's certainly not worth the full price, but just playing through it is worth it nonetheless.

I would like to start by saying I havn't tried the PvP side of the game and doubt i will, its just not my thing so I will leave that for people that play that way to comment on that side of things, so that said i will comment on the PVE side which is the way I play my main MMo's (WoW, FFXI, FFXIV and Rift).
I've found this nice fun, easy to play and learn, although im not through to end game content yet Im still questing through and leveling my mage I am finding it nicely paced and not too rushed. If you play other mmo's ou'll find the quests are of the usual variety collect X of this, kill Y of those monsters, one feature i do like and wish a few others would pick up and incorperate into thier games is that not only do the quests show on the mini map each quest has a little arrow and distance marker beside it showing where to go and how far it is, nice touch thanks, quest text is clear and easily readable and understandable and also conveys the game lore without it being bashed over your head with it.
The single player dungeons are also a nice touch aswell, it gives you  the chance run off do a dungeon without having to hang around either waiting for a group finder to get a group for you or you tring to PUG a group, the instances are not insainely difficault and can be done with quest dropped items and also give good rewards without spending ages to finish   there are some simple tactics to each boss which are easy to pick up and learn, and the usual rule applies "Dont stand in the Fire".
To the big question being as it is free to play is it pay to win?   As far as PVE goes not really, you can get boosts and safegaurds to your crafting and things of that fayre but most of the pay for items I've seen so far are vanaty Items and these can be perchased in game from merchants with gold and silver anyway.
Conclusion...
Would i recommend this game to other people? Yes, it makes an ideal starter MMo for people comming into the genre its not overly complicated and everything is explained for you, its not as "grindy" as some i could mention and has a nice pace to it. It does not have the cutting edge graphics that some of the latest MMo's have so can be played on an average  PC or Laptop which is no bad thing, not everyone can afford a top end gaming rig. TLDR: This game is fun for the first 10 hours and after you start to get better gear you start to realize that you have nothing left to do but ration food and sleep.
Story mode added nothing new except for the story, which was not special. The writing is cringy and as many people have said, the quests are very tedious fetch this fetch that. Not all bad however, hidden caches were cool and the new region was good, but no AI survivors added (which was heavily hinted at for years).
You may notice that I have 300 hrs in this game. Ive owned this since the first new region was added back, 3 years now. If you check my achievements for this game you will see I have never survived to 100 days. This is because the most fun in this game you can have is within the first 20 days of survival. After that there is nothing to do. I have often deleted saves when I had everything I needed to live for 100 days. But there was no fun to be had at that point. That and playing the game when a new region came out, or an update to content, amounts for the 300 hrs. Also I personally like games that feel realistic (even though this game is not realistic) and as a result I dumped a fair number of hrs into this game.
Developers do not intend to add any form of late game/goals to the sandbox. They frequently say they want it to be a goalless game. There is still nothing to do once you have all you need to survive.
They added challenge modes (mini missions, like get chased by a bear, or chase the bear), which is in the right direction frankly. However, what really needs to be added is something to the sandbox, so that its not all about finding loot and surviving for the longest period of time because that is boring and really is not fun.
Lastly, the developers have said that this is not a realistic game in response to negative reviews talking about aspects of the game being unrealistic. Its odd that their steam page description seems to describe a game about "true survival" fight against "mother nature". Its not realistic at all.
In this game:
Wolves and bears will attack you as soon as you get within about 50m. Wolves are the zombies of this game. No wolf packs.
The rifle bullets literally stop existing after they travel about 50-100m.  There is no bullet drop, bullet time, bullet effects.
Tools degrade extremely quickly
3 seconds in real life is 1 min in this game, however you walk at the same pace as real life though. You will also therefore become thirsty and hungry extremely quickly.
No alive people.
No jumping, climbing, vaulting.
Crafting is limited to a few things, bow, clothing items. Nothing special.
When cooking, you cannot move or do anything.
Overall. This game is not worth £27. More stuff will be added but don't wait on it. Get this game when its less than £10 for value for money and play it in 5 years when there is more to do.
Also this is not really important to the game as such. The devs get a little defensive over criticism of their game. Doesn't feel very professional to see them banning people on forums for voicing complaints.

Unlike a lot of "Early Access" games, v0.1.1 of Dungeon of The Endless feels like a relatively complete game.  It's stable and has a great mix of overall game mechanics that work well to produce a coherent game.
To try to describe this game in conventional terms might just confuse you.  Yes, it has aspects of roguelike games, real time strategy games, role playing games, tower defense games, and board games.  Personally, I think of it as mostly a board game with each "turn" divided into a time before you open another door, which will reveal treasure, a merchant, waves of enemies, blueprints, or something else - you never know!  Then it's a mad scramble reminiscent of a real time strategy/tower defensive hybrid to keep everything upright until the next turn.  When deciding who to level up or equip with gear, that's where the RPG aspect enters the picture.
This board-game like mechanic can be a good thing because it introduces a lot of interesting choices.  If I assign my hero here, will they be able to make it back to where they need to be if enemies appear there?  Do I spend my industry points on producing more industry points, producing things I need, or do I try to scimp on points now so I have more avaialble to use on the next map?  Do I invest my dust in that great piece of equipment, or is it more important that I power rooms?  These choices are clever in that many of them are just comprimises; there's often not a "right" choice, just a good guess at what might work out in the long run.
I like a game that makes me think.  Yet, Endless Dungeon is rarely ever overwhelming, just rich with important choices to make and requiring you pay attention when your heroes are fighting so they don't get slain needlessly.
It's quite remarkable they consider this quite-playable product such an early version.  True, you're limited to just three (four?) random map levels per game (which you can exhaust in an hour), there's not yet skills on the heroes, the tech tree systems isn't in yet, and so on.  Yet, the game is more complete than many $15 titles I've bought.  Amplitude studios seems to know what they're doing, and if they call this version v0.1.x, then it's clear this game should be of staggering, epic proportions if they see their plans through to completion.

You can tell this game is old as the graphics are really outdated and all the characters talk in the "Sim's speek" version of pig latin while "thought bubbles" with vage pictures in them float over their heads which I guess is suposed to tell you something but most the time I have no clue what I'm looking at till I check the bio. Natrualy once everyone starts telling me what their scared of most of them are already fleeing in bind terror so I have to wonder what the whole point was.
The Second issue is the frustration factor. The clues droped though out the game are often so cryptic and unhelpful you ether have to replay the same haunt over and over again till you figure out the right combos or just look up the guide which can quickly kill the fun. I'm sure the developers thought they had come up with some clever puzzles but with no real hints and a rather impatient tutorial at the begining I forsee many ragequits. At times the dialog with the traped sprits can come off as a bit lazy as well, like the writers just threw togeather a placeholder statement intending to come up with something better later on, but never did.
All and all this game has a lot of potential, unfortunately most of it goes untaped but it's still fun to experiment with all the diffrent types of ghost and powers just to see what happens, there's no downside to simply reseting a haunt until you get the results you wanted. If your willing to be patient this game can be a lot of fun, otherwise I'd look somewhere elce. I could see this game benfiting from a reboot.

Overall, a very fun, tense, and comical survival game.
The atmosphere feels perfect. Especially when the sun goes down and you jump at any sound that sounds remotely like a bleep and/or bloop. I've yet to find a gun through my few attepts but I've managed to get by with using rocks for distractions when I need to. Improvising should be something you should always keep in mind while playing. Your butler Walters also helps you get an idea of what you should be doing upon your first time playing.
There are a few things that can and WILL screw you over though. Such as the robot's pathing glitching into eachother...on one of the pieces you need to collect. The music (being very well done btw) is a bit of an annoyance. It starts playing when you need to keep your ears open when you've got your face buried in some shrubery and is completely silent when you're being chased.
If you can overlook the small problems/bugs you find in the game then I would say, buy it. you'll get a lot of fun out of it and you won't regret it. Unless they release a patch that breaks the game forever. Then I imagine you would.

Bioshock is an amazing, fun and definately addictive game that keeps you interested from the beginning to the end of the game with an incredible twist at the end of the game. Its action packed with an amazing story line yet very creepy/scary/disturbing due to its gore and horror.
Here are some advantages and disadvantages about the game:
# Good things #
1. A very well constructed, amazing story line
2. Theres always something to do and you never get bored
3. Altough it uses the classic single player objective game, its unique design changes the way you think of single player games forever.
4. You don't need an amazing super beefy computer to play, although you might want to have a good graphics card to get the real image of the game.
# Bad things #
1. Objectives may be hard to complete and possible need to look up a walkthrough for some (This isn't a major issue)
2. Possible need a good graphics card/headphones etc. to get the best feeling out of it.
Overall, this game is an absolute must have as it has all the things that you want in a signle player horror type game.
Thats my review for Bioshock, hope this helps whoever reads this.

Typical stories you find in books or movies usually follow a linear path. Event A happens because event B happened which happened because event C happened, so on and so forth. Now this isn't like real life where events are always caused by a combination of different events. Event A in real life might've happened because of events B, C, D, E, and F. However obviously for books or movies you can't write stories like that because they would be convoluted messes. In games however the narrative has the potential to be much stronger not just because you are telling a story, but also because in a game, the world, all the surrounding elements, are the story. In games you can have event A be a result of some combination B, C, D, E, and F and yet still have a coherent storyline. Infact truly great games are able to make every single aspect of the world enhance the story. Bioshock is one such game.
Do not buy Bioshock for the graphics or the combat. Both aren't bad at all, but both also aren't the point of the game. Instead buy Bioshock to be immersed in the underwater city of Rapture, A once beautiful city destroyed by capitalistic human greed and lust. Every corner of this game's world tells a story. Couple that with excellent lighting/sound design and one of the best plot twists I've experienced in a while, and you get one of the best first person shooters I've ever played.

You have 4 bars representing the Church, the People, the Army and the Treasury. If any of these bars reach the top or bottom then you end up brutally murdered, otherthrown etc... and your reign is over. Your goal is therfore to keep these 4 bars equalized through a sequence of political choices where the flavour text hints at the outcome, but the exact impact is unknown.
The presentation is excellent and gameplay is fun and satisfying with some nice variations (duels and dungeons). Each reign gives you 3 mini-objectives and some encounters unlock additional characters which provides progression. Its also easy to pick up and put down as reigns tend to be short and the game is mostly turn-based.
Unfortunately the sequence of encounters has the main impact on the game, rather than skill or judgement. Ultimately I found the game to be too luck based to hold my attention for long. Given the sale price however, I'm not sure thats a problem and I'd still say I got my moneys worth.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a brilliant First-person-sneaker, set in a typically quaint British countryside populated with sadistic killer robots.
The game is definitely inspired by classic sneakers like Thief, and the focus is on using stealth and deception instead of brute force to fool the robots, and collect fragments of a mysterious device to enable your escape from the islands.
The five islands are procedurally generated, and are absolutely stunning, with beautiful sunsets, dark woods, and eerie moonlit moors. Everywhere the robotic voices of your pursuers pierce the silence, and hearing the thumping and screams of the Landowner approaching is a truly terrifying thing.
I highly recommend this game for anyone looking for a stealth/horror game which at times leaves you with heart beating, running like mad through the woods with crazy robots in pursuit.

This review was done with the Founder Pack version.
Pretty fun game from what I've played so far. It's a tower defense dungeon crawler/RPG. For the stage the game is at the moment I think it's very polished and the artwork is fantastic. The game generates random dungeons so there is a lot of replayabilty.  Another thing that I thought that was neat was DOTE follows the lore of Endless Space (Another fantastic game, especially if you like a more simplistic Civ game in space). Which I think is a nice touch.
I'd highly recommend this game if you like FTL (Faster than Light). Pretty similar gameplay but in a dungeon and you have to protect your Crystal reactor. Which you use to power up rooms with open slots for upgrades for industry,agriculture and science. Dust much like Endless Space is the currency but also doubles as a fuel source in this game. Which you would use to power up the rooms or to buy items from the merchant. Also you can level up your heros with agricuture, instead of experience like Endless Space. I think it would have been cool to get Xp from slaying mobs but it is still early access so the developers may change that (The developer is very active with the community and takes feedback. They also have votes for changes in the game via their forums that you got from buying the game).
I'm going to play this game a lot more and would recommend it but to someone who hasn't played Endless Space (They use a lot of of the resources, tech trees and lore, that Endless Space uses.) or doesn't likes tower defense games. You should probably wait until it's on sale or when it's out of early access (As of right now there is only 3 levels).
Founder Pack version notes:
This part of the review will go over the Founder pack extras that are included in-game and cross game. I'll add in the other in-game items and extras once they are released (Or if I even remember to :D). The to be released items and extras are the Ship Pack: The Library, the Hero: Josh 'Ntello, the Official soundtrack and Vaulterskins for Endless Legends (Game will be out next 2014).
At the moment you get 50% off for Endless Space and the expansion pack (This is an awesome game, a more simplicated Civ game in space with tons of lore), 2 community badges on the Amplitude forums (So you can feel special over people with no badges, just kidding) and The Vaulter faction for Endless Space. The Vaulter faction for Endless Space is a bit disapointing for me at least.
I had a chance to play today and they do have nice stats and nice abilites but the ships were disapointing and also that there was no introduction video for their faction, like other factions have. They're really similar to the United Empire ships. Unlike the the Piligrims ships where you can see the differences in ship design there is little to none with the Vaulters. Where as it's understandable with Sheredyn faction sense they're still close to the United Empire and were the Emperors  personal guards. But other then that, as of now the Founder pack was worth it (My opinion). Hopefully they will redesign the ships and add a introduction video in a future update.
Founder Pack and can be a hit and miss for some and would recommend that you buy the Pixel pack instead, if you're unsure. Amplitude have been known to have an option to upgrade for Endless Space so it's possible that you will be able to upgrade later but at the same time it's a "Founder pack" it may be limited time only.
Update: Now that the game has officially been released, a couple of things have changed. See below.
- Currency is now randomized (FIDS) and is not just Dust. FIDS is Food, Industry, Dust and Food.
- Science is now used to update modules and you research via Endless Artefact.
- Updated the intro movie, main menu and some parts of the Hero UI. (I like it)
- Soundtrack has been updated.
- You can now save items in a backpack now, that are not in your heros inventory for the next level. (I was waiting so long for this)
- Ships can be unlocked now, by completing certain conidtions in a successful playthough.
- Heros can be unlocked now, by meeting them in a playthrough and meeting certain conditions.
- Monuments also have been added which give random buffs or debuff for a  random duration.
- And a multiplayer mode has been added but have yet to try it.
- You have to click exit to move to the next level.
- Loading screen to next level has been changed.
- 13 levels to complete a playthough. Unlimited levels, if you use the Drill ship. (Unlockable)
- Steam cards and Steam achievements have also been added with DOTE's release.
My thoughts; game is amazing now that it has released and awesome updates to the DOTE. Updates will probably be continued just like it's sister games ot the Endless Universe.

Ready to run into gunfire and gun down half the enemy team at once? Slow down there cowboy, this isn't the Call of Duty you're familiar with. Only your accuracy with a bolt action riffle and ability to follow orders will lead your team to victory. Welcome to Red Orchestra 2, a realistic team based first person shooter with squad elements. Aside from the laughable single player mode and poor squad co-operation, RO2 delivers a very immersive rewarding team based experience where a good commander can make or break the battle.
Already dead? Don't be surprised. Death is so sudden and violent here that you're constantly going to be on edge, especially when everyone is dying around you. This is only furthered by your inability to fire accurately while bullets and explosions land a few feet away. Now before we fire your weapon lets discuss uniforms.
At a glance there is no easy, instant way to tell if a soldier is on your side. That's not to say the uniforms are not distinct, they are. But things are not always so clear, especially when battle lines are not as they may first appear to be. Just be careful and forgive honest mistakes.
Before you run off and lead your squad to its death lets dial back and pick a role. Remember that bolt action we were talking about? The Rifleman is the heart and soul of any army. RO2 has a steep learning curve at first and before we take command we need to have a basic understanding of what's going on. With this role you will not only learn to shoot accurately and stay alive, but you also form up the main fighting force for taking and defending objectives. Rifleman, when supported by other soldiers, rain down with fire so accurate that the enemy will most likely have to call for artillery to kill them. Let's grasp a good understanding of the game before we jump into a leadership position.
Ohh your buddy just blew up by an artillery shell? Artillery comes in waves and will most likely kill anyone caught up in the barrage. If you survive the first volley get away or find some shelter. Some players will try to slip through between the volleys but you need to be fast. It's dangerous at will likely be suicidal to attempt this. Artillery is used for area denial. When placed properly artillery inhibits both advancing and defending reinforcements from capturing or defending a point.
I see you've finally made it up near the objective without being killed, I'm impressed. Most soldiers don't make it this far and fewer survive capturing it. In RO2 capturing points is the most basic way to win a game. Defenders can end a game early by holding these points letting the game time expire. Attacking forces on the other hand can extend the total time for a game by capturing these objectives. There is more than one way to win a battle in RO2 however this is the most straightforward objective of any RO2 battle.
Don't die. Each death costs your team a ticket. Run out of tickets, lose the game. Staying alive in RO2 is important. Sometimes just sitting tight and defending a point is better than running off only to be shot without ever seeing anyone.
Listen to your team leader and everything will be fine. Communication is crucial and sometimes you might see enemy troops flanking before anyone else does. Call it out so your team leader and teammates can respond accordingly.
"Banzai!!!!!!!!"
Congratulations you're ready to play RO2. There is so much more we could discuss but you've learned the basics. Keep your head down and I'll see you on the battlefield.

NOTE: The first half of this review was written before the release of the full game.
"A first person danmaku? That will never work!" Ohhh how wrong I was...
This is a spectacular game full of intense bullet dodging action and lots of shooting. It is so very satisfying to shoot the limbs off of a giant death machine and then blow up the core. Some of the missions that would be more "gimicky" are actually really solid (such as the muffin collecting which I adore. Srsly. Keep the collectables muffins.) The humor is wonderful and I can't wait to see what sort of fun changes the future of this game holds. To top it off the soundtrack is AMAZING. Every song is spot on and matches the lighthearted feel of the game.
The only issue I take is the difficulty curve. Some missions are aboslutely burtally hard while others are laughably easy. I'm sure that will get ironed out but it really doesn't detract from the overall game. This is a must own gem for anyone who likes a challenge and making things blow up.
Edit: Now that the full game is out I felt it was best that I update this. First and foremost I want to state that my opinion of the game has largely stayed the same in terms of its quality and fun factor so take my criticisms with a grain of salt.
First and foremost: The voice acting. It's good, quality voice acting and the dialouge is sharp and funny. It just... Was unneeded. The game was already hilarious with just the premise and I suppose if the dialogue was just limited to the suit talking and/or making some quips at the robots it would be fine. But I thought the limited story silent protagonist was fine. So i'm kind of on the fence about it. I'd have to lean toward not liking it though. (The threats by the robot bartender on the answering machine and the pestering news lady etc are hilarious though and need to be there) The voice of the pickups also changed which is fine but I kinda miss the original.
Secondly: The gun. Ohhhhh boy... Part of the funness of the gun was the feeling that you were just obliterating everything on screen. Especially with how you could see the bullets go faaaaaar and watch them break stuff. But the bullets were changed from spheres to these little illogical laser beams (not that there was much logic in this game in the first place) and some of their impact went away. I suppose its nitpicky for me to feel this way but I liked the spheres better. They felt more satisfying. I can see why they were possibly changed since th spheres could possibly hide bullets that you wanted to dodge, but it wasn't so problematic that it warrented a change. Maybe a small drop in opacity and thats it.
Thirdly: The graphics and sound. OH MY GOD ITS SO SHINY! also the sounds are wonderful. The sounds of the explosions rivals the ones in Colony Wars in terms of the satisfaction one gets from hearing them. Also, the bright and upbeat colors just make the entire game a treat to look at. Music is great too. If a soundtrack was released I'd put it on my iPod.
Again, this game is still a must buy. The addition of extra missions and the sheer insanity of this game is great. The difficulty makes it very fun and makes you want to keep playing. Now, due to REAL LIFE I havent' finished the game yet. Here's hoping they didn't remove the muffin collection missions. They were some of the best things in the early access.

Is Evolve worth £34.99? ($60)
yes.
And heres why,
Most titles for the past few years have been remakes of remakes with little to change between titles as not to alienate their fanbase, any sort of change to the norm as of late as been dealt with with severe backlash and i think this is mainly what evolve suffers from.
People first major concern is that the game is repeatitive, is it? yes it has a simple formula at first glance but to name a few examples of games with a simple premise but deeper gameplay like Left 4 Dead or League of Legends with huge replay value but both are also very repeatitive, does it make them any less of a game.... no and the same can be said for evolve.
Each creature plays truely unique and every player will in turn play those creatuires a totally different way in order to survive an win, each hunter class plays differently and also so does each character within those classes creating a true tapestry of unique situations and stories to be told depending on their composition.
The maps are varied the game types fun and engaging, there may not be many but it does all of them incredibly well that it doesnt feel like the experice is missing something as a whole.
Even as a game with only multiplayer to offer its a truely next gen game with true next gen ideas to mix up the old outdated formula of multiplayer games. The unlock system is a tad flawed but in essence its not what the game is about... the game from my perspective is as the Rock would say "know your role" you are part of a team once which quickly breaks down at the loss of a player this creates frantic quick encounters than can turn from planned cunning engagement to panicked and confusing survival creating a huge sense of tension, play your part and you win, dont and you use that experience to learn and fight again.
Granted playing this game with friends is a much more satisfying experience, but as a purely SOLO player iv enjoyed countless battles with chatty like minded players just looking to shoot the heck out of a giant badass creature, and some of the greatest spontanious moments have been created with players i dont even know!

But to return to the starting question if  you want 100 hours of gameplay out of this you could, its gonna take time to truely master a class but lets be honest its multiplayer only it is what it is...... but if your experience with a game is more important to the price tag it upholds over the amount of hours played then honestly Evolve is on of the best games your money can buy right now.

At first I thought it's gonna be an RPG, but after reading tags I figured out that it's just a FPS. A little disappointed, I decided to go for it anyway (this may not seem obvious to you; I'm just not a huge FPS fan), especially after seeing overwhelmingly positive reviews and high metacritic score.
It was surely the best decision I could have made.
While being a FPS, Bioshock includes a few RPG elements - there is no experience gaining or levelling up, but still there are 4 fields of enhancing main character's abilities - via so called plasmids.
The setting is an underwater, dystopian, a bit steampunk city in 1960s. These facts make the game feel more like Fallout than Fallout 3 - and it's the thing I love the most in Bioshock.
The script is quite interesting; beginning with no knowledge of what's going on here, step by step we collect more and more facts, getting to know the whole story. It turns out to be really good. Some plot twists are also to be expected.
There are only a 2 little cons of this game I've noticed. The ending could be a little more exhaustive, maybe giving a little more explanation, or some more details of what happened next. The second thing is the essence of gameplay - it gets a bit repetitive after a while. In this light I think that about 15 hours needed to complete Bioshock is exactly the right time to spend on it.
I'm glad there are two more games in the franchise, waiting for me to complete :)

TLDR: This game is fun for the first 10 hours and after you start to get better gear you start to realize that you have nothing left to do but ration food and sleep.
Story mode added nothing new except for the story, which was not special. The writing is cringy and as many people have said, the quests are very tedious fetch this fetch that. Not all bad however, hidden caches were cool and the new region was good, but no AI survivors added (which was heavily hinted at for years).
You may notice that I have 300 hrs in this game. Ive owned this since the first new region was added back, 3 years now. If you check my achievements for this game you will see I have never survived to 100 days. This is because the most fun in this game you can have is within the first 20 days of survival. After that there is nothing to do. I have often deleted saves when I had everything I needed to live for 100 days. But there was no fun to be had at that point. That and playing the game when a new region came out, or an update to content, amounts for the 300 hrs. Also I personally like games that feel realistic (even though this game is not realistic) and as a result I dumped a fair number of hrs into this game.
Developers do not intend to add any form of late game/goals to the sandbox. They frequently say they want it to be a goalless game. There is still nothing to do once you have all you need to survive.
They added challenge modes (mini missions, like get chased by a bear, or chase the bear), which is in the right direction frankly. However, what really needs to be added is something to the sandbox, so that its not all about finding loot and surviving for the longest period of time because that is boring and really is not fun.
Lastly, the developers have said that this is not a realistic game in response to negative reviews talking about aspects of the game being unrealistic. Its odd that their steam page description seems to describe a game about "true survival" fight against "mother nature". Its not realistic at all.
In this game:
Wolves and bears will attack you as soon as you get within about 50m. Wolves are the zombies of this game. No wolf packs.
The rifle bullets literally stop existing after they travel about 50-100m.  There is no bullet drop, bullet time, bullet effects.
Tools degrade extremely quickly
3 seconds in real life is 1 min in this game, however you walk at the same pace as real life though. You will also therefore become thirsty and hungry extremely quickly.
No alive people.
No jumping, climbing, vaulting.
Crafting is limited to a few things, bow, clothing items. Nothing special.
When cooking, you cannot move or do anything.
Overall. This game is not worth £27. More stuff will be added but don't wait on it. Get this game when its less than £10 for value for money and play it in 5 years when there is more to do.
Also this is not really important to the game as such. The devs get a little defensive over criticism of their game. Doesn't feel very professional to see them banning people on forums for voicing complaints.

Bioshock was something that I had intentions of playing for a very long time. My first memories of it were from watching an early playthrough trailer of the game on an old Xbox magazine disc when I was around 12. Obviously seeing images of the splicers and the dark underwater setting kinda put me off from playing it for a very long while. But while browsing various game shops it would always be somewhere where I could see so eventually I borrowed it off my friend for a bit to play it.
And overall, it was fine.
Nothing hugely amazing but fine.
Of course the dark brooding underwater atmosphere was something of note as well as the general lore to Rapture itself. Finding various audio recordings of the inhabitants of Rapture really brought around the atmosphere of the place and added the sufficient element of creepyness it deserved. But the combat felt a bit lacklustre to say the least, guns never really had that much weight to them and the plasmids although spectacular were repetitive to use. The little sister mechanic of saving/harvesting seemed to be the only thing that affected the story which was a pity because I felt more could've been done to exploit other areas of the game in order to affect the story as well.
I wouldn't recommend playing this game by itself. Play with Bioshock 2 and Infinite in order to gain a better understanding of the mythos as well as produce more variety in playing the series in general.

I gave Echo of Soul a fair try, as with those other games. In the end I must say, that I am positively surprised.
The PvE balancing and Quest goals are done in a way, that does not halt your progression through the game. The flow feels like Diablo 3 i.e. you keep moving through the game without being forced to stop and grind in one area.
They also use the phasing system that games like World of Warcraft used, so that the world around you actually is able to change in response to completed quests. For example, early in the game you arrive at a town, which is on fire and overrun by enemies. After you save it, the world changes and the town is normal again, functioning as a regular in-game hub with merchants and players etc.
The graphics and design are nothing new or spectacular, but EOS does look very nice and inviting. In addition it has it's own charm, as you can create quite extravagant characters. You have a variety of unusual hair and skin colors to select from and the size slider has a big range as well. It is not as expansive as some other games, but definitely good enough to not be limiting.
I read in other reviews, that the game feels Pay to Win for them. Looking at the items available on the Cash Shop, I can understand this notion, as some items seem quite powerful. But in all the time I played, I never actually felt compelled to buy anything there, as the game's balancing does not feel, like I would really need any of them. The only thing that really is of interest, are the extended bags, as there is quite some loot to carry around after some time of play. Even the standard mounts, of which you get one very early in the game, are sufficient, so you do not need to buy a better one.
I did not encounter any serious lag or other technical issues. The game ran smooth and stable for me. There was only some lags on the release day, a couple of weeks ago, but that is completely normal for an MMO. I read that some people's Antivirus software is giving warnings, but this also happens with many online games, as the Anti-Hack tools can be seen as false positives by those Antivirus tools. I personally did not have this issue.
Echo of Soul is nothing new or extravagant. It is competent, solid and the actual gameplay is done in a way that it is entertaining without any grind. It might not be made for the hardcore players or those that want a great PvP game. But if you are looking for a good time in PvE, Echo of Soul is definitely worth a try.

Despite the target audience above, saying that Cuphead is this revolutionary difficult game is a little misleading. Not in a gaming industry with japanese SHMUPs thats for sure. But Cuphead will kill you over and over again: and that's alright. It's a game that relies on pattern/attack recognition and clawing your way further and further to the end of a boss. The combat mechanics are simple yet effective: as you have a limited set of moves and weapons to work with: but enough to change up  your strategy just enough to deal with specific bosses. Speaking of which, bosses all are unique and aren't altered versions of prior ones. Each battle teaches you something to use in your arsenal, and you have to adapt that lesson to the next ones. Hell, you may even need to throw it away if needed.
This is all held together by a presentation that had a LOT of effort put into it....and it shows. The hand drawn characters without digital effects (ok, coloring, but really that's it) must have taken ages to do. But the end result is some of the cleanest animation you've ever seen in a video game, as the ccartoons look as authentic as they possibly could be for emulating the 1930s. The over the top nature of the presentation tells you a lot about all these various bosses without forcing exposition down your throat. And the music and sound design is pretty brilliant, able to emphasize the right parts of gameplay while not emphasizing what you don't need to pay immediate attention to.
Where the game falls short for me in that next level of gameplay. The structure of the game is at the core of this problem: once you've mastered a boss, you may get a slight addition to the challenge in expert mode, but not a lot of replayability beyond that. Sure, you'll die a bunch, but it's not like the game requires a lot of skill to get past all of these challenges. Some yes, but not the hand eye coordination of a gaming god. I just, I don't know, I was expecting another layer, something to bring out more of the game when all was said and done.
It's not the Game of the Year, not in a year where there's so many top level games coming out. It's just a cut under the top games of 2017, but it's still worth an immediate buy.

You can view Ghost Master in two ways. Either its an admittedly aged, but nonetheless original and fun game. OR its ostensibly broken. A good idea poorly implemented. I like to see it as a good game for a Sunday. I can play it for a good few hours before it starts to irritate me. Then I stop and do something else.
In short, you own a stable of ghosts and are tasked with haunting an area, either to rid the area of its occupants (in as quick time as possible) or to encourage said occupants to perform certain tasks for you (in as quick time as possible).  In each area there are up to 4 ghosts you also need to rescue. Underpinning this is a 'Ghoul Room' where you upgrade your ghosts abilities, and a revisit function where you are marked on your performance - the highest being a 5x multiplier to your score. Neither of these parts of the game are particularly well done and it is these facets of the game that disappoint. The ghosts you acquire earlier in the game are obviously the strongest as they are the only ones you can use in all the scenarios; and so the Ghoul Room concentrates solely on the 7 or 8 'must have' skills and ignores all the others. Also it is quite clear that Terror is much easier to achieve than Madness, instantly removing a potential 50% of the game. In short, its imbalanced
Hidden within the constraints of the game is the concept of the 'perfect' game. i.e a revisit to a scenario and achieving a 5x multiplier plus rescuing all ghosts. This is how I like to play it, but there are two scenarios, "Deadfellas" and "Phantom of The Operating Theatre" where this goal is basically impossible. The latter of those two scenarios, "Phantom" is so annoying that this is where I usually draw the line on a Sunday's play. There is also the concept of 'Luck', if you want to get an Ai to do something for you - sometimes it will, sometimes it will EVENTUALLY. When you are being timed, this is just a little annoying. You can minimize this luck with some astute timing, but some bad AI pathfinding will always exist. Sometimes the AI wont go into a room, not because he/she isnt programmed to, but because its pathfinding abilities have become messed up. The game is not massively glitchy, but you feel that a remake would be better implemented (plus, of course, have better graphics - be ready for some unobtainable chest sizes).
I often wonder how I would remake this game - because there is definitely a game worth playing here - but the only conclusion I can come to is that, although I do have an obvious soft spot for this game, its some way from where it could and should be.

The Sims suddenly wake up to an even bigger terror than a chair in the doorway: ZOMBIES. Nah, but seriously, this is a fantastic isometric C(lassic)RPG that plops you down into a neighbourhood where things have suddenly gone horribly wrong and it is up to you (and your chosen character skills) to see how long you last. The game, to its gameplay, asks you: How will you die? There is no coming out alive from this, but how long can you last - and how far will you go to push back death for as long as possible?
The view, as mentioned, is isometric but unlike the joking comparison to The Sims you are in full control of your character. It reminds me of The Sims because you have to FULLY manage your avatar's body needs. Sleeping in a bedroom while there are 50 zombies outside banging on the walls will result in you not having any shut eye and even potentially going into a panic metal state. If you get infected...then you will slowly start wearing down before the inevitable catches up with up and turns you into one of "them" (game over). You can carry only as much as your body can handle, meaning you will have to find a place to fortify and stash your survival gear. It won't be a matter of just finding lots of guns and (re)killing everything in sight, though...because guess what happens when you shoot your gun? It will be very loud...and catch unwanted attention. You will have to make life or death decisions wether to eliminate a zombie quickly with a gun and hope you can outrun the horde, or make the mistake of alerting an entire mall of zombies to your presence and becoming a small fish in a very large pond full of crocodiles.
As many have said, this game is incredibly depressing and bleak but that is exactly what the scenario is here - the♥♥♥♥♥♥has hit the fan, everyone is dead or dying, and despite being dead, they are still walking around trying to make YOU dead too.

First of all, this is not a good game to play for an hour right before playing CS:GO. It's a mindf*ck when you get into CS, and you'll stop moving all the time but time won't slow down and you will get killed.
As has been said in at least half of the reviews on here, SUPERHOT's "plot" is basically the player as Neo from The Matrix. Buuuuuuut Neo never left his desk and instead had an inane conversation with Tinity about how the Matrix is great and how he should tell everyone about it, then Trinity says "KYS" and disconnects. The "story mode" is really just a tutorial with a bunch of idiotic, tedious, time wasting, fake IRC crap thrown in. It's one of those games which forces you to stop playing several times for way more time than necessary to tell you something you can't skip, which you don't care about and which doesn't move the
"plot" forward. Just take this BS out and call the top option in the menu "tutorial.exe" and get on with it.
The actual gameplay is based on a fairly simple mechanic: the slower you move, the slower time moves. Time never stops completely, even when you're totally still, but it gets pretty slow. That said, this is the ONLY mechanic the game has to offer (excepting the aforementioned tedious IRC crap), and while it is fun for a while, it does get old, and the game just keeps serving up the same time mechanic until you quit forever.
A lot of people have suggested that players skip through the story and get to the challenge modes. While this is where the meat of the game is, there are really only a few challenges and then a bunch of arenas to play them in. Kill x enemies as fast as possible, kill as many enemies within x seconds (game time), kill as many enemies as possible in x seconds (real time), kill as many enemies as possible until you die (endless). These are fun for a while, but there is no in-game leaderboard, no way to compare how Steam friends did, and the only interaction you can have with the game's "community" (I'm not sure there really is one, most people seem to quit pretty fast) is to upload replays to a website which you can't access in-game. Wasted opportunity.
If I'm calculating how much I paid over with how much I've played, I think I did alright, because I bought this for like $3. Also, five of my recorded game hours came from using IdleMaster to get cards. Don't pay more than $5, because at that price, you're going to end up spending a dollar per hour to read this rambling IRC drivel.
So yeah, tl;dr: fun for a while, but also way more excruciating than necessary. Buy for nothing more than 20% of retail. And, much like eating before swimming, wait at least twenty minutes between this and CS:GO.
Note: the PC version of the game also has a fairly large flaw. If you're playing with a mouse and keyboard, you have two options for speed: FULL and STOP. Any time you move with the keyboard you are RUNNING, which makes things a bit more challenging, but also kind of breaks the game's mechanic. If you play with a controller, the analog input allows you to move yourself (and time) as slowly or as quickly as you choose. Splinter Cell handled this by using the mouse wheel as a speed control, but this game basically says "I hate you, buy a controller."
