This game is an instant classic. You won't see any scaring games being released around this era of gaming.
Ghost Master is game where you bind and equip ghosts into the houses/places of people you want to scare. You can also unlock new ghosts that are somewhat trapped in the houses you try to clear out. The game offers not just scaring out of the blue but it also makes use of certain situations like for example if the residents are non-believers then you have initiate a certain event like a hidden dead body to be spotted by the residents. By doing so, they will slowly become vulnerable to your scaring tactics and powers. Each ghost has its own specialty and powers and their binding points depend whether they are fitted for indoors, outdoors, or both. You can also train your ghosts so that they can learn new powers or enhance their scaring abilities. It's your choice of strategy whether how you want to scare the current residents. The main goal of the game is to scare out all the residents from the house.
I recommend this game to anyone who loves the classic scaring games genre.
NOTE: If you want this game, you should buy it during a sale. This game is more likely to be on sale during the Fall Sale.

Ready to run into gunfire and gun down half the enemy team at once? Slow down there cowboy, this isn't the Call of Duty you're familiar with. Only your accuracy with a bolt action riffle and ability to follow orders will lead your team to victory. Welcome to Red Orchestra 2, a realistic team based first person shooter with squad elements. Aside from the laughable single player mode and poor squad co-operation, RO2 delivers a very immersive rewarding team based experience where a good commander can make or break the battle.
Already dead? Don't be surprised. Death is so sudden and violent here that you're constantly going to be on edge, especially when everyone is dying around you. This is only furthered by your inability to fire accurately while bullets and explosions land a few feet away. Now before we fire your weapon lets discuss uniforms.
At a glance there is no easy, instant way to tell if a soldier is on your side. That's not to say the uniforms are not distinct, they are. But things are not always so clear, especially when battle lines are not as they may first appear to be. Just be careful and forgive honest mistakes.
Before you run off and lead your squad to its death lets dial back and pick a role. Remember that bolt action we were talking about? The Rifleman is the heart and soul of any army. RO2 has a steep learning curve at first and before we take command we need to have a basic understanding of what's going on. With this role you will not only learn to shoot accurately and stay alive, but you also form up the main fighting force for taking and defending objectives. Rifleman, when supported by other soldiers, rain down with fire so accurate that the enemy will most likely have to call for artillery to kill them. Let's grasp a good understanding of the game before we jump into a leadership position.
Ohh your buddy just blew up by an artillery shell? Artillery comes in waves and will most likely kill anyone caught up in the barrage. If you survive the first volley get away or find some shelter. Some players will try to slip through between the volleys but you need to be fast. It's dangerous at will likely be suicidal to attempt this. Artillery is used for area denial. When placed properly artillery inhibits both advancing and defending reinforcements from capturing or defending a point.
I see you've finally made it up near the objective without being killed, I'm impressed. Most soldiers don't make it this far and fewer survive capturing it. In RO2 capturing points is the most basic way to win a game. Defenders can end a game early by holding these points letting the game time expire. Attacking forces on the other hand can extend the total time for a game by capturing these objectives. There is more than one way to win a battle in RO2 however this is the most straightforward objective of any RO2 battle.
Don't die. Each death costs your team a ticket. Run out of tickets, lose the game. Staying alive in RO2 is important. Sometimes just sitting tight and defending a point is better than running off only to be shot without ever seeing anyone.
Listen to your team leader and everything will be fine. Communication is crucial and sometimes you might see enemy troops flanking before anyone else does. Call it out so your team leader and teammates can respond accordingly.
"Banzai!!!!!!!!"
Congratulations you're ready to play RO2. There is so much more we could discuss but you've learned the basics. Keep your head down and I'll see you on the battlefield.

Rogue-like games are normally games which offer some form of level randomization and permanent death; your character dies and you must either start over or keep going until everything is lost. These types of games are normally unforgiving.
If you have an interest in Rogue-like games and think that an intermixed concept of base defense is a good idea, keep reading. If you do not like traditional Rogue-like games where it is turn based, you might still like this since it is a hybred of turn-based and real-time with a pause feature. However if you do not like either concept of Rogue-like “permadeath” or base defense you may want to consider doing more research or finding something else.
Also with a Rogue-like game the graphics are not normally the main focus, thus if you are turned off by anything below 3D graphics you should consider something else.
This will be a breakdown of concept and features, atmosphere and stability.
The concept of mixing Rouge-like with base defense is interesting; it gives an interesting way to progress. Including Dungeon of the Endless uses real-time with waves verse the traditional turn based method.
Right now the game has three available resource types, Food, Dust (energy) and Industry (tech). Food is used to recruit new members to your team, heal them and level them up. Industry is used to create defenses in powered rooms. Dust is used in two ways first to buy things from random merchants and to power rooms beyond the starting room with the core. Dust currently resets every level while Food and Industry do not.
Progressing in the dungeon you will have to make decisions on if it is correct to save Food to heal or on the chance to recruit someone or even to level someone up. The current max level is five and five makes a large difference verses a level one however it is expensive.
The player will have to decide what rooms to open to since they will not have enough Dust to supply all the rooms at the start. When you have access to merchant the player will have to decide if they are going to give up Dust used for defenses to buy equipment or sell equipment for dust. Defenses can be used to also increase your income while exploring.
Progression also at this time also includes finding chests and blueprints for building new defenses.
The interface is rather clean and easy to use after you have it down. It also allows short-cut keys while building defenses, so you can hold shift and click to place multiple defenses instead of reusing the menu.
The game also employs a monster wave system, where waves occur over time from unpowered rooms. Thus if the room remains unpowered monsters come from the vast darkness to kill the team.
The overall objective is to find the room to the next level and then move the core there using one of the heroes to do so. You will find that the rooms begain to lose power while doing this and waves of monsters start to show up to stop you.
Overall the feeling is deployed correctly for alpha; the story is short and sweet and not overly lengthy or bulky. Basically your team of two is on a ship and become stranded and must progress through the dungeon. The generated two characters the player start with have a slight background to have the player interested and give a hint on how they should be used to progress.
The graphics are a very nicely done pixel art format, with effects and seem to pay homage to older graphical related Rouge-likes very well. Personally I found the graphics enjoyable.
Music was interesting and seems to fit well with the current atmosphere of the game however it may become bland unintentionally over extended play.
Overall the game /did not/ hang or crash on older machines that lacked the graphics requirement. I tried on older desktop machines and laptops under windows Vista and Windows 7; it was pretty efficient and was not a complete resource hog on the system. I also did not run into any critical errors which cased instability and the program failed to run. While I’m unable to speak for everyone and their systems it seems to be overall pretty solid. Most of the time games in alpha or beta still are unstable while this game seems to be nicely polished in respect to stability in the listed windows environments.
I would currently recommend this to someone who is /interested and willing/ to try a Rogue-like combined with base defense which is implemented in hybred fasion of real-time and turn-based. This game will most likely have a very interesting development process from Amplitude Studios and I look forward to it.

To me, that's all worth $60 (or lets be honest, you're going to buy it on sale anyway) and the mere existence of other content that I don't want to pay extra for doesn't tarnish that.
Lastly and more esoterically, it's important to encourage publishers to take risks on new games that aren't Call of Duty.

Sir is something like a British S.T.A.L.K.E.R., full of tea and English countryside and terrifying robots with monocles and pipes. Or maybe a DayZ, with a twist of Minecraft’s procedurally-generated landscapes, and a ton of tweedy charm. The environments are beautiful, and the robots are equal parts terrifying and amusing. Sir is everything that’s wonderful about systemic games, and I felt like a goddamn genius when I lured some robots away from a piece of the device by lighting a cooking fire, then snuck around behind them to grab the piece and bugger off.
I really, really like this game, but I have two concerns. First, “collect the MacGuffins” is becoming overly familiar as a goal in procedurally-generated games. Second, and more complicated, is that procedurally-generated games always make me feel like I’ve seen pretty much everything I’m likely to see, far earlier than their promise of endless variations might suggest. While the environments are never identical, variations that feel significantly different are fairly rare, and the nature of procedural generation means you’ll mostly see stuff that falls within a certain band of stuff that looks much the same. It’s nice that the monkeys occasionally produce some Shakespeare, but the truth is, mostly they don’t.

So, you've played DayZ, H1Z1 etc. and fancy yourself as a survival expert? If you can survive the zombie apocalypse you can survive a desolate Canadian winter right?
Nope. Prepare to die in a series of humiliating, heart breaking and just downright depressing ways as you attempt to scratch out an existence in the mysterious landscape you get dropped into. Everything about the game is gruelling and unforgiving - overlook one thing and you die.
For example, I had survived for 2 weeks. I had a stocked cabin, with a decent supply of meat, drying hides, water and medecine. One day, I went for a forage but forgot to check the temperature outside - it was a clear day, didn't look like a storm. Turned out to be -31C with a string wind...I was in trouble within about 5 minutes, realised there was no way I could make it home and ended up having to dig a snow hole and set up a campfire to try and sit it out. 2 wolves saw the fire, I was too weak to scare them away properly (vision was really screwed up at this point) so they eventually attacked me. I killed them both with a knife, bandaged my wounds, and crawled back into my hole to try and sleep. Died of blood poisoning and hypothermia a few hours later.
On another occasion, I literally passed out and died within what I later worked out must have been around 20 steps of my home cabin because a blizzard blew in, and it became a complete whiteout while I was out on a frozen lake. Couldn't see anything, my tracks in the snow were wiped out, and I got lost.
The mechanics of the game are amazing, especially with its handling of the cold. There is a temperature reading and a windchill - the wind blows in a direction (changeable) and you can shelter from it behind cover. Forests for example will cause you a lower windchill factor than open plain.
So basically my opinion is:
- This is the best damn survival game I've ever played.
- It is seriously, seriously hard but just as rewarding when you do well.
- It is absolutely frickin' beautiful. Seriously Hinterland, I'm not normally a fan of these cartoon-ish art styles in games but holy sh**. Every single time I remember to look up from trying not to die, there's an oil painting looking at me.
- It never feels unfair. I've never died and thought "well that's stupid", just "well I was stupid".
- The developers are awesome. I got the game really early on and have been keeping up with development waiting on the storyline mode, and they are very good. To me these days, that can be more important than anything.
- I HIGHLY recommend this to any survival fans, but be prepared that it is hard,  you will die, and don't expect to be fighting zombies or humans etc. The only combat is bow/gun against animal, or hand to hand fight-for-your-life when a wolf or other jumps you.
TIP: I had a problem where I found the game really boring and not at all entertaining. If you find this, turn the difficulty up. Seriously this game is designed to be hard, and is not nearly as good when you aren't under pressure 24/7.

I embarked at sunrise
with a flask of water, a samurai sword
in the cockpit, a shaven head
full of powerful incantations
and enough fuel for a one-way
journey into history
but half way there, my wife thought,
recounting it later to her children,
I looked far down
at the little fishing boats
strung out like bunting
on a green-blue translucent sea
and beneath them, arcing in swathes
like a huge flag waved first one way
then the other in a figure of eight,
the dark shoals of fishes
flashing silver as their bellies
swivelled towards the sun
and remembered how he
and his brothers waiting on the shore
built cairns of pearl-grey pebbles
to see whose withstood longest
the turbulent inrush of breakers
bringing their father’s boat safe
- yes, grandfather’s boat – safe
to the shore, salt-sodden, awash
with cloud-marked mackerel,
black crabs, feathery prawns,
the loose silver of whitebait and once
a tuna, the dark prince, muscular, dangerous.
And though he came back
my mother never spoke again
in his presence, nor did she meet his eyes
and the neighbours too, they treated him
as though I no longer existed,
only children still chattered and laughed
till gradually we too learned
to be silent, to live as though
I had never returned, that this
was no longer the father they loved.
And sometimes, she said, i must have wondered
which had been the better way to die.

If you ever need a game to calm you down after a long dreary day at work, or a relaxing game on your laptop while on a long traintrip, this is the game to go. Don't be decieved by the minimalistic graphics. Squares, diamonds, trangles and lines is all you need to enjoy the game. Connect the same shapes with a single line, without crossing other lines (except at HUB-like octagons). Each move and each completed level is accompanied by a smooth chime sound. So the more you test out possibilities, the more musical the game becomes, without being disruptive at any time.
The game offers unlockable color palettes. Even if this is no big deal, the change of color can change the way of perception drastically, and also every player can select his/her favorite palette later on, without being forced to the standard turquise one.
Every day there are new daily levels offered (internet connection required) that makes this game an infinite plethora of mind twisting but relaxing puzzles.

Empire At War is an RTS  Set in the Star Wars Universe. The game itself has 2 Primary Modes, and several Modes wihin that. The Primary are Galatic Conquest, Similar to the Battlefront Gamemode, and Instan Action, in which you just pick a map and begin. The two of three sub modes apply to the other two, Those two being the Land Battle Mode, where you use various troops, vehicles, and heroes of the Universe to engage an opposing side, either the Rebel scum or the Mighty Empire. Another is Space Battles, a mode where you use Everything from fighters to Star Destroyers to fight your opponent's.
The gameplay itself is more or less just a simplified RTS; It focus's more on the War and Battle part than building structures, although a basic Unit Upgrade system is in place. The empire has a Slight Advantage in Space Battles in my experience,  as with even basic units, the basic Tactic of Swarm with many troops is efficient enough to win most Encounters. However, having not played much as The Rebel Scum, That may be true for both sides.
The modding community for this game has created a large amount of Mods, with mods in The Clone Wars Era, to the Imperial Remnant Era.
All in all, I enjoy this game, and, despite some small bits being dislikeable, such as the fact the Empire Can eventually just Death Star Planets to death, I give it a 8/10. Some things could have been changed, but asides from that, I Highly reccomend it, as it is a Fleshed out, enjoyable game.

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

The Beginner's Guide is heavily dependant on its narrative, so it's hard to review a game like this without giving away spoilers. While I won't mention anything specific, just explaining certain parts felt like a spoiler to me, so reader beware.
***SPOILERS***
Now The Beginner's Guide is a walking simulator, and like any other walking simulator it depends on the narrative to succeed or fail. The problem is that The Beginner's Guide's narrative is one about the meta relationship between the game and the player, and The Beginner's Guide fails to handle that relationship very well. This is largely because The Beginner's Guide is completely linear.
The game feels like the clumsy translation from a book to a movie or a movie to a game. A meta game that is completely linear, that explores the relationship between a player and the game, without actually letting you have any meaningful interaction as a player to the game. This is especially noticeable because The Stanley Parable made by the same creator covers a lot of the same ground, but actually allowed the player to well, play with it. Even as a walking simulator, it gave you choices and let you change the game. The Stanley Parable played with your expectations about what would happen and what actually did happen.
Now a central conceit of The Beginner's Guide is a "real" story about a creator and the player. How you feel about the game in the end is probably going to depend a lot on how much of that story you actually believe. Because that "real" story is the justification the game has for its linear narrative, for why it restricts your choice as the player. At least for me that felt like a cop-out. I don't think it's a real story, and if it isn't completely fictionalized, it is at least partly falsified. And for the narrative the game tries to spin, what's the point if that's the case? What's the point if it isn't true?
Creators make fictionalized worlds and stories all the time. You don't need it to be real to make you feel something. But when someone tries to tell you something's true and you think they're lying, well it's hard to feel anything about it then. But what if it was true?
If the "real" story that The Beginner's Guide tells is actually true, then it's a completely linear game that plays with the idea of being a meta game. The narrative is used to justify a weaker type of game and restrictive mechanics, just for the sake of the narrative.
And if it isn't true? Then there's no point making a linear game playing with the idea of being a meta game. No point playing The Beginner's Guide instead of The Stanley Parable. If the whole point of the game is just about the player and the game he plays, then we've seen this done better in a dozen different ways.
***SPOILERS***

Since this game and the developers have always been pretty good in general, I thought the game was deserving of a review to solidify any skeptical want-to-buy-but-not-sure-if-game-is-actually-terrible browsers.
It is a sandbox zombie game. The gameplay is how you play. Singleplayer, multiplayer--doesn't matter. Pick a combination of skills and just create a person to become. For example, you can be a doctor/medic that will heal other players,(PVE or PVP) or a bandit on a PVP server. Or build a HUGE complex base. Or just drift and collect items. Or take off the clothes of every zombie you can find and make swatstikas by dropping each piece of clothing by hand on the ground. I've seen it all. That's another thing, just cruising a server is also very fun, the community usually entertains me legitimately through roleplay or through drama/absurdity.
Personally, I enjoy running around collecting all the items I MIGHT need, fighting zombies, leveling up skills, etc. Essentially I play this game to satisfy my hoarding and completionistic tendencies while somewhat interacting with other human beings. Who said videogames aren't good for you?

I was alive. Now I'm not.
I started in my house. It was a small little cottage, in a suburb close to the city.
But there was a couple of pieces of food in the fridge, so I knew I needed to go out and actually scavenge.
I did not know things were this bad though. Right when I stepped outside, one of them spotted me.
Not wanting to lead it inside, I ran around the outside of my house. Little did I know that an entire group of them waited around the other side.
I panicked and they spotted me. As they slowly shambled towards me, I ran back into my house into the bathroom. I frantically shut the door behind me. As soon as I did that I heard my windows shatter, along with pounding on my door and many low groans.
I knew I couldn't stay there.
I, as quietly as possible, snuck out my bathroom window while the horde pounded down my doors. I snuck past them and made my way to another small house down the road.
On my way I had to take down one of them with my fists. I frantically beat the infected woman down until each my blows were responded with a crunch. I searched her body to find a pistol and six bullets.
With that I felt invincible! Finally I had a weapon to use against them.
Now when I got there I was exhausted. My house was destroyed and I had nowhere to go and no one to even talk to. I didn't even bother to check the house or close the curtains. I just immediately sunk into the closest bed I could find. I quickly fell into a deep slumber...
Suddenly, I sprung up. I heard a window smash, and two figures were climbing through it, into my room. Terrified, I grab my pistol and fired at them, only landing about two shots.
That was my mistake. I heard hundreds of more groans outside. The sound was deafening. I sprinted through the house to escape. But just as I opened the door, another one of them was right behind it! I fell back, only to have one of the ones from earlier grab and bite my hand. I jerked it away, leaving my left hand cut and bleeding bad. I scrambled past them to the nearest room I could find.
As soon as I got in I slammed the door behind me. I was in another bathroom. But this one had no windows, no other doors, no ways to escape. As I turned back the way I came there was a loud 'thunk' on the door. It was quickly followed by another one.
Scared for my life, I sunk back into the corner. I was still bleeding badly and was starting to hurt real bad. I had no meds, so I took of my sweater and tore it up to form a makeshift bandage.
Hours pass. The banging on the door had continued relentlessly. I was still bleeding real bad and hurting even worse now. It felt like my bones would break with each move.
I was now starting to think I was infected.
That sudden thought of dying sparked something in me. I suddenly felt brave. I could take on whatever was outside. It didn't matter that I was half awake and starving. I could do it.
I powerfully swung the door open, only to knock back one of them onto the floor. It seems as if the rest of them just straight up and left after their meal "got away". I bravely stomped it down, and opened the door to take on the world.
I ran straight to the city in my fit of bravery.
But the city quickly ended my fit of bravery.

I bought this game when it was a tech demo. Back before Steam. Back before the game could even be called a game. I've watched it grow and evolve over the years. I really want to recommend it at this time, but I just can't.
They've essentially given up on creating any kind of single-player experience. They made a lot of promises early on about how it would be immersive and feel like a real world, but they constantly keep putting the immersive elements of the game on the backburner to cater to things that make multiplayer more appealing. Initially they said multiplayer would be "much further off" if it was a feature at all. I guess they decided against that plan.
The community is screaming at them, and any "official" comment is that "they're still working on NPCs". They've been working on NPCs for like seven years now. It's not going to happen, just face it.
I like the progress the game has made over the years, sure. But I bought the game for the things they said it would become. I supported THAT Project Zomboid. Not this one.
At this point, the game is essentially a survival game like ARK, RUST or Conan Exiles that requires heavy modification to get any immersive elements. If that is appealing to you, go for it. For anybody looking for a dark, gritty and immersive (and complete) single-player experience.... you won't find it here. This game is an inventory managment sim with a little bit of crafting, a little bit of farming, a little bit of gun handling, a little bit of everything, but nothing substantial in any one area.
If you want an example of what I'm talking about.... look at the store page image. The man with the backpack. It has been their image for a LONG time, and you can neither see your backpack on your body, nor can you carry a weapon in one hand. Seriously. What are these devs even doing that simple cosmetic features do not get added after like five years of having a functional game...?

Disappointment. That's what I feel after playing this game. I wanted to like it so much and it has a lot of potential and appealing aspects, but looking beyond the amazing atmosphere of a black and white platformer and there's only disappointment.
I expected a fun puzzle game that provided a good challenge, but instead it's a do-everything-at-the-perfect-time-or-you-fail-while-being-timed-already type of game where every task feels trivial and doesn't give you with a sense of achieving anything. The puzzles aren't even difficult, simply tedious, and after completing one and moving on to the next there's no feeling of excitement to overcome the challenge of the game but rather dread that the next puzzle is going to take even longer to get the timing right. And the one after that even longer. And the one after that even longer.
I was hoping for some sense of a story, for some feeling that accompanied the atmosphere and haunting connection of being in LIMBO, but it's simply not there. And the lack of any sense of this makes everything you do in the game feel like you are mindlessly completing poorly designed puzzles. Not to mention the physics in the game can be a bit questionable and the controls have issues with response, and you're only getting more tedious things to deal with to make the challenge of the game.
Unless you are passionate about this genre, I can't even suggest picking it up in a sale. It feels highly overhyped simply because of its atmosphere and potential.

This is an old 2D side scroller that might be called a "precision platformer" if it was released today. Although your character can run and jump, the game is largely based around using your laser beam both to shoot enemies and as a jetpack type thruster. It is difficult to describe how poorly this is implemented. The "jetpack" provides different arbitrary levels of thrust depending on which direction it is pointed and when it's fired. Some reviewers claim that some hidden random number generator controls the output, but that is not true -- the physics are total nonsense but they are the same nonsense every time. Aiming directly at the ground and firing always produces the same strange slo-mo super jump. Aiming to the left or right on the ground always pushes you the opposite direction with no acceration whatsoever. Jumping and firing left or right  sends you hurtling across the screen like scarecrow strapped to a jet engine. Jumping and firing down does basically nothing. Firing right/left and then swinging the thruster down results in nothing: no super jump, even if you are grounded. It makes no sense and feels deeply unsatisfying but it can be learned. Helpfully, the checkpoints come quickly and the game is mercifully over after three hours or so. Sprinkled on top of the central dysfunction are various other mechanics, including a piece of cake that transformes you into a fat bowling ball and a truly  wretched bullet hell sequence. These are mere diversions though -- little more than mini games. The meat of NTTE is imprecise "precision" platforming punctuated by infuriating boss fights. All of this is wrapped in a moldy layer of newgrounds style early internet humor. I hated hated HATED this game. Forget paying, this is just not worth your time.

This is what I'd call an atmospheric trial and error simulator.
The strong point is the atmosphere: the lighting, the ambient sound and the minimalist contextual storytelling which slowly, horror by horror, unveils one of the grimmest video game worlds the medium has ever seen. Bravo on that point.
Then we have the mechanics, inevitably the core of any game. The verb set is fairly rudimentary; you can run, jump, climb, push and pull things, and that about summarises it. The mileage you can get out of these basic actions, coupled with some rudimentary physics, is fairly limiting. But from what I saw of Limbo, the designers compensated somewhat for the repetitive nature of the puzzles by dressing them up in some inventive and creepy set pieces, each one revealing more about the world you find yourself in. So I was ok with the mechanics, at first.
Where the game fell apart for me is the checkpoint trial and error nature of the gameplay. The world of Limbo is so perilous that you're only ever a few footsteps away from the next new death animation, and the problem is that for the most part these are not telegraphed to the player. By telegraphed I mean to have just a second where the player senses imminent danger and can react accordingly if they are thinking on their feet. There are too many cases where this doesn't happen in Limbo, such is the sudden and unpredictable nature of many of the traps and hazards. The result of this is that the player is soon conditioned to move forward expectant of death. And the designers know this, that's why there is a checkpoint before and after every little puzzle, trap and monster. So the combined effect of both expecting death and knowing that it's of no consequence results in the player pushing onward carelessly, allowing themselves to be killed and then hoping to learn from their death how to overcome the section on the next attempt. Or the third, fourth or fifth attempt.
Unfortunately this no-consequence, checkpoint kind of gameplay adds an extra layer of repetition onto mechanics already inherently repetitive (as mentioned). But worse, much worse, is that it saps any kind of fear or tension from this wonderfully atmospheric world that has been crafted. With no reason to worry about death, no reason to feel triumphant at a near-miss, and no reason for the palms to sweat because of the high stakes and terror, the power of that atmosphere is stripped away. And without that atmosphere what is left behind amounts to an assault course of trial and error physics puzzles that you will attempt dispassionately, again and again, until eventually they just come to bore and irritate you.

It's often hilarious, and there will always be someone to step up and rule the throne after a king dies. They can earn nicknames through feats of heroism, love, treachery and everything in between.
If ruling a kingdom is your fantasy, but you can't be bothered with the tedium of grand strategy games, this is the game for you.

If you've ever played a creepy black-and-white platformer, it doubtless owes Limbo a debt for paving the way. Its release on Xbox Live Arcade nearly seven years ago practically opened up a new genre of platformers to explore, those that unsettle and perplex with their ominous atmosphere and threatening aesthetic. We're a long way out from those heady days, and it's worth considering how well Limbo holds up now especially in the wake of its spiritual successor, Inside. But I can tell you up front, even coming to it now for the first time you won't be disappointed.
Limbo starts you off with no fanfare whatsoever, as a silhouetted child awakening in a forest. With no guidance you head rightward in search of something, probably not the deadly traps and machines and creatures that you find, though. Your journey will take you through the darkest parts of the forest, the forgotten corners of industry, and the decrepit heights of the city, with death awaiting you at every turn. There are no items and no real enemies, just you scrambling through a world that feels like it very much does not want you there.
As far as gameplay goes, you run, jump, climb, and push things. Your jump is a sad little hop that skews pretty hard on the realistic side, but levels are designed with this in mind and being more ground-bound helps keep your options focused. You'll need to do plenty of mantling up ledges and swinging on ropes, along with no shortage of crate pushing, log pushing, rock pushing, and so on. These skills will help you traverse the dangerous territories of Limbo, usually by overcoming some basic trap or hazard but later by clearing a path through more complex puzzle rooms.
It's important to note that the traps and puzzles never feel contrived, as they always have some discernible purpose in the bleak world you find yourself in. Spike pits and bear traps were clearly built by someone, machines have gears and hatches to negotiate, and the creatures you meet behave in strange and wild ways as suits their designs. Puzzles in Limbo tend to be the gratifying kind, the ones that make you feel clever for sorting them out even if they're simple to begin with. It's thanks to some straight-forward design that makes solutions seem obvious, along with some excellent environmental detailing that helps obscure the most obvious parts.
There are aspects of the game that are left too vague, however. Limbo has no shortage of ways to kill your hapless child but isn't always clear on how it plans to do it. A lot of deaths can easily be described as cheap the first time you encounter them by springing an unseen trap or not reacting to some new mechanic quick enough. The prime example for me is a pair of crushers in a cave about 1/3 of the way in. The first one has a raised plate, and if you step on it, you're safe; stepping on any other part kills you. The second one is the exact opposite, with the plate calling down instant death. This kind of design guarantees that nearly every single player will die at least once here, with survival being a literal matter of luck.
Death isn't a big deal in Limbo because the checkpoints are numerous and respawning happens swiftly. Still, the frequent unforeseen deaths have the potential to frustrate and are only really mitigated by how well they fit with the atmosphere. The lo-fi monochrome graphics give the game a terribly ominous and solitary feel that is built upon by the many unsettling and downright disturbing sights you'll come across. Atmosphere is Limbo's greatest asset, with few games even getting close to its horrific feel. Every time you see a new creature or device or even a shadow in the background you'll be wondering if you should fear it, even though you likely will already.
The sharp design elements that made Limbo an instant classic so many years ago have not dulled in the slightest. The aesthetic is still at the top of the genre, the puzzles remain clever and rewarding despite a glut of similar platformers, and the simple gameplay does not get old through the 2 or so hours it will take to finish (though be prepared for an extremely abrupt and unclear ending). There are some secrets to find if you're diligent, but really the beautiful, haunting journey is what you want to focus on here. It's just as good as it was at release, and anyone who likes their platformers creepy should have already gotten on this by now.

I want to start off by saying the first time I sat down to play this with my friends, we played for 8 hours straight.  I don't really remember the last time I did that.
The teams are well balanced, which is quite impressive given the default 1v4 setup.  The feeling of trampling hunters as the Monster is quite satisfying, but is counteracted by the first stage or two of the match by the feeling of being hunted while your are vulnerable.  Likewise, the thrill of hunting your prey as the Hunter starts to diminish into despair as the creature steadily gets more and more dangerous.  Regardless, at no point do I feel like the fight is hopeless and I should just give up.
The characters themselves are well done as well.  Despite being part of the same class, each different hunter has varying abilities that change their approach to filling that role.  This gives you great variety in how you deal with each situation, and gives you more options to make sure you have fun no matter what role you are filling.
Now all this said there are a couple of drawbacks.  I'm sure I'm not the only one that feels this way, but for me, games like this are only as fun as the people I can play them with.  Playing solo with bots just isn't as satisfying as playing with your buddies.  If you don't have a few friends you can jump into a match with, this may not be the game for you.  The other draw back is the DLC.  Most people that have rated this game poorly did so because they disagreed with the nickel and dime approach that 2K and Turtle Rock seem to have implemented.  While I do dislike the way they seem to be trying to money grab with this, I feel if you simply don't buy the DLC that sends a pretty clear message.  Most of the DLC is just alternate skins for the monsters, or hunter weapons, so they make zero difference to the game play anyway.
In summary, I would absolutely recommend this to anyone looking for a fun coop experience.  All of the Pros outweigh the Cons and it comes together into something that is not quite like anything else out there.

Be very careful when deciding whether or not you should buy this game. I’ve purchased it and found it to be a massive let-down. The game has a distinct lack of features, is very difficult to learn, and is a very frustrating game to play.
The game extremely confusing to play; upon joining a server for the first time, I found it impossible to find any enemies. I searched the map for at least 15 minutes before being taken out by a sniper in the distance. Upon re-spawning, I didn’t have any issues finding enemies; however, I did have issues killing them. Every time I ran towards the enemy lines, I would just get gunned down every time. This was a very frustrating experience; because I am used to other similar games (such as Call of Duty) I was using the normal tactic commonly found in COD. This, for whatever reason, is not effective in Red Orchestra 2, and instead you must camp and wait for enemies to come into your line of sight. The most frowned upon “tactic” used in Call of Duty is the only valid tactic in Red Orchestra 2. In my opinion, that is just due to lazy game design.
Something else which I found to be extremely stupid is that not everyone can have access to an automatic weapon. Instead, most players on the server are forced to use a bolt action rifle against their will. This is not only a bad game design choice (since we are forced to use a weapon that we might not want to use), but it also doesn’t make any sense from a realistic point of view. If both sides had access to automatic weapons, wouldn’t they arm all of their soldiers with them? Doesn’t make any sense to use the out-dated weaponry.
I also was disappointed to find that this game is set in the olden days. I find that modern warfare is much more exciting, strategic and enjoyable to play. There are a larger variety of weapons to choose from, alongside a diverse range of vehicles to choose from. I think that the game should have implemented both “olden day” and “modern day” game modes, at least in doing this there would be some variety in the game.
My final point is regarding the kill feed. There seems to be a glitch with the kill feed, in the sense that there is a delay between getting a kill and the kill appearing on the kill feed. In superior titles (such as COD), the kill feed can be used as a means of checking to see if the enemy is dead. For example, if an enemy is in the distance, you can fire a few rounds at the enemy, and then simply check the kill feed to see if they are dead. In Red Orchestra 2, the enemy will often lie down after being shot at. It then becomes very difficult to tell if you have killed the enemy or not, which is often misleading. Fixing the kill feed bug will fix this issue, but the devs do not seem interested in fixing it.
Whatever you do, stay away from Red Orchestra 2. It’s nowhere near as good as others are saying it is. There are a magnitude of poor design decisions which have made this game unplayable. Avoid!

A refreshing & alternative take on the "lone wolf survivor" genre - which (if you include co-op survival games) has essentially been overdone in recent times.  The core element of the game is to survive.  Loot, sneak, kill, repeat to paraphrase a popular song of 2013.
The thing that impressed me the most about the game was the environment - the randomly generated areas are great and depending on where you are (industrial, moors, mountains etc.) you will have a different experience dependant on how easily you can get from point A to point B, who you may or may not encounter along the way and how much cover you might be afforded.
The humour is another element of the game which is great, from the robots screaming "Ah! me leg" when they're caught in a bear trap, to the ability for the player to set up an alarm clock or a model train set as a distraction, the game will both surprise and humour you.
Would easily recommend it to someone who is jaded with the whole zombie scene of survival games or is a bit of a steam-punk fan - or they just want a fun & humourous game.  Whatever way you look at it, Sir (or Madame), you are being hunted is a bit of fun and you can make it as casual or intense as you like.

A neat gem of a game from the past that I think would be worth your time and money, Ghost Master explores a concept that will maybe remind you of Dungeon Keeper and other games where you are the "bad guy". In this case, you'll control a group of ghosts, called "haunters", in an attempt to scare the hell out of mortals. It's a Strategy/Puzzle game, and some missions require you to complete different tasks from scaring. Most of these special tasks involve using mortals to interact with certain objects that your ghosts can't use (not correctly, at least). All the ghosts are unique as each one of them as their starting skills and base behaviour (altough many details are never addressed by the game, it's something you pick up with experience). All of them have their special fetter, or a place where you can "bind" them, or summon them in the livings' world. Fetters vary from free roaming to being linked to a peculiar condition, with varying rarity. Often, strict links mean powerful ghosts. Most of the ghosts will be locked at the beginning, and will need to be rescued during missions. Each one of them as its unique rescuing requirement. But I already spoiled too much, I'll let your curiosity take over and try out this little art piece ;).

This is what I'd call an atmospheric trial and error simulator.
The strong point is the atmosphere: the lighting, the ambient sound and the minimalist contextual storytelling which slowly, horror by horror, unveils one of the grimmest video game worlds the medium has ever seen. Bravo on that point.
Then we have the mechanics, inevitably the core of any game. The verb set is fairly rudimentary; you can run, jump, climb, push and pull things, and that about summarises it. The mileage you can get out of these basic actions, coupled with some rudimentary physics, is fairly limiting. But from what I saw of Limbo, the designers compensated somewhat for the repetitive nature of the puzzles by dressing them up in some inventive and creepy set pieces, each one revealing more about the world you find yourself in. So I was ok with the mechanics, at first.
Where the game fell apart for me is the checkpoint trial and error nature of the gameplay. The world of Limbo is so perilous that you're only ever a few footsteps away from the next new death animation, and the problem is that for the most part these are not telegraphed to the player. By telegraphed I mean to have just a second where the player senses imminent danger and can react accordingly if they are thinking on their feet. There are too many cases where this doesn't happen in Limbo, such is the sudden and unpredictable nature of many of the traps and hazards. The result of this is that the player is soon conditioned to move forward expectant of death. And the designers know this, that's why there is a checkpoint before and after every little puzzle, trap and monster. So the combined effect of both expecting death and knowing that it's of no consequence results in the player pushing onward carelessly, allowing themselves to be killed and then hoping to learn from their death how to overcome the section on the next attempt. Or the third, fourth or fifth attempt.
Unfortunately this no-consequence, checkpoint kind of gameplay adds an extra layer of repetition onto mechanics already inherently repetitive (as mentioned). But worse, much worse, is that it saps any kind of fear or tension from this wonderfully atmospheric world that has been crafted. With no reason to worry about death, no reason to feel triumphant at a near-miss, and no reason for the palms to sweat because of the high stakes and terror, the power of that atmosphere is stripped away. And without that atmosphere what is left behind amounts to an assault course of trial and error physics puzzles that you will attempt dispassionately, again and again, until eventually they just come to bore and irritate you.

If you've ever played a creepy black-and-white platformer, it doubtless owes Limbo a debt for paving the way. Its release on Xbox Live Arcade nearly seven years ago practically opened up a new genre of platformers to explore, those that unsettle and perplex with their ominous atmosphere and threatening aesthetic. We're a long way out from those heady days, and it's worth considering how well Limbo holds up now especially in the wake of its spiritual successor, Inside. But I can tell you up front, even coming to it now for the first time you won't be disappointed.
Limbo starts you off with no fanfare whatsoever, as a silhouetted child awakening in a forest. With no guidance you head rightward in search of something, probably not the deadly traps and machines and creatures that you find, though. Your journey will take you through the darkest parts of the forest, the forgotten corners of industry, and the decrepit heights of the city, with death awaiting you at every turn. There are no items and no real enemies, just you scrambling through a world that feels like it very much does not want you there.
As far as gameplay goes, you run, jump, climb, and push things. Your jump is a sad little hop that skews pretty hard on the realistic side, but levels are designed with this in mind and being more ground-bound helps keep your options focused. You'll need to do plenty of mantling up ledges and swinging on ropes, along with no shortage of crate pushing, log pushing, rock pushing, and so on. These skills will help you traverse the dangerous territories of Limbo, usually by overcoming some basic trap or hazard but later by clearing a path through more complex puzzle rooms.
It's important to note that the traps and puzzles never feel contrived, as they always have some discernible purpose in the bleak world you find yourself in. Spike pits and bear traps were clearly built by someone, machines have gears and hatches to negotiate, and the creatures you meet behave in strange and wild ways as suits their designs. Puzzles in Limbo tend to be the gratifying kind, the ones that make you feel clever for sorting them out even if they're simple to begin with. It's thanks to some straight-forward design that makes solutions seem obvious, along with some excellent environmental detailing that helps obscure the most obvious parts.
There are aspects of the game that are left too vague, however. Limbo has no shortage of ways to kill your hapless child but isn't always clear on how it plans to do it. A lot of deaths can easily be described as cheap the first time you encounter them by springing an unseen trap or not reacting to some new mechanic quick enough. The prime example for me is a pair of crushers in a cave about 1/3 of the way in. The first one has a raised plate, and if you step on it, you're safe; stepping on any other part kills you. The second one is the exact opposite, with the plate calling down instant death. This kind of design guarantees that nearly every single player will die at least once here, with survival being a literal matter of luck.
Death isn't a big deal in Limbo because the checkpoints are numerous and respawning happens swiftly. Still, the frequent unforeseen deaths have the potential to frustrate and are only really mitigated by how well they fit with the atmosphere. The lo-fi monochrome graphics give the game a terribly ominous and solitary feel that is built upon by the many unsettling and downright disturbing sights you'll come across. Atmosphere is Limbo's greatest asset, with few games even getting close to its horrific feel. Every time you see a new creature or device or even a shadow in the background you'll be wondering if you should fear it, even though you likely will already.
The sharp design elements that made Limbo an instant classic so many years ago have not dulled in the slightest. The aesthetic is still at the top of the genre, the puzzles remain clever and rewarding despite a glut of similar platformers, and the simple gameplay does not get old through the 2 or so hours it will take to finish (though be prepared for an extremely abrupt and unclear ending). There are some secrets to find if you're diligent, but really the beautiful, haunting journey is what you want to focus on here. It's just as good as it was at release, and anyone who likes their platformers creepy should have already gotten on this by now.

BioShock is more than just a normal first-person shooter. The combat system is innovative, the game design suits the late 1960s style of the story and the story itself is stunning. Nearly every electronic device such as vending machines, safes, doors and security bots can be hacked. Nevertheless, the crucial element is the story. The story is set in the 1960s and takes place in the underwater city Rapture, where the player encounters different charackters, one being more crazy than the other. The game creates a dark atmosphere with moments of horror, which underline the plot. All in all, BioShock is still worth its money!

I've played a lot of different puzzle/logic games in my time, and I've come to be a bit picky about what I'm willing to sit down and spend time on. Usually the difficulty ratchets up way too fast, or never goes up at all, and I end up either disappointed or frustrated into a ragequit. LYNE, however, creates just enough of a good curve with each level to make me feel the difficulty is increasing without feeling like each new puzzle is impossible to beat.
It has a simple interface, just lines, colors, and shapes, which I find is much more pleasing than the alternative of a complex, intricate, and sometimes deceptive setting trying to cover up the lack of good content in a game. It's not a game you can sit down in one go and complete fully. But to me, that's a really good thing.
There's a flow to the game, and sometimes you can complete 3 or 4 levels in a row without much thought only to get stuck on solving the next level. But often the flow will come back, and you'll breeze through 3 or 4 more. Like I said, it's not a game that can be completed in one sitting, but I've never found myself on the edge of ragequitting no matter how long I have to spend on a level to finish it.
10/10 would recommend for the puzzle/logic game lover out there.

I purchased Bioshock as part of the triple pack.  Before playing through the trilogy, if it can be called that, I didn't know anything at all about the series other than there was something called a Big Daddy.  I wasn't wearing nostalgia goggles while going into this one.
The first Bioshock plays like a survival horror first person shooter.  It has tons of jump scares, eerie sounds, and gory scenery.  That said, I'm not a fan of jump scares, they have always felt banal to me.  Survival horror has never been my genre. I remember enjoying watching friends play through the Resident Evil series more than playing the games myself.  Eventually, perhaps due to overuse, the shock of the jump scares wear off.
Not unlike Resident Evil 1 and 2, Bioshock's storyline is more interesting than its gameplay.  It is what kept me playing the game.  The undersea wonderland of Rapture, Andrew Ryan, and the unfortunately underutilized licensed music were all spectacular.  It made me wish we were somehow able to see more of the city before it descended into its current state.  It is easy to see why so many people still talk about the Bioshock series today.  As far as the gameplay goes, it is worth mentioning that upgrading your character was fun, and that the hacking mechanic felt fairly creative.  There seemed to be enough variety of upgrades to grant the game some level of replay value.
If you see the triple pack on sale (or perhaps just Bioshock 1) I'd say that it is worth picking up. I don't feel that the game has aged well enough to warrant the full price cost of $19.99 USD.  Out of the three games it has the best story and the worst gameplay.

I want to start off by saying the first time I sat down to play this with my friends, we played for 8 hours straight.  I don't really remember the last time I did that.
The teams are well balanced, which is quite impressive given the default 1v4 setup.  The feeling of trampling hunters as the Monster is quite satisfying, but is counteracted by the first stage or two of the match by the feeling of being hunted while your are vulnerable.  Likewise, the thrill of hunting your prey as the Hunter starts to diminish into despair as the creature steadily gets more and more dangerous.  Regardless, at no point do I feel like the fight is hopeless and I should just give up.
The characters themselves are well done as well.  Despite being part of the same class, each different hunter has varying abilities that change their approach to filling that role.  This gives you great variety in how you deal with each situation, and gives you more options to make sure you have fun no matter what role you are filling.
Now all this said there are a couple of drawbacks.  I'm sure I'm not the only one that feels this way, but for me, games like this are only as fun as the people I can play them with.  Playing solo with bots just isn't as satisfying as playing with your buddies.  If you don't have a few friends you can jump into a match with, this may not be the game for you.  The other draw back is the DLC.  Most people that have rated this game poorly did so because they disagreed with the nickel and dime approach that 2K and Turtle Rock seem to have implemented.  While I do dislike the way they seem to be trying to money grab with this, I feel if you simply don't buy the DLC that sends a pretty clear message.  Most of the DLC is just alternate skins for the monsters, or hunter weapons, so they make zero difference to the game play anyway.
In summary, I would absolutely recommend this to anyone looking for a fun coop experience.  All of the Pros outweigh the Cons and it comes together into something that is not quite like anything else out there.

I remember this game rather fondly when I played it when it  first came out a few years back, Playing it now I only have one word, for it: Stale.
It's kinda hard to pin down why, because on paper it all should work. It's a Star Wars game where they add Ground control style combat on land, Star trek Armada Style space combat (which was a pretty good RTS, not AMAZING but it worked) with Hyperspacing mechanics that allow you to reinforce just about anywhere.

Sounds great right?
Well it just doesn't play as well as it sounds on paper. Again it's  hard to describe but it all just feels so bland. The units aren't terribly interesting (except some heroes), the textures are plain, yet muddy, and it all feels like they took a lot of concepts that were AMAZING in other RTS games (Ground Control's Dropzone mechanics, CNC Tanks, Company of Heroes' Squads, Dawn of War: Dark Crusade's Risk map, Yes I am aware some of these came after this, but they still did it better) but didn't properly understand WHY those mechanics worked the way they did in those games and thus it ended up watering it all down.
Granted if you are a fan of the Extended Universe before Disney De-canonized it you'll get a kick out of the extra units and characters (Where else will you have Kyle Kataran throw down with Mara Jade?). but all in all, to me it feels very bland and watered down.

Will it ever NOT be in early access? This is getting ridiculous, and I regret supporting an unfinished game, just like Starbound. It's been more than 4 years. 4 YEARS.
The main menu's 'theme song' or whatever it is of the women moaning and ooo-ing is infuriating to listen to, you get injured once and your speed goes down to a crawl, and only injure yourself farther the more you move. Realistic, sure, but that doesn't mean it's fun when you get in 1 minor scuffle with a zombie and die 2 days later just trying to recover in bed.
The world is dead, no NPC's around ever, it's just you waking up in some house surrounded by thousands of zombies in a town. I sometimes hear helicopters pass by over head, but I don't think those are actually for anything.
I remember playing it a few years ago with that starting tutorial story with the injured wife and husband, that showed promise! where is that? where is ANYTHING like that? theres almost nothing to this game it feels. Theres farming, but you can just scavenge for food forever it seems. You can build safe houses, but why not just fortify an already built house?
There are 2 maps and I can't tell the difference between either of them. You can level up your character but it doesn't seem to have any real impact on gameplay.
You can venture around outside and get weapons and guns to make finding food easier because you don't need to worry about zombies so much, but then they break or run out of ammo and you need to find more weapons so you can find more food so you can survive longer so you can just repeat until you die.
If there was actual NPC's to interact with then the game could start getting some semblence of a goal, you find some guy out in the city, befriend him, trade resources & help each other out, find more survivors and make a community together, all while dealing with zombies and hunger problems and other hostile survivors!
But no, the game doesn't have that.
This wouldn't annoy me so much if the game has only been around for a few months, but this simply isn't the case and the game has just sat in my library for years now even when I bought it back on Desura because it wasn't avaliable on steam.  Is 4 years not enough time to make a game and get it out of early access? Apparently not!
It feels like they're just using the term "Early Access" as a shield for their unfinished game they don't want to work on. But I don't know that, it's just what it feels like after waiting so long.
The 15 hours i've played is more like 15 1 hour sessions checking to see if the game has gotten any better, and so far, I wish that I could refund this game.

I've been following Project Zomboid on and off since very early builds, and can say I definitely recommend it maybe.
The UI is clunky as hell, but other than that, the game is incredibly clever and ambitious and continues to get moreso with each update. Everything about it is pretty much the paradigm of a zombie-survival simulation. Good loot is rare and requires a great deal of fairly risk scavenging. The game's systems make each and every zombie encounter feel like a real threat, whether it's just one zed that came in through a window or a thousand zombies rushing in as the horde shambles by your home base. And they're just part of the problem! Issues arise if your character gets hungry, tired, scared, or even bored. Not to mention the issues of learning to live with the appliances in game and not burn down your base. Or learning to live without your appliances as the zombie apocalypse starts to take its toll on the power supply and other norms of everyday life.
If you like roguelikes and survival games and have a fascination with zombies, definitely give it a go; it's already great and constantly getting better. If you're kind of burned out on the whole zombie thing, you might want to keep looking.

This game is so interesting and fresh, amidst a genre that doesn't feel particularly fresh most of the time. My only complaint is that it's pretty short, outside of endless mode. I would get it at a discount, if possible. However, I really liked it and now I want to play it in VR.

It's a good game, I definitely think it's unique with the old cartoon esque art style and the amazing jazz/music. I am slightly disappointed with how short it felt, but understood why it was relatively short (It has an expert difficulty setting that  makes the game more difficult after you beat the final boss the first time, but I still wanted there to be more bosses, I honestly didn't want it to end, but also hoped for more gameplay wise and etc).
There's not too much content that comes with this game besides unique boss stages ( they were all amazingly different from one another, so they never really got old), annoying run and gun levels, and these protect the urn levels. This game is all action with little dialogue and some cutscenes/story to it (besides the map that you can explore). That being said, the gameplay is very smooth and polished from what I have seen. I believe it plays out like Megaman, it's a 2d platformer  where you simply dodge enemies, continously shoot at them, and "parry" pink objects. It isn't as difficult as everyone says.  It's only punishing unless it has reached expert mode *even if you can only get hit 3 times *( there is no penalty for losing). But even if you are struggling with the game, the OST and sound of the game is amazing to listen to while failing/leaning the enemy patterns .
The game also has a sign of forgiveness with the items that can be bought in game or simply lowering the difficulty if necessary, or the game can be played to extreme and trying to make it as hard as possible.
Yeah, it's pretty fun, don't really see it as a game that can be played over and over again though.  I do hope to see more or even just a continuation from the devs as dlc....I was hoping for more content tbh, but I was pleased with what I got or at least satisfied . I don't know if I am going to be able to play this on expert mode for too long though, probably will attempt to finish this up, but overall, it's a good game.

Well, was not expecting to like Reigns this much, anything that looks like it belongs on a phone I tend to avoid, but I heard good things, and as it turns out what I heard was accurate. For it being a simple game of yes or no or this or that, it's actually pretty deep if you want to reign for any real amount of time. Choices you make will either come back to bite you, or save your bacon, some making the game easier and others harder. Reigns has a very suitable sense of humor, it never made me laugh out loud, but I found myself with a frequently recurring smirk that was accompanied by a chuckle from time to time. The humor of the game is very fitting for the art style and the game itself, and knowing what you are is an underrated trait; a trait this game has in spades and then clearly used to tailor the rest of the game around it to form a very concise and tight gameplay package wrapped in charming wit and a simple yet visually entertaining art style.

I got this game a while ago and seeing it pop up in the Humble Bundle made me think this was a good time to revisit it.
Unfortunately, I can't *not* recommend this game enough. I know I haven't played much of it but that's not for lack of trying.
Pros:
Apparently, if you play enough of it, it has a story that's not too bad?
Cons:
- Controls.
The controls are absolutely infuriating. You walk at a snail's pace and the jump is so pitiful that it may as well have been removed from the game. You "jump" about as high as your character is tall which makes it good for literally nothing. All of your movement comes from your weapon.
- Sound.
The music seems to be a poor attempt at a callback to retro games but it's repetetive and grating. It's a fully-voiced game, and on top of the poor sound quality the "jokes" fall flat. All of its humor comes from a "lol so randomz!" standpoint, resulting in a weak chuckle the first time one comes up and an apologetic sigh the following times. In my half hour of play I heard "My insides and my outsides are in pain!" literally 10 times.
- Gameplay.
The biggest issue I have with this is that the gameplay itself just... isn't fun. Sure, it's a difficult platformer, but the difficulty comes from the controls rather than clever design. It has a few ideas that it toys around with for a level or two but never revisits them. It's usually an infinite-life platformer but will then toss you into a boss fight where suddenly lives are a thing. The boss fights are frustrating and give no information on what a boss can or will do until you've already died to it, a problem worsened by the fact that you die while just trying to get into position thanks to the poor controls.
Tl;dr, it's an interesting game that looks far more fun in the trailers than it actually is. The game just isn't worth it to play but looks interesting enough to try. It'd be a dissappointing game if it were $5, but selling this for $15 is insane.

is a small, ported-from-mobile game that is nonetheless very interesting. You "swipe" left and right (more on that in a moment) to perform decisions which will affect your kingdom. The land is represented by three groups, the Church, the people, and the army, with the last factor being your treasury. From a pure gameplay perspective, the difficulty comes from trying to balance all four "meters", because both too little and too much focus put into any of them leads to a game over. This is hard at first but after a while, you simply remember what each card and each decision do, and learn to act on them instinctively.
You may actually be surprised that there is a story to this game — a kind of meta-storyline that occurs in between the lives of your many monarchs. I don't want to spoil anything here but the game maneuvers very deftly between a funny and light-hearted atmosphere and something more horror-like.
The atmosphere in the game, by the way, is overall really great. The soundtrack features something like a medieval monk choir, the illustrations are simple but fantastic, and even the flavor text, anachronistic as it is, somehow manages to reflect, in a humorous and irreverent way, the realities of the middle ages.
The game, unfortunately, has some flaws, mostly related to the interface. The controls were clearly designed for touchscreens and just don't make as much sense in a desktop environment. Whilst they're nice when you get used to them, for all their simplicity they were surprisingly hard for me to figure out initially. The game offers very little in the way of explanation (of anything, really), so that didn't help. Also, scrolling feels sort of laggy for me.
(There is also the obvious fact that the game, even with its hundreds of cards, is rather small when compared to many other, especially mainstream games. I've seen some people complain about that in other reviews. You really should be able to tell what you're getting by looking at the screenshots and the description, and the price is entirely appropriate. Also, if you aspire to find out all the secrets this game has, it will still take you many hours.)

is that it is one of the few, I think, games that bridge the divide between "casual" and "hardcore" gaming. I mean, I don't believe there are many "gamers" who could honestly say they never played any timewaster mobile game. But still, there is a big distinction between the kind of video games one part of the population tends to find enjoyable and the kind that the other part prefers.

I want to start off by saying the first time I sat down to play this with my friends, we played for 8 hours straight.  I don't really remember the last time I did that.
The teams are well balanced, which is quite impressive given the default 1v4 setup.  The feeling of trampling hunters as the Monster is quite satisfying, but is counteracted by the first stage or two of the match by the feeling of being hunted while your are vulnerable.  Likewise, the thrill of hunting your prey as the Hunter starts to diminish into despair as the creature steadily gets more and more dangerous.  Regardless, at no point do I feel like the fight is hopeless and I should just give up.
The characters themselves are well done as well.  Despite being part of the same class, each different hunter has varying abilities that change their approach to filling that role.  This gives you great variety in how you deal with each situation, and gives you more options to make sure you have fun no matter what role you are filling.
Now all this said there are a couple of drawbacks.  I'm sure I'm not the only one that feels this way, but for me, games like this are only as fun as the people I can play them with.  Playing solo with bots just isn't as satisfying as playing with your buddies.  If you don't have a few friends you can jump into a match with, this may not be the game for you.  The other draw back is the DLC.  Most people that have rated this game poorly did so because they disagreed with the nickel and dime approach that 2K and Turtle Rock seem to have implemented.  While I do dislike the way they seem to be trying to money grab with this, I feel if you simply don't buy the DLC that sends a pretty clear message.  Most of the DLC is just alternate skins for the monsters, or hunter weapons, so they make zero difference to the game play anyway.
In summary, I would absolutely recommend this to anyone looking for a fun coop experience.  All of the Pros outweigh the Cons and it comes together into something that is not quite like anything else out there.

Contrary to popular opinion, I believe Cuphead is an extremely accessible game. It's like riding a bike, it seems impossible until you learn what you need to do, then it clicks and you never forget it. But the actual triumph of Cuphead is that it retains this accessibility while remaining very challenging.
The difficulty in Cuphead is extremely consistent and always comes from the same source--the attacks are designed to trip you up. What this means is that less skilled players will find the game challenging because the act of dodging is new and overwhelming, but more experienced players will
find the game challenging because the attacks are very unpredictable and heavily punish false prediction or overconfidence. The shot types are incredibly well balanced in that no matter what weapon you choose, or how often you use your supers, no phase of any boss can be "brute forced"--you HAVE to learn the boss, and once you do so, the game is very reliably complient. The feel of the control is incredibly tight and no boss in the game requires anything more than the basics: move, jump, parry. The hard part is always learning what to do, the easy point is executing it. Cuphead is an extremely responsive game.
The biggest flaw of Cuphead is, ironically, that the developers have focused so much work on this
great art style, that a certain degree of "gamey feedback" is lost due to the (very commendable) authenticity of the 1930s-visuals. The game looks EXACTLY like a technicolor cartoon, but health bars never appeared in cartoons, so they do not appear in Cuphead. This leads to a lot of situations where the player is somewhat unsure about what is actually going on--how much damage they're actually doing, whether or not an object has a hitbox or not, etc. In the absolute worst cases the background can actually cover up key information like bullets or Cuphead himself, which can lead to unexpected death--though thankfully this very rarely occurs.
I'm dead certain that this lack of feedback is
because of a lack of commitment towards accessibility. Quite the contrary, I believe Cuphead is as accessible as can possibly be without compromising it's art style--but in a select few cases, I think that compromising the art would have been worth it.

The Forest is a rare charm of a game which is a bit rough around the edges and has its fair share of bugs, but you can tell it is the love child of a developer with a vision rather than a heartless AAA project with a hundred contrasting ideas. The game itself take an interesting turn on the survival genre, forcing players to put quiet a fair amount of effort and experiment on different ways to survive against the cannibals.
The player learns the game incrementally, discovering different ways to use tools, different locations, buildings, and structures. Woven into the survival is the ‘story’ which is played out through a serious of dungeon like caves, caverns, and experiences. Nothing feels ‘tacked on’ and the survival/story elements work together seamlessly, even if the game only ‘truly’ opens up once the player learns the game. It manages to successfully pull off the typical rather steep but rewarding learning curve rarely seen in newer games. There’s a sense of accomplishment after finding a helpful item in a cave, beating the first mutant or creating the first base that can fend off cannibals without much personal input.
Some might be worried when they see what looks like a default Unity Engine launcher from the start, but after getting in the game I often found myself forgetting that I was in the Unity Engine. There are certainly some improvements to be made to the game, but in 3 years I think the game has come pretty far and I’ll be excited to see what else the developers choose to add to this game.
It’s hard to really target who the forest really appeals too. It’s got quiet a few elements built into one. There’s times it feels like a horror game, other times a survival/crafting games, sometimes a strategy game and now and again a dungeon crawler type RPG. I wouldn’t say there’s “Something for everyone” but If any 4 of those appeal, then it’s certainly worth a try.
