Here's the 10 steps of my first playthrough:
1) While looking for shelter, a wolf spots me.
2) I duck into a train tunnel to hide from the wolf.
3) Hours later, I see a buck run by - so I run like an idiot boy scout to chase it with a my gear clanking with each step.
4) Out of breath, I round the corner and see the buck! ...and I startle the wolf that was sneaking up on the same buck.
5) Wolf wants to kill me for spoiling his hunt, and charges me. I calmly aim down the sites of my rifle and pull the trigger. Oops, didn't load it...
6) Wolf attacks, and somehow I get a few good blows in with my rifle, before passing out in the snow from blood loss.
7) Miraculously, I wake up hours later and limp to the train tunnel to bandage my wounds. I may actually survive!
8) Night sets in. I try starting two fires, but both fail. I realize I survived a wolf attack, just to freeze to death tonight.
9) I limp from the train tunnel through a blizzard. I see a house in the distance! Within a stone's throw of the house, I collapse from my wounds and exhaustion, and freeze to death from the bitter cold - just as the sun was rising.
10) Stare at my screen, stunned at my epic permadeath, and start a new round.

.. One of my most played, if not THE most played game, and it's always surprising how I've bought this game back when it came out on Desura ages ago, I boot it up after going on hiatus a few months, and it's an all-new experience.
I'm sure you'll remember the first time you've bought yourself a copy of Photoshop and you couldn't even draw a line, right? Well, it's pretty much the same with Project Zomboid! If you're one of the lucky ones that picked it up from its very beginnings, it certainly was a more gentle learning curve. Back when you could jump through windows without needing a doctor's degree in how to mend simpe cutting wounds, but nonetheless, the game is fun.
In my opionion, the game is not for "casuals",
It's a harsh mistress, and it'll make you bend and kneel down for its own entertainment until you give it what it wants, so take the negative reviews with a grain of salt, unless you're certain people aren't whining about the game's difficulty.
Even though there's sandbox modes that make the game terribly easy, the moment you get yourself out there, the game is a harsh, unforgiving experience. Get bit? Eat dirt. That's how it goes. Jump through a window and get a cut? No first aid at hand? You bleed out. Managed to bandage your wound and get infected? Better stay in bed and drink those last bottles of whiskey. Sometimes, deaths can be depressing, but every single one of them is a harsh learning experience that you'll need to face to reach your goal of establishing a well-armed, self-sustaining camp some time in the future.
And that's just a small share, the list goes on and on. It's the small things that keep me coming back for more, be it that every patch, every new version brings such a great deal of nice, new features with it, or be it that this game just doesn't seem to die, ever. I can certainly remember a lot of other EA titles that *NEVER* got finished, and won't ever be touched again by their developers, but this game's developers seem to still run the game with a passion!
There's been regular updates for what - well over 5 years, if not more now, and each of them leaves you coming back for more, so if you're looking for a long-term game investment, this one is certainly worth the money!

I actually Live in Kentucky. :)
PZ doesn't kill you, bad decisions do. ;)
Pros
-----------------------------------
- The Map? HUGE, the devs are going to add Louisville(So I've heard) as well.
The map itself already sports four small towns, two of which are like mini cities in game, they are so big. The other two are like small towns(Still pretty big) Tons of woodland, farmhouses, hunting cabins and lakehouses. Gunstores, clothestores, supermarkets, trailer parks, and the Dreaded "The Mall."
The Mall has every item you could possibly want, But don't go there.
Saying "The Mall" to a PZ player is like saying "Voldemort" to Harry Potter.
*Everybody Shudders* (o.o)
The map is so big, you will probably never explore all of it in a week. I still haven't done it with all the hours I clocked in, I've barely scratched the surface.
You are currently only allowed to spawn in places like West Point and Muldraugh (the two mini cities)
but there are two smaller towns as well. One being called "Dixie" and the other Bedford (I think)
- Realism (You will find no other game like this, it is incredibly challenging and makes you feel like you're actually surviving a zombie apocalypse.)
The water and power gets shut off, Nature overgrowth after a period of time, roads crack, food rots, seasons change affecting survival dramatically.
You could live off berries and trapping in the summer, but expect to survive solely on traps in the winter, as food is scarce.
- Zombies (Because who doesnt love getting eaten at 3AM when you peek out of your safehouse)
-Zombies beat down doors, smash windows and follow you out of two story windows, albeit jumping.
They Also Horde up, so dont be suprised. :P
- Survival (Build traps, farm, build rain collectors, build your own house, walls, fish, forage, etc.)
- Live practically anywhere (Its definately a game about decisions, tactics, and overall using your head. If you try to be A Rambo, you generally wind up dead within about 2 game days at the least (Standard Survival mode time, about 1 whole hour) Though I have been killed in just mere 16 in game hours. That being said, You can live anywhere you want, in any house, or just live in the woods.
-Ridiculously challenging (Expect 1 zombie to do nothing to a door, but set off a house alarm and fail to leave the house in time, massive hordes will be beating down the front door in 20 seconds or less. Its realism in the game also makes it incredibly difficult as one bite and you're done. Zombies are everywhere, and one jump from a window, one untreated wound, eating a rotten bird or rabbit or just dehydration and you're done.
Just like in real life, death is everywhere in this game; and it finds you eventually. It's not really combat based, the gameplay is more centered towards survival, so it makes you think.
-It has Several mini games about trying to defend a house with randomly spawned items from hordes that increase in number. Great for Ingame strategy practice.
Hide behind that Bar with your ol' Twelve gauge and make a final stand, or barricade the windows and doors and ready that kitchen knife.
There was also a mini game where you wake up drunk in a burning house, but that brings back bad memories. I don't like to talk about it. ._.
-Sandbox Mode, which is probably the most played game mode in PZ. Customise everything about your game, from Make zombies Sprinters (Like 28 Days later) or make them Shamblers like "Night of the living dead". You can customize their senses, i.e. how well they can smell fresh blood(Dont cut yourself on broken glass from those windows. :P), how well they detect sound, how well they can see...
You can increase the Zombie amount, Loot amount, season, time, The abundance of farming, foraging etc.
You can basically set the scenario how you want.
But Survival mode is the challenge, the default play of the game. Few make it past 3 months, even fewer live to see winter.
There are those who have survived over a Year in game, and they are what our little PZ community like to call "Gods" because if you bought the game an knew the situation we PZ players face, you too would call them "Gods" :P
-Weapons: Whether you like it or not, sooner or later, you're going to have to fight. How you do that depends on what you prefer in real life. If you wanna kick open your safehouse and send the Undead back to hell with your sawnoff shotgun that you made, Go for it.
If you don't like guns and don't like the thought of stabbing with a knife, then nothing says "I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; like flailing a claw hammer or some other blunt instrument in an attempt to fight the undead.
If you like Sticking to the shadows or Sniping from the rooftops with your hunting rifle, they got Sniper rifles with Scopes.
If you're passive aggressive they got pistols, meaning whilst you're trying to get out of that Gun store you're looting alive, you pop a couple zombies that are in your way and flee into the night with your 9mm as the Undead hordes chase after you.
Keep to the shadows and live a quiet life with just your Club or blade, or be a tactical warrior who always looks to weigh any situation to their advantage, even if that means a couple boxes of 00 buckshot. (But Nothing says I'm pro like wiping out an undead horde with a camp fire.) :3
-Guns: they got em. Shotguns, pistols and hunting rifles(Pretty accurate for Kentucky) with Customizations from long range scopes, ammo straps and using a Hacksaw to really polish your scattergun, if you know what I mean. ;)
Lasers for the pistols, red dot sights, etc.
Ammo is pretty abundant if you know where to look. There are places to find guns all over the map, and zombies tend to drop pistols and ammo often (With the Lucky trait)
-Fortify your base: Just like in real life, you can desperately kick in doors and make planks to barricade windows if you think that a zombie eating you alive whilst you sleep is gonna be a problem.
Though nothing will save you if a horde comes and you chose to live in a one story house. D:
-Jobs: Your character will be who you want them to be. If you choose the police officer as the job you had before the outbreak, then you will be calm in panicky situations and good with a gun.
Lots of Jobs to choose from though.
- The Devs themselves are really loving, down to earth folks and respond to their customers and even ask for suggestions to add to the game. (Sometimes they even add it if they think its a good Idea) Which makes them unique. :)
Of course I could go on and on (Which I already have done) :P But you get the idea.
Its a really good game in that spectrum it offers far more than I mentioned, and I know its in Early access, so it isn't complete.
Cons
------------------------------------------------------------------
I live in Kentucky as I have stated, and the biggest problem I have seen that take away from realism in this game (Since it is based in Muldraugh) is that Kentucky is like most other states, except the people here, almost everyone and their grandmother owns guns, and hunting equipment. It rarely snows, and the summer heat is extremely intense, and it barely ever rains.
They got the extremely rural part right though. :P
-It rains too often in game (Kentucky rarely gets rain, so our crops die alot. And the snow thing, we get a good snow about every 3 years, so ingame it should probably be rarer. It's usually just rainy and cold.)
-Hunting and kitchen knives are rare in game, but in reality, Kentuckians own more knives than baseball bats, and golf clubs.
-Guns are extremely Rare,  in reality as I have stated, every other household has a Gun here. I would expect it to be different in Project Zomboid.
Shoot, I watched my little 60 year old granny cut tree branches down with a Scattergun. Wait, what are we talkin about again? :P Yall take it easy and be sure an give this review a like or two.

I've always been fascinated by the idea of an assymetric PvP Game, and
has been on my radar since reading about it in Game Infomer in January of 2014.
And i have got to say, Turtle Rock has delivered, the game is an absolute
to play.
In the premier "Hunt" Game mode it's 4 v 1 -- 4 hunters ranging in classes from support to damage, and your goal is to hunt down the monster and destroy it. If you're the monster, your job is to either wipe out the hunters or destroy the com relay.
I really enjoy the game, like a ton, and I am glad i ended up picking it up after waffling around following "DLC-gate" (more on that in a bit.). To be quite frank, the game gives me an adrenaline rush, particularly when i play with a competent team against a good monster(or vice versa but i'm a terrible monster). The classes are fun, and the way the leveling system is set up really forces you to understand the role before you can unlock the more advanced variations of said role. It sort of reminds me of the way Battlefield 3 did unlocks in terms of functionality, but it just doesn't feel as grindy. Also, the game looks spectacular, though i guess thats subjective.
So far i have always ended up with balanced teams (I play on PC) when i play with randoms, and for me at least, I've almost always been paired with some pretty fun folks when they had coms active. The gameplay itself also, has largely felt balanced-- though vs wraith is frustrating, but apparently there is a nerf coming.
I have found that the game has a pretty steep learning curve. Yeah sure, you can get the basics of each class/monster down in a couple of games, but if you approach Evolve as a generic cookie cutter CoD Shooter,
. Everything from sounds to carcasses to broken tree branches can point you in the direction of the monster. A good team can split in two and drive the monster into your own ambush-- where you place your arena matters just as much as placing it(Don't do it in a cavern!), and understanding when to engage and when to flee is incredibly important, And those are just a couple of examples. Really, Turtle Rock did a great job of delivering the feeling of an FPS with the strategic depth of a solid moba... and if you don't play moba's, they tend to have insane amount of depth.
This however, brings me to my next point.
It's possible to have great games with randoms, i've had a couple-- but if you really want a consistently fun experience, and really amp up your strategic depth, get your friends to buy the game or find a group on reddit or Gridom. That having been said, so far i still usually play solo and i still quite enjoy the experience.
like the rest of most, i was initially really turned off when this came out, but i have since made peace with it. The game in my opinion, carries tons of merit on it's own, and if you look at the majority of the negative reviews on steam they will all echo this sentiment, before launching into complaints about the DLC. These are some of the top negative reviews:
“Great Game, Solid all round in gameplay, competitive and a lot of replayability with different strats/compesitions...” - Mr. Farenheit
“Let me be perfectly honest, I absolutely had a blast playing this game in Alpha and Beta..” - Giddy Wraith
“So far I'm really liking this game...” - N8
The reason why i changed my mind is largely... well, honestly, it's several things. A major reason is because i later read somewhere that the reason why it was made so (DLC) compatible is so that they have the funding available to continually expand the game, rather than go on a bi-annual release like CoD or BF do (to name the two most prominent examples). And i can get behind that. I understand tyhat the cost of development has gone up, and that eventually intial sales of the game will taper off, so if devs want to continue expanding on the game they need to generate new revenue somehow through DLC-- or abandon the game and begin developing a brand new title (Evolve: Black ops the presequel anyone?!). The second, and perhaps this is a leap of faith on my part, but i sincerely believe that turtlerock studios really really cares about this game, just judging from how amped they are when i saw them speak on their twitch stream or whatever, how much emphasis they keep putting on wanting feedback from the community for balancing purposes... and i just don't think there is a deliberate attempt to fleece us by the devs-- hell, if anyone was watching the launch day stream yesterday, they are ultimately just a bunch of nerds that really ♥♥♥♥ing love video games.
I also want to point out that all DLC currently available, contrary to popular belief, is cosmetic. So what? I mean if the fact that you have to pay 5$ extra to plau 'wendigo' goliath (or whatever it is) detracts THAT much from your gaming experience, then you should reevaluate your priorities. And even beyond
I think turtle rock created a really fun and original multiplayer game, with tons of strategic depth, and is a game i think most of you would actually enjoy if you'd give it a chance. DLC isn't inherently a bad thing.
So if the premise of the game interests you, check out some videos on youtube, and if it interests you enough to buy it, please do so!

The Beginner's Guide starts with a promise. A promise that the developer will be as open with us as he can be if we are willing to open ourselves up to listen. And I did listen. This game enthralled me, because it was bold and unafraid to do things differently. I wasn't sure what the point was, exactly, but I trusted that Davey Wreden had something to say, something worth saying, and that he was speaking with a sincere voice.
He was not.
This doesn't have anything to do with how "real" the events of the game may or may not be. That doesn't much matter to me. What Davey Wreden reveals with The Beginner's Guide is that he refuses to play by his own rules. He uses the appearance of sincerity to win over the player's trust, then betrays them when they're most invested. For The Beginner's Guide, getting someone to feel strong emotions is a goal in and of itself. It wants to shock you, to be impactful by any means necessary. It takes no prisoners. The Beginner's Guide is like Lucy with the football, beckoning the Charlie Brown sitting behind their keyboard to run ten miles before kicking it, then pulling it away at the last second.
This game made me feel genuinely emotionally manipulated. As the credits started to roll, I got up and crawled into bed and cried. Not because the story itself was particularly sad, and not because I needed a healthy emotional release. I cried because I felt hopeless. I wondered how someone could be so cruel. I paid this person ten dollars and they fed me two hours of lies, then revealed the truth and kicked me in the gut and ran away. It was like I met someone who wanted to be my friend, and I opened up to them, made myself vulnerable to them, only to discover they were pretending the whole time. This game is a betrayal.
I know. I know how crazy this all sounds. It's a game, right? It's a video game. You know it's not real. It can't hurt you. But if games and stories can make you feel fear, joy, anger, exhilaration, and comfort, why couldn't it hurt you? Make you feel betrayed, manipulated?
I don't know Davey Wreden. I only know him through his work. I loved The Stanley Parable, and I admired him and empathized with him when he wrote a blogpost about his depression. I am also someone who has suffered from depression and anxiety. So I cannot for the life of me understand why he would create a game that treats emotion like nothing more than a tool, a means to an end. Why try to make people feel genuine discomfort and loss, when games, like all art at its best, can be used to spread joy and understanding and belonging? It might be okay if it was a horror game - you know what you're getting into. But that's not what The Beginner's Guide is, nor what it advertises itself to be.
The Beginner's Guide starts with a promise. A promise it spends over an hour doing everything it can to convince you is genuine. Then it takes all of five minutes to not just take it back, but reveal it was all a ruse, constructed solely to make you feel shock and terror and sadness.
The Beginner's Guide is a game about what it means to be an artist, from the perspective of someone who has entirely lost sight of that meaning. An artist reveals truths, presents with utmost sincerity some aspect of themselves. But Davey Wreden - both versions, the developer of The Beginner's Guide and its narrator/protagonist - speaks with no sincerity. I don't doubt that he's been through some very difficult emotions, experienced depression. I know what that can be like. But how he could wish someone else feel that too, I have no idea. Sincerity requires understanding that the person you're speaking with has opened themselves up to you just as you've opened up to them. Feigning sincerity to catch someone off guard when they're most emotionally vulnerable is manipulative and cruel. Davey is not acting here as an artist - he is a con man. The Beginner's Guide is a cruel trick. A promise made and a promise broken.
The Stanley Parable remains one of my favorite games ever. And I wanted to like this game too. I bought it the day it came out. All in all, there's some really cool ideas in it, and it's exciting to see people try new ways of designing games and constructing stories. And honestly, part of me wants to give The Beginner's Guide credit for making me feel such strong emotions - that's an admirable goal of art, right? The fact that it made me feel something and examine myself and think hard about what it was talking about - maybe The Beginner's Guide was a rousing success. But no. I hate this game. I hate how it made me feel. No game, or movie or show or book for that matter, has ever made me feel so dejected and depressed, brought about such deep anger. Maybe it'll be different for you - I hope it is. The amount of positive reviews clearly suggest that I'm in the minority. But as an aspiring artist myself, as well as just a human being, I never want to make anyone feel what The Beginner's Guide made me feel.

Not only does it feel nostalgic in animation and gameplay, but it also reminds me of when video games were actually difficult and didn't feel like you were just clicking the screen and something happened. Additionally, the game grades you on how well you do in a certain area, and does so fairly. Although this is a great game and I wouldn't discourage buying it, I feel as though the game is a little overrated and if it gets too out of hand it might burn out quickly. So if you plan on buying this game just because people have confused you into believing it is like Undertale, you may want to rethink your descision unless you like this type of game as well. I just played through this game's main storyline in one session. Here's what I think:
The Good:
+ The beam gun and the flinging shotgun are innovative plattforming mechanics.
+ The levels are visually varied and generally well designed. Checkpoints are usually placed quite generously and fairly.
+ Each chapter introduces new temporary environmental mechanics, which makes for a shortwhiled experience.
+ The overall pacing of the levels is quite good, none of the chapters or mechanics outstay their welcome.
+ Collecting hats is  a fun way to customise your character and provides a nice layer of additional challenge in most stages.
+ Some of the hats are downright ridiculous and so is the main stoyline. The humour is definitely debatable, very slapstick-esque and lol-so-random, but I think it's safe to say that if the trailer for this game appeals to you then you will enjoy the plot.
+ The original soundtrack kicks♥♥♥♥♥and is surprisingly varied.
+ The voice acting is ridiculously over the top and probably the main contributing factor to this game's hillarity.
+ The meta-commentary on video games and game design seemed a little out of place, but I enjoyed it regardless.
+ Steam Workshop support, additional levels, and the challenge of trying to collect all the hats and all the achievements should be enough incentive to keep playing for those masochistic enough to want to do so.
The Bad:
- In almost every chapter there will be one stage that is extremely hard in comparison to the rest. This seems in part due to these stages having less generous checkpoints than usual or sometimes none at all. These random difficulty spikes can be very frustrating and are a testament to the fact that this was a debut game by a small company. Definitely could have used some more playtesting.
- The game keeps its promise to not explain anything. You have to figure out every new mechanic by yourself and make creative use of your movement abilites to forge your path through the levels. This is of course where the challenge of the game comes from, but I think it is safe to say it does not hold your hand. As a result, I sometimes found myself having to cross-references videos of other people's playthroughs to make sure my approach to traversing the level was correct and it was only my execution that sucked.
- The bossfights in particular are quite hard. They all have set rotations that you'll have to figure out for yourself. The game generally tries to give visual and auditive clues as to what you should be doing, but oftentimes it is unclear how many stages a fight has. Bosses also never have a healthbar, instead the game relies purely on different visual stages of the bosses' models which makes the progress of the fight feel vague at times.
-Playing the game with a controller seemed fine, but there were a few stages where I found myself switching back to mouse and keyboard as the chapter-specific mechanics seemed easier to handle that way.
- The main campaign can be finished in around 3-4 hours. This might be a consideration for some people, although as I said the game is overall very enjoyable and shortwhiled.
- The original price tag of 15 euros/dollars is a little too high in my opinion. Although it's definitely worth picking up on sale for a reduced price, probably more around the 5-8 euros/dollars mark.

First off my guild(The Oran'Thul) was personally contacted by the devs of Echo of Soul to test the game. This is an unbiased, truthful review of the game.
Let me start by saying I plan to give this game a negative review. Now that's not saying its terrible and its not worth playing, but for those who take their MMOs seriously and competitively, you are going to want to steer clear of this one.
Echo of Soul at its core is a pretty decent MMO, entertaining pve and pvp. It does not stand out from the rest of the MMO's but for the features it does have, it does do them pretty well.
The MAJOR issues that this game suffers from is pretty much what plagues every other MMO that has been released for the past few years.
1. PAY TO WIN.
This is a MAJOR issue for those who wish to play MMOs competitively and take their MMOs seriously. This game comes from Aeria games, for those of you who have played their games before you most likely are not surprised to hear that this game is P2W.
2. BALANCE ISSUES.
My god.....my guild and I looked past the pay to win issue in this game and said "meh its an MMO to kill time with". When we got into the battlegrounds....  the balance...MY GOD THE BALANCE!!!!
The issue became apparent when we were still low levels, so we brushed it off as a balance issue at lower level pvp. As we leveled the issue became much...MUCH worse.
There are currently 5 classes in the game, 3 are nearly unplayable vs the other 2. Can you guess who the underpowered ones are? As always, its the melee. The sorceress and the Archer are disgustingly overpowered to the point that you shouldn't even bother pvping at all as a melee.
3. CHANNEL SYSTEM
The channel system...the bane on all open world MMOs. For those of you who dont know what a channel system is....here is a quick explanation.
A channel system is pretty much a way to take one server and break it up into a ton of mini servers. This allows the developers to spread out a congested world so players arent overcrowding everything to the point that there are no mobs to kill and you cant move an inch without being ganked.
There is a right way, and a wrong way to implement a system like this. Echo of Soul does it the wrong way.
As you progress through the game you are constantly entering little instance portals, this hurts the game as you get the feeling that the world is not an open worlds, its just a bunch of mini instances smashed together with load screens between each of them.
When you enter these portals you are thrown into a random channel of that specific zone.
For instance...
FOREST ZONE (CHANNEL 2) --> CAVE ZONE (CHANNEL 4)
As you can see above, when you progress from one zone to another you are thrown into a random channel. This may be packed full of players, or have none at all.
This really destroys the feeling of being in an open, growing world filled with players.
In addition this absolutely KILLS world pvp. My guild and I found it nearly impossible to join a friend in a channel to participate in world pvp becuase the channel was filled.
Lastely this also allows players to leave the channel to run away from potential pvp.
This truly makes for a babies MMO and anyone serious about their MMOs should stay away.

LIMBO is a game that I first played upon its release in 2011, though I played it on my Xbox 360. Just a handful of years ago, I remember being very creeped out by the game's premise and dark world.
However, after replaying the game just now, I find that it was not that exciting. It seems that I look at LIMBO and other games differently than some years ago. I thought that the minimalist story of the game back then was some magic answer, as if it was free of criticism - especially with the ending of the game. But that is not quite right. While the set-up of the game is definitely eerie, this time around I seemed to have wanted more. LIMBO definitely could have had more to it.
The early part of the game gives you that weird feeling because there are other creatures and seemingly human beings in this place with you. But in the later part of the game, all of that vanishes, and it becomes nothing but boxes and water and saws and gravity. The disappearance of other life could have been done as a means to make you feel even worse about the place you are in, but it did not have such an effect. If anything, it just seems like the developers did not know what else to do with other life.
Environment-wise, the game's appearance and sound fit the overall idea. In fact, music does not exist at all, and you only hear your footsteps and random objects clashing around here and there. Fitting for the "dead" world that you are helplessly navigating. Darkness. Fog. Minimal light. The visuals also fit that bad realm of LIMBO.
While I am not necessarily saying that the game is bad, I was just not as impressed as I was when I first played it. I feel like the game is a one-time-go, and then it's not really good to return. I also think that it is easy for you to overrate it (as I did myself years ago), because of things like the black and white shadow artwork. People seem to just look at the game and because of the visuals, it is already pulling them in and ready to say that it is good.
As LIMBO is a game, the gameplay itself is actually not that amazing. The game is literally die-and-repeat-until-you-win. Most of the puzzles have hidden obstacles or traps which are not easy to tell until you run through the first time. It may seem funny at first, but is actually not that amazing once you find out that a lot of the challenge is simply that. You have to repeat until you understand how to get around something.
For instance (slight spoilers if you care about single-pass obstacles), one of the sillier examples is early in the game. You are running through an area and you see two sets of mini-platforms that look like buttons, each of which are sitting on top of panels and underneath giant weights. If you run onto the first panel, then the weight comes down and crushes you. So you must jump onto the mini-platform button, and then jump across to the regular floor again. Now, as you'll probably know where it's going from my context, the next panel and button are swapped. If you jump onto the second button, you get crushed again. So this time you must use the panel and jump over the button, avoiding it.
The developers did the above example as a means to simply trick you easily and add a little artificial time to the game, as you'll have to repeat getting around it - but you only do so once. And that is very common in this game, with you having to die here and there until you are able to know what is ahead of you, and what you need to use to stop yourself from dying. That is not necessarily a good design, in my opinion. It would be alright to happen a little bit, but not as often as it really does.
And you also have the amount of gameplay there is, which is very little. Despite having already played the game years ago, I did not really remember much of the puzzles and still died quite a bit. Even so, I was able to complete the game in about 2 hours or a bit less. There is not a tremendous amount of content in the game; and quite a few of the puzzles are meticulous in a bad way, meaning a good chunk of the 2 hours was repeating attempts to get past the same obstacles over and over.
Sadly, I did not have that much enjoyment, excitement, or feeling of accomplishment playing through LIMBO. While I still intend to try out Playdead's INSIDE game, I do not see myself returning to this one.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

SUPERHOT is a pretty mixed bag. It has the base for what potentially could have been a truly revolutionary first person shooter, but somehow fell short; SUPERHOT is a totally stellar idea with frustratingly underwhelming executiuon, resulting in another one of those niche indie titles that's pretty dang fun, but mindlessly so.
Let's start with the good. SUPERHOT's main gimmick is that time will only move normally when you move. When you stand still, time will drop into very slow motion (but it will not stop) allowing you to plan your next move. Everything in the game, including both enemies and yourself, will die from one bullet, or from several consecutive melee attacks. Combining the concepts of time manipulation and swift, quick death, SUPERHOT straddles the line between frantic action and slow, strategic planning. This mix is largely satisfying, and the short levels combined with quick respawn times encourages experimentation and variation. Enemy AI is simple, and the game's difficulty relies more on throwing a bunch of people at you at once rather than clever tactics, but it doesn't detract from SUPERHOT as much as it would in other games. Later in the game you'll pick up the ability to switch bodies, keeping the gameplay fresh for a little while longer. At the end of every level, you can watch your replay at full speed to see what it would look like if SUPERHOT was a regular shooter and you just happened to have superhuman reflexes. The presentation is great too; with a minimalistic artstyle and a story that gets pretty meta on you multiple times over, SUPERHOT leaves you longing for more.
Which becomes the game's biggest downfall. It's just too. Damn. Short. I finished the game in 115 minutes, 5 minutes short of Steam's 2 hour limit on refunds. You can play the whole game from start to finish and then get all your money back if you wanted to. And, understandably, had they just added more levels then people probably would have labeled the game as too repetitive. This is the problem with any game that revolves around one simple gimmick. You can only milk it for so long before it gets boring. SUPERHOT is as short as it is because, other than its main gimmick, the game has nothing interesting or unique to offer. Again, it's a fantastic idea...but that's all it is. SUPERHOT probably would have done better if it was labeled as a tech demo for something rather than a full blown game. Completing the game will unlock endless mode, but that doesn't stay fresh for very long. SUPERHOT is an amazing game until it isn't anymore, and then you'll move on to something else. With a playtime of less than 2 hours for the main part of the game, SUPERHOT remains (as of the time of this writing) the same price that it did when it first came out over a year ago: a steep, unfairly priced $25. What I'm about to say is something I haven't really said in any of my other reviews...
I bought this game during Steam's 2017 Summer Sale, for $14.99. That should have been the game's regular price. At full price, you are paying almost half the price of a fully fledged AAA title for a game so short you can easily burn through almost all the content in one sitting. I think that's unacceptable. I am giving SUPERHOT a positive review because its a fun game; very unique in what it offers. But I cannot stress enough that
SUPERHOT is enjoyable, but there is no way in hell that it is worth $25. Not even close.

On August 11, 1999, the cult classic System Shock 2 was released to the world from a studio known only as Irrational Games. 8 years later, and BioShock, a game that got nearly everybodies attention was released. Taking their abilities to create excellent atmospheric experiences, littered with Role-Playing elements, Irrational Games created a game that is now widely adored, which is why it surprised me how long it's been in my Library without being played. In all honesty, I haven't played this game in quite a while, so, some of the things I say may not be 100% accurate.
BioShock is an underwater experience that has no swimming, but walking around in buildings and corridors built around that water. I really do not wish to say anything about the story, but, from what I've played, it's pretty good. The guns and special abilities also feel pretty cool, and the Role-Playing elements work pretty well. This said, though, this game does have flaws. The first and foremost is simple: this game has some pretty big compatibility issues on newer systems (which I find strange because games like HL2: Episode 2 which were released in the same year don't have these same issues), and it's really annoying having to spend an hour or two wondering why the hell everything is not functional. Secondly, this game makes you backtrack, and wander around... A LOT. This is the reason I haven't beaten this game yet, or played it in a while... because I got a headache even trying.
Despite those 2 issues, I still recommend BioShock if you want a good, atmospheric experience. Will I continue playing this? Probably!

This is a great game, a blast all the way through, but I don't think it's a fully realized idea quite yet. You see the 1.8 hours I have on record? That's the entire campaign all the way through. That's pretty bad for 25$, but I think the unique experience is worth it IF IT'S ON SALE! The puzzle fps is a fun concept, and the game does so much stuff really well it's hard not to have a blast going through it for the first time.
The gameplay is always really fresh and exciting, the punches and headshots and throws feel so satisfying as you learn to lead enemies and have them move into it. You feel like a super hacker badass when you are just gunning and slicing right and left, and the levels are varied and complement the mechanics fantastically. Also, it isn't very linear either, there are a ton of different ways you can go about dispatching your foes, and I feel like it would be interesting to revisit the game later for another playthrough.
The "story" or fragmented bits that are fed to you is intriguing, and while there isn't a total payoff in the end, it is fun and interesting enough to string you along for the ride. The game takes control of your menu and game at certain points, and "glitches" and screws up your graphics for a surreal, drug like experience (never taken drugs, it seems that way though).
Overall, this game is fresh, and fun, and interesting, and I felt like if they have another few hours of gameplay with some new abilities gained along the way, this game would be way more worth it. I still recommend it, but DEFINITELY wait for a sale unless you are made of money.

status report.....where do i begin......
Lets start with the basics, making an account. You can either make one with steam or gravity. I would recomend gravity if you play ragnarok as well so you can have all your accounts in one place. The character creation system is not that good, in fact it is pretty basic and not all that good. The options that you have are even LESS then ragnarok.....? With ragnarok your archer can go hunter then rebirth to bring more to the table when it comes with skills and gear. in RO2 however you go from archer to ranger... or even better you can go from archer to a druid, i ment a wow rip off.....i ment beastmaster. OK i am going to get this off the table now and say this is what happens when someone takes what people don't like about ragnarok and have it make love to a half♥♥♥♥♥world of warcraft.
Next up is graphics. It might just be what i like but i would rather go with the graphics of ragnarok then wow rip off RO2. While it looks good it still has a long ways to go in order to look like a good game. There are plenty of games that look better then this and have smoother game play. The fact that RO2 has cutscenes can be rather fun to watch but only the first time through.
Skills is one of the things that make ragnarok so good. the ability to test out different skills and see what works with your play style. RO2 is back to the basic (but good) skill tree. While it looks rather solid it still forces people to use the same skills and thus not much in making different options. A good example is comparing RO1 and RO2's swordsmen. In RO2 it is pretty much between dps and tanking. In Ragnarok however there is several kinds of swordy alone. AGI sword, AGI spear, zerk, tanking, and so on. While you will pretty much get the same skills as a swordy you can still choose different weapons and builds to costomize your toon. There are also things that you have to think about before doing some quests in Ragnarok such as what the monster is strong and weak again. RO2 does not have this at all which makes the game more dull in my opinion.
WHAT I HATE MOST ABOUT RO2. I have been comparing Ragnarok and RO2 from the start...and that is mainly because this is Ragnarok 2, if it had been its own game (like the Ragnarok games on your phone) then i might not be so crule in this review. Something that is nice to get in Ragnarok is VIP. It allows you to use more warps, more experience, less experience loss from death, buffs, the ability to go into VIP only areas that allows quick levels and could allow you to go second job with max job level in less then a day. In RO2 it also has VIP but is lacking is what it offers. You get an exp bonus, stats bonus, movement speed, and a few other things....that is pretty much it. It does not even allow a different tab for storage like in Ragnarok. Speaking of storage.....RO2's storage is the worst i have ever seen in any mmo i have ever played (15 years and still going), even runescape had better. In Ragnarok there is a 600 item limit in the basic storage, 600 more in VIP storage, and i believe 600 MORE in the special Kefra storage. The storage in RO2 is pathetic as you only have ~30 slots. You can get more but it will cost you REAL MONEY. In RO2 you also have to get VIP FOR EVERY SINGLE ONE OF YOUR TOONS!!! Ragnarok is a once and you are good with all of your toons. You also can't share items with the Kefra storage like in the Ragnarok. You can make items to your other toons but you can only do that one item at a time. Storage on your toon is back to the WoW bag slots unlike Ragnarok weight limit. It does also have a max amount of different items you can have but the numer is large enough that you will not likely hit it normally. You can get rather nice bags with....you might have guessed it....real money. three bags will only run you 60 bucks.....ONLY.....and PER TOON......if you want to have 5 toons with those bags then you are down 300 bucks......WTF Storage keys are also pretty pricey. You can drop a grand on this game and not even try too hard.
Proffesions.... In Ragnarok only alchemists can make potions and blacksmiths can make weapons....and it was good. In RO2 you have a larger rage to be able to make and you can have anyone with blacksmithing and alchemy. This is most likely due to the profession system in WoW. This addition to the game is actually a nice bit better then Ragnaok as it allows you to make full gear with little effort and is the only thing that i think that RO2 does better. The titles in this game is easily the best aspect of the game. Unlike most games, the titles in this game help you out by giving you extra stats such as strength and agility. For the people that played this game when it first came out (like me) then they have a few toons with the "founder" title which will give you a massive bonus that will carry you into late game. The other titles are gotten through objectives.
Transportation. Transportation is simple enough in this game. They have flight points instead of warps like in Ragnarok. The main way to get around is by a mount. You can get mounts by spending real money to allow you to use a mount.....for a limited time. You can get lucky however and get a unlimited mount (only for one toon) that will allow you to use it whever you want. Other then that there is walking....have fun with that.
Final thoughts. When you compare Ragnarok and Ragnarok 2 then there is a large difference in the games. Ragnarok just has alot more to offer and makes you want to play more and more. With more class choices and the newly added doram class. Ragnarok is a much better game and knows how to treat the players right. Ragnarok 2 just has too many things that cost money in order to let you play the game to the best ability.
Final score: 2/10

As many of the other reviews have stated, Iron Fisticle is similar to classic arcade games such as Robotron and Smash TV.
This is a twin-stick shooter.
You go in a room.
You kill everything.
You move onto the next.
In a number of ways, this game is designed to follow Smash TV's template. Your throwing axe isn't particularly good, so you have to take every chance to get hold of the good (but temporary) weapons. This changes things from merely being about slaughter to carving a path to the next weapon, all just to capture those precious seconds of relative safety. In terms of aesthetics and mechanics, Iron Fisticle is quite appealing. The graphics are nice and clean, resembling something from the Toaplan age. The controls are perfectly solid, and the hit-box is suitable for what needs to be done. This makes for an easy game to just pick up, play, and enjoy.
This game certainly isn't as difficult as Smash TV. As the store description goes, you can level-up to boost your health, abilities, and unlock new & items and weapons. Unlike seemingly every other rogue-like on Steam, these level-ups are permanent. You're free to purchase stat upgrades, so you'll start the next game with a nice boost. HP-restoring hearts are very prevalent as well. If you're particularly adept at the platforming bonus rounds, you can grab a full-healing before your next stage. Is it all really necessary? Yes and no.
In standard rogue-like fashion, merely beating the game isn't enough. Sure you might have defeated some great evil and saved the legendary turnip or radish or whatever the hell it is. However, when you've accomplished your task, you get kicked back to the beginning. Everything is a little more difficult now, and your luck will run out eventually. Now here's where things get interesting. Aside from Smash TV, Iron Fisticle also takes ideas from Bubble Bobble.
Within each stage, you'll find the silver weapon-holding chests, but you'll also collect a myriad of items that award points. Zombies drop food, which can award up to 800 points each. There are also special items, that are found in gold chests (one per stage). Sometimes the right special item can make a huge difference, and so can finding the right weapons. This adds a slight luck factor to the whole affair. Your dodging skills might be adept, but weapons are what keep you from getting cornered and overwhelmed. There is a dash move, which is pretty useful. However, zombies eventually roll extremely deep, and you could end up dashing into a crowd.
So for most players, beating the game isn't much trouble, but going for those pesky leaderboard spots will cause headaches. Theoretically you could beat the game an innumerable amount of times without dying, but you're always one streak of bad luck away from death. If you want the top score, you'll have to play for a several hours straight. This can get pretty dull, since you'll be so strong the first 30 minutes or so won't pose any threat. Last I checked, the top-score was around 8 million, that's at least 8 play-throughs in a row. Mercifully, the challenge mode is only four stages, though luck still plays a slight factor due to food-drops and other potential bonus points (and using spare iron fists to milk the "hurry-up" golems). There's also playing for the shortest time, which has some merit as well.
Whatever the case, Iron Fisticle's long-term replay value isn't very high. Once you hit max level (which doesn't take very long) there aren't many incentives to play the game. The normal mode takes too long to become interesting, and there's a little too much randomness to make playing for score very compelling in the challenge mode. Even with that in mind, I still give this game a recommendation. It is fun, well-constructed, and does an admirable job of blending the design philosophies of multiple classic arcade games.

I've had hours of fun playing this game and I was very glad to see it on steam so I could enjoy replaying it. At its heart the game is resource management, you manage your ghost's power's from a shared meter, which you can increase by scaring mortals, which in turn you manage so that they are capable of being manipulated to fulfil your goals while providing you with enough power. The Beginner's Guide starts with a promise. A promise that the developer will be as open with us as he can be if we are willing to open ourselves up to listen. And I did listen. This game enthralled me, because it was bold and unafraid to do things differently. I wasn't sure what the point was, exactly, but I trusted that Davey Wreden had something to say, something worth saying, and that he was speaking with a sincere voice.
He was not.
This doesn't have anything to do with how "real" the events of the game may or may not be. That doesn't much matter to me. What Davey Wreden reveals with The Beginner's Guide is that he refuses to play by his own rules. He uses the appearance of sincerity to win over the player's trust, then betrays them when they're most invested. For The Beginner's Guide, getting someone to feel strong emotions is a goal in and of itself. It wants to shock you, to be impactful by any means necessary. It takes no prisoners. The Beginner's Guide is like Lucy with the football, beckoning the Charlie Brown sitting behind their keyboard to run ten miles before kicking it, then pulling it away at the last second.
This game made me feel genuinely emotionally manipulated. As the credits started to roll, I got up and crawled into bed and cried. Not because the story itself was particularly sad, and not because I needed a healthy emotional release. I cried because I felt hopeless. I wondered how someone could be so cruel. I paid this person ten dollars and they fed me two hours of lies, then revealed the truth and kicked me in the gut and ran away. It was like I met someone who wanted to be my friend, and I opened up to them, made myself vulnerable to them, only to discover they were pretending the whole time. This game is a betrayal.
I know. I know how crazy this all sounds. It's a game, right? It's a video game. You know it's not real. It can't hurt you. But if games and stories can make you feel fear, joy, anger, exhilaration, and comfort, why couldn't it hurt you? Make you feel betrayed, manipulated?
I don't know Davey Wreden. I only know him through his work. I loved The Stanley Parable, and I admired him and empathized with him when he wrote a blogpost about his depression. I am also someone who has suffered from depression and anxiety. So I cannot for the life of me understand why he would create a game that treats emotion like nothing more than a tool, a means to an end. Why try to make people feel genuine discomfort and loss, when games, like all art at its best, can be used to spread joy and understanding and belonging? It might be okay if it was a horror game - you know what you're getting into. But that's not what The Beginner's Guide is, nor what it advertises itself to be.
The Beginner's Guide starts with a promise. A promise it spends over an hour doing everything it can to convince you is genuine. Then it takes all of five minutes to not just take it back, but reveal it was all a ruse, constructed solely to make you feel shock and terror and sadness.
The Beginner's Guide is a game about what it means to be an artist, from the perspective of someone who has entirely lost sight of that meaning. An artist reveals truths, presents with utmost sincerity some aspect of themselves. But Davey Wreden - both versions, the developer of The Beginner's Guide and its narrator/protagonist - speaks with no sincerity. I don't doubt that he's been through some very difficult emotions, experienced depression. I know what that can be like. But how he could wish someone else feel that too, I have no idea. Sincerity requires understanding that the person you're speaking with has opened themselves up to you just as you've opened up to them. Feigning sincerity to catch someone off guard when they're most emotionally vulnerable is manipulative and cruel. Davey is not acting here as an artist - he is a con man. The Beginner's Guide is a cruel trick. A promise made and a promise broken.
The Stanley Parable remains one of my favorite games ever. And I wanted to like this game too. I bought it the day it came out. All in all, there's some really cool ideas in it, and it's exciting to see people try new ways of designing games and constructing stories. And honestly, part of me wants to give The Beginner's Guide credit for making me feel such strong emotions - that's an admirable goal of art, right? The fact that it made me feel something and examine myself and think hard about what it was talking about - maybe The Beginner's Guide was a rousing success. But no. I hate this game. I hate how it made me feel. No game, or movie or show or book for that matter, has ever made me feel so dejected and depressed, brought about such deep anger. Maybe it'll be different for you - I hope it is. The amount of positive reviews clearly suggest that I'm in the minority. But as an aspiring artist myself, as well as just a human being, I never want to make anyone feel what The Beginner's Guide made me feel.

Iron Fisticle is what I would call a spiritual successor to games like SMASH TV, where killing is possible in your primary and secondary directions.

LIMBO is a game that I first played upon its release in 2011, though I played it on my Xbox 360. Just a handful of years ago, I remember being very creeped out by the game's premise and dark world.
However, after replaying the game just now, I find that it was not that exciting. It seems that I look at LIMBO and other games differently than some years ago. I thought that the minimalist story of the game back then was some magic answer, as if it was free of criticism - especially with the ending of the game. But that is not quite right. While the set-up of the game is definitely eerie, this time around I seemed to have wanted more. LIMBO definitely could have had more to it.
The early part of the game gives you that weird feeling because there are other creatures and seemingly human beings in this place with you. But in the later part of the game, all of that vanishes, and it becomes nothing but boxes and water and saws and gravity. The disappearance of other life could have been done as a means to make you feel even worse about the place you are in, but it did not have such an effect. If anything, it just seems like the developers did not know what else to do with other life.
Environment-wise, the game's appearance and sound fit the overall idea. In fact, music does not exist at all, and you only hear your footsteps and random objects clashing around here and there. Fitting for the "dead" world that you are helplessly navigating. Darkness. Fog. Minimal light. The visuals also fit that bad realm of LIMBO.
While I am not necessarily saying that the game is bad, I was just not as impressed as I was when I first played it. I feel like the game is a one-time-go, and then it's not really good to return. I also think that it is easy for you to overrate it (as I did myself years ago), because of things like the black and white shadow artwork. People seem to just look at the game and because of the visuals, it is already pulling them in and ready to say that it is good.
As LIMBO is a game, the gameplay itself is actually not that amazing. The game is literally die-and-repeat-until-you-win. Most of the puzzles have hidden obstacles or traps which are not easy to tell until you run through the first time. It may seem funny at first, but is actually not that amazing once you find out that a lot of the challenge is simply that. You have to repeat until you understand how to get around something.
For instance (slight spoilers if you care about single-pass obstacles), one of the sillier examples is early in the game. You are running through an area and you see two sets of mini-platforms that look like buttons, each of which are sitting on top of panels and underneath giant weights. If you run onto the first panel, then the weight comes down and crushes you. So you must jump onto the mini-platform button, and then jump across to the regular floor again. Now, as you'll probably know where it's going from my context, the next panel and button are swapped. If you jump onto the second button, you get crushed again. So this time you must use the panel and jump over the button, avoiding it.
The developers did the above example as a means to simply trick you easily and add a little artificial time to the game, as you'll have to repeat getting around it - but you only do so once. And that is very common in this game, with you having to die here and there until you are able to know what is ahead of you, and what you need to use to stop yourself from dying. That is not necessarily a good design, in my opinion. It would be alright to happen a little bit, but not as often as it really does.
And you also have the amount of gameplay there is, which is very little. Despite having already played the game years ago, I did not really remember much of the puzzles and still died quite a bit. Even so, I was able to complete the game in about 2 hours or a bit less. There is not a tremendous amount of content in the game; and quite a few of the puzzles are meticulous in a bad way, meaning a good chunk of the 2 hours was repeating attempts to get past the same obstacles over and over.
Sadly, I did not have that much enjoyment, excitement, or feeling of accomplishment playing through LIMBO. While I still intend to try out Playdead's INSIDE game, I do not see myself returning to this one.

The Beginner's Guide tries to be more than what it is, and this attempt falls short. Despite my own personal opinions, one might very much enjoy this game if they're into interactive storytelling and games that make you think (but not too hard). I want to like this game, but it was profoundly boring and the last half hour had me constantly checking the time. I loved The Stanley Parable, so I can confidently say that my distaste for The Beginner's Guide has nothing to do with the lack of action or the inability to do anything except walk around. Yet, for some reason, in this game a found myself constantly wishing I could do something, anything, except for inexorably continue forward into the story. Perhaps I'm just not cut out for a game that's so unflinchingly linear.
There's no question that many would consider this game art, and it's possible that I fall into that category of person, but the original style of The Beginner's Guide, as well as the deeper meanings that definitely lurk within, fails to make up for the fact that I just wasn't entertained and didn't enjoy myself.
Pros
+ Unique and original

Cons
- Nothing to keep the player entertained
- Comes across as trying too hard to be artsy

I've been playing this game quite a lot during the closed beta and I have to say I had much fun with my friends. I came here looking for a fun Free-2-Play MMORPG, and I got what I wanted. I would give it a 90% rating in the MMO category. For my group of friends it was kind of a WoW/Lineage 2 revival. Easy to get into it, fun PvP and dungeons, and I especially like the game-design and art style (even though on the tech side the game is not The Witcher III, let's face it ^^ But my laptop could run it pretty smooth in high, it looks sharp).
Sure it's not revolutionary and it doesn't have a special feature that stands out, but it becomes more and more attractive and interesting as you play the game. It has all the features I was looking for, different types of PvP, a ton of dungeons to farm gear, cool mounts and pets (if you like lamas you'll love riding them in this game lol), nice crafting systems, a pretty extensive job system and the end-game content seems huge (even though I have done much myself after I hit level 60, I need a bit more time to look into it as I was having some fun in PvP for a while and put the dungeons/questing on the side).
It's pretty easy to get into it even for MMORPG beginners, the interface is user friendly, and I found the learning curve well done. I felt I actually needed some time to master some skills and to start feeling powerful, which is a good thing IMO (I don't like hen its too easy). I got crushed my first few times in PvP but now I actually do quite well without spending a single penny and without having amazing skills myself.
On the negative side, I would say that there is some grinding involved that can become a bit boring at some point. I don't mind farming personally, but I know some friend wanted to progress a bit faster. Yet, nothing crazy either, still in line with many other MMORPGs, especially those coming from Asia.
Regarding the debate "P2W or not", it didn't felt Pay-2Win to my eyes, especially in comparison to some other Free-2-Play MMOs. Sure there is a shop, but you can get most stuff via in-game drops, via the magic egg system (cool idea for free players), or by buying in the auction house. I have some friends who spent some cash on the game to buy some mounts and costumes plus some boosts for leveling, but in PvP we were on the same level. So all good from my point of view on that side. Might consider spending if I continue to play for a while, but I don't feel forced to do so...
So overall I really like the game and will continue to play for a while. It's perfect for casual MMO players but also interesting for experienced players. Found the game well balanced and not Pay-2-Win so far. A good example of what a F2P MMORPG should be!

first game in a year:
- me and a friend meet up near muldraugh, when I get there he tells me he's got attacked, he's wounded.
- fleeing the undead, he got lost and bumped into an abbandoned lumber mill with solid metal doors.
- he gives me directions. I see where he is.
while I struggle to get drugs, bandages and disinfectant, he discovers the joys of stitching oneself.
- we join and, while he recovers from his wounds, I board the place up and gather all the wood and tools I can.
we sleep in the break room. they're 5 feets away, clawing at the boards. they never break in.
- after a few days we start scavenging the suburbs, just what we need, we have projects.
- a few weeks later, we're settled, the crops we planted on the roof after transporting some dirt there is flourishing.
days passed by, peacefully. the place is clear and we start to feel in control.
he picks up cooking.
- one night, I hear moans and cracks, the building's on fire. whole groups of them came to see it.
my friend passed out while cooking and canning food for the winter.
- he almost dies in the fire to save the seeds and tools we couldn't survive without.
- once set up in a smaller building, we heal and consume all our reserves, the meds are gone and the water shuts off.
we peek outside.
- the Z's have massed, we can't reclaim enough terrain for a field or rain collectors.
after making an inventory of what's left we decide to loot the gun store, one town away.
we'll have to get out anyway and at least, if we go there, we could clean our home afterwards.
- the way there is easy, we're well rested, fed and hydrated.
we run there, only stopping for the night in a gas station half way
- just before we arrive, we're starving. we ate all our food, drank all our water.... we see a supermarket!
- we drink soda and eat meat for the first time in a month. we're safe in the offices, the stairs are broken.
we can rest peacefully and the shop is within a stone throw.
-the next morning we silently climb down the roof with a rope made of bloody clothes.
- the score is easy. I distract them, shooting our few last bullets and run into the woods while he brings down the metal roll-up door of the gunshop as fast as he can with a sledgehammer.
- we've got 'em! we're armed to the teeth and we paint our way out of town red.
- I already aim better by the time we reach the gas station.
it's a tough fight to reclaim it and I get scrached. a cold gives me fever and I freak out at the idea I might be infected.
I drink and smoke all night to forget the worries.
- by the morning I'm all better (besides the hangover but who cares, I live!) but my friend is nauseous.
he didn't rest and looks sickly. he tells me he thought we were above use-by dates.
after surviving what we did. he couldn't just die from bad cabbage... could he?
- a few miles later, he can't run anymore. I run my lungs out, straight to the city.
he'll die if I can't get him supplies.
- before he stops answering he says this:
"I can't run anymore. I'm exhausted, sick, wounded. they'll catch me soon"
I have to go back.
- I put the gun bags down, raid the first house I find for basic pharmacy goods and just run his way.
- I battled to find his bright orange shirt in what's left of his last stand and found him.
brought him peace, losing some flesh on the way.
-I was now the one wounded, exhausted, sick and lost.
alone on a country road with a dead friend, his murderers and three sports bags full of guns and bullets...
we had played 13 hrs straight at that point. no rage or regrets. just ideas for next time... seriously, buy it. now.

I don't get why people complain about "Day 1 DLC". Considering the fact that the dlc in the store is purely cosemetic and does not affect the gameplay what so ever. And the season pass doesn't give anything but just few skins you can start out and the extra monster and 4 hunters when its released in another update. There is no such thing as Day 1 DLC, as it does not affect gameplay what so ever, just cosemetics, you guys are overreacting to it. The base game already gives alot of content, you can just unlock all the hunters and monsters threw the player progression found within the Base game.

But anyways, back to topic with my experience.
Evolve is a action packed co-op 4 vs 1 game, pitting 4 hunters against 1 monster. Currently at the time I am reviewing this, theres 3 monsters and 12 hunters, each with their own progression tree, leading up to a elite skin when you complete it.
I played hunt in multiplayer as the monster. I was certainly scared, and you get that adrenaline feel as you don't know what tactics the hunters might pull out, or when they catch you, or spot you, it's very unexpected and each match is different. Especially Evacuation which I'll explain in a bit. Wildlife around the map can help or even harm any team. Such as Carnivorous plants that eat any hunter that steps on it, or packs of trapjaws that can deal a significant amount of damage to either team.
Evacuation is a series of gamemodes put together that allows each match to have a game changing experience. Winning orbital drill as the monster causes satellite debris to fall on hunters. Or winning the armory as hunters and attack drones come and absolutely dominate the monster. Each evacuation match is always different from another (Unless your lucky enough to get the same result out of 800,000 combos) match.
To end it off, there are many mechanics in the game I can't really tell much, from the littlest detail, to probably the most obvious, its a good game from Turtle Rock Studios.

Every once and a while, I go looking for an oddball game. Something that I want to be silly and campy, instead of overly serious and full of aliens, zombies, and muscleheads with tortured pasts. Ghost Master is just that.

Each ghost has their own set of abilities, with all of them forming small groups that share similar abilities.
The gameplay itself, to me, feels like a cross between Sims and Tecmo's Deception, with each level requiring a bit of looking around to scout out spots that might make for a good scare, like using a water spirit to fill all the kitchen sinks with blood, or using one ghosts lure power to bring a group of people into the room, just as another ghost splits himself down the middle for everyone to see. All in all it's a fun game, with levels that are fun to replay, lots of ghosts and powers to work with, and all on the cheap.

I don't usually buy games with mixed steam reviews, but I was too interested in the concept and gameplay to ignore it. So here is what I have to say about why I bought it, what I think of it, and why you should be careful what reviews you read first.
To save you from wall of text have an early TLDR: No day 1 dlc, only cosmetics and season pass for future content. Fun solid gameplay, could use some balancing of wraith but mostly very good. If you want negative reviews to give some contrast, look past the ones to do with dlc.
It is just too interesting to pass up being how different it is. It is a game that pits 1 against 4, and every match can go differently. One match you could be playing cat and mouse for 15 mins, constantly chasing a fleeing monster. Sometimes skirmishing and wearing each other down. Or sometimes just going all in. The second option is the most fun as the fights can be quick, brutal, and exciting, and lead up to a final showdown where you stand your ground against a powerful, deadly, and smart opponent. The tide can turn in a fight very quickly and requires teamwork and co-ordination for the hunters, and cunning and strategy from the monster. The hunt game mode is fun with the right team and enemy, the evac campaign brings a bit of variation into an already unpredictable situation. So yeah, can be fun as hell, but can also leave you unsatisfied or frustrated, all depending on who you play with.
It is a good game, may not be worth the full price but I managed to grab it for £26 and I think it was very worth it for the base game. The full price and the dlc is probably too expensive for my taste, but I prefer playing hunter, so I probably wont bother with monster dlc at least at first.
This game had a lot of hype. And the devs made a mistake by releasing a bunch of content and packages as day 1 dlc which rustled a lot of jimmies. When I saw the new about it I was not happy myself. But when I looked into it I noticed it was not anywhere near as bad as people made it out to be. But hey everyone loves a good bad wagon that is bashing big studios.
So what is the deal with it then? In short, we have several packages such as a season pass, monster race bundle, and digital deluxe edition. And a very large amount of cosmetic skins. All this on day 1. But thats not a problem, because all of the bundles give you access to different cosmetics, and FUTURE content. There is no day 1 DLC. It is just season passes for content that is still in development, which as far as I remember is perfectly normal. The rest of it is just cosmetics to make you look a bit different from everyone else, and as far as I am concerned cosmetic skins are NOT dlc, they are in game items purchaseable with real money. Micro transactions, completely optional and non game changing ones.
However, I will state again that the current prices for the game and new hunters and monsters that will come later, is too high. So it may be best to wait for a sale or see if you can get a discount on a legitimate 3rd party site.
So yeah if you want to find some useful negative reviews, ignore the ones about dlc, and look for ones that criticize game play. The game is currently fairly well balanced apart from wraith, who is slightly broken.

is a twin-stick arcade shooter with procedurally generated dungeons. In this game, you play as an axe-throwing knight who's been whisked away through a portal by a monster who's stolen your castle's precious food. You have to fight through four levels with waves of monsters swarming around you. It's pretty awesome.
As with most arcade games, there is no save-functionality; every run is fresh and new. However, you can obtain permanent stat increases that persist between games. In this way, you can start each game with a slight advantage and build toward a strong loadout. Also, as your score increases, you level up, unlocking more items and raising your max stats. Along the way, you can grab temporary weapons which add variety to your attacks and items that help you survive, like armor and magic trinkets.
The difficulty scales quite well, with 3 different levels to choose from, as well as a challenge option. At first, swarms will steadily increase in size. As you progress, monster types will change and give you more of a challenge. The amount of different enemies to fight keeps the game fun and engaging. Bosses are fun to fight, and you'll need to raise your stats efficiently to handle the ever-mounting danger. I feel that the game is best played with a gamepad; you'll get more control out of it.
The game isn't perfect, however. I've experienced some periods of lag that occur at times they shouldn't, especially when there aren't even that many enemies onscreen. Players might get turned off by
's retro aesthetic. I don't see anything wrong with a chiptune soundtrack and pixel graphics, but I do know a lot of players absolutely hate it, so it is something to consider. Feelings about the replayability of the game can be mixed; it's really fun to pick up and play for a while, but once you've beaten everything, you might find the gameplay to be quite stale.
Still, the game makes for a really enjoyable experience, especially if you have a friend around. The $9.00 price-tag might be a little steep to some for the game's content, but it's a game that can give hours of entertainment. It's fun, addicting, and it makes for really relaxing playing. If you see it on sale, I would say you should definitely grab it.

Here's the 10 steps of my first playthrough:
1) While looking for shelter, a wolf spots me.
2) I duck into a train tunnel to hide from the wolf.
3) Hours later, I see a buck run by - so I run like an idiot boy scout to chase it with a my gear clanking with each step.
4) Out of breath, I round the corner and see the buck! ...and I startle the wolf that was sneaking up on the same buck.
5) Wolf wants to kill me for spoiling his hunt, and charges me. I calmly aim down the sites of my rifle and pull the trigger. Oops, didn't load it...
6) Wolf attacks, and somehow I get a few good blows in with my rifle, before passing out in the snow from blood loss.
7) Miraculously, I wake up hours later and limp to the train tunnel to bandage my wounds. I may actually survive!
8) Night sets in. I try starting two fires, but both fail. I realize I survived a wolf attack, just to freeze to death tonight.
9) I limp from the train tunnel through a blizzard. I see a house in the distance! Within a stone's throw of the house, I collapse from my wounds and exhaustion, and freeze to death from the bitter cold - just as the sun was rising.
10) Stare at my screen, stunned at my epic permadeath, and start a new round.

I think you will like this game if:
1) You're a big fan of puzzle platformers
2) You're a hardcore speedrunner
3) You're an extreme sucker for noir and atmospheric stuff
I dabble in all three of the above, but not enough to truly like this game, which I got for free and am glad that I did. Obviously I'm in the minority here, and I won't deny that Limbo does some things well. The environments are interesting, especially in the forest levels, and I quite liked the parts that have you fighting against giant spiders and strange children that seem right out of Lord of the Flies. The whole concept of a brave little boy stuck in some kind of shadowy world is a good one, and I like white noise, so the game's quite pleasant to listen to.
But I just got bored. Once you're out of the forest the puzzles devolve into block pushing/physics manipulation sections, which have to be some of my least favorite game mechanics. Everything just drags and drags until it all abruptly ends, and the game relies on style to stick out in your mind way more than interesting gameplay.
I can see why a lot of people like this, and I think it may have played better in 2010 when it first came out. But even back then you already had great puzzle platformers like Prince of Persia, Flashback, Another World and Heart of Darkness on the market, and I'd rather play any of those than Limbo again.
I'd recommend it.
