I loved my time with this game, quite honestly, in a large part thanks to the perfect understanding of what made the old shows amusing. Cheesy lines, silly storylines played up until you get a shiver saying "epic" despite your best reasoning and a sense of satisfaction from the repeated, well-made sequences of transformation, finishing moves and whatnot. Giving the ability to customise often used lines and even the team name allows to turn this factor up to eleven.
This is backed up by a very well made content of missions, each of them a chain of several tactical fights, sometimes ending with a quick-timey battle in your Mecha. While this last part might sound bad, its execution is better than you would expect - the fights are basically just timing button presses with a little bit of strategy sprinkled in, but the audio-visual effects and plenty of impactful, meaty slowdowns make this feel better. And honestly, how interesting can you make something as awkward as the kaiju fights from Power Rangers and the like?
The on-foot combat is much more nuanced, with a few enemy types introduced over the course of the game and a tonne of boss monsters. Fair warning, some of them are very similar, including two that are basically reskinned - I didn't like that decision, but thankfully the RNG in those fights made it actually engaging. Equipment and skills are drip fed to the player as well, helping to familiarize yourself slowly with how the game works. Puzzlingly, that doesn't mean everything is explained all that well; skill regen is the main example, it is more convoluted than you would expect, requiring some digging to familiarize yourself with the inner workings of it. At the same time, this might be just me being pedantic - for a normal player, the idea that the higher it is, the better for your skills is probably everything needed.
The combat stands out from a run-of-the-mill tactical grid in two ways. First, there is a big focus on 'teamwork' stance, another engine for sentai nostalgia. Your characters can propel each other around for high-distance jumps, join forces in an attack and even perform a finishing move when the entire squad joins in (with a bonus,
Power Ranger-esque animation if that is done with weapon attacks). Several nuances are built into this mechanic - Lead boosts your Audience and damage if he is a part of a team move, Assault can throw people really far while Support heals in AoE every time they enter teamwork.
And yes, I said Audience, that is the second thing. Your team is a bunch of stuntmen working on an indie super sentai show, which means you have to go through every mission (dubbed 'episode') in a possibly most fan-pleasing way. There are special goals (director's instruction) that give you bonus audience, aside from steady income on teamwork moves and just beating baddies. Each character can unlock skills catering to their fanbase: Support lovers will want to see them heal even more, while Scout is cheered for when they zip across the battlefield. The audience is no small deal, and sometimes you will have to either sacrifice fan growth (and thus money) for efficiency in combat or vice versa. Later on, director's instructions become quite the challenge, satisfying to fulfil.
The game is not without its fault, and the difficulty curve is pretty uneven; I played on Challenging, which meant that most of the time game required reasonable tactical thinking, but some episodes/instructions can send you back to the drawing board many-many times. I already touched on the problems with copy-pasted enemies and not everything being perfectly clear, so let me add two more to this list. One, it is pretty hard to switch your strategy on the inventory level. The crafting system demands a lot of materials, so destroying old weapons is mandatory. Now, that wouldn't be so bad if not for the inherently random nature of crafting, that means you might go up a tier of equipment but finish with a substandard set of traits (especially dangerous on class-specific items). You can still make it through the game, or lower the difficulty if you are desperate, but the problem exists.
All in all, however, we have a loveable indie title here, one that brings you back to the time when you rushed, as a kid, to the TV for yet another same-ish episode of Power Rangers. Except here, it is self-aware of everything that entails.

It's not finished yet, true, but it feels sort of... empty. The premise of the game seems to be: Find the special glowy things while running away a lot. Sometimes you'll find a weapon, but using one is usually more dangerous than not. That sounds great in theory, and the game has potential, certainly, but currently the game feels a lot emptier than the time it takes to generate each world would have you believe. There are several buildings, but you can't actually enter any of them. The reasons for this are well explained in a developer blog (and essentially boil down to "it'd be too easy to escape from the robots if you could and would take too much time away from things that are far more important") but that doesn't help with the emptyness factor.
I'm not sure if it's actually true (or if it's something to be worked on later), but it feels like you're literally the only non-robot in the world; every time I play it I'm left with a feeling of loneliness which makes me want to stop playing. My one hour of game time on record (which I'm sure is slightly more than that in reality but probably not much) is spread over at least 4 sessions, because I just couldn't keep playing it any longer. Not because the game is bad, per se, but because there (currently!) isn't much to do other than run away from robots. Nobody to interact with, no side-quests or missions to complete (that I've ever found). It feels less like a singleplayer game, and more like a multiplayer game with nobody else on the server. That kind of 'there should be something else here but there isn't" kind of feeling. Admittedly, that could very well be due to it's Early Access status, but nevertheless it's for sale now, so worth mentioning. The fact that your opponents are literally a bunch of machines intentionally devoid of any individual personality doesn't help here either (they're characterful, certainly, but they're all basically the same other than 'Baloon Guy' and the new Poacher).
I like the ideas in the game, and I'll keep checking back every now and then, but so far it's not a game I enjoy playing. And not in a Spec Ops: The Line style "you're not supposed to enjoy it" way. Entirely willing to admit however that it might just "not be my sort of game", because a lot of other people love it.

I got the chance to play Evolve at E3 in 2014, and I was a huge fan just from those short experiences playing on a controller with strangers. I was really looking forward to the release, and was hyping it up to all my buddies.
Then they released the pricing for the game... and the ten tons of DLC.
Let's cut to the chase: The gameplay is great. Levels are well thought out and provide ample room for battles, monster and hunter alike. There are multiple game modes out of the gate (a problem that made Titanfall far less palatable on launch) so the action never gets dull. Each class of hunter and monster requires some level of study to get down, and when you do, you become the amazing teammate that pulls through at the last minute for the win. Give Turtle Rock your money for this bit, at least, because they've taken the concepts behind Left 4 Dead and MADE THEM BETTER! HOW???
Now the bad bits: it's Cryengine, so your system will weep. I'm running dual GTX 770's and I'm running at medium settings. The unlocks are painfully slow. You'd think people would have learned from Diablo 3 that people don't enjoy grinding for gear, but what do I know? Finally, that DLC. I bought the PC Monster Race edition, and that comes with more content when it gets released over time. That being said, the game is awfully skimpy for content to start, and then asking for more bucks up front to get the "full game" sucks. I guess this is how the industry is going to monetize going forward, but it's crap no matter which way you look at it.
I conned a buddy of mine into buying this game. and he was skeptical as hell going in. 3 matches later and he's trying to figure out who else we can get to buy the game so we can have a full team.
Buy the game, skip the DLC for now. If you're having fun? Buy the DLC and go bananas.
And for god's sake be a good medic.

-v-v-v-FINAL UPDATE AT BOTTOM-v-v-v-
I never like to see a game, that was once paid for, go free-to-play. This is an act of desperation, by the developers at this point. Unfortunately, rather than stick to their original vision, the devs listened to the vocal minority in the community. The same vocal minority that probably dropped this game as soon as the next game was available. They didn't understand how to overcome challenges, and instead demanded the devs change the game - the very core of it - so they wouldn't have to live up to the expectation the game presented. There are probably a few other expectations, unrelated, that they haven't lived up to. Nonetheless, the devs listened to these people and the game was ruined. The core of it fractured, and so easily penetrated now the challenge was gone.
Fear not, however, for there is a light at the end of this dark passage. There's a new update out, and a few play throughs will determine if this is a rejuvenating future, or the gateway to Heaven. Why the non-recommendation then? More often than not, it is never a good sign when a game, that was once paid for, goes free-to-play. Team Fortress 2 did it - though to be honest it died a long time ago when valve introduced hats. Forge did it. Even Guild Wars 2 is planning to do it. This is a bad omen, potentially. With the new update, however there is hope. Only a few hours of gameplay will determine the exact fate of Evolve - despite its name, it certainly appears to be evolving in the wrong direction. While it's free though, go a head and give it a try. It couldn't hurt.
-------EDIT-------
So this new version appears to be gimped. The co-op feature is completely gone, and I assume with it the cutscenes and story - for anyone who cared about that. More information will be added to this review as my evaluation continues.
-------EDIT-------
The trapper class is now the tracker class, if not in name. While the trappers had an ability, or tool, to track the monster, their main purpose was to trap it. With the new update, however, every hunter now has the ability to trap the monster - which I'm still not sure is a bad thing. The ability the devs chose to replace the trapper's primary ability, unfortunately, is aweful. Anyone remember the DOOM multiplayer abilities controversy? The trapper (tracker) now has the ability to see the monster, as well as a few wild life, through the terrain. Essentially allowing the trapper to track the monster with absolute ease. The trapper's old tracking ability is now relegated to back-up status. If the trapper uses it, and his new primary ability, there is literally nowhere for the monster to hide. There's no more, actual, tracking, or what is known in the real world as spot-and-stalk. This was an essential, and immersive part of Evolve. This not only forced the trapper to rely on his tracking ability, but it also gave the monster time to hunt and, evolve. This was a core aspect of Evolve and it's gutted now, for some reason only the devs can explain. However, as explained in the original review, this whole free-to-play thing is an act of desperation, and I think the new trapper ability resulted from a similar act of desperation - as if they didn't know what else to do. Whatever the specifics of this decision were, the tracker is now a broken class.
-------EDIT-------
I think, perhaps, the biggest flaw in this recently changed Evolve is one that has been carried over from the original version. As I firmly believed back in the day, and still do class based games suck, usually. Evolve is one such game that would have benefitted and seen much greater longevity if it had a loadout system, instead of the class system. But Evolve was designed from the ground up to be a competitive multiplayer, e-sport title. Somehow the silly idea that classes make an e-sport title has been popularized, and appears to be a foundation for many games these days. Yet loadouts would have saved Evolve from its fate. Just like save states, loadouts are thought to be an antiquity. A product of the times and lack of modern resources. Sometimes, however the old ways are the best ways, and not everything is as antiquated as some would like others to believe. Just as those who believe the Constitution (of the United States of America) is antiquated, the people who believe loadouts are the same are wrong. Loadouts would have made Evolve far more dynamic and competitive. The class system is too restrictive in their intended roles. Which is why Evolve appears to be broken, and even more broken now than before. Can the developers still save Evolve at this point? Is all hope lost? Where does that tin-can get replacement heads from?! The answer to the first two questions at least is, probably. Evolve having gone F2P does not bode well for any sort of hope the devs, and publishers have for the title. As such, it is safe to assume Evolve is pretty much abandoned. It's simply too far too late, for any major change for the better to occur - at the very least it is highly unlikely.

This game is being sold on its resemblance to the early two-stick top-down shooter games of the 1980s, in particular Robotron 2084. This game does share in common two traits of that game: the stages are static full-screen rooms and enemies spawn in fixed quantities at random positions throughout the arena. What it doesn't share is its high pace and intensity. The default weapon has both very low firing speed and range, which makes clearing rooms a chore more than anything else, and the player is expected to upgrade them through grinding. Player reviews also commonly compare Iron Fisticle to Smash TV, an all-time favorite of mine. And while the two games are closer in graphical style, enemy behavior and co-op features, the gap in pacing is far more apparent. In a market where there are at least two other games that play similarly that give the player much more power from the start without slowly doling out more, Iron Fisticle can be recommended only for the very patient and those somehow amused by the double entendre in its title, which isn't played up much in the game proper.

Ghost Master is great fun.You are a spiritual entity who commands ghost. Your main resouce is ectoplasm, with which you pay for your ghosts' abilities. There are many different ghosts at your disposal since in each level, there is a ghost or ghosts you can free by fulfilling their wishes. Their abilities also vary; while some focus mainly on scaring mortals (Clatterclaws being one of the best and cheapest you can get), others have more specific abilities, such as creating artificial bond (a gift) or attracting mortals to their location. Your objectives also vary: sometimes you have to scare away everyone at the current location, sometimes you have to uncover a mystery or free a particular ghost.
Even though the game is highly enjoyable, there's one thing that really got on my nerves. MORTALS. Some of them are stupid beyond belief. Imagine you have to uncover a dead body in order to free the ghost that once resided in it. You use that ghost's ability to attract a mortal to see it. He walks right next to it, shrugs his shoulders and leaves the room. Sometimes it seems like they would rather be killed than help you to fulfill your objective. Oh, the frustration.
So, long story short...ghosts, scaring mortals, funny references (Hardboiled) and various objectives, classic game...and cheap. You shouldn't miss this one.

This is a unique game with great potentials. There's a lot of creeping around, looting houses, evading/fighting robots and being thrilled by all the dangers lurking around you and hunting you from the shadows. In this game the whole world seems to be against you, including the mad scientist who started it all, his evil/funny robots, the hot air balloon chasing you silently from above, the houses storing only rotten food when you're starving, scarecrows and sea monsters giving away your position, camp fires attracting the evil robots, and robodogs woofing as you try to outrun them. All in all, the game is a great challenge and a lot of scary fun. Depending on the patches, the game gets either really challenging or too easy at times, but this is part of the development process. One of the most odd name choices I've ever seen for a game, but also very fun. Great smooth responsive gameplay, great sound and music, and fantastic art direction. The enemies, weapons, and effects are all very well done and the game has great lighting. The graphics are fantastic. They are new-age retro rather than pure retro which is good because we do not want to see games nowadays with straight up NES graphics. Shooting thousands of Frankenstein monsters in the face never gets old. A lot of people are describing this as a twin stick shooter although there is no shooting involved. There is not a constant stream of projectiles anyway, although a couple weapons do fire very rapidly. It is more like a twin stick axe thrower. The weapons are all great, although I don't much care for the random spread of the ninja stars and I don't like the canon balls. Their hit box is too small compared to the normal axe but the aoe is cool. The upgrade system is great and is the only way you will be able to progress in the game and eventually beat it. Save your coins as much as you can so you can afford permanent upgrades. I try to not spend coins on temporary upgrades unless I am in a pinch or have extra coin. The game gets hard around floor 3 then harder on floor 4, but not for any other reason than the game starts flooding the screen with enemies and when you can't move a millimeter without touching an enemy, you are gonna be in trouble.

Lyne is an excellent pure puzzler that challenges your spacial awareness.  No quick reflexes or special items required.  No in-game purchases.  Relaxing visual layout and sound effects.  It's one of the best kinds of puzzle games in which you figure out how to play in minutes (thanks to a simple tutorial set), and can find yourself playing for hours to get just one more level completed.  All you do is create lines to connect like-colored shapes together.  The challenge involves passing through various hubs and not crossing over any lines you've already drawn.  If you need to start over, you just click on any shape to erase any lines previously drawn from that point.  For those who like Steam achievements, you get one for every set of 25 puzzles you complete, plus there are random daily sets.  Lyne is a highly addictive and satisfying mental workout.

Story: 6/10
Black Rose properly establishes it's classic atmosphere as a haunted home. Ignore the fact that this is a Funeral Home, this place is straight haunted from the core. Right off the bat, you're locked inside with no way out. Although there's little reason as to why you're there, the story within it's walls is thick and juicy enough to keep your attention. It feels like you're exploring the Haunted Mansion at Disney World, except this time around the monsters are real. There's a bit of an extravagant, hilarity to some of the text, the audio, even the story. It sounds so unbelievable but within the walls of this Funeral Home, it's all plausible.
There's an excellent attention to horror creep. By this, I mean that the story is able to teach you how to play whilst introducing new horrors to explore. Although you instantly see the first monster, you probably won't see her again (at least, not intentionally.) Then you jump into the next area and there's something new, but it's slightly creepier. Slightly more terrifying. Slightly above the previous encounter. After that, you keep going up, but it's so subtle that you're never expecting it to get worse. Even as I'm telling you this, you'll experience some horrors and scares that are so precise that you'll definitely keep talking about it.
Since the narrative is restricted to pieces of papers scattered randomly throughout the home, it makes you wonder how they showed up. And, if someone decides to skip a paper, how are they going to learn where to go? The papers are helpful as plot points, but immersion is lost when you imagine someone terrified of monsters taking time to write a novel. And, with such clarity, the narrator had time to contemplate philosophical questions of horror. Can he really spend time thinking about that? It makes little sense, but it doesn't ruin the experience. It's a minor issue that does little to dampen the lore of the narrative.
While there's mentions of horror philosophy, or dreadful themes that you'll experience in other narratives (Any Frictional Games production) they're not really indulged in. That's fine, since the story already feels a little crowded, and can be confusing, but it makes you wonder if someone helped edit this story for the developer. There were things that could have been edited out even in the text that you find. It's fine, but it's still a bit funky. It can ruin some of the realism.
Gameplay: 7/10
Proper understanding of development theory. We're taught multiple mechanics in the game before they're officially used. There are specific things such as quick times that teach you to use them again later, but then there's even more subtle things that you won't realize you were taught until afterwards. It's incredibly intelligent. It makes puzzle solving much, much easier. But, even with that above thing, you probably saw me mention quick times. Yikes. Well, there's not many, which is nice, but the final event has a quick time that was never established before, so be ready. I have no shame sharing this. Just be prepared!
Puzzles are handled well, but they're a little strange. They have an in world reason, but they're a little bit... well, you'll see. The puzzles were handled well, however. One particular thing that's strange about this game as that there are awkward save points that are set after certain events. Thankfully, most puzzles aren't super long or obnoxious so that when you restart a checkpoint you're not getting totally screwed with running around like mad.
Despite the proper ambience of the home, the home itself has some terrible architecture. This makes for horrendous exploration in a few rooms. There's one or two rooms that are empty, there's a room that cannot be explored, there's a tiny, tiny chapel. There's just a lot of strange set up that makes it weird to run around. And, on the topic of running, it's kind of ridiculous that you can just sprint around certain locations and the monsters will vanish. However, the developer is smart enough to recognize this, and they end up making a couple scenes where that doesn't happen. It keeps you on your toes. That said, the running space is crap. There's a few loops, but it's a tight squeeze. There's a lot of this pacing that makes the experience memorable, as well as intended false-reassurance to make the player feel safe when they aren't. It's fantastic.
One section I was completely lost. There was no direction. Only by pressing M1 was a location found to progress the plot. This is a little ridiculous, especially when the gameplay handles itself fairly well everywhere else. Also, clipping through doors. If the door is opening, a player can clip through them. You won't get stuck, but an item or two that's important the plot might. Be careful.
One small mention: There's a score system. This is neat, but the monster will earn you more points the closer he is. If you're playing the game, you can't really focus on that. If you're playing with friends, they'll tell you if you're safe. It's a bit of an exploit but it's not terrible. Everyone is freaking out anyway.
Sound: 9/10
Brilliant work! There's a ton of detail put into the audio. No complaints in this department. Ambience changes with each section, Voice Acting is pretty great, audio is recorded in high quality, non-repetative sound FX, songs all sound good and change depending on events, consistent sounds that align with the lore, there's so much good stuff.
Something really enjoyable is the fact that audio wasn't used for jumpscares. By that, I mean the audio didn't turn down to make the jump scare louder. Audio remains the same so encounters happen out of nowhere. It's excellent.
Art: 5/10
Character models are bear minimum. However, they don't really take away any effect. You're spending too much time running anyway.
Scripted animations look pretty great. Non-scripted (general walking animations) look kind of jank.
The textures are all good enough. Nobody is spending a lot of time focusing on the wallpaper. It does it's job.
Enjoyment: 7/10
Tons of fun. I played this with a lot of friends and we binged it from beginning to end. We all came to the conclusions you've read above and were almost unanimous on every subject. It's a good game, no doubt about it, but the attention to the sound effects along with a wonderful horror creep made things completely memorable. There isn't much to replay here, but that's fine considering the game is free. If anything, this is a great game to show off what a developer can do, so I'll definitely keep my eye on future releases.
OVERALL SCORE: 7/10

While this game has a some unique mecahnics it has 3 major problems.
1) Lack of a tutorial. It wasn't until the Shotgun guy that I realise I could move my character other than using their weapon.
2) Poor level design in some levels. You automatically respawn on the last land you touched but on some levels it's possible to fall back to a lower level, forcing you to repeat most of the level. Some levels also lack any land so you have to repeat the whole level if you make a single mistake.
3) You can only select a stage but not an individual level. So if you stop playing part way through a stage you have to repeat all the levels in this stage. This is especially annoying when there's a lot of levels or a few are very difficult.
Until you can select levels the player will continue to be punished for giving up half way through a stage.

I actually like this game and find it to be a nice simple game to play after you have nothing better to do, or you want to play a quick night because your bored. I like the balance of the gameplay and the formula of the Animatronics becoming active as the nights progress which adds a challenge. The jumpscares are not really scary as they just scream in your face but I don't mind them. The characters are all different from eachother and balance the game out. The characters are Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie the Bunnie, Chica the Chicken and Foxy the Pirate Fox. They have a different formular so its best to keep a good eye on them so they don't end you early in the night. I recommend that you keep your camera on Pirate Cove and Freddy most of the time as Foxy is the danger of not checking on him frequently. Freddy is also your main worry as he is pretty difficult to spot because he hides in the shade, and if he is at your right door I recommend that you close the door from time to time as he will sneak in the office and eventually kill you. I know Bonnie tends to leave first but whenever I'm playing Chica is the most active and continues to bug me, maybe its because Chica is my second favorite because she is creepy and I like her exagerated expressions.
The only minor issue I have with this game is it tends to lag a bit, but its probably because my laptop is old so maybe that's why.
While this game has been around for a year now, I actually like the game because it has a interesting story, the gameplay is simple and the characters balance the game pretty well and I like them overall. While this may seem like a bad idea for anybody who gets startled easily, I recommend using headphones because sound plays a important factor and can hint whether their close or not for example if you hear pots and pans clattering its obvious Chica is in the kitchen making a loud ruckus, and footsteps meaning their walking. If you listen closely in the later nights when you hear garbling but your not hallucinating it means that Bonnie or Chica are next to you in the corners of the hallways. The garbling happens when you see their heads twiching so that is a good hint that their close when your not checking the cameras.

Black Rose is sort of hard to talk about in my opinion. The thing is when I usually write up my reviews, my opinion to a game I usually have before even writing a review but Black Rose is just sort of average.
The story of Black Rose is that you're this unknown guy investigating this old abandoned funeral parlour for some reason and you need to figure out what the backstory is to the place and what happened to the owners. However there's a woman who is chasing after you so while you're discovering the mysterious backstory of the funeral parlour, you need to avoid her as well.
Gameplay is basically your typical horror game you'd expect to go along with this kind of story, you're wandering around a building with a flashlight looking around for stuff, meanwhile you need to avoid ghosts that haunt the place otherwise it's game over. Now you're probably wanting to know if, since this is a horror game, is it scary, well that's sort of hard to answer. To me, elements of Black Rose was scary, particularly the creepy voice coming from a baby monitor that you pick up, that was probably the scariest part of the game for me, however the issue with it is that it isn't the primary horror elements that it focuses on, this game heavily relies on jumpscares to scare the player, now I know that there are some people get scared by jumpscares but to me jumpscares are a cheap and tacky way to make a horror game if that's the only element that the game has going for it (Five Nights at Freddy's) but what I will give Black Rose credit for is that I can see that it actually tries. It tries to bring in some other horror elements into it but the majority of the time it doesn't really do much. The atmosphere about 80% of the time doesn't really build up anything the only exceptions being the basement with the coffin and the morgue, those areas actually fealt like I was bein stalked by a ghost somewhere. Now the jumpscares in this game are pretty bad. First off the game gives you a warning when the jumpscare is going to happen. The first warning is your flashlight starts to fliccker, that's telling you the ghost is near and when the jumpscare is about to happen, your flashlight turns to normal again but you're locked in place then in the span of 5 seconds, the ghost slowly animates it's self into place and then the lioud scream happens. Not exactly a good way to use jumpscares.
The graphics are mostly decent. The floor textures look pretty good, the walls also look really good for Unity however the models of the ghosts look terrible. They sort of look like what would happen if you tried to put a google jpeg image into the Unity engine and try to animate it. The doors and locks look liek they're out of place with each other. The locks look like they're pretty good but the dorrs don't look too good and doesn't seem like they fit in with each other either. So in a nutshell, if you don't closely analyse everything it looks decent however could look better.
The sound is primarily quite basic in this game. There are 2 things in the sound department that stood out however and that was the voice on the baby monitor and the jumpscare sound. The sound on the baby monitor was great and was one of the 3 things that I was actually really scare dof in this game. The jumpscare sound is terrible. I'm not entirely sure why but I think it's mainly just the build up done for the jumpscare (or the lack of a build up) that butchers it
However, the one thing that I need to take into consideration is that it's a free to play title but this sort of thing is the sort of common thing that you would expect from a free to play title. There are some really good titles that have a fre to play tag and are worth your time more than this one I think.
Pros
+ At times good atmosphere
+ Some good horror moments
+ No bug encounters
+ Decent graphics
Cons
- For the most part not scary
- Bad jumpscares
- Bad build ups
- Generic
- Some models seem out of place
Final verdict: 4/10

This game is really fun if you know what you're doing.  It will not hold anyone's hand beyond highlighting footprints/animals on the map. In the case of the hunters, communication is paramount, as is playing each role properly.  In the case of the monster, each action must be chosen with careful consideration. Play and counterplay abound.
Not much can top hunting down a big boss-like character being controlled by another human being, or being the monster crushing the four hunters.
Evolve does feature a horrid DLC structure, so if you do buy the game, please do not buy any DLC. There is day 1 DLC in the form of skins, which, I feel is inconsequential, and of course the ubiquitous season pass.  I'm not entirely sure if content was cut to sell as DLC, as balancing in this game requires lots of testing, iteration, etc.; the release date may give us a hint, although it could be purposely held back to deceive us.  However, given that the game was delayed by 3 months from it's original release date, I'm more inclined to believe the answer is no.
I think that people sell this game short when they point to a lack of content, as the content that is present in the game is balanced superbly, giving replayability through varying strategies and meta.

This game has very little to do about objectivism and capitalism. Because in a capitalist society people would buy,sell,trade and barter resources,goods and services even in a natural,financial or man-made disaster and in this game there is no such notion. You are forced to do use violence as your only option. This implies that any time that there is anarchy or little government that every human being would act like savages would only kill and loot everything in sight even though some of the resident of Rapture still retained some of their sentience and consiousness free of illness.
The game only allows you to buy upgrades and ammo from vending machines and never buy,sell and trade with the residents of Rapture which are literally placed all over the entire game. The game developers/writers deliberately designed the game to label capitalism as "evil". You are never given a choice to use non-violence to as an alternative or use non-lethal weapons to take hostile enemies down.
Here is the full definition of capitalism: "an economic system characterized by private or corporate ownership of capital goods, by investments that are determined by private decision, and by prices, production, and the distribution of goods that are determined mainly by competition in a free market"
The the huge irony is that all of these vending machines are all seem to be own by one single company and from the state of Rapture there doesn't seem to be anyone repairing and maintaining these machines as well as restocking them. I am surprised that 90% of these machines are still working and haven't been looted already by the locals themselves. This only proves that the developers were either too lazy or tried in a fail attempt to percieve capitalism as evil.
The story plot is also seriously bad as the writers made Andrew Ryan as the villain and delibrately made him the catalyst for "interfering" with the free market. The game writers also refused to mention that it was in fact that the SJWs,activists,socialists,altruists and communists that are the true villains of the story and that in a society that is well educated and capitalistic would have never been allowed such a disaster to occur.
The Resident Evil 4 merchant is a fine example that he is willing to exchange his goods and services for equal value. Do you need a pistol? Do you want it upgraded? Even though the obviously has more guns and weapons than you ever could he isn't forcing you to buy his weapons and he isn't robbing you either.
The game is definitely fun to play but it is simply just another Resident Evil 4 + Half-Life clone without the merchant. I will even compare these two game rather accurately.
+ A good community ravaged with an infection or epidemic? Check.
+ A zombie-like set of enemies known as Splicers that are the equivalent to the Ganadaos? Check.
+ A cult leader that is the one controlling and manipulating them? Check.
+ A game surrounded with quicktime events? Check.
+ A game with an item (herbs = adam) progression system? Check.
+ A game where a white man only kills white people? Check.
+ A game that is pretty linear and a limited open world? Check.
+ A silent protaganist that only follows orders? Check.
+ A ton of conveniently placed healing and fueling stations scattered across the game? Check.
The game in a nutshell is fun but the story is obviously poorly written and this poor written stories are pretty much repeated throughout the sequels in both Bioshock 2 and Bioshock Infinite. There is literally no real plot in both of those games which only solidifies this fact.

Before I start off this review, you probably already know what this game is about. But what you know of it from the countless YouTube videos of people screaming, breaking down the lore, etc. is very different from experiencing it yourself.
I feel as if some people have somewhat of a bad assumption of the FNAF games solely based on all of the reception the series has recieved over the past year. But coming from someone who's experienced all of the games first-hand, I can truly recommend them to anyone who likes the horror genre.
As you know, you play the role of a night security guard at Freddy Fazbear's Restaurant and you're tasked with monitoring security cameras to make sure the four animatronics don't goof off. The gameplay consists of closing your office doors, monitoring the camera, and using your door lights all while making sure you don't run out of power by the time 6AM rolls around.
The scariness factor in this game spawns from the inability to move or see certain spots. It's the fear of the unknown. You never truly know where the animatronics are at all times. They could be hidden in a blind spot outside your office, or possibly waiting to jump out at you from inside your office!
Even if the horror gameplay doesn't appeal to you, the game packs some pretty interesting lore that even hardcore theorists can appreciate.
In short, it's no wonder the game has become the gaming phoenomenon it is now. Looking at the games themselves, I can really grow to appreciate the FNAF series as they are. It's just the cancerous 8 year-old fanbase that really makes me get a bad taste in my mouth.

This game really requires both hunter and monster players to think every step during the game. Hunter and monsters have their own playing style.
Like monsters you should know how to avoid hunters in the early game. How to evolve as soon as possible and how to defeat well-teamed hunters in a right timing.
As hunters, you should know how to find monsters as quick as you can. Monsters will become very powerful when they evolve. Your advantage is in the early game. Kill monsters quick or you die.

So there are a lot of things to think about and to play with. It is really a fun game to play. Especially when you use monster to defeat hunters, you will feel like you really achieve something that is really big since you not only 1 VS 4 but also you win the game. Playing as other players' boss is amazing. I have played plenty of games and all bosses in the games are the most impressive elements. However, they are all AI. In this game, you can be the boss for other players. To crash them and destory them. Really a new and interesting feeling to me.

TL;DR: The concept of Evolve is great, but it was executed poorly. 2015's Titanfall, fun for a week, then done. Also, get an attention span so people like me don't have to dumb down reviews for idiots like you.... TL;DR indeed...
I think the idea of tracking/hunting down a creature using various methods in a beautiful locale is a great idea. Unfortunately this is not what we got from Evolve. I think many were expecting this game to be the next Left 4 Dead, which it definitely is NOT.
I thought that it would be a bit slower paced, you would follow tracks and other evidence, and ultimately, after a decent amount of time, find the beast and face off with it. I thought it would take skill and brains to track it, I thought it would make you THINK, god forbid. Instead what do we get? Follow the big glowy tracks that any idiot can see, or follow your hunting dog, or follow the sound of disturbed birds. No matter what you do, you end up spending about 90% of your time jetpacking around the map, often in circles, doing nothing. Just run and jetpack, run and jetpack. What happens when you finally find the monster? A battle, sure, but it's a big, chaotic, hectic mess. Often the monster runs away and you spend another several minutes running and jumping.... running and jumping. Find it again, big, chaotic mess, rinse and repeat. And you always have the sense of urgency looming over you because the longer you take to find the beast, the more powerful it becomes. It's always RUSH RUSH RUSH, FIGHT FIGHT FIGHT! Great for your typical ADD-riddled gamer of today, I suppose, but not for me.
There are several game modes, but ultimately you are doing as described above, with slightly different objectives. I feel like it was a lazy way to get more replay value, personally. I will also say, as patient as I am, the load times are INSANE for a modern game. In the game mode "Evacuation", you are essentially playing a multi-mission campaign, with one big payout at the end. The amount of downtime between these missions is frustrating to no end, 95% of is spent waiting for match start countdowns or just ludicrous load times. Pile on the rage.
The character abilities are well-thought-out, but some characters have rather unbalanced loadouts. Take, for example Lazarus, the medic. His only heal ability is an area-of-effect health burst with an all-too-long cooldown. "Don't use him", you say? Well to unlock the third and final medic character, you will need to master the abilities of the first 2 medics, Lazarus included. This makes matches with Lazarus very irritating to play in, but forces medic players to use him if they want to unlock the third medic character. Overall, the playable hunters are fairly solid in their design and balance with the aforementioned exception (and possibly a few more)
What bothers me the most, however, is how UNSATISFYING the game is. When you finally corner the monster, it doesn't feel like a reward, it feels like a pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥ You can never do any real damage to any of the monster types and they have so many attacks that knock you around and juggle you that combat is just frustrating and ultimately it's just NOT FUN. Even if you could get off uninterrupted attacks on the beast, you do so little damage to it that it doesn't even matter. It's not that killing a monster is impossible, or even hard, it's just not satisfying. The hunting isn't satisfying, the combat isn't satisfying, the winning isn't satisfying. It all just feels like work... and you don't even get paid for it!
Ultimately, to make this game good in my eyes, it would take a complete pacing, damage scale and combat revamp from top to bottom. I know that will never happen, so once I've put a little more time into it to justify the amount of money spent, I will not be returning to this game and I defintely don't recommend it to anybody unless you find the above written to sound appealing.

All this game has is the Ragnarok game, but it doesn't have anything unique and only uses the War of Emperium from RO1, but nothing else to honor the name, so to speak.
Well, RO1 was a huge part of my kid and teenage years, and even today I play it on and off, but on private servers, because the free extra character slots and ease of movement when it comes to teleporting to cities and a few areas is just so convenient.
Don't get me wrong, I liked this RO, but not enough to recommend it. I just wish the devs took aspects of RO1 and used in this game.
And one of them is inventory space, I like keeping crafting materials handy, and saving exp scrolls and some other utilities for later, and keeping monster cards. This was a piece of cake in RO1, because there's the cart for merchants, plus 300 inventory slots only otherwise limited by item weigth, and 500 storage slots. But here I caught myself not able to collect cards and save useful stuff because there's just not enough storage and inventory space, and I refuse to pay real money or tons of in-game money to get just a few extra slots in the storage and inventory. As for cards, there's a card album that you can put as many cards as you want, you get one with your newbie character, but you can use it only for 10 days, and if you want a permanent album, well, guess what... there's one in the cash shop. But even with the inventory expansions from the cash shop, it's nowhere near what RO1 had.
Another thing is community guides, what I could find about character builds and skills is pretty much all outdated, and even some 1+ year old posts on the official forums asking for help are left unanswered. This is frustrating because I want to know how a certain class works before I make a new character.
I also think it lacks build options, from what I could find, something that was different even in the first versions of RO1, even before the 2-2 jobs and rebirth jobs.
It also feels kinda rail-y, there aren't enough areas to explore, in my opinion, and there's just one path to go, something that RO1 (again) has a lot of - like at least two or three areas to grind at for each level range and job, if you're not into doing gramps quests, for those that play renewal IRO.
This one has Prontera, Izlude and Payon (kinda), Alberta, and Morocc, You follow this path in this order, and that's it. There's no big Payon with the archer village, no Al De Baran, Lutie, Comodo, Geffen, orc village, goblin village, toy factory,  just to name a few places from RO1. I know RO2 is way younger than RO1, but all these places I mentioned, and others, were present in earlier versions of RO1.
Another thing I liked, but at the same time disliked, was merging the merchant job, blacksmith and alchemist with the other classes. Of course it's nice to get some loot with your assassin and just open a shop with him to sell them later, or to be a knight that can craft his own equipment, and to be able to craft armor, and have the artisan and chef/cook classes, but I feel they "killed" content by excluding the merchant job tree as a character "main"/combat class, In RO1 blacksmiths have attack power and atk speed buffs for parties, in Renewal they can have a flipping mecha, and alchemists can summon plants, throw bombs and acid, throw potions to buff atk speed and heal, have a flipping homunculus to help in combat by dealing some damage, or buffing, or helping with stat boosts to have a better success chance with crafting. In RO2, blacksmiths and alchemists just gather and craft stuff, and that's it.
Maybe if they just remade RO1 with the graphics from RO2, but "merged" some RO1 maps so it doesn't have too many individual areas, and at kept the mounts from RO2, it would be a much better game.
One more thing, leveling up as a support class, well you can do it solo in RO1, just use Heal on undead monsters and it works like an attack, well there isn't this kind of thing here, as every monster has the same element/type, kind of.
Well, time to get back to RO1.

So finally ready to write a review of Evolve.
Evolve is by far one of the most fun online FPS games I´ve played for a long long time.
So to break it down.
Graphic wise Evolve is top of the line, nothing to complain about at all, I´m running everything maxed and my GPU has no issues running it, however make sure your GPU doesn´t overheat when running this game at those settings as it is a demanding game but it is sooo worth it in every aspect.
Gameplay wise Evolve is pretty simple and very easy to understand, you are either hunters or a monster, the hunters job is to kill the monster and the monters job is to survive, evolve and kill the hunters, pretty stright forward really.  However there is different gamemodes atm there is Hunt and Evacuation both brings different challanges and unique things into the game.
As you play you unlock new hunters or monster types and perks that will help you with either survival or killing whatever you prefer. Personally I´ve fallen in love with beeing a monster sneaking around and picking people off one by one soooo much fun hearing them rage in the map change screens ^_^
Community this game is top of the line too, there is build in voice chat, however unlike a LOT of other games, people here seems to in fact only talk and use it for game related things, even the games I´ve played with completely random people they have been good at team play, nice, polite well minus one guy who I`m sure was fapping ><
All in all this game is great and one of those games I will keep returning to for sure as more content gets added with DLC´s and we know it will as it is published by 2K who is masters of DLC´s (Check borderlands 2) but honestly I cannot wait.
If the price is scaring you a bit then wait for a sale, but if you like online FPS team play do NOT miss out on this title!

NOTE: THERE ARE NO SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW
Bioshock is a well-polished game with a great storyline, and was interesting all the way through. The environment/setting alone is worth the price of admission. It's obvious this game was created with a lot of love. It's too bad this game was created as a console game and ported to PC. I feel like it could have been so much more if it had treated PCs as first-class citizens. But back when this game was made, if you wanted to pitch a game you had to release on consoles first. Overall, I highly recommend this game. I played it for the first time in 2015, and it holds up very well despite its age.
+ Random loot.
+ Atmosphere. Very well themed - everywhere you look, there is something interesting to see.
+ FPS controls work well and seem polished.
+ Lore tapes are really enjoyable and help deliver the story in an interesting fashion.
+ Progression of weapon power is good - not too slow or too fast.
+ The tutorial was nicely integrated into the starting area. I didn't feel like I was going through a tutorial.
+ It's nice that death has no penalty in this game, especially since you die so much.
+ Ability to re-search containers is nice, but kinda gimmicky. Better to not *need* to search containers a second time. Plus, it makes no sense.
+ Ammo variations were cool. Anti-personnel rounds, armor-piercing rounds, electric rounds.
+ Enemies can get hit by their own friendly fire - very nice.
+ Taking pictures of creatures to research them for bonuses was a neat concept.
- Most loot containers are empty - kind of a time waster.
- Switching back and forth between Windows and the game requires you to change your graphics setting back from "windowed" mode, which it resets to. Every. Single. Time.
- I wish there were more tactical options in combat, like quick dodge/roll, leaning around corners, etc.
- Could have used a bit more backstory or exposition for setting up the world and what happened. Just a plane crash in 1960...and a light house...BAM, done, go.
- Enemies (and the player) are bullet sponges. Also, there is no reduction of effectiveness for being damage. You're just as effective at 1% health as you are at 100%.
- I crashed to desktop almost every time I exited the game to Windows.
- Enemies respawn way too much. I don't like enemy respawns at all, but if you're going to do them, at least keep them low. I would clear and area and 5 mins later it's full of enemies again.
- If you don't use the exact correct ammo, guns will do very little damage to enemies. You can unload a full magazine of armor piercing ammo on a creature that is resistant to AP, and it barely scratches it. Damage resistance seems a little too heavy.
Just remind you that, don't buy this game if you want to play this by using your phone. There is a phone version for you in Google play. And I have bought a phone version after refunding this.

Ok, so I've played this game off and on prior to downloading it here on steam and got to about mid-level. So here's what I think about the game! It's not nearly as bad as some people might make it out to be, and I think people would be less upset if this game had nothing to do with the Ragnarok universe and just had its own. But obviously that's not the case here.
So onto the main problems with the game, the first one being that it's generic. Painfully generic. HELLA generic. In fact, one of the only features about this game that even remotely help it stand out is the fact that it's a Ragnarok game--and in my opinion, in name only. RO2 has none of what made the original so great...The charming pixelated sprites being replaced with generic animu models, bland (and again, generic) combat mechanics you'll find in just about every tab-targetting game, a lacking soundtrack, and shady behavior from the GMs are all reasons why this game and the original Ragnarok Online just can't compare.
In conclusion...
If you're looking for a new MMO to try and hold you over for a little bit and aren't too picky, go ahead and give it a try. I still find myself briefly coming back to it when I'm bored and up for a simple game to keep me entertained for a while myself.
However, if you're coming into this game expecting anything even remotely close to the original Ragnarok, then you'll be very disappointed.
Final Verdict: Play Tree Of Savior instead.

This game is a hidden gem. You have an arsenal of ghosts available to you and you want to scare people in a Sims type environment. The game starts of great with a cheesy fmv, you get to scare people in different ways with different ghosts.
Unfortunately, they took it a step too far for me. The third and fourth mission were very puzzly. You needed to use certain ghosts in certain situations or you wouldn't be able to progress.
I completed the third mission a little bit aggrevated because you needed to guide people to certain locations which was a chore. The mission after that was straight up "use this ghost in this situation to trigger this event, then use another ghost to do this and that".
I wish they just kept it to scaring people and didn't make you solve puzzles. There is depth in just scaring people since certain people are scared of certain things.
I wouldn't recommend it if you're not into the puzzles. Still, it's quite an unique game and I might persevere to see if things change.
EDIT: I made it to the final mission before I became too frustrated to continue. As expected, most of the later missions are puzzle based and can be quite frustrating without a guide (in some cases even with a guide). The final mission is completely bonkers, in a bad way. You're reliant on luck for a correct scenario to occur and you pretty much need a certain secret ghost to complete it.
If you do pick this up, I would recommend using a guide if you're feeling frustated.
Unfortunately even with a guide I was able to get stuck in a mission because I didn't have the proper ghost power to proceed. My only options were to go replay a previous mission and unlock a secret ghost that had that ghost power or go buy it for one of my existing ghosts (which wasn't an option as I already spent my coin for powers on other ghosts). I ended up editing my game with a save game editor to get that power.
This game was an unique experience. Gameplay mechanics were great, the strong focus on puzzles was a letdown.

Sir is an incredibly addictive game with a great gameplay foundation -a survival simulation based in an open environment, in which you have to manage your energy, health, and what you're carrying while searching for 25 artifact fragments strewn about 5 islands...all the while being hunted by intelligent, agressive robot gentlemen. This supposedly simple setup of 'get the fragments and escape with your life', spirals into a remarkably dense balance of combat and resource management, due to its underlying gamplay mechanics -not unlike Sir's spiritual predecessor, the STALKER series.
Also of note: the procedural generation of the islands and buildings insures that your experience is unique (you won't find a "let's play" video walkthrough of this one), and the aggressive enemy AI and their deliberately overpowered weaponry always keeps you on your toes.
I'd recommend this game to anyone looking for the next hardcore first-person shooter challenge. Despite it's semi-cartoonish trappings, this game is only for the brave.

This is an old favorite of mine. Ghost Master is a game which is quite one of a kind. You play as a 'Ghost Master' who is the leader of a gang of ghosts who's task it is to scare the people of Gravenville.
Each level is a parody of a well known horror movie. For example, there's a level called Poultrygeist. The level is set in a house which was built where a slaughterhouse for turkeys once stood. The goal is to free a poltergeist, who looks like a ball of light with feathers foating around it. Other settings range from sorority houses to hospitals to a military base.
Each level has its own goal. Most of the time, that goal is to scare all humans untill they flee the location, or to drive them insane. In more complex levels, you need to manipulate the humans into doing certain tasks for you. Some humans (priests, wiccans,...) will fight back and try to banish your ghosts. You will find trapped ghosts in each level, who are stuck to an object. If you manage to free the ghost by doing a certain task/solving a certain puzzle, they will join your team. Each ghost has its own skills, and you can teach it new abilities following a skill tree. You can revisit each level and try a new team of ghosts and see if you can get a higher score with them. This adds a lot of replayability.
The best part of this game is in my opinion the sound design. When starting a level, all you hear is some sort of astral choir, singing in the distance. As your ghosts start interfering with the world, the music reacts to their actions. This builds up untill all hell breaks loose, and then, well, you should hear it for yourself. The music is awesome.

Long before the likes of Geometry Wars or Waves, twin stick shooting gameplay has been reimagined countless times since the 80's first gave us classics like Robotron or Berzerk. Introducing the directional shooting and arena based challenges was the start of a new genre, and soon we saw deeper level progression in the form of dungeon crawlers like Gauntlet or SMASH T.V. Iron Fisticle seeks to bring modern twin-stick action and 80's arcade arena shooting into a classic RPG setting of medieval madness.
Iron Fisticle stays true to the classic formula with the classic 8-directional shooting we remember from the best of arcade classics while adding its own brand of modern flashiness through crisp and highly stylised pixel art provided by the ever talented Tikipod of Aqua Kitty fame. The game spices up the basic high-score arena shooting gameplay with a few elements of randomization and persistence giving roguelike depth to a generally simple arcade concept.
The dungeons are laid out in a grid starting you in one corner and the boss in the other, with layouts being randomized each playthrough. Defeating any given room leaves you faced with the decision of which direction to travel in, taking into consideration upgrades and powerups needed along the way to properly defeat the bullet-hell action of each of the four floor bosses. Different routes will provide you with either a shop for upgrades or a platforming minigame for earning coins, and sufficently powering up your character along the way is vital before facing any of the floors bosses.
Even though the game stays mostly true to the shoot-'em-up roots of SMASH T.V. it includes the addictive properties of an RPG or roguelike. You also occasionally come across permanent upgrades that carry over on consecutive playthroughs, which raise any particular stat and is where the persistence comes from. These are very valuable, making future trips into the dungeon much more manageable and high scores more obtainable for diligent explorers who are keen to find and collect a good amount of upgrades.
Aside from the stat modifying upgrades you find are weapons you can gain from leveling up, and the selection is impressive. From walls of throwing daggers, streams of blue flamethrowers, to rows of area effecting bombs, there's plenty reason to keep playing and discover all of the devastating ways you can end your foes and rush through the levels even faster than before. Despite having beat the game, I still find new tools to play around with on each playthrough that make me re-evaluate how I could tackle it again.
Iron Fisticle is retro done right and a dream come true for score chasers. The adrenaline gives you an arcade high as you make a mad dash around each map collecting the pixelated food that drops to keep your multiplier going and test your skill against the world on the leaderboards. Even though a single playthrough can be experienced in one sitting, its the kind of game you'll want to visit everyday just to see how much better you can do the same way many of us revisit our favorite arcade classics.
With a solid brand of arcadey twin-stick chaos chock-full of addictive RPG properties that push you towards multiple playthroughs, excellent couch co-op, a heavy and groovy chiptune soundtrack complimenting crisp and attractive pixel art visuals all rolled into one package Iron Fisticle is one nostalgic experience that should not be passed up.

This project explains why every interactive work is not supposed to be consistently about entertainment; and how it can harm the way of creation. Think of this as a piece of art. A movie, if you like. But this is not a game. It is a form of communication, a way of expressing feelings.
I would like to keep going, but anything said beyond this would ruin it. Just don't try to explore the games, try to explore the mind behind it. Try to observe the changes. I am sure you will find a piece of yourself in there.

Wow... I am fairly impressed with this game.
Had a random coupon for 25% off, wanted to see what it was about.
Ended up being one of the better uses of six bucks lately.
This game is basically a strange Smash TV reboot with a more zombie/monster theme to it.
The biggest difference is the rougelike aspect of it.
As you play, you get points and level up... easy, but you don't directly choose what to upgrade that way.
Rather, you must make it to the shops with enough loot to BUY upgrades from the random list of 4 or so.
Some are permanent, and cost more then twice as much, others are for that game alone.
What leveling up does is unlock things for you to work with, be it new items that will drop in game, or greater max stats to invest into/ upgrade during game.
This adds an interesting layer to the chaotic nature of this kind of game.
HOWEVER... it is only LOCAL co-op, which can be fairly dissapointing.
It does a GREAT job of recreating the 16bit era. Lots of action, controller support, local co-op, and responds/looks like an authentic SNES/Genisis game.
It's the kind of 'retro' old schoolers typically refer to when they keep forgetting just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ a lot of 8 bit games were.

Initially I thought a game that was made in black and white would be too dreary and monotone to hold my attention for very long.  However the dark, atmospheric environments combined with the grainy light effects creates a really engrossing 2d world.  The subtle use of sound, with little to no music, adds to the eeriness of the game.  There were times where the music would kick in towards the end of a chapter/zone and make me wish that it played for most of the game.  Some of the levels, especially those that took a while to solve, got a little bare for me and I think music would've added quite a bit.
The game is very minimilast in general.  There are direction keys and an interact button.  Its strictly linear, and there is really nothing to explore.  The game consists of chapters, each of which take place in the same environment with similar puzzle physics.  The first half of the game containst mostly creatures and other enemies, while the second half seemed to only have puzzles.  The real challening puzzles probably didn't kick in until the last hour or two.  And I almost wish there were zone bosses or something bigger that you were progressing to, other than different puzzles.
So shortly after playing the game I had one major complaint, and that was rooted in the games minimilast style.  I've never been a fan of games or movies where the player or viewer is supposed to create their own story through imagination.  I have no problem when open-endeness adds to the story or create conversation.  For example, the spinning top at the end of Inception adds to the movie, the film doesn't depend on it.  But when your game or movie has a wide open gap that is supposedly intended for you to supplement with your own version, I think its just lazy or an excuse for poor writing.
But, after thinking about it, the game is certainly catered to be more episodic.  It's not intended to be completed in 1-2 sittings like I did (4 hours total).  There is no plot or characters for you to worry about. There is a minimal story to hang the framework of the game on, and the rest is just fun, atmospheric puzzles to explore zone to zone.  And in this way it succeeds.
I would almost recommend you purchase it on iOS than PC, or at least plan to play it in short sittings. I believe I got it on sale but even for $10 you get your mon

If you've been anywhere on the internet you've probably seen something of Five Nights at Freddy's. Or if you walked around a mall in a really white neighborhood, and saw some little 8 year old fat kid wearing a t-shirt with Five Nights at Freddy's on it, that's an easy way to learn that it exists too. It's a meme, no doubt about it. Let's not beat around the bush about it. Becoming a meme is a double-edged sword to an indie upstart. On one hand, everyone on the internet will know you. Whether they like it or not. On the other hand, not liking it is very common, and they're always on par with or more passionate than the ones that like you.
Aside from being the dankest meme of 2014, Five Nights at Freddy's is a humble little survival-horror game. It didn't exactly have it easy. Imagine you're an indie guy, trying to make a game. And people like you. They really like you. But, oh, now they're making furry porn of your characters, and, oh, now they're making cringey memes of your game. Now everyone hates you. Now all of your hard work will forever be remembered as degenerate furry garbage. That's exactly what you get for using anthropomorphic animal characters for your game you ♥♥♥♥ing furry.
In Five Nights at Freddy's, you're tasked with staying alive in a Chuck E Cheese full of♥♥♥♥♥♥machines. They want to stuff you in a fur suit and yiff you to death. With no escape, you lock yourself in your office and try to survive the night by closing the doors and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself. Conceptually, it's definitely different. It's not a zombie-ridden stereotype fest. It's not a cheap knockoff of another horror game. It's unique. It's almost like a genre that the game industry rarely taps into has come to life through this. The wonderful world of horror B-movies. Are they meant to be scary? Yeah, a little. Are they? Sometimes. But they're more than that. They're fun. They don't take themselves too seriously. Or they take themselves too seriously, to the point where no one else can take them seriously. That's kinda where this game falls, between those.
It's easy to see that this game is low-budget. It was developed by one man, and he's not a billionaire. This ain't Bill Gates. He's off in Africa somewhere carrying small African children on his back like a spider, trying to find the fountain of youth and wrestle lions that keep attacking his villages. This game came up from the streets. It's not a very pretty game. The art style works. But it's just not done very well. It's definitely dark, and atmospheric, and gets you in the mood to yiff♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with murderous robots. It gets the job done. But you can see visible warping in the environment as you move around. And you can't really move much in the game anyway, you're stuck in a room defending yourself from furries, so it's not like they had a lot of environments to design. The least they could've done was make the one room you're stuck in look nicer.
At the same time, the art style seems to help make the game. Something about the entire game's slightly off appearance makes it creepier. It invokes the uncanny valley feel, and in a way seems fitting when you consider it's a game about animatronics. Which are creepy as ♥♥♥♥ to stare at. Their lifeless, mechanically blinking eyes.... Its mouth, hinging and unhinging unnaturally, as it sings you Happy Birthday in a southern American accent... It's vile. Disgusts me in a deep, spiritual way. It's just wrong. Animatronics are just a crime against the greater good. Yes, this game is very personal to me. I stopped going to Chuck E Cheese a long time ago. We don't talk about it anymore.
The atmosphere and feel are done very well, as low-budget as the game may be. The core mechanics tie directly into the tense feel of the game. Or rather, mechanic, as there's only really one game mechanic. All you can really do in the game is check cameras, open lights, and close doors. You're a security guard locked in a room. You check your cameras to make sure you know where your horny robot friends are. If they're not where you can see them, you open your lights. If you don't♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants, turn off the lights. If you do, make sure you close the door or else you're dead. That's the game in a nutshell. Incredibly simple, yes. It's not a complex game. But there's beauty in subtlety and minimalist design. The fact that you have very little control over what's happening builds the tension. You're helpless in the truest of senses. All you can do to stop death is check to make sure it's not there, and if it is, close the door. And not only that, your defense is crippled even further by your limited resources. Everything you do will consume electricity. And should you run out, you suddenly can't do things anymore. Which leaves you at the mercy of the robots.
It's an incredibly tense game. It's paranoia-inducing, and drives home a sense of terror. And yes, when the monster gets you, he pops out and goes "Boo" like monsters do. Five Nights at Freddy's thrives on the jump-scare. Is that a bad thing? Yes and no. They definitely do rely on it. But jump-scares are a staple of horror. Everyone uses them. Do they use it a little too much? Yes. The game can be summed up with "I looked in the spot. The monster was in the spot. Nope. I'm not looking in that spot ever again. Let's just turn this game off and go take a long shower. Forever."
The jump-scares are done decently. They're adequate pay-off, but the tension is the best part. The stress, fear, and paranoia are the things that make this game great. Not the jump-scares. They're scary, yeah. But they definitely do bring with a little baggage. As the nights go on, you'll find yourself being assaulted more often. The patterns that the animatronics follow will get mixed up, and they'll be more active. A lot more tense when suddenly they're not where you expect them to be and actually right there in the room with you. But at the same time, dying much more often for the sake of difficulty can also be frustrating.
A good jump-scare is like taking it up the butt. You can't rush it. You need lube, you need to go slow, and you need to be in the mood. No matter how ready you think you are, it's gonna surprise you when suddenly there's something in your butt that shouldn't be there. When done right, it's an enjoyable experience for everyone. But when suddenly it's happening too often, too fast, and when you're not in the mood, you're not gonna be happy. You're just gonna have♥♥♥♥♥♥♥up your butt and be very upset about it. That's how Five Nights at Freddy's starts to feel at the end. Not to mention the jump-scare is a little ridiculous. It sounds like a baby pterodactyl. Or maybe like you stuffed a box full of gerbils into a wood-chipper. But, as Five Nights at Freddy's sort of embodies the horror B-movie, I feel like how stupid it comes across as is really just part of the fun. No one is actually really terrified by the Killer Klowns from Outer Space. It's all part of the fun. The people tearing this game up about how "dis game is so bad, i showed babby and didnt even cry, 0/10 not scary, anoyone that older than 2 year old do not buy" miss the point.
If you can't appreciate the nature of a bad horror movie, this might not be for you. It's not a perfect game. It's clearly low-budget and gets by on cheap thrills. But to neglect the clever mechanics that promote paranoia and fear in unique ways because people enjoy it is stupid.
It's like watching amine. You don't tell normal people that you enjoy it. It's just a secret that you talk to your loser internet friends about. You can wear your Five Nights at Freddy's t-shirt in the safety of your own home. In your closet, when your parents aren't home, while you jack off to furry porn.
I won't tell anyone you do it. It's okay.

When I approached the house, what I did not expect was another survivor, we teamed and decided it was for the better.
Pans smacking against a head in the school, we kill a zombie that blocked out only exit, we ran.
Later on we found an old broken-down house that seemed to be cracking and moldy. We cooked up some stir-fried eggs and thought, this isn't the life. We set out looking for meat, bacon, eggs, cheese and sausage.
Coming back, we feasted on out mutton and bacon stir-fry. In the middle of our meal, I heard gunshots and ran back to the safehouse. "DUDE!" I yelled. "What?" He said quickly."I heard gunshots, hide, lock the doors." We scrambled desperately, for our lives were on stake. After I closed all the blinds, a man with a gun ran through the back door, "Hey,"
"You scared us!" I hoped desperatley it wouldn't agro him. "You guys fine?" He said with a gun in hand. I answered back nervously, I was anxious (real 'symptom' in the game). "Yeah." He dropped peanut butter and chips.
He later offered us an escort to the city, and we agreed. All three of us running down the street, knowing we were close.
Then a man with a gun appeared around the corner of the intersection. I yelled out, "Over here!" Then began to speak.
Suddenly, he opened fire. We desperatley tried to pull off a shot with out hammers and pans, but we weren't lucky.
In a life or death situation, I ran for the nearest house, and so did my first friend. "I'm dying." He said, I checked, (literal stats from the game) I had two bullet holes in my chest, hitting one of my lungs, somehow still alive and running, one in the leg and one in my upper pelvis. Without a word, I opened the nearest window, and ran.
I saw another house and broke into it, I ran to the bedroom and opened the window. From the back of the house, I saw my friend, get shot and killed, the other was right next to him, trying to fight back with his gun, but got shot by the man too. I went back to the window and tried to bandage myself up. First, the chest. Then I gave up, I knew I was dying slowly from the blood pouring out my legs and pelvis. I sat there and bled out.
Pretty good narrative for a pretty simple game mechanic. But it's pure awesomeness.
