TL;DR: The concept of Evolve is great, but it was executed poorly. 2015's Titanfall, fun for a week, then done. Also, get an attention span so people like me don't have to dumb down reviews for idiots like you.... TL;DR indeed...
I think the idea of tracking/hunting down a creature using various methods in a beautiful locale is a great idea. Unfortunately this is not what we got from Evolve. I think many were expecting this game to be the next Left 4 Dead, which it definitely is NOT.
I thought that it would be a bit slower paced, you would follow tracks and other evidence, and ultimately, after a decent amount of time, find the beast and face off with it. I thought it would take skill and brains to track it, I thought it would make you THINK, god forbid. Instead what do we get? Follow the big glowy tracks that any idiot can see, or follow your hunting dog, or follow the sound of disturbed birds. No matter what you do, you end up spending about 90% of your time jetpacking around the map, often in circles, doing nothing. Just run and jetpack, run and jetpack. What happens when you finally find the monster? A battle, sure, but it's a big, chaotic, hectic mess. Often the monster runs away and you spend another several minutes running and jumping.... running and jumping. Find it again, big, chaotic mess, rinse and repeat. And you always have the sense of urgency looming over you because the longer you take to find the beast, the more powerful it becomes. It's always RUSH RUSH RUSH, FIGHT FIGHT FIGHT! Great for your typical ADD-riddled gamer of today, I suppose, but not for me.
There are several game modes, but ultimately you are doing as described above, with slightly different objectives. I feel like it was a lazy way to get more replay value, personally. I will also say, as patient as I am, the load times are INSANE for a modern game. In the game mode "Evacuation", you are essentially playing a multi-mission campaign, with one big payout at the end. The amount of downtime between these missions is frustrating to no end, 95% of is spent waiting for match start countdowns or just ludicrous load times. Pile on the rage.
The character abilities are well-thought-out, but some characters have rather unbalanced loadouts. Take, for example Lazarus, the medic. His only heal ability is an area-of-effect health burst with an all-too-long cooldown. "Don't use him", you say? Well to unlock the third and final medic character, you will need to master the abilities of the first 2 medics, Lazarus included. This makes matches with Lazarus very irritating to play in, but forces medic players to use him if they want to unlock the third medic character. Overall, the playable hunters are fairly solid in their design and balance with the aforementioned exception (and possibly a few more)
What bothers me the most, however, is how UNSATISFYING the game is. When you finally corner the monster, it doesn't feel like a reward, it feels like a pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥ You can never do any real damage to any of the monster types and they have so many attacks that knock you around and juggle you that combat is just frustrating and ultimately it's just NOT FUN. Even if you could get off uninterrupted attacks on the beast, you do so little damage to it that it doesn't even matter. It's not that killing a monster is impossible, or even hard, it's just not satisfying. The hunting isn't satisfying, the combat isn't satisfying, the winning isn't satisfying. It all just feels like work... and you don't even get paid for it!
Ultimately, to make this game good in my eyes, it would take a complete pacing, damage scale and combat revamp from top to bottom. I know that will never happen, so once I've put a little more time into it to justify the amount of money spent, I will not be returning to this game and I defintely don't recommend it to anybody unless you find the above written to sound appealing.

I am mostly going to review the Forces of Corruption expansion and compare it to the base game. Although I will also say that this is one of the best Real-time strategy games I have played so far. The new things that were added to the campaign are the ability to sabotage Rebel or Empire bases in other planets as well as the ability to view their formations secretly. The expansion also gave the ability to travel to other systems undetected using bribery, which could prove extremely useful if you do not want to engage a considerable fleet and rather just simply bypass them. Although the Zann Consortium has only 4 buildings in which it can produce units which is a drawback for me as the enemy AI has fewer buildings to destroy in Skirmish or Galactic Conquest mode, it is rectified by the ability to corrupt planets in the Campaign or GC mode. Once you corrupt a planet, either Rebel or Empire, you have the ability to acheive a unit exclusive to it (such as a Tartan Patrol Cruiser or a Marauder-Class corvette) using the balck market and other benefits such as Bribery and Corrupt Militia. The best addition to the game is that they added a few more units in skirmish mode, in addition to more buildables in skirmish games. The new units and ships in-game means that you would have more options into bringing reinforcements as opposed to just simply generating all the units and sending them all in one skirmish game. Another great addition is that three-way battles are now playable on certain maps in both land and space battles as well as the AI in skirmish games improving considerably.  Even though the Zann Consortium has fewer ships and units than the Rebels and The Empire, they rectify it with the firepower they have such as the Aggressor-class Star Destroyer and the Destroyer Droid Mark II. Overall, this expansion had more postive aspects than negative ones and I enjoyed the additions this game had to offer. Dissapointing to note though is that they completely shut down the multiplayer servers back in 2014. At least the LAN option is still available.

This is a zombie survival simulator RPG. A proper one. And quite possibly the only proper one, because every other so called 'zombie RPG' out there either tries to do a silly gimmick to make itself unique or really isn't a 'sim' at all.
Not Project Zomboid. From the very start, Zomboid has been dead set focused on creating a realistic survival experience that is both challenging and exciting. It is what it is; hard, cold, realistic. No run and gunning. The focus is not on killing the undead, but avoiding them wherever possible.
And you will die. A lot.
With the upcoming implementation of NPCs (of which are set to be some of the most dynamic and interesting in RPG history), vehicles and an ever expanding map, if you're into zombie survival simulators or RPGs, then this game is for you.

So finally ready to write a review of Evolve.
Evolve is by far one of the most fun online FPS games I´ve played for a long long time.
So to break it down.
Graphic wise Evolve is top of the line, nothing to complain about at all, I´m running everything maxed and my GPU has no issues running it, however make sure your GPU doesn´t overheat when running this game at those settings as it is a demanding game but it is sooo worth it in every aspect.
Gameplay wise Evolve is pretty simple and very easy to understand, you are either hunters or a monster, the hunters job is to kill the monster and the monters job is to survive, evolve and kill the hunters, pretty stright forward really.  However there is different gamemodes atm there is Hunt and Evacuation both brings different challanges and unique things into the game.
As you play you unlock new hunters or monster types and perks that will help you with either survival or killing whatever you prefer. Personally I´ve fallen in love with beeing a monster sneaking around and picking people off one by one soooo much fun hearing them rage in the map change screens ^_^
Community this game is top of the line too, there is build in voice chat, however unlike a LOT of other games, people here seems to in fact only talk and use it for game related things, even the games I´ve played with completely random people they have been good at team play, nice, polite well minus one guy who I`m sure was fapping ><
All in all this game is great and one of those games I will keep returning to for sure as more content gets added with DLC´s and we know it will as it is published by 2K who is masters of DLC´s (Check borderlands 2) but honestly I cannot wait.
If the price is scaring you a bit then wait for a sale, but if you like online FPS team play do NOT miss out on this title!

I'm not gonna comment on the graphics or on the scary portions.
Instead, I'm gonna talk about the gameplay. You start inside the house, then you navigate to point A, open a door, grab an item, then move back down to point B, then move up and down to point C... Doing so takes some time, and you still have to wait a couple of seconds for each "cutscene". Then you finally get something new, some action, some game-over state.
And after the game-over, you are forced to walk everything again. And wait/watch the cutscenes again. And then you can avoid the first game-over, but then, a few minutes later, you get another game-over. And you have to restart everything from the start.
The game gets very repetitive and boring because the player has to redo all the parts again and again. The game is mostly a trial-and-error. Try something, fail, then restart from the beginning and try again.
The core gameplay is not good: it is time-wasting. And that's why I don't recommend this game.

This is a good, albeit flawed gem.
On one side, the combat is solid, with the need to control the battlefield being the top priority, movement can be enhanced through partnership and powers, and it has a good-ish story that don't deviate from the 'power of friendship and hope' from older shows. Every member of the squad has specific roles that can and will be needed at all times, and some references are spot-on. The music is based on the super nintendo era, and some pieces are really good, specially "Hardboiled" and "Monster Jam".
On the other hand...
The loot and crafting is messy and can be quite a headache if you need specific gear for your team, everything is randomized, how many items you get, if you get said items, and which items. There are two kinds of gear, crafted, and bought. Bought items always have specific stats, and crafted ones have the advantage of two or three 'extra' stats. The problem is, said stats are randomized too.
And boy, it can be quite buggy. In my run, the game auto-skipped the first speech of every character in a scene, the music would suddenly stop, and sometimes it interloped with the menu music if I started the stage too fast.
So, if you want a nice strategy game, and are not afraid of some minor bugs, get this gem!

is a real time game in which you assemble a team of haunters to scare off mortals and release trapped spirits to join your cause. You start out with a handful of ghosts to send a group of college girls screaming from their sorority house. Over time, you get to recruit spirits to tackle more challenging scenarios.
Many of the characters and scenarios in this game are inspired by TV shows, movies, and comics. Recognizing these pop culture references may get you chuckling. I’ve spotted references to
,
,
, The Three Stooges, and many more. The whole concept of gathering ghosts to scare off mortals makes this game immensely fun, especially when plenty of humor is thrown in. It certainly helps that many of the scenarios are cleverly designed.
Despite all the good things going for this game, some of the fun is sapped out of it when trying to figure out what powers should be activated to get mortals to do certain actions. For example, in one scenario, you need to send three mortals to a cabin to complete a ritual, but the mortals would first have to find a way to cross a raging river and a deep chasm. Since the solution to these and other problems isn’t always obvious, you may need to experiment with different powers before making headway.
This wouldn’t have been a problem if not for the fact that mortals move around the map randomly like characters in
. Some will use the bathroom, take a drink of water, or converse with their friends at random moments. While it does seem natural to have mortals behaving in this manner, it doesn’t help if you have to wait a long time for a mortal to do a particular action, such as bringing a gift to a specific room. If you aren’t even sure that what you’re attempting will work as intended, then having to wait more than a minute becomes an exercise in frustration.
Even with these problems,
is highly entertaining. If scaring the bejesus out of little computer people sounds like fun (and believe me, it is), do yourself a favor and get yourself a copy now.

As a disclaimer, I love the concept of survival.  I love the show 'Alone.'  I enjoyed the Flame in the Flood, Miasmata, and Don't Starve.  But The Long Dark is the most fantastic piece of survival media out there.  It feels real.  It teaches you to be patient, to minimize risk, and to discard most of the cheats you've learned in other games.
It is, alas, an alpha game and therefore imperfect.  I have suffered a handful of glitches and there are some features that don't really make sense to me from an administrative perspective.  That said, even in its current state, it is one of my favorite games of all time and an absolute joy to experience.
The game is a challenge, although not to an impassable degree, and I progressed to Wolf Mode (Stalker Level) over time because I began to learn how to actually survive.  Don't misread this and throw yourself into the Northwest Territories because you learned how to handle a video game, but I truly felt like my experience with singular wilderness survival improved and that, accordingly, I was able to progress to higher difficulties in the game.
It is difficult to make a parallel to other games, where you might increase your difficulty level as you memorize button combinations, improve your trigger finger, or take advantage of predictable conversation or pixel patterns.  Instead, you start to appreciate the relationship between your vitals and weigh the risks and rewards of going out in a blizzard for food because you're starving or risking a wolf pack encounter in order to change locations because your safe house is no longer sustainable in the long-term.
Keeping in mind my original disclosure,
I cannot recommend this game enough.

Probably one of the better shooters that I have played, though the experience was slightly muddied by various audio bugs I kept running into while playing.  Still, by far one of the better single-player shooters; something I wished kind of carried over into other shooters of today.
Story-wise, this game clicks with me a lot.  I'm not usually a fan of 50's Noir; I grew up obsessed with the Space Age and the advances made in the space race during the Cold War.  But this game still clicks with me.  I have a bit of a 'fetish' of sorts that involves deep, isolated places where the civilization that had built them and came before had fallen apart due to their own hubris, which is why I'm such a fan of games like Dead Space and the like.  Bioshock has that in hypos full of Adam.  Combine that with the amazing 50's era music, the undersea environment (another setting I absolutely adore in games), and the 50's-punk art style and you've got an amazing experience.
I'd go into further details but this was one of the best games of its year, there isn't much else in the way of praise that I can say that hasn't been said already.  If you enjoy shooters and creepy environments that are isolated from the rest of the world, this is for you.

You either hate or love this game. Limbo is an experience, and what makes it awesome is also what lets it down so chose wisely according to the type of gamer you are. Also be careful if you've got a fear of spiders.
Here are the main features which made me love Limbo:
Very short puzzles. I never played more than 30min / one hour at a time, it also means that if you're stuck you can exit the game and start again later whithout losing much of your progression. If you're the type of player who likes to spend hours on end playing the same game you might be disappointed.
Very simple gameplay, very minimal story; there is a lot left to your imagination. Gameplay basically is: run, jump, push objects, press buttons. I loved it, but it means the game can feel linear or boring to some.
Ability to fail and try again over and over which helps if you're like me and you're a doer as opposed to a thinker.
Steam achievements.

Okay - I'm quite hidden, don't think he will see me at all, just have to be quiet. Gonna be you or me, sparky, blunderbuss to blunderbuss - I get one chance at this, don't rooster it up. Despite all of the negative reviews for this game, it is one of the best games I have played. The environment in the game is so immersive and rich. The dialogue from the hunters is actually pretty hilarious. Game play is pretty smooth, atleast I have had no problems, haven't found any bugs, other than occasionaly my curser does not appear on the screen, but I play with a controller, so this does not effect me. The hunters are pretty balanced and fairly easy to play, before you start a match on a new hunter, you get to watch a quick tutorial with tips that will help defeat the monster.
It is a great game to play with your friends, as it takes a lot of coordination and communication (which is why I think most people gave it bad reviews, they just didn't know what type of game this is). Also, I enjoyed the "grind" to unlock third tier hunters, you get to learn each hunter pretty well by the time the next tier unlocks. most people complained about this, but just like in real life, you can't just have everything handed to you.
I play this game usually with 1-3 other people, most of the time all of us are hunters, but when we have a group of 5 playing, one of us plays the monster (they out on noise cancelling headphones and listen to music so they can't hear the hunters), while the other 4 of us either play the hunters we're best at or try to play hunters we haven't played much. When I play by myself, I do find it a little difficult to stay on the monsters trail or to even defeat the monster, but again, it's the lack of communication between the hunters and usually a bad mix of different hunters, as some hunters abilities can benefit from other hunter abilities.
The DLC is impertinent, it will not make or break matches. It's mostly cosemetic aside from the 4 new hunters and new monster, which are included in the $25 Season Pass.
If you want a game to play with your friends or a game that's actually a challenge, This is a must have game.

I've bought this game before it was even on Steam, I was instantly given the Steam copy with my old account. It seems trivial but this leads into the greater scale of the developers commitment to delivering to the consumer. Each Monday they release a "Mondoid"on their site, a news article letting us players know what they have been working on and how things are going.
There have been ups and downs but this game progressively keeps getting tuned up and bit by bit, better. For an early access, every form of this game has been completely functional. The impressive amount of features they've been pumping into the game has made this ride worth it.
After stroking the developers ego a little bit to much for even my own liking, I want to get into the game play. I'm sure others can describe it more eloquently than I, but it is pretty much the closest thing you will ever get to a real life zombie simulator. Fracture a leg? Tough luck, you're going to have to baby it for about a week until you might be able to run again? Hopping through a broken window? Ack! Cut your groin up on entry.
There's plenty of examples to go with but the fact is, this game is unrelenting. I can't tell you how frustrating it is to get a scratch and having to wait to see if you are infected. Frustrating is generally bad but in the scheme of this game, you are trying to hang on to your survival at any means necessary. Sometimes the small achievements are good ones. Like when I was able to gather enough ammunition in an apocalyptic wasteland to fend off bandits, that resonated somewhere that I achieved something. The game punishes you, every success is awesome. Every failure, depressing.
The thought that goes into this is unparalleled, with water and power turning off after a few weeks. This game is literally trying to cover every imaginable angle.
I'd ramble on about every feature, but all I wanted/needed to convey was A) The Development team is solid and B) This is the best zombie survival sim I've ever played.

First off, I wanted to say that while I disagree with the majority of the reviews on here, I do understand where they are coming from.
However, I want to reiterate what you get for people on the fence about buying the game. I think you should go for it. I honestly don't think you will regret it.
Most of the "negative" reviews on Steam aren't about game play. In fact, almost all these "negative" reviews say that it is a GREAT game, just not worth the price.
I want to make people aware of what they get for the base game:
-12 unique and beautiful maps (plus all future maps for free)
-12 unique hunters (each feel and play like a completely different character)
-3 unique monsters (who play and feel even more different than the hunters respectively)
-5 game modes all which have merits and add replayability
-a custom mode to change all variables of the map that create countless possibilities for each game
-a skin for each character (monster and hunters) that you can unlock through game play
RIGHT NOW the only DLC is cosmetic. Just weapon skins or monster skins that give you no in game advantage.
IN THE FUTURE 2 more monsters and 6 more hunters will be released which will cost money.
Do you need to buy these? No. Will they enhance the game? Yes.
I can understand why some people think that the base game content is not worth the $60, but honestly if you haven't really given it a shot, I think most people would be MORE than happy with what there is from the start. Plus, if you are paying $60 for the game, you are being pretty lazy. It is really easy to find at least 20% off online for this game Which brings the game down to $45-$50... which is damn good.
If you are unsure about this game, I hope you find this review and reconsider. There really is more than people are giving credit to. I personally think people are more mad at the idea of it all (I'm not ecstatic about it either), but THE GAME ITSELF is great.

I have mixed feelings for this game.
Keep in mind that I have played and given this game a chance twice, with several years gap between.
I first played when it was newly-released, for around 2 days, then quit because of the disappointment of the game being completely different from RO1 and boring.
I played it a second time recently in Spring of 2016... and this time I did not care if it was nothing like RO1. Sadly it had me leaving in just 1 full day from how unplayable it was.
On the up-side, I do recommend TRYING it at least once, because it's free (to start), decent character creation options, low-lag, the armor is beautifully-designed, and overall the game has beautiful art, especially if you are into the anime or hand-painted aesthetic and wanted to see more stylish, late-teenage, anime-style characters in games.
It has a few features which are fairly unique(the card system, job costume, etc), but aside from that it's a very standard point-click-hotkeyspam combat MMORPG. There will be many familiar monsters from the first Ragnarok Online game, which can be nostalgic, and they look beautifully-made with nice animations.
I liked the beautiful male NPC "Eremes Guile" as well, who is also from RO1. Nostalgia again (and eye candy which is fairly rare in gaming to be made for female taste).
However, even with all of these things that I liked, the cons simply outweighed the pros for me.
Also, if you get addicted to all MMORPGs easily, and are poor, I recommend that you don't even try. You will save more money by buying and playing a non-DLC console game than this.
The biggest con of all, would have to be the inventory. All throughout the game, before I could even reach the first town (Prontera), I was struggling like crazy to manage my inventory. No matter how much I tossed out useless items or stored stuff in the storage, the inventory kept getting jammed with things I wanted to keep like good armor I could use soon and good/rare cards.
At this point, you really can tell that the game is using a fairly aggressive psychological manipulation to get you into buying inventory bags/slots/whatever. It's not "BUY THIS OR WE BAN YOU" type of coercion, it's "BUY THIS OR TOSS YOUR FAVORITE ITEM", and to me, this is really still a similar concept to blackmail, and even for an F2P game it felt like an incredibly heavy pressure. I probably have played every F2P anime-style MMORPG out there, and this may be one of the worst offenders.
At this point, I simply just quit the game even though I had been enjoying the actual game fine a few minutes before.
This is really a game-breaker for me, and even if the game is an F2P model, I expect F2P games to be free-playable without so much stress and pressured near-coercion. Otherwise I would stayed and have bought tons of costumes since I am a fashion addict in MMORPGs. Then again, if the costumes were gachapon-only (I cannot remember if RO2 was), I would also not buy them.
So, if you want to play a game without spending money, and not tossing every precious in-game item you have earned, this is not for you in the long-term.
Honestly, the scrapped old version of RO2 (Gate of the World) was way funner even when it was still in-development with many bugs. Mainly because it had no cash shop to restrict your gameplay, and it was actually unique in many ways (weapon leveling, movement physics, etc), but sadly it doesn't exist anymore, because why make a fun unique game, when you can make a cash-grab instead?

Cuphead may be one of my favorite games of the year. The 1930s Fleischer-esque style hooked me and the prospect of a meaty challenge only made me want to play it even more.
I'll say this much, Cuphead is a challenging game, but it's not impossible or unfair. Most of the game is boss battles filled with various attack patterns to duck and weave while you chip away at the boss's health. It's easy to back yourself into a corner, but as long as you're smart about your positioning, the game always gives you a window of opportunity to avoid attacks.... it's just sometimes that window is very very small. This game will beat you down, but as long as you're tenacious and pay attention, you can only get better.
Gameplay aside, the sheer amount of love and care put into this game shows in the artwork and music. Every sprite has been animated by hand tradtionally (animated with pencil and paper) as opposed to digitally (in a program like Photoshop or Flash) as seen in games like Skullgirls or Indivisible. The sprites were colored digitally to be brought into the game, but are processed in a way to give a genuinely aged film feel.
There's enough gaming references to keep gamers happy (Sally's Divekicks, Ribby and Croaks doubling as a Street Fighter and Battletoads Mashup, Dr. Kahl's allusion to both Dr. Wily and Dr. Robotnik, etc), but also plenty of Golden Age cartoon references to keep the animation buffs happy. I feel like every boss, every stage has a connection to some old Fleischer, Iwerks, or Famous Studios short I've seen before, but without being carbon copies of any characters in those shorts. I can't be the only one that thought of Balloon Land when fighting Beppi the Clown. Or Somewhere in Dreamland while battling Baroness Von Bon Bon. I especially love the watercolor backgrounds, which not only reflect how backgrounds were made back then, but also make the animated characters (like you and the enemies) stand out. It's used to great effect on the overworld map, as the stages and things youi can interact with are slightly animated, appearing wobbly and lighter than other parts of the map. A great touch that works with this style but also works from a gameplay perspective. I'm still floored at how the Moldenhauers were able to make this all come together so naturally.
The music is also incredible. The majority of tracks in the game are played by a full jazz band, and it hits a sweet spot between a style that suits the game's aesthetic, but also works to keep you focused on the game. The music is dynamic enough that the speed and pitch will change depending on if you use a super, pause or even die (where the music sort of dies down to a crawl). Great attention to detail. The musicians deserve as much credit as the artists.
Cuphead's a great game, but it's not for everyone. Some people won't find the challenge or style all that fun or engaging. But for those who love a challenge, or are willing to go the distance to see more of the game's crazy art and animation, this is definitely the game for you.

As a "Ghost Master", you recruit a team of ghosts for each mission to rid the residence of mortals and in turn gain new ghosts and skills to progress through the game. There are around 50 ghosts in total and each haunter has its own personality, strengths and weaknesses. The spooks that work for you fall under six categories: sprites, disturbances, elementals, vapours, frighteners, and horrors named after their characteristics and skills. Skills can range from "Rattle Chains" and "Fog" to "Ghostly Apparition" and "Paralyze". Some ghosts are more beneficial in certain situations than others depending on the mission. Each time you scare a mortal you will increase your plasm; the energy that's needed to frighten them to begin with (ghost skills cost plasm to use). Scare them too much and people will flee from the building before all your goals are met, which can make your job more difficult. Mortals also have their own levels of belief, terror, and madness rendering them at times irrational, afraid or even insane! That can affect gameplay for the ghosts assigned to haunt them.  Watch out for  priests, witches, mediums and ghostbreakers, these humans have the ability to banish your ghosts until the misson is over. Missions can be both fun & humorous, poking fun at movies and TV shows (Titles like eg. Ghostbreakers, Poultrygeist, and Phantom of the Operating Room). Once the goals for a level have been met, the game rates your progress. It factors in time, the impact on the mortals your ghosts haunted, and how many mortals fled. If you completed the mission fairly quickly, a multiplier is added to the final score. This score relates the amount of "Gold Plasm" given, which can now be used to add more skills to spook crew!

The Long Dark is an amazing and sometimes scary adventure, Venturing through endless cold only to find more and more snow. Throughout the game your one and only focus is survival which I really love about this game, My heart races when I don't have enough food, water, or fuel for fire, Wondering if I will survive just one more night.
This game is a Walking simulator but in a good sense, The ambient wind and music plus the vast landscape keeps you going and wondering what might be over the next hilltop, It takes time to get to know the world, How much to eat and drink at any given time, When and how long to sleep, When to move to a new location, One wrong move could lead to your death, And don't give up If you feel like you might die, Have hope and press on even if your injured or in the pitch dark: There is always a chance for survival.
The heart of the game is what adventure you create, What trail you blaze, I encourage you to take notes in the In-game journal, Write down your own map and Take notes about your day, You get a sense of achievement looking through all of the days you survived.
All and all a very relaxing and at times intense experience, With a very real depiction of a frozen planet that wants you dead, But provides life to the courageous.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a game where you take on the role of a Sir or Madam and are placed in a randomly generated terrain based off of the British Isles.  You have two goals: assemble pieces of some sort of mysterious artifact to return home, and most importantly survive.
Surviving is easier said than done, however, with well armed hunters, poachers, robodogs, and even a scarecrow that follows you around all trying to exterminate you.  Even if you get your hands on a gun the sound of gunfire will attract other nearby robots and they will rush to your location to investigate, so attacking quickly and quietly with an axe is your best option if you can't avoid a fight.  You have a vitality meter which acts as a hunger meter that you have to constantly keep your eyes on.  You can't run most of the time unless you're positive the coast is clear, for these robots have 2000x2000 vision and will instantly spot you.
This is not the game for you if you desire a casual romp through the fields, and it's unlikely the devs will make it any easier.
You will run, you will hide, you will loot, you will kill and almost certainly be killed.  Sleep with one eye open and bring some extra tea bags for it's hunting season, and you're the prey!

Overall I'd recommend this game. The guy behind it was also behind the Stanley Parable. I'd recommend this game, but I strongly advise anyone reading this to give Stanley Parable several thorough playthroughs first. This game is not as good as Stanley Parable in two important ways.
In terms of graphics it's largely nothing special. Your typical indie Source engine game. You might like some of the lighting effects here and there. The graphics are not important, especially for a game about a person who basically makes lots of proof-of-concept games and forgets about them.
Sound is near non-existent in this game and the few sound effects you get are unimportant. However, "Davey's" narration is not hard to understand or follow. But that's all that's important. The narrative is all you need.
In terms of gameplay, this is an extremely, almost painfully linear game with little to nothing interesting about it. This is overall where this game actually pales compared to Stanley Parable. Stanley Parable's entire premise is the idea that the narrative changes as you make each decision either in defiance of or in compliance with what the narrator says Stanley is doing. The game was non-linear and very solid. Beginner's Guide is, at best, a walking simulator. In a couple instances of the game you DO get a weapon, but you do little of note with it.
Like with Stanley Parable, the entire point of this game is the story. You're there to listen to "Davey," a fictionalized version of the creator of this and Stanley Parable, talk about his relationship and treatment of another developer named "Coda" and his games. I won't get into any details on how this goes, simply because just explaining the story would effective nullify any point in playing this game as the narrative is literally all this game has.
At about $10, this game should still maybe be considered worth a buy when it's on sale, as I think it still doesn't quite have $10 worth of content or gameplay. The developer could have easily just recorded one sixty minute podcast and delivered the same effect as this game. Do not buy it thinking it'll be as clever or as interesting as Stanley Parable. It absolutely is not as non-linear as the other game in any other way.
On a technical standpoint, there's really nothing that stands out with this game. Playing this in 2017, it reminds me of how Valve has overextended Source without really drastically upgrading it the way Epic kept overhauling Unreal. That's not really within the scope of this review. My point is that this game doesn't exactly push the limits of Source in any way.
On the whole: A good game with a nice story. I'd even suggest just buying it, playing through it in one sitting, then refunding it. You won't get much value out of this game otherwise.

How can you review this game?
is something beyond the norm. Which gameplay elements can you properly review about it?
Is it walking? Left clicking on the mouse? Cause that's all about the gameplay you'll find in The Beginner's Guide.
Yet, it's still an immensely powerful experience. It is something abstract yet at the same time incredibly specific and familiar for some people.
You could argue that at the very core, this is the definition of a walking simulator and regardless of any negative connotation the genre's very own name might have had in the past, even classifying The Beginner's Guide as any type of game genre would be doing the creative thought and work that was put into the game a huge disservice.
The Beginner's Guide is an interactive experience. It is a series of short levels where the narrator, the creator of
Davey Wreden, remembers and tells a story about events that transpired with his 'friend' Coda, a game developer, during 2008-2011. Regardless of the real or fictitious nature of the events, there's an important message underlying throughout the game.
The are many different interpretations of the game's meaning but what ultimately matters is
. Call me old-fashioned but I'm a firm believer that you must play a game before you form an opinion on it.
And despite the fact it lasts for no more than 90 minutes, despite the primary telling of the story is via an unreliable narrator trope, despite there's very few interactivity for the player, despite it does get a bit weird at times and too mundane at others, despite the old age of the source engine, despite that some of its meaning in particular about game development might be lost for many of us, despite
of that, The Beginner's Guide is a game I would consider art.
It is something unique, something abstract, something that makes the player think above and beyond rather than how to stealth kill a guard, or how to micromanage that squad, or which spells are on cooldown. I'm not saying those things are not fun. All I'm saying is that not every game
to be about them. Couple that with a superb sound design and soundtrack, and you're on a trip down emotion lane.
And that's the ultimate beauty of the The Beginner's Guide. It's not just about your thoughts, but also about what you feel. What emotions you experience are part of your own reality. I think that's is a mark of the brilliant albeit bizarre experience that the game has to offer.
I could write an entire essay on the inner workings and messages that the game features but it would be all for naught. So I'll keep it simple:
For 90 minutes, you'll embark on a small journey inside the psyche of a troubled person. If there's a good chance it might be
, then do not miss on this opportunity. An absolute recommendation.

LIMBO is a very atmospheric game that is both punishing and rewarding.
LIMBO is not something you can just walk through without dying. You will die, and die, and die. You will die over and over again (unless you guide, then you cheater :P). However, you will learn from those death experiences and solve the different environmental puzzles and situations. LIMBO has a very nice saving system so that there is rarely ever a headbang rage moment. Some of the puzzles are actually quite difficult if you don't think outside the box and use all of the environment. The game is punishing if you are impatient and do not closely observe the environment. However, LIMBO truly has a good progression and none of the situations are hard beyond belief. The environment is also what makes the game so good, it is so well crafted and fits the atmosphere perfectly. The sounds and music also match the game very well.
The only bad thing about LIMBO is that I hate the weak and short hops of this little boy. It's like he has never jumped before in his life and it is honestly the most insanely stupid short jump. Although this isn't really a big problem because that's the way the game is designed, it still annoyed me.

At the risk of being flamed by idiots with nothing better to do, I'd like to explain something about this game series.
First let me say I am by no means a fanboy of this series.  I have only bought two of them.  The two I felt worth bothering with.
What many of the fanboys, and most of the haters don't seem to understand is that this game series is not what it appears to be.  It's not a jumpscarefest.  The whole point of these games is that the jumpscares (and defeat) are in your hands.  Typical jumpscare games just throw random jumpscares at you to startle you.  Other than FNAF clones (the best of which is Boogeyman) no other horror game gives you the ability to prevent a jumpscare.   This game does quite obviously have them yes, but that isn't what the games are really about.  What makes this series a horror series is the tension of knowing you can prevent the jumpscares, and need to to win.  It isn't the jumpscares that make these games worth playing, it's the dread of failing to prevent them.
Do I recommend these games?  Only to people with an IQ high enough to get it.  If you think it's all about the jumpscares then do us all a favor and don't waste your money or anyone's time bashing the series.

One of many attempts to bring Star Wars into the RTS genre, Empire at War and its sole expansion pack succeed brilliantly. Vast battles across land and space still look pretty fantastic, and the array of units among the three factions, combined with the dozens of systems and special abilities at their disposal, ought to give any player a good deal of fun. And when you're bored of those, there's a healthy mod community waiting for you.

So, I've played this game for almost a year and a half now, but only recently have gotten the funds to buy it on Steam, too, so I could leave this review. It's still in Early Access, but it's increasing in quality in steady amounts, and by the months. On the official website, the developers keep you updated about the game and its development, and there's an well-established Wiki about the game already.
The game is fun. It's the best survival game for me out there. Never before have I had the thrill of actually having to _avoid_ being bitten or scratched, and gotten exited when I scavenged together the medical supplies to apply first aid to my character. It's thrilling to run though the streets, turning a corner, and seeing a horde of zombies turn tail and chase you down, forcing you to (often) run and dodge, find a way to distract them, or go absolutely nuts with a shotgun. Which, in turn, will lead to more zombies being attracted to where you are, only making the danger grow larger.
I have to say, though, the video and screenshots don't do it justice. Slightly outdated in comparison to the newest build, and a large part of the thrill has to be experienced, and can't be advertised as easily as that. You really have to give it a shot to experience it yourself.
The trait system is a thing; You can put skill points into abilities you've levelled, and you get a choice to put certain traits in, with a few negative traits to counteract it. (If you want to be Strong, it'll cost 6 trait points, so you need to take negative points such as Clumsy and Heavy Eater to balance out that with 6 points.)
See those buildings in the 5th and 6th screenshot? Those are player-built bases, and more and more customization options are added every so often.
The only real downside I have to this game is that, very rarely, though, the forced camera angle will prevent you from seeing proper depth in some rooms, and when stepping through a broken window or something, you might fall down a floor.
The game is best experienced with other players, be it on a public or private server. Then, you can group up, build your base together, go out scavenging together, or maybe even start opposing factions.
Long story short, I think this is one of the Early Access games that is definitely worth your time and money, for a survival-experience like no game offered, to this point.

Evolve is the recent game to be added to Turtle Rock Studio's small collection of games. Most known for their development of Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2, they have yet again tried something new with the development of Evolve. This game carries a lot of controversy mainly in regards to the price range. I agree with the concerns of the price point of this game and the amount of content you get for such a price. Do I believe the game is worth $60.00? No. Plus the additional editions which can raise the price up to 20 dollars or even an additional 40 dollars? No. You might be wondering what Turtle Rock Studios is offering you for such a price. Let me go ahead and tell you what you get.
For $60.00, you'll get the base game, nothing less, nothing more. 12 characters, four game modes, and three monsters. Pre-ordering the game gave you a copy of Left 4 Dead and magma skins for the monsters.
$80.00 got you the Evolve Digital Deluxe edition. This includes the base game plus the Evolve Hunting Season Pass which includes four new hunters at a future date.
$100.00 gets you the Evolve PC Monster Race edition. This includes the base game, the season pass, a fifth playable monster called the Behemoth at a future date, the magma skins as well as the four new characters. I do not believe that this comes with all of the optional skins, it may or may not.
Whether or not you're willing to spend that much for the items I just listed is up to you. For me, it isn't enough. I believe that the behemoth is a ploy to keep you from trading away the game.
Gameplay-wise, how is the game? Well, the gameplay of Evolve is tense and very smooth. The characters are very easy to control as well as use. Although some of the characters are harder to use than others, everyone has the skills necessary to learn and perfect a class with a little time and effort. The game does come with a tutorial for every hunter and monster that you unlock. This makes it easier for you to understand how to play a match with your characters. The AI has been drastically increased from that of Left 4 Dead. When playing Evacuation mode you have the option to play with a group of four other players against an AI controlled monster. Or four players against a human controlled monster. The AI controlled monster is pretty much hard mode as it does target those important hunters first making the coordination of your team crucial.
Without communication in this game, you're doomed to fail. By default, you can ping with the q button. This will make a ping noise and mark in the area where your crosshair is pointed. A necessary tool for those with and without communication. Although microphones are always best. This game is better played with a group of friends as opposed to random players.
But what about the actual hunters and monsters? Is there any point to upgrading? Yes. As stated earlier, the base game gives you 12 hunters and 3 monsters listed below. Each of the hunters have flaws and unique abilities that make them special.
Medic Class:
Val - First
Lazarus - Second
Caira - Third
Support Class:
Hank - First
Bucket - Second
Cabot - Third
Trapper Class:
Maggie & Daisy - First
Griffin - Second
Abe - Third
Assault Class:
Markov - First
Hyde - Second
Parnell - Third
Monster Class:
Goliath - First
Kraken - Second
Wraith - Third
The game modes consist of the regular hunt mode, survivor rescue, defend, and Nest.
Hunt - Goal: Hunters vs Monster, monster must reach level 3 in order to destroy the relay or kill the hunters. Hunters must kill the monster.
Rescue - Goal: Hunters must rescue and escort the survivors to an extraction point. The monster must kill a certain amount of survivors or kill the hunters.
Nest - Goal: Hunters must destroy a certain amount of eggs before the monster is able to hatch or kill the hunters.
Defend - Goal: The monster must destroy all three of the hunter's generators before the time reaches 0. The hunters must defend their generator until the time limit is up or kill the monster.
My personal feelings for the modes are below.
Hunt - Fun, fair, cat and mouse mode.
Nest - Hunter-sided if you have a team that knows what they're doing.
Rescue - Fair as long as the monster isn't an idiot.
Defend - Monster-sided, the monster has respawning minons every 30 seconds, and the hunter's generators cannot regenerate power.
What about the gameplay? What can this game possibly offer to make you continously interested? Well, people are right to have fears about being bored of this game after several hours of gameplay. It really is the same thing over and over again and it does get boring. I didn't expect to get bored of this game so soon, but I did.
There are several mechanics in this game that just make me believe this game is a cash-in from Turtle Rock Studios.
Day one DLC, skins. Why? For a game that is 60 dollars there must be some sort of replayability right? Wrong. The replayability that comes with this game eventually turns into a grind to get "elite" status for a character. This begins a series of questions for the terrible matchmaking. Here are a series of issues I have with the game to sum up this review.
#1. Why are we restricted from filtering out certain monsters from a "server"? Not everyone wants to play against a certain type of monster, in my scenario and almost anyone else's, wraith. It's such a lame monster. High damage, and high evading capabilities. It's also a real ♥♥♥♥♥ to track making the match a grind and forcing people to resort to abandoning a server if they are just not in the mood to go through the process.
#2. Why are we restricted from having a party member be allowed to be the monster? If your worries pertain to something along the lines of "well, you can sit there and grind elites with your friends and cheat experience", then that's invalid. You're able to create a customized match and set the map settings to pretty in depth settings. The thing about these customized servers that only your party can join is that you can still gain regular experience and character progression. So if you need 900 direct hits with Parnell's rocket launcher to reach your elite skin, no worries! Just grab a buddy, set the game to monster favored, set the strikes to 0, and have him kill your AI partners. Once done, feel free to hammer away and exploit the game's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ elite skin game design.
#3. Why is our only means of customization through the elite skins? Yes, I get that you can purchase weapon skins and a couple skins for the monsters but why? Why isn't something like that already in the game? For Turtle Rock Studios to hold the Behemoth and extra four hunters until a later date, you'd want to be continously interested in the game. You wouldn't want to get bored so fast into to the game. Sure, there are perks that you unlock as you get further into levels, you can also customize a badge with little pieces and different colors as you progress through levels. But that kind of stuff doesn't give me something to work for. I don't log into a game and say "yes, I can't wait to play all day and unlock this particular badge piece." I'd want to sit there and randomly stumble upon different skins and such.
#4. Why do the characters feel so limited as to what they could do? They should at least have different loadouts in which you can fool around with. It really makes the game feel empty. Val only gets this and that, Markov only gets that and that. There's no mixing up their weapons with other class specific items. I'm not saying have Markov have the ability to use Parnell's super soldier or shotgun. Give each hunter unique skills that they can reassign and fool around with.
#5. What is so hard about making an efficient matchmaking system? Many other game devs have been able to pull off a decent matchmaking server. I'm tired of having monster so far away from first place and the game constantly makes me the monster.

I have been having more fun with this game than I have had with any other in a long time.  Leading up to its release I have tried doing some Diablo 3, Warframe, Payday 2, Elite Dangerous and Dont Starve Together with friends, but none of them really seemed to hold our interests.  But so far with Evolve I have been seeing more of my online buddies than I have in some time.
For me, Evolve is actually something that lives up to its name.  The whole thing that keeps us going is watching how things progress as we learn more and more.  First few days were the usual Benny Hill style chase the monster step for step, never gaining on it, never seeing it till stage 3.  Then we moved to the spread out and sweep sectors, until the inevitable loss of a Trapper to a Megamouth.  Then our tactics have evolved to keeping within a reachable distance of each other and trying to think like the monster, predict crossing areas, use deployables as place markers.   Its almost to the point where we actually enjoy seeing a Wraith as the monster because its a chance for us to improve our ability.
Now its not all sunshine and bubblegum.  The matchmaking is a bit schizophrenic, especially if you have a wide level spread in your group.  You would think with a full party of 4 it should only take a few moments to plonk a monster in, but there have been Evac matches where the AI was in control for half of it.  Then there is the lack of in game friends list management, coupled with Steam not tracking last played with. (It seems that Steam may only track VAC enabled games) Late game skill progression, not to be confused with character unlock progression, is a slog fest to go through normal games. It is boostable if you have a full group, but still a boring grind.   And dear god the load screens.  I dont know why you can't just lock in a class prior to pre-loading the next map, whether this is just a design decision made solely so I can have a cig between matches, or a peculiarity of the CryTek engine, but it is a bit mind numbing.
All in all, the fun I have squeezed out of this game is worth the between round screwups.  As for the money grabbing complaints.  Considering I stated earlier that I play Warframe, this game has gotten no where near those levels of costs for in game assets (Talking up to $20 for a single class or 10-20hrs of grinding in some cases) and thankfully there is no EA style buy progression packs either.  Couple that with the fact that even if you don't buy DLC you can still play with and against any future Monster/Hunter releases and play on all the new maps.  You dont have to sit behind a pay wall like you would with your friends that got the COD expansions.

Chroma Squad is a pleasant, but somewhat janky TRPG with a solid grasp of Super Sentai's themes and feel. The game is quite easy, at least on Normal difficulty, but adds challenge via special instructions for each mission. While it is linear, you are also able to choose the order of regular missions building up to the season boss.
As a TRPG, it works. Each class has unique skills available to them, though I found little-to-no reason to ever change from the build I assembled, and as there's no way to change actors once a file has been made, it's possible to give a character an asynergetic role, especially when salaries are presented as a factor you'll need to concern yourself with when they're meaningless beyond Season 1.
Chroma Squad brings a few fresh concepts to the table, as well. A "Teamwork" button allows gang-up attacks and throwing allies, but because gang-ups must be basic attacks and throwing distance is individualized, I ended up just having my slow strongman pitch my leader where I want the team, then using his group up skill to bring everyone else over. Teamwork also enables you to use the often-mission-fulfilling finishing move, but it can be a bit awkward positioning every ally adjacent to the boss, especially when many foes have knockback and at least one unit is range-based. Finally, Teamwork locks in a turn. If anything results in your not being adjacent to the target when it's time to combo them, such as the fixed camera angle concealing a tile or random knockback, the turn is wasted.
Assembling a mecha is one of the more enjoyable parts of the game, and adds some variety. Mecha battles used to be pure RNG, but have been updated to a more timed-hit basis. Still, even a perfect guard takes chip damage, which I imagine can frustrate players.
Overall, Chroma Squad is palpably a mobile game, but an excellent one, only lacking in freedom of variety due to locking in characters and having such static roles for static missions. The soundtrack is also excellent, but $5 is a little steep for any soundtrack, if you ask me.

This game is amazing. I wouldn't give it a ten out of ten, after all it is just in the Alpha stage of develpoment. But I would recommend this game for ANYONE who is tired of the current stealth and survival game and wants a breath of fresh air in the genre. Sir, You Are Being Hunted puts you in the shoes of a person who can wield a gun and axe, but can't survive many bullet wounds. And that is another thing, the weapons in the game. These are realistic weapons that are more like their real life counter-parts if there was one. The revolver is good at medium distance, better at closer ranges. The rifle is a long range highly accurate gun that can kill most robots in one hit. The shotgun is terrible at long and medium range which is to be expected from a shotgun. Then there is the wood axe, not a battle axe. A wood axe. You usually won't get in range with this weapon without taking one or two shots first, and it can't take out a robot in one hit as one would expect. The enemy A.I. whether it be the normal hunting robots to the nightmare inducing Scarecrows that I screamed a little at the first sight of after I hit it... is great. I wouldn't call it grade A but you can expect an enemy that will search for you until you are dead unlike in games like Assassin's Creed or Dishonored. At first there are barely any robots to be seen, but as you gather the pieces to the device which has trapped you in this world (which is part of the story) more and more robots start appearing. Don't try to be ballsy and think you are some superhuman just because you have a weapon or two, these robots will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ (Sorry for the profanity, but I couldn't get the point across any other way.) These robots are faster than you, more accurate than you, but aren't smarter than you. You really have to use your brain in this game if you want to survive and get all the pieces back and escape from your own version of big game hunting, where you are the big game being hunted. Robots will follow any sound they hear, this counts as bottles, rocks, and even alarm clocks. Use this to your advantage. Usually there are about two robots guarding each piece of the device. You can engage with a good rifle shot or two, or use your brain and plant and alarm clock or throw a bottle and take the piece while they investigate the sound. There are also classes at the start before you create your own personal hell. Each class has good items or useless items that you instantly start out with when you spawn in which you can use to your advantage. The first class that it recommends is the hardest to master, for it has no items that you start out with. In short, this game is great. It has intense and interesting gameplay, a good amount of difficulty that takes a little bit of time to get past, and good mechanics that make the game fun. This game is a must own. I know, I have played it.
P.S. Anything I have not mentioned or anything that you are curious about (enemies, weapons, ect.) you can visit the Sir, You Are Being Hunted wikia page and check out everything else there. Big Robot, don't change a thing.

No time to explain is a platformer where the larger part of gameplay consists of you using the recoil of a LAZOR to navigate and sometimes shoot at stuff. I say the larger part because this is also the first part where it shines: gameplay.
There is a surprising amount of different gameplay mechanics and they are why the game stays fresh each level. Perhaps some of them could have been explored further as they go on for like 4 levels and maybe a bossfight and then are dropped again forever.
Then again the game is very very short all together and can be beat in just a small handful of hours. I think it is too short for full price but adequate at a decent sale. However if you add community created levels you have nigh infinite gametime, so that is nice.
The music is very nice and fitting to the levels. Maybe not a soundtrack you'd buy but one you will totally enjoy.
The story is barely there but there is no time to explain and it isnt neccesary either.
One last thing: respawn points. This game can be pretty damn tough and you will die quite a lot. However the respawn is always whereever you stood on safe and solid ground last. This isnt too frequent but actually important as it is often that one jump you fail 20 times, so that it is good that all you have to actually do is that one jump. There is a couple of situations with differing gameplay (fire anyone?) where death sets you back much farther and it gets annoying pretty quickly in those cases.
Some decent humor strewn throughout too.
Really if that first trailer convinces you and its cheap at the moment I would totally reccommend you get this.

Project Zomboid has rapidly become one of my favorite games.
The Good:
- You can adjust your world/zombies to your preference. Making the game as easy or hardcore as you want. Apart from being able to adjust your world/zombies, you also have a other options: Beginner, Sandbox, Survival....I have about 50 hours on this game and I still play on ´beginner´ otherwise it´s impossible for me to survive longer than a few weeks. Oh, did I tell you all about servers and the freaking awesome multiplayer options?? *pees in pants*
- The realistic: You´re gonna be that guy that survives the zombie apocalypse, right? You´re gonna do it. Hell, I was gonna do it! How hard can it be right?? Well... as it turns out... quite hard. You could get scratched once, and infected. You can get bitten 3 times and still get out unscathed. The randomness is awesome. Aaah... and then there is food and water. All is good in the beginning, but then all of the sudden your watertab doesn´t work  anymore... and then your stove bugs out too. Well, better run out and get some bottles of water or get some pots to fill with the few drops left in the tab... but holy hell... that zombie that creeped up on you scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you! Yes... you cant see where normal humans can´t see. As does skilling, it takes a while and practise. Weapons? They break, making stuff requires other stuff.
- Items are spread a realistic way, you´ll get lots of the same crap, you´ll get some of the good stuff and very rarely you´ll find something awesome. I only figured out there were sledgehammers in the game a few days ago. Windows need to be barricaded and so on...
The Bad:
For it being in alpha there are not many bugs. I´m not going to nag about anything that hasn´t been implemented in the game since you can read that on their page.
Sometimes you will find you need to move to pick something up and retry it. But that´s just a minor thing imo. Another thing  is the lack of knowing how to build stuff... it´s kinda touch and go... trying to find your own way.
Soooo....
GET IT, it´s really worth it! If you´ll like it half as much as I do... you´ll deff. get your money´s worth.

Granted, I initially missed a certain component in the system requirements: section, which requires the player to have Visual C++ Redistributable for Visual Studio 2015 installed  in order for the game to run successfully.
Now, that I've managed to remedy this issue, I'm having a blast! (pun intended)
The game nicely integrates components of bullet-hell style SHMUPS with a buyable upgrade system, enabling you to augment your weapon systems to your liking from one level to the next levels.
With attractive visuals, nice particle effects, and an invigorating orchestral soundtrack, this title effectively captures the steampunk vibe integral to its setting that is every bit as fun as it is pretty.
One may find the player's hit-circle to encompass a slightly larger surface area than the miniscule center-of-the-center-of-the-center-of-the-center hit detection component prevalent in CAVE-style shooters, so veterans of this genre may wish to steer slightly clearer of incoming projectiles than they're accustomed to.  Not to suggest that the game isn't well balanced, and the difficulty level is nicely compensated for with the ability to replay the most recent level in which you perished.
Definitely a recommendation. A+

Despite all of the negative reviews for this game, it is one of the best games I have played. The environment in the game is so immersive and rich. The dialogue from the hunters is actually pretty hilarious. Game play is pretty smooth, atleast I have had no problems, haven't found any bugs, other than occasionaly my curser does not appear on the screen, but I play with a controller, so this does not effect me. The hunters are pretty balanced and fairly easy to play, before you start a match on a new hunter, you get to watch a quick tutorial with tips that will help defeat the monster.
It is a great game to play with your friends, as it takes a lot of coordination and communication (which is why I think most people gave it bad reviews, they just didn't know what type of game this is). Also, I enjoyed the "grind" to unlock third tier hunters, you get to learn each hunter pretty well by the time the next tier unlocks. most people complained about this, but just like in real life, you can't just have everything handed to you.
I play this game usually with 1-3 other people, most of the time all of us are hunters, but when we have a group of 5 playing, one of us plays the monster (they out on noise cancelling headphones and listen to music so they can't hear the hunters), while the other 4 of us either play the hunters we're best at or try to play hunters we haven't played much. When I play by myself, I do find it a little difficult to stay on the monsters trail or to even defeat the monster, but again, it's the lack of communication between the hunters and usually a bad mix of different hunters, as some hunters abilities can benefit from other hunter abilities.
The DLC is impertinent, it will not make or break matches. It's mostly cosemetic aside from the 4 new hunters and new monster, which are included in the $25 Season Pass.
If you want a game to play with your friends or a game that's actually a challenge, This is a must have game.

First off, I wanted to say that while I disagree with the majority of the reviews on here, I do understand where they are coming from.

Most of the "negative" reviews on Steam aren't about game play. In fact, almost all these "negative" reviews say that it is a GREAT game, just not worth the price.
I want to make people aware of what they get for the base game:
-12 unique and beautiful maps (plus all future maps for free)
-12 unique hunters (each feel and play like a completely different character)
-3 unique monsters (who play and feel even more different than the hunters respectively)
-5 game modes all which have merits and add replayability
-a custom mode to change all variables of the map that create countless possibilities for each game
-a skin for each character (monster and hunters) that you can unlock through game play
RIGHT NOW the only DLC is cosmetic. Just weapon skins or monster skins that give you no in game advantage.
IN THE FUTURE 2 more monsters and 6 more hunters will be released which will cost money.
Do you need to buy these? No. Will they enhance the game? Yes.
I can understand why some people think that the base game content is not worth the $60, but honestly if you haven't really given it a shot, I think most people would be MORE than happy with what there is from the start. Reigns is a kingdom-running simulation card game from Nerial and Devolver Digital. Let’s get rocking.
Here’s What’s Up
I liked this game. There’s not much to it, so I don’t feel like a long review is really that necessary. I’m just going to go ahead and get down to brass tacks here.
This game is very minimalist. The entire game consists of you being presented with choices and having to choose between one of two courses of action. Either choice will affect your reign as King. It could lengthen it or it could shorten it. Sometimes it doesn’t do anything at all (at least, not at first). You need to strike a balance between the Church, the people, the army, and your wealth if you want to rule for a long time. When I played, my longest time on the throne was 33 or 35 years. My shortest time was, I think, 4 years. Things can go sideways fast and, honestly, it’s really entertaining.
Each time your King dies, is deposed, etc, a new king takes his place. The game essentially starts over and you continue making choices. That’s all there is to it.
Verdict: Yea
For how cheap it is, Reigns is a fun game and solid time killer. It’s definitely one of those games that evokes the “just one more” mentality and you’ll find yourself playing it for longer than you’d expect. If you’ve got a couple bucks sitting around, I’d definitely recommend adding Reigns to your collection.

Overall great game with an awesome sense of humour and a very unique enviornment.
Graphics:
- Graphics are good, a little outdated now, but not bad.
- Motion of objects looks strange.
- Enemies can cast shadows but I can't?
Sound:

- The voice-diaries you collect along the way are a nice teaser that elaborate the story but keep it interesting with characters from different parts of the world, like Germany, Ireland, Australia, China. It also adds to the bohemia that a large metropolis would inhabit.
Gameplay:
- The AI can be a bit stupid sometimes. In my run-through Dr. Steinman got stuck in a corner and I just blew him away that way. Big Daddies also react very stupidly sometimes.
- The humour is so wicked and the imagery is sometimes very grotesque. I thoroughly enjoyed it.
- The hacking mini-game is a lot of fun (although, by the end you will be so sick of it).
- It much longer than the average First Person Shooter and took me 15.5hrs to finish in Hard difficulty.
Environments:
- It's all fundamentally down in Rapture, but the use of creativity and ideas never gets boring. I never felt claustrophobic and I really feel like they managed to create this living breathing city.
Story:
- Story is great, very unique. It progresses well as you learn about the decline of the situation. The voice-diaries add clarity as you go along and are a nice incentive to keep exploring.
- The game has 3 endings, depending on some of the choices you make. But really, there should only be two endings, as two of them are pretty identical.
- I was disappointed with the moral under-tone of the endings. For a game that had such brutal off-the-cuff humour, they slapped you in the end with a Christian moral indicative ending which left me quite irritated.
Enraging, but equally rewarding. One of the best games I've played in a long time.

Chroma Squad is by all accounts an entertaining game, and if you have been craving a Tactical RPG - and you're willing to overlook many a flaw - it will certainly satisfy that desire; but will it leave you coming back for more?
Probably not.
Chroma Squad has so much going for it: the visuals are vibrant, the music is catchy, the battles are fun, the upgrades are plentiful, and the ability to create your own Squad is a dream come true; which is why its flaws are so infuriating.
Chroma Squad suffers from an incredibly bad story. More often than not, I found myself skipping through painfully stale dialogue that constantly fails to make any sense at all. Chroma Squad attempts to replicate the 'terrible-but-entertaining' stories of the TV shows it's influenced by, but it doesn't quite manage to achieve the same effect. The story is tongue-in-cheek and far too self-aware, causing an already incoherent plot to throw any hope of logic out the window.
Now if it sounds like I'm being too hard on a game that doesn't take itself too seriously, remember that a Tactical RPG generally focuses heavily on two areas: strategy and story, and when the one element is lacking, it's usually left up to the other to compensate.
Unfortunately Chroma Squad doesn't involve much strategy at all.
Each character fills a specific role in your squad; the Assist squad member has supporting skills that allows them to heal other members, the Scout squad member has a larger movement range, etc. As you complete seasons, you unlock more skills, gaining the ability to further customise your characters to fit your play style. These skills - while fun to execute - serve only to hasten the inevitable victory.
The battles are simple; while that isn't a bad thing, it does cause the game to lose its appeal with the limited challenge the game presents. Episodes generally devolve into a routine of clearing waves of enemies and then battling a giant-sized version of the boss with your Mech while completing a set of tasks called 'Director's Instructions' for bonuses to your Audience meter. This means more long-term fans and money.
Speaking of money, you'll be able to outfit your squad with a number of different items purchasable from the store or crafted yourself from the materials enemies drop. It's such a treat to watch as your squad who started out wearing buckets for helmets progress to wearing awesome space helmets.
The soundtrack is catchy at best and repetitive at worst. At the start of the game, the music will seem like a beautiful work of Chiptune - which it is - but as you approach Season 5, the limited number of tracks becomes annoyingly obvious.
Chroma Squad is rife with bad design choices, but it isn't an entirely bad game, and you'll either love it or hate depending on whether you can get behind its story and one-tone gameplay. I had fun with it for little over two hours, but two hours do not justify that price.
I would suggest looking elsewhere for your Tactical RPG fix.

I actually have plenty of time to explain this train wreck, and boy do I need it.
So, a platforming shooter where you use your gun for both damage and movement. Pretty unique concept, and each world uses a unique mechanic to keep things interesting. However, it's riddled with control problems. Most significantly, this is the only platformer of this type that I've played where your crosshair moves WITH your character, so if you're moving quickly it's nigh impossible to aim. What's more, if you move your cursor off the screen it actually goes off the screen. You'd expect it to stay around the edge so you can see where you're aiming, but no. There's also a moronic feature where if you fall a long distance your character lands on his face and has to stand up, preventing you from moving for a second. I don't know if this was added for "comedic" value or to make the game harder, but it feels terrible and goes against the core idea of a platformer.
The level design is just bad and unintuitive. There are so many parts where you need precision and the game isn't capable of being that precise, so you're stuck throwing yourself around until you get the angle just right. At least you aren't punished for dying.
The writing is bland, it's the sort of "random" style that's targeted at kids and young teenagers and typical of a flash game. I won't fault them for that, I know I used to enjoy that type of humour. The music is unremarkable, and I even noticed that they blatantly ripped of a song from an SNES game. Worst of all, somehow the game's optimized poorly enough that I actually dipped below 60fps on occasion, and I don't think I've ever lagged in a flash game before.
I think I got to the second last world before I called it quits. There were more frustrating elements than what I detailed here, just so many terrible design choices and make for a truly frustrating experience. It's playable, so I rate it a 2/10, but it sure isn't fun, and it certainly isn't worth $15.

Framed Wings is indeed an very unique and amazing RPG Maker game, that is very different from the generic run-of-the-mill type of games in this genre.
The game is mainly a single player, single character game (sometimes you alternate between Faust and Elena, but it is still single character at a time). What is unique is that the player and wield different accessories which will interact with the game environment in unique ways. For example, if the player wields a "Hook and Chain" he can swing across chasms. If he wields a Bow, he can activate switches that are far away by shooting. If he uses a large hammer, the he can smash Boulders blocking the game enviroment, so they can get to various unreachable paths. As a result, once you get a new accessories, you might have to go back to earlier maps because the new accessories will open up new game pathways. This make the gameplay really different.
Furthermore there are a lot of unique game bosses, each of which require radically different strategies. There are also a lot of different and innovative puzzles that the user have to solve in order to reach each of these game bosses. Some of these puzzles can only be solved by 2 single player characters, and the game allows you to alternate between Faust and Elena (the 2 main protagonists).
All in all, I enjoyed this game tremendously, and would highly recommend it to any RPG Maker fans out there.

A very nice little ARPG. It took me 20hrs (with 13hrs ingame, no idea what happened to the 7hrs difference) to finish. Most, if not all, of the bugs have been squashed by now. I played it with a controller and it worked fine, no need to remap the buttons. The keyboard layout made playing a bit weird but possible. If you have a controller, use it. If not, you can try to change the configuration with F1. And that reminds me. If you're new to RPGMaker games, don't press F12. It'll reset the game.
The maps varies from small to big but they are all nicely detailed. The exits can be hard to find though there are clues (like footprints and obvious openings).
There are a few secrets like easter eggs, chests and hidden areas to find. Pay attention to what NPCs says and what you see or read (although there are red herrings). There are sidequests, magic, a crafting system, a fast travel system (it's very much needed) and enemies that gets harder to kill the further you get in the game. Just keep levelling up and you'll be fine.
There are no handholding in this game. You start in an area, pick up items and info and then travel to the next area. Sometimes you need to backtrack in order to finish a sidequest or find that chest you needed to leave for later.
The only thing I didn't actually really like, was the story. It started out good and mostly stayed there throughout the game. By story, I think I mean the plot since there were no scenes besides those that pointed me towards the next area. That's ok, though. It didn't feel lacking. However, I feel the end was missing an answer or two. I won't spoil it, though. Perhaps the answers will be in a sequel? (Hint, hint.)
