Honestly, I think this game gets more hype than it deserves. I mostly finished this to prove that I could rather than because I wanted to. The environment is eerie, beautiful, and quite unique as well, certainly offering an enticing atmosphere like the title would suggest. Most notably for me was the soundtrack. Though consisting of only a few pieces, the music is haunting and enjoyable to listen to, helping to build onto the world. I only wish it was more present in the game since my main dose of it came from listening to the soundtrack that I acquired with my bundle purchase. The controls are also simple, intuitive, and tight so most things are down to player timing and ability rather than mushy controls.
Other than that... a lot of the puzzles were kind of tedious. Many deaths felt kind of cheap, because so many things just felt unavoidable the first time you're playing through something, so multiple attempts at puzzles were a must. Additionally, while I did mention this as a plus, the controls make it so your timing needs to be SPOT ON. A fraction of a second could mean yet another infuriating death.
While a lot of people praise the story in this game, I felt like it wasn't there at all. It's so open ended that it doesn't even feel like a plot exists. You're dropped into gameplay and after a few hours it ends. Nothing explaining who you are, why you're there, or what your goal is aside from not dying a ridiculous number of times. So overall, I don't think I'd really recommend this game unless all you're looking for is a puzzle/platformer and you don't mind the lack of a story.

Quick first impression, I'll change this later when I have more time in the game:  It's a survival game but there's so much open space and the robots can see so far that it's very difficult to do anything.
You don't get very much in the way of weapons with the default character, so you're left with some distraction techniques and that's it.  The rest has to be scavenged from the island, except good luck with that.  Also, visibility is really poor no matter if it's day or night, but again, that seems to hinder you and not the robots very much.
If there was a simple takedown, even if only temporary that I could do, this would be a cool mashup of survival and stealth.  So far as I can tell though, there isn't one, or at least the game hasn't told me about any takedown techniques.  Then again I did find a book in one playthrough so maybe it's something you're supposed to scavenge as well... books about how to deal with the robots?
Anyway, this is early access, but it looks OK... just way too dark, gloomy and yet way too wide open with few areas you can really hide out or sneak in.  The name of the game is to find these pieces of something and bring them back to a set of "Standing stones" like the standing stones in Skyrim...
You can change the layout of the various islands to certain set archetypes (fens, industrial, rural, and one I can't remember right now).  Unfortunately that's 4 different island types but there are 5 islands (a center island with four islands to the cardinal directions).  I guess if you fancy a specific type of terriain you could make the whole thing the same, or you could try to make every part somewhat different (but two islands have to be the same).
It's procedurally generated so you won't be able to get used to the landscape too much, but at the same time, it's not so different that it will look unfamiliar either.
The bottom line is that right now, the default character is a tad difficult.  An easier character starts out with lots of traps and ways to stop the enemy from chasing you, but that may well be TOO easy.  Updated review coming when I've had time to play with it more.   RIght now it's a thumbs down though.

The game is so much fun. As a hunter, you need good teamwork to win. While it can be frustating when everyone is on a different page, when you're in a good group, seeing everyone work together is an extremely satisfying feeling. Conversely, the Monster requires no cooperation, but has a fairly high learning curve. When you play well, it is very fun to see the hunters go from angry hornets buzzing around you, to scared cockroaches skittering away from you. Overall the game is well balanced, although if you're playing against people who are good at their role, it will always be a struggle to win. Graphics are beautiful, the characters have funny backstory, and my experiece has been quite stable and bug free, outside of a few party matchmaking issues.
Variety is a little lacking (everything is basically monsters versus hunters) but there are different game modes/objectives and you can play offline with bots if you want to practice. The DLC is whatever; skins are overpriced, but that's pretty much always the case in my opinion, and future monster/hunter packs are expensive, but if you end up really loving the game, spending an extra 10-15 bucks isn't too bad. Maps and modes will be free, so even if you don't have the cash for new characters, you'll still get new content. Seems worth it to me overall and I highly reccomend the game.

When it comes down to it, If this game was delivered in the exact state that it was and there was no buzz about DLC, I don't think there would be any complaints.
This is a full game for $60.  There are 12 hunters and 3 monsters.  That's plenty; the developers don't owe us more.  We don't have any rights to a ton of characters or limitless content.  They like money, though, and I can't blame them for wanting to ask for compensation for their extra efforts.
I don't want to make assumptions, but I feel as if many people are complaining without knowing how much work goes in to what the developers have made and how much work is going in to the DLC they are going to deliver.  I'm ignorant, too, I'll admit; for all I know, it takes one guy a single hour to make a character, but chances are likely that it takes a lot more work and man hours.
Bottom line, it's a solid, full game.  If there were no mention of DLC, the complaints would be less verbose.

I heard about the DLC fiasco surrounding this game before I had actually tried it out. I pre-ordered the game for myself and 3 friends because I saw that it was a co-operative game that we could play together similar to the L4D games. I was just excited for another game with high replayability with friends. I was slightly skeptical going into it from all of the things I heard surrounding the DLC, but I have to stand up for this game and say don't let that affect your decision to buy it. If you disagree with the business practice that much to not buy the game, fine. However, I think it is highly unfair that the game is receiving poor reviews based on its business model and not the gameplay.
The game is extremely fun. I had no issues connecting to servers with a friend and the games lasted anywhere from 10 to 30 minutes on the longer end. Evolve in NO WAY pressures you do buy DLC. There aren't notifications on the main menu like with Call of Duty. Honestly, I forgot that so much DLC was out there while playing. I did not feel like I was lacking any content and there was plenty for me to look forward to as a player. Seriously, there are a number of games already out there that remind you of its DLC for sale more than this game does. The variety in classes is enough to inspire me to try all of them. Plus, the characters within classes have builds that vary depending on the team strategy you want to do. I like that you get experience points as a player and then for character mastery separately. I feel like the content is very deep in terms of what there is to learn about the monster, hunters, and the wildlife. I would definitely recommend this game to any friends looking for a fresh new co op game to dive into that will be worth their while for a long time.

Overall, I really like this game and I definitely recommend it.

Red Orchestra's mechanics are really good.  While the graphics and environmental factors are somewhat dated, the game holds up well.  The level of realism with regards to weapons manipulation is excellent.  Where the game starts to falter is the online community.
The game has a very steep learning curve, and online players are unforgiving.  Even as an experienced player the constant riticule of the other players makes the game more akin to re-living the nightmare of middle school, which is probably the demographic that consitutes the majority of its players.  I've enjoyed the game, but as I've gained experience playing the game, my tolerance of the constant game play corruption by hackers/cheaters, and the abusive language used by other players, ruins the game.
The servers need to be better monitored, and abusive players need to be removed.  Additionally, you need to be able to mute players easier.  Trying to figure out who's using profanity, or blasting music in the background is impossible without going through and one by one muting all the players on the board. Micromanage a team of rangers as they try and save Earth!
Graphics:
Being a loved of pixel graphics, this game immediatley appealed to me.  The art style and bright colors really popped out to me and made me smile.  All the spites are well detailed and animated.  A lot of love whent into the graphics!
Sound:
Bieng that I bought the soundtrack, that tells you that I LOVED the sound of this game.  The soundtrack was always a joy to listen to and the sound effects were funny and great!  So much as that I BOUGHT the soundtrack! I especially loved the impact sounds when you got a critical on enemies!
Control:
Bieng this was point and click, there were few issues with it, save for an instance here or there were it would seem you can click a spot when you can't.  Other than that, no issues whatsoever!  I did not get to try the addiction joystick controls that were recently added.
Gameplay:
Managing a team of stuntment as they evolve into actual rangers may seem silly, but it works well!  You have a finite amount of resources to deal with as your try to buy equipment or crafting supplies and crafting equipment or new parts for your mech.  You gain money from beginning of season grants, completing episodes and crafting supplies from enemy drops.  You also control what abilities they bring into battle, and they gain more as you complete seasons.
Each battle is a careful dance of keeping your rangers alive and trying to complete Director Instructions, additional episode objectives that gain you extra money and audiance, but can be difficult to do at time.  Many battles were very difficult but never unfair or cheap, and at least for me, you could always come back from a major screw up.  The mecha battles used to be difficult, having to deal the RNG, btu after the Director's Cut, this is now alleviated by a reaction bar minigame, making it easier to perform combos and survive battles.
The story also gave me a smile with each episode, which felt like I was watching an old tokusatsu show!  From dealing with a silly moment to saving citizens from petrification, this game's episodes were always fun to play!  The jokes werte always funny and never ham fisted.  Props to the writers!

I will start this review by stating this is actually the second copy of this game I have bought, after it became so popular in my house I was unable to actually to ever get on to play, so I just bought my own copy.
Now with that out of the way, to the game:
There have been a lot of games that have come into existance promising to be the "definitive" survival game, but none of them have ever come close. The Long Dark however IS the definitive survival game, and one I recommend to everyone.
At the time of this review, it is still in early access but the changes over the years have been amazing. The developer clearly cares about the game and the audience and work hard to improve it with every major patch. There will be a story mode, which was promised in Sping of 2016 which has obviously been delayed. I am not worried however, as the devs do there best to keep everyone informed and are clearly hard at work and instead of releasing an unfinished product, they delayed until it is done. I respect that, especially since most smaller studios just pump and run, but not HinterLand.
Now, what is The Long Dark. Well it is a game about trying to survive in the harsh winter of the Canadian north. Now, as a Canadian who has had the pleasure of living in the north for a period of time, I can see that the look and feel has been weel done. The art style is amazing and every little detail is present, making for an enticing game. The game play is semi-realistic, with a nice balance towards both realism and fun.
Let me tell you, if you get complacint, you will not lost long in The Long Dark. You need to be thinking at least 2 full days of in game time ahead or else you will find yourself starting a new file after dying a silly and needless death. During my first play through, I was to cocky and figured I had enough supplies to make a long trek, and found myself quickly starving and freezing until I died. My mistake was thinking that mother nature was in any way forgiving, in this game, it is not. The devs have created a very realistic weather system, in that it is totally random. You could set out at dawn in a clear, warmer day and within 2 hours you are facing a blizzard with bone chilling winds. Lost and disoriented, you will have learned your first lesson, to learn how to read the weather (for the record, I recommend finding a semi sheltered spot near by, getting a fire going and cooking any food/hot beverages you may have and wait it out. Thinking you can find your way back, even over a short distance will just likely end with you dead, after walking circles.)
This game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥over and over and you will learn, with each play through making it longer and longer. I am still discovering things. Don't think you are an expert though, as you will end up making a small mistake which ends really quickly with your demise.
With the addition of challenges, a new, fun story-lite element has been added, with mini-stories designed to take many hours to complete and a lot of risk vs reward type situations.
I could go on and on, but if by now you have not made up your mind, more words are unlikely to make you do so. However, if you are interested in this game but decide not to buy, you are doing yourself a big disservice and missing out on a once in a generation, genre defining games. In the years to come, you will see media outlets comparing other survival games to The Long Dark.

I know I've only played 43 minutes, but that's about all of this game I can take. There's just not a lot to be liked here, and quite frankly I don't know why it has so many positive reviews. (character to character) and studio dialog (actor to actor out of character) This makes the game feel really jerky, and the transitions don't make any sense. The game play is repetitive and confusing. The way you move to determine your attack range isn't intuitive, and doesn't really make a whole lot of sense. One character might be able to make a hit from a specific distance, but another character (even with the same general stats) can't make the same hit.
As stated above, the game can't decide if it's going to be serious or not. The game can't decide if it's going to be an action oriented, turn based RPG, or just a humorous game with RPG elements thrown it. When it tries to be serious it never succeeds, and when it tries to be funny the humor just falls flat. It's full of all the kitschy cliches you could ask for, and not even the endearing kind.  The game also has a real “what the hell are we doing?” kind of vibe. No single idea in the game seems to be fleshed out enough. It's very jerky, and can't really stick to one plot line long enough.
I can't really recommend this one, and will be asking for a refund. It's even more of a disappointment because I had heard such good things about this game, and had such high hopes for it.

Excluding the expansion, I've always like this game, however, there are some weird qualities this game has that will leave your head scratching, but before I get to that, lets look at the positives.
Single player modes, there are quite a few, but you either play as the rebels or empire, for an RTS game that kinda sucks because most RTS have multiple factions, but this is star wars so whatever, each side has their own story in their respective campaign modes, they follow the story but as soon as you get farther into the campaign the less the story matters.  As far as timeline is concerned it's more along the lines of A New Hope than any other point.  Anyway, what's nice about this game is that there's space combat and ground combat, and the campaigns dive into both.  You build an army, send it to a planet, space combat if necessary, then land on the planet for a ground assault.  Simple, effective, and fun.
There's Galactic Conquest which follows the same type of gameplay as the main campaign but a more do at your own pace and strategy.  This is where balance imo becomes more lopsided.  After playing a few rounds with either side, I've come to this conclusion.  The Rebels ARE FAR stronger than the Empire in terms of Navy and Army.  Empire have certain units that are most definitely stronger, IE Star Destroyers and AT-AT's, but as a unit the Rebels just kick so much♥♥♥♥♥ even the heroes are more than a match for Empire heroes.  Each side also has special abilities, Empire can build a deathstar and instant blow up planets and systems, while the Rebels can sneak attack a planet they deem weak enough to liberate under the Empire's noses.
Every planet is different however, some side with Rebels making it harder to win for Empire and vice versa.  Some can't have speeders on the planet, so yes, strategy abounds in this game.
Then there's the skirmish mode, it's so weird.  You don't have to build any main buildings (like a barrecks), they're already prebuilt, you just upgrade your soldiers, build mines/turrets, summon soldiers, and that's it, but this is where my biggest gripe comes in.
The enemy players regardless of difficulty, WILL BUM RUSH YOU!  They will send every available soldier they have straight to your base, so if you don't build anti-infantry turrets right away, you're going to have a bad time, seriously.  What's more annoying is that even if you build turrents, they will try to run straight past them straight for a target at your base.  The ai logic is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor to the max.  It's also randomized so sometimes games will be harder than others, again regardless of difficulty.  All in all, the game has held up for quite a while as it came out almost 10 years ago, but the poor ai logic can sometimes just kill the game.  I give it a solid 8/10, great game, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ai

Quell Reflect is a follow-up to the amazingly polished puzzle game Quell. This sequel takes to mechanics of the first game and adds a simple yet complex tweak to it. Controlling two (or more) droplets on the screen at the same time!
The game even has a few remixed versions of levels from the first game, but that you must solve in new and challenging ways! A few other mechanics have been implemented to allow for a greater variety of level designs.
Just as polished as Quell, and with even more beautiful music, Quell Reflect is truly worth any price as a sequel, and is amazing even as a standalone game. I really recommend picking this up today!

The game's narrator will find it the hard way. He invites us to discover the world of one of his friends, a fellow programmer named Coda. We're moving through Coda's creations, getting to know him/her more. Davey's voice tell us where to look and what we have to understand. Coda's creations are just so fascinating and full of amazing gameplay ideas.
Minute after minute, the story is slowly unfolding.
But at the end, no one will agree about what actually happened.
"The Beginner's Guide" will be a different game for every player who tries it. It's just impossible to find a comparison in the video game world. The game goes beyond words and resonate deeply within the player's mind, provided he's ready to experience this disturbing yet attractive feeling.
This game will forever haunt me. And I cannot do anything but to recommend it to other people. Maybe they will find out just like me that the video game industry can give us pleasures that we thought didn't exist.

This is one of those "experiences" that can be likened to movies such as Funny Games and The Usual Suspects. A game that asks "how can I understand the creator by playing his game" and "what does it say about me that I played it". Like these movies, the audience of challenging media with a metanarrative can be split roughly into three groups:
Those who found it enjoyable, enlightening, or at least positive.
Those who found it repulsive, boring, and pretentious.
Those who didn't get it at all and just left confused.
For this title, like Funny Games, I fall into the second category. I hate to say this to the creator of the excellent Stanly Parable, but it's just not very well done. At no point was my belief suspended and forcing myself to play through it was a slog. All for a twist that is less enlightening and less enjoyable than Bioshock, in my opinion. To me, this matters becuase Bioshock was already an enjoyable game. The metanarrative twist as the cherry on top. This game has no additional aspects to bolster the weak premise.
If you've never experienced a meta narrative of truth, maybe you will find this one interesting. However, there are far better experiences out there. Perhaps this is what Michael Haneke meant when he said "Anyone who leaves the cinema doesn't need the film, and anybody who stays does."

The Forest, What lies behind the trees.
Introduction
As a middle aged actor, you set flight on an airplane. Everything is fine and going smoothly. You experience minor turbulence when it happens. The airplane glides down into an unknown terrain. You see a man take your son Timmy away from you. You try to get him but you are too weak to get up. You faint for hours and wake up suddenly, You then realize you are stuck to fend for yourself in a world of creatures and monsters and things straight out of nightmares. You must step up to the plate and show them who's the boss. Build, explore, kill and struggle to stay alive. This is The Forest.
Game Play
This game requires loads of time and effort. Time is needed or you won't get very far in this game or get many achievements. In order to survive you must put in effort to get logs. Logs are needed to make walls and or houses. You need to build houses get materials and to get tools and all sorts of things to accomplish finding Timmy. As my saying goes, Matter over mind because this game is beyond fear. Let's define fear, Fear is an unpleasant emotion caused by the belief that someone or something is dangerous, likely to cause pain, or a threat (Oxford dictionaries). The cannibals pose danger and they will hurt you. They also show a huge threat to yourself and your walls and house and other things.
Graphics
As you walk through the forest, you notice all of the effort put in by End night Games. As you look at the grass to the rocks to the water, everything shows great detail. The animals and cannibals look very real. I would recommend to have a good computer to run medium or high, and if you have a decent laptop use low quality. If you use medium or high, It is shockingly realistic in graphics it shows they put hours of work into it.
The A.I/Bugs and glitches
The A.I is great most of the time but it could use a little bit of work. The A.I has improved but if you are near water they might disappear on you. For example if you chase a rabbit near water there is a chance it will go across the water. The cannibals and monsters can get stuck since they can't crouch but it does help you a lot but it can be a little unrealistic. But the game itself is an amazing game.
Content
This game is a challenging horror game with amazing graphics and with a great plot with it. As I said it requires time  and effort. This game has hundreds of hours worth of game play if you take that long to do it. It has everything a game should have in my opinion. It keeps you involved in both day and night. In the daytime you work to make a shelter and walls, And in the night you must defend it from cannibals and monsters. It lives up to my expectations of a good video game.
Sounds and music
The music can start playing in many different ways. One way is that you find something that Timmy drew or had, or something strange and or unusual. Another way is that you can go to a boat in the water to find a cassette player and CD's and you combine and play them. The music for when you find strange things or things from Timmy sounds mysterious and scary. When you play the cassette player CD's you get a throwback to the 90's music with guitars and keyboards. Another way is in the starter menu with the iconic creepy music, scares you when you're alone.

THIS IS NOT STANLEY PARABLE. Just letting you know.
There are no choices here and this is very linear compared to the former.
This is not a ''game''. It is a storytelling medium. You listen to a narrator as he guides you to specific ''games and explain to you his interpretation of said ''games''. Think of it like listening to an extra developer commentary on a specific level as they give their thoughts of how they designed it but instead its in the eyes of that developer's friend. That is not a reason why I gave this a thumb down. I didn't mistake this game for another Stanley Parable. This is actually a decent product with great storytelling. Hell, might as well call it art. The reason why I gave it a thumbs down is just I didn't agree with it.
Buy this on sale, 10 dollars is not worth it IMO.
My rant (spoiler alert):
I went through this ''interesting but quickly got boring'' levels while listening to the narrator's interpretation. Davey's narrations were very interesting and he made you curious about the levels and keep going. However, we were stuck in his own perspective. We as players/audience were forced to look at Coda's games in his own way. His interpretations were very interesting but annoying. Its like listening to your very enthusiastic literature teacher over analyze a piece of work
not meant to take itself seriously. The incident about Coda dissolving his friendship with Davey I didn't agree. Anyone who is willing to disolve their friendship over some ''horrible trash source engine games he made that got shown to other people without his permission''is not worth being friends with. Yea, Davey might have overreacted but he was just trying to help doesn't matter if he got the wrong idea and he did it for validation. Thats what friends are for, helping each other out. Well, one shoudn't show other people's trash to everybody in the first place anyway. I don't know if Koda is real or not or is he just Davey's inner psyche etc. I don't know, maybe I took this too literally, maybe there is some hidden ideas that flew over my head but, whatever.

After almost two and-a-half days of my life invested into playing this game, and it now being one of my favourite games of all time, I feel it was only fair that I spent a little time writing a proper review for it. So, here goes.
This game, is actually the greatest of the great, to say the least, in the whole 'Zombie Sandbox-Survival' and now 'PVP/PVE Multiplayer Survival' genres.
The gameplay, to begin with is intense, fast-paced and complex to the greatest extent of these phrases I use to begin to even attempt to describe my feelings. The Indie-Stone, a small, multicultural dev-team have now spent day-in, day-out on this... Masterpiece, the first word to come to mind, since 2013. And boy, has it come far.
Each patch, brings more and more depth and accompanying excitement, time and time again. And with the full-release 1.0 Update on the horizon, being in full manufacture by the small, yet just so detrimental and capable Indie-Stone most likely at this very moment.
I am excited, to say the least. Off-topic, but back on track - Gameplay.
This isn't just your run-of-the-mill, chop-zombies-heads-off kind of game - Deep systems of mechanics, player development through skill points and experience, micro-management to the extent that we're keeping our own little person alive, in the same ways we keep ourselves alive today.
You will need to deal with fatigue, sickness, poisoning, infection, dehydration, malnutrition, exertion, broken bones, burns and our favourite; boredom. All fueled by decline in living standards accompanied by surviving successfully - Or in most cases, unsuccessfully, in a Zombie-Infested Knox County, Kentucky.
- Combat is superb, with all the basic stuff; damage increase with skill levels, defense increase with skill levels. But then you throw in the fact that an average fire-axe used by Fire Departments in the United States weighs up to ten pounds, and your character only got five hours sleep because he got home from that loot run the night before far too late, you're gonna have a bad time - Damage decrease with exertion, damage decrease with ill-effects on the body, damage decrease if you just jumped from a second-story window to escape near-death.
- Mechanics and Micro-management, eat, drink, farm, rest, stockpile, make a run to town, get scratched on your left arm trying to face one-too-many zombies with only a spoon for a means of self-defense, run home, open your first aid kit, tip everything out, clean your wound with whiskey, stitch the wound, disinfect a bandage with the same bottle of whiskey, apply the bandage, take some freakin' pain killers like Max Payne, sleep it off, bandage is dirty when you wake up, repeat steps 700-9,000,000. This game, will make you stress, more than you do, in real life - Especially if you are running a 5 month character, and your character is a hypochondriac. (One of the many customizable traits offered to you upon creating a character.)
Farming is a huge thing, especially late game, depending on the fruit/vegetable you are growing, your harvest can take weeks of careful nurturing before you are able to reap your 230 Fresh Potatoes, and not be able to eat them, tortured by the fact you have to watch them go rotten, because you were simply unable to eat them all before the lack of refrigeration got to them. (Which may not be a problem, as alternate means of electricity generation are speculated/planned for the game's future! But that doesn't mean everyone will be able to wrap their thick mind around operating a 2,200-Watt Ryobi Generator! Professions, in their linear current state, are planned for a huge overhaul, in which certain lines of work, will restrict certain commodities to a particular person with the appropriate experience.)
This is enough for now I feel, I've spent about twenty minutes typing this, sharing my opinions and what-not.
If I think of anything else to add, I'll be sure to edit this and make additions where appropriate, setting aside this is already a massive wall of blabbering text to begin with.
Saying that I 'recommend' this game, is an understatement, in all honesty.
If there was a way to donate, without purchasing the game over and over, I probably would have by now. There just isn't any words that begin to describe how exceptional Project Zomboid is, nor are there ways I can begin to thank the Indie-Stone for providing me with *days* of entertainment, at such a low cost, and with such an up-to-date forum and blog, providing your weekly Mondoids every Tuesday (Monday for America, I'm an Australian :P ) , there are no words other than : "You are one of the most amazing Development Teams to ever exist in the Indie Game content-base, and this is one of the greatest games ever created to date."
Well done.

A gaming masterpiece, no doubts.
The story is wonderfully crafted, in fact it's so good you shouldn't watch any videos on it just to prevent you from getting spoiled.
Graphics are amazing, on extremely low-end hardware it looks fantastic (minus you can barely read signs unless you get really close, and statues look more deformed than they should be) and runs well, my graphics card is dreadful, at 128mb of VRAM and I was able to beat the game start to finish without having any technical issues or crashes, with a playable framerate. (~24 fps not much on screen and standing still, ~19 fps when there was lots on screen and tons of action, but it felt like 30 oddly and didn't really run into many huge gaping framerate dips)
Gameplay is near perfect, there are two ways you can engage your enemies, Plasmids and normal Weapons. Normal Weapons are your, well, normal weapons, like a machine gun, an oddly satisfying shotgun which I unfortunately rarely used, and a crossbow which I actually never used, probably due to the fact there was no ammo for the damn thing until the last level, where you can buy some in a vending machine, but that's a fat lot of use because that vending machine is right next to the final boss! Slightly less flawed, however, is the plasmids. Plasmids are useful tools that can shock enemies with lightning, light them on fire, freeze them, or summon a load of bees. Now, onto the flaws with the gameplay. First up is hacking, this is very useful, as you can hack security cameras and turrets to aid you against the enemies. Unfortunately, about halfway through the game hacking is near impossible just to hack something as simple as a vending machine, it also kills the pacing as you could be just about to hack as a enemy is shooting at you, then time stops completely as you hack. During my first ever playthrough of the game on the XBox 360, I only hacked once, and that was when you had to hack a Security Bot to progress. Second, is the wrench. It is immensely overpowered. From the second level of the game, you can pick up a tonic called Wrench Jockey which increases the wrench's damage. This tonic is the best in the game, as at the beginning, it takes about four hits to kill a Thuggish Splicer, and about six to kill a Leadhead Splicer. With the tonic, though, you can kill both in 1-2 hits. Wow.
Ignoring the somewhat minor flaws with the gameplay above, this is a must-buy and is one of the best games EVER MADE, and would you believe it's nine years old already? I will note that if you own a Playstation 3, that version of Bioshock is the best, since it has a new difficulty setting called Survivor, along with PS3 exclusive dlc called the Challenge  Room which is not availible for PC or XBox 360. Now, that being said,
buy this game?
EDIT: I have access to a laptop with a gig of vram, it can run the game on highest settings at 30-60fps now :)

If I could, I'd give this game a neutral rating. It surely has a refreshing concept, some humor and a fair prize, so I'm not gonna refund it. But still it disappointed me a little.
To explain my issues with this game, I have to go a little deeper into the mechanics. There are four bars in this game - indicators of church, people, army and wealth. If any of these bars drops too low or raises too high, you die.
It turns out that the "choices" you make during the game aren't real choices at all. If you don't plan on dying in the very first year, you aren't allowed to make decisions based on roleplay or your own point of view. That's because the only thing the "choices" do is raising or lowering certain indicators. So the whole point of the game basically is to memorize the several scenarios and their outcome (=how they influence the indication bars) in order to keep everything steady.
And while that certainly can be fun for a while (although the scenarios do repeat themselves a lot and you are basically forced to choose the same things over and over again), it's not what I had expected: a game with a real free will, real choices and real diversion in how to develop your kingdom. No moral dilemmas, nothing. At least there are two endings, but I don't really want to play through the whole thing again, because, like I already said, you are forced to do the same things over and over again.

First Impression of 'Sir, You Are Being Hunted', Alpha Beta.
I blindly bought this game knowing absolutely nothing about it and having not heard even the title before.  However something about the first 30 seconds into the quick video "December Festive Teapot" had me hooked and before even finishing the trailer, I bought it.
Now obviously this is a Beta, this does have bugs and is not a final product but this is a very exciting opportunity as a gamer to be a part of the continuation of improvements it will undertake, ultimately ending up as a finished project.  That being said, as it stands, it's remarkable!  Coming from someone who always looks for reviews or some form of general acceptance or denial helps me at times to filter through the vast array of games available.

This one bypassed a frequent filtering system and found its way into my game collection - boy am I glad it did.  Right from the beginning I was hooked on the art style, the Steam-Punk appearance to the UI.  It was nice to have a handful of choices prior to starting the game as to who you want to wonder the eerie islands as.  Once in the game and quickly advancing past the "tutorial" if you will, I began my journey - no idea what kind of journey or what to expect.  But with my binoculars, and rags, I began to walk.  As I said, I had no prior knowledge as to what the game was about I just installed it and started playing and before I knew it was I quiet literally being hunted, and yes I feared for my life.
The audio is raw, it's intense, it really suites the environment and the atmosphere.  It felt like I was actually being gunned down as I ran for my life and literally jumping in my seat at each sound of gunfire.  This was intense as very few games legitimately have me jumping out of my seat but the sounds of gun shots in the atmosphere had me completely engaged in my survival.  By seeking shelter in a field with some form of grain I crouched and managed to get away only with a few shots making contact.
As the environment goes through its day to night time cycle there were times my eyes played tricks on me making me think there were people around me, this was effectively conveyed through the spooky as hell tree shadows.  These shadows sway along the ground and surrounding environment displaying some eerie shapes.  The sound design for the environment at this time compliments the eerie environment the night time paints around you, equally so when the suns shining.
However there is a fairly long wait time to actually start a new game, this of course is because the game is procedurally generating new environment layouts and such for a fresh experience every time, but the wait time can take a few minutes.  Once in, the game runs smooth other than a few laggy moments when looting buildings, this of course was to be expected.  The graphics in game are quiet nice considering the stage of development, though my only comment is they are lacking in the building areas as the resolution on some doors and walls is quiet poor.
I can't be too critical at this time as I'm certain they are aware of all these comments and graphics really are of no concern for a Beta experience.  As for gameplay i've only encountered those few laggy moments - as it stands, it's extremely impressive and am happy I pushed aside my usual routine of check up and went through with purchasing it.  I look forward to future development and advancement and will most definitely be an active player along the way!

This is the premiere zombie survival game though. I have died more times than I care to count and each death is something me and my friends share as a story. You can easily get absorbed into your character's struggle to survive. You can die to a simple infection, malnutrition, exposure to the elements, and much more.
Playing multiplayer can make the experience more fun, but also more harrowing. I had a playthrough where I was bitten and had to split off from my group and leave my supplies. I found a house on the edge of town and nursed my wound til it became clear I was not going to get better and then I burned the house down took pain killers and drank some bleach.
All in all, this is the real deal for zombie survival and I highly recommend it.

I'd like to preface by saying that Limbo is not a bad game.  But I still found myself dissappointed, due in large part to the way that it is talked about on the Internet.  So, I'm writing this negative review as a warning for the consumer who is skimming through the negative review filter.
Now, there is a reason that every video ever made about Limbo on the Internet puts such heavy emphasis on the spider.  Because it is terrifying.  I felt actual dread when it showed up, and I don't even find horror classics like Jaws or Poltergeist to be all that scary.  Unfortunately, it is only found in the first fourth, maybe first third of the game.  This is ultimately what dissappointed me so much, because there isn't a single point where Limbo ever manages to claim as much interest  from me as it did when the spider is on screen.  Because they frontloaded all of their best material into the beginning, the rest of the game is very "meh" by comparison.
But that's fine, it may not be the most well crafted horror experience as a whole, but what about the gameplay?  Is that really solid at least?  The gameplay experience can be divided into two types, puzzle and platformer.
Taken as just a platformer, I'd say the game is actually pretty bad.  Your jump has no height to it, fall damage is a thing, and you run extremely slowly with no dash function.  This is forgiveable as they could be stylistic decisions, to feed into the horror of the game as well as make the puzzles a little more challenging.  What's not forgiveable, though, is the fact that the jump button and the button for grabbing ropes and ladders is the same.  This means that there are many occassions where you'll accidentally leap to your death after grabbing onto the rope, because you forgot to take your finger off the jump button.
Taken as just a puzzle game the game ranges from alright to good.  Some of the puzzles are inventive and creative, and they can be challenging, there was at least one time where I had to look up a solution because I couldn't figure out the way forward.  However, many of the puzzles are incredibly simple and just cheap.  They consist of you blindly charging headfirst into a deathtrap, and then the moment you see the deathtrap sprung, you think "oh, so I just don't do that next time".  The worst offender I can think of is a puzzle involving two hydraulic presses.
But what are the positives of the game?  Well, the game is only a few hours long, so the stuff with the spider is so good, and the whole thing so short, that it doesn't quite overstay it's welcome and is still an overall positive experience.  The level design is...weird, but in a good way.  Settings flow together like the entire game is a dream sequence, and in some respects it is.  Your character is trying to escape limbo.  So it doesn't particularly matter that there's a massive factory full of deadly buzzsaws next to a primitive village with people who use bows and blowguns.  That said, I do feel like there is far too much emphasis put on the factory area.  Not only is it the most dull of the environments, but about half the game seems to be spent in it.  But enough about that, back to positives, there is creativity put into the puzzles and the locales which I do appreciate.
Ultimately, Limbo isn't a bad game, especially for the price.  I just expected a lot more of it due to its reputation.

Id love to recommend this game, but there is such a widespread, inherent issue with crashes that is unfit for a finished product. With an AMD rig there is constant game-breaking hang crashes - and forums are flooded with this issue. You name it, I've tried it. I will reinstall the entire game and see if that solves my issues. Otherwise I'm stuck waiting for the devs to to help players on that sort of hardware. Gamplay wise, however, the game is engaging, challenging, and hilariously good: Theres so many moments to cheer or curse at your screen. The PVP is interesting to say the least: as a tier 1 monster you run from the hunters in a panic, trying to eat enough wildlife to level up - once that happens, you start hunting them. The dynamics of the hunter parties changes every match: the 4 roles remain static while the character and some abilities may be different depending on the player and thier unlocks. The DLC is all skins, the season pass is a pre-order for another batch of hunters on top of the 12 already in and another monster. All in all, the DLC has no impact on the game at this point, so don't sweat the negative reviews on that. Like I said initially, I would worry more about whether or not this game is going to crash every 5 mins or run smoothly for you.

Full disclosure, I know one of the devs and even helped to game test it a bit.
But with that said, I’m going to try to be as unbiased as I can with this review, this is both for the consumer and the devs.
With this out of the way, let's jump into it.
Grimrush is a bullet hell, boss rush game. There are many different bosses and 3 character classes.
Each character has different abilities and stats, catering to any kind of playstyle. I found myself personally changing classes quite often, depending on what kind of experience I wanted at the time.
The bosses are brutal in a really fun and challenging way, each being pretty different from one another and offering a varied set of challenges, I actually really liked the variety in this game.
The game surprisingly felt really different depending on what combination of class and enemy you’re fighting. Something I really enjoyed was the music, with each different phase of the boss the music would dynamically change and ramp up the energy in the fight, couple that with the insane amount of projectiles on screen and you have a fantastically blood pumping experience.
I found myself muttering the words “just one more try.” Quite often and clicking the restart button before even having a chance to think about it.
Another thing that I found to be a strength to the game is the combo mechanic, if you can manage to go for a considerable amount of time without getting hit, you can get your attack power to raise up to really high amounts.
It feels great knowing that you have +%100 attack combo and this is by far the strongest mechanic in the game, seeing the bosses health drop is incredibly rewarding and it urges you to keep on your toes and pay close attention to your character.
While the game is difficult I would also say it pays off really well. Being able to choose a new ability after defeating a boss is great feeling.
Now for some of the issues, while I enjoyed the game, nothing is perfect.
For the most part the enemies do a really good job of projecting their attacks, warning you that something is coming, this is a strength but sometimes the game has issues communicating exactly what it wants you to do.
For example, there is one monster that requires you to kill all of his minions before he will take damage. I didn’t know this so naturally I just thought it was a bug, it wasn’t and I soon realized what was expected of me, but that was after a few tries.
I would also say that keeping track of the bullets on screen and the energy bars on the bottom right hand of the screen can be a really taxing experience. I often found myself trying to dodge but not being able to because of my lack energy points. While I like this mechanic I think it could have been remedied by a sound effect or on screen filter, communicating that you were low on energy.
With that said though, these were the only two issues I had with the game.
The combat is fluid, the music is good and the characters and bosses are varied, I think $8 is a fair price and I would urge you to at least try the game out.
I’m excited to see what the future holds for this team, for a first game this is pretty good and a nice little distraction from all of the big budget games out there.
I’d give this game a 7/10 score.

Grimrush is a nice little fast paced action game that provides a decent amount of entertainment value considering it's low price point. Especially for perfectionists and speedrunners who wish to polish and perfect their scores and builds for each boss, it's a nice little "snack" of a game.
The bosses are varied and pretty much all of them are memorable and unique. Every single fight escalates at a nice rate to give the player the time to get used to the patterns and especially the last stage of each fight provides a nice rush of heart pounding action.
Some cons worth mentioning are slight player feedback issues (with taking damage and such) and occasional rough around the edges visuals, but thankfully at least the latter does not interfere with the enjoyment of the game.
As far as the difficulty goes, the game is challenging, which is the point I'm sure. However, the game is not TOO difficult to beat for an average gamer. If you want a great score however, prepare to adapt and perfect your playstyle with a lot of trial and error.
Each character has their own unique playstyle, so every player will surely be able to find a preferred style of play after some experimentation. It also adds decent replay value to the game due to how different each character's approach is for beating the bosses.
In summary:
Cons:
- Occasional rough visuals
- Some player feedback issues
Pros:
+ Just the right amount of challenge
+ Unique character playstyles
+ A lot of replay value
+ Memorable bosses
+ Min-maxing goodness

EDIT: An actual review.  Maybe i'll edit again after even more game time.
50+ hours in, my thoughts:
Visually, I think the game looks awesome.  Everything looks beautiful in game, effects are crisp but aren't distracting.  You will always know exactly which effect belongs to which ability.  Player models are alright, nothing amazing but are still pleasing to the eye.  Terrain is pretty neat, there are certain maps that purposely try to hinder your vision (human and monster), and others that could be clear as day.
Gameplay is hard hitting.  As stated in trailers, teamwork is essential as the hunters.  If one of your members die, you are going to notice a huge difference in your ability to take down the monster.  Every role is equally important in this game and you must work together to win.  It isn't possible to just go on your own, you can't win the game by yourself as a hunter.  I honestly believe they hit the ball out of the park as far as teamwork goes.
There are some issues with the game however.  There are very few bugs i've come across, but they can become annoying.  First, your cursor will occasionally bug and you can see your cursor roaming across your screen as you move your mouse to look in a different direction.  This is the most common bug and it happens around 1/5 games.  Second bug being wonky interractions between the Goliath and certain walls.  Very rarely, the Goliath could get knocked back (no damage) from a wall.  This could send you across the map if nothing is in the way.  Never happened to me on any monster besides Goliath.  This bug is so rare though, can't even give a frequency at which it happens.
Bugs aren't the only issues in the game, but balance.  Every game has those people that say X is OP and Y needs a buff.  The game was just released recently and everyone is still learning.  As far as my experience goes, the game seems to be in an -okay- place.  The hunters all have their strengths and weaknesses, and so do the monsters.  However, there are some characters that are a little too good at what they do.  The Wraith monster being a prime example of this.  Hunt being the primary game mode for multiplayer, any somewhat experienced Wraith will never be caught.  With the amount of speed and stealth it has, it's near impossible to keep up with it.  This leads to the hunters running around the map for most of the game trying to locate/trap it, rather than any actual combat against it.  I don't really care too much about something being too strong, but I do care when the game gets boring.  That's what the Wraith does, it makes the match boring for the hunters.  I'm completely happy fighting a Wraith if it fights, but most don't.  It just feels like one of those cheesy things to do.
Content.  Unlockable characters are all fairly easy to obtain.  Reaching their elite skin is another story however.  It will take days to unlock the elite skin for a single hunter, and it's enjoyable along the way.  In multiplayer, Hunt is the primary game mode so you could say you are playing the same thing over and over again.  But you aren't.  Every match is different, it doesn't ever get repetitive.  You never know what to expect.  In Evacuation, you play five matches back to back.  Shuffling through various game modes and maps in between each game, you obtain different advantages or disadvantages depending on the outcome of the last game.  Massive rewards at the end of all five matches.
Now for the most controversial part of the review.  Game value and DLC.
Is the game worth it?  You can't even debate this.  It's different for every person.  Some hate the game, some enjoy the hell out of the game.  I am for the latter.  50 hours in, long sessions of gameplay, still not one bit tired of the game.  DLC, however, is what is putting this game down.  There were some DLC packs that were released on the same day as launch.  The fact that the DLC could have been in the game does bug me, but the fact that it is cosmetic DLC makes me not care at the same time.  As stated many times by many people, the DLC as of now is purely cosmetic and does not affect gameplay in any way.  There is nothing that you can't do without the DLC.  The whole controversy on this topic is really bemusing.  The fact that the DLC wasn't already in the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but there is really nothing forcing you to buy it considering that it doesn't really do anything besides change what some stuff looks like a little bit.
There are some people who don't even care about any of this.
Let those people buy the DLC if they want.  Who cares.  As for me?  I sure as hell am not buying DLC that should have been in the game already, but I definitely am not going to let that ruin my experience.
As a closing statement, I would just like to say that the top rated "helpful" reviews are quite the opposite.  I find it amusing that most of these top rated reviews are from people with below ten hours of gameplay.  Many of which hardly understand the game yet, I see some things written off as bugs which are actual features in the game.
tl;dr?
Nice visuals
Great non-reptetitive gameplay (heavily encourages teamwork)
Some annoying bugs
Some balance(?) issues
Day 1 DLC is pure cosmetic but still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t
Top rated helpful reviews are not helpful

I used to be a moderator for gPotato (official host) & a volunteer for the official game Luna Online which became Luna Plus back then. Then everything was broken because the game was rushed due to the fact that the Luna community was asking us to release the expansion early & to fix the bugs later which turned out to be bad.
At the end, the official game was strangely balanced but still so much fun. It was much easier to achieve higher levels because of new features such as gift boxes every 10 - 15 levels giving you useful stuff, permanent Dungeon Date tickets allowing you to do more than 2 instance in a day with a friend or a partner, crafting which was giving you some awesome rare & legendary items that you could create if you had the right materials or stones, cooking, houses, simpler enchantment systems, items reinforcement, rides to increases various stats, party buffs, guild buffs & crazy philosopher stones giving you stats by percentage instead of value for enormous buffs, along with a 6th tier class for Fighter, Rogue & Mage, giving you the most insane builds possible in an MMORPG with so many skills that you do not know what to do with. The game had no restrictions, no requirements for whatever class you picked. You want to be a mage but you randomly want to fight with a bow or a sword? No one will stop you, the game won't stop you. Some of your skills will still work even if you're using a sword instead of a wand or a staff, the game won't give you a barrier. But what was cool about that, you could turn your character into a deadly machine. For instance, I had a friend who was a Crusader, it's a Fighter class, turned into a Tank, but it does some magical damages because of their support side. In Luna, magic was everyone's weakness, no matter who you are, what class you are, mages are the most feared class in the game because in PVP, you can't dodge magic, passively your magical defense is very low except for a mage who become a Priest, or Monk then later a Bishop or an Elemental Master for the extra magical defense, they're the only class who can survive passively without extra effort required. So naturally, when you're a tank class & you randomly start dealing some crazy magical attacks to another melee class, it's scary for those who have low magical defense, because they can't kill a tank quickly enough. Because from level 40 to level 60, you had a quest to complete to advance to a new class (tier 3), & monsters around those levels weren't really easy to kill. Then you could grind at a Dark Portal, starting at 60 until you reach level 85 then you had another quest to advance to (tier 4 at level 75), & then the nightmare begun between 85 to 105 where it was more grinding & then you had to complete the longest, hardest & most annoying quest ever to finally advance to the next & final class (tier 5) in Luna Online. First impressions:
Grimrush is a boss rush shoot em up with a juicy amount of depth. Bosses have interesting, varied, challenging to avoid attacks. Although they cover a lot of space, all attacks have generous tells, so with some practice, every attack can be dodged reliably. For new players like me, taking a hit isn't too punishing hp-wise. However, hitting the boss without getting hit yourself builds up your combo and gives you a stacking damage buff. A skilled player will narrowly avoid crazy attack patterns, rack up a huge combo, and kill bosses quickly. At that skill level, since you get a score bonus and mana boost for performing a "perfect dodge" right as an attack is about to hit you, you're still incentivized to keep things exciting for yourself.
Boss fights escalate in a very pleasing way as the boss loses health. Their attacks get faster and more complex, the boss will start to mix attacks and get some brand new ones. All of the bosses are cool: an evil mechanical heart surrounded by defenses, a giant electric sea creature, a shadowy lantern-toting wraith: the themes here are memorable. Each boss feels different to fight, and all are fun to fight in their own way. Their movesets are all very fleshed out; for me, the bosses are the highlight of Grimrush.
Each of the 3 player characters has a different playstyle, and you can choose from 3 starting abilities for each, plus one ability (from a random selection of 4) for each boss you defeat that will alter your playstyle further. The bosses themselves are in a different order every time. All of this means that your games will all be different, instead of being stuck on one boss forever and fighting them over and over again as you learn the game or are going for a good score. If you do want to fight one boss over and over again, there is a retry option when you die, although you'll lose score for using it.
The music in Grimrush is a real treat. You can check out the soundtrack here if you'd like
, but in my opinion, it works best when you're facing down a big baddie. There's also a cool music effect whenever you perform a perfect dodge, which I love.
All in all, Grimrush has left a very good impression on me, and I want more. Beating the game will be a fun little challenge, but after that I want to really dig in and try to do a masterful run with a good time and score, with tons of perfect dodges and huge combos. If you like shoot em ups like I do, I think you'll enjoy Grimrush too!

This is a fun and inexpensive logic puzzler.  The gameplay is basic and increasing in difficulty as you unlock the latter levels. The player must connect the lines without intersecting, unless through a junction box, to go from a start place to the end place.  All pieces must be connected and in some instances a certain number of intersections must occur through junction boxes.  There is also a dailly puzzle generator that can be used to generate puzzles of differing difficulties randomly each day.
Achievements are based upon completing sets of 25 puzzles.  There are 26 sets going from A-Z with an achievement for each one plus achievements for doing certain amounts of dailly puzzles. An achievement is also given for opening different color pallets.  Which are opened by completing puzzles.
My personal experience of the gameplay it was fun right at first.  Then got a lil old, but, I was glad I stuck with it because over time my mind seemed to become more attuned to how the lines had to flow in order to complete the puzzles.

I picked this up on a whim using a coupon; I generally like this type of game in small doses to kill time so I figured it couldn't hurt to give it a try.  I couldn't be happier that I gave it the chance and in hindsight, had I known, I would've been fine paying the full price for it.
The puzzles range from very simple to VERY challenging, and yet with enough thought even the hardest ones can be worked out.  I'm finding myself sitting down with this game far more than I expected and far more than similar games I've played.  Even better (for me) is that the levels aren't timed in any way.  It's laid back and relaxed, and that's just what I need sometimes rather than a game that will make me anxious!
As you clear levels, you unlock new color palettes if you want to change up the look.  For a visual puzzle like this, I like that there's some variety.  Otherwise, it's graphically simple, but it's appropriate to this kind of game.
I would personally recommend this if you like challenging-yet-solveable puzzles; there's enough here to keep you occupied for a long time with 25 levels per "Set" and over twenty sets to work on (not even counting two "daily" sets each day).  Sales are always nice but honestly, it's not expensive at full price and it's worth it.

This puzzle game has just about the simplest mechanics possible - draw lines from start to finish points hitting every point on the grid the prescribed number of times, without ever crossing your path outside of points that need to be hit more than once - but it manages to ring very deep changes on top of that.
There are a daunting set of over 500 puzzles in the "main game" as well as automatically generated daily challenge sets. The main game is organized into levels that are subtly thematically grouped - when working in a specific set of levels you will often get into habits of thought that let you progress rapidly, only have those habits punished a few worlds later. This is a game that rewards walking away for awhile and them coming back with a fresh outlook.
Unlike other "infinite" puzzle games, the automatically generated sets are set at a high level of challenge and usually do not let you get into the habits of thought I mentioned earlier. This makes them a lot of work to play through, which means they are also rewarding in their own right.
LYNE has earned a proud place in my library of puzzlegames alongside Hexcells Infinite.

In a market filled with gaming companies trying to milk every cent out of it's players, Cuphead is an absolute blessing to the gaming community.
On the fictional Inwell Isle, Cuphead and his brother Mugman are on a winning streak at the Devil's casino. Cuphead and Mugman were so caught up in the game that they end up betting their souls to the devil and lose. The brothers beg for mercy from the devil, so he makes a deal with them: they must collect contracts from the other creatures who have lost their souls to the Devil across Inwell Isle.
The game is like nothing I've ever seen before. The 1930s cartoon style graphics are hand drawn beautifully and with great attention to detail. The game has tons of excellent imagery but doesn't dwell on a certain image for too long making you want more.
One of the reasons that Cuphead great is because of it's infuriatingly hard difficulty. In order to beat one of the many ruthlessly designed bosses, you must be constantly shooting at it while simultaneously dodging, jumping and ducking over all of the clutter that the boss throws at you. One of my favorite instances of this was early on in the game where you have to dodge all of the tears of a crying onion. I love that this game doesn't hold your hand. It pushes you in the deep end right from the get-go and once you finally beat one of these insanely challenging bosses, you feel astounding. A lot of these games these days lack this feeling of true achievement because of how much they hold your hand but not Cuphead. Certainly not Cuphead.
If you're looking for a unique gaming experience that is challenging and visually stunning then check out Cuphead. At only $20 dollars it's an absolute steal.

To be honest, my "recommend" is more of a mixed opinion than a full blown recommendation.
So let's hit the technical issues first:
On the non-technical faults part, Sam & Max: Season One has the same issue that almost every adventure game has: there are some puzzles that will probably require a walkthrough for you to be able to complete due to their non-obvious nature. It's usually not too bad, but there were a few here and there that I needed help with. Then again, I'm not great at adventure games.
The writing and voice acting are both pretty good. The humor hits more than it misses. That said, the quality seems to rise the later you get into the season, so expect the first couple episodes to be good introductions, but less than stellar in terms of adventure games.
Why am I mixed, then? Because you'll encounter quite a few situations where you know what the solution is, but you have to spend a lot of time traveling back and forth to make any progress. There's a ton of downtime, and while the comedy is good, I don't think it's good enough to justify the amount of downtime there is.
Sam & Max: Season One is by no means bad; I am still recommending it, after all. But if you're not finding it funny, and you're getting bored of having to travel back and forth so much, I won't blame you for skipping it, either.

I did not get what I really expected from this game. I bought it for the cheap price and expected something very relaxing, where I'd get to make some silly decisions as king without any required thought or care. Technically, that still exists to some extent - but in reality, the game punishes you a lot more often (and I mean a lot!) than it should, and the developers seem like they were stuck between a thought-less version or planning-required version of the game. I also feel like it is definitely overrated and that the cheap price is not a reason to say it is good.
To sum up the premise of the game as quickly as possible, you are a king who sits and makes binary decisions (usually just a yes/no for performing an action or doing nothing) for an indefinite period of time. As you make decisions, things may go bad for you and you die. But the game does not end if this happens. Instead, you are just reborn as the next king and continue on, over and over, until you find a way to reach some "endings."
The game keeps four stats for you as king: religion, kingdom health, your army, and money. As you make your decisions, you'll see little dots saying which stats the choice will affect, but it won't tell you how it affects them (i.e., whether it will increase or decrease the stat). Some decisions will make it obvious whether it will harm your army, for instance, or really help the health of your people, just based on reading what you are actually deciding upon. However, not all decisions are exactly straightforward and can lead to unexpected changes in your stats.
Why does this matter? The game only allows a very small amount of each stat for you to have, and it sets a maximum boundary as well as minimum boundary for the stat. What this means is that if any of the four stats hit either boundary ("too much" or "too little"), the game will kill your king character. And let me tell you - this happens OFTEN unless you are very lucky or are scrutinizing everything forever, especially if you get surprised by a decision that triggers a large, unexpected change.
To make matters worse, the game will have you stumble upon "curses," some of which should actually be good things but are not, due to the game's mechanics. Certain event cards trigger a curse, which means from that point forward, usually until you die, one of your four stats will either increase or decrease at a constant rate as time goes on. This basically means that you must now make faster decisions than before in order to offset the new stat change, and also means that you likely want to avoid any decisions that will push that stat in the same direction as the curse. The maximum boundary death trigger is completely silly, especially because of things like curses - why is increasing money for the kingdom bad, for instance?
Now, some of the events that the game randomly draws for you are funny or interesting to read over; but unless you hit specific paths in your decisions, you will end up redrawing the same events over and over, and things get somewhat boring quickly. Even as I started getting newer events, I got bored with the "game" pretty easily because it was simultaneously trying to be so simple and thoughtless but then required planning.
At some point, after 45 minutes or so, I decided to give the game a test. The test was to see how fast I could meet all of the characters and go through all of the events and so on, without giving into planning the stat changes much. It turned out that the random chance of the game allowed me to trigger many characters, many king deaths, and many general events without caring at all. I would just leave the mouse on one side of the cards and keep clicking over and over, and I ended up "unlocking" more than half of the cards in just a handful of minutes. So the game really is a paradox.
I cannot recommend this simply because the developers did not seem to know what kind of game they wanted. If they wanted it to just be silly and fun with crazy decisions, they should have removed the actual stats management and just focused more on drawing scenarios based on what you do as the king, making more of a relaxing, laidback decision simulator. If they wanted to make it more difficult with some actual planning, then this format was not the right choice at all.

I was totally immersed in this game, but I'm struggling to capture why I liked it so much. I think, in the end, it comes down to the incredible voice acting and script. Without the narration it would just have been a random string of odd half-completed set pieces, but with the voice providing a back story and trying to interpret what it all meant... I got totally hooked. It made it less like a "game", and more like a movie you were exploring. Or the creator's mental world. I wasn't focused on traditional gameplay mechanics, like puzzles or quests or collecting anything  - suddenly I was looking at the game like I would a David Lynch movie - what does it all mean? What was he trying to convey here? Where is this going? I think everyone will have their own interpretation, but for me this game struck on notes relating to depression, creativity, and the pressures of external validation.
In a way, it feels like a bit of a cautionary tale against reading too much into someone else's work, and forcing your own world view and expectations onto it - but paradoxically, this game made me long for more games just like this one. A game which makes me curious as to what the creator was thinking and feeling. A game where I instantly jump onto forums the moment I've finished, to see what other people's theories are and to share my own. A game that leaves you thinking about it for days after you've finished playing.

I'd like to preface by saying that Limbo is not a bad game.  But I still found myself dissappointed, due in large part to the way that it is talked about on the Internet.  So, I'm writing this negative review as a warning for the consumer who is skimming through the negative review filter.
Now, there is a reason that every video ever made about Limbo on the Internet puts such heavy emphasis on the spider.  Because it is terrifying.  I felt actual dread when it showed up, and I don't even find horror classics like Jaws or Poltergeist to be all that scary.  Unfortunately, it is only found in the first fourth, maybe first third of the game.  This is ultimately what dissappointed me so much, because there isn't a single point where Limbo ever manages to claim as much interest  from me as it did when the spider is on screen.  Because they frontloaded all of their best material into the beginning, the rest of the game is very "meh" by comparison.
But that's fine, it may not be the most well crafted horror experience as a whole, but what about the gameplay?  Is that really solid at least?  The gameplay experience can be divided into two types, puzzle and platformer.
Taken as just a platformer, I'd say the game is actually pretty bad.  Your jump has no height to it, fall damage is a thing, and you run extremely slowly with no dash function.  This is forgiveable as they could be stylistic decisions, to feed into the horror of the game as well as make the puzzles a little more challenging.  What's not forgiveable, though, is the fact that the jump button and the button for grabbing ropes and ladders is the same.  This means that there are many occassions where you'll accidentally leap to your death after grabbing onto the rope, because you forgot to take your finger off the jump button.
Taken as just a puzzle game the game ranges from alright to good.  Some of the puzzles are inventive and creative, and they can be challenging, there was at least one time where I had to look up a solution because I couldn't figure out the way forward.  However, many of the puzzles are incredibly simple and just cheap.  They consist of you blindly charging headfirst into a deathtrap, and then the moment you see the deathtrap sprung, you think "oh, so I just don't do that next time".  The worst offender I can think of is a puzzle involving two hydraulic presses.
But what are the positives of the game?  Well, the game is only a few hours long, so the stuff with the spider is so good, and the whole thing so short, that it doesn't quite overstay it's welcome and is still an overall positive experience.  The level design is...weird, but in a good way.  Settings flow together like the entire game is a dream sequence, and in some respects it is.  Your character is trying to escape limbo.  So it doesn't particularly matter that there's a massive factory full of deadly buzzsaws next to a primitive village with people who use bows and blowguns.  That said, I do feel like there is far too much emphasis put on the factory area.  Not only is it the most dull of the environments, but about half the game seems to be spent in it.  But enough about that, back to positives, there is creativity put into the puzzles and the locales which I do appreciate.
Ultimately, Limbo isn't a bad game, especially for the price.  I just expected a lot more of it due to its reputation.
