July, 2017 Update: At this point, I think I am officially giving up hope on the development of this game. I still have hope buried deep down somewhere, but I feel like the chances of this game getting the core combat and stability update it needs are basically gone. I feel like this game is constantly insistent on ruining it's on fun.
Pros:
+ Very fun and unique concept. Stands out among the sea of lame zombie games.
+ Realism and simulation are a strong focus, if you enjoy that. (I do)
+ Tons of sliders and dials to tweak the zombies behavior and lore to your exact preference.
+ Adorable raccoon mascot, who gives a mixture of helpful and confusing advice.
+ Super deep, involved, well designed character creation and development system.
+ Iron man, one life only. You die, you die. (Not always a positive)
Cons:
- Key promised features like NPCs, better animations, and combat improvements are no where to be seen even after years of owning this game. After 2 years they finally released vehicles, but I would much rather seen some of the other listed features first.
- Serious flaws in the combat make it totally random, requiring good luck and gaming the system to not instantly permanently lose your character. Do you like games where strategy and skill keep you alive? Move on. Long term strategy is super fun, but you'll never survive long enough for that without sinking 100+ hours into this game learning it's quarks through sheer attrition. This drags the game down more than anything. A coherent and enjoyable combat system would single-handedly change my review to posative.
- Glitchy. I don't get why this game has gone this long with so many serious bugs left in it. One of the most common is your character suddenly spinning when you have your weapon raised when it shouldn't. Far to many of my deaths in this game are to my character suddenly spinning around, shoving his back into the zombies I was fighting and holding still so they can casually, slowly eat me to death.
- Horribly balanced. Pretty easy 98% of the time, horrifically frustrating 2% of the time, and no amount of skill or planning will save you in those situations. Stubborn refusal to tweak or improve this system because of the communities enabling, claiming it's "hard" when it's just really, really badly balanced dice rolling. (In other words, a flaw likely never to be fixed)
- Default settings seem design to exacerbate it's flaws. The "zombie infection" is literally a dice roll to instantly kill your character every single time you get hit. Totally destroys the whole injury/medical system included in this game, that I like a lot better than this zombie infection mechanic. I highly, highly, highly suggest disabling the auto-death zombie infection if you do try this game. (at least at first) You still get normal infections that can be lethal if left untreated. It makes the random bugs and missclicks auto-kill you a lot less.
- The game seems very proud of itself for killing you, when most often it's the game's fault you died. I'll finish this list off with some of my recent deaths. (Plus about twice this many to the sudden-spin-around death mentioned before)
1: 18 hour old character - Lit fire - Didn't realize instant death block around fire extended beyond the visual campfire. - Instantly died.
2: 11 hour old character - Tried to place sheet over window - character sprinted out door to place it on the outside of the window instead (I guess?) - Passing herd that hadn't noticed be previously turned and obliterated my house and killed me.
3: 8 hour old character - Forget to clear glass out of broken window - got infection - died slowly and horribly. Technically 100% my fault I guess.. ? Fun use of 8 hours of my life.
4: 4 hour old character - Climbed out window onto roof - Roof didn't exist apparently? - Fell down to porch, injuring leg and riling up a zombie half a foot away that wasn't there when I cleared the area a minute before. - zombie bait.
These flaws greatly outweigh what makes this game great. If the developers ever fix them, you will have an amazing, amazing game. But I don't think that will ever happen. They seem very proud of their poorly balanced mess. It's so very sad, because a little balancing and bit better combat that isn't pure RNG could make this one of the funnest indie games around.
Long story short, it's a great game, you'll enjoy it, then you'll missclick or the game will have something that works fatality opposite to how you would expect with the "realism" mentality of the game, or maybe it will just bug out the tiniest bit... then your character you spent the last 5~10+ hours developing will be instantly dead, and there is nothing you can do to stop it."Gaming the system" to stay alive for longer is possible, but ruins the fun of it. It makes you very aware you are playing a game... Wasn't the point realism and simulation? But it's basically all you can do. It's almost like it punishes you for actually trying to play and enjoy the game, and just calls that difficulty.
So, just skip buying it. Before I would have said follow and watch it, wait for that update that makes you go "wow, maybe I should finally get this game!" ... But I am now convinced that update will never come. So just don't. Unless you are literally a gaming masochist, and you don't care at all about the feeling of "challenge and reward" you get from a good game. That's completely absent here.
Tl:Dr: Buy a whip for your girlfriend to use on you, you'll enjoy that masochistic punishment a lot more than this. There is no challenge or feeling of reward. Just empty punishment, often for things beyond your control.

I picked this up on a whim using a coupon; I generally like this type of game in small doses to kill time so I figured it couldn't hurt to give it a try.  I couldn't be happier that I gave it the chance and in hindsight, had I known, I would've been fine paying the full price for it.
The puzzles range from very simple to VERY challenging, and yet with enough thought even the hardest ones can be worked out.  I'm finding myself sitting down with this game far more than I expected and far more than similar games I've played.  Even better (for me) is that the levels aren't timed in any way.  It's laid back and relaxed, and that's just what I need sometimes rather than a game that will make me anxious!
As you clear levels, you unlock new color palettes if you want to change up the look.  For a visual puzzle like this, I like that there's some variety.  Otherwise, it's graphically simple, but it's appropriate to this kind of game.
I would personally recommend this if you like challenging-yet-solveable puzzles; there's enough here to keep you occupied for a long time with 25 levels per "Set" and over twenty sets to work on (not even counting two "daily" sets each day).  Sales are always nice but honestly, it's not expensive at full price and it's worth it.

This puzzle game has just about the simplest mechanics possible - draw lines from start to finish points hitting every point on the grid the prescribed number of times, without ever crossing your path outside of points that need to be hit more than once - but it manages to ring very deep changes on top of that.
There are a daunting set of over 500 puzzles in the "main game" as well as automatically generated daily challenge sets. The main game is organized into levels that are subtly thematically grouped - when working in a specific set of levels you will often get into habits of thought that let you progress rapidly, only have those habits punished a few worlds later. This is a game that rewards walking away for awhile and them coming back with a fresh outlook.
Unlike other "infinite" puzzle games, the automatically generated sets are set at a high level of challenge and usually do not let you get into the habits of thought I mentioned earlier. This makes them a lot of work to play through, which means they are also rewarding in their own right.
LYNE has earned a proud place in my library of puzzlegames alongside Hexcells Infinite.

An intuitive little visual puzzle game, with a wonderful minimalist style, mellow soundtrack and engaging gameplay.
LYNE is incredibly simple: join the dots, but with rules. Create lines on a grid joining matching coloured shapes, making sure not to miss any or leave any paths untravelled. Sounds easy? It’s not. Each Puzzle is part of a Set; 25 Puzzles to a Set, 26 Sets in the main Game, so 650 puzzles in just the main Game, which continues with new Daily Sets. As you progress through the sets, they increase in size and difficulty, getting very challenging; the daily sets can also vary in difficulty, so no day is the same.
The elegant and abstract style of the game really helps to engage the player, focusing on just the puzzle, with no superfluous window dressing, just a simple layout and interface for such a devious challenge. It’s chilled out, almost zen-like, soundtrack also helps set the mood for a relaxed and engaging puzzle solving session. After I finish playing, I usually feel relaxed and focused; it’s almost meditative. The accessible play style makes the game great for casual gaming, able to drop in and out of gameplay whenever you like. You can hardcore through the game pretty quickly, but really, it’s made for casual play, whiling away 15-30 minutes here or there, enjoying soothing music and mentally challenging puzzles.
LYNE has various achievements to unlock, as well as collectible triangles with each puzzle solved, which in turn unlock different colour palettes for the game dependent on amount of triangles collected, as well as unlocking hidden features such as a sub-game involving Twitter and a hidden cypher - I don’t use Twitter, so not too sure what’s involved there, but it’s cool that games are expanding to use social media in such ways.
I bought this during the Xmas sale, after spotting a review that mentioned you could spell out words with the LYNE achievement badges - each Set is a Letter of the Alphabet, and each unlocked Achievement is a corresponding Letter Badge - and actually thought that was a worthwhile idea, but after playing it I’m glad I bought it, regardless, because it’s a great game for casual play. It’s immediately recognisable as similar in concept to various casual games on Mobile devices (e.g. Flow), but none have pulled it off with the style and elegance of LYNE; it’s so pretty, simple and fun!
Thumbs up, and definitely recommended!

TL;DR: Yes. Yes, yes, yes.
Wow! I as a rule dislike survival games. Not my stuff. But I have to say, TLD is a nice - no, SUPERLATIVE change of pace. All the others try to get you in a big hurry, or have some NPC nonsense which ends up always screwing you over, and sometimes even they go for cheap jumpscares. But The Long Dark? It is an exceptional variety of game which deserves its space as one of the best, in my opinion, survival games. It could serve as a nice role model for what a truly good, truly fun survival game should look like, and I feel a successful launch out of early access is all it needs to get its worth in attention. Not only is it a worthy adversary towards others of its genre, the Hinterland team also serves as a great role model for what other indie and early access devs should be. Now, I realize that many are upset about the rather belated story mode; however, I am excited to see what they do with the extra time!
Here's why I love this game:
- As I said before: It's definitely a change from other survival games like Rust or The Forest.
- It's a healthy balance between realistic and reasonable, two aspirations for survival games to reach.
- The devs seem to genuinely care for the game, and respond to - or at least heed - the community.
- And - and I hate to judge a general game off of this, but must comment about this on The Long Dark - the atmosphere: WOW. The Long Dark, even with its particularly... surreal, may I call it? art style, can completely captivate you, have you listening to the beautiful sounds and looking at the rather stunning world in the midst of your struggle to survive. It's amazing what you can do with pixels.
Some things I (personally) would like in the game:
- A few more bug fixes. I.e., random fall damage (still happens to me), sound cutting out every once in a while. That is not to say bugs are a major issue; no, no, in fact I wouldn't call them an issue at all, for me (except for those two, of course).
- Maybe a map with a few more shelters for individuals such as I who aren't too good at the "actually-doing-what-the-game-is-trying-to-get-you-to-do" - survival.
- More... interaction, within the game. Hopefully the story mode will have solved this issue with its NPCs; as of now, there is not much to do but survive and hear your character talk about surviving, and then move and do it all over again (of course, the very fact that a game can get away with that and still be fun is mind-blowing, and shows the splendor of the game).
Welp, that was a little long-winded, I know, but I had a lot to say, and I've been holding it in too long. This Halloween update jumped me back into the game, and then I realized how fun it was and felt as if I was letting the hard-working devs down by not letting them know, Hey - your game? It's great. Keep it up.

Ghost Master is a game most people have never heard of. In fact, even during its release in 2003 it never received much publicity or commercialism. This is because it wasn't really a "big project" in the first place. Basically no one ever heard of Sick Puppies, the developing company, because they had only released one other game before: Pipe Dreams 3D, two years prior to this game. Sick Puppies remained true to its name in the business due to the fact they were, well, a sick company. They disbanded only a year after the release of Ghost Master, though to this day the game still has a cult following, and for very good reasons.
Ghost Master is an extremely original game, with unique, haunting and spiritual music (of which is perhaps my favorite aspect of this game), gameplay and level design. You play the role of a Ghost Master, which is basically just a name for you as you scroll around in this RTS 3D world and try to best command the spirits in your arsenal to accomplish certain objectives - mostly involving the casting of "spells" (powers) to scare mortals until they run away from the level, earning you victory when all mortals are gone - or else left insane, which I might add is hard to do, but really funny to see. The abilities of your ghosts depend on the individual and type, and you can unlock more ghosts by playing levels and finding "restless spirits" which you can talk to, and they give you a quest-like objective which you must find a way to complete before you finish their unfinished business, or else free them.
The diversity and imagination of the ghosts themselves is really interesting as many are inspired by many spiritual cultures and myths, or even pop-culture as some are obvious parodies of famous horror movies. Some ghosts are elementals, others are Gremlins, which are the wild spirits of animals, and others are poltregiests, the tortured spirits of humans who were once mortals. Each ghost has a unique mini-profile with an amusing backstory, and a semi-unique set of powers you can purchas as training with the points you earn for completing levels. This currency is called Gold Plasm.
Every ghost has a specific kind of fetter (a place or a type of thing) they can bind themselves to at your command when playing a level, based on their type or perhaps how they died. This also can relate to how a restless spirit might be trapped in a level, waiting for you to free them and unlock them. One of my more favorite spirits was an air elemental named Whisperwind, a fairy-like being who was trapped in a dream-catcher which you have to destroy.
The game itself is quite tacky with its graphics, but at the same time the art style and atmosphere sends a very good at making you feel immersed in the creepiness of it all. It's easy to imagine how scared the mortals must be of you, walking around in all those locations you haunt because of how weirdly mystical everything seems, though you will sometimes still chuckle at the plastic hair of mortals and french-fry fingers of some of your ghosts with all their silly low quality models.
The gameplay, as mentioned before, is extremely unique, as I've never seen a single game to this day that really has the same kind of mechanics you see in this classic gem. However, the game is also quite buggy sometimes, and I can't promis you you wont ever flip your table in rage due to mortals not doing what you want them to. This is the most frusterating part of the game, because manipulating the mortals into doing something or triggering something is usually the only way to unlock new ghosts as you use them to do something to set other spirits free. An example of frustration would be this one ghost of a murdered sales woman, whom would be unlocked after you help her with her unfinished business by lurring a woman to her makeup tray which was resting on a table near her hidden corpse. For some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason, the woman would actually use this product despite all the dust and the DEAD BODY, but the real trick is getting the female mortal to notice it. It takes several different lurring spells, and for what ever reason, this is the one ghost I have the most trouble saving because it's completely random. I've literally tried for hours sometimes to get her and the mortals keep glitching out and avoiding her room too soon, but then other times I get her unlocked WITH OUT EVEN DOING ANYTHING! That's right, sometimes, when there's a blue moon out in real life, and the stars align perfectly for you, your objectives for a few certain things in the game may be accomplished COMPLETELY ON THEIR OWN with no prompt from you. The game is stupid like this sometimes. Mortals will also teleport sometimes.
When starting a level, first you select your ghosts. You use their powers to manipulate the environment and the mortals to complete various objectives, but it always ends with you scaring them all off. You assign your spirits a room or area based on their fetters - a gremlin for example will stay at any electronic you bind him to. In doing this, you strategize by looking at the path-finding patterns of the mortals to see how to lay traps. Some fetters however are semi-mobile, as in, a mortal may pick your object up and carry your spirit somewhere else. To stop this, just make your ghost scare that person.
Almost every level, even without the ghosts, is a giant refference to a famous horror story or novel. You will play a parody of The Amityville Horror, Sleepy Hollow and Blair Witch for example. The game is a strange mix of humor and horror involving tacky and almost slap-stick themes while at the same time having a disturbingly chilling environment at times. This is perhaps one of the game's strongest qualties - the combination of a spooky atmosphere, fun gameplay and a light air of occasional black comedy that keeps the player on their toes as they enjoy the ride - up until at some point they trip and fall over due to one of the game's occasionally irritatingly hard levels. This game isn't perfect, and sometimes you *will* get mad at it.
In the end, I think it's still a great classic and a shame that no sequels are being made. Not officially anyway. Though some indi developers are trying somewhat to get something going (you can find them easily by googling Ghost Master 2), there's no telling if they'll ever really finish, as very little is shown so far. Right now, Ghost Master is availabe to everyone here at the stock price of 5 USD, which in my opinion is a great price. It's definetly not a fancy game. It doesn't have amazing graphics (despite its interesting theme and art style), it's kind of glitchy sometimes, and hardly anyone knows about it and the developing company is literally dead now.
If you're still unsure about this game, then wait for halloween. In all the time I've been on Steam, I've seen Ghost Master go on sale for 1.50 USD or so every single time, as one of the first things to go on sale. That's practically making this game free, and once its in your hands, it's easy to get addicted to. It has decent replayability, and I've finished it like 5 times already in all the time I've had this game. I actually grew up with this, but I lost the disc and recently saw the game for sale here. It was so cheap, I couldn't resist just getting it again.
PS: Look for the popular All Ghosts Mod which brings very welcome rebalancing to the game's level select. Also, this game works for me on Windows 10, but some may have to use work-arounds.

TellTale’s first take on Sam & Max starts slow but builds into the familiar hilarious absurdity that characterises the Freelance Police. It also shows the ingenuity of the developers, who managed to build a funny, entertaining adventure game on a small budget and even smaller playing areas.
Sam & Max Save the World is one of the earliest point ‘n’ clicks made by TellTale Games, where we can find many of the elements that later bloomed into their staple adventure game formula.
The developers obviously had to operate on a small budget: the graphics and animation are mundane and the playing field usually consists of the same neighbourhood with one additional area in each episode.
Therefore, they had to rely on sheer creativity to keep things interesting. Every joke is spot-on and it is easy to see the contribution of the original creator, Steve Purcell in each moment that represents the absurdity of the old Sam & Max comics. We even get glimpses of the old 1992 LucasArts game in the puzzle design, although most of them are a lot less tame for those who are familiar with adventure game logic.
Since this was originally an episodic release, each new case has to escalate an arcing mystery on top of the current predicament. This is the only place where the game stretched beyond its limits, as the plot starts to struggle after the fourth episode and cannot deliver a cathartic ending.
Still, it does not matter if our duo has to tackle a crazy talk show host or two presidents of the United States; they easily ensure that Sam & Max Save the World remains one of the funniest adventure games ever made (assuming one start it on a modern system).

A Great game, but unfortunately fell under the radar.
To those who has never played the original (Classic), this might seem a bit strange.  The writing is dense, and the wordplay of jokes might be overwhelming and complex – some of the humor truly is designed for a written medium, not a video game.  However, with each episode, the linguistic complexity of dialogues subsides, bringing it closer to the level of the target audience – video gamers.  And even though I love and appreciate the advance depth, intelligence, and wit behind satiric constructs of the series, dumbing it down as the Season progresses helps to bring in the audience (alas, perhaps, too late).
Nonetheless.
Solid Adventure – puzzles range from easy to medium, voice acting is exemplary, plot of the First Season is fun and fit the mood of the protagonist duo Sam and Max (and the lore, of course), characters are lovable and well developed.  Some of the music gets pretty annoying and repetitive – staying, in fact, unchanged, from episode to episode – but that’s a minor price to pay for a great Adventure.
Absolutely and Highly Recommend.
You might also enjoy and/or appreciate the inspiration behind Edna and Harvey.

Okay, so there's more to it than that. After a science experiment gone-awry, you're alone on a small group of islands occupied solely by birds and murderbots. Your helpful butler informs you, voice in the head style, that you need to find fragments of a machine to get home safely. And that's it. The islands are procedural generated at world creation, and look like you would expect rural Britain to (if you have never been there like myself). Outwit and avoid the robots, gather the pieces, scav the tools and food you need to survive, and escape the islands.

Project Zomboid is one of my favorite games on Steam. The thought of semi-realistic survival appeals to me, and I love the realistic map (Takes you 30 minutes to go to the next town). Water and Electricity will eventually shut down leaving you to kill to find food and water, and if that watermelon goes bad, better find some chips fast. The developers are very active with the community as well, the community is fairly decent compared to most games (Unturned, Roblox, Garry's Mod). You also WILL eventually die from carelessness or drought.
Pros
. Semi-realistic
. Map size (Still growing)
. Zombies can easily overwhelm you
Cons
. Some minor bugs (Stairs)
. Found two pistols on normal loot spawn in a kitchen cupboard
Overall, I highly recommend this game

A decent platformer in the "super hard but small levels with easy restarts" hardcore sub-genre of platformers whose poster child is Super Meat Boy.
The controls are a bit floaty/unpredictable, but the game always restart you instantly at the last platform so failure doesn't sting and it's easy to retry again and again until you succeed. Though many levels are standard fare for that type of game, the "laser beam jump" mechanic is well exploited, with many variations, and there are a few levels that are really clever and/or funny.
Finally, the crazy story and different settings for levels will keep the game fresh enough. If you stick to it, you should be able to finish this game in a few hours, making it a good time waster that doesn't outlast its welcome.

In a market filled with gaming companies trying to milk every cent out of it's players, Cuphead is an absolute blessing to the gaming community.
On the fictional Inwell Isle, Cuphead and his brother Mugman are on a winning streak at the Devil's casino. Cuphead and Mugman were so caught up in the game that they end up betting their souls to the devil and lose. The brothers beg for mercy from the devil, so he makes a deal with them: they must collect contracts from the other creatures who have lost their souls to the Devil across Inwell Isle.
The game is like nothing I've ever seen before. The 1930s cartoon style graphics are hand drawn beautifully and with great attention to detail. The game has tons of excellent imagery but doesn't dwell on a certain image for too long making you want more.
One of the reasons that Cuphead great is because of it's infuriatingly hard difficulty. In order to beat one of the many ruthlessly designed bosses, you must be constantly shooting at it while simultaneously dodging, jumping and ducking over all of the clutter that the boss throws at you. One of my favorite instances of this was early on in the game where you have to dodge all of the tears of a crying onion. I love that this game doesn't hold your hand. It pushes you in the deep end right from the get-go and once you finally beat one of these insanely challenging bosses, you feel astounding. A lot of these games these days lack this feeling of true achievement because of how much they hold your hand but not Cuphead. Certainly not Cuphead.
If you're looking for a unique gaming experience that is challenging and visually stunning then check out Cuphead. At only $20 dollars it's an absolute steal.

Some people have argued that The Beginner's Guide is not a game since the player cannot lose. They are mistaken: I tried to understand The Beginner's Guide, and thereby lost at it.
Other people have argued that The Beginner's Guide is not a game since it is single-player only. They, too, are mistaken: The Beginner's Guide is a two-player game, in which Davey Wreden (playing in 2015) defeated me (playing in 2017.)
This is clearly a game. It is also a commentary upon games (including itself), a commentary upon game designers (including Wreden himself) and upon people who play games (including me.)
If you think this game wasn't made for people like you, let me assure you that you're mistaken. If you think this game was made for people like you, let me assure you that you're right, but not in the way that you think you are.
Play it.

Limbo, the game, is special in that while it does not wholly depict that mysterious dimension as my mind did, it captures its essence. You are a boy who wakes up in a lonely world made up only of black, white, and shades of gray. Video game logic demands you walk from left to right, jumping over obstacles as they appear, a simple task that needs little attention in the initial moments. This is your chance to absorb your surroundings. The background provides an illusion of depth, but its branches and bridges are out of focus, as if you are dreaming them into existence. The pint-sized hero, his bright blinking eyes shining from his blackened silhouette, trots ahead with the charming gangliness of a six-year-old.
- Striking atmosphere that chills the heart
- Excellent, poignant moments that stay with you
- Cold, gruesome deaths are presented with memorable and horrific apathy
- Introduces more involved puzzles at a satisfying pace
- The most haunting imagery is limited to the first half
- Ending doesn't emerge organically from the hour leading to it
Summary :
Limbo is an incredible achievement. Very few games are as original, atmospheric, and consistently brilliant. It belongs in everybody's collection. The journey may be over too quickly, but you will be entertained every minute. This is one of my favorite games. I give it a 8/10.
You can play this for hours or just for a few minutes to pass some spare time. Nearly unbeatable in terms of cost versus entertainment value.

They're respresented by a metre and so if any one of them is too high or too low then you'll face one of many types of deaths. It's not that complicated of a game but the hook for it is that the more you play the more you uncover. You have goals to accomplish like ruling for king for sixty years or be involved in an affair. You unlock new decks that carry out new questlines and encounters which helps spice things up every now and again.
This is quite a nice little game with a fun idea. It does it well and the presentation is well done plus it's one of those games with good water cooler talk so you can tell your friends weird stories on how you met the Devil or how you arranged a wedding for some werewolves. The price of admission is also very nice. It does get a bit repetitive after awhile so I'd suggest playing it in short bursts or maybe get the iOS or Android version. It looks very much designed for those platforms. Still as is it's a good game that'll give a couple of hours of entertainment. I give it a 7/10.

A very interesting concept of a stealth / strategy first-person.  The maps are very detailed and robust; when you first start a "world" it is generated and saved, which can take a few minutes to build.  First impressions is it is a simple game but as it is a stealth / strategy game, a single game looks like it could take a very long time to complete if you stuck with stealth and assassination (~3-4 hours), or if you just want to tank and spank you can but there are no difficulty controls so you may die a lot and well, that also may take ~3-4 hours too!
The overall gameplay is also quite challenging in many senses - limited inventory so when you find an objective piece you usually won't have the space for it and have to decide to ditch items.  Easy enough, but, you also have to continue eating so that can be rough too.  There are two variables - Life and Vitality.  Eating restores Vitality, which decreases over time to 0.  Once at 0, then your Life begins to decrease over time to 0 in which you die.  This type of challenge is also what make this game very challenging even for simple concept.
Highly recommend and can't wait for it to be out of alpha release, but do know this is alpha - there are bugs and missing features.  For example I had t restart a few times in order to get resolution up to 1920x1080, when moving from one world to the other it locks up on the Loading Map screen and I have to CTRL+ALT+DEL to get out and start over.  No difficulty controls.  Small things like that and you will absolutely run into them, but considering the developer(s) are putting out patches every month and doing a great job (the best of any software development I've come across) with video updates, I can overlook this for now as an alpha and just restart the game.
Oh, and there are only two times you can save - when at the "recall" point, or when moving to another map, so be sure to save each and every time both for the alpha bugs but also well, you are almost guarantee to die a few times :)
Cheers.

After Telltale dropped the ball on their Bone game series for reasons unknown. They put their focus on another comic property that this time they made more than two games out of it. And that comic property is the crime fighting anthropomorphic rabbit and dog, Sam & Max themselves! This duo made their first debut in an underground comic series dating back to 1987, but it wouldn't be until the release of the widely acclaimed LucasArts computer game "Sam & Max: Hit the Road" was when the characters started to become recognize to a wider audience. Then came an animated tv series that while tone down to meet the standards for a qualified kids show, it proved to be a funny and creative show. It ran on the defunct Fox Kids line up for one season and had the additions of a bat cave like basement for Sam & Max's operations and the child prodigy Geek as their weapons specialist.
After the show ended it run, there were plans for there to be a sequal to the "Hit the Road" titled "Sam & Max: Plunge Through Space". The game was intended to be an XBox exclusive title that revolves on Sam & Max retrieving the stolen Statue of Liberty by traveling through space. The development team consisted of former employees from LucasArts and Steve Purcell the creator of Sam & Max would of pitched the story. The project fell threw when the development company Infinite Machine went bankrupt a year after production began and the sequal was abandoned. After the cancelation, LucasArts annouced that they themselves will develop a new sequel to the game titled "Sam & Max Freelance Police". It was conceived as a point and click adventure game like its predessor except in a 3-D enviroment similar to the games "Grim Fandango" & "Escape From Monkey Island". This project had the co-director of the Hit the Road game Michael Stemmle leading the project along with Steve Purcell as creative consultant, with the plot being a string of six stories forming a climax. This time around it seem like this game was going to be a reality only for the whole thing to collapse when LucasArts pulled the plug on the sequel citing market/economic conditions and the loss of interest in adventure games as their reason for cancelling it. This news didn't please Sam & Max fans, Steve Purcell, & video game fans too lightly when there was an audience for it, but at the time of the game's cancellation it was when "point and click" adventure genre games were becoming fewer in numbers.
For nearly a decade it seem like we will never see another adaption of Sam & Max in computer game or animated form a like. That all change when LucasArts license on Sam & Max expired in 2005, and Steve Purcell kindly gave the video game rights to the newly formed Telltale Games, formed by mostly LucasArts employees who either left or got fired from the company to form a company that does adventure games as a focus. The cancelled "Sam & Max Freelance Police" game helped inspired this very game we see right now "Culture Shock" the first episode of a six part episode season focusing on newer adventures focused on Sam & Max themselves. Sorry for the long ranting there, but I felt this was too good of a back story to ignore, I will now give out the plot outline. Culture Shock starts up with Sam & Max receiving a phone call from the commissioner giving them a case for the first time in a while. Their mission is to investigate the recent vandalism that is taking place in town. Graffiti art of a washed up 1970s TV star Brady Culture is seen on all of the building walls, while mysterious video tapes are being circulated via video dumping that are causing viewers to become hypnotised. The culprits are three washed up 1970s former child stars the Soda Poppers(Peepers, Wizzer, & Specs). The three celebrities are not themselves as all three of them are overly obcess with Brady despite that he was their rival during their heyday. The only way for Sam and Max to put an end to this nonsense is by some how trying to snap the Soda Poppers out of their trances, as well as learning the whereabouts and the motive of Brady Culture. This game is everything you'd want to see in an ideal Sam & Max 3-D adventure game.
The game is on par with the "Hit the Road" game as oppose to the animated tv series. Which means the sub basement and the character Geek are omitted from the game. Believe me, I would of love to seen Geek as a supporting character for this game, but unfortunately royal rights and legal issues are often the reason we don't see characters from expanded universes cross over. But don't feel blue this game provided some new supporting characters to fill the void. Bosco who was mentioned but not seen in "Hit the Road" is finally given an identity as a raspy voice conspiracy fearing black guy along with the new female character Sybil, a multi career woman who previously was a tattoo artist is now a psycho-analyist. These two characters provide Sam and Max help in some form or another. Even if you never played the "Hit the Road" game or seen the tv show, you are able to enjoy this game without the previously said titles. This game helped put Telltale on the map of innovating game companies to keep an eye, they were able to obtain rights to develop other properties with the years that followed since their foundation date. Culture Shock was a great start to the six part episode season that is known as the "Save The World" season, it's exsistence is proof that point and click adventure games are alive and well. If you are a fan of Sam & Max or like to play a fun adventure game then don't hesitate to play this one.

The Forest is currently an Early Access Survival Horror game. The core concept and execution of the game are excellent thus far. The Developers for this game are very active in the community and regularly release updates. Detailed breakdown:
What we know about the Story:
The story is in development. This means the whole Story is not there. You cannot "beat" the game as is. While exploring the island you will find clues as to what happened to "Timmy" (who is assumed to be your son). Parts of his toy, pictures, cave sketches. The game has basically zero handholding and refuses to point you in any direction at all. Most people will never find all the hidden story components. If you do find them, you will learn where "Timmy" has been taken
Gameplay:
The game is played in First Person. The core aspects of the game are survival based. Hunger, Thirst, Rest, and Energy all make an appearance. You must hunt for food (or forage, alternatively), drink water, and sleep. So far, the survival aspects are pretty well balanced, and always being improved upon.
You are going to establish a "base" or camp of sorts. Shelters, fires, walls, traps, gardens, resource management, and food storage all come into play here. There are quite a few creatable structures/devices already, and more are going to be added. Base creation takes time. You must gather resources to build things. Many people feel this is "grindy" but I enjoy it a lot. You will find yourself collecting rocks, sticks, logs from trees, leaves, and other objects and transporting them back to your base. This takes time, but seeing your base take shape feels extremely rewarding.
Combat is a necessary part of the game. You are stuck on an island populated by cannibal tribes. Hungry cannibal tribes. There is so much to say for the AI in this game. They are already impressive and quirky and only getting better. The cannibals are currently broken into three tribes.
Starving/Skinnies. These cannibals are very thin/lanky, often naked and covered in blood. They are almost always hostile to the player and have even been seen killing and eating fellow cannibals. Often acting as scouts, it is common to see solo skinnies roaming the island. When they find something of interest (deforestation, foreign structures, you) they will often hide and observe for a while. When satisfied, they will run back to their camp and alert fellow cannibals. If they located your base, expect to see patrols coming and going from now on. Skinnies are the weakest of all the cannibals, but they are EXTREMELY fast and agile. It is very easy for skinnies to dodge your attacks and get behind you when in combat.
Cannibals. The regular cannibals look like normal humans, with a few skin tones, often covered in dirt or decorations. They usually travel in groups of 2-4. They are not always hostile to the player, but it's always safer to assume they are. If they know your location it's common to see them roaming around the edges of your base. they are slower than skinnies but they usually carry clubs and hit much harder. They are prone to splitting up in combat, flanking and coming from behind the player.
Cave Cannibals. Gray skinned aliens, basically. Stronger than regular cannibals but a bit slower. use the same tactics and skills as above.
The AI is so awesome. They stalk you, they observe you, leave effigies outside your base (body parts on sticks) to mess with you, ambush you, scare you. You will find yourself fearing them, looking over your shoulder when doing even the simplest things. there are special varieties of mutants deep in the caves, but I'll leave that for you to discover.
All in all this game is excellent. The core concept and foundation are very well done. The developers add more and more, and try to stay on top of glitches and bugs. More is being added and the game is only 14.99 on Steam. 9.5/10 for me, I love this game and would recommend it to anyone.

You get to build creative structures with the resources you have; buildings, traps, rafts (although not to escape). The multiplayer option does not detatch the game from its horror setting. Buidling a fortress to fall back on with other people, of whom you may have never met, allows from a rapid and smooth progression through the game making it all the more fun.
Although the game is still buggy at times and requires some polishing, I still highly recommend the game. I think this game is getting so many "Recommended" reviews due to the low price. In my opinion, Reigns is interesting and funny, but not particularly fun to play for more than an hour.
You have 4 guages in this game. Religion, Population, Militia, and Finance. A card appears and says something like:
"Sir your people are sick!"
You then can choose from two options and you can guess how the stat guages will be affected. This scenario is easy. You pay for medicine and your Finance guage drops and population goes up. If you do nothing, then only the population goes down.
The object of the game is to keep the guages from going too low OR too high. If one stat hits zero, it's game over. If a stat hits 100%, it's game over again (For example if Militia hits 100% the army kills you and takes over).
Honestly it's very fun for the first hour. After that I had my fill and decided to keep playing and get some achievements. I think I'd recommend this game as well if each card was treated like a word puzzle...but the random cards just add to the monotony.
Cost factored into this review....I'd recommend as well. $3 for an interesting experience like this is worth it. However ignoring the cost, I'd give the game a 5/10. It excels from it's originality, but suffers from it's continued fun factor.

As a child of the 1980s, I saw two things pretty much everywhere: NES games and cartoons.  In the glory days of the 8-bit NES, we had "Nintendo-hard" games where pattern recognition was key.  Levels and bosses that seemed unfair were actually operating on relatively simple pattern-based algorithms, and a keen-eyed gamer could exploit those patterns for a win that made the whole affair look easy.  Mess up, though, and you were punished for it.  Bosses didn't have checkpoints no matter how many phases they had.
The cartoons were ubiquitous.  Sure, we had our campy 80s action shows, but you were just as likely to find Looney Tunes/Merry Melodies or old Disney cartoons on TV.  If you had the right channels, you might have even been graced with the old black and white cartoons of days past.  These cartoons often eschewed modern sensibilities and political correctness for snappy action and silly gags.  Things didn't have to make real-world sense in these shows, but there was a sort of internal logic to them.
Cuphead is the marriage of these two glorious things.  If Mega Man had noodly arms, he would be Cuphead.  If Mickey Mouse fired shotgun blasts out of his gloves, he would be Cuphead.
Let's make no mistake: the game is hard, and you will die.  You may find yourself cursing your computer, your controller, the creators of the game, or perhaps even your chosen deity.  None of these things is to blame.  Cuphead is fair.  You just haven't gotten good enough yet.
Stick with Cuphead, and you'll find a game that has some of the most exciting character design, music direction, and pure charm of anything you've ever seen.  It draws inspiration from so many areas, and yet it's a creature all its own.  If you have any love for classic games or classic cartoons, give it a shot.

You oversee a group of actors as they film a knock off Power Rangers TV series and gain popularity. The main gameplay offers very basic turn based strategy battles where you fight monsters and power up for mech duels. Between filming episodes you organise your squad, buying and crafting new gear, reply to fan mail and activate bonuses with ‘fan power’ that is earned by completing goals in each episode.
The game has been updated recently. The mech battles have been changed to use timed button presses. They seem very easy but they aren’t long so they don’t become annoying.
The graphics are well designed with different sets and monsters. Each characters has a different class with unique abilities. However the fighting quickly becomes tedious, there is very little enemy variation or new mechanics, so virtually every battle plays the same. The main strategy is just to use your special abilities when possible.
Although there is a story the player has little input so it lacks involvement. It focuses on the actors rather than the characters in the TV show. It fell flat for me because it was written for laughs but the jokes were too referential. I appreciate that the source material is not serious but I feel that focusing on each episode as a quest where you could make key choices would make each episode feel more unique.
Overall it’s decent but I don’t recommend it at full price unless you want something to play without much thought required and don’t mind repetitive battles.

A seriously addicting game that puts you in the shoes of several dozen cursed medieval kings. You're tasked with keeping the kingdom - consisting of the Church, the people, the Army, and the treasury - in balance; nothing can be too powerful or too weak, or you'll meet a sorry end.
Gameplay is super simple; the game started out as an Android and iOS app, and the basic swiping mechanics carried over. You can use either the mouse or the spacebar and arrow keys to make decisions and progress in the game. Your choices are generally pretty limited to "yes" or "no", but the scenarios and characters are interesting enough that that doesn't matter, and with over 600+ cards in-game, it's going to take a handful of playthroughs to get bored.
The only negatives I've got to offer on Reigns are: 1. "Winning" the campaign is a ridiculously difficult puzzle; even if you can figure out what you're supposed to aim for, actually getting there is tricky, with the majority of critical in-game clues being impossibly subtle. 2. Getting all the achievements isn't realistic - not only because viewing all 600+ cards is, in the dev's own words, all but impossible, but because the game is so absurdly repetitive after 5-6 consequetive playthroughs you'll be left wanting to smash your head against the wall (although maybe that's just a me problem). 3. The kings' names. Oh, my God. It's like the dev's never read anything but an English history textbook. You're a king in a world where witches, werewolves, and dragons run abound, but there's only two or three fantasy names thrown in the mix, and the rest are just endless repeats of Henrys, Roberts, Geralds, and Harrys (with the occasional "Thomas" and "Cedric" for variety).
TL;DR: Really fun game. Super addicting. Gets boring after 5-6 consequetive playthroughs.

This is episode one of the first season of a series of point-and-click games based on the original comics with loads of references to them as well as other media they may have appeared in. You can only buy them bundled in what season number they're in despite every episode being individual games. This is the only season out of Telltale's three that consists of six episodes with their own individual story that only somewhat connects with the next one until the season's last episode where it all falls together. Each episode won't take longer than a few hours if you're halfway competent at making sense of the puzzles.
Like the comics, everything about this series is very cartoon-y; the artwork, the story, and the writing. Most of the writing is very clever to say the least, even if you don't happen to find the current joke funny.
These games aren't particularly hard, but they are entertaining, especially for fans of the franchise given that Steve Purcell had a huge hand in this particular series in trying to keep the game as true to the comics as possible in visuals, tone, and content. The visuals may differ too greatly from its 2D counterparts as well as the voice tones of Sam & Max themselves. A few "puzzles" may be a little too out-of-the-box, so to speak, but other than those none of them are mind-bending. Regardless, a lot of the results from them are satisfying to see.
It's not exactly an innovative point-and-click game or anything like that but it's definitely fun to go through for those that can get into this franchise's style of humor.

Incredibly charming top-down tactical RPG w/ base management elements.
You play as a studio / group of stunt actors who create their own TV show similar to Power Rangers. You'll go through 5 or 6 "seasons" with multiple episodes (read: battles) each, in which not only do you have to survive and defeat the bad guys, but you have to try to follow additional "Director's Orders" to maximize your audience gain. In between, you do some studio management in which you can craft gear for your heroes, upgrade your mech, and enhance your studio.
The game is very earnest in a way that charmingly captures that sense of silly enthusiasm that you find in shows like Power Rangers. You can tell the game creators knew their genre very well.
I thoroughly recommend this game for fans of tactical RPGs (XCom, FFT, Disgaea, etc).
An extra word on difficulty: As a veteran of tactics RPG, I played & beat this on challenging (the hardest available starting difficulty). It was indeed challenging and often frustrating (sometimes in a good way, sometimes not). If you're not a fan of difficulty, I'd recommend the middle difficulty setting instead.

Now first of all. It's a great game and worth every cent. Maybe the best early access game I've ever played. Keep it going.
The combination of survival in the wild and the constant threat of being eaten alive is amazing. The dark and hostile caves
gave me one of the best experiences in gaming ever. Went into a cave, well equipped, about 30 minutes later I found myself lost and trapped, shaking, scared, poking in the dark with my spear, barely made it out alive with only a lighter and an axe. There should also be an evaluation of the player's sanity. That was maybe the most tense hour in my gaming life...
Nevertheless I would like to give the devs some suggestions:
- Survival in the wild is too easy. Only 4 days in my first game and I found myself so well equipped with meat, water and resources. There was no real challenge. Even when I set out to explore the island, I made it through 5 days without having any difficulty finding food or water. Deers would run around in front of me, just wating to be killed. So please: Make the hunting feel like real hunting! Let me track the blood of an injured animal.
- A skill system would be nice. Not that I always need skill systems in games, but progress in this game should have a skill system. I mean, I'm some guy used to supermarkets, plastic wrapped meat, flat screens and netflix and I crash in the wild. Hunting should be a mess and very difficult at the beginning. After killing a couple of rabbits I might get better at this.
- Please add more wildlife. I bet there's more to find on an island than lizards, rabbits, birds and deer. How about insects?
- Animations are a little off. Especially for the spear and arrows when they hit an animal or enemy. would be nice to see them get stuck. Limb damage would be amazing
- "Real" Dodging would be great
- Why dont't I get bones from deers?
- A greater variety of environments/maps would be awesome
- Dead bodies should spread infections. Would be great to be able to dig a grave or burn bodies to keep myself from getting sick.
- Sanity level doesn't really have an effect. Or at least I didn't feel it. I start to chop up humans and eat them for god sake. And that doesn't have any consequnece?
- Using mud as camouflage. In general I would like some more "Lord of the flies" feeling
- Bandages and more variety in medics, damage zones would be great
Thanks for reading, whoever finds this useful. Great game and I'm really looking forward to the finished game! Keep up the good work!

I have to say that I have never given a review before but I felt like this game is worth my time. So far, I have spent 180 hours in this game and I have to admit, it is the most fun game I have played in a long time.
This game is for people who like to micro manage. You have to learn the details of the game to make the most of it Simple stuff as carpentery, cooking and even first aid become a lot of fun, and due to the development team it only gets better.
Project Zomboid is basically a game like the Sims, except on Steroids, or maybe Zomboids. You play for survival and depending on your difficulty setting it can be totally frustrating to an almost endless adventure of fun.
The only downside is being early access, meaning sometimes things change a lot and you have to learn the new mechanics, but the development team has been nice enough to allow you to carry over your existing save to the new mechanics so at least you don't have to start over.
Currently, I am playing a character who used to be a Police Officer in Muldraugh. I made my home base in the home I started in, and I have probably spent a good 80 days of real life playing time on this game. I am having tons of fun expanding my property, having created a garden, settings traps to catch animals for meat and gathering survival tools.
My wife watched me for a while and thought I was stupid for wasting time on this kind of game. I ended up buying the game for her, and now she cannot stop playing it and is asking me for advice on certain techniques such as carpentry or trapping.

SUPERHOT tells you to tell everyone else that it is the most innovative shooter you’ve played in years.
While this is probably true, what it doesn’t tell you is that the game is only about two hours long, is extremely simple, and yet retails for $25.
SUPERHOT is a very simplistic game with a very cool central mechanic – time moves at an incredibly slow rate of speed, to the point where bullets are crawling through the air towards you as they’re shot. The catch is that when you take actions – picking stuff up, moving around, firing your own weapon – time temporarily moves at normal speed.
Thus, this game is basically like being in bullet time all the time, except when you’re moving.
That is the central conceit of this game, and what little there is revolves around it. As much a puzzle game as a FPS, the real goal of this game is to figure out how to kill all of the enemies which are often coming at you from multiple directions without getting killed yourself. Time progressing at a very slow rate won’t stop you from being gunned down from behind or dying in a hail of bullets down a narrow hallway. Moreover, your own weapons have sharply limited ammo clips and rates of fire, which means that you are constantly having to throw your weapons away (stunning your enemies in the process) to nab new ones.
The game really centers around this – firing your weapon, tossing it (and whatever nearby pick-upable objects you can) at people to make them drop their weapons, grabbing the dropped weapons out of midair, and repeating the process. And in the end, while this is pretty cool in one sense, the game is very limited in another.
There’s only one type of enemy – the red dude – and there are only five types of weapon – pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, baseball bats, and katanas. The pistol fires slowly, the shotgun fires a couple of blasts before you have to toss it away, the assault rifle fires off four bullets in rapid succession with no waiting between bursts, the baseball bat is a bad melee weapon, and the katana is a one-hit kill melee weapon which can be thrown at people to impale them or even slice bullets in half in midair.
All of this SOUNDS really cool, but honestly in practice the game doesn’t feel nearly as cool as it sounds to play. I feel like the central mechanic is really neat, but the limited environments, the limited environmental interaction, the fact that I didn’t have other neat powers (like, say, wall-running or something similar), the fact that the weapons were all kind of samey, and the fact that bullets felt surprisingly slow even in supposed “real-time” all sort of contributed to the game not really feeling much like the power fantasy you’d expect. Rather, it is much more of a puzzle game, about using your attacks in the right order and positioning yourself properly while dodging bullets, as one shot will kill you and force you to start over the (very short) levels.
All in all, the game’s story mode (which is strange and does little to explain itself) takes about two hours to beat, and you’re likely to get bored with the game’s limited mechanics around the point that you beat it. There are challenge and endless modes, but there’s not much more to the game beyond that point, so what’s the point, really?
All in all, this feels like a very short diversion, and the $25 asking price is just not likely to leave you very happy. I got this as part of a bundle, and it was fine there, but as a stand-alone game, this is very much an indie project which feels sort of like a proof of concept for a future game down the line which will be much cooler.
It is somewhat interesting, but it isn’t really all that great, and it isn’t nearly as clever as it thinks it is. Innovative it may be, but it just executes the most basic game possible with these mechanics. Hopefully someone else does more with it down the line.

Red Orchestra 2 is hands down one of the best multiplayer first person shooters of all time.
It's ingenuity lies not only in its original gameplay mechanics, but its atmosphere, its leveling system and the community it has built around itself. A truly amazing experience. Recommended for every hardcore gamer, and well worth its asking price.

I would recommend watching some of the better Evolve players out there (such as maniacsquirrel or sacriel) to get an idea of how this game plays at a high level.  Its main problem is playing with new players who don't know how to play classes to the best of their ability, since if even a single hunter is not on top of their game, a good monster player will dominate.  When played skillfully, with other skilled players, Evolve is a gem.  Intense battles are scattered throughout tense chases, and most of the time, wins feel deserved rather than luck of the draw.  Communication is key, but not necessarily vocal communication, as some of the best matches I've played have been silent, with each hunter focused on the task at hand of finding the monster, or dealing damage while avoiding the monster's flailing limbs and special abilities.  Watch the basic and advanced hunter tutorial videos in the extras menu to gain an understanding of how each unique hunter plays before jumping into multiplayer, and you'll be far ahead of most of the gamers who jump in and expect to bunny hop around the map and Leroy Jenkins the monster to death.  This is a simple game with impossible depth, and giving it just a cursory look isn't enough.  If you're not sold, watch the streams, and pay attention.  And if you purchase it, realize that you've got a learning curve ahead of you, but the accomplishment you feel after gaining some semblance of skill is astonishing, and well worth $60.

This game has a lot of mixed reviews, so in the interest of helping out the undecided, here is a basic review of the current pros and cons. I am recommending the game and I feel the pros out weigh the cons fairly significantly if you are a fan 4 v 1 and hunt games.
First the pros:
The balancing is pretty good, niether side ever feels like they are absolutely the hunter and not the hunted.
The classes are well thought out and each character has unique strengths and weakness's even within their own class, so nobody feels like just a reskin of a previous character.
The rounds are always pretty action packed, if you get into the hunt in games then you will feel the adrenalin pumping.
The game looks nice and the sound design matches everything well.
The modes and characters are all failry easy to learn, but require skill to master.
Even without DLC there is a ton of continuous play value.
Most importantly in my opinion, the game requires you to think on your feet and make split second decisions. It takes thought and skill to get good, there is no spam to win class.
Now for the negatives (some of these will likely be subject to change as patches come out) note: none of these make the game unplayable.
The match maker is buggy, especially if you are trying to find a match while platooned with one or more friend. Some times it will kick your friend, or make one of you the monster despite the monster slot being closed when you are platooned. (this doesn't happen a lot, but enough to be worth mentioning.)
Even if your machine more than meets recommended specs, high graphics settings seem to cause the cutseens to lag and some in game lag. Might be an issue with optimization. The game look really nice even on low settings so it's not a huge hit.
No ingame video replays, or in game means of saving them.
The game is heavily geared towards the sale of DLC, (however if you have no issue with playing the characters that come with the game, then you don't miss out any game modes or maps.)
Currently the number of modes is rather limitied. Just skirmish and evacuation. Skirmish is what you think it is. Evacuation is 5 battles, the first one is always a standard hunt and the last is always a defence/ assault depending if you are the hunter or monster, and the other 3 battle could be hunt ( kill the monster), nest (destroy all 6 monster eggs/ minions, rescue (revive survivors and get 6 of them safely evaced). Different maps offer different bonuses to whomever wins. This mode also has a balance system which gives the side with the least wins a damage buff.
The character audio gets a little repetetive (you do get hints at the story in the dialog, and the first time you hear a particular conversation it is usually pretty good.)
I hope this helps

The game is based on squad tactics, communication and co-operation where personal skill or your kill count does not matter, and the primary goal of the player is to fulfill the objectives for the team. This is a real tactical war sim, and as you would not go to war on your own, you would not survive on your own in this game. Team play is a must.
The theatres in the base-game are limited into Stalingrad and Pacific but there is an active modding community and the game is Steam Workshop compatible. Therefore the game allows te community members to mod and add multiple maps and other theaters too. Heroes of the Wet mod is a prime example of this, and is a must if you want to experience the western front of WW2..
Also, you can experience attacking enemy soldiers only with your katana in your hand, shouting "TENNO HEKKA BANZAI" from your lungs while charging the enemy, evading artillery shells and flame throwers, first hand.

Honestly, when I first heard about this game and saw it in action, I was thrilled by it. However, now that I got my hands on it and got to play it, I came to the quick realization that while the idea was sound on paper, in reality it is anything but.
Aside the DLC fiasco that's been all over the internet, my main problem with the game is that it doesn't feel any fun. As a hunter you spend most of the time just running around with nothing happening, while as a monster you jump around and eat other animals - playing hide 'n seek - until you hit level 3 and completely crush the hunters. The level of skill it takes to be good monster player is insanely low compared to being an average hunter, which requires good coordination, situational awareness, and constant communication between your team-mates. If you start playing with a team of hunters, prepare to lose - a lot - before you get your skills up high enough to challenge a good (or even an average) monster player. This game requires insane amount of patience to become good at, and I'm afraid not too many - myself included - simply do not have that kind of patience.
Yes, I'm aware that there are videos of players who are completely dominating as hunters, but you can tell they're good at it. I mean really, really good at it. For an average person who works for 32 hours a week, sleeps 8 hours a day, and has other hobbies/duties aside playing video games, attaining that level of skill is simply not plausible in a week or so.
Co-op games succeed only if they're fun to play, and this unfortunately just doesn't feel fun. At all. It just boring, whether I'm playing as a monster or a hunter. I feel like I'm playing Final Fantasy 13 of First Person Shooters.
So no, I'm not recommending this game to anyone. And I feel sorry because I was really looking towards to this game six months ago.

A seriously addicting game that puts you in the shoes of several dozen cursed medieval kings. You're tasked with keeping the kingdom - consisting of the Church, the people, the Army, and the treasury - in balance; nothing can be too powerful or too weak, or you'll meet a sorry end.
Gameplay is super simple; the game started out as an Android and iOS app, and the basic swiping mechanics carried over. You can use either the mouse or the spacebar and arrow keys to make decisions and progress in the game. Your choices are generally pretty limited to "yes" or "no", but the scenarios and characters are interesting enough that that doesn't matter, and with over 600+ cards in-game, it's going to take a handful of playthroughs to get bored.
The only negatives I've got to offer on Reigns are: 1. "Winning" the campaign is a ridiculously difficult puzzle; even if you can figure out what you're supposed to aim for, actually getting there is tricky, with the majority of critical in-game clues being impossibly subtle. 2. Getting all the achievements isn't realistic - not only because viewing all 600+ cards is, in the dev's own words, all but impossible, but because the game is so absurdly repetitive after 5-6 consequetive playthroughs you'll be left wanting to smash your head against the wall (although maybe that's just a me problem). 3. The kings' names. Oh, my God. It's like the dev's never read anything but an English history textbook. You're a king in a world where witches, werewolves, and dragons run abound, but there's only two or three fantasy names thrown in the mix, and the rest are just endless repeats of Henrys, Roberts, Geralds, and Harrys (with the occasional "Thomas" and "Cedric" for variety).
TL;DR: Really fun game. Super addicting. Gets boring after 5-6 consequetive playthroughs.

Chroma Squad is a Strategy RPG in the style of the Disgaea games that has a lot of strong ideas that are implemented fairly well.
It has a nice snap to the combat, there's lots of neat little ways you can customize your crew. The game also has very little fat to it - the whole thing from start to finish will run you between 8-12 hours. There's no need for grinding, which is great, because there isn't a convenient way to grind. So to that end everything requires strategy - every decision about marketing and team building matters because they're all permanent.
It would be incredibly difficult to have a fully decked out team by the end of the game, which is fine. The game is balanced well, and you can lower your difficulty at any point in the game.
The music is very nice, the graphics are vibrant, well animated, and have lots of variety. The camera zooms around a lot, so if you're prone to some kinds of motion sickness it could possibly set you off in story heavy chunks of the game.
If you do not like a dash of meta in your story telling - AVOID - this game's story is 100% meta. It's one of the first games I've ever played that has essentially no forth wall at all. It being SO abundant made it less grating than it can sometimes come across in games that rely on it a lot but not always.
I didn't care for the mech battles. They're a little on the slow side.
I feel this game has enough content that they could have stretched it a little further. While I appreciate that the game has very little padding, some optional bonus episodes within the seasons wouldn't have hurt. There are several monsters you only see once or twice, several backgrounds you only see a couple times, mechanics that don't get explored to the fullest they could be. While I appreciate the brevity of this game, especially in a genre where games tend to stretch well past the 60 hour mark pretty frequently, I wouldn't have minded a little more optional padding.

The humor was definitely there in the beginning, what with your future self being severely mutilated right in front of you, but after a little while, the humor dies down when you realize that's it. Every level you start off in shows another version of you being dragged off with spurts of blood and screaming in agony, but it starts to get tedious and annoying, especially when you keep dying while trying to figure out how to proceed to the next level. And once that humor is gone, all you're left with is a kind of mediocre platformer. The idea of using your gun's momentum to traverse the area is pretty cool, but it falls kind of flat simply because what sells this game is the weird, quirky randomness of the trailer, not so much the game.
I think another major difference here is the controller. It has the full support, but if you're someone like me who always prefers the controller to the mouse and keyboard, you'll have a harder time. Like with almost any FPS game, using the mouse is infinitely more accurate and quicker than trying to orient yourself with the stick. Normally that's not too much of a problem, but when the difference between a success and failure is a split second decision of where to aim the gun, it can be pretty jarring since you have no clear indicator of where you're aiming until you shoot. Not only that, but the stick just feels sluggish anfd I always feel like I'm overcompensating on turns trying to figure out where to orient myself when the mouse would probably feel more fluid.
If you fall into my kind of category, where you bought the game because you thought it would be a good laugh, and you prefer the gamepad, the novelty will wear off really quick. This is more like a game that you play with your drinking buddies on the weekends to just laugh at each other's failings. And maybe most importantly, is the price. This game doesn't scream out $15 to me. I feel that's too overpriced. If you really want to get this, I would wait for a sale.

First off, I will start off with a couple of things I don't like about the gameplay.
1.) Sometimes you get stuck in a loop where you can't find the things you need, and you find a ton of the things you don't need. In my current game I'm still having an issue finding a gardening spray can.
2.) Related to #1. Since the game introduced guns other than pistols or shotguns, I still haven't found any of the new guns. In my current game the last place I have to look is the mall, which is totally zombie infested. By the time I'm finished with that area I will have no need for the new guns.
3.) The items get kind of boring after a while, and some of the ones you come across still have no function as far as I can tell. Things like rubber ducks, lipstick, necklaces, etc.
4.) I want more things to do. It's more than just surviving. You grow crops, you build bases, you scavenge, you kill anything that stands in your way. But once you got all of that covered you will start wandering aimlessly just trying to think of things to do.
5.) Nasty, pesky bugs. This happens to games developed by major companies, and this happens to indie developers. Patience is a virtue, but even with that, I can say I have been playing this game for a REALLY long time and I'm still having to make backups of my SP saves after I'm done playing. It's not worth losing everything over a really dumb glitch. But hey, it's still an early access game after all. Everyone buying needs to keep that in mind.
---
Things I like:
1.) The blend of sandbox and RPG. You make your goals and you work to achieve them. You have an open world that is getting bigger. There's a lot to explore.
2.) First aid, fishing, and trapping made this game a whole heck of a lot better. Sometimes it makes me nostalgic for Oregon Trail.
3.) I am jumping out of my seat very often. It's a negative trait, but I like playing with bad eye sight because I like the rush I get from having a close near death encounter.
4.) The stategy you have to put into it. Getting to the police station may not be as easy as you thought. You'll need to take inventory of what you have and prepare the attack.
5.) It's getting a lot more realistic. With that you have extra challenges. You can't just build a rain barrel and drink the water anymore. Now you need to boil it or you will get sick. With multiplayer you could probably even roleplay and have people take on different responsiblities that keep the group alive.
Overall, I will say that I love this game. Even with the limitability I still find myself coming back to it pretty often. What most people take for granted is the fact that the developers are still incredibly decicated to working on the game. They slowly but surely will add things to keep people interested. There are some early access games that get abandoned and I'm glad the developers haven't given up. Even if in it's finished state the game is a still a little bare, I hope this garners enough attention from the gaming community and there is demand for more like it.

A couple things I think one should note before playing and/or buying this game...
- This game IS NOT for everyone.
The Beginner's Guide demands it's audiences' fullest attention, so that it may grab you, and pull you into itself. This is not a game that you, the player, control, but rather a game where the naritive controls you, as you are more or less dragged helplessly through the story.
I think that if you are someone that can appreciate story and dialogue over gameplay, please, do yourself a favour and buy this. If you want a game where you can stack achievements, and mold into your own player-driven sandbox, this game may only disappoint you.
- This game is short. But brilliant.
Too many games these days seem to saturate themselves with hours upon hours of meaningless content (ex. "the underwater level"), whilst providing minimal story and little significant gameplay to compare. I've played many AAA games that seem to just drag on in an attempt to perserve my attention, ironically only succeeding in boring me out of my mind (similar to this review). The Beginner's Guide is the opposite, as it's over saturated with meaningful content that can succeed in capturing and maintaining one's attention indefinitely.  I believe that this, in itself, makes the game worth the pricetag.
Furthermore, I think because it's so short, this game deserves to be played in one sitting. Don't let this story be cut into little pieces.
- Although you can totally just watch someone's playthrough on Youtube, don't.
As I said before, this game doesn't actually have much gameplay. It's more of a narrative pulling you along into a story, and I think that makes a lot of people interpret the game as a movie. But it's not. Part of what made me enjoy this game so much is just the experience of exploring the different worlds and levels provided for me at my own pace, so that I could interpret each of them for myself, which can't be experienced through watching a Youtube video. Just because this game relies heavily on narrative does not mean it leaves a player without anything to play.

I am now 60+ hrs in the game, level 30, and love it. The graphics are good (cryengine), the sound is great and together they form an amazing atmosphere. The gameplay is really intense on both sides and replayability is unlimited because of so many different aspects of the game changing each match (different hunter setup, dome fights, neutrals, buffs and so on..).
The developers are really active and discuss a lot with the community. Sadly, their publisher 2K is not that great and they created a ♥♥♥♥♥torm on Evolve mostly based on misinformation. To clear some things up:
There are 12 hunters, 3 monsters and 12 maps currently available. All of those, so the complete playable content is included in the base game. There is no day 1 DLC. You can however buy cosmetic skins if you feel like it. Also the advertised "Hunting Season"-Pack is a PREORDER for the next 4 hunters yet to come. Even if you decide not to buy the next 4 hunters when they come out, you will be able to play with and against others who own the content, so the community won't be split like in Battlefield (future maps will always be free btw!).
