I would recommend watching some of the better Evolve players out there (such as maniacsquirrel or sacriel) to get an idea of how this game plays at a high level.  Its main problem is playing with new players who don't know how to play classes to the best of their ability, since if even a single hunter is not on top of their game, a good monster player will dominate.  When played skillfully, with other skilled players, Evolve is a gem.  Intense battles are scattered throughout tense chases, and most of the time, wins feel deserved rather than luck of the draw.  Communication is key, but not necessarily vocal communication, as some of the best matches I've played have been silent, with each hunter focused on the task at hand of finding the monster, or dealing damage while avoiding the monster's flailing limbs and special abilities.  Watch the basic and advanced hunter tutorial videos in the extras menu to gain an understanding of how each unique hunter plays before jumping into multiplayer, and you'll be far ahead of most of the gamers who jump in and expect to bunny hop around the map and Leroy Jenkins the monster to death.  This is a simple game with impossible depth, and giving it just a cursory look isn't enough.  If you're not sold, watch the streams, and pay attention.  And if you purchase it, realize that you've got a learning curve ahead of you, but the accomplishment you feel after gaining some semblance of skill is astonishing, and well worth $60.

This game has a lot of mixed reviews, so in the interest of helping out the undecided, here is a basic review of the current pros and cons. I am recommending the game and I feel the pros out weigh the cons fairly significantly if you are a fan 4 v 1 and hunt games.
First the pros:
The balancing is pretty good, niether side ever feels like they are absolutely the hunter and not the hunted.
The classes are well thought out and each character has unique strengths and weakness's even within their own class, so nobody feels like just a reskin of a previous character.
The rounds are always pretty action packed, if you get into the hunt in games then you will feel the adrenalin pumping.
The game looks nice and the sound design matches everything well.
The modes and characters are all failry easy to learn, but require skill to master.
Even without DLC there is a ton of continuous play value.
Most importantly in my opinion, the game requires you to think on your feet and make split second decisions. It takes thought and skill to get good, there is no spam to win class.
Now for the negatives (some of these will likely be subject to change as patches come out) note: none of these make the game unplayable.
The match maker is buggy, especially if you are trying to find a match while platooned with one or more friend. Some times it will kick your friend, or make one of you the monster despite the monster slot being closed when you are platooned. (this doesn't happen a lot, but enough to be worth mentioning.)
Even if your machine more than meets recommended specs, high graphics settings seem to cause the cutseens to lag and some in game lag. Might be an issue with optimization. The game look really nice even on low settings so it's not a huge hit.
No ingame video replays, or in game means of saving them.
The game is heavily geared towards the sale of DLC, (however if you have no issue with playing the characters that come with the game, then you don't miss out any game modes or maps.)
Currently the number of modes is rather limitied. Just skirmish and evacuation. Skirmish is what you think it is. Evacuation is 5 battles, the first one is always a standard hunt and the last is always a defence/ assault depending if you are the hunter or monster, and the other 3 battle could be hunt ( kill the monster), nest (destroy all 6 monster eggs/ minions, rescue (revive survivors and get 6 of them safely evaced). Different maps offer different bonuses to whomever wins. This mode also has a balance system which gives the side with the least wins a damage buff.
The character audio gets a little repetetive (you do get hints at the story in the dialog, and the first time you hear a particular conversation it is usually pretty good.)

Reigns is a decision-making game. Each card is a choice between A and B, and which one you choose will usually affect your four stats (Religion, People, Army, and Wealth) and can often have a longer-lasting effect when other cards reference back to the decision you made.
At least in theory. You can in fact see the effects of your past decisions, but the truth is that it feels like the RNG has a much bigger influence on the game than any decision you make. This is especially true in the Fencing and Dungeon minigames that occasionally pop up. And then in order to progress the meta-game forward, you have to make certain decisions on certain cards (e.g., "Meet the clumsy prophet"), but often those cards give you almost no hint as to which decision to make to accomplish the objective.
I'm not against games that are brutally punishing, where your character dies frequently, but they still have to be a GAME in the first place. I'd hardly call Reigns a game; I feel like I'd be exactly as successful if I made every card decision by flipping a coin.

The first two seasons of Sam and Max are among the best adventure games I've ever played -- great puzzles, hilarious writing, musical numbers, and the unmistakeable signs of psychopathy. The third is... unfortunate, but still worth it. The level of detail drops significantly, presumably so they could focus on implementing Max's new psychic powers, and the interface is overhauled but ends up worse than the original. And the humour changes, dipping into a little bit of sentimentalism which the real humour of Sam and Max scrupulously avoids (even so, the third season's climax hits the right buttons). They removed the ability to indiscriminately shoot objects, the minigames, and a lot of the funny but irrelevant comments that result from examining the decor. The thing is, you'll get stuck pretty often, and all those things they remove in S03 helped make even being stuck a fun experience. Still, the third season has some great moments; one of my favourites was the Phoenix Wright-esque interrogation sequences at the start of 304. So buy the first two seasons and see if you just can't get enough, or if you're already a big Sam and Max fan, buy the complete Sam and Max right away.

My friend and I start up a private server, and these are our (mainly mine) moments caught through the eyes of my character in a journal I made in-game. His name was Mordeci Flents.
Day 1
"I don't know what is happening. everyone has gone.. mad, attacking on sight. I found this journal and decided to write in it every now and then, just to ease the boredom."
Day 3
"i've been traveling from house to house, scavenging for food and avoiding those things. I haven't came accross any other survivors, could i be the only one left? I'll have to keep moving east until Im out of Muldraugh."
Day 10
"Damn window. I guess its my fault for not better equiping myself for the broken glass, now I got a scratch on my left hand and a large shard of glass in my forearm. God I hope i can find the supplies i'll going to need soon... I feel like i've already lost too much blood."
Day 11
"I stumbled accross Cortman Medical and was able to find the supplies but thats not the only bit of good news. I met a man named Scotty that was also scavenging Cortman Medical. At first, he was hesitant to allow me to group with him but I told him that I was a skilled carpenter and I could help with building any fortifications down the road. He's leading me back to his 'safehouse', said it'd take a couple days or so."
Day 14
"We were stopped by a horde moving through the previous day so we held up in a house but we've made it to Scotty's 'safehouse'. It was just a simple little house with a large wooden fence around it. Scotty then told me where everything was stored and said the next day he was going to go scavenge for more food and told me to work on whatever I could to improve our defence."
Day 15
"Well, Scotty went out to get more food but I've been hard at work building walls and cutting trees down. In one day i was able to get a large segment of the outer wall done and tomorrow I'm gonna start working on building actualy structures. I feel like I'm experienced enough now.
Day 16
"A few of the Zombies were banging on the doors to our compound today. I was able to dispatch them with ease with my hammer but I worry that my continued building will attract even more.."
Day 17
"Scotty returned with a large bundle of food and informed me off where the hordes were the thickest. said to the North and West were the highest points. The rest of the day we both worked on our houses. I started building the upstairs but ran into a bit of a snag... or fell into. I fell from the second floor and fractured my foot. I splinted it but I don't know how long i'll be out of building, or fighting. I rest now, and Scotty leaves again tomorrow for West Point, in search of supplies."

Day 22
"I havent been able to do much therefore I havent wrote much. This fracture slows my movement to where I'm at a crawl. Luckily, we had plenty of painkillers from Cortman Medical so I'm doped up good. Scotty hasn't returned yet, its been a few days."
Day 24
"Scotty finally returned but he had a huge chunk missing from his leg. He said he was scavenging a house when he ran into a zombie in one of the rooms, he killed it but the fighting attracted a nearby horde and while escaping one got a bite out of him. He told me that he has seen other be biten and not survive long."
Day 25
"Scotty's wound didn't look any better the next day, he handed me his shotgun and asked me to mercy kill him, for the sake of not turning. I tried to tell him there had to be a way but he had made his mind up..."
Day 26
"The blast echoes in my ears. I am alone again. I went about moving the corspe outside to the burn pile but it was difficult with my fractured foot. After disposing of the body. I noticed something moving up the road and quickly returned inside. Moment later I hear bangs on the doors, the Mercy kill attracted a small horde to the compound, and I couldnt fight with my fractue and ironically, the shell I used on Scotty was his last one.. I hid in the best spot i could think of and waited.... with the sounds banging in the background... Will I survive another day in this 'new world'?"
Unfortunately I recently build a computer and the entire time up to day 26 was played on my laptop and when i began again on our server I lost my save of Mordeci, but after I wrote that last entry, I was saved by my friend respawning as another person and planned to incorporate more into the story but since that was the last entry and when i began a new character, I lost the journal and never got to add anymore entries.
10/10 would write a journal again.

I could not run to save my life so I decided to stay home and work on building my fort and finish the renovations I have started. Luckily I had already rid myself of the pestering neighbors so I can do my work in peace. phew~
It took about 3 weeks until I was able to run again. Another 7 days until my fracture was healed and my fort completed. Was a flippin sweet day!
On that same night I had just finished setting up my farm when I heard some crackling behind the walls.
I had left the stove on.
The flames escalated rather quickly. (note to future zomboid players: please remember to turn your appliances off)
Gathered all of my food and what percious loot I could carry and got the hell out of there. Before running off I had to look back at my beautiful fort with deep remorse (why didn't I turn that damn stove off!?). My home was completely engulfed in flames, my crops were burning. It was just terrible. Terrible.
So I ran for it.
Or more like fast paste walking. I had to drop my backpack with the thought that I will return to retrieve it.
Decided to retreat to a werehouse I had cleared out. Barricaded the entire frist floor so to get out I had to go down the rope ladder I had instaled on the second floor... Was a plan that usually worked for me until I went out the wrong window without thinking.
Fratured my leg again. I can not run again. There is a horde south of me and all it will take is a helicopter for them to come storm the place. But, I will not give up! I will survive!
So potential buyers!

Honestly, when I first heard about this game and saw it in action, I was thrilled by it. However, now that I got my hands on it and got to play it, I came to the quick realization that while the idea was sound on paper, in reality it is anything but.
Aside the DLC fiasco that's been all over the internet, my main problem with the game is that it doesn't feel any fun. As a hunter you spend most of the time just running around with nothing happening, while as a monster you jump around and eat other animals - playing hide 'n seek - until you hit level 3 and completely crush the hunters. The level of skill it takes to be good monster player is insanely low compared to being an average hunter, which requires good coordination, situational awareness, and constant communication between your team-mates. If you start playing with a team of hunters, prepare to lose - a lot - before you get your skills up high enough to challenge a good (or even an average) monster player. This game requires insane amount of patience to become good at, and I'm afraid not too many - myself included - simply do not have that kind of patience.
Yes, I'm aware that there are videos of players who are completely dominating as hunters, but you can tell they're good at it. I mean really, really good at it. For an average person who works for 32 hours a week, sleeps 8 hours a day, and has other hobbies/duties aside playing video games, attaining that level of skill is simply not plausible in a week or so.
Co-op games succeed only if they're fun to play, and this unfortunately just doesn't feel fun. At all. It just boring, whether I'm playing as a monster or a hunter. I feel like I'm playing Final Fantasy 13 of First Person Shooters.
So no, I'm not recommending this game to anyone. And I feel sorry because I was really looking towards to this game six months ago.

Red Orchestra 2, or RO2, is an amazing game. It is, by far, my favourite shooter, because of its stunning grahpics, amazing visual effects, and great audio. It also stays true to the historical events of WW2, and is set around 1941, during Operation Barbarossa, with Soviet Soldiers clashing with the German invaders. The game also features vehical combat, which is a nice touch. There is a large ammount of weapons in the game, too, which are, for the most part, well-balanced. The majority of the maps in the game are quite vast and open, save for a few close-quarters combat maps. Red Orchestra 2 is all about tactics. The Team Leader is a key asset to every team, as he can call in artillery strikes and recon planes. Squad Leaders are important because they are a mobile spawn point for any player of the team. Riflemen and submachine gunners are the main fighting force for either side. Marksmen usually hide in bushes like the cykas they are and pick off enemies from a distance. And engineers can stop a tank in its tracks. But every class plays a key role in leading their team to victory.
In summary, Red Orchestra 2 is a phenomenal game with a few minor flaws that are made up for by the amazing gameplay, visuals, audio effects, and realism. It's a great game, and anyone who hasn't played it should give it a try.
PS, if you're a rookie player, be sure to have a keen eye, or you'll get shot by some unnatural force that you cannot see.
PS again, Soviets have the best rifle in the game and Germans have the best SMG.

Oh Lucasarts where did you go?
This game, which is basically a spiritual successor to Star Wars Rebellion (which I unfortunately have never played because it apparently doesn't work on Windows 7...) is probably my favorite Star Wars game and definitely one of my favorite real time strategies too.
This thing has got EVERYTHING, and if you get ANY of the decent mods, the quality goes up through the roof (it already was touching the ceiling with having all the lovely super weapons the empire can build, like the Super Star Destroyer and the 2nd Death Star) - only for Forces of Corruption though.
The original is still great though. The ability to play both the Rebels AND the Empire and even start before the Battle of Yavin is amazing, and in fully voice-acted and fleshed out campaigns too? As M. Bison would say: YES! YES!
The ground combat is kinda silly, but it's epic. Darth Vader, Luke, Obi-Wan, Yoda (yes Yoda) and the Emperor himself can lead swarms of rebel troopers, AT-ATs and everything else in between in huge clashes that take place on many different worlds, most of which are actually from the Expanded Universe (but don't worry, the originals like Hoth, Tatooine, Endor and Naboo are still there and even have the proper indigenous peoples as well).
The Space Combat is where this game really shines though. Despite the lack of "technically" 3-D combat, it still manages to hold up really well after 10 or so years.
The Death Star II has a big role to play in the space combat by the way (I think you can probably guess how).
I didn't even mention the Zann Consortium did I?
The Zann Consortium is only available in Forces of Corruption, but they have their own campaign (which has some ups and downs and kind of a meh ending, but is still fun) and basically are the cooler version of the Black Sun Pirates (yes even Xizor makes an appearance from Shadows of the Empire). So does Thrawn...and IG-88...and Bossk...and Jabba the Hutt.
White-haired Tyber Zann and his wannabe Jedi (but not really) alien partner Urai Fen try to build up their criminal enterprise after losing virtually everything when Tyber gets captured in the tutorial, and they do this through two ways: One, the conventional way, CONQUERING EVERYTHING IN SIGHT, and Two, the more interesting way, Corruption.
The way this new game mechanic works is that it will basically "corrupt" the planet that it is executed on (which usually involves doing a specialized ground or space mission) and give you extra special bonuses from holding the planet.
This can come in the form of just extra credits, or even being able to build ships that the faction's planet that you corrupted build!
I'm not sure if you can build Star Destroyers because that would be a little OP, but considering that the ENTIRE CONSORTIUM is OP, from their massive canderous death tanks that slaughter AT-ATs to their Mandalorian capital ships and specialized capital ships that shoot GIANT BEAMS OF DEATH, getting the half-finished Eclipse at the end just seals the deal.
By the way, the Eclipse had a scaled down superlaser, that was a little less powerful than the Death Star's.
On the other hand, it shoots faster, and kills any ship it hits instantly (just like the Death Star II), so that's always a nice plus.
10/10
P.S. I know you're probably getting tired of seeing these P.S.'s but I'm DOING EM ANYWAY.
Anyway, the P.S. I had to say here is that if we ever get an RTS that is star-wars themed, you should always think of this before you make the decision of whether to buy it or not. If it's not any better than this, don't bother. Just play this. The modding community is VERY active.
Some mods I recommend (mostly for Forces of Corruption):
Ultimate Empire at War (it's inactive, but a lot of work was done on it and it's a solid mod)
Thrawn's Revenge (haven't actually played this one, but it looks very, very good)
Awakening of the Rebellion (made by a German team oddly enough, has had a lot of updates and even has some story to it - unfortunately the voice acting's only in German, but it's great, and the combat is vastly improved on the realism front).

Limbo is a puzzle platforming indie game from 2010 where you play as a boy traversing some sort of spooky landscape, who and where you are never really explained, but many people have given their two cents on what it all means.  It is a game that was released to almost universal acclaim and one that is often used as an example to show how videogames can be art.  You see, above being a platformer or a puzzle game, Limbo is trying to be an experience, and as such has had great effort put into the art design.  The first thing that struck me about the game is the monochrome grainy look, which combined with some stellar sound design reminds me of David Lynch's film Eraserhead.  The game looks great beyond the aforementioned visual style, the boy as well as the other inhabitants of the strange world are well animated, backgrounds are detailed and multilayered, and lighting is well utilized to create a game with fantastic visuals.
Unfortunately, this is where my praise for the game end, and where the problems begin, play dead nailed that experience part of the game, but the actual game part of Limbo leaves much to be desired.  The bulk of the game is spent on the puzzles, which though are serviceable, are nothing great.  Limbo is a mechanically simple game; you can walk, jump (though not very high), climb ladders and ropes, push and pull objects, and activate certain mechanisms.  As such, many of the puzzles are simple in design, and do not require much effort to solve.  Most of them are some variation of moving objects to climb a ledge/ cross a pit, or moving an object to avoid some sort of hazard.  Things get a bit more interesting near the end when machines are introduced which activate magnets, or alter gravity, but even these puzzles feel barebones and easy.  What is annoying however is that many of the puzzles (especially near the end) rely more on precise timing as opposed to problem solving, the result are puzzles which can be solved quickly, but take several more minutes trying over and over to get just right (one puzzle involving a ladder on wheels and a ramp struck me as especially bad).  Additionally, some puzzles have hazards that you could not have realistically saw coming (also worth noting that everything in Limbo kills you in one hit).  Although death really only sets you back to the start of the puzzle you're on (no lives exist, so you can die as much as you want) because many rely on slow mechanisms, having to start a puzzle from start because of a cheap death feels grating.  An example of this is early on where you see a large piston on the ceiling, and a pressure plate under it.  Obviously, most players will be expecting a trap at this point, so you want to avoid the plate.  After this you come across another piston and another plate, but this piston will only not crush you if you land on the plate.  What sense this makes is beyond me, and the end result is a “gotch’ya” death which is unfortunately all too common in this game.
Lackluster puzzles would be fine if the "experience" side of Limbo was better, but this side is flawed as well.  The game is trying to be scary (at least I think it is, it is tagged as horror anyway) but I was never once scared, or even tense.  The game kills you far too much, and often through no fault of the player, that when the "scary" bits happen, they just feel like another hazard that the game is throwing at you.  The game is also too liner and scripted for anything to be scary, as real horror cannot exist unless the events feel spontaneous (which they never do).  In terms of the story, well there is no story.  You are a kid, and you must go right to progress.  No characters, only a few cut scenes, no dialogue, and virtually no explanation of anything.  The best theory I could find is that
but even this is pretty skimpy premise to base an experience on.  The game often felt as if it was trying too hard to shock or disturb me with all of its elaborate death animations.  Over the course of the journey, the kid you play as will be crushed, disemboweled, electrocuted, impaled, drowned and shoot, yet the game kills you so often that none of it carries any weight, and is more likely to  come off as manipulative and try hard.  Beyond this, the game is paced poorly.  Without a good story (or any story) to hold the gme together, it all just feels like a series of things that happen, until it ends an abrupt and unsatisfying ending.  The game never builds to anything, and it felt like these areas could have been arranged in any order without anything being lost, for example, the spider you fight is probably the most effective part in the game, and it is at the beginning of the game.  I would expect a horror game like this to get more disturbing as it progresses, but if anything, Limbo gets more tame.  The swamps and forests of the early game have a real grit and grotesqueness to them.  The latter portions of the game take place mostly in generic urban/factory settings that feel like they could have been from any game.  It's such a shame to see such good and unique art direction wasted on levels that feel so "videogamey".
Lastly, I should mention the game's length, and how it only took me about 200 minutes to beat it.  The game is also extremely liner so there is not much point in replaying it unless you want to find the hidden collectables (which don't do anything beyond give you achievements).  Honestly, I usually wouldn’t mind paying ten or twenty dollars for a game that's over in a few hours as long as it is good, I mean portal and Braid were short, and those are some of my favorite games ever, but Limbo just doesn’t have anything too memorable in it.  My point is I don’t oppose paying $10 for a short game; I oppose paying $10 for a game that isn't very good
So that’s just about it.  I know I was mostly negative in this review, but the game wasn't horrible, hell, I probably wouldn't even call it bad, just disappointing after I finally played it after years of hearing people rave about it.  If I had to give it a rating, I would say 2/5.  This dev team made a more recent and much better game called Inside which is very similar to this (a stylish horror puzzle platformer where you play as a kid in a spooky world).  Though Inside doesn't fix all the problems of its predecessor (cheep, often gratuitous deaths, fairly simple puzzles) it is a far better experience.  Unlike Limbo, Inside has setting that is fully realized, an actual story with themes and ideas, and it is a game which actually builds and builds as it progresses and then delivers with a memorable climax.  So yeah, if you're interested in Limbo, play Inside first, and if you are still interested, try to grab Limbo when it is on sale or free.  I simply cannot recommend buying this game at full price.

Chroma Squad is unexpectedly genius in its design. I came into this game with very low expectations, having not followed the kickstarter at all and getting the game as part of a massive bundle with other games. But the premise of the game, which is that you're not just trying to defeat the enemies, but defeat the enemies in ways that increases views for your show, makes the game actually really fun. All the things that usually seem tedious in tactical RPGs, repositioning units and maneuvering, here are all part of the 'show' and often get you views on their own. Beyond that, the teamwork function, giving increased mobility to allied units and also setting up high damage combos, means that individual units being out of position can still often have functionality. I've only gotten through "Season 1" but for someone that does not have a fixation on the tokusatsu genre (and really never has), I found this a surprisingly satisfying tactical RPG. It's fundamentally a good game, and that it's also charming and ripe with in-jokes is really just a perk.

TL;DR: Fun, Simple Time-Waster.
Buy this.
Longer Version:
---------------
You get a lot for what you pay in this game. It's a simple decision-making, almost text-based game.
Graphics: I enjoy the art style in this game, it is simple and unique, interesting to look at, but not distracting. Very easy to run even on low-spec systems.
Audio: The soundtrack and sound effects are are good and do their job, but are not over-the-top. I enjoy the soundtrack, it fits the theme and the sound effects are satisfying.
Gameplay: The gameplay is very simple. Your kingdom has 4 core systems: The Church, The People, The Army, and The Bank. It is your job to balance out these 4 aspects of your kingdom, without letting any of them get too far to either extreme, high or low.
To do this, you are given a short bit of text and a portrait of who you are speaking to and must make a choice by clicking on 1 of 2 possible options. These choices will affect your kingdom's 4 core systems, and while you can see how big of an effect the choice will have, you are not shown for sure whether it will make the part of your kindgom better or worse. Many times, you can guess this, however. For example, saying "Yes" to building a new church will increase The Church, and decrease The Bank.
If any of the 4 aspects gets too high or low, you will be dethroned/decapitated/exiled/burned at the stake, etc etc, which will lead to the end of your reign. But it's OK, that's why this game is called ReignS, not just Reign. You take control of the next leader of the country and begin a new reign, and things like advisors you hired or people added to your court will persist. This game is a randomly-generated, persistant, perma-death game, and it requires little skill/practice to play. The repetitive clicking left or right is broken up by unique events that happen, such as being cursed, a famine, getting lost in your own dungeon, meeting the devil, being sieged, and more.
Conclusion:
I enjoy this game and usually play it when I have anywhere from 5 minutes to an hour to burn and I just want to kick back and relax and play a no-stress, interesting, fun game that requires little effort.
For the price, I would definitely recommend buying this game. It has so many cool little things that occur that keep me entertained and interested.

This is one of the most fun turn-based games I've played in a while. The idea of pandering each hero pandering to the audience by taking certain actions (along with "dramatic" optional objectives) to rack up points while you fight is great fun in concept, and breathes a bit of life into combat. The focus on using "teamwork" to launch people through the air and perform combo attacks is also very fun and helps sell the feel they're going for. Each party member feels very different and can be built several ways, and skills feel varied and useful. The humor is also top-notch and lends to a light-hearted but entertaining story.
Other pluses: It's quite long and has multiple endings, and also multiple actors to pick from. There's also great music and good pixel art. And lots of good jokes.
It's not perfect though. The audience system, despite being a central mechanic, isn't fully explained in-game (specifically which actions each person can perform to earn points, what effect death has, how much director's instructions are worth, and whether the mecha battles affect it). On some particularly easy levels (or levels with nigh-impossible director instructions) it can also lead to you wasting turns farming audience to max it out (which could have been mitigated a lot if it told you how much each director instruction is worth).
Also, the difficulty curve is backwards; the first season is the hardest because you have very few skills, and in the last few missions your heroes are ridiculously durable if you have the best available equipment. It's probably balanced towards you NOT maxing out your audience every level, but perfectionists will almost always do that. Still doesn't keep it from being fun though.
Those are small complaints though. By the time you notice those problems you should already be hooked. I'd definitely recommend this game.

Although it may not be important for some, I originally got this game after playing the PS3 demo hoping to add it to the list of low spec games playable on my netbook. Linux users please note that Limbo will not run on the GMA3150 included with most netbooks, and likely laptops or computers using the same on board graphics, even with OpenGL 2.1 support enabled.
Nonetheless the game runs beautifully on my main computer. The puzzles in game are interesting, but not too complicated, making it a nice casual platformer. Checkpoints (or "chapters" in game) save after most puzzles, so if you die you never have to backtrack too far.
Overall if you're looking for a casual platformer with a dark atmosphere, I'd highly recommend this game, albeit with the caveat that Linux users should be aware that it may not run at all on older hardware.
For those who've played the demo and are wondering if the full version is much better, I can say that the game only gets more interesting once you've passed the demo section.

If you’re not sure what the game Broforce is, then I suggest you go read my review for that game to familiarize yourself. If you can’t be arsed to do so, I’ll give you a quick run-down right now. Broforce is an action game, drawing heavy influence from Contra, where you play as various action heroes, as you fight the forces of evil with the power of machine guns and grenades. Got it? Yes? Good.
So, what exactly is The Exendabros then? It’s a, I suppose you could call it a spin-off of Broforce, though I’m not sure that’s entirely accurate. It plays the same as Broforce, but instead of featuring the bros from that game, this game’s bros are based on The Exendabros, and the game does spend some time advertising for the movie. Of course, an interactive advertisement that lets you shoot things and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up is far from the worst type of advertisement. Another way to look at the game (and the view I prefer to take) is that it serves as a short demo for Broforce if you’re not if you’re sold on the game, or as another shot of the testosterone fueled action if you need a bit more after completing Broforce.
As for the bros in the game (and I’ll confess I’ve not yet seen The Expendabros, so I can’t comment too much on the characters) are unique bros compared to the full Broforce game, but the way they play isn’t entirely unique. You have some repeat weapons, though they’re paired with a different special weapon than the character that wields it in Broforce. But again, some of the special weapons are also repeats. Thankfully, there are a few new ones too, but they aren’t as thrilling as many of your offensive choices available in Broforce, or even as much as some of the repeat weapons featured in The Expendabros.
The game itself is very short, and it’ll probably only take you an hour, at most to complete it. I ran through it in 45 minutes myself.
All in all though, it’s not the greatest game ever, and it doesn’t live up to the actual Broforce game. But it is free, and it’s not a bad way to kill an hour, but it’s by no means a must have. If you dig it, then make sure to give Broforce a change. Hell, give Broforce a chance even you you aren’t feeling this one, as it’s a lot of fun.

First off I want to say that I don't really play the single player of this game, so the review is based entirely on multiplay.
I personally love playing this game with friends... it's the only multiplayer zombie survival game I've come across that I've enjoyed.  It's incredibly simple, yet incredibly complicated at the same time.  Don't expect to just jump in the game and do well... the wiki is an incredibly valued resource that you will need to read over at least once.  I'll also mention that this is an early access game, but doesn't play like one.  Far too often we see games launch as early access which are barely playable... project zomboid however is wonderful.  Take note devs... this is how you early access.
What really caused me to love this game was that they actually managed to get zombies right.  Far too often do zombie games have overpowered, super monsters.  Zombies are slow, stupid, and easy to kill... their danger comes in their numbers... this is something almost every piece in zombie related media screws up.  Project zomboid nails it though.  Suburbs have fewer zombies than cities, and a city has the number you would expect (note: it's a lot).
The game very accurately lets you feel what it would be like to be an ordinary person thrust deep into a zombie apocalypse... think you'd be able to survive? Think again.  I strongly recommend this game to people (at least if you have friends to play with... I've heard a lot of complaints about single player not being nearly as entertaining).  The greatest thing the creators of this game did was give you the option to modify the world.  You can alter how long it takes for the electricity and water to turn off, how sparse loot is, how many zombies there are, experience multipliers, whether or not loot respawns, how quick zombies are... all of it.  You can really try out all sorts of scenarios.  And how easily the game is modded... this allows a lot of user generated content to enhance the experience.
Cons of the game:
- Combat takes a little bit to get used to and can be frustrating to newcomers.  It's a shame, but practice and I guarantee you'll get over it.
- The zombie virus infection rate can't be altered.  Currently it's 96% infection rate on a bite, and 25% on a scratch.  I'd love to see these numbers be customizable to the server (personally I'd love 100% bite and 0% scratch)... but I think them adding this feature would improve the game drastically
- There is no in game map.  You would think if you lived in a city you would know your way around it... unfortunately you have to figure this out for yourself.  There is a map online, but I think either having a map option or adding a map as a rare loot would be a wonderful addition.
- Multiplay can be tough to set up at first... especially if you need to port forward.  I would love to see them implement some form of steam assisted multiplayer setup including "Invite to Game" option.
- [EDIT: THIS HAS BEEN FIXED] Having items with durability or that are equipped that stack in your inventory can cause issues.  When you want to drop one but can't specify which one you can spend a bit of time fumbling.  Nothing is worse when you're running from zombies, but carrying too much weight so you decide you want to drop your second baseball bat, only to find that you dropped the one you had equipped and now you have no weapon equipped to defend yourself.  And I can't tell you how many times I've chosen to rip a spare shirt into bandages only for my character to disrobe and rip the one he's wearing instead.
The cons seem many and the pros seem few, but I assure you they aren't... that's just my inability to articulate properly.  The game is really enjoyable and I recommend it to everyone.  The pricetag is a little high in my opinion, but still a wonderful game to pick up.

I would recommend you play this while in an introspective mood, though, in order to get a fuller experience.
The game itself does wonders with its aging engine, creating vignette-like games of often startling beauty.  Wreden's narration is masterful, and is on a similar level of quality as the narrator of the Stanley Parable, though the two games are quite different in tone.  Both are extremely meta analyses of gaming, but while the Stanley Parable is at heart a comedy the Beginner's Guide is more melancholic and has a gravitas all its own.
10/10.  Would recommend to anyone who has ever spent any time thinking about the games they play.

This is easily one of the best games I've ever played. Everyone seems to be complaining about the optional DLC rather than discussing if the game is actually worth your money. I'll make it easy for you. Do you like Left 4 Dead 2's versus mode? Are you tired of the same symmetrical FPS? Do you enjoy games that actually require team work? Do you want a game that you can play by yourself, against human opponents and still have a satisfying experience without the hassle of low skill teammates? If you answered yes to any of those questions, buy this game.
Regarding the DLC, if you feel compelled to have every colorization possible for your monsters and your hunter's guns, then you're going to spend some money. These skins do not add anything extra to the game play experience. It would have been nice if the skins were unlockable through gameplay, but they aren't. Will I ever be able to walk around with a baby poop green Goliath? No, I won't. I will not spend $7 to have my monsters recolored. THIS DECISION IN NO WAY REDUCES THE AMOUNT OF ENJOYMENT I GET FROM THE GAME BECAUSE I AM A REASONABLE ADULT. If logic and my rational disposition fail to persuade you, you should believe me, and think the same way as I do because I wrote that all in caps.
The fact that this game has "mixed" reviews at the moment is a shame. This game is fresh, difficult, and a ton of fun. I look forward to throwing my money at 2K and Turtle Rock when they come out with DLC that will have a material impact on my enjoyment of the game (hunters and monsters), but until then I will enjoy the fact that I paid money for a product that had a clear disclosure of the contents rather than whine about not being able to treat my hunter's hue like a mood ring without a larger investment.
Again, buy this game.

Another lackluster console port to PCs.
Even before you get into "The Game" you've got a bunch of unskippable videos of company logos to go through, before you get to the intro video that is skippable if you hover over the press the awkwardly placed "skip" button.  When you do that you're treated to...additional loading before you get to the actual menu.
From here, you have an awkward console-ported to PC interface.  You know the kind where the mouse feels like it downed about 10 shots of Jager before the game.  It's not smooth, it's quicker in some directions than in others, it's not enough to merely place the cursor over the button you want to press, but you have to find the "sweet spot" to actually activate it (because someone spent all of 4 seconds doing a sloppy conversion from gamepad to mouse interface).  All that's when you're lucky enough for the cursor to even show up, which is a fairly common problem (judging from my experience and a lot of other reviews).
This shows the general level of polish the game has.
The match making is horrendous.  It takes about 5-10 mins to find a match.  I think I've only started a match from the beginning two out of the fifteen or so rounds I've played.  More likely than not you'll end up getting dumped into a game midstream, usually because someone left, and that side is getting its butt kicked.  i.e. you're a first-stage monster stuck in an arena with 20% of your health left, or you port into a dead guy watching the one last surviving teammate getting pummeled by the monster.  It's very confusing because it's often a character you'll have no experience how to use ...and I still don't know every time I'm the monster the skills are different/inconsistent (perhaps this mystery would be solved if I got to start a match for once).
Theoretically the group stays together for another round, but all I get is a screen that says "waiting for players to load" or some such for eternity.  Well, ok, I've never waited longer than about 25 minutes before finally exitting out (for which you are penalized for doing so by the way).
In the even that you get to play the game for longer than 30 seconds before it's game over (and an infinite wait screen) you'll find the usual problem.  If your a hunter, your teammates suck.  Trackers think they're assault and don't use tethering or arena skills, healers think they're assault and only use their offensive weapon without ever healing, support think's it's assault and only uses its offensive weapon, and assault...well, those guys usually do ok.  I suppose this can't really be blamed on the game...that's just the nature of pickup groups on the internet.
Perhaps in general most of the above problem can be avoided if you can manage to group up with some friends before embarking on the game.  If you were hoping to drop into a group of unknowns...well: I wouldn't recommend it.
Additionally, there are other issues with the structure of the game.  It appears to be setup for a rather long grind.  each class type only has one character available initially.  You have to acquire so many points with the different skills to unlock to the next hunter in that class.  Perhaps it goes quicker if you can start a match from the beginning, but at my "join game in progress for 30 seconds before its over" pace, it would likely take me 40-50 hrs to unlock another character.
You can read any of the other 10,000 negative reviews griping about the DLC issues with the game as well.  I'm sure at least one of them has expressed the issues with that more eloqently than I could.

Posting my Heroes of the West Review here because according to Steam, I've only played one minute of it(?).
Really well-done and thought through mod. I'm in love with the British faction.
Pros -
+ British Faction w/classic WW2 British arms (Lee Enfield, Bren, Sten etc)
+ Expanded German Arsenal (Gewehr 43, Browning Hi-Power)
+ 4 New Maps
+ Really good textures
+ Fun, refreshing
+ Instant LVL 50 on all guns on the mod (can't tell whether I like this or not yet)
Cons (A bit nitpicky but it's all in good nature) -
+ Browning Hi-Power needs to be less block-y. I suggest retexturing the 1911 and making some slide and handle changes, since this is what John Browning basically did to this gun.
+ Omaha Beach needs balancing on the beach head on the first two objectives
+ The wait times between spawning and arriving on Omaha Beach as the Allies needs shorting by at least 2/3rds of the length
+ The spawns need bringing a LOT closer to the objectives
+ MORE BRITISH MAPS
+ Minor object changes - put in some cover to make maps more attacker-sided.
Overall this is a really great mod with a few bad things that even AAA game designers get wrong on release so don't be put off by those. Regardless, these things still need to be changed to compete with the original game's content. In the wait for Rising Storm II, this mod has DEFINITELY increased this game's lifespan for me and I'll be playing a lot more of it. I hope the developers read my review and take these things into account because this mod has amazing potential.

Full Impressions:

There is a big misconception about the game being pay to win. Definitely disagree. You can farm your way up to be #1 easily. It's pay to speed up, not to win. I played many mmorpg's over the years. None that i liked as much as metin. Game has an amazing feel to it. And i'd still recommend for everyone to start and/or atleast give it a go. Learn the basics of it and then judge it.
This game is very unique. It has a skill system like no other. Simple and crazy good. Every single skill can be upgraded to be 5x stronger than the basic. It's item system was ahead of it's time as well, many games coppied it later on, upgrading items from +0 to +9(I believe it was first created in metin - Correct me if i'm wrong, but i believe i'm not.). PVE is insanely enjoyable, 1 against a 100. Massive mob killing sprees. PVP: Basically in other games the only way to be strong if you're max level for PVP... NOT THE CASE HERE! There can be a lvl 30 character stronger than 80. How? If you developed your skills, and if you got very strong gear. You can easily fight against people that are way above your level. This is a game where you can create your 1 man army character. 1 man with very good pvp gear can kill a dozen of other! Item progression reaches much much further than many other mmorpg's. The whole world has open PVP, almost every single spot anywhere. There are few safe zones in cities, and that's it. You can litteraly attack anyone anywhere. All you have to do is go to options click two times, and that's it!. There are definitely many more things that make this game stick out, and that are unique but i won't list them all. Now tell me this isn't worth giving a go. Peace out.. Even fishing is fun!

Black Rose is one of the best horror games around. You play as Linda, a curious and mysterious girl who tries to find the disappearances of the people that lived in the old funeral home. Throughout the game, you search around for secrets, hints, and items that are scattered throughout the funeral home to help you find the mysteries of this haunted place. Later in the game, you encounter Myrtle and Sullivan, who are enemies that will chase you throughout the funeral home until you are dead. The story is presented well, with a vast amount of characters and bios about them. There are two modes to play with, timed and story mode, which bring players the option to play easier and harder modes and to get your best times. You can also get high scores and compete with other players, which brings a score addicting factor into hand. The game is one of the most scariest games I've ever seen, with the death animations, music, and atmosphere that really defines what a horror game is. The graphics are textures are amazing, the soundtrack is catchy for scare standards, and there are even multiple endings. In conclusion, Black Rose is a amazing horror game that brings a lot of content for a free game and will keep you on the top of your feet for hours.

)Go to the near bottom for pro's and con's) This may be the best early access game i've seen.
First off, you could sell this game as it is for about $20 and i don't think people would absolutely hate it.
To give you a rundown of the game, it's basically like this: You are a plane crash survivor, you wake up after said crash to see your son being taken away by some pale man. Then you have to gather materials and build a base aswell as defend it from cannibals (Which are very creepy and have very interesting A.I when you first play the game) the crafting system is pretty typical but collecting wood (or logs) from trees is alot better than most games, you chop down the tree and it turns into logs.
Then, you have to carry the logs back to your base to build onto it, you can build a log cart to carry more aswell.
So now, for those of you who don't wanna read a review and just want the pros and cons, here you go.
Pros
-A game with a pretty nice crafting library, when this game is done you can bet it'll have huge amounts of recipes.
-Very different and unique building system, you don't just punch or axe a tree and get wood in your invetory, you chop it down, then you carry the logs back to your structure in order to continue adding onto it.
-Building bases can be fun if you're creative. This game allows you to customize your base quite a bit for an early access game
-The story is initially a bit typical, your loved one has been kidnapped or killed blah blah save them but as you go on and if you read up on it on the wiki page, you'll realize it's pretty complex yet creepy/weird
-The cannibals have great A.I, they don't just attack you on sight (unless you've been killing them an awful lot) when you encounter your first cannibal(s) they will typically just stand a distance away from you and observe you, however be careful as to not turn your back to them, they're still unpredictable at times.
-Lots of tools and weapons for an early access game.
Cons
-No random world gen, but it's very understandable why.
-Replayability is soso once you beat all the gamemodes
-The lighting seems to be a bit off..even on ultra, i just don't like it at times.
-Game can be complicated for new players
Overall, amazing early access game, if you see it on sale, GET IT.

Good:
Fun.  A good mix of things I recognize mixed with new material.  I enjoyed it once I got used to it (see bad).
Just the right amount of challenge.  It takes a bit of getting used to, but once I figured out how it works it was all smooth sailing and I completed the game quickly (including black armor).

Lots of secrets to find.  This game has great replay value if you want to see everything.  Plenty of "ah ha" moments as I figure things out.
Bad:
Noticeable input lag.  Yes, set game resolution to my monitors native resolution, no prerendered frames or vsync, etc.  I play tons of twitchy games under the same setup and this one lags.  If you're the type of person who notices it, this game will take some adjusting to.
Armor/weapon combos are not very well balanced.  Some are nearly useless, some completely overpowered to the point of trivializing the game.

Conclusion:
This game has some rough edges but lots of style and fun gameplay.  It's worth the asking price and I don't regret this one.  I'll follow this developer and see if their future releases improve on it.

Black Rose is a free to play horror title by indie developer Sir Bedlam Productions. The story is simple enough, you take on the role of a girl name Linda who is exploring an old, abandoned, haunted funeral home. Your overall goal is to figure out what is going on, and what happened to the people who worked there.
The gameplay is equally as simple as the story, you will explore the funeral home and pick up notes along the way to unravel the plot. You will also find various items scattered about, although ultimately you need to find a couple of keys to open a door that is locked with two padlocks. Eventually, you will begin encountering enemies; there are only two within the game, Sullivan and Myrtle. After you find their initial resting place, they will randomly spawn and chase you around; if you get to close to them, it's game over. However, the game rewards you with score points for staying as close to the enemies as possible without dying. This is an unfortunately useless feature, as there are no rewards or leaderboards.
The graphics are alright, and the ambient atmosphere is suspenseful and inspires a sense of dread in the player. It's good to note that the game even has 5.1 surround sound capability. It also runs at a smooth 60 FPS and doesn't suffer from any random drops; it's a very well optimized title, which I commend the developer on. However, there are some bugs and glitches that need to be ironed out; such as getting stuck on doors, chairs, and the fact that enemies can spawn right on top of you. A save feature would also be a welcome addition, as not everyone would be willing to sit down and spend an hour to finish the game in one go.
Black Rose is one of the better, and more well optimized, free indie horror titles to come about, and for that reason I am going to recommend it. Yes, the game utilizes jumpscares a bit, but it more so relies on the tense, thick atmosphere that is set up by the use of ambient sound. Yes, the enemies do look a bit cheap and cheesy, but I have seen far worse models in far worse games. If you're a fan of horror titles, give this one a shot... you've really got nothing to lose, it's free after all.

LYNE is a logic puzzle game where you attempt to connect all shapes of similar type/color with a single line. Each tile can connect to any active tiles of the same shape (and a few which allow for multiple lines to pass through) in any adjacent or diagonal direction.
It takes this relatively simple mechanic and has a nearly endless supply of levels - each group has 25 levels, and there's 26 groups included in the game, along with a daily feature which has up to three groups of varying difficulty.
This is a game best played in short bursts, as too much of it at one time can become tiresome. That being said, for those short periods of time, it ends up being a very relaxing and satisfying puzzle game, with some of the harder levels leaving you scratching your head for a great deal of time.

If you are looking for an action game you are in the wrong place. PZ is more of a simulation of life during a zombie apocalypse with more of a focus on surviving than mashing in the heads of zombies (which is still quite an important part ;) ). I have been playing this game for 4 years now. It has come a very long way from alpha and many improvements have been made. This game is a blast to play either by yourself or with a group of friends online even at this stage in it's development. There is still NPC's to be re-implemented into the game and vehicles. It is very unforgiving but the perma-death gives you more incentive to fight for your last breath! The leveling system is quite in depth and there are plenty of recipies to cook and items to craft. PZ is one of the best video games I have ever played and I can guarantee if you are looking for a realistic zombie rpg then you will sink hours and days into this game. With it being a sandbox game in nature the possibilties are endless, especially with a very strong modding community which has a good relationship with the devs.
TL;DR
A realistic zombie survival game which will suck away hours of your life. Very much playable in early access. Even more fun/amusing with a group of friends. What are you waiting for? Go out and buy this game ;)

Well, this is a sad day. Superhot looked like a really cool game. I played the whole game in around 2 hours. I explored all of the menus. I found a couple of the in-level secrets. I did not try endless mode or the challenges.
Let me start with the horrible flaw in this game and the main reason I simply cannot recommend it.
Superhot Team has taken a cue from TinyBuild and gone down the rabbit hole that is mistaking tedium for difficulty. And it certainly is tedious. One can only shoot, bash, and slice up so many arbitrary red enemies before the game becomes a slog of the same repetitious crap.
From a development standpoint, the Hotswap ability (the ability to switch into enemies) is introduced much too late. The one ability that can truly save the player only shows up for a short portion of the game before being entirely useless in the hardest part of the game.
Before I get into what I do like about this game, I need to talk about a severe design problem. Enemies make no sense whatsoever. Hotswapped into an enemy directly behind one frames about to shoot you? Worry not; that enemy can pull a full 180 and fire with perfect aim because the enemies have no regards for the rules of the game. They are always perfectly accurate in aim and they can fire instantaneously at any target in any direction. Even Portal's turrets are more forgiving than these red aimbots.
What makes this all the more depressing is how much more the game could be with more reasonable enemies. When enemies are slower to react, don't have perfect aim, and don't have omni-vision, a lot more of them can go into one level. Much of the game is restricted by not forcing simple restrictions onto the enemies. As it stands, the game already oversteps its bounds on the limits of how many enemies one should be required to face (as anyone who has played the final level will understand).
The greatest asset Superhot has to offer is its visual quality. It looks quite nice. With its minimalistic visual design, contrast is great and shadows are sharp. The menus are fun and add to the experience, as do the wonderful work that has been done with the visuals involving the menu. It is just too bad all of the narrative related experience falls flat with by handling its concepts more hamfistedly than I have ever seen in video games.
I am not going into the poorly written narrative at the moment. To sum it up, it is forced, uninspired, poorly executed trash. First draft quality at best. I really don't think this game deserves the effort to explain it more.
With all that said, there actually are people I would recommend this to. I would recommend this to someone interested in playing the VR version of this game. I believe the unique experience should very well make up for the mechanical flaws in big ways. While the standard version struggles to create a sense of immersion, VR has an inherent immersive quality to it.
That is the place of this game: a cool looking VR tech demo. It is the quality of one and should be treated as such. A two hour adventure of boredom to moderate enjoyment.

The first paragraph is my story of experiences with the game, and the second is akin to an actual review.
I first learned about the game when I was like 7 and I was watching the Bonus Features disc for Revenge of the Sith and I saw the trailer. I instantly fell in love with the idea of a Star Wars strategy game. I got on my mother's computer, downloaded the demo, and played all the tutorials and the 3 planet Galactic Conquest. I begged my mom to buy the game for me, but she said no so I did the most logical thing for a young kid to do. I got on my mom's computer, went to Amazon where she was already logged in, and bought the Star Wars Best of PC Collection, which came with Empire at War, Knights of the Old Republic, Battlefront, Jedi Outcast, and Republic Commando (the last 4 being stories for other reviews). I was mainly interested in Empire at War though. I chose One-Day shipping so the next day when I got home from school, I saw a package a the front door. I grapped it, ripped it open, installed EaW, and played the Empire Campaign non-stop. The next night, I here my mother screaming at me, "WHAT
ORDER?!?!" I told her about it, said that I was sorry and begged her not to tell my father, and I got grounded for the first time in my life. She ended up letting me keep it though, but I had to pay her the $60 it cost plus the shipping, so I was out of money for a while. For like my 9th birthday, I asked my grandmother if she could buy me the Empire at War Gold Pack at Walmart, (which I had just discovered) and I got it. I played through the new campaign, but soon delved into Galactic Conquest as the Empire. I wondered why I didn't have Vader as a hero like in the original game, and then I saw he could be constructed for 12500 credits. I did it, brought him into battle, saw the Executor, and then I truly fell in love with the game. If Steam counted the hours I had on my cd copies, I might even be into the thousands in all honesty.
Onto an actual review though, Empire at War is a Real Time Strategy game set in the Star Wars galaxy. You can choose from either the Empire or Rebellion (or the Zann Consortium, a criminal empire with many unique gameplay elements in the Forces of Corruption expansion) in either story driven campaigns, galaxy wide Galactic Conquests, or small skirmish battles. Once you've familiarized yourself the game however, I would reccomend delving into the huge modding community for this game. There are many great mods such as Thrawn's Revenge (Setsthe game after Return of the Jedi with new factions, planets, mechanics, and a more accurate Galaxy map), Republic at War (Take a guess), and Awakening of the Rebellion (Which gives the Galactic Conquest much more depth, rebalances everything so the Empire is a hulking behemoth of a war machine and the Rebellion is just a ragtag group of freedom fighters, and just adds to the overall feel of the original Galactic Civil War Era). Even without these mods though, Empire at War is still a great game and is definitely worth your money.

When I was transitioning between games until FFXIV came out, I played a lot of this. Even now when I play FFXIV, there's times I actually missed playing this game. I played it on the release day up until shortly before Noel came out, and there were a ton of bugs after release. But the bugs were mostly funny to me, and as someone who has played a lot of both Free to Play and subscription MMOs, it's extremely understandable for a game to have a slew of bugs after release or post-patch. What matters is how they were handled.
The bosses were fun, the Emnity list for tanking was actually EXTREMELY useful (something I've always missed is the ability to see the parties' exact emnity values as I'm tanking), the game is colourful and pretty, mobs range from adorable to awesome in appearance, and above all, the game is maintained on micro transactions that -are not required pay to wins-. Although you can buy items that'll enhnce your abilities for a certain time and progress quicker through the game, you dont -have- to in order to keep going.
People seem to forget how great this is when you play something Free to Play. Tons of micro transaction games will have you "Pay-to-Win" in order to become anything of value beyond the beginning levels and some players would literally pour thousands of dollars per week into specials just to gain and if you didn't have that kind of money, you'd have to spend days grinding or competing with bots in order to earn enough of the in-game currency to trade with someone for it in order to just do the real content. Despite the exorbitant amounts of money some communities would dump into these games, they would -still- be rife with game breaking bugs. So what is everyone's complaint with RO2 when compared to the majority of F2P MMOs?
This game is fun, is enhanced by but not dominated by it's cash shop, and is a good casual thing to play without requiring a huge time sink. Yes, it has bots, bugs, and elitists, but what MMO doesn't?

I played Evolve during the Beta and got pretty hyped about it. I brought the pre-order pack for around 60 euros which included an extra monster (Garg) and a skin for the Goliath on launch.
I tried to play a lot, but three major factors have put me off:
1) It's a co-op game that can force you to play solo. I found that if queued solo, with the monster as your least favourite role, you would still often get picked to play the monster, mostly against a 4man pre-made team of friends.
It's a core problem with the game, when you want to compare it to something like L4D, people buy L4D because they love co-op play, a group of players working together for common survival. Whilst people loved the competitive mode in L4D2, you still at least got to coordinate and play as a team, even when playing the bad guys.
If you really truely love co-operative play, but don't really enjoy the 1vs4 aspect, you must queue with other players to avoid being forced to play a round as the monster.
2) Due to how heavily hunters rely on their team, European servers can suck when English speaking players are paired up with Russians, Romanians, French etc, and I mean no slight to these people, but it sucks when you have a co-op game and 3 of the 4 people can't understand each other. Evolve really should have split it's match making down by some level of language division since communication is such a vital aspect of the game
3) Payment model is rediculous. Around the stage I was getting tired of Evolve after release and starting to feel resentful of my pre-purchase and that I really hadn't gotten my value for money from my original purchase, I gained access to my new pre-order Monster, but at the same time 4 new heroes were added at a cost of another 15 euros.
Whilst 15 euro's for that much content in a lot of games isn't too bad, I can't justify it after feeling I've not gotten value out of the original 60 euro purchase of the game and will not keep pouring money onto Evolve in the hopes that the new hunters give me the satifaction I want.
It's practically impossible to try out the new hunters (of which there are two waves now, costing 30 euros to have all 8 plus even more for the new monsters), so all you could do is watch a youtube video of their abilities, pay for it, find you don't enjoy it then kind of 'well tough' where as with most other games with unlocked heroes, there are features that let you try out a hero to decide if you want to earn your hard-earned money.
As my general advice to anyone thinking of buying this game, if you can get hold of it during a sale for <20 euros, perhaps consider it, knowing that if you want to have access to the full range of hunters and monsters, you're looking at dishing out another 40-50 euros.
Ultimately, I would recommend people do not buy this game (and none of this is mentioning the gigantic store of skins, 99% of which you can't even see due to First-person view).

Put 24 hours into this game over a less than 48 hour period of time. Time just escaped me while playing it.
You should know that I'm reviewing this from the perspective of someone who has never touched a tactical RPG in his life. I just like Super Sentai/Power Rangers and superhero games. I bought this on a whim and haven't regretted it since.
The game is fairly short. I beat it on Casual in less than a day and am probably 65 or so % of the way through my Normal mode playthrough about a day later. That said, the game warrants at least 3 replays due to the branching story which leads to multiple endings (not Mass Effect 3 style endings. REAL alternate endings). So far I've already encountered 2 brand new bosses and one new stage that I didn't play on my first time through during my second run.
The pixel art is really fun and doesn't take away from the experience at all. It runs like a dream and only takes about 5 minutes to download due to the small set of files. The music is very reminiscent of my Game Boy days and brings me back. It'll stick in your head in a good way and definitely helps you feel pride when you finish a really tough Megazord fight. The real selling point for me was the ability to fully customize your ranger team from what they shout when they morph to what they yell to summon the Megazord - you really feel like you're running a season of the show.
A couple of negatives include an inability to undo accidental purchases in the in-game currency shop system. I have to quit without saving and go through buying everything again which can be a pain if I regret buying a certain piece of gear or crafting a certain item. You can't preview the stat changes on craftable items before making them which pushes you to do the quit without saving thing a decent amount on your first playthrough. The RNG side of Megazord fights basically makes them a big gamble as my stats don't seem to be doing me any favors in my second playthrough. It's also somewhat boring compared to the ranger parts of the game due to basically only having the choice of attacking or defending as your pray to RNGesus to bless your next move.
Other than that, I can't praise this game more highly for fellow casual strategy game players. If you're more hardcore, you might find it too simplistic, but maybe the game's humor and charm can win you over into donating a few hours of your life to a little Power Rangers nostalgia.

As a child of the 1980s, I saw two things pretty much everywhere: NES games and cartoons.  In the glory days of the 8-bit NES, we had "Nintendo-hard" games where pattern recognition was key.  Levels and bosses that seemed unfair were actually operating on relatively simple pattern-based algorithms, and a keen-eyed gamer could exploit those patterns for a win that made the whole affair look easy.  Mess up, though, and you were punished for it.  Bosses didn't have checkpoints no matter how many phases they had.
The cartoons were ubiquitous.  Sure, we had our campy 80s action shows, but you were just as likely to find Looney Tunes/Merry Melodies or old Disney cartoons on TV.  If you had the right channels, you might have even been graced with the old black and white cartoons of days past.  These cartoons often eschewed modern sensibilities and political correctness for snappy action and silly gags.  Things didn't have to make real-world sense in these shows, but there was a sort of internal logic to them.
Cuphead is the marriage of these two glorious things.  If Mega Man had noodly arms, he would be Cuphead.  If Mickey Mouse fired shotgun blasts out of his gloves, he would be Cuphead.
Let's make no mistake: the game is hard, and you will die.  You may find yourself cursing your computer, your controller, the creators of the game, or perhaps even your chosen deity.  None of these things is to blame.  Cuphead is fair.  You just haven't gotten good enough yet.
Stick with Cuphead, and you'll find a game that has some of the most exciting character design, music direction, and pure charm of anything you've ever seen.  It draws inspiration from so many areas, and yet it's a creature all its own.  If you have any love for classic games or classic cartoons, give it a shot.

Let's Play: REIGNS
Reigns is a great little game that really captures that classic choose your own adventure feel. You play as a young king who assumes the throne after the previous king died. Each turn is 1 year and each year you are presented with a request, problem, or event which requires you to decide between two options. The result of your choice will effect one or more of your kingdoms 4 groups, the church, the people, the military, and the treasury. Your object is to rule as long as possible, keeping all 4 groups happy, while completing objectives. You do this until you inevitably die to the plauge, the angry mob, the religious zealots, your dinner, or any other number of things that can kill you in this game. You then assume the role of the next young king and do it again.
-PROS:
- Great content for the price
- Decent replayability
- Easy to pickup and learn
- Enjoyable and funny gameplay
- Steam Achievements
-CONS:
- Events tend to repeat, could use more events
- At certain points there is no way to keep your king alive
TLDR: Great game to just sit down and play. For the price, absolutely recommend!!!

LYNE is a puzzle game that lives up their tagline: deceptively simple, infinitely complex. Your goal is to connect the colored shapes from their respective beginning and end points with the multicells filled up should there be any. But as you finish each set (there are 26 sets named after each alphabet with 25 puzzles/set), the puzzles gradually increase in difficulty. As you complete more sets you will realize that your original intuitive approach in solving the puzzles will eventually be replaced with a logical approach, especially for the 4-slot multicells.
The puzzles are fun to complete, but the game is repetitive so I would advise against completing several sets in one sitting, especially in the later sets. Even if you have completed all 26 normal sets, the game also introduces daily sets, so you can still do new puzzles every day.
By completing sets, you earn badges in the form of the letter of the set which you can use to display in your profile. And completion of normal or daily sets will earn you trytes, limited to 999 of them. With enough of these trytes you will be able to change the background color, which is a nice touch. What is the ??? achievement for btw?
Overall this game is fun, addictive and worth every penny. Every now and then I mess up using the pattern lock in my tablet thanks to this game.
TL;DR 10/10 will play until the LYNE effect kicks in

I've got a thing for puzzle games. I like to sort of just swallow them whole, kind of sink myself into them until I'm drowning on puzzles. Most puzzle games I go through in one night of glorious puzzle binging—but Lyne was never like that. It's a much more insidious game, one that I come back to again and again when I'm looking for a casual mix of mind-bending and mindless. It's, just as it claims to be, a game that will "knot your brain as it calms your soul". I put on some music in the background, fire up Lyne, and sit back and relax while my mouse sort of glides through the puzzles and my mind struggles futilely to keep up with my intuition.
Other users have compared Lyne to a much more complex game of connect the dots. The goal of the game is simple: you have a board with different colored shapes. Connect the shapes. Make a line. Fill the board. Repeat. It's never more or less complex than that. It becomes a sort of mantra the farther you go in the game: Connect the shapes. Make a line. Fill the board. Connect the shapes. Make a line. Fill the board. Connect the shapes . . .
Until you get stuck, of course—and you will get stuck. Sometimes your brain tries to think about the puzzle more than it should and then suddenly you aren't actually going any where at all anymore. That's when you set aside the game, do something else for a while, and then come back to it when the urge to play strikes you again. That is the most intriguing thing about Lyne: it seems to be a game that you can only win by trying not to win. Too much effort breaks the peace that Lyne tries to create and will only serve to frustrate and annoy you.  You don't solve a Lyne puzzle, you just know the answer and complete it.
Lyne is, without a doubt, my favorite puzzle time-waster. It's what I play late at night, when it's too close to bed time for more video games, but I'm too far away from falling asleep to actually put my head down on the pillow. It goes well with a hazy sort of pre-sleep understanding and logic, one that can only be recreated during the day time by a fiercely zen attitude and some slow tunes playing in the background. I'd even call it the most productive sort of "zoning out" that I've ever managed to achieve.

A puzzle game where the objective is to connect all shapes of similar shape/color along finite number of lines. LInes cannot cross, but some shapes will accept any line color and can accept a line multiple times.
That's it.
Pros:
+ Easy to pick up
+ Gets gradually difficult
+ You will not run out of levels, because the game generates daily puzzles
+ There's like 650 pre-built puzzles anyway, this game will take you at least 10 hours
+ Steam trading cards
+ The achievements are letters, and you can use them to spell things in your steam achievement showcase. If you're bad at puzzles, you can just look at one of the many walkthroughs and enjoy your ill-gotten showcase; nobody will know.
+ Costs less than a couple of tacos
+ Soothing flute
Cons:
-
Points of note:
? No soundtrack (there is audio as you interact with the pieces and finish stages), but this lets you put on any kind of ambient music that you want. This would be a con, but I don't think it's reasonable to expect this game to have a 10+ hour soundtrack.
? It's a puzzle game, so if you don't like puzzle games, don't buy it.
? Casual
Edit: After beating the game (all the puzzles and some of the random daily ones) I can't say this game was mind-bendingly difficult, but I did get stuck on a few levels from time to time. The solution to that was usually to just go away and do somthing else and then come back to the puzzle with a fresh mind after a day or a few.
