This must be one of my favourite games ever. These are some of the things that make it so great:
- The visuals in the game are stunning: picturesque landscapes and sunrises rich with colour will make you want to climb higher and wake up early in the game, even though it's usually a bad idea.
- Learning: you get no map and only some very basic hints on how to survive in the game. As you play you learn, if not through common sense and experimentation, then by reading community content. You need to give the sandbox a few attempts if you feel lost at first. Trust me it's worth it.
- Audio: I think it's a very important and often overlooked feature of this game. Each item when used has unique, realistic sounds. Sounds in the environment indulge you and make you feel like a part of the game. Listening is also really important from the practical perspective e.g. to avoid predator attacks, to detect the weather outdoors etc.
- Replayability: I think that static and dynamic, procedurally generated elements of the game are very well balanced. The world is very recognisable between the games, yet some elements change e.g. where the items are spawned, whether the indoor interiors are accessible etc.
- Nature: for someone who enjoys staying outdoors and resting from other people I greatly enjoy the fact that there are no other humans in the sandbox. Only your character and the harsh nature.
These are only a few points in this ever evolving game. I can recommend it with no reservations

I really liked this.
I was never into the Power Rangers myself, nor a lot of the anime this game pays tribute to. But I don't think that's really required here to appreciate that this game is a love letter to cheesy TV and all the fun people have had with it. Everything in this game is so goofy and so fourth wall breaking wink wink, but it's done in a way I found really charming and sweet, as opposed to, say, Retro City Rampage which just bashed you over the head with how funny it thought it was every 5 seconds (hot tip: it wasn't).
There are about five million of these faux-16 bit games now, but here is one that actually uses that effect correctly and accurately. The target audience for this game is, at least in part, people like me that actually remember when 16-bit was real and spectacular, and tactics RPG's were just an emerging thing. There's just enough depth here to be interesting without being something overwhelming to work out, both in terms of the combat and the crafting system. The gimmick with the game is you are playing a fight scene in each episode of the show, and you can get bonuses for fulfilling director's instructions, things like "kill three enemies on a turn" or "use team attacks 4 times", these add enough spice for completionist types without, technically, being neccessary to advance the game.
The game isn't flawless, I hit a couple annoying but inconsequential bugs (there's an annoying one with one of the Space Sherrifs where his finisher doesn't actually count as a finisher). There are a couple spelling errors that aren't part of the on-purpose narrator gag (breath/breathe mixup happened at least twice). And I really, really wish this game had saving mid-chapter.
But on the whole, I had way more fun with this than I could have ever anticipated. It's cute, almost disgustingly so. But not quite. I got this in the Humble Freedom Bundle which was so large it was inevitable there were several indie games I'd never heard of there. This was the first of those I tried becaue the premise of "some stuntmen quit a TV show to start their own knockoff" is a hilarious, great premise. And I really did enjoy the game from start to finish.

Enjoyable niche pvp game -- at release there are three monsters available and a total of 12 hunters (4 original of each role, with the ability to unlock two more of each role). Hunt (deathmatch), Rescue (Hunters recuse and escort human survivors to extracation points, monster attempt to kill survivors or hunters), and Nest (Hunters attempt to destroy monster eggs around the map, monster attempts to kill them or defend till time runs out) are the three available game modes with Evacuation serving as a version of game mode that mixes the three in a "week" of fighting and then introduces Defend as the final encounter (which is basically reversed Nest with some added bells and whistles).
Now, to the million dollar question.. is it worth the price? And the answer if we look at the content released by pretty much any other game, would be a shoulder shrug and a not really. Does this make the game less fun? No, it doesn't... but their money making model is going to hurt them in the long game by ostracizing players who both see the glaring flaws in their content-starved release as well as have become insanely entitled by many F2P titles (Even in this genre one could look at Nosgoth as a F2P competitior)
As far as how the game handles itself within the pvp space -- I'd say it does a good job. You have pretty solid balance with a few minor and non-game breaking exceptions and the game doesn't spoon feed you on what to do or how to do it, which does lead to the inevitable "X IS OP!!1111" cries on the forums. You also have a pretty wild skillcap difference from the players who have been with the game since mid-alpha, as well as some early indications of working hacks (neither of which is anything new, or specific to Evolve). The limited number of game modes and maps does yield some serious repitition early on, which will drive away heavy players earlier than many games do.. so hopefully Turtle Rock will stay on it's content release, and not try and charge players every time they push out a new tidbit of code.
For what it does, I'd give Evolve an 7.5 of 10 with the caveat that the game should be doing considerably more given it's pricetag. A single player campaign would've gone a long way with the playerbase, as well as given Turtle Rock a chance to throw a little more backstory on the hunters and monsters into the mix... and only four game types is a little odd, especially considering that once of them is purely just deathmatch and the others really aren't anything truly new within the space.
I'm having fun with the game, but I can certainly see how gamers on limited budgets would pass this one over.

The most amazing "inside a MMORPG" game
This game is about an average player that wants revenge on a hacker that messed up with his friend. At first, Haseo is a rebel young guy who treats everyone poorly and thinks he can do everything by himself. But as the story progresses, he grows as a person, and a lot starts to change in his objective as the truth unveils.
The port is decent. The game has this old PS2 game look to it, but it's easy to get used to it. The only problem I had was with the shadows - having them activated would sometimes kill my FPS randomly (like staring at a door would make it go below 20fps). There is a notable slowdown when many effects are happening at the same time, but this problem was also present on the PS2 and doesn't happen often
The controls are a bit clunky at first, considering the combat is action-oriented (it doesn't have the same flow of Bayonetta and DmC, for example). It's something you get used to as well, especially with animation cancelling
There were some additions to the game, like the cheat mode, which puts you in the max level and gives you a ton of items and gold. The experience gain after battles has been increased, which makes the pacing a lot better (you will outlevel some story dungeons that were supposed to be used to level though). The terminal disc is included, which contains videos about the .hack games before G.U. and some more info about what's going on
The addition of a new volume is debatable. The story feels complete at the end of Vol 3, and Vol 4 seems to be a "good ending" to the series. It suffers from bad design though, like making you talk to every ally before a big battle (so they can say 2 phrases), and the new mechanics are only available for several dungeons. All in all, it seems to be an advertisement for a new series
In the end, the G.U. series is amazing and definitely worth buying. The game runs well, the story is very interesting, and it's easy to get used to the game's limitations

This series was a crazy ride from start to finish. The story was amazing with a lot of feels and unexpected twists. It starts off a little slow but quickly starts to pick up as Haseo, the main character starts to learn more and more about whats going on in "The World" and what he has to do to meet his own goals. Most of the characters Haseo meets are very likable and you get to see them grow throughout the whole series and also help Haseo grow into a better character himself. Everytime you get a new party member you add them to your friends list like you would in an actual MMO style game which lets you invite them into your party for the story, quests, dungeons, etc. You also get the ability to trade with them and give them gifts while in a party. The game does a really good job of making you feel immersed into "The World" with how it has you logging out to a desktop and back into the game as if you're the one actually playing it and having a friends list full of the characters you meet throughout the story.
Gameplay wise the combat is rather simple at first but gets more fun later on as you get more weapons and fight harder enemies and such. You have the option sometimes of inviting any of the party members you have into a group of 3 so you can have whatever two party members  you want for quests. The way the dungeons worked in this game was really unique to me since you had to combine 3 words to essentially create a dungeon for yourself. Sometimes the story gave you 3 words to use for story quest dungeons and other times you could create your own dungeon to go into by using any combination of 3 words. Music in this series was amazing and really fit for each of the fights/cutscenes it was for. Having the ability to unlock the music from boss fights and cutscenes to use as your background music on the desktop was a really nice feature.
Overall I would definitely recommend anyone that loves RPGS and MMOs to play this amazing series because it was truly a great experience.

Limbo is horrifically beautiful.  It’s horrible, but startlingly pretty. A 2D puzzle-platformer built in black, grey and white. The figure of a young child hangs limply from a noose. Death is everywhere. White butterflies that flutter gently by are the only sign of hope.
The boy you control has a twee outline, all floppy hair and short trousers. The boy’s task? To find his sister. That’s all you need to know. There is no back story, no dialogue or cutscenes. Just the drive to push on through the shifting mists and silhouettes of the game’s environments and puzzles.
Trial-and-error makes up a large park of Limbo, a game where death isn’t just likely but often a prerequisite to understand the mechanics of a puzzle. But these tasks usually delight more than they frustrate. Most are fiendishly clever without being obtuse and the satisfaction comes in pulling each apart piece by piece. They’re tremendously varied too; some play with perception, while others see fit to flip gravity. There’s plenty of puzzles that run through the game’s short but perfectly formed running time of around five hours. And underpinning them all is good old-fashioned twitch platforming, with you maneuvering the boy; jumping, moving crates, and swinging across bottomless ravines.
Overall verdict:
Highly recommended!

Ladies and gents... I present to you Outlast, aka: Door Slamming Simulator.
Now before I start, let me give you my personal opinion, despite my recommendation being a thumbs down.
I actually enjoyed the game to an extent enough to beat it- BUT. The game has many flaws.
Let's start with my gameplay first. When I first played, I decided to go on Nightmare difficulty because hey, I'm not a wuss. I later guessed that with higher difficulty your battery life probably drains faster and *maybe* enemies are more difficult? (I honestly haven't tested this on the easier difficulties.) I found myself strobe-lighting my camera's nightvision function just so I could see through the dark 6/10 times so I wouldn't be trapped in might-as-well-be-wearing-a-blindfold-pitch-black darkness.
When I'd encountered my first enemy, my first thought was to hide, obviously. Stealth mechanics=♥♥♥♥♥♥ Your ONLY options of hiding are either to move around in the darkness, hide in lockers/under beds and tables/ in crawl spaces. You can't hide behind most objects. I'm almost 100% sure someone is going to give me♥♥♥♥♥♥about that last point, but if there's to be a stealth mechanic like that, I'd like to hide behind something that looks like decent cover such as a laundry cart.
Also, since I gave up on stealth long ago by abusing the "Stealth" mechanic, I simply just walked around in the darkness when it was safe to do so or whenever the enemy was a good distance away. Honestly, halfway in, I abandoned stealth altogether and just ran everywhere while slamming doors in front of their faces. Works every time.
Now let's move on to the "Horror" part of this game. Honestly, I was only surprised 2 or 3 times. The rest of the time I was so afraid of losing battery life because then I'd be stuck in pitch black purgatory. The *ONLY* fear factor from my perspective was being trapped in the dark with terrible lighting(if any, depending on the area) and the occasional "jumpscare". For people who've played Alien: Isolation, Dead Space 2, and others similar to those, they should be hardened enough to anticipate those.
Overall I enjoyed the concept, but not the execution of the game. If others are fine with these flaws, then I'm not one to judge. But in my opinion, stay away from this game unless it's on sale.

"No plot, no story, just killing red dudes" - what I wish this game had
SUPERHOT is an interesting mix of a decent idea with cool level design bogged down by an absolutely terrible story and puzzling inconsistencies. People have gone over and over about how the story is pretentious and too full of itself, and I'll agree 100%. But let me add my own personal experience to the mix:
At one point in the game some dude tells you to never run superhot.exe ever again after some long drawn out cutscene about how you have no control or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ So I thought "maybe there's some cool easteregg if I quit the game completely and boot it back up". Well, there wasn't. But what doing that did was start me over from the very beginning of the long cutscene again. After skipping through it as fast as I could, a chat section appeared. I took this opportunity to use the "press esc to skip chat" feature- only to have the game stop me from skipping it with the message "THIS IS FOR YOUR OWN GOOD. LISTEN." It was at that point that I felt compelled to do what the game was telling me, quit and never come back.
But hell, the game is only two hours long, so I decided to play through the rest.
Beyond the story, I have issues with the gameplay as well. I played the original flash version before the full version came out, and I enjoyed the little it showed off with the stop-and-go gameplay. And in the full game, I really love the level design. It reminds me of a game I grew up playing called "Indiana Jones and the Emperor's Tomb" where the fun was going through each room finding creative ways to use the scenery around you to dispatch your enemies who are far more equipped than you. The problem comes where each room feels less designed around the level and more "let's create this area and then dump waves of enemies with machine guns in it". It gets tedious after a short while and even nearing the end of the pitifully brief 2 hour campaign I was feeling fatigued of the gameplay. You shoot a dude, strafe right a step and shoot another dude, 5 more dudes spawn at various hallways, rinse and repeat. Occasionally you do something really cool like throw a shotglass at a guy to get a katana to dismember two other dudes behind you... but these moments are too few and far between to keep me interested. It usually boils down to a fancy looking hallway sporting 4 dudes with guns.
And if you really like the gameplay, buckle up because you are forced to go through the campaign until you unlock the speedrun and challenge levels. Unless there is some secret I'm unaware of you can't just access the gameplay, you have to listen to the game berating you for playing it for a few hours.
Beyond the story and the main game, I really liked the secret side stuff and sound design of the whole package. I enjoy the "old demoscene" look to the UI, and there are funny bonuses laid around the file explorer. I personally like "Tree Dude", in which you are an ascii lumberjack cutting down a tree. It also features a more gripping and compelling story than the main game itself.
Bottom line, SUPERHOT didn't hold my attention. The gameplay is grating after a while due to it just being waves of enemies pouring through hallways and the story is absolute misery to slog through. It's also short and overpriced for what you get. There's a part in the game where you are required to quit out of the game and boot it back up, and boy did I have a tough time gathering the willpower to not just give up and forget it exists on my harddrive.
This game is coming together fast, plenty of patches and loads of fun.

Wow.  Check this refreshing game out.  I wish Fallout had this level of detail and simulation when it comes to pure Survival Game time.
So, The Long Dark is essentially a Sandbox game (and I can not WAIT for the Sory Mode!) where you must survive the Canadian wilderness.  It is not Sandbox, in the Minecraft sense lets say, in that it is not a truly random map, but it is a (roughly) random spawn point on existing, lovingly crafted maps, with varying levels of loot tuned to the difficulty level you are playing.  Your four stats are Cold, Fatigue, Thirst, and Hunger - in that order.  You will probably die of hypothermia.  There are wolves and bears, and rabbits and deer, and if you are lucky enough not to get eaten by the former, you may survive long enough to find decent shelter and start a fire!  Assuming, as I mentioned, that you haven't already frozen to death.  Oh, and everything you do burns calories.  EVERYTHING.
Better find a knife or a hatchet soon!
Super immersive, and an incredible effort by this small Canadian dev team.  I am in love with it.  I don't want to give any more away, as trial-and-error are part of the excitement of this game. This review is for all seasons of the Sam & Max video game series:
Being a avid cartoon fan, I would've expected something as breakneck fast and energetic as the show. What we got from one of Taletale's earlier games is a bunch of moments that feel like Sam & Max after a long day of freelance crime-solving, and it's in 3D instead of Steve Purcell's lovely hand-drawn art style.
The writing is fairly funny, but most of the experience just feels flat or shallow - probably better off buying the complete series on DVD rather than playing a game based off of it. Plus, Sam's new voice is annoying to listen to compared to the original voice actor Harvey Atkin - shame they couldn't get him for these games.
Still, even if the game, the acting, the puzzles, and the story doesn't always seem appealing, it's an enjoyable, quirky Point & Click adventure to blaze through.
The good news is that the writing improves slightly each season as well as the graphics. It's also amusing to see the same location altered due to the events of past game episodes as well as deviate to some new ones connected to the game's Main st.
7/10: worth one playthrough, not much else.

Honestly one of the best RPGs I've played in years. its fun, pretty, with an exciting story. 21 hours in and I've finished volume 1 (of 4), and loved every second of it. I'm now actually going out of my way to do some completionist things before moving on to volume 2, which is out of character for me.
quick pros and cons:
PROS:
-cutscenes are crisp and pretty
-voice acting is mostly good for an "anime" type game
-combat is solid, fun, and simple if you wanted to be, more complex if not
-same goes for equipment
-LOTS of things to collect and do, if you're into it. All optional, though.
-many QOL changes from the original release, but I can't name many since I never played those. Things like faster move speed, AI party members kicking chims for you, etc
-The music is memorable and enjoyable
-The "desktop" outside of the game itself, along with the forums and continuing news stories for world building
CONS:
-areas are very limited. Aside from the special story areas, most everything looks pretty similar. I didn't feel this took away from the experience, though, yet I do hope this isn't the case for volumes and onward
-the game is very generous with exp, and it is easy to overlevel without trying. Fights meant to be challenging were sometimes cakewalks, though a cerain post game boss was still a challenge despite this.
-in engine cutscenes don't have lip movement. not something that bothers me, but something that's worth mentioning
So, yeah, I'd definitely recommend this based just on the first volume. I'll update the review as I go on. Maybe.

I've played the first volume and 30 minutes of the second. 70% of the game was not enjoyable. I think the gameplay is hit or miss. A little simple, but maybe that's fine. My problems are mostly with the game's story, and this is what this review will cover. Spoiler alert btw.
---The Good---
This is a game where you play as a person playing an MMO called "The World". You are able to play "The World", or log out and be on your desktop. Here, you can open forums and news websites to get information about "The World" and "the real world" (the fictional real world outside the fictional MMO). This is where you will get most of your world building, and the only thing I thought was great about this game's storytelling. You can read about real-world events like rockets being sent to space, or watch some trashy news program (trashy in the sense that most things on TV these days are kinda bad) that is closely related to what happens in "The World". The forums provide world building for "The World", and it makes you feel like there is an active player base for "The World" (even if it is all fake). You friends (in the game), also use this forum, and you can learn a few things about them through here.
This was what made me go over my 2-hour refund playtime, and I hate how the world building was good enough to make me play for 20 more hours.
---The Bad---
The rest of the story is really bad. Or... Well... It is delivered really badly. You are this main character called Haseo, who got PK'ed (Player Killed) on his first day in "The World", by the players who learned him the basics. This serves as the tutorial, and it kinda treats you like you are an idiot, who can't remember what they are told. I normally don't have a problem with this in tutorials, but I'll get back to this later.
After this tutorial, you a treated with a cutscene from 8 months later. You learn that Haseo has become a PKK (PK Killer), and is known as the Terror of Death. The reason for this is that during these 8 months he had a friend who got PK'ed by someone called Tri-Edge and ended up in a coma IRL because of it. So basically Haseo is seeking revenge.
He finally finds Tri-Edge, who then performs some weird supernatural thing on Haseo, and after that, he is back to level 1. So far, this is fine. It establishes some motivations and end goals.
After this Haseo meets with two new tutorial guys, and they start trying to help him just like before. Haseo tells them that he knows all the♥♥♥♥♥♥already, but they don't believe him, so they go with him on a "quest". Still no problem. THEN DURING THE ♥♥♥♥ING MISSION, THESE TUTORIAL GUYS TELL HASEO SOMETHING HE DOESN'T ♥♥♥♥ING KNOW! HOW? HOW DOES THIS HAPPENED? HASEO WAS LEVEL 133 OR SOMETHING! HE SHOULD ♥♥♥♥ING KNOW EVERYTHING! HE WAS A FAMOUS PKK, WHO NOBODY COULD BEAT!
Ok, ok... It's fine... NO, IT'S ♥♥♥♥ING NOT! This keeps happening during the story. Apparently. Haseo doesn't know about "The Arena", a place where official PvP matches take place or most things about guilds (even though he's been in one).
Now you might be saying: "Don't be stupid baka baka. If they didn't tell Haseo, then how would you, the player, know about all this.". Yes, that is a valid point, but then why did the game do the "after 8 months" cutscene when it did. It could have waited, have you join Haseo first guild, have you join Haseo in his first arena battle because he wanted to get stronger for revenge. Then, after this, we could have had this cutscene. All problems solved.
Sadly, this disconnect between what Haseo should know and what he actually knows is not the only problem with this game. Remember what I said about the first tutorial. The entire game is like this. Every time you go into a room and the doors lock, you get: "You can put in these spheres and then the doors will open.". Every time Haseo read an email telling him where to go, he then repeats it in his head. THEN WHEN YOU LOG INTO "THE WORLD", HE SAIS IT AGAIN! WHY?!?! IM NOT A ♥♥♥♥ING IDIOT! ONE TIME IS ENOUGH! Also, after every major plot point, Haseo will end all cutscenes with: "Well, I guess I will go check my email or something.". This happens without exception (this could be a fun drinking game). The problem here is, that you will get a popup when you actually get an email, so there is no reason for him to say it.
Ok, so I've deviated a little from the plot, let's get back to that. Haseo get's to know this girl Atoli, who looks exactly like his friend in a coma. This girl seems to kinda fall for him(?) or at least wants his attention really badly. The problem here is, that I really don't see why she cares. Haseo is only ever a jerk to her. He literally bad mouths her guild, the first time they meet. When she then tries to show him what she cares about in "The World", like looking at the scenery and taking it easy, he verbally abuses her, tell her to never show her face again. Why does she care for Haseo? Why hasn't she at least blocked him? She probably even has the rights to report him.
Btw, Haseo is also an awfully unlikeable character, if you haven't already noticed. Now, I really don't like to call things "edgy", as it is the most uninforming thing people can say as criticism. Sadly, Haseo tries his hardest to be this edgy guy, who cares about no one and always tries to say this "cool" and sarcastic lines to whoever he talks to. Sadly, he is never cool, and all his lines sound ♥♥♥♥ing stupid, especially when he talks to people smarter than him, and gets his word showed back up his♥♥♥♥♥ He also didn't have any character growths in all the time I played the game. You would think that after his verbal harassment nearly gets Atoli hurt badly (because she does something to get his attention), that he would stop... Sadly, he still just yells at her at the start of volume two, soo... And it's not like he doesn't care for Atoli (I think). It seems to me, that he seems to regret things whenever he actually hurts his friends... That is, when they tell him, that he hurt them. This is especially true for Atoli.
The dialog in this game is also ♥♥♥♥ing awful. The English dub is partly to blame, but I assume that they are just reading the subtitles, so even if I had Japanese on, it would still be the same. There is one point where Atoli's voice is kinda weird, and they other people say that they can't hear her. So I assume that this weird voice is to portray her thoughts to me, the player, but NOPE! Everyone responds to her when she talks, and when she tells her guild master about what happened HE LITERALLY SAIS: "Oooh, so that's why I can't hear you.". This was where I was about to drop everything. Maybe this is a translation issue, but I can't understand Japanese, so the original script is useless to me.
I think you all get the point by now. If you don't care about the story, or if all this is not a problem, then this may be a game for you. It seems that a lot of people actually enjoy this game, I mean, look at all the positive reviews. I think the premise is strong, and there are some interesting supernatural mysteries that I still want to know the answer to. Sadly, if a story is gonna do something for 27 hours, then it is likely that the rest is done the same way, so I'm done.

.Hack G.U. the second series in the series that popularized the "mmo" plot. With its 15 year anniversary we have this collection release giving all 3 volumes in one quick access launcher and a previously unreleased 4th volume along with small extras here and there. I've decided to split the review up slightly between the volumes and it should go without saying there's likely to be some spoilers in this, but I will try to avoid as many major ones I can.
Volumes 1-3
The original ps2 games. These games do slightly show their age. They upscale the graphics as much as they can, but they can't exactly upgrade the gameplay, which is a little dated. To be fair however their gameplay was repetitive even back when they were new. The "jrpg" curse of being very repetitive is present here but its surprisingly one of the less offensive even in recent memory due to how it is structured. There is also the option now of using what the game calls cheat mode, essentially a "tell me a story" difficulty this cuts out all leveling and gear hunting and just lets you experience the story. For anyone else actually interested how the game plays keep reading.
This game uses scaling to base how its entire system is structured, to put this simply a core statistic (typically your level) is picked by the game to "weigh" more than others and has much more bearing on how the other statistics will perform. So in .Hack level is everything. You could have 1 million HP, but if enemy was 20 levels higher than you it'd still kill you in just a few hits. Once you realize this the game will feel a grind at first cause you feel shoehorned into leveling, except G.U. is the extreme end of this scaling so it allows leveling to be abused. The tolerance gap is 10 levels, if you fight anything outside of 10 levels from you the scaling gets extreme and murders you quickly, but if you stay just on the bleeding edge of the 10 levels you gain experience extremely fast and cap out for the respective volume in around just a couple hours each volume if that. That brings me to something else that should be discussed, the volume splits.
Back in the ps2 era these volumes were completely separate games connected solely by the player's save data, one of the larger hopes when they released Re;code would be they connected the games together fully. They did not do this but instead put them all in a sort of emulated launcher which while is not ideal, it works well enough. It also shows the progression of the series very clear as each volume got more added to it, vol 1 feeling very barren. This kinda adds to the pseudo mmo feel as this makes you feel like you're experiencing content updates. Which of course is important to the whole experience of giving you a fake mmo experience.
This comes to the biggest draw of the games, the pseudo mmo experience and its story. This is the thing that kept me playing despite faults, I loved the story and setting of this series. They go to great lengths to try to make you feel immersed in a fictional breathing world, from other players posting on forums and communicating, to world news posts explaining the issues of this game's "real" world. This latter aspect also becomes an interesting time capsule showing what were issues back when the game was made, and can be neat in its own right. The main plot of the games can be a little hard to follow at times as it never truly explains some aspects and leaves it up to the imagination, this is fine so long as you take it simply as that. In all the characters and story to me are the biggest selling point of the game and kept me playing even through its more dull points.
I would have had a very large complaint on them releasing G.U. without the original .hack cause people would be lost story wise if not for one thing, they had the forethought to include the terminal disc from the original ps2 release. The terminal disc was an extra mode that is purely story content that not only explains the original .hack which is handy for people new to the series, it also explains some of the real world happenings leading up to and during G.U.
Vol 4 Reconnection
This will be short as the game itself is pretty dang short, vol 4 can be finished in about 2 hours. This new volume was an extra that came with the re;code repackaging that concludes the G.U. story pretty much definitively. I sort of have a mixed feeling about this, without spoilers there is a bonus ending in vol 3 that acted as the true end at the time, and while it left some things up in the air, I thought it was a decent enough ending. Vol 4's ending and content puts a very bittersweet feeling to how everything ends which I am not sure I like. As for the gameplay there's not much to say as you barely get to play anything and most of the games features are disabled in this volume. The games cut scenes take step forward and step back at the same time by being fully animated yet having some uncanny motion to them, making them feel sort of stop motion.
Its clear to me that they took what they had of the at the time canceled vol 4 and stitched it together so the game could run. The story becomes boarderlne incoherent at points as the "middle" that would fill in details is missing, it jumps from main story beat to main story beat till it finishes. In all there's not much to complain about I guess if you think of this simply as an extra to the whole package, but if you were going to get this purely for Reconnection, I'd think about it a bit more.
In all however the package is great for its price and still a top notch story as long as we leave vol 4 out of the equation. I recommend this.

So I have been a fan of .hack for about a good 10 years now and when I heard that Last Recode was coming out with a new volume I was very excited. To those of you who havent played .hack before granted this isnt the best starting point but it should do if you wanna get interested in the series (The original Quadrilogy you cant get anymore but you can probably still watch the anime for it.)
(Warning I will probably spoil a tiny bit of Volume 4 but only in a gameplay sense)
The first game of this series Rebirth feels a little bit sluggish from the other 3 games. The story can start off a bit slow and you will be doing a lot of grinding that doesnt feel contributes to the game. That being said if you can get through the first game you will be through most of the slow parts of the game (When I mean slow parts I mean that the story feels like it doesnt progress as well as the other games do.)
The second game is personally my favourite out of the original GU games because it fixes a lot of problems that the first game had. The new Multi-Trigger system allows you to change weapons on the fly when you use that weapons skill. So say if you wanna switch from Dual Sword to Scythe you can do so while in battle instead of having to change and waiting like a few seconds in battle to switch from the first game. This story will tear you up it probably has the most character development and if you are emotionally attached to characters you will learn a bit more about them.
The Third game in the series is my second favourite cause it keeps the same formula as all the other games. Haseo grows a lot in personality and learns a lot from every person you have met in the world. This game is probably the game you will be spending the most Post game time on instead of the actual game because there is a LOT to do at the end of this game. Back when I played this I probably spent 10 hours on the main game with 30-40 hours in Post Game.
And then we get to Volume 4. Which honestly shouldnt be called its own volume but rather half of a volume with nothing but linear storyline. When you open up Volume 4 EVERYTHING you could do on the desktop you cannot access. When you go through the game you will soon realize that there is no free roam of what you want to do. The game locks you to the story and it feels very iffy. I feel like after all this work I have done in the post game for Volume 3 to only find everything locked it doesnt feel good. Really good atmosphere and general artstyle could make this game rise above the others. Unfortunately, I feel that when compared to other puzzle \ platformer games, visuals and sounds are really the only thing that Limbo does well.
There are a few puzzles that are very smart and challenging, but most of the times you'll find the solution right away and you'll have to push some block or run very slowly to the solution. It's boring and irritating to have to spend so much time to solve a puzzle that you could have solved right away... and it's even more irritating to die while solving it, because you jumped a tenth of a second too early ( timing is really the essential skill in here) Other times I felt deaths were a little cheap, with objects that are virtually unavoidable on your first try, since you can't \ won't really see them hanging out in the darkness.
Also, the story. This is very much a personal opinion (as the rest of the review, btw)  and I know plenty of people like open ended stories or having to fill in the spots. Still, this is way too much if you ask me. There are so many websites arguing about what this game means, and that's because nothing is explained at all. You wake up in a forest, run away from a spider, then other things, at some point from other humans, then machines, then you find a girl. And I know lots of hints can be gathered by visual imagery, yet these are the only elements that one can know for sure about the plot.
Overall, this game is very short, unexplained and with a gameplay that can be both frustrating and boring. Yes, there are things to be loved here, but I'd suggest thinking twice before buying it (basically if you want something short, visually appealing and interesting, this might actually be for you)

Come on Down is a stereotypical movie that creates nonsterotypical scenarios, allowing its cast to explore the boundaries of this indie film. Although at times it drags, and other movies have already trod this path, Come on Down still manages to – if for a moment – create some comedic drama in a small town. For the current sale price, it is worthwhile if you have some time to burn and not much else going on.
Although the settings and scene may feel familiar from other films, here they allow the cast and actors to explore their connections and build a tentative, but enjoyable, rapport with each other. The clear breakout star is Mark the Manager (played by none other than Jon Robert Stafford), who succeeds in turning his character into that one person we all know and hate. This can be seen quite clearly in the motivational speech Stafford gives at the start of the film, ending with the inspiring and memorable “GO TEAM”.
Ultimately, despite its various shortcomings, Come on Down still manages to entertain for the short time it is in front of you. I wouldn’t trumpet this movie from the mountaintops, but certainly did pass the time. Watch it when it’s available on sale, or just look for the inevitable gifs that will be created.

LYNE is a game for people, who love to use their brain even in the spare time. It's perfectly suited for everyone, who wants to play just some minutes or long sessions up to 2 hours. Your task is simple. Connect the two main knots for each color and all knots of the color on the way between both. All knots have to be used. You're not allowed to cross lines or to use the same way, you've already used before. Sounds simple, right? But it can become very challenging, if you have to deal with several colors and neutral knots, which have to be used multiple times. Your brain can really melt in longer sessions and you should seriously stop, if you're starting to see lines, where they aren't supposed to be.
The game has 2 game modes: chapter mode (26 chapters (A-Z) with 25 levels per chapter) and daily challenges (3 chapters with 25 levels per chapter), which will be random generated every day.
Excellent game for a good brain workout. It's very cheap, addicting, easy to learn, offers difficulty levels in form of different chapters for everyone and has a very high replayability. If you love to use your brain, then LYNE will be perfect for you. Not recommendable for stones. Absolutely recommendable for everyone with a working human brain.

2 years ago this game was released as Ragnarok Online 2: Legend of the Second, a wonderful & more challenging time. Everything was kind of difficult to do and most of the time people rejected you because of not having a specific amount of health for raid dungeons.
September 12, 2013, they released the Noel class.
December 2013, (can't remember the specific date like the previous one) this game was renamed to Ragnarok Online 2: Advent of Valkyrie introducing Master Level. ***[Side Note, master level is pretty much rebirth on RO1 but ONLY your display level is reset back to 1 (51).]*** With master level, the older content became easy to do. Until the ramped up the difficultly on the raid dungeons, still soloable if you have the right gears and junk. That same year, the korean server closed.
October 2014, the SEA server merged with us making the game iRO2 (International Ragnarok Online 2) and a sperate server called "Freyja."
July 28, 2015, the TW server merging with Freyja.
---UPDATE---
The last major update was the remake of Forgotten Payon and boosting the level cap to 85 (ML35). In August they will be releasing Jawaii, the honeymoon place from RO1. Awhile back they said that a marriage system would not be added with Jawaii but according to the "Will you marry me?" event on the forums, it might be added. (Ovvvvvver jooooooyed)

There are folks on the forums here on steam saying that the camera and movement is terrible. This is a re-review of this game post-release. I don't usually write reviews of games, but I felt compelled to write this in response to some of the fair yet slightly misleading user reviews I see on the front page.
** THE PROBLEM WITH USER REVIEWS **
Firstly, I don't like steam's user review system. I have no idea how to fix it either. The problem is apparent with games like this, which have some legit criticisms from some gamers, but others would find it immensely enjoyable. The button that "upvotes" reviews is labelled "helpful", but I do believe that a bad review can be helpful without my holding the same opinion. On top of that, it seems that people with a lot of review "helpfuls" have a large group of friends or are in guilds, etc. I am not criticizing anyone...just a flawed system that might lead people away from a niche game that many would enjoy.
** GAMEPLAY **
In fiction, there is a thing called a trope. A trope is a often used device, such as a fallen hero or a damsel in distress. These things can be over used, and genre fiction has a habit of creating whole works based on them. The point of a trope is to use something people are comfortable with so that they can spend their efforts enjoying the important bits...like characterization, or sometimes a fresh look at an old trope. Tropes are a creators shorthand because wholly new things are dense and difficult. The greatest works of literature and film use tropes, some creating new tropes, so that they aren't over long and dull.
The gameplay in this game is the trope. It is resource management, fetch quests and stealth. While the game is not quite a survival horror game, it uses the same limitations for an effect that I will get into in the next section. There are games which expand what a game can do...some successful, some not. This is not one of those games, nor does it try to be. You will understand what is expected from you early on and you will be doing it a lot. I would like to point out that the combat in this game can be easy for some, but I would contend that this game is not about hammering through with a weapon and those people who do are missing the point.
** MOOD **
This is where this game shines. Back in the 1960's, some folks at a small British movie company decided to remake an old classic film, Dracula. By that time everyone had seen the original Bela Lugosi film, so really what is the point in remaking a film when everyone already knows the plot? The answer is mood. Hammer films are not gory in the way contemporary films are, they are not jump scary, they ooze creepy. There is something of the molester in Cristopher Lee's performance in Dracula: Prince of Darkness, something that is in the original text, but sadly missing in Bela Lugosi's self-indulgent performance. And yet, Hammer films always have a wit. It is a mood that had never been reproduced in gaming...until now.
I roleplay this game. What I mean is that it might be possible to manhandle the robots, but I refuse to try because I let the mood sink in. I am more quick to run from the dogs than wisely set a trap for them. Not because I am a bad gamer, but because I let myself get into the environment. In sucking at this game I heighten my enjoyment of it. Winning is not the point of a game like this, experiencing it is. Ultimately, Dracula gets a stake in the heart, the end. This could have happened on page one, but it didn't.
** STORY **
There isn't one, and thank god for that. I am so sick of game makers thinking they are novelists because they largely suck at it. With some exceptions, almost all being in the adventure game category (I hated Bioshock Infinite,) good stories in games are second rate rehashes of better novels or movies. If I want character development or a solid plot I will read a book. If you don't read books and need videogames to get some narrative, well then please don't breed.
That isn't to say there isn't a narrative. There is, but it is one that I felt I was creating myself. Gone are the overwrought cgi cutscenes. Gone are the "easter egg hunt" notes on why we are here. What you have is a series of islands, some evil robots, and an attempt at surviving impossible odds.
** CONCLUSION **
This game isn't for everyone. Anyone who reads the negative reviews should take them to heart. But I am aware that people will see the number of "helpfuls" and think that is a vindication of their opinion, rather than what it says...it is helpful. I greatly enjoyed this game for the mood and emotive character of the world and level design. I had no problem jumping through the fake hoops required to spend some time within. But fake hoops they are. If you want an original experience, a successful experiment, check this one out.

I don't think I've ever said this about a game before, but the writing makes me want to punch myself in the face. It's not bad English, it's just supernaturally bland. Banal is not a word I've ever had cause to use before, and I'm using it now.
It's like...
You know how five year olds write? Maybe all the words are in the right places because the teacher helped them out a bit, and maybe their spelling's all been fixed with red pen, but the story still reads like a grocery list?
That's Chroma Squad. That's Chroma Squad in its excruciating, every-mission-is-a-plot-mission tedium.
This would be tolerable, I guess, but the gameplay is boring too. Even on the hardest difficulty, missions just take longer to clear, and most of that time is hammering away at putties waiting for something to actually threaten you.
There's a whole resource management/business sim back end to the game and that, at least, isn't boring, but it's grindy and obnoxious instead. You try to farm enough resources to craft new gear while deploying advertising bonuses to get new fans and increase revenue from viewership, while pumping your stats with a few small global bonuses, so that you can quickly and efficiently win the next mission with lots of style and max out your money gain.
That's not awful, but it ends with you playing the mission, which is.
If you liked Knights of Pen and Paper, you'll like this. It's a time-waster with bright colors and a surprisingly pleasant soundtrack. It has good design ideas but they're somehow lost in the implementation - like a cannoli and kidney milkshake.
I tried hard to enjoy Chroma Squad, and I recognize that other people may have quite different experiences with the game, but at the end of the day, it's still just...

Chroma Squad is a little, cute game that has spend a fair bit of time just laying in my library. I liked the premise and got my hands on the game, but didn't feel the pressure to try and play it for a while.
I have finally decided to give it a shot, and I honestly can't say that I regret that decision. The game is a tactical RPG with minor management elements - you control a squad of five (and later - six) characters, who will fight against sets of enemy minions and bosses. I am not going to discuss a premise, because it is very clearly stated in the description.
What I will say, that gameplay-wise, the game is pretty good at what it does. Game is split in two phases - episodes (which consist of combat) and studio management. The combat system is simple, but enjoyable - your characters can use simple melee attacks, weapons and their abilities. There is also a teamwork system, which allows you to attack with a few characters at the same time. In some episodes you also get control of special characters which have some unique abilities of their own.
The management part of the game is less robust and in many ways confusing. You can craft equipment for your squad, you can upgrade studio equipment which comes with different bonuses, and you can choose a marketing agency, which also provides you with a set of benefits based on your fans. That part of it all is, however, fairly simplistic and lacks any real depth.
The game makes good use of it's theme, and most of the game is enjoyably cheesy. If that's something you are not into, you will probably not enjoy your time with Chroma Squad. It does also take a bizzare twist half way through, but it only adds to the experience in my opinion.
There is a single place where the story diverges. It isn't a huge difference, honestly, and happens very late into the game. If you are going to unlock all the achievements, you will have to play through the game three times - and about 80% of each playthrough is going to be identical, sadly.
There are some minor issues that I have with the game. The mech combat is extremely repetitive, and if you are planning on finishing up the game in short period of time (I personally did last 2 seasons in one sitting), you will have to do A LOT of mech fighting. A system which is a cool idea, but execution of it is rather lackluster, and you will always be doing the same thing. No matter who you are fighting, the enemy will always have the same pattern - either three basic attacks or one large attack. You just sit there and click the same button time after time, hoping for RNG to work out for you.
Another issue right now is the scarcity of information - or at least information which is not being presented in a clear way. There are some terms thrown around without much explanation at all, and at other times information that you could need at any given time is not given to you in the right place. Sure, you could remember it - but you shouldn't have to. I didn't realise you could read buffs and debuffs on your enemy until the last season, because of how unintuitive it is.
While the game has it's flaws, I would still recommend it. There is nothing that actively makes it less fun - the mech combat is a bit of a drag, and management could use more work, but the episodes themselves, with turn-based combat and abilities to use, can be really fun.
It's a small and enjoyable experience overall.

READ CONCLUSION FIRST IF YOU TL;DR.
HD remaster of PS2 games + a short vol 4 to give a closing. Has its issues but not a bad port (I'm looking at you, Fractured But Whole).
Bad things:
* Random Crashes, which are not often.
* Difficulty (laughable, but we are waiting for difficulty mods).
* Poor graphic optimization (makes FPS drop to 30 or below in cities), which can be turned off for performance and it still looks beautiful (or you can just add a mod that fix this)
Good things:
* Amazing story that happens in a MMORPG
* Fun gameplay (though it can be outdated to today standards, but remember; it's a 2006 game)
* "web and forum interaction", meaning you can read forums (which you can get wallpapers, advices and unlock in-game stuff) and news that tells the current state of that universe (everything electronic and computarized, VR goggles, etc), which basically mirrors our current world (though this game was released in 2006).
Note: This game offers 20 hs average per volume, and it offers replayability to max everything. Also has data transfer, so if you finish game 1 and use that save for game 2 everything you had carries over.
Conclusion: Buy it on sale or after a patch, because unless you're a fan of the saga, 50 bucks (though I got it cheaper) for a game that crashes is not worth it, even though you're actually paying 50 bucks for 4 games.

It really is hard for a gamer, when a game put you between loving a game or just hating it. Now for a moment, close your eyes and forget about all the DLC's they have put out in the first week of it's release (Let's stop the Hate for a second). Now my review is based solely on the Base game that they have released.
The idea when it was first shown really interested me and I am definitely sure that like me, many gamers were waiting for this game eagerly. I for one constantly kept tracking the Game's news, video reveals of the monsters, gameplays shown at game conferences. It really got me hyped, plus I was happy that Turtle Rock Studios got a good Game at their hands - A game which was getting positive reviews. Now that the game released, what's my reaction? Read on to know.
Evacuation, Hunt, Rescue, Nest and Defend <- Individually all these game modes are fun, at least for me it was fun and I am enjoying it.
The Hunters must kill the Monster before it can destroy the power relay located in the map. The Monster must reach stage 3 in order to destroy the relay, though it can also opt to kill all of the Hunters.
Six Monster eggs are located in random locations on the map. The Monster must protect them from the Hunters for 18 minutes, and can hatch one of the eggs to spawn a minion to help it. The Hunters must destroy all six eggs, as well as any minions, within the time limit to win.
Injured colonists trying to escape the Monsters are placed randomly on the map. Hunters need to locate, revive and protect them as they make their escape. The monster needs to kill as many of these colonists as possible and keep them from getting away. Whoever saves—or kills—five colonists first wins.
A starship's refueling station comes under the assault of a player-controlled fully evolved monster and smaller Goliath minions. The hunters must stop the monster from causing a catastrophic accident by protecting the power generators until the ship is fully powered, while the monster must destroy two generators to reach the ship's power source. These are the 4 Base game modes available in the game and Evacuation is an interesting concept which boasts about having more than 800,000 different outcomes - Evacuation is a short Campaign style game where all these 4 game modes may be included. Average time for an Evacuation campaign is around 45-60 mins.
I will keep the Game Play part short as it is quite easy to get a hold off. Once you go through the tutorial and watch the videos provided, you will be ready to tackle the game head on. Controls are okay, controlling the hunters feels like the usual FPS style and controlling the monster is a whole different ball game but it is quite fun in the end.
Who said the game had any story? jokes aside, Evolve is set on Shear, a distant planet located in the "Far Arm" of space, that humanity has traveled to in the distant future. The established colonies, considered the most valuable in this region of space, are soon attacked by malevolent alien Monsters (Where did I hear this before?). As the Monsters destroy the colonies on Shear, a former planet tamer named William Cabot is brought out of retirement to deal with the threat, in order to evacuate the remaining colonists from Shear. In response, Cabot assembles a team of Hunters—consisting of war veterans, psychopaths, professionals, and expendables—to eliminate the Monsters, setting the main conflict of Evolve
The Ambient sound is beautiful - the environment really gets you in. The Voice acting has been done pretty good and it really makes you care a little about the characters that you are playing. (You usually hear them talking throughout the game and usually at the start - it's quite neat). Now the Monster part - When it Roars and it keeps running around in the distance, an uncertain fear gets inside your heart - you wait in uncertainty as to when you're gonna find him. Whether you will win or die? If he gets to Stage 3, than find a place to die :) No seriously.

This is probably the best multiplayer shooter up to date.
The game is semi-realistic, which means it tries to be both realistic and fast at the same time. A single bullet means death if it hits head, heart or lungs (in case of lungs it's not an immediate death though as you can still shoot while dying), but a bullet to less vital parts of a body will only cause a wound. A bullet shot into enemy's weapon will effectively disarm him. Granades are very deadly as they should be, which is important to mention, because in many games their effectiveness is downplayed. Wounded legs will slow you down, wounded arms will negatively affect your accuracy.
The game is very fast as there are "tickets" that let players respawn until they run out, hence there usually isn't too much turtling and the game heavily discourages such tactics anyway due to maps, use of artillery and so on. Many maps allow multiple tactics as they usually allow two (sometimes even more) points to attack for a team, hence the defenders need to spread out, and attackers can decide where to focus on pushing the enemy forces.
The game provides multiple classes to choose from, but the better and more important ones are limited, and interestingly not every player is equal - some get better weapons, some get worse, but also some are leaders, while others are cannon fodder. But it is fun regardless of what class you are playing (although you might have your favourite one). The game isn't about being the best in the team, it's about helping the team. It is very encouraged by the game's mechanics and affects the game in a very significant way, hence why the game doesn't play like another random multiplayer shooter #241221. It's unique in its own way. I definitely recommend it to everyone who enjoy multiplayer action games, regardless if they prefer realism or arcade, as this game is somewhere in-between (albeit inclines more towards realism than arcade). The only negative things I can say about this game is that albeit its realism, bullets do not penetrate objects (which is a serious flaw), and the fact that unlike previous games by Tripwire RO2 doesn't support anything besides Windows operating system.

When I first went to the store page and saw the wave of negative revierws, I was startled and confused. Turtle Rock has done provably well with co-op shooters in the past, and from the Alpha and Beta experiences I had, Evolve was gearing up to be a game I'd really enjoy. And so far, the backlash is all the same- compalints about the dlc,a nd not the actual game itself.
I must emphasize this point- THIS GAME IS QUITE FUN. The characters all have their own playstyles and utility, and the levelling system rewards you for fully utilizing and learning to use each character's kit. The monster play is more difficult than one would think at first, but it still is every sort of rewarding when you get to play a hulking beast made of terror and Godzilla copyright infringement.
The complaints about day-one dlc is fair, I suppose, but seeing as all the dlc is vanity items or the season pass, i am in no way offended. The skins are fairly priced for a non-vital vanity set, and look great. And as for the season pass, that is an industry standard now, and it isn't Evolve's fault for joining in. One would be wise to acknowledge that all upcoming maps will be given for free to all owners of the game, which is something that much of the industry fails to do (Call of Duty, I'm looking at you). The only egregious price imbalance is that of the monster slated for release, both of them coming in at a hefty $14.99. Though one is a free bonus to all who pre-ordered, the price tag still feels notably steep.
All in all, though, if you really want to judge this game for what you find in the bax, here are the facts:
It is a multiplayer game that has a single-player option that is actually still fun by yourself.
The gameplay is fun, polished, and challenging.
The graphics are gorgeous.
I recommend this game, and in a standard out-of-ten scale, I would rate this an 8.5.

Buy? Yes.
LYNE is a simple and crisp puzzler that requires players to connect shapes on a grid with lines that are not allowed to overlap (unless there is a later mechanic in the game for such a thing). The player must use limited space and combination of connector pieces to have all shapes connected to their "endpoints".
This game is very clever and I think it hits the difficulty curve mostly right on the head (I found some puzzles easier than prior ones). It also seems like the player can eventually figure out any puzzle through pure trial of elimination, though that may take much time. So even if you have a hard time with a puzzle, just try all the possible combinations until you win. Lyne is also often used by Steam users to decorate their profile with words using the alphabetical acheivements from beating each "world".
I can easily recommend, especially due to it's low price. When it's on sale, it is often less than $1 which is arguably a steal for the quality and value of the game.

SUPERHOT is a FPS game in which you need to overcome obstacles and kill "red dudes" to progress while you have the ability that time only moves when you move.
Pros:
-The concept behind SUPERHOT is superb, with time only moving when you move. The game thus feels like it strays from true FPS to more of a puzzle/FPS game to me, as you need to plan each move you make before you make them, or be killed by the red dudes.
-The endless mode and challenge mode kept me entertained for quite a few hours, as killing red dudes constantly brought me joy
-The simple ploygonal graphics combined with only red, white and black as colours used within the game add a nice contrast and draw your attention to what is happening aroung you within the game
-Controls are smooth and extremely responsive
-The game has a slight learning curve, but once you get into it, it is really good. Almost anyone can pick-up this game and figure out how to play it and have a good time
-There is a lot of bonuses within the game which are always fun to find
Cons:
-The story itself is extremely pretentious, and to top it off very short. Would've liked a more solid story and one that doesn't function as a time filler cause it is so short.
-The game feels overpriced at R269 (~$25), because of how short the story is
SUPERHOT is a great game, and one of the games I've had the most fun with in a long time. Pick it up on a sale if you can.

Reigns is an interactive, erm, how-are-you-gonna-die story that lets you play as a King in charge of a Kingdom. You simply choose from two possible options by clicking/swiping/etc either left or right.
The main goal is to stay alive for as long as possible, while the background story develops. To that end, you manage four main resources (I believe they would go as: Church, Population, Army, Treasury) and try to keep a fragile balance between them. The game isn't simply about stacking the resources: in fact, you'll die in an event if you cap out the Treasury bar.
Of course, as the background story requires, there's more to it than just those resources.
You might just die seemingly randomly at times... Then take a look at the bigger picture, things might be going on behind the scenes.
Overall, the game itself is rather simple, but can keep you busy for a while as you try to understand just what's going on in the background, while your kings are just dying one after another for idiotic reasons. It's not without flaws, but it's very well polished, and definitely an interesting concept.
Did I mention it's just 3$/3€ too ?

RTS is my favourite genre though I mainly like base building RTS games like Age of Empires 2 and Red Alert 2.
I never really liked the games where you just have some units and you will have to do everything with that.
However, one day I won a steam key for this game and since I like Petroglyph Games and saw the first (oldest) 3 Star Wars movies I was pretty excited.
Since I mostly played base building games and didn't focus much on micro management I had to take some time to get into this game. At first I didn't fully understand why this game was received so well beside it's nice (Star Wars) atmosphere. However when I played some more and got further into the campaign I began to understand that also the gameplay was quite fun :).
Positive:
- The Star Wars part of the game is VERY well done. The models look great, the landscapes, flora, fauna and weather are nicely done, the sound effects and music are good and the Star Wars characters are also well done. If you are a Star Wars fan, that part of the game won't disappoint you. The atmosphere of the game is just really nice.
- Apart from the Star Wars part the graphics and design is well done. The user interface looks nice and is easy to use, the graphics look good, the models are pretty detailed, the terrain is detailed, effects are also nice.
- The gameplay is quite nice. You have a galaxy  map on which you can manage your planets. You can build structures on planets, trains/produce units if you have the necessary structures, research/steal tech, spy etc. There are units for on land and units for in space. All units can freely travel to planets in real time (though the galaxy map can be paused). Some planets are connected via some sort of travel lane which makes travelling between those planets faster which may prove benificial when controlling the planets. some planets have room for more building than others and planets may have bonuses if you control them. You can capture planets by destroying all ground buildings and units of the opponent controlling the planet. Before you can land your ground units on a planet you need to clear the space units around the planet (in a space battle) along with the space station and perhaps defences though none of these thing may be present (which makes it more easy :)).
On land battles you need to destroy the enemy base (if there is one, can be build on the galaxy map) and all enemy units. The map layouts are quite nice. There are hardpoints spread around the map which can be captured and then used to put turrets on. There are infantry only zones, native threats (or allies) and wheather effects. If you got bombers in orbit of the planet you can call in bombing runs.
Negative:
- Gameplay may become somewhat monotone. Though this may also just be me, because I get that more often.
Conclusion:
If you like Star Wars and RTS games that focus more on tactics then this is probably a very nice game for you. If you mostly like basebuilding RTS games then you should be somewhat more carefull. I think this is a pretty good game and would rate it somewhere around 80/100, but it just isn't for everybody.

Five stunt doubles quit their job and start their own sentai show in Chroma Squad, a turn based tactical RPG. If you’re not familiar with the sentai genre, it’s basically costumed people doing goofy acrobatics and occasionally piloting giant robots to fight space monsters and other wacky stuff, and this game features all of that. You even get to name your team (I picked Colorblind Crusaders to be ironic) and can customize all of their catch phrases.
Each of your team members has a role that defines how you will use them in combat. The scout typically runs ahead to stun groups of enemies or pick off individual monsters. Support heals and technician has a variety of useful skills and long distance attacks. Lead and Assault are for tanking and damage dealing respectively. All characters have their own skill tree that expands with new selectable skills every season.
This game features an assist system where a character ends their turn and becomes available for throwing other characters across the battlefield. If you put characters in assist mode while surrounding a monster and attack with a non-assist character, you will perform a team attack for additional damage. Finally, placing all five members of your squad in assist mode surrounding a monster initiates a special finishing move that does a lot of damage.
A major underlying system in Chroma Squad is the audience meter. You gain audience by successfully completing levels. To keep things interesting, each level has director’s instructions that are essentially mini-quests ranging from “defeat the monster with a finishing move” or “attack the monster with lead 5 times”. Audience is turned into cash at the end of each episode and can be used with various marketing agencies to give your squad various different bonuses as well as additional cash. Cash is then used to buy armor or weapons or crafting materials to make specialized gear.
If I had to sum up Chroma Squad with one word it would probably be “cozy”, if only because of the soundtrack and overall graphic theme. Try listening to the OST on youtube and you’ll see (or hear rather) what I mean. I really liked the simplified retro-look as well, it has sort of a late-era SNES feel to it which fits perfectly with the game’s style. There are all sorts of little campy details like the characters doing different silly poses when they’re the focus of conversation or the omnipresent recording crew following you to every single battle and staying just out of harm’s way.
All of this comes with a nasty catch though; there are some significant performance issues in this game. My rig is capable of doing VR games no problem but I still had loads of framerate drops at random parts of the game. The good news about this is that it typically won’t effect your playthrough due to the tactical nature of the game, but it will be a bit of a pain for giant robot fights where you have a QTE during the monster’s turn that requires you to click at a precise time to defend.
If you are in to sentai-style stuff at all, you will probably love Chroma Squad. Even if you aren’t though, this game is still fun for anyone who would enjoy a tactical rpg like Disgaea or Final Fantasy Tactics.

text:
I really want to like this game. I really, really do. I'm a huge fan of Tokusatu shows and I love Power Rangers and Super Sentai. I also love strategy games, business managers and RPGs. This game is based off Power Rangers, is a strategy game and has business manager elements. Sounds like a combo made in heaven, right? Well...I've tried to play through it over 3 times now and every time I just get tired of it. It's not a bad game, really, but it reeks of poor design choices.
But I don't want it to seem like I hate the game, so lets talk about the positives of the game.
The game looks gorgeous. Pixel art sometimes feels lazy, but this game makes it look really nice. Sprites are put together nicely and are animated well. The maps in particular look sweet, I especially love the city block with the toy store map.  The pieces of gear you can craft also look great, most end game gear even looks like cool Power Ranger suits. The animations your characters do when they fight enemies are also done really well and just feel like they really connected. The sound effects really help in making every hit feel like it landed too.
The gameplay itself is also fun. It's simple, very simple, but fun. It's a basic SRPG affair. Units move across a grid map and punch enemies in the face. Some classes like the Tech Guy can hit enemies from afar and each class has their own skills to spice it up a bit. You only get 5 Rangers (missed opportunity for a dope 6th Ranger to join you), so the actual strategy element is a bit lite.
Now for the bad...
The story...oh dear the writing. The writing in this game can range from just plain boring to borderline offensive statements that make no sense, but I want to avoid that can of worms so let's just talk about the other way the writing just isn't very good.
First of all, the actual show you produce doesn't seem to have any sense of internal continuity with itself. You don't really see this unbelievably powerful alien king plotting his plan to take over earth in the show itself. That's like, a trait in Power Rangers since MMPR. Lord Zedd, Emperor Gruumm, Master Sledge etc, even the more fantasy ones had a similar antagonist. Almost every episode feels like a basic "Monster of the Week" episode. You only get to see the action elements of the show too, not the character development or world building Power Rangers is known for. The show you're running is boring and none of the episodes stand out. It's ironic because the actors you play as complain about the former show being all action and no substance.
Next off, the monsters you fight all seem like jokes with no substance or personality. Yes, Power Rangers had silly looking villains (Diabolico still makes me chuckle), but most of them are still meant to be taken seriously, and to an extent, are. Some monsters in Power Rangers look downright
. Lord Arcanon, Lord Zedd, Loki, Badussa, Koragg, Ransik, etc all look awesome and threatening. Meanwhile in Chroma Squad we get...that "has science gone to far" meme from a few years ago and a stop sign wizard...it's not very riveting.
Your characters have no portraits for dialogue either, nor do they change expression at all, which makes the mood hard to read. It's hard to take a serious seeming role with a half naked boxer perpetually in a "1-2 punch" animation cycle. Those issues I listed, plus the fact that if you get down to it, the plot boils down to a basic "leader who got full of himself and has to get back down to earth" scenario (Man, Power Rangers SPD had that plot resolved in like, an episode...) that just isn't fun or interesting.
When the plot actually does get going...it's just a typical villain arc with no flair or personality. The main bad guy is a joke in both literal and metaphorical senses. He has no menace to him. It's just a lady gaga parody. Imagine if we got someone like Lord Zedd, Octomus The Master, Emperor Gruumm or even King Mondo or Rita Repulsa to hijack the plot? That would've been 10 times more interesting then what we got. Heck, Power Rangers even had a similar villain to Lord Gaga named Heckyl...and they made him so much more interesting by giving him more depth then "he's feminine and girly".
Now, the bad parts of the gameplay. The bosses just feel like they're tailored made to be as counter productive to a strategy game as possible. The first major boss teleports around every turn -- which makes gaining distance to regroup feel pointless, can scatter your units -- which makes positioning feel pointless, can attack multiple times per turn -- which is just mean and can stun your units -- which just removes an aspect of strategy. Not only that, but he constantly summons ranged units, which widdle you down while he attacks your units twice a turn. What makes this even worse is that you're healer in this game is borderline worthless. 1 heal per 5 turns? Are you serious?
And it doesn't get better...Season 5 is where I always just give up. It's just not fun in the slightest at that point. Stage gimmicks become bull and enemies have way to much health. The fact that you can't save in episodes -- which can take up to an hour -- is just painful. Theirs no check points, once you feel an episode, that's GG, gotta re-do it unless you want those major drawbacks. What makes this even worse are the mech fights. Oh god the mech fights. The mech fights have literally no strategy to them at all. No extra skills, no items, no techniques, just "punch" and "super move". Winning or losing is based off your luck with RNG.
Character customization is also plagued with RNG. Getting crafting items is based off enemy drops or you can buy them in the store (Money is painfully scarce, mind you), so getting that piece of gear you need is up to chance. You think your characters are under equipped? Just got to live with it, I guess. You can't re-do episodes and theirs no way to grind reliably. If you're doing bad with drops, you just have to deal with it. Because of this, my squad always feels so lopsided, with my frail healer and scout getting all the good gear to cover their bad defenses, while my fighter and Red Ranger lack behind.
Speaking of your squad. You can create your own Ranger squad with 5 classes. Pretty basic stuff, you got your Red Ranger, Blue Ranger, Black Ranger, Yellow Ranger and Pink Ranger, but you can customize the colors. Each has a different bonus and skill variety. My issue with this is the actual people you get for your Rangers. Most characters you pick just seem like jokes. I would've liked a variety of normal looking humans. In the words of the wise Zordon "Alpha, Rita's escaped! Recruit a team of teenagers with attitude!".
That's probably just a nitpick on my end, but I just wish this game took something serious, you know? Everything feels like a joke. The characters are jokes, the mentor character is a joke, the plot is a joke, the monsters are jokes, the main villain is a joke. Theirs nothing to take seriously, nothing to really get into. Power Rangers had silly moments, but was meant to be taken seriously. This is just nothing but a joke. It's not a funny one either.
All in all, this game isn't bad, but it lacks substance, balance, depth and just fun.

Cuphead is a bullet hell game that mixes a '30s cartoon style with great graphics and incredibly smooth animation. It's got great gameplay and it can be a very difficult or normal difficulty game. You can either go for 100% grades, which, for your own sanity, I do not reccomend, unless you know what you're doing, or you can simply fight each boss and progress that way, which is how sane people will do it.
You will die plenty of times either way, but it doesn't punish you for dying, which is a very cheap move that most 'difficult' games, like Dark Souls, use. Instead of beating everything on your first try, you have to learn the patterns of the bosses, and try and try again until you eventually beat the boss, but once you do, it's very satisfying.
There are a few problems I have with this game, such as:
-The 8-direction aiming. It's very hard to use, although certain weapons like the Roundabout and Chaser don't really require aim
