It's a very interesting game, you have elements of a 4x4 game, a normal RTS game, and capture point RTS.
Simple explantion of a game: Many planets, some have perks. You first sent your fleet over, than you attack it and take control. You have pre-made units that you deploy to the plant. Than you build on the planet whatever you want.
I enjoyed the concept that you need more than one fleet to protect choke point planets and sometimes you need a ground presence, but generally if your fleet is destroyed and your planted is invaded it's not going to be much of a battle because you can only keep "X" amount of units actually on a planet.
The game starts to go wrong half way through the game:
1. Space battles. As the Empire you can not build normal tie fighters, they come from your crusiers. The Empire does feel stronger in space when you are the rebels, but when you play them they are capped at 20 compared to Rebels being caped at 25. Which would be fine, but you're two major big ships cost more points compared to the Rebels big ships.
Overall the space battles are interesting but at the same time you're fleet doesn't seem to respond very well to what you want them to do. More so when you hit a ships special ability.
2. Ground battles
When you play as the rebels your missle soilders are a key fuction, they deal a great deal of damage to vehicels. When you play as the Empire they seem to do even more against you. Which is fine in the long run, yet as the Empire you don't have any missle toting storm troopers.
Vehicles are too easily defeated, they seem to die quicker than soilders. More so they don't seem to deal a lot of damage, even the big ATT shots at the rebels soilders and the damage isn't near what you would think it would be. Yet somehow you need them.
The speeder bikes for the Empire are sort of pointless. They are suppose to drop a little bomb, but by the time you click on it your bike is blown apart, and your lone storm trooper is doomed. They are meant for exploring and doing quick bombing runs but it never works out. You don't need to scout...You know there are a ton of baddies (or goodies-depends how you feel about the rebels) in the location where you are sending them.
The Rebels assult speeder is basically untouchable, nothing the rebels have can really damage it. It's not like they do a lot of damage, but they can bring down your ATT with the cable lines. Since none of their soilders or tech have something to bring a flying unit down you have to hope there is a pod where you can build a missle bay. Even than your range is very limited.
The main isssue is the balance, there is not a lot of countering. Your standard battle is mostly about getting another capture point to bring in more units, and getting close enough to do a bombing run which destroys a building in one shot along with anything around it.  It's pretty much a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥contest latter in the game and you fighting till you can bomb again, 2-3 bombing and a capture point is how you win.  Strategy goes out the window.
With that said it's a fun game and even when the game isn't on sale it's worth playing. This is one of the games where it's not a thumbs up or a thumbs down, it's just OKAY. Hardcore Star war fans will probably love it, but it just seems like they could have done a lot more with the game.

The Positive: Cuphead is a BEAUTIFUL game. The graphics, the sound, the music - are completely accurate to what a 1930's cartoon would be in the day, and I've seen my fair share. The story is classic-feeling and (again) something a 1930's era cartoon would be about, and it's not complex. The price is fair, and there's no BS like in-game DLC, loot boxes, or the other junk that companies like *COUGH* [MOSTLY ALL OF THEM NOW] add to their games in order to repeatedly try and tap your wallet. The controls are basic and not overly-complex (I cover more on this - see "The Mixed" below) and the tutorial is fast and covers them quickly and makes you aware of what you need to know in order to progress through the game - which isn't too many. Overall, I think the developers did a great job and focused on the aspects that many companies sadly overlook - the gameplay. The level navigation, progression, and design is diverse and well thought-out. The only bug I found was a graphic that didn't disappear when it should have - the "crying tears" of the 'onion boss' didn't disappear after I had defeated it, and it remained during the rest of the level. However, I was only able to produce it once time and it didn't affect the gameplay.
The Mixed: While the game is themed around a 1930's cartoon, don't let the cartoon-style looks fool you - this game is BLOODY DIFFICULT! You can lower the difficulty down a notch but only on the battle-styled levels, not on the "gun and run" stages. The controls aren't complex and neither are the number of moves you're required to learn in order to play, but you better memorize them and you better become a master at which key does which, or you're not progressing at all. You press the X key instead of the Shift key and make a mistake, you're not finishing the level and you're better off just selecting "RETRY" in the pause menu and starting over. I don't count this as a negative, as I love challenges and I can't knock a game down because of that. This difficulty can be disheartening for some and motivating for others. However, I feel that when I play, there's a big frustration factor that the difficulty absolutely plays into. I'll play for one hour and exit the game having not progressed a single level. However, it's not frustrating to the level that I stop playing - I find myself coming back after taking a break and having at it some more. I will say this, however: I feel that I am progressing through the game partially by mastering the controls, but also because I'm memorizing exactly how the level plays and when I should move, jump, shoot, or dash. Again, I'm mixed on the difficulty. I feel that if I could knock the difficulty down a notch on all stages and take a lower score, the game would appeal to those who just want to play and without yelling a curse word after dying for the 10th time on the same level.
The Negative: Pretty much nothing. The only thing I call BS on is how I'll attempt to hit a pink object and it'll occasionally both count as a "success" (as in I successfully hit the object) and also count as a "hit" (meaning that the object hit me and knocks off 1 HP). It's miniscule and really not worth mentioning as a negative, but sorry - if you're going to make a game this difficult, you should expect people to call you out on things like that. Other than this, that's pretty much it.

This is probably the best multiplayer shooter up to date.
The game is semi-realistic, which means it tries to be both realistic and fast at the same time. A single bullet means death if it hits head, heart or lungs (in case of lungs it's not an immediate death though as you can still shoot while dying), but a bullet to less vital parts of a body will only cause a wound. A bullet shot into enemy's weapon will effectively disarm him. Granades are very deadly as they should be, which is important to mention, because in many games their effectiveness is downplayed. Wounded legs will slow you down, wounded arms will negatively affect your accuracy.
The game is very fast as there are "tickets" that let players respawn until they run out, hence there usually isn't too much turtling and the game heavily discourages such tactics anyway due to maps, use of artillery and so on. Many maps allow multiple tactics as they usually allow two (sometimes even more) points to attack for a team, hence the defenders need to spread out, and attackers can decide where to focus on pushing the enemy forces.
The game provides multiple classes to choose from, but the better and more important ones are limited, and interestingly not every player is equal - some get better weapons, some get worse, but also some are leaders, while others are cannon fodder. But it is fun regardless of what class you are playing (although you might have your favourite one). The game isn't about being the best in the team, it's about helping the team. It is very encouraged by the game's mechanics and affects the game in a very significant way, hence why the game doesn't play like another random multiplayer shooter #241221. It's unique in its own way. I definitely recommend it to everyone who enjoy multiplayer action games, regardless if they prefer realism or arcade, as this game is somewhere in-between (albeit inclines more towards realism than arcade). The only negative things I can say about this game is that albeit its realism, bullets do not penetrate objects (which is a serious flaw), and the fact that unlike previous games by Tripwire RO2 doesn't support anything besides Windows operating system.

I was a fan of the .hack//Quarantine series and picked this up to relive some nostalgia.
I was really surprised. Currently still on Rebirth, so if things change through the series I'm unaware of it. In my opinion, these games individually are worth the single price tag alone still if you are a fan of the series, so 4-in-1 is a great value.
Pros:
-Excellent remastering. The graphics weren't the only thing they touched on and there was clearly a LOT of work that went into this, it wasn't just a nostalgia cash grab.
-The remastered graphics actually look pretty good. It's not current-gen by any means, but there's times you'll have trouble believing this game is 11 years old.
-The combat is not quite what I loved from the Quarantine series, but it's still unique and fun and it keeps the player engaged.
-Tons of content. Like, a lot. The .hack world is so well built, it's a shame The World never made it to a full blown MMORPG spinoff in NA. Plus, this is 4-games in one.
-The option to either play through the game as it was originally intended, or accelerated with a built-in cheat mode if all you care about is the story. Very nice player comfort feature.
-Content is not just within the game itself. There's a simulated social hub featuring clips and stories that is actually really well done.
Cons
-Character voice acting is inconsistent. Sometimes it's great, other times it's awful.
-Not a fan of the generation or combat in this series. The Quarantine series felt a lot more open to me, but it's fair to say there are benefits to this style as well.
-Game is 11 years old. While this is a proper remaster with a lot of new content, it still suffers from the limitations of 11 year old mechanics.
-Not releasing a Quarantine remaster before this. Playing the Quarantine series at the very least is helpful to understanding what's going on in the story. If you are new to the series, I'd highly recommend playing the first half of the .hack games first.
Here's to hoping this remastering was intended to help a new team develop a next-gen .hack game.

LIMBO follows a young boy out in the woods, alone, and with no further purpose but to walk forward. The story is very silent but the subtlty and atmosphere within it do far more justice to it than an entire paragraph of dialogue could ever do. The world that you walk through feels like a world that was abandonded by giants that inhabited long ago, and left their ancient machinery to rot as the only memorandum of their existence. This also could be designer's anxieties for a world we're slowly sucking the life out of with our technology.
The world is very claustrophobic, ominous, and tense for every step you take forward. But within this desolate, post-apocalyptic landscape, there is a shimmering hope that extends before you: the butterfly and the girl. Those brief glimpses urged me onwards, believing that there was something good in this world inhabited by horrible monsters, untrustworthy people, and deadly machinery. But the game is as depressing from its immediate beginning to its abrupt ending. From how heartlessly you forge onward as the protagonist, you might start to realize how much of a psychopath he is. Perhaps the world is dangerous... but isn't he just as much of a dangerous force inside it? And what do you think that says about you, the player?
Philosophy aside, the game is a wonderful 2D platformer. The shadow child controls well and the puzzles are all excellently laid out so that you can figure them out within a reasonable amount of time. There are a few denser puzzles here and there, but nothing too ridiculous. The game is pretty straightforward.
The sound design is also top-notch, save a few moments where I noticed some stock sounds (Like the a-oo-ga of a car engine used in cartoons, and some sound effects I'm pretty sure were ripped from Half-Life). The world feels empty and dead, yet flickering with the faintest amount of life somewhere deep inside it. And the visuals are obviously gorgeously. I'm sure you can see the screenshots for the game page yourself. This is a beautiful game that uses its black, white, and grey palette to produce some magnificent backgrounds and truly memorable enemies.
Despite the over-reliance on puzzles here and there, LIMBO is a truly magnificent game. There are few games out there that choose to have absolutely no sound within the game (the only few exceptions I can think of are ICO and the original DOOM... to a certain extent), and it serves this ominous and depressing video game. This is a truly artistic game that deserves a score of 9/10.

And as  a monster you are sneaking, feeding, evolving, then surgically picking off the other players. Or if your a goliath, brutally bashing there skulls and spamming all your abilities by rolling your face across the keys.
It also takes some time to experience all that the game has to offer, as you must play and level for several hours to unlock more abilities and characters.
The game is simple, no campaign, (well not a traditional one), with very few game modes and monsters. But it doesn't matter. It's still fun as hell. Trust me you wouldn't want too many classes, it would be too hard to form your strategy on either side with so many variables to consider. Even amongst the small selection there are many diverse strategies to employ.
I held of on giving this game a verdict before clocking in a great amount of hours, in fear of the repetition growing boring over time. 50 matches later, and I am leagues from having my fill with this game. I sometimes skip doing other important things to play more Evolve, regrettably, such as sleeping... don't judge me.
"But what about the overpriced DLC?" What? You mean the skins that you don't even notice. I purchased one of them just to see if it would make an impact. I didn't even realize they were there. I wouldn't even use these items if they were free. So don't waste your money on them.
The only thing of worth is the season pass which includes new classes, but as for the rest of the DLC, its worthless so who cares how much it costs. It doesn't withhold game modes, or content from the game itself. Think of it as paying an extra $50 for a collector's edition which many do. It's only decoration. Crappy decoration.
The last complaint i get is that the game cost too much. Your on PC, why the hell are you buying a game for full price? That's what♥♥♥♥♥is for!
This game is fantastic, and I will most likely never stop playing this game until the servers stop working, should that day ever come. I would buy the sequel if it came out tomorrow, at full price even just because it was that damn good.

You begin alone, in littlemore then a loin cloth with a crude sword.  From there you are in much the same situation as your character. Your trying to figure everything out, But unlike your character you will survive the errors aspect of the many trials and errors you are going to experience.

At first, I went into a boss battle unprepared, and the 2 characters I had died. I tried again. The 2nd time, I forgot to load healing items onto them, because I forgot that even potions had to be manually loaded into each character's inventory slots. (Each character has 3 inventory slots, and items do not stack.)
I considered those efforts part of a learning curve, and didn't mind too much. I also hit ALT+F4 a few times in the second attempt, and reloaded in, just to see if there was any way to win without those healing items. Doing that would restart the battle at the beginning, and forget the bruising the characters just took. Yet, despite a fresh try, there wasn't a way to win without those healing items. This means that, at least sometimes, your characters need every bit of help they can get. The boss battle, which ended this second attempt, was one such time.
With these lessons learned, I tried a third time. I did better but it still wasn't being enjoyable. I found decent loot, but the battles were tedious. I led enemies into grenades, into poison spouts of blue on the map and, when there were bug-like creatures, then I let the human and bug NPCs fight each other, since they didn't get along. But this wasn't any sort of high-strategy ordeal, and it was repetitive and boring to keep doing.
Then, suddenly, a fight went poorly. An electric grenade was thrown and, unlike other grenades, it went off on impact and did a large amount of damage. My character had a healing item, used it, and was fine. I thought his survival was due to his armor, since he was decently decked out. I was being good about putting the best armor that I could find onto them. The battle was won, and things went the same as before. Then another grenade was used in a fight, and did an instant one-hit kill. There was no way to avoid it. It happened at the beginning of the battle, when the character was fine on health.
This means that not only is the gameplay tedious, but scavenged items might not even keep your characters alive. One-hit kills are irritating when there's no strategy to avoid them. Plus, I was already bored by that point. There wasn't much to do, and what there was to do wasn't any fun. For example, there was also a crafting system in place, but it only had one recipe. It seemed like you had to discover recipes as you clicked around the base. Discovering things wasn't fun, either. You click on a circle to move your characters into a room. If there are items in it, then you see a single, glowing box/terminal, click, and get items. Otherwise, you get items from fights, and a text/sprites scroll up at the top to show "You found" x, y, z. The single-click, single-point gathering/exploration was limiting, and made this feel more like a phone game than a PC game to me.

Buy? Yes.
LYNE is a simple and crisp puzzler that requires players to connect shapes on a grid with lines that are not allowed to overlap (unless there is a later mechanic in the game for such a thing). The player must use limited space and combination of connector pieces to have all shapes connected to their "endpoints".
This game is very clever and I think it hits the difficulty curve mostly right on the head (I found some puzzles easier than prior ones). It also seems like the player can eventually figure out any puzzle through pure trial of elimination, though that may take much time. So even if you have a hard time with a puzzle, just try all the possible combinations until you win. Lyne is also often used by Steam users to decorate their profile with words using the alphabetical acheivements from beating each "world".
I can easily recommend, especially due to it's low price. When it's on sale, it is often less than $1 which is arguably a steal for the quality and value of the game.

Tactical RPG fans interested in a Power Rangers parody should buy.
I would like to give it a thumbs up. However, while I personally enjoyed the game, it has far too many issues and bugs. Behold Studios can do better.
*
The core of the battle system is the Teamwork system. I overall really like it. During a character's turn, you can end it by selecting "Teamwork". That character can then do one of two things: A. Join another team member's attack on an enemy.  B. Throw another team member to a further space.
*
A lot of games simply have a "skip scene" option, but that's a very binary choice. With fast forward, I can selectively skip through parts of scenes.
*
- In a lot of RPG's, the character models are the same regardless of what you've equipped. In Chroma Squad, the characters look different depending on what you've equipped!
*
- The background Studio music got stuck in my head. In a good way.
- The music that plays in the Mecha battles is good and gives the appropriate feeling.
- Japanese theme songs are great.
*
- Each Season, there are 5 to 6 Episodes. Except for the first and last Episode, you can choose which order you play the Episodes in.
*
- Great to have branching
- But the branching is simplistic. There's only
- If you want to see all 3 different endings, you have to replay from the beginning. And because the branching is so simplistic, you'll be mostly replaying the same content.
*
- What's Crafting Rate? Fan Conversion Rate? Income Conversion? Skill Regin? None of these are clearly explained by the game.
- Some abilities boost Defense. Wait, how do I see my character's Defense stat? Well, you can't. They hid it.
*
In Chroma Squad, you'll often want to use Team Acrobatics to have one team member throw another to a further tile. But this is tough to plan and I was often off by one.
- You don't get to see the member's throwing range until after you've already put them into Teamwork mode.
- The grid is only explicitly drawn as you're moving a character. And it is only drawn covering the area that that member can cover.
The ability to undo actions that don't trigger RNG would be helpful. So you could undo movement or putting a member into Teamwork (exception: the Support class can heal neighboring members when put into Teamwork mode, which does trigger RNG).
*
You can either buy equipment or craft it yourself. Crafting is neat in concept, but it has several issues:
- The bought equipment is unique from the crafted equipment. You'll often be asking yourself whether you should buy Equipment B or craft Equipment C.  However, the Shop and Crafting screens are separate, so there is no direct way to compare the two. I found myself constantly jumping between the two screens. (And you can't jump directly between them. You have to back out to the main Studio screen first. Bleh.)
- I generally found the Crafted equipment to be worse than the bought equipment.
- Some crafted items get random properties, which are basically boosts to one of the stats. But there's no explanation of what to expect. If you get Health +10 is that a good roll or a bad roll? Also, sometimes your rolls can be for the same stat. I found that a bit surprising at first and wondered if the game maybe failed to give me one of my random properties.
*
- In many scenes, the enemies are shown appearing one... by... one...  by... one... Why? No one want to see that.
- Do you like watching characters move across the screen with nothing happening?
- There are significant pauses between characters saying lines
- The fast forward system doesn't have an option to let you stop fast-forwarding at speech lines. That's what I really want. I want to read the dialog, but I don't want to have to wait through poorly choreagraphed scenes.
*
- Every monster you fight behaves the same way. And so you never have to change your strategy in how to fight them.
- The setting where you fight is always the exact same. (The game lampshades this, but that doesn't excuse it.)
- This was a huge missed opportunity. Imagine monsters that attack in unique ways that require unique responses. Or unique environments that you can use as part of the fight.
*

*
- About 20+ minutes into the final battle, the game wouldn't advance. I had to restart from the beginning of the battle.
- After finishing an Episode, I pressed escape while it was totalling how much Money and Fans I had earned. The game got in a messed up state and never gave me credit for the Money or Fans.
- For a game that fails to explain its mechanics, it compounds this by showing incorrect information around those mechanics:
-- The game often improperly calculates Expected Income.
-- One Ad Agency gives you a bonus of 35 Fans per Episode. The game improperly shows that the Fan Conversion rate is increased by 35, instead of just a flat increase of 35 Fans.
-- The game is often incorrect about the number of Fans and Money you earned the previous Episode
- When defending in the Mecha battles, you basically have to time when you press your mouse. Unfortunately, this is exactly when the game would decide to stutter on me.
- Sometimes a character is attacked offscreen and the camera doesn't move to show you what's happening.
- If you click the upper right corner, you can submit a bug report, which is great. But, the form to report bugs has bugs! The arrow keys where you're writing text don't work.

This game was built for Early Access. Here's the big glaring issue - While the game was in early access, establishing yourself on the island (Shelter, storage, traps, weapons, boats etc) was a fun, albiet slow part of the game that you could focus on besides exploring and surviving, because there was NOTHING ELSE TO DO! But the end-game result is to find your missing son. With this in mind, what does establishing yourself with a mansion and walls and traps, food and water and the other plethora of things you can build for days and days have to do with the end-game? If this was sold as a finished product the goal of the player would be to build temporary shelters throughout the forest until you find what is needed to find your son and get out of there. I see no point in spending hours/days on end building a huge and elaborate base with all the fixin's, when your ultimate goal is to get off the island with your son in tow.
The Forest is a great open world game with a greater identity crises. Hopefully the devs can balance the end-game and the adventure that gets you there, better than what it is already, because at the moment it is very much "build your own village until you get bored, then go find your son" Hard to recommend a game thats unfinished, but if you HAD to buy an early access game, then this would probably be the one to get.

Sam and Max is a moderately funny click adventure game that features a bunny and a dog as detective. The puzzles are simplistic, the humor is simplistic. If you are looking for profound dialogue and/or puzzles, you will not be finding it in season one.
I was not too surprised to find out that Sam and Max, like most other click adventures, have no re-playability. However, I was surprised to find how dull episode 1,2,3 is in this series. The three episodes are chock full of simple fedex delivery puzzles with esoteric solutions. Good luck solving them without a walk-through. Luckily the game does pick up it’s pace by episode 4, and the game took a turn for the best. Puzzles solutions remain esoteric, but the results of solving the puzzles can create quite amusing consequences. You also will not remain stuck at your boring♥♥♥♥♥apartment block which is a plus!
Telltale nailed the voice acting in this series. Intentionally annoying characters have intentionally annoying voices; you will feel like punching the screen every single time the soda poppers talk. Humor is not universal, so the jokes in this game can either strike you as “ROFL” quality or downright immature. Luckily none of the jokes are nearly as stupid or overused as the ones you find in Duke Nukem Forever.
I recommend this game solely on the basis that’s a very well polished click adventure with a unique brand of humor. It’s not immersive or challenging, but it does make for a fantastic change of pace in between long sessions of Elder Scrolls, Counter Strike, DOTA 2, etc.

Well I didn't, but I knew of it, and even watched some scattered episodes here and there, but I always found it too hard to get into and really corny (And I know, it is part of the charm of the series, your hand is probably shaking right now to tell me that, but as a kid, that didn't grab my attention.), and well, this game surely nails on corniness, it feels just like the show, which I nowadays respect a lot, everything is here, the music, the silly costumes, the fights, the megazord, even Zordon is in it; and, in gameplay, this game surprised me, it's really fun!
In Chroma Squad, 5 stuntman for an lackluster action show get bored of their current contract and their director, so they decide to quit and make their own independent studio to film an action packed show, starting in a humble warehouse with Chroma Key and a text to speech giant brain prop, up to a real professional studio, and throughout the game you have to manage the costumes, the advertisement, the props, reply to fan letters, and of course, film the show. And it's all tongue-in-cheek and very corny, just like the original Power Rangers. It's amazing to see the big Mecha fights against a giant enemy, or the exaggerated moves, or EXPLOSIONS!!
The game has a really cool battle system, it is somewhat basic, but still fun. You watch over the battle field and you can either move or attack an enemy, you also have skills you can activate and a teamwork mechanic, which I think it's really well done. But that's just when you're filming, when you are between shoots, you can manage and improve your studio and show, by buying or crafting clothes and weapons for your rangers and improvements for your mecha, purchasing new filming equipment, signing contracts with advertising agents, and answering fan mail. Everything is really creative and well done.
The game looks really good, it has a wonderful 32 bit style to it, and sometimes there's also a 90s TV filter in the studio management screen, which sets the tone pretty well, all the sprites are really well drawn, and the enemies design is also fantastic, especially the bosses, who are a ton of fun.
The music and sound effects though, those are the best part, in the title screen, the game has an Japanese opening music playing, which already sets the mood to the game, and the rest of the soundtrack, is really good and somewhat catchy, I love it!
Overall, this game is great, I absolutely recommend it, it has the soul of the Power Rangers in it, with all the fun corniness the show had, the developers did a wonderful job! Now they just need to make 23 movies and iterations of it, and it truly will be Power Rangers, the game.

The best Star Wars strategy game you will find. Galactic conquest mode is great, allowing for battles across land and space of 50+ planets as any of the game's three factions. Bonuses gained while occupying planets diversify it quite a bit and sometimes makes you want to keep the planet rather than blow it up with the Death Star. Don't look for great depth in this game. You have money that is given on a regular interval, which is determined by planets controlled and mining facilities built on them. Use this money To build units or buildings. Diversify units to counter enemy units well.Conquer the galaxy.
The space battles are amazing and what really make this game great. Being able to target specific functions on larger ships (smaller ones like a Nebulon B Frigate, up to a Star Destroyer or Mon Calamari Cruiser, even to a Super Star Destroyer) serves great purpose. The ability to send bombers in to take down shields with proton torpedoes, for example, is a great use of this as it disables the shields on the ships and makes them vulnerable to laser fire. Units  are well balanced, Empire may get the Executor or Death Star to conquer space and destroy planets, but Rebels get Garm Bel Iblis who can sneak past fleets and invade the ground with his powerful shielded tank- capable of winning over many planet systems.
Overall, a great game. I mostly played this as a child when I had it on CD and played a ton, but I do not regret buying this again. However, if you are looking simply for a RTS there are better ones out there (Age of Empires 2, for example). Get this for the impressive Star Wars universe.

Played this game back when it came out on Playstation 2, but the opinion still applies to the PC version. dotHack franchise is rather diverse in that it includes anime, manga and games, the latter being more recognizable even in western world. As the game by itself it has pretty good action combat (although it might get rather repetetive later on), likable characters and very good music.  And even though it's a game about people playing a game it manages to be serious when it is needed. It won't take too long to beat it when playing just for the main story, boss fights are not really too challenging, but it wouldn't hurt to try and get into the whole "The World" setting with logging into your game, interacting with other players via emails and reading outside world news describing the events tied into the story.
Graphics do show that this is a PS2 game, but all the minimal options like resolution, shadows, antialiasing are present. Voiceover can be switched between English and Japanese. Controls can be remapped for keyboard or better yet just use the gamepad. It is better optimized for that type of control.
Overall it is a solid game which may interest people who are into JRPGs.

Disclaimer: DO NOT BUY FOR FULL PRICE ($9.99). There is only about an hour and a half of gameplay. My 3+ hours comes from idling in the background while eating dinner and watching a Star Trek TNG episode.
Disclaimer 2: I didn't factor price into my score of this game, but I mention it in my review.
Tl;dr: A beautiful game with fun puzzles but only 1.5 hours of gameplay. 8/10.
Limbo is one of the more beautiful 2d games I've played. The art style (As seen in the trailer) is very ghost-like, and to progress the pun, at times very haunting. You play as a boy who awakens in a forest and then travels along a path where various things happen. There isn't much of a story, as in there is no text or voice to speak of, but there are some things that happen that give you a hint of something else going on. That being said, there isn't really anything going on. But it's fun to play and watch unfold anyways.
The puzzles range from the obvious to the impossible. I don't mean that there are impossible puzzles in the game, although there is one that is almost worthy of rage quitting (cart in the ladder before the mine car, for those curious). I mean impossible because they are not possible to be solved based on wits alone. More than a few puzzles require you to die in order to figure out what the trick is and then from there you can solve the puzzle. Those ones aren't really difficult, they're just lame in that you have to fail in order to solve them. Although, that could be what the story is supposed to be, that you are stuck in limbo, even if you die.
The achievements in the game are pretty lame. You get one achievement for actually playing and completing the game. The rest of the achievements are for doing stuff not on the game path (like the first one is going the wrong way at the start). So there's no take home or enjoyment from the achievements. The only replay value in the game comes from watching a guide to complete the ill-described achievements. Or you might lucky enough to go the wrong way and complete an achievement. The game is linear in that you follow the 2d path and solve puzzles. There is no variety (other than in the puzzles themselves). So expect a platformer game and nothing more.
The only other thing to really talk about (since there is only 1.5 hours of gameplay) is the price. I get that this is a very polished game and that this game came out on the xbox 360 live store. There is usually a premium added to games on exclusive markets like that. I get it. But honestly even if this game were brand new it is not worth 10 dollars. Paying $6.60 for each hour of gameplay is pretty absurd imho. The absurdity only continues when you see that this game is almost 6 years old, still only has 1.5 hours of gameplay, and is still marked at $10. And as I said, the game is not worth $10 brand new.
Overall the game can be challenging, looks great, and can be fun to play. but get it on sale for <$5. Or <$2 if you're smart. 8/10.

With all the new jrpgs coming to steam, I hoped that .hack might one day come as well since it's one of my favorite series.  THE TIME IS NOW, with an extra epilogue even!
First, going to start off with Volume 4
Volume 4 was made on a budget, and is moreso a playable epilogue than an actual chapter.  I finished it in a bit under 2 and half hours.
Instead of cutscenes, a majority of the story is told through incredibly janky looking anime scenes.  The new form is pretty fun to play as, for the one dungeon you're able to.
Much, much more enjoyable to play with the graphical improvements and most importantly, 60 fps.  Gameplay, story, and ost (apart from a few very, very repetitive tracks) are all still excellent.  The achievements aren't anything special, you'll get 99% of them from naturally playing the game.  There's no grindy achievements, or "find this secret!" types.
The port is one of the best I've seen of all the jrpgs currently ported.  The title screen is a game selection one, with additional options for the Terminal Disk and Parody Mode (which is amazing)
I haven't experienced a crash or any sort of slowdown in the 124 hours I have clocked in.  There's some basic quality settings; shadows, anti-aliasing, and texture filtering.  You're able to choose either the english dub or the original japanese voices.
Note that you CAN play this with a keyboard.  The control settings are located in the "Steam" subsection, which you can open on the title screen with Q (by default)

I would only recommend this game if you played the original .hack series and have an interest in either feeling some nostalgia or simply like the flashy but simplified fighting style that g.u. brought to the .hack universe. The game expects you to know things are important from the original game series as well as .hack // sign and if you are coming in without any background knowledge this game will feel incredibly disjointed and confusing.
I originally avoided picking up g.u. because I thought the idea of Skeith/the other phases being used as fanservice was increidbly irritating. I never liked the idea of something that was supposed to be this terrifying fragment of corrupted data that would data drain humans resulting in them becoming comatose being turned into this "cool" anime thing you are supposed to be cheering for when he appears. The worst example of this is the abomination Gorre being turned into a cutesy set of twin robots but that is just my personal gripe with the concept of Avatars.
After managing to ignore these issues I enjoyed the games for what they were and had fun. The avatar battles are incredibly easy but there were some satisfying moments in seeing Skeith data draining your nemeses at the end of a battle. Combat overall is done fairly well but the weapons besides the daggers are largely useless unless you want to juggle enemies that are significantly higher than your level. Also, I feel like the dodging ability in part 3 should have been part of the entire series but that is just my opinion. The story has some pacing issues mainly with an obnoxious pink dog-eared warlock wanting you to do side quests randomly but other than that was well written and enjoyable.
The games get gradually better as they go along with the exception of the added part 4 so if (when) you find yourself trodding through the seemingly endless trivial and almost insulting objectives in part 1 do know that the games do eventually pick up.
And sort of spoiler warning but I do sincerely hope that what Piros says at the end of part 4 turns out to be true and not just in-game chatter.

That said; this is one of the most thought-provoking and wholly unique experiences I've ever had. It raises more questions than it answers, and by the end of it you're left with a swirling mind and a deep-seated sense of unease. Don't google anything about this game. Don't read too many reviews. Experience it, form your own opinions.
I bought this game on sale, but I would pay the full ten dollar price tag for the experience I had.

I have a lot of things to say about Rencounter but I'm going to start out by being forthright; I really like Rencounter. I have played it on & off & on again. I feel I need to say however that, despite my seemingly limited number of hours, I have felt the change and growth over the time that it has gone up until now. It has gotten a lot better as in comparison to the early stages.
I remember back in the day, the first thing I did was just die. I died a lot and this genuinely made me angry because I simply didn't understand, but after dying a few times, trying to use stuff and my inventory was filling up with junk equipment I finally saw the disassemble button. The game then opened its' doors and said "welcome".
Rencounter is a Dungeon Crawler with turn-based tactical elements, minor roguelite elements &  nearly no RPG elements. These aren't points against it. I like my random name the game gives me every time. It adds flavor to my run. I don't like I can't get a random clone when I die, and always end up coming back as the model I call♥♥♥♥♥♥Rockjaw, just slightly bigger or smaller but what it does have is:
Stat building, passive traits, a minor crafting system, gear management & Food rationing. This is enough for me right now because I really find myself very interested in the world that we are playing in.
I haven't beat Rencounter yet but I have high speculation and a ton of the in-game scrolls and I get pictures of the overall plot. I imagine the ending will be along the lines of "you are in a VR program to see if you are worthy for real life" kind of situation. That's why I think you're allowed to come back as your character, until they die.
Edit: I beat the game. I have seen the surface. I hope there will be a sequel. This game has so much potential for an expanded sequel. I am glad that my guess was wrong.
REAL WARNING: if you're playing and you are invested in your main character, if he dies, You will play whoever is left over. I know this should seem obvious but it really comes as a super hard shock to you as a player, so Remember this: Invest in your team mates. They could be your new Player Character.
I have had many good team mates. In the early days, I actually didn't understand what the rooms meant. I didn't understand what Ice was or anything. So I just killed them and looted their bodies. Some people will tell you that this is a good strategy for early on in the game, but you Will Need friends.
I've had characters that I have admittedly abused through perk manipulation. Had one guy that used Path of Pain and a few other things and got my character up to 10K health. There is mechanical fun and challenge to be had if you know what you're doing.
I like the lighting, the shadows- I like the Look of Rencounter. I like the ruins, the fungal altars, the drowned rooms, the nearly-aztec style masks, the shift to near-medieval with plate and then the severe comparison to things like the Hacksaw, or the Star Killer. You feel very lost in time if that wasn't already felt from your slow departure from the cloning pods.
I intend to beat Rencounter soon. I have been inspired by a rare instance in-game that meant something to me.

Never before has the line drawing game genre had such a giant in the field.  I imagine that if you could somehow go back in time and show LYNE to the ancient cavemen on their primitive stone tablets, that they would hardly believe what they were seeing.  They would probably club you to death and burn your body as a sacrifice to the sun god or something, but hey, what do those crazy cavemen know.
Fast forward to today, where we can play LYNE without being beaten to death, mostly, and the awe and wonder this game exudes are no less than they were in the hypothetical caveman days.  Let us take a look at what has made LYNE the number one line connecting game released on March 17th, 2014.
Shapes.  We all love shapes, and LYNE delivers several of the greatest shapes known to man.  Square?  Got it.  Triangle?  Bam!  Octagon?  You know it!  But there is more to LYNE than that.  You have to draw lines between the shapes!  Draw the lines the way they want you to and you get to move on to the next level; fail, and your life is an empty meaningless shell.  It really is perfection, a grim balance between glory and abject failure, a balancing act so delicate that one false move could send you spiralling into a vortex of existential dread so severe you would need thirteen Kierkegaards to bring you back.  Also, LYNE is great for kids.  Teaches them things and such.

Truffle Saga is a mobile game that somehow made it's way onto steam. But will you want to play it here ?
We play as Truffle. We need to destroy the pesky mushrooms by throwing acorns at them. It's just as random as it sounds.
Gameplay is really simple. You throw down an acorn and try to destroy the mushrooms and you can also collect crystals. But you can only use one shot.
While the gameplay is really simple, controls are the reason this game is quite hard. It feels really clunky and it's really hard to aim. In later levels you can change the layout by flipping snakes, opening parts of level and use bees to bounce the acorn. But it's really tough with the clunky controls.
Graphics are probably the only good thing about this game. It looks really cute and the art style is really cool but that's not saying a lot.
The soundtrack is painful. It get's so tedious and it could make someones ears bleed. My suggestion if you do play the game is turn off the music as soon as possible.
The game is really easy. Even the harder levels are pretty easy and with enough patience you can beat any level within minutes.
The game is also incredibly short. Even though there's 60 levels, I finished the entire game in 1 hour. If you do want you can try and go back and collect all crystals and all crowns, but no one would attempt that. The developer promised new levels (not that I want any) but nothing has been announced.
The game isn't buggy, but the controls are a big problem. It's hard to aim when the line doesn't go where you want it to go.
Overall Truffle Saga is a horrible game and not worth your time and money. It's easy, short and not worth the money.  I don't suggest getting the game even at a sale. I give Truffle Saga a 2/10

Short version:
This is a rouge zombie game.  Death sends you right back to the start menu.  No special zombies, but a large amount of regulars.  Game focuses more on survival than mindlessly blasting through hoards.
Normally something i'd be into but.....  Basic mechanics were a deal breaker.  I feel as though the game developers had some really great ideas when it came to the higher concepts but then said '♥♥♥♥ it' when it came time to work on the basic gameplay.
I'd love to recomend this game based on its subject matter and potential for exelent survivally fun.  Unforunately in its current state i can't because I didn't enjoy it.
Pros:
Atmospheric.  You feel as though something might be about to get you every second.  No room feels safe.  Going outside scares the crap out of your character.  You can honestly feel your iminent demise closing in on you.
Deep crafting system?:  At least it looks deep.  I haven't gotten deep enough into the game to throughly explore this.
Stress, traits, and other customizable characteristics.  Good idea, still needs to be balanced somewhat, but I like where the Dev's head is at.
Good customization on Zombie effects:  Can turn on and off death from a tiny scratch and other features.  I would always play on hardcore, but I like options.
Cons:
Poor basic mechanics:  This is what killed the game for me.  I can't see, or fight, or even manage basic things like doors and windows very well.  Characters are forced to play in a third person radius effect.  Meaning that you can't see things above a certain radius on the front side of your character.  Camera angle is static.  This makes it hard to see if there is a zombie on the other side of say: a now transparent wall with a door or some other object providing more clutter.  The upper left side of buildings scare the crap out of you.  For the life of me, I still can't reliably stomp a zombie on the ground.  I'm sure a person who really takes the time to learn all the tricks of walking can play this game just fine.  But for me, it's not worth the time investment, especially not if I can pick up a title like Don't Starve and start playing immediately.  I just wish more care had been taken to get the controls to feel more fluid.
Graphics are a little basic, but nothing you can't work around.
Buy if:
You really like zombie games. +
You don't mind some weird stuff with cameras +
Are more forgiving of works in progress.

I really enjoyed this game. I started on "interesting" as a difficulty setting as I've played plenty of tactical rpgs. And, boy, did Chroma Squad deliver an enjoyable experience. Not accounting for times when I left to get food in my bidge-play of this game, you can complete it within a reasonable 10-12 hours, even faster if you skip the dialog on replays.
But onto the important stuff, what was good?
+ Customization of characters, studio, and your OMEGA SUPREME mech. (eh, couldn't help it).
+ Storyline does develop overtime but is slow in the first season.
+ Multiple endings
+ Quirky narrator
+ Crafting options for your squad and your mech
+ High level of detail (clouds hang from strings, cardboard backdrops, etc).
+ Multitude of bosses
+ Required episodes of annoying red leader being an annoying red leader
+ Character development(?), some people have stated that they didn't think the characters were developed enough, but I think part of that has to deal with being involved with your squad. By the end of the game I new what each team member's personality was, their flaws, and dislikes. (I.e. overzealous, not liking violence, etc). To get more out of the game maybe name rangers after friends or read the dialog out loud (oh, what a concept) to bring more life to them. Regardless I thought the charactization was good.
Stuff I wished there was more of:
- More characters to choose from. I'm on my third playthrough of the game and I do have favorites that I like to use, but there are other characters available that don't work well for the "challenge" level of difficulty where you need to spend money and upgrades for the studio and characters wisely.  This is not to complain about the difficulty, I think it is fine, but more characters would add more variety and depth to playthroughs.
- Possibly less marketing partners.I know I just said I want more variety, but sometimes there can be too much of a good thing. I honestly only used 2-3 depending on my need for the episode. More options for other sections of the game could have been prioritized more instead.
- Side-characters. I include this lightly as Chroma Squad does pay homage to other rangers coming to save our would be heroes by introducing different characters throughout different episodes, but some of them fall to the way side and don't re-appear (besides when you make choices that cause that to happen).
If it were a perfect world:
Keep in mind that this development team has been wanting to add more to Chroma Squad but, has been bogged down in bureaucratic nonsense due to licensing agreements with the Power Rangers franchise. I am sure that there is a lot more that they would like to add to the game. I look forward to more Chroma Squad in the future.
The price:
I bought this when it was on sale, that being said, I still would have paid the 14.99 to get the game. You can tell a lot of time was spent on settings, dialog, etc. That doesn't mean this game is entirely perfect, but the price is suitable to the experience I had.

Cuphead is a game that is as fun as it is creative, and as creative as it can be frustrating.
The art work is beautiful to look at, the bosses are all original, well thought out, challenging but never impossible. You basically have 3 modes throughout the game, regular boss fights, plane boss fight (where you fight a usually flying boss in an actual plane) and run & gun. All of them, spread out in the game, present a good amount of variety and are all different enough from each other so that you feel like you're actually playing something different. A great deal of effort was made to make this game's art, groovy music and boss fights! The game encourages you to replay the game for higher scores, different visual filters, and upgrades. You even have a small slider that tells you how close you were to beat a boss, allowing you to know if you were on a good track about your strategies while facing him/her!
All gripes i could possibly have with this game are fairly minor. The visual filters are neat but they can sometimes stop you from seeing certain parry able objects. Certain attacks, special attacks and super moves feel extremely weak compared to others. The 3rd super move you get feels like a letdown, and some charms in the game feel somewhat useless. Theres no real reason to take the heart or twin hearts charms when others like instant parry,  going through objects or a passive meter boost are way more useful.
All in all, an amazing game.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad / Rising Storm GOTY
Pros:
- Immersion, immersion, immersion
- No biased point of view ( A rare thing in WWII games )
- Good gameplay
- Good AI
Many people have commented on this game being a "PTSD Simulator". This claim is far from unjustified. This game is super-immersive ( Even more so when using the Immersion Overhaul Simulator -
). Realistic graphics, along with good ballistics, suppression affects and an amazing atmosphere of constant danger give this game an edge over other WWII games of the genre.
No biased Point of View is another big tick for me. No more evil Germans or unbalanced mechanics that impact how the Germans play. This is a big step forward and a great way of seeing how the front was ACTUALLY LIKE. No more of the lies made up about the Germans by the victors.
Gameplay strives to be as realistic as possible, while also catering to beginners. Most weapons take one shot to kill, but are balanced by accuracy and weapon sway, etc. Tank gameplay is extremely impressive with full internal views and great combat elements.
The AI are not easy to say the least. They are only slightly less competent than a human player. There are also always servers with lots of bots to practice with.
Cons:
- Flamethrowers...

An extremely fun and balanced game. A tense cat-and-mouse type game. 4 unique hunter classes, each with 3 distinct characters which all play different roles. 3 monsters with unique playstyles. When considering the previous release title was Left for Dead, Evolve's base game gives plenty of content.
The developers careful thought and planning in the game really shines through with the minor nuances of the game: Plenty of unique character dialogue, incredible map/texture details and designs. A game with a steep learning curve, but very rewarding when you develop a thorough understanding of gameplay mechanics and an understanding of how to play. The way the game is meant to be played heavily punishes a lack of teamwork and communication- hence the pitchfork mentality with balance. Communicate well, whether it be with your friends or a lobby of strangers- the playing community is friendly and always open to communicate.
Slight problem with matchmaking, there are very occasional games where I have been matched with people who are clearly at a higher level than myself- however this has been very rare. Hopefully the developers continue to release more content and provide the game with the TLC it deserves. Recommend!

I remember playing this game on PS2 many years ago and throughly enjoyed all the 3 volumes, almost getting everything 100% completion, only didn't do so because something glitched in the second volume and I didn't feel like reloading MANY hours of gameplay just for one quest. This game is not for everyone.  This is a challenging, turn based, dungeon crawling RPG.
The game puts you on the bottom of a 10 level duneon.  To win, you must escape.  You work with 1-3 characters to clear rooms, gain loot and improve your characters so that you can tackle the next level of the dungeon.  When you start the game, you won't get any tutorials or much in the way of help.  However, the game isn't hard to learn and exploring is part of the fun (though many will not agree with this).
The game is hard.  You will die.  You will need to learn which weapons are the best, how to spend your money, when to eat and how to craft.
Combat is a hex turn based system.  Each room can have different environments (foggy, hot, jungle etc) and/or a few obstacles in the way (ex. corrosive acid) which can add complexity/variety to the fights.   The AI is decent, but not amazing by any stretch.  A room that leads to the next level of the dungeon is always a boss fight.  You will have a tough character with a small number of minions helping him.
As you progress, you can buy equipment and/or attribute upgrades (str, dex, agil, etc).  The game has special abilities called "T.A.L.A.N.T.S." that you find randomly and after a boss fight.  These abilities can make a big difference, but its a RNG on which ones you will find.
There is a story to the game, but it is pretty hidden.  You actually have to work to understand the story.  Graphics on this game are not great.  If you have top tier graphics to play a game, move on.
If you like a challenge and turn based strategy, this is an inexpensive game that can give you several hours of entertainment.

Chroma Squad is a tactical role-playing game, released for personal computers in early goings of 2015. It was heavily influenced by various Tokusatsu series, two of the chief inspirations being Saban's Power Rangers and Shotaro Ishinomori's Kamen Rider.
Five professional stuntmen who've grown tired of the poor production values and tyranical director of their current television series decide to uproot and take their talent elsewhere. Soon after impulsively deciding to leave, the group begins developing an original Sentai series, and must work through a myriad of problems to ensure that the series is successful.
Before the game rears into action, the player is given several options to tailor their experience: A choice between three difficulty settings, helping to accommodate players of all skill levels; selecting your squad and studio names, colors and transformation shout; and finally, designating the actors to the roles that you see fit.
Each of those actors have unique bonuses, which help to determine how they'll influence the team for the better. Several of these bonuses are especially beneficial with a particular role, e.g.; Skill Regen for an Assist character to improve the rate at which they can heal the rest of the group. Some actors go so as far as to impose combat penalties on themselves, so that they can provide a heavy boost in another area.
Branching paths are another feature that help to provide some elements of customization. The studio will occasionally receive an email with several options for replies. While most of these only lead to an audience bonus, others can provide weaponry that otherwise wouldn't be available. The largest branch in the game is accessed during one particular battle: depending on how one chooses to complete an objective, the game determines how the second half of the journey will play out. All of these add a great degree of value to subsequent plays.
The foundation that the game is built upon is squad based combat, which plays out on a turn-by-turn basis in which the rangers move around on an isometric grid. The team use their varied skill sets to turn the tide of battle, in whatever way they can. Be they used for healing, or rapidly bursting down the health of nearby enemies, each member is prepared to put up a fight, whether they're alone, or working together.
Should they choose the latter, teamwork is used as a mechanic that allow them to launch one another to distant locations, as well as attacking enemies as a group for higher damage. Still, sometimes even a team of powerful heroes need a little more help to defeat a daunting foe.
At times like these, our heroes call upon their Mecha to participate in Kaiju battles; essentially, giant robots fighting giant monsters. These also play out turn-by-turn, but here the objective is to create combos with your abilities, all the while paying close attention to a percentage representing you're likelihood of hitting the target. The significance of this is that combo-chains determine your damage multiplier, and missing an enemy breaks this chain, resets it to 0, and proceeds to the the next turn. While these sections aren't especially interesting on their own, they do add enough variety to keep the core gameplay relatively fresh.
Personally, I've never been particularly compatible with isometric tactics, as they tend to be very slow paced, without providing something that makes it feel necessary. That said, I found Chroma Squad to be a game that meaningfully improves the pace of the genre. Perhaps the kindest thing I can say about it in that regard is, while the gameplay is familiar, the time you spend in battle doesn't feel like it massively exceeds the amount of time allocated to plot and cutscenes, as it does in many tactical titles.
As a longtime enthusiast of the source material, Chroma Squad had an easy time getting through to me, as it shows an incredible amount of reverence for the style, and does a wonderful job of presenting it in a unique way. Going beyond that incredibly initial premise, there's an incredible amount of charm to be found here. From the moment you launch the game, the main theme mimics the vocal styling of many classic Tokusatsu themes, and perfectly sets the tone for the adventure. Something as simple as skipping through cutscenes is done as though someone was fast forwarding through a VHS tape, showing an immense amount of character for something that otherwise wouldn't be noteworthy in the slightest. Here we have an incredibly quirky game that makes for a very engaging experience and is absolutely worth the price of admission.

This game is wonderful.  It's self aware, funny, and one big homage to sentai, while playing like Final Fantasy Tactics and Disgaea in combat, and like nothing I have ever played in the management aspects.
Pros:  Combat.  You have team attacks, acrobatics, heals, buffs, stuns, and special attacks.  The studio management stuff seems a bit overwhelming at first, but you get used to it.  You can use marketing to increase your income, buff the actors in combat, increase your fanbase, etc.  You can choose to make all your costume pieces, or buy them instead, while getting rare items during episodes (missions).
Cons:  Might be a relatively short playtime.  I'm at 12 hours now, and that's just because I screwed up my first playthrough and wanted a fresh start, might have 4 more hours of play left.  Aside from the first few missions you get, and some emails you read in game, you kinda have to learn a lot of stuff on your own.  I'll give you an example, the game teaches you if you get all 5 actors next to an enemy, have 4 locked into team action, and then attack with the last, you'll get a finishing move.  What the game didn't teach me and I found on my own, you can have some attack from afar with others in range of the target, and get a finishing move with a mega laser gun where all the actors merge their weapons together.  All that being said, these are still minor cons.
I love this game and I recommend you get it if you enjoy some light to intermediate management gameplay and tactical rpg combat similar to Disgaea and FFTactics.  Also, if you like sentai and don't take it too seriously.  If you like playing these type of games on difficult, buy it no matter the price.  If you play on casual or normal (you'll probably finish a lot sooner), then I recommend waiting til its 10 or less.
Have fun.

This is my favorite WW2 game by far. This a great and realistic game with a lot of depth.
Here is a quick overview:
You will play as a soldier of either the Red Army, the Wehrmacht, The U.S. Marines, or the Imperial Japanese Army. The game is set in two theaters of war, The Pacific (U.S. Vs Japs), and the Eastern front (Russians Vs Germans). In each army, there are different classes such as rifleman, assault, marksman, and so on. As you progress in the game, your weapons will level up and get attachments/upgrades, and look like they are in better condition. The class you are playing itself can be leveled up to give you more weapon/sidearm choices. Finally, you can level up your account with "Honor". The higher that level is, the more battle hardened your soldier is and the more things overall you can choose from.

On Steam it says I've barely played this game, but I played a TON of it when it first came out and didn't have it on Steam. Anyways, it's an old game, and I HATE to say it, but it has not aged well. At all. In fact, if I ever play it again, it will be entirely for nostalgia's sake, unfortunately. The problem is the balance, especially in land battles.
The way everything is set up just feels weird. It feels like vehicles can die too easily, the Empire infantry weirdly stack up into box formations that just doesn't really fit with the Star Wars atmosphere, and the rocket artillery on the Rebel's side is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥LY overpowered, to the point where they can almost take out your entire military force at the beginning of a match (yet when you use them, they don't feel nearly as powerful). It's just kind of a weird game, and yes, the space battles are cool, but they have also aged to the point where unfortunately, it's just not worth it anymore. The meta game  (galactic conquest or whatever it's called) is also weird. A lot of time there are strangely fast time limits to win the game, which annoys me because it gives little time to really develop a nice army and tech that can really do damage. And since it's all in real time, it sometimes devolves into a game of tag, where each side has their core planets, and then all the outlying planets are taken by one side, then taken by another, and so on and so forth, and this is due to the unit cap, which restricts you from truly building a large enough force to take over the empire. There's so many connections to all of the planets that it's not easy to actually form a stronghold, and while there is strategy in that, the game isn't quite good enough to compell you to want to develop the skills to master that strategy. I don't think I ever finished a single galactic conquest map. I ended up just reverting to multiplayer (which I can only assume is dead now).
If you played the game before, and just want nostalgia to kick in, maybe pick it up on a sale, but if you've never played it before, I'd say move on to better RTS games.

So I'll avoid another review and instead offer advice for noobs where they're likely to read it.
The community is generally welcoming but providing you follow two easy rules.
1. Do NOT take the Team Leader position.
2. Do NOT take a Squad Leader position.
OK, 4 rules.
3. Do NOT play this like COD.
4. Shout out that you're new and ask for advice. Many of us like to show off our experience so will gladly help when asked.
Red Orchestra is a team game, played over a number of battles in a campaign (usually). A TEAM game. As an example, if you're a points ♥♥♥♥♥, the top of the leader board is the person with the most TEAM points. NOT highest number of kills. Team points can win games.
The issue with those two roles, TL and SL, is they have to be played properly if the team is to win. And TL, and preferably SL's, need a microphone and experience.
So thats it. Do not got TL or SL  until you have a lot of experience OR .. you're willing to tell the team you are new and want advice. Then listen and follow.
Also be aware of the role you pick or are allocated.
MG's usually move to the flanks and provide cross covering fire. Keeping the enemies heads low. Accuracy and kills is actually less important than scaring the enemy. Make them keep their heads down. When you get low on Ammo shout out using your command keys .. ask for ammo and riflemen should bring it to you.
Snipers .. your job is to take out enemy MG's and Squad Leaders. Anyone else is just going to give your position away for little benefit.
Tanks ... always operate best with a crew who communicate with microphones. Use the 6 key to swap between shell types. AP for armour, HE for everything else. Remember that you have 2 mgs. One in the hull, one parrallel with the main gun. commander, stay inside the tank. You are an easy target.  Driver, hatch closed.
SL's, including Tank SL. You have 5 jobs. Do them and your team might win.
1. Stay alive. DO NOT DIE. DO NOT BE A HERO. If you want points, do your job. You can get to the top of the leader board without firing a round.
2. Mark artillery targets. If attacking, locate it just past a cap, preventing the enemy from entering. If defending, in a position in the cap furthest away from you .. ie where they enter the cap.  There are many variations of this on the different maps. Learn them. Always be thinking ahead to the next cap point and try to get your marks in early so your TL isn't waiting. You get team points for any enemy killed by artillery.
3. You are a mobile spawn point for your squad. Get close to the cap and stay down. Stay alive. Your squad can spawn next to you rather than all the way back at the previous spawn. this enable syou to quickly cap and advance.
4. Smoke.  You start with one smoke and can pick a second at the nearest ammo point. Use it to keep your squad alive. Position it to alllow them to get into caps safely. Not too far away so as to be of little use. You are their surrogate father. Look after them. Keep them safe. Its possible to use smoke in defence but it has to be done VERY carefully so as not to block your line of fire or benefit the enemy.
5. Talk to your squad. (Press T to find out who they are, Press I to chat to just them). Encourage them, instruct them. Tell them where to expect arty, when you're popping smoke etc. Organise them so you can mount a strong attack.
TL .. you need to be talking to your team constantly. Letting us know when and where arty will drop. Which area to attack and when NOT to attack.
You need to call in recon at the appropriate time, instructing your SL's to check their maps and provide new updated marks if required. You HAVE TO STAY next to the radio while the recon plane is up other wise enemies are not shown on th emap.
If you need to support an attack in a certain way then tell you SL's where you want their marks. Keep a constant eye on the chat and relay any important infor to the team (thats why you need a microphone).
Anti Tankers .. clue is in the name. You keep the team safe from tanks. If you don't do your job and instead decide to go sniping, your team will get slaughtered. DESTROY TANKS.
Engineers ..  you destroy tanks and tank barricades. When attacking you make a path for YOUR tank with the satchel. Blow fortifications to cripple defenders or alow ingress. When defending you destroy enemy tanks but your're also tasked with defending baricades etc. from enemy engineers.  It's your job to STOP them from being blown up.
Assault .. as it says .. when attacking your are the main thrust of the attack.
Auto Riflemen .. you are essentially an assault with greater range.
Riflemen .. You provide cover for the assault squads .. forcing the enemy to hide.  You then follow the assault into the cap and help consolidate. You then hold and defend the cap while the assaulters move onto the next cap, again providing them with cover and preparing to move on again once the assaulters have nearly secured the cap.
You can also resupply MG's. Walk, run or crawl up to them and press USE. This is an essential job since if an MG has to run back for ammo they're both at isk and leaving you without vital support.
Always use transports when provided. They allow you to follow up an attack much faster and to concentrate forces where needed. Therefor, never drive off in a transport on your own. Always wait until its mostly full.
Enemy recon planes can be shot down. Russian is a bi-plane, German mono. It loses them team points and recon info.
Team Kills, TK's, happen. they just do. If you TK, say sorry. If you're TK'd and the person says sorry, type np  (no problem), the TK will be forgiven, the person won't be kicked and your team will get a point .. because you were nice. Always forgive, np, TK's by arty .. it's usually your fault.

I think this is a very clever game with a lot of potential.  It is not of course a fully featured AAA title, and so it isn't priced as one.  Clearly some people have had difficulty with the lack of a manual, but if you go into it knowing that it is Roguelike, and how Roguelikes work, you should be fine.
Thematically, and narratively, the game can certyainly do with more development, and I hope the devs will be sufficiently encouraged to keep working on the project.  But what it is at present is a combat encounter system, wrapped in just enough structure to make a certain kind of sense, although frankly, this is not much less than something like Grimrock might offer.
I think the combat system on which it operates is very clever and well designed, and indeed, reminded me of the experience of playing Xcom.  Lovely clever, thoughtful battles with little fluff in between, I think it;s great fun.  If this is your sort of thing, you may find it highly addictive in a "just one more turn" sort of way, as I did.  But when they say the game is hard, they are not kidding.  This is a game for people who enjoy the challenge of mastering the way a system works, in the face of stiff resistance.  This is the kind of game that expects the player to be emotionally tough enough to accept defeat anf to keep coming back, the same sort of thing that games like Rimworld and Dwarf Fortress offer. HNNNNNNGGGGG. This game is a survival fps, a mix of STALKER and Don't Starve. The genre it self is already my GOTY. I am recommending this as of Aug 22, 2013. Its currently in alpha so don't say I didn't warn you.
You are a human. You are stuck in this dark/grim looking world with robots hunting you (you are an alien to them).  Your mission is to collect pieces of these magic rocks to power up this mechine that takes you back home. Along the way, you must stay alive and don't starve. You must search houses or robots you killed for supplies to stay alive till get back to the real world.

Weapons ranges from currently that I see in game are, axes, bear traps, revolver, 2 barrel shotty and a hunting rifle. Guns seems inaccurate so you do need to conserve ammo ALOT. Robots consists or dogs, normal huntsman in various cloths (seen in title art), fat town mayor guy and a flying ballonist spotter with floodlights that alarm nearby robots. To stay healthy you need to eat things, some things are bad for you like rotten food but you can cook some game. Currently you can't hunt game yourself so you have to find them in houses/robots and cook them at bonfire. Stealth is a BIG part of your survival. As someone who likes RPG's, roguelikes, and challenging games like XCOM or Fallout, or even Pixel Dungeon I've really enjoyed this game so far. The controls are nice and simple, so it's great for kicking back on a tablet. The atmosphere is cool, and I'd love to see some more story elements fleshed out--but as a roguelike this isn't a huge expectation.
Combat is well paced and really rewards thoughtful strategy. It punishes you big time for bad decisions. Entering a room you're unprepared for, or making a bad move, means dead squad members. Great if you want to re-live that horrible feeling you got when watching your soldiers in XCOM get gunned down.
All that being said, the game doesn't feel totally finished. There's absolutely zero instruction provided to the player on how to play, other than a scroll that starts in your inventory which says "Press LMB to equip items". Not super helpful, but the controls and the UI are simple enough to figure it out as you go. Just adds to the challenge! Each playthrough I learn something new and have been able to make it further into the game. Character customization is decent, but I'd love to see the option to set your name, appearance, or stats before beginning a new game.
