The Positive: Cuphead is a BEAUTIFUL game. The graphics, the sound, the music - are completely accurate to what a 1930's cartoon would be in the day, and I've seen my fair share. The story is classic-feeling and (again) something a 1930's era cartoon would be about, and it's not complex. The price is fair, and there's no BS like in-game DLC, loot boxes, or the other junk that companies like *COUGH* [MOSTLY ALL OF THEM NOW] add to their games in order to repeatedly try and tap your wallet. The controls are basic and not overly-complex (I cover more on this - see "The Mixed" below) and the tutorial is fast and covers them quickly and makes you aware of what you need to know in order to progress through the game - which isn't too many. Overall, I think the developers did a great job and focused on the aspects that many companies sadly overlook - the gameplay. The level navigation, progression, and design is diverse and well thought-out. The only bug I found was a graphic that didn't disappear when it should have - the "crying tears" of the 'onion boss' didn't disappear after I had defeated it, and it remained during the rest of the level. However, I was only able to produce it once time and it didn't affect the gameplay.
The Mixed: While the game is themed around a 1930's cartoon, don't let the cartoon-style looks fool you - this game is BLOODY DIFFICULT! You can lower the difficulty down a notch but only on the battle-styled levels, not on the "gun and run" stages. The controls aren't complex and neither are the number of moves you're required to learn in order to play, but you better memorize them and you better become a master at which key does which, or you're not progressing at all. You press the X key instead of the Shift key and make a mistake, you're not finishing the level and you're better off just selecting "RETRY" in the pause menu and starting over. I don't count this as a negative, as I love challenges and I can't knock a game down because of that. This difficulty can be disheartening for some and motivating for others. However, I feel that when I play, there's a big frustration factor that the difficulty absolutely plays into. I'll play for one hour and exit the game having not progressed a single level. However, it's not frustrating to the level that I stop playing - I find myself coming back after taking a break and having at it some more. I will say this, however: I feel that I am progressing through the game partially by mastering the controls, but also because I'm memorizing exactly how the level plays and when I should move, jump, shoot, or dash. Again, I'm mixed on the difficulty. I feel that if I could knock the difficulty down a notch on all stages and take a lower score, the game would appeal to those who just want to play and without yelling a curse word after dying for the 10th time on the same level.
The Negative: Pretty much nothing. The only thing I call BS on is how I'll attempt to hit a pink object and it'll occasionally both count as a "success" (as in I successfully hit the object) and also count as a "hit" (meaning that the object hit me and knocks off 1 HP). It's miniscule and really not worth mentioning as a negative, but sorry - if you're going to make a game this difficult, you should expect people to call you out on things like that. Other than this, that's pretty much it.

★★★⋆☆ (3.5/5 - Decent)
(WARNING: This review contains mild spoilers)
LYNE is one of those clever minimalistic games that focuses on providing simple but entertaining casual gameplay. Your aim in LYNE is to connect nodes of the same shape and colour in order to create one single line between them. Lines can travel between nodes and shapes in eight possible directions. Although this may seem like a simple procedure, there are certain elements in the game that can provide challenging and thought-provoking problems for the player.
LYNE only requires the mouse to fully utilise the game, this along with simple gameplay makes LYNE very easy to pick up and play. You create lines by dragging between two nodes, to delete a node you simply reverse the process and drag back to the previous node. Occasionally clicking in the wrong location can also remove linked lines but this is rarely a problem and most players will only have this happen to them a couple of times so long as they're careful. The gameplay is smooth and menu and level transitions are practically flawless.
When you begin the game you have access to a simple yet informative tutorial and getting your bearings on the game and understanding it is painless, within minutes you'll be clearing LYNE boards like there is no tomorrow.
The graphics and effects in LYNE are minimal (hence the reason the game is classified as a minimalist game) but the effects and use of colours is relaxing and a high level of detail is definitely still present. Palettes help to excel the game and provide interesting colour and pattern combinations. The graphics all appear to be vector images and this makes the game clean and enhances its sense of tranquility further.
The music of LYNE is probably the most important and most effective part of the game. The game prides itself as being a  "relaxing puzzle game". The music and sound effects is what makes this claim so abundantly true. The music itself is a relaxing blend of trance and drone-style ambience. Every time you join a line between nodes a soft calming note plays. Although simple, the gentle qualities of the notes and sounds used within the game easily ties it together as a whole.
I would consider only playing this game in short periods to recieve the full effect of the game, playing it in long sessions can destroy the game for some people who see it as repetitive and boring. The game is fairly repetitive with each level set getting gradually more and more difficult, but if you play it in short bursts you should still find it fresh and enjoyable.
This brings me to my next comment - replay value. The game as many have said can get boring after a while, but daily random levels of differing difficulty can help to provide more entertainment between the regular level sets. Also, as you complete level sets, both daily sets and the regular ones, you will recieve strange codebits known as "Cipher" which help you to unlock new colour palettes and other interesting content.
The difficulty is almost spot on and rarely will you get stumped on levels that cannot be solved with 10 - 15 minutes. The amount of Cipher you earn in any given set correlates to the difficulty of the puzzle (e.g. 1 = easy set, 5 = very challenging etc.).
Overall I would highly recommend LYNE to anyone who likes puzzle games or any casual gamers that are looking for a relaxing and fun game to ease their mind after a troubling day. Basically anyone can pick this game up and I encourage those interested to do so, I almost guarantee you will not be disappointed!

Hooray.
Every so often I would see herds of zombies (zomboids?) shuffling through the woods or on the city streets, and while one or two would attempt to give chase, they were slow shuffling meatbags that I quickly outpaced. I assume they got bored or just ran into trees, but when I arrived at the Country Market convienience store, I stopped to check the path I had taken. No zombies had followed.
F**k it. Time to raid the store.
There was nothing in the store except a jar of mayonnaise. It was half eaten.
As I stared in confusion at the jar, I heard a voice from outside. "Hey!" it called, "Over here!" it continued. I looked, surprised to see another human. Hey, the text said this was how -I- died, didn't expect I'd have to share my dying spotlight with some other jerk. He climbed through the broken window of the store and cut his hand open on the glass.
I laughed at him, and then shouted in surprise as he'd led a zombie directly into the store, shambling through the window after him. We both fled out of a window opposite the entrance it arrived, where I proceeded to cut my hand on escape. Why did karma always screw me? When we had cleared the zombies, we exchanged. . . something akin to pleasantries. He was a lumberjack, though his name isn't important. This is my story, screw you.
We decided to stick together, to find tweezers. You wouldn't believe how difficult it was to find tweezers. Instead of tweezers, sick of that word yet?, we found a third person to join our parade of misfortune; Billy Mays.  At least, he kept saying "BILLY MAYS HERE! WITH..." before any actual sentence.
Good to know the zombie apocalypse happened circa 2008.
A short time later, he'd found a home to call our safehouse. It was secluded, mostly free of zombies, and all the windows were boarded; meaning the dead couldn't see in. We'd found our new home. Alas, tragedy struck mere minutes after we settled in.
Dexter the Lumberjack wasn't happy. He demanded to know why I would put my food in my bedside cabinet instead of in the fridge. "It spoils that way!" he said, "All this is rotten now!"
I munched on a stick of butter while glaring daggers into him. And then I ate a second. He wouldn't stop mouthing off, so while shirtless (oh yeah, Billy Mays had taken his shirt off at some point and was rushing around the town showing off his self-described 'beautiful chest hair') Billy Mays was out. . . I attacked Dexter.
Being a lumberjack he was pretty fit, but my sneak attack gave me the upper hand, helping me win the duel in the end. I stood over his dead body, satisfied, as I looted his corpse.
I mean this literally. I looted his corpse. I put his body in our fridge, on the top shelf. I didn't want it to rot. He laid right next to my jar of pickles, when I noticed a rotting, dead mouse in his shirt pocket.
Waste not, want not, right?
I flipped the oven on and tossed the rotting carcass in.  Shirtless Billy Mays returned around this time, and I asked him to get a Leek from the fridge to help with the meal. For some reason he screamed and called me "disgusting" as he stormed out of the house. He left the fridge door open.
Seriously, what'd I do?
The smell of the cooked rat meat was delicious, I can't describe anything like it. By the time I pulled the baking tray out of the oven, I was salivating at the taste. Without hesitation, I bit into the charred fur. And then I took another bite. I ate it all in one sitting; organs, spine, fur and all, though I feel this angered a passerby who happened to barge in, shouting obscenities at me. His name was. . . eh. . . I don't know. I think he was Dexter's brother.
We broke out in a fight, where neither of us would give in. This was my land, he'd have to earn it.
We both died.
Choking and sputtering as I bled out, I wasn't sure if I was laying in my blood or his. Shirtless Billy Mays must have heard the cries of battle, as he returned one final time to ease me in to the next life.
"You guys are both f**king idiots."

**A bit of a mixed review but altogether I do recommend**
While making this review I had 7hrs played on The Long Dark. This time was enough to experience the first map fully. Exploring was great in the game and I give a big plus for that. The survival had a nice feeling as well. It took me a few hours of gameplay to even find the next map (which I have not explored fully yet). Overall for an early access game I was content with what I got and enjoyed it. It comes with a wide variety of playstyles so if you don't like as much of a challenge don't worry! Plus for only $20 you can get a lot of hours on this game which makes it very worth it in my opinion. All together If you like survival games, especially ones that challenge you, you're bound to like this game.
Now my complaints/suggestions
Because this game is early access I don't exactly know what they have planned for the game so some of these things they may be trying to fix or add.
-All around a bit more content. Even though it is sandbox mode there should be small objectives that people want to get to help their survival. It would be really interesting to see a way to get power for the main shelters. A way to move slightly faster by crafting snowshoes. Crafting in general just seems a bit bland. Although they want the game to be challenging, you should also be able to craft things to make living a bit easier as you play.
-Because of the lack of crafting new things I feel like it makes survival tedious. You don't really have new ways to get food or make a shelters better so you're stuck doing the same things.
-Lastly the biggest complaint would have to be how long we have waited for story mode. If you are looking for the story mode I'd say wait until it leaves early access (which could be a long time from now.) Otherwise you only have sandbox mode and some challenge modes.

I figured I would provide a review that isn't just whining about DLC and comes from someone who actually bought and plays the game.
Overall I'd give it an 8 out of 10
Pros:
1. Turtle Rock Studios-one of the most open and honest developers I've seen. They're constantly re-evaluating the balancing in the game and when they make a change, even if you don't agree with it, they provide the data that the decision was based on.
2.Gameplay is fun and consuming-the people that say the opposite aren't playing the game correctly. As a hunter to be truly successful you're using site and sound to better track the monster and force those early engagements.  The synergy of matching the hunter’s abilities to your advantage is an art form and finding new ways to use those abilities is compelling. As the monster, your constantly walking the line between running, fighting, or sneaking and finding new and better ways to get the upper hand.  The audio elements, landscape, and game style provide an immersive experience.
3.Ability to play solo-this is missing from so many games in the Multiplayer genre. The AI is intelligent enough to have a challenging and enjoyable experience. You can fully customize the match by map, mode, hunters, and monster; you can play against any character regardless if you've unlocked them; it provides an entertaining training and proving ground; you can play with friends mixed with bots and put in match bonuses like healing pads, teleporters, colonists, dropship spotters and more; you still gain experience and mastery points for unlocks in this mode so it's great if you're having trouble with a specific unlock
4.Game Modes-though they're not wholly original they do a good job of putting twists on them to keep them fresh. For example, "Rescue" at it's core is capture the flag. Except, your flag is a survivor who helps you fight as you return to base, there are multiple survivors who you then have to defend while you wait for the dropship, and there is more than one way to win or lose the match.
5. Progression in game play-this is fairly obvious with the monster as you evolve and choose different abilities during the match but there is more to it than that. You find yourself having to constantly change your strategies based on every encounter during the match, on what combination of characters are being used, and how each player chooses to compensate. Unlike many multiplayer arena style games, where you shoot, die, and repeat, you really have to consider your choices as the match progresses and there are many ways to come back from devastating blows that keep you pushing forward and not feeling defeated if you go down or lose the match.
Cons:
1. Progression system-I have mixed feelings on this one but ultimately I'll list it as a con. The progression system does what it should by compelling you to continue to play and rewards you for doing so. However, the means by which you have to progress can be a bit frustrating and detrimental to your success in a match depending on what character you play. Many of the Tier 1 unlocks are easily acheivable during normal gameplay but some of them force you to abandon a skill in favor of unlocking rather than winning a match. This seems to only get worse with Tier 2 and 3 and some characters and skills are worse than others. You can combat this by playing in the solo mode where your win/loss doesn't affect a team and/or you can unlock 50% of the skill by spending mastery points in the mobile app Hunters Quest. (app is free and mastery points are gained through gameplay. no money involved) Grinding like this can help the longevity of a game and also helps keep balancing by preventing everyone from immediately having Tier 3 abilities but there is a fine line to walk between keeping a player interested and driving them away. I fear that once players get to tier 2 and 3 of abilities it may discourage rather than encourage.
2. Lack of campaign/story-this one doesn't bother me as much in Evolve but I thought I'd add it for transparency to anyone who may not know it and because it is something that normally bothers me with multiplayer only games. I've always insisted on a campaign because of the rich story and the ability to just go it alone and immerse myself. However, I knew going in that Evolve was not that type of game and it still provides the ability to play solo. The dialogue and story that is there is well acted and written but I definitely wish there was more.  Unlike Titanfall that promised a campaign but delivered a halfhearted attempt with some cut scenes, I'm glad that Evolve spent the time to make what I feel is a more compelling multiplayer experience.
3. Tweaks still need to be made- alot of the complaints out there seem to stem more from the player ability but there are definitely things that need attention. Luckily, so far none of them are game stopping and I'm confident TRS will continue to address them as they have throughout the alphas and beta.
Comments/Suggestions:
1. DLC-none of the day 1 DLC is necessary and will not help you win matches. It's all skins. If you don't want to make these micro transactions then don't and you'll still enjoy the game.
2. Game Price-between the Alpha, Big Alpha, Beta, and now the game I've played at least 100 hours which is worth $60 to me. Yes I agree that games are getting expensive and DLC is getting out of hand but if you calm down and consider the economy, games studios are going out of business left and right, and a large population of gamers wait for games to go on sale for $20 ( I'm talking to you Jeff ;-) ) you start to wonder how much is warranted and how much is big business. This game was in development for 4 years and that costs alot of money. Maybe think about these things before going on a rant about price and DLC with any game.
3. If you primarily play story driven games with RPG elements don't buy this game and then gripe about how they're not in there. Ignore the hype machine, educate yourself about the game (there is so much game footage), and if it's your style of game then buy it.

While Reigns is a neat little game (and cheap) and was fun for about 30-40 mins. You have different cards (or different skenarios) with each of them having a two choice and it will have positives/negative consequences (or in some caes, nothing) for your kingdom. Unfortunately it gets boring pretty fast, but it's not the only reason.
Your king dies if one of your four elements/resources get depleted, but also having too much stuff leads to the same result. I would understand the religion and military, but really....having the people meter filled up will lead to anarchy and having too much money will make your king unintentionally kill himself for eating too much expensive food.
When time passes, you'll might get a different bonuses that will give you free stuff automaticlly (in real-time btw), but you can also get a negative trait that does the opposite. The problem is that you have to make your choices really fast and you probably won't have the time to read the cards and you WILL make a bad decision eventually. But what about the positives traits/buffs....well here's the thing, as I said earlier, having too much stuff will lead your king to his death, so it's actually a bad thing to have
When you are scared for making too much money, increasing your army strength or making your people's well being rather flawlessly, then there is definitely something wrong with the game.
If some of these issues are fixed, maybe I would enjoy it more, but it feels more like a time consumer than an actual game, but it seems that Reigns is a mobile game and I might recommend this game for a mobile. It has a big layout and a really simple game mechanic, which is underwhelming for a PC and that's why it should stay as a mobile game in my opinion. In short, the game is not broken or awful, but not that enjoyable.
If you want a good mobile-originated game, download Fallout Shelter, because atleast that game is actually fun, even when playing with the PC. However, if you are really interested in a simple mobile game for PC and don't think that the issues I mentioned are that bad, I suggest you give it a go, but i'll give this game, a non-recommended status and requested a refund for my game. (cheap or not, I like to save my money, sorry)
P.S: Reigns is not a bad game by any means for many people (92% approval rate with 500 reviews at the time writing this), but for me, I didn't have much fun with it after an hour and some gameplay elements made me stressed. I understand if you strongly disagree with my opinion and that's fine, but clearly this game is not meant for me.

Project Zomboid offers a lot of good things to the zombie survivalist- the main emphasis of the gameplay is almost entirely around trying to survive each day, with supplies growing scarce, the horde growing larger, in constant fear if that scratch you got from one of those zombies that jumped you when you were going through the kitchen cabinets managed to pass on their deadly disease.
Survival in Zomboid is not of course, entirely dominated by avoiding or doing battle with the infected. You must brave the elements, weather storms, sickness, boredom, panic attacks, food poisonings, food spoilage, tainted water, and trying to make do without the myriad of other everyday conveniences like refrigeration, healthcare, food and shelter.
Zomboid is also grimly fatalistic- you will die. Even the game's opening intro always ends with 'This is a story of how you died.' You may survive, but accidents, bad luck or just plain bad planning can end your life in a heartbeat. Thankfully, the game does not end with death, and you're allowed to create another character in the world, perhaps a bit wiser this time.
The game features an extensive crafting, building and farming system, already fully implemented, even 'tho the game is in EA. Latest additions also added fishing, and the game world is still growing, with new features such as character classes, new items and areas being added in a steady pace.
My only major grievance with the game is the inexplainably high ping, even on servers that are not remote from my location. I've seen pings rise from 40 ms to 1000, and on one occasion, even 18k. Hopefully, the devs can finetune the game code for servers and such in the future, allowing smoother multiplayer experiences.
So far, I've generally played on cooperative and non-hostile PvE servers- the community is nice enough, unlike on most FPS gaming communities, but not free of griefers, player killers or people abusing external voice chat to annoy others. Thankfully, the latter can always be muted, but one should be wary of players coming at you with an axe or handgun, either out of sadistic troll mentality, or interest in the contents of your backpack.
All in all, the game doesn't offer much interest in the singleplayer department as of yet- the scenarios originally released with the game involving Baldspot and his wife Kate have been removed for now, as have been the NPCs, which would have definitely added more colour to the game world. Still, supposing you can find an adequetely populated server, I guess you can set up a survivalist commune, and fight the zombies (and humans) together, bringing extra fun to the game experience.

This game is brutal.
I returned after a long period of not playing and am very satisfied with the changes that are currently in the beta build. The addition of more occupations for your character + perks/debuffs make for some very interesting character builds.
With almost no hand holding, you're plonked into a random house in the middle of a map that you'll have no idea how to navigate. With nothing but the clothes on your back and food in your fridge "plus anything else you're lucky to find" You set off on your adventure! Looting shops, houses, warehouses, farms, petrol stations all in the hopes you'll find a little more loot to help you survive that extra day.
All the while you're battling the hordes of the undead. The sandbox mod allows you to tweak the nasty biters any way you like. Want old school zombies? Sure! Want to try and survive in a scenario like 28 days later? Go for it! "although not recommended" You'll fight with whatever you can find. Kitchen knives, bats, axes, planks of wood. There are also firearms, but remember! the zombies react to sounds and a gunshot will likely make all your problems worse. Hordes of zombies migrate at random events that happen in game so don't ever think that large group won't think twice about seeing what tasty morsel hides in your home when a chopper goes overhead.
Along with the copious amounts of brains you'll be ejecting from skulls you will also have to contend with the isolation that is the zombie apocalypse. You'll be holed up in a house for days on end, fortifying, all whilst your character becomes bored, lonely and depressed at the thought they're the only one left.
If I could give a few tips to anyone new playing, It'd be invest in the future. Read the books and learn how to farm, fish and build. The power shuts off and any fresh food will go mouldy. The water will go and you will have to find other ways to sustain your thirst. So spend time learning how you're going to extend your life without the comforts we all take for granted.
Good luck! You're going to need it.

It was really pleasant surprise, this game.
I've been looking for a while for a Survival game that actually was about survival rather than a Battle Royale in disguise (granted, lately games finally dropped that disguise).
I mean, I started with Rust, back when the environment provided 'some' threat. Tried Day-Z standalone, which is to this day the game I regret the most buying. By the way, I thought I was done with early access since that damned thing.
So, steam sales, I had a friend that had this game under his radar too, and BAM! One game we've enjoyed for hours and hours, with many more to come as it would seem.
We were really enjoying that survival aspect of the game, not really caring about plot. Plot? Plot. But you know, you go exploring caves, one cave leads to another, and you suddenly find yourself pushing harder and longer than you should to find out how it ends (boy, this paragraph >.>).
Concluding, a game I enjoyed as it went, and I even get an awesome surprise I wasn't really expecting from it, with a twist.
So, pros:
+ PVE Co-Op, where the "E" is actually something, and the Co-Op is actually needed (well, as far as hardest difficulty setting goes).
+ What you learn from playing actually makes your life easier (player xp opposed to character xp).
+ Subtle mechanics (which I won't spoil) that have a noticeable effect on the game without making it or breakint it.
+ Very polished, I didn't have any crashes or performance issues on my old rig (gtx 680, ivy bridge i5). I did have problems when I tried running a dedicated server and the client at the same time (which were solved by moving the dedicated server to my even older rig - r7 200 something I can't recall atm, and a phenom II x4)
Cons:
- Survival is harsh mostly because of enemies, the environment itself is a bit too easy.
- Can't support a harsher environment due lack of variety in crafting.
- Bit over simplistic for my tastes (Project Zomboid fan here).

I figured I would provide a review that isn't just whining about DLC and comes from someone who actually bought and plays the game.
Overall I'd give it an 8 out of 10
Pros:
1. Turtle Rock Studios-one of the most open and honest developers I've seen. They're constantly re-evaluating the balancing in the game and when they make a change, even if you don't agree with it, they provide the data that the decision was based on.
2.Gameplay is fun and consuming-the people that say the opposite aren't playing the game correctly. As a hunter to be truly successful you're using site and sound to better track the monster and force those early engagements.  The synergy of matching the hunter’s abilities to your advantage is an art form and finding new ways to use those abilities is compelling. As the monster, your constantly walking the line between running, fighting, or sneaking and finding new and better ways to get the upper hand.  The audio elements, landscape, and game style provide an immersive experience.
3.Ability to play solo-this is missing from so many games in the Multiplayer genre. The AI is intelligent enough to have a challenging and enjoyable experience. You can fully customize the match by map, mode, hunters, and monster; you can play against any character regardless if you've unlocked them; it provides an entertaining training and proving ground; you can play with friends mixed with bots and put in match bonuses like healing pads, teleporters, colonists, dropship spotters and more; you still gain experience and mastery points for unlocks in this mode so it's great if you're having trouble with a specific unlock
4.Game Modes-though they're not wholly original they do a good job of putting twists on them to keep them fresh. For example, "Rescue" at it's core is capture the flag. Except, your flag is a survivor who helps you fight as you return to base, there are multiple survivors who you then have to defend while you wait for the dropship, and there is more than one way to win or lose the match.
5. Progression in game play-this is fairly obvious with the monster as you evolve and choose different abilities during the match but there is more to it than that. You find yourself having to constantly change your strategies based on every encounter during the match, on what combination of characters are being used, and how each player chooses to compensate. Unlike many multiplayer arena style games, where you shoot, die, and repeat, you really have to consider your choices as the match progresses and there are many ways to come back from devastating blows that keep you pushing forward and not feeling defeated if you go down or lose the match.
Cons:
1. Progression system-I have mixed feelings on this one but ultimately I'll list it as a con. The progression system does what it should by compelling you to continue to play and rewards you for doing so. However, the means by which you have to progress can be a bit frustrating and detrimental to your success in a match depending on what character you play. Many of the Tier 1 unlocks are easily acheivable during normal gameplay but some of them force you to abandon a skill in favor of unlocking rather than winning a match. This seems to only get worse with Tier 2 and 3 and some characters and skills are worse than others. You can combat this by playing in the solo mode where your win/loss doesn't affect a team and/or you can unlock 50% of the skill by spending mastery points in the mobile app Hunters Quest. (app is free and mastery points are gained through gameplay. no money involved) Grinding like this can help the longevity of a game and also helps keep balancing by preventing everyone from immediately having Tier 3 abilities but there is a fine line to walk between keeping a player interested and driving them away. I fear that once players get to tier 2 and 3 of abilities it may discourage rather than encourage.
2. Lack of campaign/story-this one doesn't bother me as much in Evolve but I thought I'd add it for transparency to anyone who may not know it and because it is something that normally bothers me with multiplayer only games. I've always insisted on a campaign because of the rich story and the ability to just go it alone and immerse myself. However, I knew going in that Evolve was not that type of game and it still provides the ability to play solo. The dialogue and story that is there is well acted and written but I definitely wish there was more.  Unlike Titanfall that promised a campaign but delivered a halfhearted attempt with some cut scenes, I'm glad that Evolve spent the time to make what I feel is a more compelling multiplayer experience.
3. Tweaks still need to be made- alot of the complaints out there seem to stem more from the player ability but there are definitely things that need attention. Luckily, so far none of them are game stopping and I'm confident TRS will continue to address them as they have throughout the alphas and beta.
Comments/Suggestions:
1. DLC-none of the day 1 DLC is necessary and will not help you win matches. It's all skins. If you don't want to make these micro transactions then don't and you'll still enjoy the game.
2. Game Price-between the Alpha, Big Alpha, Beta, and now the game I've played at least 100 hours which is worth $60 to me. Yes I agree that games are getting expensive and DLC is getting out of hand but if you calm down and consider the economy, games studios are going out of business left and right, and a large population of gamers wait for games to go on sale for $20 ( I'm talking to you Jeff ;-) ) you start to wonder how much is warranted and how much is big business. This game was in development for 4 years and that costs alot of money. Maybe think about these things before going on a rant about price and DLC with any game.
3. If you primarily play story driven games with RPG elements don't buy this game and then gripe about how they're not in there. Ignore the hype machine, educate yourself about the game (there is so much game footage), and if it's your style of game then buy it.

Corruption brings to bear all that is shown in Star Wars VI: The Return of the Jedi, employing everything from X Wing and Tie fights, to superstar destroyers and death stars.  Quite simply, this game is brilliant, and I would highly recommend it to anyone looking to play a simple build and conquer game.

Replay value is also pretty good, since the difficulty ramps up a bit toward the end, you are timed, and the ability to destroy the environment makes things interesting every time. There is local multiplayer as well, but I haven't tried that.

If you're looking for a very simple game in which to waste a little bit of time, Reigns is a game for you. With it's very simple "swipe left or swipe right" mechanic to make your decisions, you are choosing whether or not your kingdom with prosper or fail. While the game does have some sense of strategy involved, it also forces a bit of randomization upon you that will make each time you play the game feel fresh and unique. And having one of your rulers die is just part of the fun!
It's all about managing your four key resources - your Religion, People, Army, and Money - all of which you  neither want to be too high or to low. If one resource is really high, you risk the chance of being overthrown by that force - if it's too low, you risk the chance of you or all of those people dying or rebelling against you. Then, of course, you have the randomization. Occasionally, your king will die from outside forces that are simply out of your control - but that's part of the fun.
The game also has the occasional battle mechanic - a cute little minigame that your swiping left or right helpts to decide the outcome of the battle. You will either want to push the battle or defend. And each time, you'll get a little better once you've gotten used to the mechanics of it.
All in all, this game is a lot of fun. I think the only thing that I'd like to see from the game is an option to choose whether you are male or female. Being able to be the queen vs always being the king, would make it a lot more appealing to a female audience, in my opinion. Or even going back and forth, depening on whether or not one of your heirs (Oh, yeah, did I forget to mention that you could get married and have children in the game?) was a male or a female, would make the game feel a lot more interesting and as if the choices and actions that happen in each game feel as if they had an impact upon your gameplay.
I'm looking forward to seeing where this game goes in the future!!

? No, that's not the ever-so-awkward pickup line spouted by hundreds of teenage boys to cute girls daily across the world, it's the name of an indie explorer game on Steam. Now, whether you can call it a game or not depends on how you define the word “game”. If you define it as an application that has interactive elements, then this would be a game; however, if you desire your games to have a defined plot-line, an actual ending, and/or a reason to actually continue playing beyond the first 10 minutes, you might find this particular offering wanting.
For the sake of this review, I won't call it a game – rather, I'll refer to it as an “interactive experience”, in some ways similar to Journey, though nowhere near as polished or meaningful.
is done in a clay animation style, which, while simple, can be a bit grating after a few minutes of play. The controls are also fairly simple – use WASD to move your character around, and the Space bar to interact with the various characters scattered throughout the world. The whole time you're wandering about this fairly barren landscape, your little puppy follows you without so much as a sound.
In actual gameplay, it is simple, almost annoyingly so. There is very little to do but talk to other characters and kick around some rocks; the biggest draw is the fact that the weather in-game is supposed to change based on your local weather. I have to admit that the developers added a bit of an interesting element by adding sounds to various things that you walk over or kick around; however, this feature would have been more intriguing if they had added variation in the sounds. It can be obnoxious when every flower you walk over creates the exact same tone, and every stone you kick sounds the same no matter the size.
Overall, while
might be ideal for young children looking to enjoy a few minutes of pointless running around with cutesy graphics, I cannot recommend it for anyone over the age of 7. The lack of purpose, interaction, and general things to do will become boring incredibly quick for anyone who enjoys truly interactive games.

The "everything only moves when you move" is actually a 'bit' untrue, everything moves when you act and different actions actually affect the worlds speed differently. The concept of this game is pretty fantasitc. Other RTS's, such as: Warcraft III and Starcraft and Command and Conqore with Red Alert as well, you build your base and then your army, and then you attack/defend. This game you build your base  on other planets, then your army, then you take your army and attack the enemy base which is on another planet. The ideal behind this is the person playing defense has the advantage. They have factories that will constantly put out troops, while you are limited to the troops that you brought. You attack their space station and their defenses, while they continually get backup. So you have to work quick to bring them down. Making this a unique and interesting approach to the classic RTS
However this game is not without its quirks. It is starting to show age and some of the units are not fully balanced. But since the multiplayer really never kicked off, they didnt keep messing with it. Yet this doesnt take away from the fact that it is a fun game to play, especially when you are with your buddies/roomies and just have a lan party for an hour or so, or just play single player. The skirmish battles with a hard AI is quite the challenge.
So dispite its setbacks, this game still pleases, even after all these years.

I bought this game on sale for $0.99 this morning, and after trying it, was really intent on leaving a negative review.  Instead, I've decided that this game has earned a "positive", but fairly critical review.  Ultimately, in its current state, I wouldn't recommend it at full price, but definitely give it a try if it's on sale.
So my biggest, BIGGEST complaint about this game is the lack of polish.  Compared to the original "bit Dungeon" flash game and "bit Dungeon II", this game feels like a rushed beta.  All the pieces are there, but it doesn't quite come together.  There are many bugs, and quite a few of them outright ruin the experience.
That being said, the developers have ended every update they've released with the statement "Dolores Entertainment and Kinto Game are working hard for polish the game".  It seems they're aware of the problem(s), and will hopefully get it into more respectable shape in the near future.
This game is a remake of the flash game "bit Dungeon".  From a gameplay perspective, it does a good job translating the mouse-based flash game (and touch-based mobile game) into a keyboard/gamepad experience.  A lot of reviews are criticizing the gameplay for not being as engaging as "bit Dungeon II".  While I can see where they're coming from, I think they should keep in mind that this was designed to be faithful to the original.  The movement and controls are NOT as fluid as "bit Dungeon II", but they weren't supposed to be.  This is a remake of an older game, treat it as such.  Also, the fact that this game uses keyboard/gamepad controls is a pretty clear indication in itself that the developers are listening to the feedback on their previous games.
The bugs in this game almost scared me away.  I really intended to stop playing it, but the gameplay was still pretty good.  The music could use some work, with several tracks being a little too "screechy".  Overall though, "bit Dungeon+" has some decent potential, and I'd love to see what it looks like with all the bugs worked out.
If you've played "bit Dungeon" or "bit Dungeon II", and consider yourself a fan of the series so far, pick this one up.  If you're hesitant (especially with all the bugs at the moment), then pick it up on sale instead.  These games are both cheap, and provide a decent amount of entertainment for their price.
---
Also, developers, if you could make a quick Linux/SteamOS port of these games, it'd be appreciated.  =D
I believe "bit Dungeon II" runs on flash, so it should be as simple as exporting/wrapping it right.  This game might take a *little* more work, but probably not that much.  Maybe something to keep in mind after the bugs get worked out.
Keep up the good work.

Pros:
-if you play on the hunters' side, you get a human-intelligence boss fight, which is better than what any boss in any game has to offer
-the game is very balanced - there are many people who keep on saying that they can't catch the monster or that one side has it much easier. It's not true - it all depends on the skill level of the players. I play on both sides and I honestly can't see any kind of bias there.
-the graphics are sweet! The lightning, textures, even things like skin definition on the monster or particle effects of hunters' weapons. This is truly a feast for the eyes
-there is a ton of possibilities and strategies you can utilize. Does the monster want to run away as fast as it can, eating wildlife along the way? Or maybe sneak around and confuse the hunters? How about just throwing them off-guard and bringing the fight to them early? This game does reward outsmarting your opponents and using your imagination and creativity
The neutral:
-the game is hardly binary. In many competitive multiplayer games you have to pay attention to the range of the opponent, to your position, to every single piece of stat you can muster. Here it's not this hardcore.  You can play this game really well if you only know how to utilize your character's strenghts. That said, the metagame here is not yet shaped, so maybe later this will change.
-you're not always going to play what you want to play as. The matchmaking system takes your preference (rated from 1 to 5) but it doesn't guarantee that it will get you the first choice. I managed to get my last option three times in a row. However it is incentive to learn other classes and explore the game more.
The bad:
-the game has several bugs that don't come up often, but when they do they're often frustrating. Bugged wall-climbing and disappearing skill points for monsters are two of them.
-the DLC is pretty pricey. I do know that they have to put a lot of effort into balance (seeing how well they managed to balance the base game). This one could be in the neutral section, it depends on how much you value your money.
-the game could use some better interface decisions, like being able to check character progression on the character selection screen, or the achievement notifications not obscuring the team's HP bars.
-Evolve is not quite easy to get into. There are many players who watched many pre-release broadcasts as well as participated in the alpha and beta, meaning that if you don't know much about the game yet, you are going to have a lot to catch up with. I suggest watching videos from the official youtube channel to learn your stuff.

Now let me say,
People complain about dlc practices but here's one thing to remember: This game came out on hard copy and on console. The game was finished about 2 months before release so they could put it on disc and ship it out.
Either the entire studio could sit and twiddle their thumbs for 2 months (all of them not getting paid), or, they could start working on supporting their game further. by developing more monsters and more hunters and more maps and more gametypes.
I don't know if you know this, but in a scenario where unknown monsters are attacking colonies on an entire planet and hunters are being brought in from around the galaxy to deal with it, there are a lot of directions you could go with any of the designs for anything in this game.
You could have twelve million designs for monsters alone, but you have to narrow that down to a few monsters that you can polish and balance against the few of the twenty million possible hunters, and design a handful of locations that could exist on an entire planet and make those balanced for both teams.
What I'm saying is, this game's concept always left it open for tons of dlc. Everyone who had been following the game knew that from the first reveal. Everyone who buys this game should understand that if they think about it even for a second.
If you buy the base game, you will always be able to play with everyone who bought any version of the game. Simple as that. If you somehow don't want new characters when they are released, don't buy them.
I will buy them because each character has a huge impact on how each team plays and I know how much work goes into creating that dynamic.

Ok, so.  The game is currently rated Overwhelmingly Positive, and there's tons of gameplay footage and hype surrounding this game, so you probably already know if you want this game and whether you'll enjoy it.  But in case you're one of the few who doesn't know already, lemme just lay it out for you.
This is a platformer bullet hell lite game.  Dying carries no penalties.  Which is good because you die a lot.  There's a guy on isle 2 that keeps track of just how much you died.  I hate that guy.  Still, it's hard.  Bosses have patterns, and the patterns are difficult to master, and sometimes you still screw up even when you know exactly what's about to happen.  It takes several tries on each boss, and each boss is its own type of challenging.  A lot of people struggled with the flower guy, but I breezed past him.  But then I had trouble with the candyland chick, and she's supposedly super easy.  So give yourself some slack.
But not too much slack.  The tutorial is easy.  If you struggle with the tutorial, you have a problem.  If you don't understand the reference, look up the cuphead tutorial videos.  I promise you'll find it.
Anyway, winning feels super rewarding because it's hard.  But it's not maddening and unforgiving like dark souls.  You get an instant retry, with basically no lost progress.  And when you finally get it, you'll get that really satisfied feeling that has me addicted to this game.  And every boss is beatable, and no boss move is broken or undodgeable, you just have to learn how, and that's part of WHY it's so rewarding.  You really feel like you earned it.
The game is very focused on boss fights.  There are some side scrolling levels with the same general feel to them.  The controls are intuitive, the animations are honestly the most fun and entertaining out of any game I've played, bar none.  The soundtrack fits perfectly.  I laughed at the shift between boss forms several times.  It's just... fun.
Try it.  You'll know before 2 hours if you like it or not.  Obviously, most people did.  Personally, I think it's the most refreshing game I've played in a while.
Easy recommend.

Gameplay & Controls
Evolve is a game that truly gives out a diverse experience. It's like Titanfall, hopefully without the short Hype-Train. The gameplay roles and mechanics help to give every player a unique roll, and truly emphasize the importance of teamwork. With every humanoid having an important roll. There is the Assault who deals significant damage, the Trapper who finds, and keeps the monster nearby, the medic heals other players, and the Support who gives supporting abilities to allies such as invisibility. Humans have a jetpack that runs out relatively quickly, and recharges relatively slow. Giving you a bunch of "are you kidding me" moments. But the cool character quotes, as well as unlimited ammo seems to make up for that.
On the Monster side of things, your main goal is to kill living creatures, and evolve into a stronger monster. Where you then must destroy a power relay to win. Or you could just kill all of the humans, which is proven difficult even with evolving. When you evolve, you gain health, and shields. Health lost is permanently gone, but eating other organisms regenerates your shield. You have the ability to smell other players, breathe fire, and more. But remember, your goal is NOT to rush into the human players, as they can overpower you if you are not smart about the way you play.
Evolve has an amazing balancing of power between the humans and the Monster.
The controls in this game are what you would expect them to be. WASD to move around, your mouse to look, left click attack, etc. But the Monster's abilities like throwing rocks, and the human's weapon switching are done with the numbers 1 through 4 on your keypad. These controls seem a little weird at first, but it doesn't take long to get used to.
Re-playability:
Evolve is a very re-playable game. I can't imagine why people don't find it playable. I have this game on PC, and most of the bad Steam reviews are complaints about having a $60 or $70 game (depending on where you are) with pricey DLC. And I can agree, I mean it costs $5.49 for a character skin. A CHARACTER SKIN! But we must always remember that DLC is optional and is not a requirement to play the game, nor should it prevent you from getting the most out of your experience of any title. Evolve has a wonking number of only 2 gamemodes. In one gamemode titled Evacuation, players are to play 5 games in one random party. The party fluxuates on who plays as who after every game, and as the games progress, your failures and successes will aid or hinder your ability to win. For example, winning as a Hunter in this mission will give you lasers and missiles shooting down from the sky to attack the Monster in the next. This gives over 8,000 possibilities on what map dynamics you have on the map, whether to encourage, or prevent you from sweet sweet victory. Surprisingly, this game has a ranking system. This system gives the players abilities that they can unlock, and use to their advantage. But I'm still yet to cross level 5, so I can't really say too much about it. But I get the feeling that this game is going to have many players on it for at least a year, before it becomes a bit of a ghost.
This review is getting quite long so let's sum it all up. On the pro side of things, Evolve has:
-Great Use of Teamwork
-Fair Player/Team Balancing
-Map Dynamics
-Witty Dialogue w/great voice acting
However the con side of things, Evolve carries:
-Pricey DLC
-Only 2 Game modes

There’s something wonderful about Lovely Weather We’re Having, by Julian Glander. Maybe it has something to do with the bright pastel colours, off-the-wall characters and adorable little pug that faithfully follows you wherever you go? It’s a delightful plaything, that’s undeniable, but it leaves me craving more than it can offer.
You and your little pug friend have been locked out of the house, and have nothing but roaming around the village and talking to the locals to pass the time. And what a weird bunch of locals they are. There’s a giant sea monster, for one thing, who is much more approachable and friendly than his exterior may suggest. Then there’s the guy with the rockin’ afro, slumped beside his house and always asking philosophical questions. I’m pretty sure he’s the game’s token stoner, though. There’s over a dozen of these lovable characters to encounter, and they will always be happy to spit out some mystifying conundrum, or piece of advice.
The game, in a clever little piece of technological jiggery-pokery, can extrapolate time and weather details based on where you are playing, and the town and townspeople will react accordingly. At night time you’ll receive a torch to run around with and so on. Little touches like that keep things interesting, and add a little variety to your encounters you’ll have with your neighbours.
You aren’t supposed to play for extended periods of time. Rather, a few short 10-15 minute bursts at different times of the day. That way you’ll get to experience the day gracefully fade to night, and the various mood changes your neighbours have throughout the day.
It’s just a kick in the pants that there’s not much more to Lovely Weather We’re Having.
I’m not new to these “goal-free” games, where exploration is your only real objective, but I’m a little disheartened nonetheless.
The game’s world and the people that inhabit it are so well-crafted, that it’s difficult to believe that there isn’t more to discover. Just a little more interaction, please, that’s all I ask.
Don’t let my slight grievances put you off, though. Lovely Weather We’re Having is a gorgeous game to explore, and Glander’s signature art style will appeal just as much to adults as it will to children.
People of a more serene disposition will glean more enjoyment out of Lovely Weather We’re Having than the rest of us, but I suspect that was the intention all along.

Review:
An interesting concept for a game. Naturally, those who are opposed to 'walking simulators' will find nothing of interest here, however, it did seem to have more to it when compared to other walking sims that are available.  That said, the world was very small (or maybe I just never found the rest of it).
The weather, supposedly, correlates with your local weather. If that's the case then I don't know where it thought I was because it was hazy and foggy in game whilst the sun blazed away outside my window without a cloud in sight.
The artstyle is fun and light. It has a claymation sort of vibe to it.  Also, the various characters that inhabit the world are quirky and, for some reason, remind me a little of Adventure Time characters.  That said, they lacked any real substance and conversations were awkwardly stilted.
In short, the game is not objectively bad but is unlikely to sustain a player's interest for more than an hour or so.  As a result, I can't recommend it.

Very awesome. In reality this is a puzzle game, but it is masked as a FPS style. The "everything only moves when you move" is actually a 'bit' untrue, everything moves when you act and different actions actually affect the worlds speed differently. However this means merely turning to look will often get you killed, as well assault rifles fire in bursts and pulling the trigger once will actually speed up the world for a few moments longer than any other weapon because it affects time the entire time the weapon is firing. As well, when you try to look around you will often die from a enemy that simply was NOT there a split second ago, but if that didn't happen probably 50% of the deaths you suffer wouldn't happen and there would be much less of a challenge. I got this through Humble Bundle, for $12 this game is awesome even if it was all I got through Humble Bundle. However, the $25 they're asking for this is a bit much. A great game, it's one of few modern games that poses you with a real challenge... All without engaging a human in any way. In the Long Dark you survive against a brutal and unforgiving Canadian wilderness. Finding my first Lee Enfield Rifle made me actually shout with happiness, and I make every shot count since you can only find at most 5 rounds in a box. Maybe a little unrealistic given how many guns Northern Canada has, nevermind ammo, but it does really make you hesitant to shoot unless a wolf or bear is directly threatening you. The food also decays rather fast, especially since you could cache it outside in many places wildlife couldn't get to (negative temps should act just as a freezer). But it's a game mechanic that stops you from getting too powerful and complacent. Then there is the deleting your save upon death feature. While I see the reason behind it (and it really does make you stop and think before doing anything risky), it also is a little harsh if you die through a glitch or some other issue that is no fault of your own. Thankfully glitches are rare, and as I'm a QA tester playing an Early Access game, 2 bugs in almost 30 hours of play is a pretty good run. A great game from a studio local to me that challenges the status quo of multiplayer-based PvP shooters. It's one of the most polished Early Access games I've ever played, more polished than many rushed modern AAA games (looking at you Battlefield).
The audio is a solid 7/10, the vocals are a little repetitive, but still good, and the environment audio is amazing, makes you feel cold just hearing the wind howling. The gun sounds horrible and nothing like a real Enfield (either with loading SFX or firing), but it's not a shooter, so it's forgivable. The visuals are okay, I'm not a HUGE fan of the art style, and would prefer a realistic style, but that's my opinion. A few things bothered me, like your player lacking arms, the rifle/lantern/flare just magically hover in front of you. It is Early Access still, so hopefully this is on the list to fix at some point soon.
If you love survival single player games, get it without thinking twice.

I used to play this game back in my college days, and when it went on sale on Steam, I got it for nostalgic value. Playing through it again, it reminded me of all the faults and all the pros of the game.
"Empire at War" is kind of like the Command and Conquer games, but placed in the Star Wars universe. You have a map of the Star Wars galaxy, and can choose to play the Empire or the Rebellion (I never played the expansion). The universe map is semi-real time, with the clock ticking while you choose to raise units and build structures on various planets to either gain resources, research better technology, be able to build more units, etc. You can move ships from planet to planet, and in the case of battles, there are two: space battles, just above the planet surface; and land battles, after you've secured the space above the planet and have troops available to attack.
Sometimes space battles can be boring. If you have the upper edge, you can pretty much just sit there and stare at the screen while the enemy is obliterated. That being said, if there's a decent fleet facing you, things can get exciting. It's also exciting if you're outnumbered: there were a couple of good fights where I had nothing but a space station and a few regular ships up against a much larger fleet, and managed to come out victorious. This is where micromanaging (a dreaded word to some) comes in really handy.
Land battles can be more engaging. One thing I must recommend in battle: USE THE SPECIAL SKILLS OF YOUR UNITS - A LOT! Not even just your hero units, but you're regular units as well. If you try to play this game with the units as is, you're going to lose every time. Trust me - I know it might sound weird, but unless you really put time and effort into your micromanaging, you're going to get overrun. When I first started playing again, I didn't do this, and got frustrated when I kept losing. When I started to use the special abilities for even foot soldiers, things turned around. The only other complaint I might have about land battles is the drop point limitation can be annoying sometimes; on some planets, you can only land three or four units, and then you need to really push and use your strategy to obtain other drop points in order to increase your army. If you're not careful, one of the annoying default units of the planet will swipe in and steal your drop point. In fact, the default (or "native") units on planets will be especially annoying given how quickly they spawn. However, this doesn't make land battles IMPOSSIBLE - you just need to be wiser and keep these things in mind.
Perhaps the saddest part about this game is the cinematic camera option. Basically, in the midst of a battle, you can choose to have the camera look at the scene from various angles, as if you're watching a movie. The problem is how the game decides to put the camera is peculiar. You could have a massive battle like the opening of Episode III...and the camera chooses to focus on a giant rock floating off to the side. What?! Sometimes it will shoot at a random part of the space station completely untouched by the battle. Again, not sure how they developed the camera system, but it's disappointing how lacking it is in delivery.
Overall, this game is a fun way to past the time, if you want a strategy game set in the Star Wars universe. It's not the greatest strategy game ever, but it can be one of those games you install and play every now and then. With Star Wars fandom picking up again, probably worth a try.

When RO2 came out I convinced 3 of my friends to buy the game based on how great the original game was. Sadly, at the time of release RO2 was a hot mess... Poor frame rates, crash to desktops and poor online performance seemed to be a daily occurance. After a month I uninstalled the game.
Fast forward about 6 months onwards >>
After I reinistalled the game it has been my go-to pick up and play game.
Nothing comes close to how this game makes you feel when you are successful and when you aren't.
Pros:
- Sound quality throughout the game is fantastic, authentic sounding weapons which have different sounds/filtering over distance. The sounds of pain/death are the best I've ever heard in a game. The music is also of the same par, very fitting the overall mood of the game.
- Graphics, while dated compared to most modern games are still nice, but more to the point they are authentic. Uniforms, weapons and maps have had a lot of research and really look the part adding to the immersion of the game.
- Realistic mechanics, aiming down sights pays off, leading targets over range, switching out mg barrels, calling in artillery from a static radio position. Bayonets, suicide charges and the list goes on and on. All without feeling too clunky.
- Multiplayer game modes that can suit long or short play times. The online campaign mode is fantastic for a long game (1-3 hours) and Firefight mode is great for a quick 20 minute game.
- Levelling & stats. This game does it right, you will not level everything up quickly in this game it takes a very very long time to level all the classes and weapons in this game. Unlike other games you will not get bored after levelling weapons, they actually allow you to try different tactics (single fire on the PPSH over range for example).
- Tactical gameplay. This game is has it in spades. Flanking attacks, sniping high level targets, laying down suppressive fire with MG crews, CQB with bayonets. When you work with a team, nothing beats the feeling of doing something right :)
Cons:
I honestly can't think of anything. Ohh hang on, maybe the bots.. The bots can one shot you from the hip at range sometimes, which can be frustrating but that is all I can think of...
Overall:
A great game, community map contests keep the map rotation fresh online and most of the players I have met are helpful. You do not get many COD kiddies playing this game. The learning curve is high, you will die a lot to start with but if you put some time in and take advice from some of the more experienced players you will enjoy this game a great deal.

Honestly, The Long Dark is in my opinion, one of the most under-rated games on steam. It's concept is simple, but its depth in mechanics continues to impress me. Even though story mode hasn't come out yet, I still enjoy playing sandbox mode!

This is a pretty solid and fun game. You play as one of four hunter classes or as the monster. You can set your preferences as to which you like to play the most and the game will try to match you to that role, but even when it can't and you have to play another role it's still fun to experience another part of the game play and not always the same thing as the class you wanted. Matchmaking works fine for putting people together. A difference between over all player level doesn't have any bearing on skill, just the amount of matches played. The in-game community, in my experience, is quite pleasant and helpful. Most matches the hunters use mics to communicate and track the monster and then chat in the lobby, answering others questions or talking about different game elements.
The current game balance seems to be weighted towards the monster's favor, which is fine since there's only 1 of them and it would be very frustrating if one mistake or event would cost you the game very early on. It makes the hunters actually work together and focus on their roles, not to mention stay together. Some monsters/hunters more easily counter others but with know how and effort any character can beat the others.
This game is worth the purchase. It is fun playing with randoms and even better when playing with a pre made team of friends.

Cuphead is a bullet hell game that mixes a '30s cartoon style with great graphics and incredibly smooth animation. It's got great gameplay and it can be a very difficult or normal difficulty game. You can either go for 100% grades, which, for your own sanity, I do not reccomend, unless you know what you're doing, or you can simply fight each boss and progress that way, which is how sane people will do it.
You will die plenty of times either way, but it doesn't punish you for dying, which is a very cheap move that most 'difficult' games, like Dark Souls, use. Instead of beating everything on your first try, you have to learn the patterns of the bosses, and try and try again until you eventually beat the boss, but once you do, it's very satisfying.
There are a few problems I have with this game, such as:
-The 8-direction aiming. It's very hard to use, although certain weapons like the Roundabout and Chaser don't really require aim
-Some bugs. There are very few bugs, however in a game like Cuphead they can be very annoying For example, one level is glitched so the time bonus never counts, making it impossible to get 100% for that level.
And that's really it for the flaws.
In conclusion, it's a great game and is definitely worth your money even when not on sale, and is very fun to play no matter how you do it. Have fun and try to keep your sanity intact!

I received Chroma Squad in the Humble Monthly Bundle earlier this year.  Having never heard of it, I decided to give it a chance.
This is a turn based game where you control a team of five stunt actors who decide to start their own power rangers show.  Every 'battle' is one episode, so you go through the setup and fundraising for the studio and costumes and such, and then enter filming, which is essentially the episode.  Failing to win the battle causes you to get bad ratings on your show.
If you have positive feelings towards Power Rangers from your childhood, and you like lighter-side story centered RPG strategy games, you'd probably like this.
Its strong points are numerous; it has item crafting, a good story, challenging but not overly brutal strategy, combat is fun, good humor, likeable characters, nostalgia (without leaning on it too heavily), etc.
Weak points might be that some mechanics can be a little tedious.  Kaiju battles never got boring for me (there's like 8 or so in the game) but they're all pretty similar.  Also, some people don't like pixel graphics, so if that's not your thing then move on.  Also, the game tries (and succeeds) in capturing the campy nature of power rangers style shows, so if that's going to make you cringe then you could consider it a weak feature.

This is the only game I've played that I don't get tired of. I have played for many, many hours, and I still look forward to every time I've got time to play it. I get the feeling of real survival, the struggles, the fights, the hunger, the lonelyness...
As I play, I enjoy the beautiful landscape, which by the way may vary from game to game. I enjoy the animals, and their realistic movements, I enjoy this whole artistic game. Absolutely love it!
I also like how the clothing gets torn when I fall or get attacked, and how my reairing skills gets better and better each time I repair something. I also like how I have to defrost and dry my clothes when I fall through thin ice. The creators have thought about every detail when they made this game (and are still improving, which is awesome).
As I have built my base, I feel like I have got more understanding of the environment around me. It's pretty cozy, gathering resources and feeling happy because I have food enough for a week. Also I have just finished the making of my own clothes, which is truly satisfying.
Therefore I'm ready for some more exploring tomorrow. You should too.

When RO2 came out I convinced 3 of my friends to buy the game based on how great the original game was. Sadly, at the time of release RO2 was a hot mess... Poor frame rates, crash to desktops and poor online performance seemed to be a daily occurance. After a month I uninstalled the game.
Fast forward about 6 months onwards >>
After I reinistalled the game it has been my go-to pick up and play game.
Nothing comes close to how this game makes you feel when you are successful and when you aren't.
Pros:
- Sound quality throughout the game is fantastic, authentic sounding weapons which have different sounds/filtering over distance. The sounds of pain/death are the best I've ever heard in a game. The music is also of the same par, very fitting the overall mood of the game.
- Graphics, while dated compared to most modern games are still nice, but more to the point they are authentic. Uniforms, weapons and maps have had a lot of research and really look the part adding to the immersion of the game.
- Realistic mechanics, aiming down sights pays off, leading targets over range, switching out mg barrels, calling in artillery from a static radio position. Bayonets, suicide charges and the list goes on and on. All without feeling too clunky.
- Multiplayer game modes that can suit long or short play times. The online campaign mode is fantastic for a long game (1-3 hours) and Firefight mode is great for a quick 20 minute game.
- Levelling & stats. This game does it right, you will not level everything up quickly in this game it takes a very very long time to level all the classes and weapons in this game. Unlike other games you will not get bored after levelling weapons, they actually allow you to try different tactics (single fire on the PPSH over range for example).
- Tactical gameplay. This game is has it in spades. Flanking attacks, sniping high level targets, laying down suppressive fire with MG crews, CQB with bayonets. When you work with a team, nothing beats the feeling of doing something right :)
Cons:
I honestly can't think of anything. Ohh hang on, maybe the bots.. The bots can one shot you from the hip at range sometimes, which can be frustrating but that is all I can think of...
Overall:
A great game, community map contests keep the map rotation fresh online and most of the players I have met are helpful. You do not get many COD kiddies playing this game. The learning curve is high, you will die a lot to start with but if you put some time in and take advice from some of the more experienced players you will enjoy this game a great deal.

TLDR: Buy this game, that's all you need to know.
So as many people know, early access can be a ♥♥♥♥♥. A lot of times the investment people make into early access games isn't worth it, and that made me sceptical of buying this game. However it was the Autumn sale and my friend had been encouraging me to play it with him for ages. I was very pleasently surprised.
This game successfully captures the feeling of survival in the wilderness. From a food and water system as well as a temperature system, it ticks the basics of a survival game. Furthermore, the game features various methods of preserving food which was very welcome. These are all basic requirements though, and not as impressive as other parts of the game.
A great part about the game is the atmosphere of it. It really feels like the world is living and breathing without you and very quickly I found myself immersed. Me surviving just with my friend was great while we built a base, then I encountered my first cannibal. The first time I saw a cannibal I was intrigued but also terrified of the body language they gives off, that brings me onto my next point, the AI.
The AI is extremely good for a game still in alpha. If you choose to stalk the cannibals you can see them burying their dead, eating the dead of enemy tribes. Even drinking water. Circling you to intimidate you. They can even climb up trees to ambush you. They really are portrayed as something to be feared. There are still rough edges but it is very impressive for a game this early in development.
Also with the help of my friend, we completed the games main story withing 7 hours and I was pleased with the amount of lore contained in this game. A large amount of AAA games lack the level of detail this UNFINISHED game has. It's amazing. The ending was a shocker so I don't want to spoil it. I recommend you experience it for yourselves.
Another great mechanic is the cave exploration. It feels extremely ominous when the miniscule flame from your lighter goes off and you find yourself in the near-complete darkness. Just experience the enjoyment of this game for youself. Don't go outside. Just stay at home and play this game.

Everyone who plays puzzle games should have at least one "light" or "casual" one, and LYNE is a good option. Very soothing and relaxing. You just connect the shapes according to some simple rules, and that's it. The game doesn't hold your hand; it doesn't punish you for taking your time, making a mistake, or starting over as much as you need to; and it isn't a huge timesink where you feel like you have to sit there for however long and can't walk away. The levels are grouped into manageable sets of 25, and you can easily do two or three sets in less than half an hour — but you don't have to. You can do as few or many levels at a time as you want. You might lose yourself in the game…but you won't feel trapped if you don't
to be trapped.
The learning curve is neither too steep nor too flat. Having done set A and B and today's two Daily sets, I never felt like I was in way over my head, but I never felt like I wasn't being challenged at all. I wasn't being challenged
, it just feels like a sustained, low-grade hum, which is sometimes exactly what the doctor ordered. The flute-like notes that play with each connection are a great addition to the atmosphere, and the light crescendo when you finish a puzzle is surprisingly satisfying.
Playing LYNE is like going for a leisurely walk in a nice neighbourhood or nature trail. It's not intense exercise, but you're burning calories and releasing endorphins all the same, you choose your pace — and the scenery is lovely.
P.S. I also commend the "Daily" sets. Each day you get two sets of procedurally-generated levels, which vary in difficulty according to the day. So in addition to the levels that are already in the game, you get what is effectively an endless supply of additional levels. It's like buying a sudoku book and then also getting a free sudoku delivered to your doorstep every day for the rest of your life.

Is Tasty Blue a well made game? No, not by any stretch of the imagination. But what it lacks in design and control, it more than makes up for with pure unbridled fun. A sequel-ish to Tasty Planet, Tasty Blue shares much of its mechanics with its predecessor, but while Tasty Planet took place on a flat plane from a birds-eye view, Tasty Blue instead is treated like a diorama of sorts, meaning gravity has an effect on the game's physics. Tasty Blue certainly does not have the same charm as Tasty Planet did, given the fact that you're eating mostly fish and people, but the gameplay remains enjoyable enough to keep playing it. There are some issues I have with the game, such as its seemingly poor optimisation on my computer and tough to use controls, but those problems are washed away by the fact that I simply enjoy the game. Getting 3 stars on a level is often very hard, and sometimes RNG based, but trying to get as many stars as you can keeps me entertained enough to keep playing the same levels over and over.
I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Tasty Planet, or Feeding Frenzy from way back in the day. While the game looks (and is) simple, that doesn't make it any less fun, and there is a certain childish whimsy to hearing that the sounds of eating accompanied by silly looking blood. If anything, this game brings me back to a simpler time when I first found sites like Big Fish Games and PopCap, and the ability to relive that odd nostalgia makes the purchase more than worth it.
