bit Dungeon+ is an upgraded version of a Flash game (which is also available on mobile devices) from a few years ago. You may have heard of it or perhaps its sequel, bit Dungeon II, which has been on Steam for a while now. So, how does the first game in the series, armed with a fresh new coat of paint fare?
Clearly, this game is inspired by quite a few popular titles, many of which are also on Steam. Games like The Legend of Zelda, Diablo, The Binding of Isaac, and even perhaps Dark Souls have inspired bit Dungeon. The game plays most closely to Zelda, but elements from the other games I mentioned are definitely present: randomized loot, randomized dungeon layouts, and (somewhat) slow-paced combat along with some giant bosses. bit Dungeon is played from an overhead perspective like most roguelikes out there, but it definitely differs in one major aspect: it feels more like an arcade game than something lengthier that might pop up in Steam's  "Rogue-like" tag section.
A standard playthrough consists of the player progressing through a randomized dungeon, killing enemies, using melee weapons or magic (both are viable), and eventually fighting a boss. After defeating it, you'll progress to the next floor of the dungeon. There's also randomized loot to be found all over the place, along with coins that you can use on shops that are hidden behind certain walls.
The game is entirely beatable in less than an hour, yet it's challenging enough to keep you coming back for multiple tries before you can finally manage to beat it. Personally, it took me a decent amount of attempts to even manage to beat it on Easy, which I managed to do with ease once I had acquired some nice gear. Speaking of gear, there's a fair amount of variety in gear types, or at least gear stats and appearance. There's 8 different rarities of gear (based on the color of the item), though unfortunately in reality every weapon and piece of armor feels and plays the same as all the rest. They may cosmetically appear to be different, but none of the items really "feel" different from one another - they just look that way.
The enemies are a bit lacking in variety as well. Sure, they have different designs, but they all generally "feel" the same. They all shoot out a small wave-shaped attack (it's hard to describe) at you, though some of them have ranged attacks while others can only attack you up close. Even if the enemies may all look fairly varied, they all functionally only fit into a few categories: melee, invisible (or rather cloaked) melee and ranged. Sometimes the game randomly spawns giant enemies, which are stronger and thus more challenging, which does admittedly add to the fun. The bosses play similarly to these larger enemies, so they're at least pretty fun even if the generic enemies get a bit repetitive after a while.
Probably my biggest complaint with the game is how unpolished it feels. There's a tutorial, but besides a few helpful tips, like how charging an attack will give you a bit of temporary invulnerability, the game doesn't help you out much. For example, in one situation I was stunned by an enemy while a "PUSH!" message repeatedly popped up above my character. I mashed buttons and moved the joysticks around, but I had no clue how to "PUSH!" so I simply had to restart the game. Another example - items have stats, but some of them are utterly confusing; what's the difference between "armor" and "defend", and what the hell is "proc" or "chop"? The game also doesn't bother to explain what its story is about unless you read the store page, which was a bit amusing to me when I reached the end of the game, only to find my supposed "loved one". It doesn't help that there's a few typos and a decent amount of grammatical errors present as well.
In terms of bugs or glitches, I really only encountered one, and that involved me moving through a door, only for it to glitch out and leave me in the entranceway. There was some rats in the room that then swarmed around me (without damaging me) and pushed me into a corner. I eventually killed them and moved on, but from there onwards the game only showed the bottom half of each room, which was pretty odd.
Despite all these complaints, however, I still enjoyed my time with bit Dungeon+. Is it worth $5? Well, that depends on your personal taste in games and how fine you would be with all the negative aspects of the game that I mentioned earlier. Personally though, for $1-$3 I think that this game would be pretty decent; with some patches (which the developer has frequently been releasing anyway) I think this game has the potential to be really good. The pixel art is lovely, and the enemy designs are pretty creative. The bosses are quite fun to battle, and the game can get fairly difficult at times. I personally died a lot even on easy mode. And hey - the game has co-op support too!
All in all, bit Dungeon+ is somewhat of an unpolished gem. It's covered in dirt and soot, but underneath all that grime is a great game. Sure, it has problems, but the base game is still quite fun, and for that I believe it deserves a recommendation.

EDIT 03/29/16: Today, I had a lengthy discussion with the creator of bitDungeon+, who has stated that the issues below will be addressed. While he has requested that I not change this review until said fixes go through, I felt it necessary to at least mention that they will be worked on. Stay tuned!
When this game released on Early Access, I was intrigued. I've spent many hours playing bit Dungeon on mobile, and I enjoy bit Dungeon II. bit Dungeon+, however, has fallen so miserably short that I am sincerely tempted to request a refund.
First and foremost, navigating the menu is a game in and of itself, considering there are no prompts to let you know what does what. Multiple keys appear to function as back and forward, yet there are no guides (only "humorous" comments like "are you a master or a chicken"), so it is not uncommon to find yourself on the wrong difficulty in the wrong mode because you hammer random keys to try to get somewhere. And no, you cannot check key bindings; accessing the control menu immediately forces you to begin rebinding all keys, and will then kick you out of the menu once you have rebound. Speaking of changing settings, there are NO audio or resolution options; by default, the game is set to an unlocked window that may or may not be largely off screen, and volume is so loud it is recommended you start the game on MUTE and adjust your operating system or speaker volume once in.
Once in game, there are, again, no prompts to let you know what does what. You have to remember what you have bound, or hammer keys until you figure it out. The "tutorial" is laughable, stepping you through rooms telling you to "push the attack button" without enlightening you as to what the attack button might be. Out of the tutorial, things pickk up, but only slightly. Accessing the map/menu, and no, there is no persistent minimap, lets you see your stats and equipment, though even this is rough as stat numbers bleed over text and become jumbled, and checking equipment is on a spring and bound to your movement keys; be careful, as holding right to check your sword may lead you into the next room unprepared since the movement controls are still active.
Save your money on this one. Spend it on a polished dungeon crawler like Sword of the Stars: The Pit or The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. If you still really want this game, wait to see if they continue to patch it (or at least fix the horrible grammar and spelling in the stupid menu messages).
To those coming back to this review, yes, I deleted my old review as I expected it to change since early access. It has: it's gotten worse. And considering these are now my impressions from the "released" game, the "pre-release" flag no longer applies. This should not have left early access in this state.

Its a good game for the price. Its pretty funny, it manages to stay relatively fresh duringthe course of the game and its fun to play and discover how your dynasty evolves through time with different councillors.
However, it has problems... several
I cant start a new game with a new dynasty. I have to continue with the one i have no matter what which is something i dont necessarly want to do.
They call your ruling family a dynasty but you dont ever feel you have one, since even if you never have childrens, and get several kings killed in quick succession, it wont affect your "dynasty". Youre also stuck with the names the game chooses for you. Youll have 34 roberts and 52 williams. Why doesnt it allow us to pick our own names if we want to? Some deaths are really arbitrary and shall we say, stupid.
If you have too much gold in your treasury, you lose/die.
The peasants are too happy?? you lose/die (wait what?)
The church loves you! they kill you and make you a martyr! (how does that even...)
You agreed to all the demands of the military? they organize a coup! (for some reason)
See the patern here?
They force you to constantly balance powers/factions/money or face defeat but its stuff that SHOULDNT cause you to lose when its in the green, and those deaths feel both forced and illogic.
Passive accumulation/decrease events ARE COMPLETELY BROKEN. They go up or down depending of a certain rate per second. (be my guest, check it! , be under the effect of the orange mushroom with an accumulate/decrease event, the rate at which it changes per second is insanely fast)

Project Zomboid is an intersting production. You become a lone survivour, in zombie-dominated world. Your duty? Stay alive as long as you can. Sounds simple, but in-game you will see it is not. At the beggining you have to create yourself a survivour. Game offers a few customisation options, such as name, hair, and skin colour - not much, but game is still in early acces. Then you pick a profession, with a few aviable at the moment. Each of them have bonus or two, like fireman has bonus to axe usage, policeman better shooting ect. Then you can get some more traits, but each of them comes with a value, with starting value of 0. So you need to pick some bad traits as unlucky or fat, to get some good ones.
When you finally end up on the map, you will find yourself in some building, picked randomly from all around the map (there are 2 maps to choose at the moment). Its a good idea to avoid fighting, as even the smalles scratch can be deadly. The best idea to start? Find yourself a house. It will be your safe place. When you find one big enough, secure it - put sheets in the windows, make sure there are no zombies inside, and then... then you can live there. Then you will need to look for food in other houses - non persistant such as chips and canned soups are a great find, while persistant ones are good at the beggining - because electricity will be turned off after some time. With electricyty you lose fridge, so your pesistant food can be gone anytime. Same with water - water bottles are great thing to store, because water can be turned off anytime. Then - survive. You can't win - even the loading screen shows: This is how you died.
While starting a game you can change a lot of things - from amount and strength of zombies to frequency of finding food and weapons. Which means - you can have difficulity as you want - from walk in the park to necessity to fight for barest scrap of progress.
As for me, even though it's an early acces game, Project Zomboid can give a lot of entertainment. Finding a first gun, figuring out how to drink and so on can be really satisfying. Although price can seem to be a bit high, its a solid piece of work.

Great game. I think it really helps if you're a fan of Super Sentai shows. Even a reasonable knowledge of Power Rangers will do. But even without that, I think what really shines through with this game is how self-referential a lot of the writing and humour is. Fake emails from viewers asking when the Kickstarter backers will get their copies, sidelong references to how similar all the enemies look, pokes at bad spell-checking of the narrator.
And the pop-culture references go beyond Power Rangers. If you look closely enough, there are littered references and parodies of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Teletubbies, Robocop - even The Devil's Advocate!
Behind all this is an extremely solid and varied strategy game. Chroma Squad comes in for a lot of criticism for being shallow - and I think this was my first impression, too. The first "season" of the game provides very limited flexibility and differences between characters and especially on normal difficulty it's easy to simply punch your way through most battles. But the action is driven by the Director's Instructions which push you to complete battle with a certain style and a certain way, which makes a difference to audience size, fans and of course studio income. Characters get an additional ability slot unlocked per-season, so by the third or fourth set of missions it's possible to really customise your squad's abilities and maximise your performance.
Arguably the weakest element is the Kaiju fights, in which you take turns trading blows with a giant enemy. I personally like them and I think they're a really satisfying end to an episode, from a narrative point of view. BUT, if you choose upgrades which give you boosted attack and hit % then there really isn't much to do apart from gamble with the decreasing hit % and occasionally defend. However I recently went for a Mecha build which game me a choice of four special abilities to choose from and this gave me a lot of flexibility, expression and interest in these fights - but that route is optional, so the devs may want to consider what needs changing for these in - dare I wish!? - a sequel.
But it's definitely one of those games where I think "ahh, one more episode" and before I know it, it's two A.M. Really fun turn-based combat, great humour and stories and I love the low bit graphic style.

I love this game. Initially I was looking for something similair to BF1942, and while there are no ships and planes to pilot, the environments are absolutely gorgeous to battle on with the Unreal engine. Granted I don't play it too much these days, simply because I've been playing LoL, it is a fantastic first person WW2 shooter. I wrote a short review in 2013, but it is no longer showing the RO2/RS image. This is a more detailed review in any case.
I especially love Rising Storm maps, because I feel they have more cover and thus all sorts of nooks and crannies to play with. The pacific theatre is also brightly coloured, and contrasts to the darker feel on the European front maps (Red Orchestra 2).
The weapons are great, and I believe the majority of weapons can 1-2 shot a target, depending on type of weapon and body location. Bolt-action rifles are powerful, automatic weapons are good in close ranges, and machine gun types can supress your enemies, essentially blurring their vision and really sending that danger message home. You are fragile, and you will get shot at/killed, so you need some patience and planning to defend/assault locations.
There are Squad Leaders and also a Team Leader (Commander). These are all familiar features on games such as BF2. Yes, there are also artilery/mortar strikes. And boy does it feel satisfying/nerve racking (depending on which end on you are!). While there is the occasional tank on some maps (RO2), the game primarily revolves around ground infantry combat.
I could go on and on, but suffice to say this is close to the epitome of a WW2 shooter IMO.
. Sometimes you will die because didn't pay attention or the enemy has dug in and can see you from afar. Sometimes you will do the killing because you have found a sweet spot and the enemy isn't aware of your location yet.
10/10. FPS lovers of WW2 will find this game enjoyable, set in richly detailed environments, where every bullet matters.

Tasty Blue; Having completed this game in normal mode and tried all the bonus levels, I have a few things to say...
PROS:
-You get to be a number of cute aquatic characters that get the opportunity to eat or be eaten in the wild world of the great blue sea, which is fun.
-The music is quirky and light hearted
-There's a bit of a story (although I'll get to this in more detail)
-The gameplay over all is cute and cartoony, ideal for children.
CONS:
-Levels very repetitive in terms of what you can do/eat and your characters abilities.
-The story was promising to begin with. Three scenarios are lined up for you to experience; the goldfish that gets overfed and escapes their prison of a bowl, the opressed dolphin that makes their escape from the mediocrity of jumping through hoops for its human overlords entertainment and the genetically engineered shark that was created to defeat the other two monster characters, but decided it was still hungry afterwards. HOWEVER, I personally felt like there could have been a slightly more in depth story, which may have broken up the repetitiveness of each characters plights. However these story introductions leave me wanting to know about more of a follow up to the characters.
-Continuity issues: One level I've grown to the size of a house, and am EATING houses, the next, I'm back to the size of a tuna fish... why? I thought there was a linear story happening here...? Also, orcas that are half the size of helicopters.
-Same old ability: space to boost, space to boost, space to boost..... Shouldn't different creatures ahve different perks?
In conclusion; 'Feeding Frenzy' did it better. Seriously, if you're considering buying this game for your kids, sure, go for it, but if you like the mechanic of playing as a creature that must eat or be eaten, and consequently grow and eat bigger things, look up Feeding Frenzy. It's fantastic, and has a great story with a touch of mystery beautiful artwork, and each character has specific attributes and abilities.
Do I recommend this game?
For kids, sure, but go google Feeding Frenzy anyway.

Project Zomboid was part of the first wave of Early Access games to hit Steam a while back. I didn't jump right into it, but had always had some interest in it. Finally picked it up a few days ago and I have to say that I am addicted. The game is great!
First off, one thing that was really pushing me away was the graphics. I know, they aren't the biggest deal... but I am into immersive games and I like to be sucked in, good graphics help with that. I would say that the game reminds me a lot of the old Postal games (before they went FPS), with a nice mix of Sims elements. Gameplay is very fluid and fun. You can dump hours into this game without even realizing it! I have yet to build a base or do much crafting, other than first aid stuff.
This game leaves a lot for you to discover. Crafting recipes have to be found on your own, and there is no map to refer to, at least that I have found. While it can be frustrating at times, I don't think I would like the game as much the other way around. You have to use a lot of common sense, which I really like.

I don't think any other zombie game has presented the same challenge, freedom, and ultimately great experience that PZ has.  Every decision, action, and day spent are absolutely crucial.  Didn't stock up on non-perishables for the long winter? Dead.  Climbed through a broken window and didn't disinfect/dress the wound? Dead.  Made a little too much noise during your loot run downtown? Most likely dead.
This game does a fine job of pushing you to survive with finite resources.  If you manage to create a sustainable lifestyle, it then gives you a push and asks "how sustainable?" as a horde migrates into your farm or the rain takes a couple weeks off.
On the flipside, while the long term survivial is challenging, it is an extremely fun game for the zombie/survival die hards.  Particularly, the sandbox mode offers plenty of options for players to craft their own experience to what they enjoy.  Considering this is early access, it is one of the most complete and enjoyable zombie games I have ever played.  Some of the things you WON'T have to deal with:
Awful/Scam Devs (WarZ/I:SS) - They update their site every Monday with progress and are constantly testing new builds.  Also, NO CASH SHOP.  Thank goodness.  Too many devs are trying nickel and dime us with junk.  If you're going to survive, you'll have to pull it off on your own.
Abandoned Game (Dead Linger - let's be honest with ourselves) - As above, they update progress often, have a great modding community - many mods end up making it into the game itself, and they have been going for a couple years strong on PZ.
Play how you want - Sandbox options can center the SP game around how you want it to be. Impossible? Sure, go for it.  Super easy? Why not? Have fun.  In multiplayer, you can privately host for friends or join a public game.  Up to you.  If you don't like PvP shoved down your throat like DayZ, stick to SP or PvE/private servers.  Hosting is very easy.
Zombies are actually a threat (H1Z1 & others) - Seeing that weapons can be limited, the decision to fight can be a tricky one.  The smallest scratch can lead to infection while bites are typically a death sentence.  If you use guns, you're going to draw a whole hell of a lot of attention, making things even more difficult.  Meanwhile in melee, even with the best weapons and high skill, you can still find yourself in trouble if you're heavily outnumbered.  Smart play and decision making will make you last longer.  PRO TIP: If zeds aren't a threat, turn up the difficulty.
I've noticed with DayZ, you'll get about 1 zombie per sq. km, and that one zombie happens to have been Usain Bolt and noclips through walls.  PZ has plenty of zombies (Friends at my fort call them our "neighbors") and a metagame to keep them coming.
I could go on for days singing PZ's praises, but I'd like to get back to playing it.  Do yourself a solid, drop the $15 and give it a shot.

As an early-access title, it's far from finished, but it sure as hell feels like it's finished! So far I have survived for a total of 5 months in game time and even though it's getting very quiet  around my fortress that I built from the ground up, There's always that paranoid feeling of living in constant threat. This game is a Sandbox rouge-like. Most people would argue that it's not but bear in mind that in this game, you never spawn in the same place twice and you only live once! Just like in the Naughty Dog game, The Last of Us, you don't want to go fighting zombies head-on unless you are better prepared to do so, you are not immune to the infection if you get bitten or scratched, yes scratched! Plus another thing I like about this game is that this game doesn't hold your hand. You have to figure everything out for yourself. Plus the healing in this game is not instant. So even though you splinted your broken leg after falling from a two-story window and you are at full health doesn't mean that you are fully healed already, plus the game never tells you when you have fully recovered from your wounds, you have to find out in due time! Plus I have heard people complain about how clunky some of the UI is for certain actions but that's how it supposed to be. It's supposed to mimmick real-life. Plus the game leaves a lot of room for role-playing. A word of warning though, later on when you have survived for around 3 months, and no zombies have wandered through you neigborhood, the best thing to do to not get bored is to go traveling across town and collect supplies you think you might need. This game has it's moments of victory and agony just like in the Walking Dead but in the end you always lose. In this game's case that's actually a good thing because it fits the mechanics of a game like this. You see this in mobile games like Flappy Bird all the time when really the only reason why it's there is so the developers ustilize it to milk money out of their customers and artifically extend replayability, this game already has a natrual form of replayability! Indie Stone, if you see this, I just want you to know, "This game has a long way to go but so far, so good!"

Superhot gives you the oppurtunity to feel like an action hero from the movies, pulling of amazing kills and dodging bullets like your Jet Li. In Superhot time is slowed down while you stay still and speeds up as you move which makes it possible to dodge incoming bullets and take out enemies in a deadly ballet. Theres loads of different levels putting you in the middle of various scenarios like fighting through a corridor of enemies or fighting enemies in an elevator.
The use of colour in the game is quite clever. All enemies are just red humanoid shaped beings with all the background invarious shades of grey and white. The contrast between the red enemies and white background really helps you identify the threats around you clearly so you can react in time. It also gives the game a very distinct look.
There is a story that ties all the levels together and its quite an interesting story too. On completing the story you unlock challenge and endless levels as well as the ability to replay levels from the story. So while the story mode is short there is at least more levels to sink your teeth into.
Superhot is a very unique game and is worth playing.

Gimmicky Campaign and Mission missions aside with their own little special objectives and goals and all that, you get 4 difficulty levels: Easy, Medium, Hard and Very Hard for both Political Difficulty (ie how hard everyone are to please basically, especially internal factions) and Economic Difficulty.
Easy and Medium (for both) basically makes the game play itself from start to finish.
Hard and Very Hard I can't even tell the difference of, but economic difficulty is a joke and political difficulty goes completely nuts sometimes.
To sum economic difficulty and the way economy works here is what you essentially have to do:
Step 1) Build 6+ Cotton Plantations with the upgrade that reduces workers and gives bonus efficency
Step 2) Build a bunch of Textile Factories
Step 3) Congratulations you beat the economy game and will now snowball so hard that you can't possibly ever lose anymore
Anything you do past that point economically will just result in you having basically unlimited money, the game just gives up after that. It only gets easier.
Instead your primary struggle lies in constantly figuring out why the heck that 20-50% of your population being constantly unhappy.
See the game keeps (basic) graphs on happiness in various areas (like food, employment, liberty, etc), and while this gives you an idea of more or less how good the respective systems are on your island it does absolutely nothing to tell you why so and such value is low or what problems people have in general.
Instead you are left to figure out a lot of the apparent issues people are having with your island based on intuition and experience, stuff like, how you can't do anything meaningful about healthcare until the cold war era, or how you need basically an amount of religious buildings equivalent to several vatican states to satisfy the religious needs of 600 people, how BROKE people are ALWAYS HOMELESS until you do tax subsidiaries to lower the minimum wealth required to live in even the crappiest houses to broke and how RICH people refuse to live in anything below a hecking mansion because reasons.
A lot of the time the happiness levels and approval rating will feel completely random and inconsistent, even between games where you do things similarly, or straight up focus on the needs of your people.
The approval rating also is based largely on these things, which self explanatory.
However it also governs how many rebels will be in your population, of which the amount then determines how many angry mobs spawn should a rebel attack happen.
At 30-50% tons of rebels appear, at 50-60% some appear, at about 70% little to no rebels appear and at 80% they just sort of cease to exist.
To make rebels disappear you can bribe them, and thats basically it, because if you do mass arrests, kill, banish or discredit people everyone will hate your guts and even more rebels appear, go figure.
Oh, unless you build an asylum, which supposedly removes the negative effects of discrediting people, but I honestly never do this because it costs hekin 5000$ compared to the usual 1000-2000 for bribing most folks.
Bribing is also a good - if vague - way of basically neutering any politically motivated people ever.
The effect of this isn't always entirely obvious and self evident, but you'll find that if you have enough money all these people pretty much go away and sit in a corner.
But so, you solve all these issues, you get approval to 70-80% and your reward is literally nothing, like you've already basically beaten the game with your unlimited money.
Congratulations, try not to fall asleep as you now proceed to spam jillions of buildings willy nilly because you CAN.
Like I kid you not, the most challenge you'll ever have in the game, is when you start out in the colonial era.
Every minute of play once you declare independance gets progressively easier and easier and easier, and as a result dramatically less fun and rewarding.
Also by the way? The military and anything military related? A joke.
None of the island invasions are in any way threatening if you have really basic military.
If you have more than one tank unit you are now also basically immune to rebels.
Don't even bother with Guard Towers and Fortresses and all that because they do ZERO DAMAGE, and serve literally no purpose other than to delay the enemy for like 10 seconds, I straight up can't tell if this is a bug or intentional.
It's okay to mess around with if you get it on sale like I did, but it's largely a complete waste of time.

The visuals and production quality holds up til this day, but as soon as the rebels get the mobile missile batteries, there's but one option: destroy their planets with the death star. The artillery makes the game feel frustratng and unbalanced.. it's a shame really.

PARAGRAPH WARNING. Yes, I have a lot to say.
I recommend ONLY if you want to see an unplayable game turn into something (potentially) cool.
Decent idea, but right now awful execution.
If you purchase this game right now and expect fun, you're in for a bad time. Details below.
I'll just say right now that, while the makers of the game aren't primarily English-speakers, it looks pretty bad to have so many spelling and grammatical errors. Get those fixed.
It's a very simple hack-and-slash thing, playing similarly to Binding of Isaac and the original Zelda.
Go through randomized dungeons and hit monsters in each room until they die. Stat-giving equipment is all over the place.
==BASIC GAMEPLAY & INTERFACE==
You're a knight with a basic melee weapon and a shield. That's currently the only starting class. You have avatar sets, but they are entirely cosmetic; that greatsword is gonna swing identically to that scythe.
You have an attack button, a magic button, and a block button (Default A S and D). That last one is important, because timing to block enemy attacks will keep you from otherwise requiring trades. A single hit can just chip at your health, but you are in rooms with three to like twenty enemies at once, and they're all attacking on their own patterns, so if you never touch that shield you're going to be dead in three rooms.
Kiting around and blocking effectively is key to getting hits in without taking damage. It's definitely trying to feel like a top-down Souls game -- a concept that is entirely responsible for keeping me around.
Unnfortunately, having three buttons doesn't mean the game is immediately accessible. Thanks to an almost complete lack of interface or instructions, I didn't even understand that I had a block button. The launch options window says 'Fire 1' 'Fire 2' and 'Fire 3'. Ignore these completely, because there's an in-game options menu for that. It says 'Controllers' but it really means 'Controls'.
They don't even have a setting to rebind Up Down Left and Right, opting to have default-blank 'Vertical' and 'Horizontal' axes. Just ignore those input settings.
Oh, don't set anything to Z, either, because that's the debug mode key for spawning a random chest, it seems.
Yes, this executable is for DEBUGGING.
==GAME FEEL & CONTROL BUGS==
The controls are meant to be a little bit clunky and require thought to timing, but the stiffness leads to exasperation more than anything. You will often find yourself stuck swinging in the wrong direction despite holding down another direction's key. If you're close enough to an enemy, you might not even be able to turn, because it seems as though turning is stopped any time movement is halted. This doesn't happen on walls because they are pushing you back instead of restricting movement entirely.
There is a completely unnecessarry delay to most actions. It's caused me to wonder if my keyboard was broken multiple times. There's a small delay before blocking, but no visual indicator that you need to take time to put up the shield. In many cases, it looks like damage went right through your shield.
==SOUND==
The music and effects themselves are mostly passable. The same dungeon tracks over and over can get pretty annoying, but whatever. Unfortunately, you can't set just the music to 0 and play your own stuff while keeping the sound, because there are no audio options anywhere. The game starts blaring at max and you're forced to change it with the volume slider.
This debug version is nigh-unplayable, making you deal with gameplay bugs and expecting you to know what you're doing. Like I said, if this becomes even a half-playable top-down Soulsish game, I'll be happy I got it.

Could not believe my eyes when I saw these 15-year-old gems being rereleased on PC and PS4. Enjoying this with my dad was such a big part of my childhood, and I am SOOOO excited to get back into it.
As I have put a few hours into it already, I can say for certain it feels exactly like it used to (with better graphics of course).
PROS:
-Updated graphics, much smoother and more pleasing than the originals.
-Soundtrack is phenominal, and most of the time it feels like it belongs in an actual MMORPG.
-While it can take some time to get used to, the main combat system is pretty tight, and knocking around enemies with big♥♥♥♥♥weapons feels awesome.
-The important boss battles still feel very grand and spectacular.
-Loads and saves MUCH faster than it did on PS2, and runs very smoothly.
-Still feels immersive, even when not in the actual game. When not in "The World", the rest of the game exists on the computer desktop of the player behind the Haseo character. In a way, you effectively ARE that person.
CONS:
-Voice acting, as could be expected from the PS2 era, is rather cringy pretty often.
-As others have stated, the gameplay is pretty repetitive and linear. The 3rd game in the series did a bit better in this regard.
-The early hours of each game feel very limiting.
-Fairly low challenge (at least in Vol. 1), as the EXP grind was tuned down more than I thought.
Great JRPG, more enjoyable than most in my opinion. It has some faults but most of them come in the form of voice acting and (sometimes) low difficulty. I highly recommend to almost anybody, especially those looking for any of the following:
1.) a new single-player experience
2.) a positive entrance into the JRPG genre
3.) NOSTALGIA

is a roguelike game where you explore an endless dungeon. Fighting bosses and getting the best loot is your top priority. Oh, and also not dying, that's the most important part.
You control your noble knight that tries to save his girlfriend or something like that. Excuses, excuses. You and I know that he just wants to kill all the innocent creatures that live peacefully in the dungeon, then pull all the gold coins and emerald rings out of their bodies, because profit. The whole dungeon idea is kinda inspired by
and the likes: You have a bunch of rooms that are connected to each other. By using the doorways you can go into another room. Enemies spawn, you get locked up, you kill them all, you go to the next room.
There is also a shop where you can buy various potions and chests with random loot. When you are done with your dungeon floor, you go to a conviently marked boss room, you fight a boss, you die, you get angry, you try again, you succeed, and you do it over and over again. The whole idea is good, but it's not really polished. When I was playing the game, I was working on an autopilot: Kill those guys, get this loot, die at the boss, repeat.
In one word:
Well, at least while playing with a DS3 controller. I had much trouble hitting my enemies, because my character would often face the wrong direction. When you attack, you also stick to the direction you are attacking at for a moment, so you have to get your finger off the trigger, and try to flip your character to face the enemy.
You have a shield that you can use to block, but it's so tedious to use that most of the times I let my enemies hit me, rather than playing peek-a-boo for 20 seconds with them. You can also stomp at the ground, it's supposed to stun the enemies for a brief moment, but sometimes they will still move and shoot at you, I don't know if it's a random element, a bug, or maybe something else.
They are alright. Enemies are not really creative (
) but their pixel sprites are nicely done. I also really liked how different parts of equipment change your appearance, so you can transform yourself from a boring knight in shining armor, to a lava demon, or a Grim Reaper (complete with a scythe!)
Sound effects are nice, although they get pretty boring after a while. You probably gonna ignore them after some time, because they are not really that interesting. But I liked the music! Enjoyable chiptune, fitting to a dungeon. What I didn't like is that you can't mute it, because no matter how great it is, it would still be nice to listen to some sweet silence without muting my volume in the Windows control panel.
It has some fun little gimmicks, like stomping on pools of blood lets you leave bloody footprints for a while, and coming back to a cleared room spawns enemies that feast on the poor creatures you have killed just a few moments ago.But it's all just not enough to let me recommend this game.
It's fun for a short while, and when you ignore all the control issues and repetition, you could play it for a while longer, but still not longer than a few hours. The game isn't packed with content for the time being, but I can understand that it's in early access, so I guess we'll see if the game evolves into a fun little roguelike, or will it still be like today:

Overall: Pretty good
Difficulty: Mostly very low
Comments:
- The second section of this article
is a good discussion that touches on why I think this is only a
puzzle game, not a
one.
Likes:
- Good for when you want to play a game while also doing something else
- Relaxing, mindless
- Has daily procedurally generated puzzles
Dislikes:
- Monotonous. This game is based only on a single idea: draw lines through all the nodes.  All of the puzzles are just reconfigurations of this same basic problem, and they are all solved using the same lines of reasoning.  Nothing new is introduced to make the puzzles more interesting or varied.
- Straightforward and lacks depth -- any difficulty comes from the number of possible paths, not from any depth of gameplay
- The number of possible paths encourages a trial and error approach to puzzle solving, rather than a more analytical, calculated approach
- Not challenging until around set U (the 21st set of puzzles, out of 26 total sets).  Many puzzles are trivial and could be removed without losing anything of value
- Puzzle sets are progress locked, so you have to go through a lot of tedious puzzles before you get to the more worthwhile ones
- Does not support Steam Cloud to sync progress

LYNE takes a very simple concept and expands upon it drastically, it's amazing to see how fleshed out some of the levels in the game get.  To begin you're giving one different colour and you're tasked to get it to connect to the other end piece while lighting up all of the same colours similtainiously, sounds easy right? Well it gets far more complicated, they begin to introduce blocks which need to be activated a certain amount of times and different colours which can't be crossed over, the puzzels get quite challenging later on.  It's somewhat addictive, I personally either found myself breezing through some levels or getting suck figuring out how to get that damn fith diamond lit up.  Either way, if you're plowing through levels like a bat out of hell or stuck figuring out how to finish a puzzel correctly the sense of satifaction you get from completeing a level, is quite thrilling.  The implimentation of daily levels for people who just can't get their fill of making lines is quite cute.  Not to mention the ambient music makes it all the more calming an experience. And the graphical makes it much easier to recognize what it is you should be focusing on. Reccomened for anyone who needs a few hours to just chill out, it's relatively inexpensive and it'll get the job done and then some, although it may not be everyone's cup of tea, especially if you're some sort of action junkie I can't see you getting much of a thrill out of connecting lines.

I'm not really sure what to say about this game. It's fun, yet after a while it becomes a chore.
However, it is really, really fun. I played this with some friends and we were all yelling at each other over certain choices, so that could have lengenthened the longevity of this game.
You basically choose left or right, usually two choices that are yes/no or two choices that seem similar and don't really have a different outcome. I don't know. After about 2 hours you might notice every choice leads to certain things happening because you have gotten them so much, and you might try to "spice" it up by picking the opposite of said choice, but it will lead to immediate failure or just nothing positive happening and making you stay with your original choice from now on.
However, at other times, you might pick the same choice you picked the previous times and something different will happen, which is definitely good even though it doesn't sound like it from just reading it. Then you might try to pick that choice again hoping for that uncommon outcome, not get it, and just feel awful because you lost or something stupid bad happened. I guess that's part of the game though.
There will also be times in the game where you just have no chance at all. A plague will come and you have to make some of your resources plummet, followed up by another event that will do the same thing, most likely ending up dead. Then in the same manner, there is times where everything goes absolutely perfectly and you get a crazy run with a possibly locked resource (when a resource can't go down.)
There's also not really any description of the stuff and it will take a while to figure out what choices will influence what (or at least how much a choice will affecta resource by how much.)
Honestly, I'm making it sound negative but I do recommend this game. It's cheap, and I've gotten plenty of fun out of it so far (7.5 hours currently.) Just wish there was a bit more information given or a way to skew the luck into your favor more often, which there very well might be and I just haven't found it yet.

Played through the entirety of the game in less than two hours. I know it's supposed to be an artsy type game but it really, REALLY dragged out in the end. Like they told you the big secret in the plot and then took another 20 minutes to add in the tear-jerking sentimentals with music etc.
There was some parts where the level design felt overly abysmal, and I'm not talking about start-to finish as the whole point of the game is not having an ending. I'm talking about the parts where it would take you 4-5 minutes just to go down a ♥♥♥♥ing hallway only to be rewarded with another hallway and more narrator-jabs and bits.
The dialogue etc. is never to the point, and the levels/games are really boring and don't provide a whole lot of interactivity while you hear the narrator drone on and on for the exact same thing he could have cleared up minutes ago with just a couple of sentences. If you expect me to listen to 10-minute biographies on a single thing while giving me nothing to do during the entire ♥♥♥♥ing game, of course its going to get boring.
You could say why the game had no interractivity was because the "developer" (guy who made the levels in the story line) liked non-interactivity and abstract things, but unfortunately it feels more like a crutch so the devs didn't have to add any more things other than walking into the game. The most interactive parts of the game were probably the parts where you could see the notes "left by other players" and the one part where you are cleaning the house, but those get repetitive quick. It just feels like that character trait was forced in to that character just to make an excuse to not add anything gameplay wise. It doesn't even play into the story either. The most that trait does it just make it so other traits that do matter make a bit more sense for his character, but that's stupid anyways as his main traits should be reinforced and not reliant on other traits.
I really feel like this game would have more than likely benefitted with the humour that Stanley's Parable had. Perhaps adding small easter eggs or things that people might miss or cracking a pun every once in a while. This game doesn't do any of that. It keeps a deadpan tone the entire game which results in a eye-gougingly boring and frustrating experience when combined with the long hallways and meh level design. It takes itself WAY to seriously.
Worst part about the game has to be that it guilts most people into not hating on it, since it tries to exhibit the pain devs go through when they start to attract a fan base and they start demanding things.
Overall a kind of meh game that is way to spread out and boring because it's trying way to hard to be "artsy". Avoid this game like the plague if you don't like "artsy" games. Good if you want to cry a little if you're really sensitive.

TO THE PERSON WHO HASN'T PLAYED THIS YET:
I'm not entirely sure if you should buy and play this game. It has been helpful for me, but I feel like I'm gaining something from another person's pain and folly. It doesn't feel right, but at the same time I'm better for having played it. If guilt is not something you're willing to dabble in then I'd stay away.
That sounds really nebulous and doesn't describe the game. Describing the game itself would break the effect of it. The only way I feel I can share without spoiling is to say this:
This game brought me out of a bubble I thought I had gotten out of and didn't know I was still living in...
Theres more to that statement below.
TO DAVEY AND CODA (and in general to add to the conversation/help anyone also going through these problems):
I am unsettled because I feel that this game is something I should not have been a part of as a buyer and player. But at the same time I needed it.
This game brought me out of a bubble I didn't know I was still living in by bringing me into someone else's and watching theirs burst. My life is better for having been shaken back to reality with this game's narrative.
To elaborate for the 0 people reading this; this game has made explict, a piece of knowledge which I have known and taken for granted over the past year or so. I've walked around for quite a while now thinking that I do not need external validation to define myself. I went through a troubling time, mentally and physically, trying to figure out what this life thing is about and finally decided that the point is for me to decide my own meaning and purpose, not for others to tell me what I mean to the universe.  I only found this after years of looping through what was probably a very destructive existence. I had considered my war against outward validation won.
However, the narrator's revelation about his relationship with the games' creator has made me realize that there are still actions in my own life (completely different from ones described in this game) which I subconciously take to attain validation from peers, family, and even strangers. This game has shown me that this war I'm fighting does not end until I am dead, because the part of me conditioned by thousands of years of human socializing is my true enemy.

Tropico 1 and 2 were some of the first city builders I ever played, and I was very excited when I saw there were new games in the series coming out. However, when I played Tropico 3, it felt a lot more cartoonish and lacking in options as the first two games. And then, Tropico 4 felt like exactly the same game as Tropico 3. However, Tropico 5 has regained my favor. It completely refactors the entire game, taking you on a journey from a fledgeling colony through the cold war to the modern era, recreating your constitution and juggling international politics. While it is still cartoonish, this time it feels like an addition to the gameplay instead of a bandaid. Compared to other city builders and strategy games, Tropico feels incredibly fast paced, blasting through the four eras of the game in quick succession, even though it will still ensnare you for multiple hours. And of course there are some underdeveloped areas, like the dynasty system and foreign trade. However, overall this is a good return to form to the original Tropico formula while at the same time not feeling like a rehash at all.

This game is fun. Although I only played a tad more than 10 hours, I'm really into this game. Collecting resources didn't get boring and all I did until now was playing co-op with a friend and fortifying our base. I did not explore the island (only entered one cave - bad idea), I did not raid a mutant camp except one and I did not continue (or even started) looking for my son.
At night it gets really dark and the terrifying shouts of the mutants get you startled while collecting this last tiny bit of needed wood to complete your defenses. It really makes me feel I should stay in my camp at night. Normally I'm not that kind of player, but those savages are dangerous! Maybe this will change when I get stronger.
There are a couple of strange mechanics, but this is due to the still early state of development, I think.
Pros:
+ nice graphics, looks beautiful at sunrise/sunset and after you've designed your base
+ threatening enemies which make you wonder if they continue getting bigger and crazier the longer you play
+ promising crafting/building system
+ huge island to explore
+ sometimes you really feel trapped in your base with all the mutants waiting and shouting outside
Cons (I guess most of them will be fixed/changed in later versions):
- When we started building our base, groups of 2 to 3 mutants visited us. This changed after some hours to hordes consisting of a maximum of 12 (!) mutants, some of them being very strong ones. No chance yet to fight them. If we played with 8 players this would've been fine, but for two this was a lot. Maybe we are too close to an emeny route or our base is too big and they get easily attracted by it.
- The building system is clearly something to work on. E.g. you choose a table. Now you can place a transparent version of this table on the ground. You then have to put the needed resources onto it and it gets built. You can put e.g. two rocks and 10 sticks on it and come back later to complete the building. If it's still fully transparent you can still remove it. But you can't move buildings any more once you've started building them and you can't easily destroy buildings. The placement is a bit odd because you move the transparent building a couple meters in front of you and can't change this distance. Detailed placement becomes a bit of a mess with this limitation.
- The mutants drown very quickly. So staying on a float and alluring them is an effective way to defeat them.
- Draw distance could be a bit higher.
- The difference from playing with 2 people compared to playing with 8 people must be huge. Maybe you're not supposed to build big bases when you're a small number of people or even alone, but when you're with 7 others you surely are able to build an empire in a short amount of time. A big pre-defined building costs about 90 Iogs. You need to cut approx. 25 trees for that. With a log sled for transportation you need to travel ~8 times between your base and your "sawmill". All in all this takes you maybe 15 minutes. With 8 players this is done in two minutes or maybe even less. I see there must be an advantage to play with more people, but maybe they could lower the resource costs a bit when playing with less people.
Neutral:
The save game system is very strange. Before you decide to host a game (which is then hosted on your own computer), you set the number of players, let's say 3. This doesn't seem to have any impact on the gamplay itself. It only limits the number of players that can join. Then two of your friends join the game and before you stop playing you save the game. It gets physically saved to your disk. But only the character who started the game gets saved. Your partners lose all their items if you load the save and continue playing. I think you could also start a game with a maximum of 8 players and only play with 2. This shouldn't make a difference (except for open games where everyone can join). You can also start a game with 2 players, save, set max players to 8 and load the game again. It's a bit unintuitive and has both its pros and cons.
+ You can always change the number of players on a "project" you want to play with.
+ You can send the save game file to your friends and they can be the host.
+ You can start a game with 2 people but play alone and continue working on your game without any other players. You have to be the host next time though to progress with other players (or send the save game file to the host).
+ Players are completely interchangeable. You can play with 7 other players on your save game the one day, the other day you'll continue working on your base with 7 other players.
- All inventory items except for the host do not get saved.
- You have to reload the save game to extend the number of players.
- No dedicated servers for game hosting. Host disconnects: other players can't do anything. Host does not come back: other players don't have the current state of the save game and won't be able to continue.
Looks like my cons are more than my pros, but this is not the case. Overall the pros win, this game has a very nice atmosphere and It's going to be a great one after they've worked on some of my points.

This is how I imagine Popcap would design a Katamari clone. It is fast, goofy, has often-questionable hit meshes, even-more-so questionable animal-to-world scales, and it's a lot of fun while it lasts. It is certainly no Katamari, nor shares the polish and budget of a Popcap title, but if you like a game that doesn't take itself seriously, you'll probably like this game.
The game is short - I finished in just over 2 hours. It is split into levels which chronicle the lives of three different aquatic animals as they grow to monster sizes. The game really shines when it drops you into a large body of water with a large variety and population of things to eat. This becomes very apparent as soon as you encounter the boring and frustrating oyster levels which there are two of. You'll know what I mean when you get there. There are also bonus levels at the end which offer some more fun after the campaign.
If you let yourself just steep in the ridiculousness of this title, you'll surely enjoy it while it lasts. Minor things like keyboard controls, repetitive (but often totally bangin') music, and those goddamn oyster levels might make you want to kill yourself briefly, but that's just a sign you've been playing this game for too long at a time. I finished my 2-hour playthrough in three sittings.
If you still want the game at this point, I wholeheartedly recommend it because it's downright fun for the price.

A positive review.
I understand the complaints and Ill-feeling with regard to the story mode, or the lack thereof,
but as a latecomer to this project, I was very impressed with sandbox and very quickly became immersed in this beautiful set of environments and sounds.
I've read many of the positive and negative reviews and can appreciate that some have issues with unrealistic reactions of animals but...It's a game.
Not only that, it's a game with a disclaimer at the start which, and I'm paraphrasing, basically says 'don't be a idiot about wolves....We get that wolves don't rush you....It's a game.'
Calories burned, energy expended, recovery from fatigue, relationship between body temperature and energy spent......
I agree, many things could be made more realistic but, personally, I have no problem adapting to how a game works, whether realistic or not.
That out of the way, this really is a beautiful set of environments with immersive, albeit cartoony, graphics, and great sound effects.
It's not for the team player or the agressive action-seeker, but if you're someone who likes to wonder solitary once in a while and doesn't mind having to wait for the right time to carry out a certain task, you might just enjoy this!
I don't think there's much point in mentioning specific small issues or nits about a rapidly developing project, but I do feel that vague maps might be useful for some players.
My sense of direction is abysmal and I know that I became frustrated with taking a punt, knowing I could survive travelling a certain distance, only to realise I took a wrong turn and was stranded.
Sure, maybe this is part of the game but, given that there's no option to save or restore, I feel that some players may benefit from, or appreciate, a rough outline.
Keeping it realistic, even a map which develops as you unchart new territory might be useful.
*edit* The final sandbox update, Faithful Cartographer, introduced this feature.
If you're looking for a decent playthrough to get a better idea of the gameplay, check out SplatterCat's youtube channel.

I find Tropico 5 to be in two places.  Yes, I like it.  It's another Tropico game.  Good job, well done, now shut up and take my money and let me get that sweet sweet fix.
The changes to Tropico from previous games include the introduction of eras, and such. The game is divided into four eras, you have to maneuver your island through, and as you do, you unlock new research, can issue new edicts, and can build new buildings.  But the result is that the eras lock your choices, and thus create a similar game each time.  For example, in previous editions of Tropico, you could build a tourist paradise very early in the game as a way to make money.  In this game, you have no tourist things unlocked until the 3rd era, and many of the better ones aren't until the 4th.  The result is that you really are unable to tap into tourist stuff until much later in the game.  And that is the same in each game, in part, because there aren't as many things do use.
There are fewer things to build - fewer homes to live, fewer recreational options, and more.  There are also fewer options with the things you do have.  In previous editions of the game, I could build a media outlet like a Newspaper and then choose if I wanted it to help a certain faction or be a propaganda arm for my state.  No longer.  I have no options any more with that. Meanwhile, gone are things like the Immigrant Office that I could use to determine my immigrant policy.  The citizenship options aren't nearly as robust in the Constitution.  Gone is the ability to choose multiple things to distinguish about your character.  I loved the traits, abilities and limitations you had to have earlier, and that really helped to distinguish the game.  When one character began with a free hotel, that was something. Another would have a free Cement Factory and a third a great relationship with the various nations.  They encouraged different play throughs.  But in this?  Just one trait that's almost nonexistant in gameplay.
A few other things are missing that I think were pretty cool in older games, like El Presidente's Childhood Home, the Movie Theater,  and the above-mentioned Cement Factory that would increase your build speed.  Little bonuses like that were great!  And getting something like the Childhood Home is awesome.   It drips flavor.
I love the Constitutional addition.  It allows you to control your policies much better (save for immigration) and in many ways where you couldn't before.  I also beeline for the Constitutional updates in each era in terms of research so I can add more policies to my nation.  And there are times I'm not really sure which policy to implement.  I've had great success with both planned economy and free market.  I think Theocracy is very strong compared to Secular State or Atheist State.
So that is an addition that is so good that once you play with it, you never want to go back!
Another great addition s the trade system. I like building trade options and purchasing things my island needs or selling steel behind the back of my dopey EU allies to Russia who pays more money.  That's good stuff.
I do think the Fog of War is an inconvenience and just an early game money sink.  It's an island, not a continent.  You don't need to explore it to find out what is in your mines or to make a road.  And later, you'll get a research (compass) that removes anything left.  I don't like FOW for this game at all. It's like adding a FOW to SimCity and you have to explore the areas before you build in them.  Would that make a lick of sense?
Multiplayer?  So awesome!
I do like some of the additions in the DLC, but they are uneven value. The one that gives you a creamery for your milk is, by far, the best of the one note stuff.  All of the spy and military line from Espionage is really powerful, and the water options are good as well.  Every a single island of mine has at least one creamery, and multiple buildings from the other options.  But some, like the Giant Ray Gun, just do nothing.  You are not building anything in those.
It is nice to have a sub, drones, and even an aircraft carrier for defense though.  I was attacked by the US recently, and just barely lost.  But you can not have commandos and tanks and such to help defend, and I like Tropico's moves in that direction.
It also makes me laugh to see rebels crushed by my tanks.
So overall, I get T5 a thumbs up.  That is qualified into two camps.  It errs.  It makes some mistakes.  It's the worst entry in the series by far.  For the first time in my life, I am not going to auto-buy Tropico 6 next year when it's released, because I don't like the potential downward progression this game series has.  And the plot in the scenarios and events have gone into bizarre territories. Time travel? Death rays? Clones?  This is not a James Bond film, and if I wanted to play as the villain in one, I'd go with Evil Genius, not Tropico.
But the game works.  It makes me smile.  I stayed up late until 4:00 am a few days ago playing it.  It's still recommended!

Brought to us by Australian indie developer Thomas Bowker, LYNE is a minimalist puzzle game that tasks you with connecting sets of colored shapes, without crossing or re-tracing any lines along the way. If it sounds simple, that’s because it is by design; LYNE claims to be “deceptively simple” yet “infinitely complex”. But does it do enough to set itself apart from the ever-growing library of puzzlers competing for gamers’ attention?
LYNE is designed to be as streamlined and polished as possible. Your first moments with the game set the tone for the entire experience as you’re met with crisp lines, pastel colors and gentle sounds, making for a very refined appearance. The menus are easily navigated as well, and overall everything feels calculated and elegant. The puzzles themselves are divided into lettered sets of 25, and completing a set earns you anywhere from one to five points, depending on the difficulty. As you accumulate points, you’ll unlock additional level sets and color palettes. There are hundreds of puzzles pre-loaded, so there's no shortage of challenges to tackle!
The puzzles start off easy, acquainting you with the controls and basic gameplay with a few stylized visual prompts. However, after the first level set you’re on your own. Still, the difficulty curve is gentle enough to welcome even those who have never tried a puzzle game before, while still appealing to even the most hardcore of puzzle masters. No lives and no time limit means the pressures of performance and progression are removed, placing the focus on the player’s experience with the game. There is a surprising amount of variety in the puzzle design, all while only ever using four different shapes. It’s not overcomplicated, and if you ever feel yourself growing tired of looking at the same colored shapes in different arrangements you can simply change the color palette for a fresh visual experience. Completing a puzzle sends it sliding off to the left to be replaced by another, and a total lack of load time helps LYNE maintain a superb flow.
As excellent as the puzzle design is, the secret of LYNE lies in its audio. Ambient and echoing but never obtrusive, the soft tones that emanate from each connected shape combine with the minimalist visuals to create an impressively immersive and calming environment. I often ended up playing it after a stressful day, and found relief in its gentle, tranquil presentation. That combined with the satisfaction of puzzle completion means it easy to lose yourself in LYNE.
At $2.99, its price is a bit steep for a seemingly simple puzzle game. It’s a shame so many people will pass over LYNE without a second thought just because it’s not free or under a buck, because it truly does offer a unique and immersive experience.
LYNE is a great game not only for its clever puzzles, but for the soul soothing elegance it emanates throughout the experience. Don’t let the price stop you: this is a game worth owning. If you’re looking for the next Tetris you won’t find it here, but LYNE distances itself from the frantic and competitive nature of other games in the genre for a gentle yet challenging experience that is perfect for nearly every gamer.

Although a lot of people say this game is overrated, it really is a unique take on the horror genre, with simple controls blended with an incredibly creepy atmosphere. Combine with lore that would make the Human Centipede frightened, and you have a recipe for success.
For those of you who don't know, Five Nights at Freddy's is a point-and-click horror game that takes place in a Chuck E. Cheese-style restaurant, where animatronics are the main attraction. The four main animatronics (Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy) were allowed to walk around freely during the day, until an incident known as "The Bite of '87" took place, in which a customer lost his/her frontal lobe, due to a bite by one of the animatronics. After that, the animatronics were restricted to being able to walk around at night. You, as the night security guard, must watch the animatronics using a camera system, closing your doors when they get too close. If they find you, they will assume that you are an endoskeleton without a suit on, and will try to stuff you in a suit, killing you in the process. The difficulty of the game is that you have limited power, and anything you do (turning on lights, checking cameras, closing doors) will use up some of that power. If you run out of power, Freddy will come out and kill you.
I would also like to point out the game's difficulty (for me, at least) as I have never made it past the 4th night. This might be because of my tendency to shut off my computer whenever an animatronic is at my door.
So that's it. If you couldn't tell already, I strongly reccomend this game to anyone, horror fanitics or casual gamers. The lore of the series alone is enough to keep me intrigued for a long time. Make sure to watch the Game Theorist videos, becaue they are amazing
(Also, it says I only played 1.2 hours, but I usually play this game when I don't have internet. It should be about 4-5 hours.)

That's the whole game.  Buy it now.

A very enjoyable and realistic zombie apocalypse survival.
An overrun town with scarce loot, and electricity and water supply eventually running out. Wound system has a sort of an HP bar included, but every wound is still counted separately and has to be tended with the first aid system. You might cut yourself while climbing through a broken window, and get some glass shards jagged inside the wound for good measure. Death is permanent, and occurs quite easily especially if you get scratched or bitten by a zed.
You can manage for a while just by running and looting, but eventually most of the lootable food will be rotten and you'll have to start looking into farming, trapping and/or fishing. The carpentry system is decent, too. You can build a proper fortress for yourself. Most tools wear down and can be repaired or replaced by fragile makeshift ones. The asphalt starts to have cracks eventually and the houses will have vines growing over their walls. Trees will pop up everywhere.
The multiplayer is well functional, and I've spent most of my game hours there actually. PVP is possible, too.
Although the game is still in early access, I haven't encountered any outstanding bugs (the few I've seen have been minor and cosmetic). The game is very playable alredy, just lacking a few features. The development seems to be active, with weekly blogs and such. The latest build was released in last December, and the versions seem to have come out every few months.

A very interesting FPS with a unique time stop mechanic. Enemies only move when you do (well...they do move otherwise, just very slowly). In addition when you run out of ammo, you can throw your weapon to stun enemies and grab their weapons mid-air while they're stunned. The entire game has a very unique vibe and overall visual quality and is quite short (I beat the game in around 2 hours for my first playthrough). It also has other modes when you beat the game such as Endless and challenge modes. If you want a shooter that's a bit different from the norm, this should scratch that itch.

This game will not blow your mind with it's graphics or it's awesome multiplayer, that's for sure.
HOWEVER...
When it comes to survival, Project Zomboid is the BEST you can get. In no other game is survival so meticulous and so well thought out. You've seen hunger and thirst meters before you say? Sleep depravation is nothing new? Sickness? Exposure? Well, you've never seen it done RIGHT until you play Project Zomboid.
PZ lets you try to survive in a Zombie Apocalypse and is even so kind as to let you choose the rules for your game. How do you get infected? Do zombies run, shamble or walk? How much do they see or smell? How long will you have power and water? How common is loot? And many other quirks that allow you to play how YOU want to play.
The map is HUGE and since the game is so mod friendly, you'll never have to worry about growing tired of it. While now there aren't many other maps out there, there are a few and there will be more.
Crafting, professions, day and night, seasons, building... all there to help you survive.
Vehicles and NPCs... on the works. Soonish.
This is the story of how you bought the best Zombie game ever made.

Epic Super Sentai Sendup!
This is a fun (if simple) SRPG with a story that's a hilarious parody of every live action superhero show.  The narrative unfolds just like the inner monologue that anyone of a certain age would have if their younger siblings watched Power Rangers.  It's spot on in terms of the humor, but it's also apparent that the creators enjoyed Power Rangers and their ilk.  There's enough strategy to keep things interesting, but it isn't so difficult as to turn of novices to the genre.  SRPG stalwarts will find the game to be pretty basic, but the storyline is entertaining enough for the game to be a solid recommendation for fans of SPRGs and Power Rangers alike.
